quality_problem.story:
The Nexus Café occupied prime real estate in Valleyview's central district, where the old quarter met the gleaming towers of new development. From its outdoor terrace, you could watch the city's transformation in real time—ancient brick buildings housing traditional artisans on one side, glass and steel structures filled with blockchain startups on the other.

Valleyview, nestled in Parkview Province, had become something of a crossroads. The city attracted an unusual mix: venture capital investors scouting the next big thing, artists fleeing the high costs of more established centers, political activists organizing grassroots movements, and a steady stream of academics researching everything from computational linguistics to consciousness studies. The local government's hands-off approach to regulation had made it a haven for those who wanted to operate outside conventional frameworks.

I sat at my usual table, reading the morning edition on my tablet. The headlines were the usual mix: new developments in nanotechnology, debates over pollution control measures, updates on space exploration programs. The coffee here was overpriced but excellent, and the people-watching was unparalleled.

"Mind if I join you?" 

I looked up to see Dominic Wagner, a slight man with an easy smile and tired eyes. I'd run into him a few times over the past year at various networking events. Something about venture capital and strategic planning for emerging markets, if I remembered correctly.

"Please," I said, gesturing to the empty chair.

He ordered an espresso and settled in, looking out at the street. A group of young activists marched by, carrying signs about societal change and environmental justice. Their chants echoed off the buildings before fading into the general din of the city.

"Quite a place, Valleyview," Dominic observed. "I've worked in a dozen cities, and I've never seen anything like it."

"It has its charms," I agreed. "Though I imagine it makes your work complicated."

"How so?"

"Well, strategic planning must be difficult when the rules keep changing. Half the businesses here exist in legal gray areas."

He laughed. "That's precisely why I'm here. Traditional markets are too predictable. The real opportunities are in places like this, where new paradigms are emerging."

A woman walked by with a portfolio under her arm—probably heading to one of the visual arts galleries that had sprung up in the converted warehouses. Dominic and I both watched her pass.

"What brings you to Valleyview?" he asked. "You're not local, are you?"

"I'm from Millbrook originally," I said, naming a city in Havencia. "But I've been here about two years now. Research work. Valleyview feels like home at this point."

"What kind of research?"

"Personal growth and leadership development," I said smoothly. "I study how people adapt to rapid change, how they develop emotional intelligence in unstable environments. Valleyview is perfect for that—it's essentially a laboratory for human adaptation."

This was true enough, though not the complete truth. My actual research had somewhat different parameters.

Dominic nodded thoughtfully. "That makes sense. I've noticed the same thing. The people who thrive here are the ones who can handle ambiguity, who don't need clear hierarchies or established rules. It's almost like they're a different species from the folks back in more traditional cities."

"Interesting way to put it," I said carefully.

He ordered another espresso. "You know what fascinates me? All these political movements that base themselves here. Valleyview has become a hub for every kind of activist and revolutionary. People organizing for societal change, developing new models of governance, experimenting with alternative economic systems."

"The local government doesn't seem to mind."

"That's what's brilliant about it. They've realized that by allowing all this experimentation, they're essentially crowdsourcing solutions to problems that stump larger governments. Some of these experiments fail spectacularly, but the ones that work get adopted elsewhere. It's like... natural selection for political systems."

I considered this. "You make it sound almost like they're studying us."

"Well, in a way, aren't they?" Dominic leaned back in his chair. "Think about it. Humanity is at this inflection point. We've got the technology to solve most of our problems—space exploration, pollution control, you name it. But we're stuck in these old patterns of thinking. Old political structures, old economic models, old ways of organizing society."

"And Valleyview is where people come to break those patterns."

"Exactly. It's why I love it here." He paused. "Though sometimes I wonder who's really learning from whom."

A young man passed by wearing augmented reality glasses, probably testing some new 3D printing design in virtual space before committing to physical production. The technology was everywhere here, seamlessly integrated into daily life in ways that would have seemed impossible a decade ago.

"What do you mean?" I asked.

Dominic looked at me with an odd expression. "You ever think about whether we're alone in the universe?"

The question caught me off guard. "That's quite a leap from political movements and venture capital."

"Is it though? Think about all the money going into space exploration. All the serious scientists talking about the possibility of extraterrestrial intelligence. What if they're already here?"

"Here as in Earth, or here as in Valleyview?" I kept my tone light, amused.

"Both, maybe. Think about it logically. If you were an advanced civilization studying humanity, where would you base your observers? Not Washington or London—too much surveillance, too many security protocols. You'd want somewhere with minimal oversight, maximum diversity, where unusual behavior is the norm rather than the exception."

I sipped my coffee. "You're saying aliens would choose Valleyview as their observation post?"

"I'm saying it would make sense. A place where nobody asks too many questions about your background. Where people from dozens of different cultures mix freely. Where you can access all the information you need—the city has one of the best research libraries in the region, plus direct feeds to every major database. And where your presence, no matter how odd, wouldn't raise eyebrows."

"That's quite a theory," I said. "But wouldn't they eventually slip up? Make some mistake that would expose them?"

Dominic shook his head. "Not necessarily. The beauty of a place like Valleyview is that everyone's a little odd. Everyone's hiding something or running from something or trying to reinvent themselves. The normal rules don't apply. You could be from another planet, and as long as you paid your bills and didn't cause trouble, nobody would care."

"But surely," I said, "with all the intelligence agencies, all the security apparatus that exists in the world today, someone would eventually catch on. There are too many cameras, too many databases, too many ways to cross-reference information. An alien would make some mistake—use the wrong idiom, miss some cultural reference, fail to understand some basic human behavior."

"Would they though?" Dominic leaned forward. "What if they were really good at it? What if they'd been studying humanity for decades, or centuries? What if they had technology that let them... I don't know, read our minds? Understand our psychology on a level we don't even understand ourselves?"

"Telepathy?" I raised an eyebrow. "That's a bit far-fetched."

"Is it? We're developing brain-computer interfaces. We're mapping neural networks. Consciousness studies are advancing rapidly. Who's to say a more advanced civilization hasn't already figured it out?"

A group of students walked by, arguing about some aspect of computational linguistics. Their voices carried snippets of jargon—neural networks, semantic parsing, machine translation.

"Even with telepathy," I said, "I'd think the risk would be too great. One mistake, one moment of carelessness, and they'd be exposed. Can you imagine what would happen if an alien was actually captured? The panic it would cause?"

Dominic smiled. "Unless they were already so integrated that we couldn't tell them apart from humans. Unless they'd been here so long, learned so well, that they were essentially invisible."

"You've really thought this through."

"I have a lot of time to think," he said. "My work involves a lot of observation, pattern recognition. You start to notice things."

"Like what?"

"Like how some people never quite fit. They're too perfect, in a way. They know all the right things to say, but there's something slightly off about their affect. They ask questions that seem naive, but in a way that suggests they're testing you rather than genuinely seeking information."

I felt a slight tingle of alarm, though I kept my expression neutral. "Sounds like you're describing half the venture capital people I've met."

He laughed. "Fair point. But sometimes I wonder if there's more to it. Like right now, for instance."

"Right now?"

"I felt something a moment ago. A sort of... probe. Like someone was reading my thoughts."

My heart rate increased slightly, though I kept my breathing steady. "That's an interesting sensation to have."

"It is, isn't it?" Dominic's smile widened. "Especially when the person you're talking to suddenly has a physiological response—elevated heart rate, slight pupil dilation, micro-expressions of concern."

"I think you've been in Valleyview too long," I said. "The conspiracy theories are getting to you."

"Maybe," he said. "Or maybe I'm finally seeing clearly. You know what I think, Leah Ford?"

The use of my name—my human name—was deliberate. A test.

"What do you think, Dominic?"

"I think we're both very far from home. And I think we've been dancing around the truth for the last twenty minutes."

I studied him carefully. His body language had shifted subtly. The easy-going manner was still there, but underneath it was something sharper, more alert.

"That's quite an accusation," I said quietly.

"Not an accusation. An observation. I've been on Earth for five years now, and I've gotten very good at spotting others like me. The way you deflected questions about your background. The way you described your research—true enough to be convincing, but vague enough to mean almost anything. The fact that you're here in Valleyview at all, in this café, at this time of day."

"Lots of people come to this café."

"But not many who can suppress their autonomic nervous system responses as well as you just did. That takes training. Or biology that's not quite human."

I considered my options. Denial seemed pointless. He was right—I had probed his thoughts, a momentary lapse in discipline. And if he was what he claimed to be, there was no real danger in confirmation.

"What gave you away?" I asked.

"Nothing specific. Just a feeling I got. Call it professional intuition. Or species recognition." He leaned back, relaxed now. "So where are you from? I'm from the Pleiades cluster myself. We're practically neighbors to Earth, astronomically speaking—just a few hundred light-years. Easy commute."

"I had a somewhat longer journey," I said carefully. "My people take a more extended view of things."

His eyebrows rose. "How extended are we talking? The Sirians complain about their eight-light-year trip, but that's nothing. Some of the Arcturians have traveled thirty-seven light-years. Are you from one of the more distant Milky Way outposts?"

"More distant than that."

Dominic paused, his espresso cup halfway to his lips. "More distant than the Arcturians? That puts you past most of the well-established observation posts. The far arms of the spiral?"

"Beyond the spiral entirely."

"Intergalactic?" He set down his cup. "That's ambitious. Most of us are born within this galaxy's arms—the Pleiadians, the Sirians, the Arcturians. We're all comfortable with the Milky Way's rhythms. Crossing the void between galaxies is another matter entirely."

"My civilization believes certain questions require external perspective. You can't fully understand a system from within it."

"I suppose that's true." He seemed genuinely curious now. "So which neighboring system? The Magellanic Clouds? They're practically attached to this galaxy—the Large Cloud is only about 160,000 light-years out."

"The Clouds are satellites," I said. "Gravitationally bound to the Milky Way. Hardly independent perspectives."

"Fair point. Triangulum then? It's the next significant spiral, about three million light-years distant. Small, but respectable—maybe forty billion stars."

I shook my head slightly. "My home is closer than Triangulum. And rather larger."

Dominic's expression shifted as he worked through the implications. "Closer than Triangulum, larger than Triangulum, but not a Milky Way satellite." He was quiet for a moment. "There aren't many options that fit those parameters."

"No," I agreed. "There aren't."

"The journey itself," he said slowly. "Even with faster-than-light methods, crossing millions of light-years... your people must have been watching Earth for a very long time. Since before human civilization began?"

"We established our first observation post here before humans developed agriculture. The distances involved require patience and long-term commitment."

"And you came personally? Made the crossing yourself?"

"I did. Though I had extensive preparation. Years of studying human culture, language, psychology. By the time I arrived, I knew more about Earth than most humans do."

A police drone flew overhead, part of the city's minimal security apparatus. We both watched it pass without concern.

"It explains something I noticed," Dominic said thoughtfully. "The way you structure your telepathic probes. There's a particular pattern to them—subtle differences in how you organize information. I couldn't place it before. Now I understand. You learned from a tradition that developed independently, in isolation from the Milky Way's networks."

"Your own probes have a distinctive signature too," I said. "Efficient but somewhat narrow-band. Optimized for the shorter distances you're accustomed to."

He laughed. "Fair criticism. We Pleiadians have never needed to push our range very far. Everything we care about is relatively close by."

"How many of us are there?" I asked. "Here in Valleyview, I mean."

"I've identified at least a dozen, though I suspect there are more. Different species, different missions. There's someone from Arcturus studying visual arts. Someone from Sirius researching emotional intelligence. A few others I haven't quite figured out yet. Most of us are locals—born in this galaxy, comfortable with its rhythms. The ones who've crossed from other island universes are rarer."

"And nobody's been caught?"

"Why would they be? We're careful. We've studied human behavior extensively before coming here. We understand their psychology, their culture, their technology. And we've chosen our base well. Valleyview is the one place on Earth where being strange is normal."

"Do you ever wonder," I said, "what will happen when they do figure it out? When humanity realizes they're being watched?"

Dominic shrugged. "By then, hopefully, they'll be ready for contact. That's part of what we're studying—when will they be mature enough to join the broader galactic community? When will they have developed the emotional intelligence and social structures necessary to interact with other species without panic or aggression?"

"And if they're never ready?"

"Then we keep watching. And documenting. And hoping they figure it out before they destroy themselves."

We sat in silence for a moment, watching the city move around us. The activists had been replaced by a group of artists setting up an impromptu exhibition. A food vendor was arguing with a city inspector about permits. A couple sat at a nearby table, absorbed in their own conversation, oblivious to the fact that two observers from vastly different origins were discussing the fate of their species just meters away.

"It's strange," I said finally. "We come from such different distances—you from within the Milky Way's spiral, me from across the intergalactic void—studying different aspects of human civilization, and yet we end up in the same café in Valleyview."

"Not so strange," Dominic said. "This is where the interesting stuff is happening. This is where humanity is experimenting with its future. If you want to understand where they're going, this is where you need to be."

He finished his espresso and stood up. "I should go. I have a meeting with a group working on new governance models. Fascinating stuff—they're trying to use blockchain technology to create decentralized decision-making structures."

"Good talking to you, Dominic."

"Same here, Leah. It's not often I get to compare notes with someone whose home is visible to the naked eye from Earth—at least on clear autumn nights in the northern hemisphere. Human astronomers love photographing it. They've even managed to resolve individual stars in the outer regions."

"They've gotten remarkably good at studying us from a distance," I agreed. "Their estimates of my home's stellar population have improved significantly in recent decades."

"How close are they to the actual number?"

"Their latest figures suggest roughly a trillion stars. They're not far off."

Dominic whistled softly. "A trillion. That's what—two, two and a half times the Milky Way?"

"Approximately."

"The nearest major spiral larger than this one," he mused. "Interesting that your people chose to come here rather than staying home. What made Earth worth crossing millions of light-years?"

"The transition point," I said. "Species that successfully navigate from planetary to interstellar civilization are rare. Earth is at that critical juncture. We've documented dozens of failures across both galaxies. The successes are worth the journey to witness."

I watched him walk away, disappearing into the crowd. Then I turned back to my tablet, scrolling through the news. A headline caught my eye: "New Space Exploration Initiative Announced." Humanity was reaching outward, slowly but surely. Soon enough, they'd be ready.

Or they wouldn't.

Either way, we'd be here, watching. Learning. Documenting. Those born within this galaxy's spiral arms, and those of us who had crossed the void from the nearest great spiral beyond.

In Valleyview, where everyone was strange, and no one asked questions, and the future was being invented one small experiment at a time.

It really was the perfect place for observers to hide.

quality_problem.story:
Dr. Sophia Edwards left her laboratory at the Oceanographic Research Institute in Oakdale Village at exactly 6:00 PM and began the evening walk she had taken, without fail, for fifteen solid years.

The walk never varied. She paced three blocks down Harbor Street, stopped at the Blue Whale Café to purchase a kelp tea, then walked to the end of the fifth block on Harbor. There she turned left on Maritime Avenue, followed Maritime to Coral Street, down Coral and so by way of Beacon back to Harbor again and to her small apartment above the institute.

She didn't walk quickly. She took her time. She always returned to her door at exactly 6:50 PM. No one ever stopped to talk with her. Even the barista at the Blue Whale Café remained silent while preparing her drink. Dr. Edwards merely nodded, the woman prepared the tea, and Dr. Edwards took her cup. That was all.

For people long ago had gathered that Dr. Edwards desired solitude. The newer generation of researchers called it dedication to her work. Certain colleagues had a different word for it. The senior scientists remembered that this intense woman with her waterproof notebook, titanium data collection tools, and ever-present rain jacket had once been a celebrated professor at Ravenswood Regional University.

A professor of oceanography, they recalled, specializing in deep-sea ecosystems and marine resource management. At any rate, a controversy of some sort was connected with her name—an academic dispute that had divided the scientific community. She had published a research paper that challenged fundamental assumptions about how humans interact with the natural world, and she had presented that research to international conferences. The paper had provocation written into its very title, something about "The Observer's Role in Environmental Stability." Industry representatives and resource extraction companies had apparently lobbied heavily against her continued employment, though accounts differed on exactly why. Whatever the full truth, it had been considered sufficiently radical to cost Dr. Edwards her tenured position at the university.

A pale moon hung over the harbor and a sharp, salt-tinged wind was blowing when Dr. Edwards started out at six o'clock.

It was a good evening, she told herself, breathing the clean ocean air and the faint scent of seaweed from the nearby docks.

She walked steadily, her notebook tucked securely in her jacket pocket. She noticed that the streetlight at the corner of Harbor and Beacon was flickering, and she frowned slightly when forced to step around construction barriers before the entrance to Building 47.

It seemed she reached the corner of Maritime and Harbor just a bit too quickly, but she told herself this couldn't be. For fifteen years, since the year following her dismissal from the university, she had lived by precise routine.

The same thing, at the same time, day after day. She had not deliberately chosen such a regimented existence. A single woman, living alone with her research stipend and savings, the timed routine had developed gradually—a framework for maintaining stability in the absence of other anchors. She had learned to pay attention to her surroundings with unusual intensity, cataloging every lamppost, every crack in the pavement, every familiar storefront. It was, she sometimes thought, as if her careful observation helped keep everything in its proper place.

So she turned on Maritime and back on Coral. The security guard at the corner of Coral and Beacon nodded to her as always, a silent acknowledgment of her nightly passage.

A news broadcast was playing from someone's open window, and fragments drifted to Dr. Edwards.

"...continuing to occur worldwide...entire research station in Larchmont Province vanished...leading marine biologist, Dr. Christopher Lane, cannot explain the phenomenon..."

The wind carried the words away and Dr. Edwards pressed her lips together. Another sensationalist report, probably. She remembered similar panic years before, something about atmospheric anomalies. And Lane! What did Lane have to do with anything? He was one of the scientists who had dismissed her paper as pseudoscience—though Lane had been primarily concerned with its implications for the deep-sea mining operations he consulted for. He had called her conclusions "an attack on sustainable resource extraction dressed up in mystical language."

But she pushed the thought away, focused on the familiar rhythm of her steps, looked at the known landmarks that emerged from the coastal darkness as she walked. For there was nothing—absolutely nothing in the world—that she would let disturb her equilibrium. That was a principle she had established fifteen years ago.

There was a group of researchers outside the institute's main entrance at the corner of Coral and Beacon, talking urgently. Dr. Edwards caught excited phrases: "It's happening in every coastal region...What could cause this...The data analysis shows nothing...Maybe Edwards was right about observation protocols..."

But as Dr. Edwards approached, they fell silent and watched her pass. She, for her part, gave them no acknowledgment. That was how it had been for many years, ever since people had accepted that she did not wish to engage.

One of the researchers, a young woman named Camila Bryant, half-stepped forward as if to speak, but then retreated, and Dr. Edwards continued her walk.

Back at her apartment door, she stopped and, as she had done a thousand times before, checked her waterproof watch.

She stared at it in confusion. It was only 6:35 PM.

For long minutes she stood examining the watch. The timepiece hadn't stopped; its second hand still swept smoothly around the face.

But fifteen minutes too early! For fifteen years, day in and day out, she had left at six and returned at ten minutes to seven. Now...

It wasn't until then that she realized something else was wrong. She had no kelp tea. For the first time, she had failed to stop at the Blue Whale Café.

Shaken, muttering to herself, Dr. Edwards unlocked her apartment and secured the door behind her.

She hung her jacket on the hook in the entryway and walked slowly into the living area. Dropping into her reading chair, she shook her head in bewilderment.

Silence filled the room. A silence measured by the soft hum of the temperature control system.

But silence was familiar to Dr. Edwards. Once she had enjoyed music—classical recordings she could stream through her speakers. But the speakers sat disconnected in the corner. Dr. Edwards had unplugged them years before, precisely on the evening when a concert had been interrupted for breaking news about environmental protests at offshore platforms.

She had stopped following news feeds and scientific journals too, had isolated herself to a few city blocks. And as the years passed, that self-imposed isolation had become absolute, an invisible but impenetrable boundary marking an area five blocks by four. Beyond that perimeter lay something she could not name, would not acknowledge. Beyond it, she never ventured.

But recluse though she was, she could not entirely escape information. Things researchers discussed in the hallways, fragments of broadcasts from open windows, headlines glimpsed on discarded tablets.

And so she knew this was the year 2089, and that the conflicts in the Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions had ended in catastrophe, followed by a mysterious phenomenon—a plague of disappearances sweeping through region after region like an invisible tide, erasing populations. Some blamed the collapse of marine ecosystems; others pointed to the wars over undersea mining rights that had depleted coastal populations. A few whispered that it had something to do with attention itself—with the way people had stopped paying careful notice to their surroundings in the chaos.

But those things she dismissed as concerns far removed from her small world. She disregarded them. She pretended she had never heard of them. Others might worry and theorize if they wished. To her, they simply did not matter.

But there were two things tonight that did matter. Two disturbing, inexplicable events. She had arrived home fifteen minutes early. She had forgotten her kelp tea.

Huddled in the chair, she frowned. It was unsettling to have her routine disrupted. There must be something wrong. Had her long isolation finally affected her mind—perhaps just slightly—enough to impair her judgment? Had she lost her sense of temporal precision, of spatial awareness?

No, she hadn't. Take this room, for example. After fifteen years, it had become as integral to her identity as her research methodology. Every detail was recorded in her mind with scientific clarity: the titanium desk with its organized specimen samples; the shelf with her carefully maintained equipment; the chronometer that displayed not only time but date, lunar phase, and tidal information; the specimen jar on the side table and, most important of all, the framed photograph.

Dr. Edwards treasured that photograph. It showed depth, she always said. It depicted an underwater scene in the foreground, a coral reef teeming with life. Far in the distance, almost at the edge of visibility, was the vague outline of a research submersible. That photograph had been taken during her last field expedition—the one where she had first begun developing her controversial ideas about what held ecosystems stable. Not conservation policy, she had concluded. Something more fundamental about the relationship between the observer and the observed.

There were other images too. The coastal landscape above the storage unit, the marine charts in the corner where she sat, the satellite imagery above the bookshelf. But the reef photograph was directly in her line of sight. She could see it without turning her head. She had positioned it there because she valued it most.

Further reflection became difficult as Dr. Edwards felt exhaustion overtaking her. She prepared for bed mechanically. For an hour she lay awake, troubled by undefined anxieties she could neither articulate nor comprehend.

When finally she slept, it was to experience a series of disturbing dreams. She dreamed first that she was conducting fieldwork on a small research platform in the open ocean, that the waters around the platform teemed with unknown organisms—bioluminescent creatures that pulsed with alien light—and that steadily those organisms were consuming the platform itself.

In another dream, she was pursued by something she could neither observe nor measure, but only sense. And as she tried to flee, she remained stationary. Her legs moved frantically, but she made no progress. It was as if she ran on a treadmill in the laboratory.

Then again the threat surrounded her, a vast, incomprehensible presence, and she tried to call out but couldn't. She opened her mouth and strained but filled her lungs to bursting with the effort to shout—but no sound emerged.

All next day she was uneasy, and as she left the apartment that evening at precisely 6:00 PM, she kept reminding herself: "You must not forget tonight! You must remember to stop for your tea!"

The streetlight at the corner of Beacon was still flickering, and in front of Building 47 the construction barriers remained in place. Everything appeared the same as the night before.

And now, she told herself, the Blue Whale Café is in the next block. I must not forget tonight. To forget twice consecutively would be unacceptable.

She held that thought firmly in mind, walked just slightly faster down the street.

But at the corner she stopped, disoriented. Bewildered, she stared down the next block. There was no blue neon sign, no welcoming light on the sidewalk to mark the small café tucked into this research district.

She stared at the street marker and read the word slowly: MARITIME. She read it again, disbelieving, for this shouldn't be Maritime Avenue, but Dock Street. She had walked two blocks, and the café was between Dock and Maritime. She hadn't reached Dock yet—and here was Maritime.

Or had she, absent-mindedly, walked one block farther than intended, passed the café as on the previous night?

For the first time in fifteen years, Dr. Edwards retraced her steps. She walked back to Beacon, then turned and went back to Maritime again and on to Coral. Then back to Maritime again, where she stood stunned while a single, impossible fact crystallized in her mind:

There wasn't any café! The block from Dock to Maritime had disappeared!

Now she understood why she had missed the café the night before, why she had arrived home fifteen minutes early.

On legs that felt numb, she stumbled back to her apartment. She locked the door behind her and made her way unsteadily to her chair in the corner.

What was this? What did it mean? By what inconceivable mechanism could a paved street with buildings, equipment, and structures be erased and the space it had occupied be closed up?

Was something happening in the world that she, in her isolated existence, knew nothing about?

Dr. Edwards shivered, started to adjust her jacket, then stopped as she realized the room temperature was regulated. The cold she felt came from somewhere else. The cold of fear and uncertainty, the chill of half-formed understanding.

A profound silence had descended, a silence still measured by the chronometer's digital display. And yet a silence that held a different quality than she had ever experienced before. Not a comfortable, familiar silence—but a silence that suggested emptiness and void.

There was something behind this, Dr. Edwards told herself. Something that connected to fragments of memory buried in her consciousness, demanding recognition. Something tied to the conversations she had overheard at the institute, pieces of broadcasts she had heard while walking, the urgent discussions among researchers. Something related to events in the world from which she had withdrawn.

She recalled them now and focused on the central theme: the wars and disappearances. Hints of Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions swept nearly clean of human presence, of the phenomenon spreading through African coastlines, of its appearance in South American ports, of the desperate efforts of North American authorities to prevent its advance. Some attributed it to ecological collapse—the consequences of decades of marine resource exploitation finally manifesting in ways no one had predicted.

Millions of people had vanished from Pacific and Asian regions, African and South American coasts. Billions, perhaps.

And somehow those grim statistics seemed connected to her own experience. Something, somewhere, some element of her earlier research, seemed to hold an explanation. But try as she might, her confused mind failed to find the answer.

The chronometer advanced silently, its display shifting from 7:29 to 7:30.

Dr. Edwards stood, walked to the window, and looked out.

Moonlight painted the harbor in silver and black, silhouetting the cranes and vessels against a luminous sky.

But the research building directly across the street was not the same. It was strangely distorted, its proportions wrong, like a structure that had suddenly become non-Euclidean.

She stared at it in shock, trying to determine what was wrong. She recalled how it had always stood, solid, a standard example of modern marine research architecture.

Then, before her eyes, the building corrected itself. Slowly it resolved, smoothed out its strange angles, readjusted its dimensions, became once again the familiar structure she knew it must be. It was as if her attention had pulled it back into proper form.

With relief, Dr. Edwards turned back toward the room.

But before she moved away from the window, she looked again. The building was distorted—as severe, perhaps worse than before!

Gasping, Dr. Edwards moved away from the window, went to her bedroom, and took sedatives from her medical kit.

Her dreams that night were the same as before. Again there was the research platform in open ocean. Again she was alone upon it. Again the bioluminescent organisms were consuming her foundation piece by piece.

She woke, body drenched with perspiration. Dim light of early dawn filtered through the window. The clock beside her bed showed 7:15 AM. For a long time she lay motionless.

Again the inexplicable events of the night before returned to haunt her, and as she lay there staring at the window, she remembered them one by one. But her mind, still clouded by sleep and confusion, processed the events mechanically, lost the sharp edge of terror that surrounded them.

The light through the window slowly brightened. Dr. Edwards slid out of bed, crossed to the window, the cold floor against her bare feet. She forced herself to look out.

There was nothing outside the window. No shapes. As if there might be fog. But no fog, however dense, could obscure the equipment storage shed that stood close to the building.

But the shed was there—shadowy, indistinct in the gray light, with rust visible on its panels, a few identification markers still attached to its surface.

The shed was there now. But it hadn't been when she first looked. Dr. Edwards was certain of that. It had materialized only when she concentrated on remembering its details.

And now she saw the faint outline of the adjacent research building—but that outline was wrong. The dimensions didn't align properly—they were distorted. As if some massive force had grasped the building and twisted it out of true. Like the building she had seen across the street the night before, the building that had painfully corrected itself when she focused on how it should appear.

Perhaps if she concentrated on how the adjacent building should look, it too might correct itself. But Dr. Edwards was exhausted. Too exhausted to focus on the building.

She turned from the window and dressed slowly. In the living area, she collapsed into her chair, rested her feet on the ottoman. For a long time she sat, trying to think.

And then, abruptly, something like an electrical shock ran through her. Rigid, she sat there, hollow inside at the realization. Minutes later she rose and almost ran across the room to the bookshelf mounted on the wall.

There were many volumes on the shelf: her reference texts on the first level, her research journals on the lower levels. The second level contained but one publication. And it was around this publication that Dr. Edwards' entire professional life had revolved.

Fifteen years ago she had written it and foolishly attempted to present its hypothesis to the international oceanographic community. The media, she remembered, had sensationalized it extensively. Environmental groups had initially celebrated what they thought was support for stronger conservation measures. The extraction industry had condemned it as anti-progress mysticism. But both sides had misunderstood her central argument entirely. Controversy had erupted. Narrow-minded colleagues, failing to understand either her methodology or her conclusions, had forced her resignation from the university.

She took down the worn volume now and turned to a page she had marked long ago, a passage she had underlined:

"The question is not whether we should protect marine environments from industrial exploitation—that debate misses the fundamental issue entirely. The question is what role human attention plays in maintaining environmental stability at the most basic level of structure."

She flipped to another section, her handwriting cramped in the margins:

"When populations decline in a region, whether through war, migration, or catastrophe, the familiar features of that region become unstable. This is not metaphor. The relationship between observer and observed is not passive..."

The industry consultants had seized on phrases like "environmental stability" to claim she opposed all resource extraction. The conservationists had celebrated her while misunderstanding that she wasn't talking about policy at all. Lane had written a scathing review in the Journal of Marine Sciences, calling her work "mysticism masquerading as environmental advocacy."

But now, holding the paper, fragments of meaning began connecting in her exhausted mind. The disappeared populations. The buildings losing their form when she didn't concentrate on them. The way her focused attention seemed to pull distorted structures back into shape.

She stared at another underlined passage:

"Theoretical frameworks from quantum mechanics suggest that observation itself may play a constitutive role in determining the state of physical systems. I propose we extend this principle beyond the microscopic..."

She closed the paper, returned it to the shelf, and retrieved her jacket.

She had to know more. She had to find someone who could provide information.

She moved through the entryway to the door, emerged onto the walkway. Outside she looked skyward, trying to locate the sun. But there wasn't any sun—only an all-pervading grayness that shrouded everything—not a gray fog, but a gray emptiness that seemed devoid of life, of any movement.

The walkway led to the street and there it ended, but as she moved forward the pavement came into view and the building ahead loomed out of the gray, but a building with distortions.

She moved forward rapidly. Visibility extended only a few meters, and as she approached them the buildings materialized like two-dimensional projections without depth, like twisted cardboard structures appearing in misty conditions.

Once she stopped and looked back and saw that the grayness had closed in behind her. The buildings were erased, the walkway faded into nothing.

She called out, hoping to attract attention. But her voice frightened her. It seemed to echo upward into higher levels of the atmosphere, as if a giant opening had appeared to a vast space high above her.

She continued until she came to the corner of Maritime. There, on the curb, she stopped and stared. The gray barrier was thicker there, but she did not realize how close it was until she glanced down and saw there was nothing, nothing at all beyond the curb. No dull gleam of wet pavement, no sign of a street. It was as if all existence ended here at the corner of Harbor and Maritime.

With a sharp cry, Dr. Edwards turned and ran. Back down the street she raced, jacket streaming behind her in the wind.

Breathing hard, she reached her building and stumbled up the walkway, grateful that it still existed.

On the threshold she stood for a moment, catching her breath. She glanced back over her shoulder, and a strange feeling of inner emptiness seemed to wash over her. At that moment, the gray nothingness appeared to thin—the enveloping curtain fell away, and she saw...

Vague and indistinct, yet cast in holographic outline, an enormous structure was silhouetted against the darkening sky. It was a structure fantastic with geometric domes, crystalline towers, and suspended platforms and connecting bridges. Corridor-like passages, flanked on either side by luminous panels and transport systems, stretched endlessly to the vanishing point. Great beams of multicolored energy probed huge patterns and spirals above the higher levels.

And beyond, like a final backdrop, rose a colossal barrier. It was from that barrier—from its angular projections and geometric features—that Dr. Edwards felt the presence observing her.

Thousands of consciousnesses focused with a single purpose.

And as she continued to observe, something else seemed to form above that barrier. A pattern this time, that swirled and shifted in the ribbons of energy and rapidly coalesced into strange mathematical configurations, without definite form or detail. A vast intelligence, an intelligence of incomprehensible power and purpose, staring down with calculating composure.

Then the structure and the intelligence slid out of focus; the vision faded like a deactivated hologram, and the grayness returned.

Dr. Edwards pushed open the door of her apartment. But she did not lock it. There was no purpose in locks—not anymore.

The temperature control was still functioning, and she adjusted it upward, though she knew the cold she felt came from within.

Without removing her jacket, she sank exhausted into her chair, closed her eyes then opened them again.

She sighed with relief as she saw the room was unchanged. Everything in its accustomed place: the chronometer, the specimen jar, the equipment on the shelf, the reef photograph on the wall.

Everything was as it should be. The chronometer measured the silence with its silent display; it advanced to the next minute and the equipment emitted its usual faint hum.

This was her room, she thought. Rooms acquire the identity of the person who inhabits them. Every object here had been noticed by her thousands of times, cataloged in her memory with perfect precision. This was her world, her own private world, and as such it would be the last to go.

But how long could she—her focused awareness—maintain its existence?

Dr. Edwards stared at the reef photograph, and for a moment a small measure of reassurance returned to her. They couldn't take this away. The rest of the world might dissolve because there were insufficient minds paying careful attention to maintain its form.

But this room was hers. She alone had furnished it. She alone, since she had first moved into this apartment, had lived here. She knew every detail.

This room would remain. It must remain—it must...

She rose from her chair and walked across the room to the bookshelf, stood staring at the second level with its single publication. Her eyes shifted to the top level, and swift terror gripped her.

For not all the books were there. Many books weren't there! Only the most familiar, the most frequently referenced ones.

So the transformation had already begun here! The unfamiliar books were gone, and that fit the pattern—for it would be the least familiar things, the things least attended to, that would disappear first.

Turning, she stared across the room. Was it her imagination, or did the specimen jar on the table blur and begin to fade?

But as she stared at it, concentrating on its familiar shape, it became clear again, a solid, substantial object.

For a moment real fear reached out and touched her with icy fingers. For she knew that this room no longer was protected against the thing that had happened out there on the street.

Or had it really happened? Might not all this exist within her own mind? Might not the street be as it always was, with researchers walking and equipment functioning? Might not the Blue Whale Café still exist, its blue neon sign glowing in the evening?

Could it be that she was losing her sanity? She had heard whispers when she had passed, whispers the gossiping researchers had not intended her to hear. And she had seen the looks when she walked by. They thought her unstable. Could she be actually unstable?

But she knew she wasn't unstable. She knew that she perhaps was the most rational of all people who walked the earth. For she, and she alone, had foreseen something like this. And the others had dismissed her for it—Lane with his industry connections, the conservationists who had thought she was on their side, the colleagues who couldn't see past their conventional assumptions.

Somewhere else the researchers might be working in a laboratory. But it would be a different laboratory. And the researchers undoubtedly would be different too.

For the matter of which the laboratory and everything within it had been formed would now be cast in a different form, shaped by different attending presences.

She understood now. There were not sufficient minds in existence, paying sufficient attention, to maintain the material world in its familiar form. Some other intelligence from beyond human experience was struggling to supersede human awareness and reshape this universe into its own framework.

Abruptly Dr. Edwards closed her eyes, trying to process what she had finally allowed herself to understand.

Humanity had played unwittingly into the hands of those other presences. Humanity had waged wars, and wars had depopulated vast regions. And perhaps the whole vast cycle of events was but a component of a strategic plan.

She could see it all now. By an insidious form of manipulation, entities beyond human perception—or was it one supreme intelligence—had deliberately created the conditions for conflict. The reduction of the world's attending minds had been carefully planned with calculated premeditation.

On impulse she suddenly turned, crossed the room, and opened the connecting door to the bedroom. She stopped on the threshold, and a sound of despair forced its way to her lips.

There was no bedroom. Where her bed and storage units had been, there was grayish nothingness.

Like an automaton, she turned again and moved to the entry door. Here, too, she found what she had expected. There was no entryway, no familiar jacket hook and equipment rack.

Nothing...

Weakly Dr. Edwards moved back to her chair in the corner.

"So here I am," she said, half aloud.

So there she was. Making a final stand in the last corner of the world that remained to her.

Perhaps there were other people like her, she thought. People who stood at bay against the emptiness that marked the transition from one state to another. People who had lived close to the things they valued, who had endowed those things with such substantial form by power of careful attention alone that they now stood out against the power of some greater attending presence.

The street was gone. The rest of her apartment was gone. This room still retained its form.

This room, she knew, would remain the longest. And when the rest of the room was gone, this corner with her chair would persist. For this was the location where she had lived for fifteen years. The bedroom was for sleeping, the kitchenette for eating. This room was for living. This was her final stand.

These were the walls and floors and photographs and equipment that had absorbed her constant attention, her will to perceive them as walls and photographs and equipment.

She looked toward the window into a blank world. The adjacent buildings were already gone. Others had not lived with them as she had lived with this room. Their attention had been divided, broadly distributed; their focused awareness had not been concentrated as hers upon an area five blocks by four, or a room fifteen by thirteen.

Staring toward the window, she saw it again. The same vision she had observed before, yet different in an indescribable way. There was the structure illuminated against the sky. There were the geometric towers and crystalline features, the dome-shaped projections and platforms. She could see with stereoscopic clarity the suspended bridges, the luminous corridors sweeping on into infinity. The vision was closer this time, but the depth and proportion had changed—as if she were viewing it from two concurrent perspectives simultaneously.

And the intelligence—the intelligence of magnitude—of power, of cosmic strategy and purpose...

Dr. Edwards turned her attention back into the room. The chronometer was advancing slowly, steadily. The grayness was infiltrating the room.

The desk and equipment were the first to go. They simply faded away, and with them went one corner of the room.

And then the specimen jar.

"Oh, well," said Dr. Edwards, "I never did pay much attention to that one."

Now as she sat there, it didn't seem strange to be without the desk or the equipment. It was as if it were something quite normal. Something one could expect to happen.

Perhaps, if she concentrated hard enough, she could restore them.

But, after all, what was the purpose? One person, alone, could not resist the irresistible advance of nothingness. One attending mind, all alone, simply couldn't do it.

She wondered what the specimen jar looked like in that other reality. It certainly wouldn't be a specimen jar, nor would the equipment be equipment, for perhaps they didn't have specimen jars or equipment in the invading dimension.

She wondered, as a matter of fact, what she herself would become when she finally transitioned into the unknown. For she was matter, too, just as the specimen jar and equipment were matter.

She wondered if she would retain her individuality—if she still would be a person. Or would she merely be a thing?

There was one answer to all of that. She simply didn't know.

Nothingness advanced upon her, consumed its way across the room, approaching her as she sat in the chair beneath the shelf. And she waited for it.

The room, or what remained of it, plunged into profound silence.

Dr. Edwards started. The chronometer had stopped. Strange—the first time in fifteen years.

She leaped from her chair and then sat down again.

The chronometer hadn't stopped.

It wasn't there.

There was a tingling sensation in her feet.
quality_problem.question: What was Dr. Edwards' academic controversy centered around?
quality_problem.correct_answer: Her research paper proposing that human consciousness maintains the physical configuration of reality
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: Her opposition to deep-sea mining and natural resource extraction in protected marine zones
answers: Her opposition to deep-sea mining and natural resource extraction in protected marine zones
Her research paper proposing that human consciousness maintains the physical configuration of reality

quality_problem.story:
The Architect of All Possible Cities
By [Author Name]

Jonathan Gibson stood in the pristine white chamber, his worn boots leaving faint dust marks on the crystalline floor. He knew exactly whom he had to thank for this opportunity—his great-grandmother.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he muttered as the technicians ushered him toward the massive architectural simulation engine that dominated the center of the room. All of them, despite the urgency of the moment, remembered to bow respectfully toward the half-dozen stern-faced individuals seated on the observation platform overlooking the chamber.

He stripped off his patched coveralls, as instructed in the preparation room, and stepped into the housing of the enormous mechanism. This was his first time seeing the actual device, having trained on a simplified model, and now he gazed at the shimmering holographic projectors and the humming quantum processors with considerable awe.

This machine, the pride and hope of 2089, represented something almost beyond his comprehension. But Jonathan Gibson knew how to operate it, and he understood, roughly, what it was supposed to accomplish. He also knew that this was the first backward projection of any significant duration and, being scientifically unpredictable, might well kill him.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he muttered again with affection.

If his great-grandmother hadn't volunteered for the earliest temporal-cognitive experiments back in the nineteen-seventies, back even before the Drought, it would never have been discovered that she and her descendants possessed unusual immunity to retro-temporal dissonance. Maria had participated in those groundbreaking studies during the same period when surveyors first began mapping potential dam sites across Thandor—both endeavors products of that era's optimistic belief in technological solutions.

And if that hadn't been discovered, the ruling powers of Earth, more than a century later, would never have plucked Jonathan Gibson out of an obscure position as a maintenance worker at the North American Water Reclamation Facility in Unity, Veldoria, to his present heroic and well-compensated prominence. He would still be monitoring the filtration systems that processed the precious water supply—about one-sixth of the pre-Drought capacity—thoroughly content with the half-ration of purified water he received each payday.

No, if his great-grandmother hadn't demonstrated long ago her unique capacity for maintaining consciousness during temporal projection, Jonathan Gibson would not now be shifting nervously in an AI research laboratory, facing the water barons of the world and awaiting their final instructions with an uncertain and submissive smile.

Men like Tarek Stephens, who controlled the desalination monopoly, Rita Jenkins, the atmospheric moisture harvesting tycoon, Carmen Russell, the recycled water magnate—would sustainable business moguls of their tremendous stature ordinarily waste a glance on someone like Gibson, let alone confer a lifetime pension on his wife and four children of a full liter each of clean water daily?

Even if he didn't return, his family would be provided for better than almost any other family on Earth. This was an excellent opportunity and he was fortunate.

Gibson noticed that Lila Cole had risen from her chair at the side of the room and was approaching him with a sealed data cube in one hand.

"We've decided to add a further precaution at the last moment," the old woman said. "That is, the AI specialists have suggested it and I have—er—I have given my approval."

The last remark was added with a slight questioning note as the Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority looked back quickly at the water barons on the observation platform. Since they stared back impassively, but offered no objection, she coughed in relief and returned to Gibson.

"I am certain, young man, that I don't need to review the details of your instructions once more. You enter the simulation engine and project back the duration for which it has been preset. You've studied the briefing materials about the target year, I trust?"

Gibson nodded. He had memorized everything about his destination—the political climate, the technology of the era, the layout of the facility. The documents had emphasized that the dam's grand opening would occur just days after his arrival, with dignitaries and celebration planned.

"Just so." Lila Cole nodded. "And at that site in Ravenswood, Thandor. You see, young man, you will materialize at the very moment and at the very spot where the control center managing the dam's AI system was—er—managing the system. You will be in an excellent position, an excellent position, to alter the dam's structural parameters and change human history for the better. Very much for the better. Yes."

She paused, having evidently lost her train of thought.

"And he adjusts the blue valve clockwise," Carmen Russell reminded her sharply, impatiently.

"Ah, yes, the blue valve. He turns the blue valve clockwise. Thank you, Ms. Russell, thank you very much. He turns the blue valve on the primary control panel clockwise, thus preventing the error that caused the dam to create a cascading water management failure and causing it, instead, to function as originally designed."

The Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority beamed. "Thus preventing the Drought, making it nonexistent, as it were, producing a present-day world in which the Drought never occurred. The catastrophe began in June of that year—mid-June, specifically. That is correct, is it not?" she asked, turning anxiously again.

None of the half-dozen figures on the platform deigned to answer her. And Gibson kept his eyes deferentially in their direction, too, as he had throughout this period of last-minute instruction.

He knew who ruled his world—these composed, well-hydrated individuals in clean garments with a minimum of patches, and where patches occurred, at least they matched the surrounding fabric.

Cole might be Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority, but that was still a civil-service position, only a few social notches higher than a water facility worker. Her clothes were nearly as worn, nearly as mismatched, as those that Gibson had removed. And the thirst in her throat was no doubt almost as great.

"You understand, do you not, young man, that if anything goes wrong," Lila Cole asked, her head nodding tremulously and anticipating the answer, "if anything unexpected, unprepared-for, occurs, you are not to continue with the experiment but return immediately?"

"He understands everything he needs to understand," Russell told her. "Let's proceed."

The old woman smiled again. "Yes. Of course, Ms. Russell." She approached where Gibson stood at the entrance of the simulation engine and handed the sealed data cube to him. "This is the precaution the AI specialists have just added. When you arrive at your destination, just before materializing, you will release it into the surrounding temporal medium. Our purpose here, as you no doubt—"

Rita Jenkins sat up on the platform and snapped her fingers peremptorily. "I just heard Russell tell you to proceed, Cole. And we're not proceeding. We're busy people. We've wasted enough time."

"I was just trying to explain a crucial final detail," the Director-General apologized. "A detail which may be highly—"

"You've explained enough details." Jenkins turned to the man inside the simulation engine. "Hey, you. Gibson. Move!"

Jonathan Gibson swallowed and nodded vigorously. He darted to the rear of the machine and pressed the sequence that activated it.

*flick!*

It was an excellent opportunity and Jon Gibson knew whom he had to thank for it—his great-grandmother.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he laughed as he looked at the concerned faces of his two colleagues. Stephen Porter and Jordan Hughes had done as much as he to build the compact simulation engine in the secret laboratory under the water reclamation facility, and they were equally eager to go, but—unfortunately for them—they were not descended from the right ancestor.

Casually, he unzipped the richly embroidered garment that, as the father of three children, he was privileged to wear, and squeezed into the housing of the intricate little mechanism. This was hardly his first time seeing it, since he'd been helping to construct the device from the moment Hughes had nodded and risen from the design terminal, and now he barely wasted a glance on the miniature holographic projectors growing out of the almost microscopic quantum processors that powered them.

This machine was the last hope of 2089, even if the world of 2089, as a whole, didn't know of its existence and would try to prevent its operation. But it meant much more to Jon Gibson than merely saving a world. It meant an adventurous mission with the risk of death.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he laughed again happily.

If his great-grandmother hadn't volunteered for the earliest temporal-cognitive experiments way back in the nineteen-seventies, back even before the Plague, it would never have been discovered that she and her descendants possessed considerable immunity to retro-temporal dissonance. The experiments had begun during the same years when the preliminary dam surveys were being conducted across Thandor.

And if that hadn't been discovered, the Gibsons would not have become architectural designers upon the passage of the United Nations law that everyone on Earth—absolutely without exception—had to choose a branch of research science in which to specialize. In the cautious, protective, life-preserving world the Earth had become, Jon Gibson would never have been reluctantly selected by his two co-workers as the one to carry the forbidden banner of dangerous experimentation.

No, if his great-grandmother hadn't demonstrated long ago her unique capacity for maintaining consciousness during temporal projection, Jon Gibson would probably be a water management specialist today like almost everyone else on Earth, laboriously working out tedious conservation problems instead of embarking on the greatest adventure humanity had known to date.

Even if he didn't return, he had at last found a socially useful escape from environmental conservation responsibility to humanity in general and his own family in particular. This was an excellent opportunity and he was fortunate.

"Wait a moment, Jon," Porter said and crossed to the other side of the narrow laboratory.

Gibson and Hughes watched him stuff several sheets of paper into a small metal container which he closed without sealing.

"You will be careful, won't you, Jon?" Jordan Hughes pleaded. "Any time you feel like taking an unnecessary risk, remember that Stephen and I will have to stand trial if you don't come back. We might be sentenced to complete loss of professional status and spend the rest of our lives supervising water filtration robots."

"Oh, it won't be that severe," Gibson reassured him absent-mindedly from where he lay contorted inside the simulation engine. He watched Porter approaching with the container.

Hughes shrugged his shoulders. "It might be much worse than even that and you know it. The disappearance of a three-time father is going to leave an enormous vacancy in the world. One-timers, like Stephen and me, are everywhere; if either of us dropped out of sight, it wouldn't cause nearly as much concern."

"But Stephen and you both tried to operate the machine," Gibson reminded him. "And you experienced dissonance after a fifteen-second temporal displacement. So I'm the only option, the only way to stop the human race from dwindling and dwindling until it reaches absolute zero, like that complacent old Security Council seems willing to let it do."

"Be cautious, Jon," Stephen Porter said as he handed the metal container to Gibson. "The Security Council is just trying to solve the problem in their way, the conservative way: a worldwide concentration on water management research coupled with the maximum preservation of existing human lives, especially those that have high reproductive potential. We three disagree with them; we've been working down here at night to solve it our way, and ours is a radical approach and plenty risky. That's the reason for the metal container—trying to cover one more explosive possibility."

Gibson turned it around curiously. "How?"

"I stayed up all last night writing the document that's inside it. Look, Jon, we've calibrated the machine to send you back to the target date. When you arrive at the Ravenswood Dam Project and turn that blue valve counterclockwise, many other things are going to happen than just altering the dam's design so that it will create the cascading failure instead of functioning properly."

"Sure. I know. If it creates the failure, the Plague doesn't occur. No Anderson's Syndrome."

Porter shook his pudgy face impatiently. "That's not what I mean. The Plague doesn't occur, but something else does. A new world, a different 2089, an alternate time sequence. It'll be a world in which humanity has a better chance to survive, but it'll be one with problems of its own. Maybe severe problems. Maybe the problems will be severe enough that they'll get the same idea we did and try to go back to the same point in time to change them."

Gibson laughed. "That's just looking for trouble."

"Maybe it is, but that's my role. Jordan's the designer of the simulation engine and you're the operator, but I'm the theoretical specialist in this research team. It's my role to look for trouble. So, just in case, I wrote a brief history of the world from the time the dam functioned properly. It explains why ours is the worst possible of futures. It's in that container."

"What do I do with it—hand it to the person from the alternate 2089?"

The small man exasperatedly hit the side of the simulation engine with a well-cushioned palm. "You know better. There won't be any alternate 2089 until you turn that blue valve. The moment you do, our world, with all its slow slide to extinction, disappears and its alternate appears—just like two light bulbs on a push-pull circuit. We and every single one of our artifacts, including the simulation engine, vanish. The problem is how to keep that document from vanishing.

"Well, all you do, if I have this figured correctly, is push the metal container with the document out into the surrounding temporal medium a moment before you materialize to do your job. That temporal medium in which you'll be traveling is something that exists independent of and autonomous to all possible futures. It's my hypothesis that something that's immersed in it will not be altered by a new time sequence."

"Remind him to be careful, Stephen," Hughes rumbled. "He thinks he's an adventure hero and this is his big chance to escape the laboratory and become a daring explorer."

Gibson grimaced in annoyance. "I am excited by doing something besides sitting in a safe little corner working out safe little abstractions for the first time in my life. But I know that this is a first experiment. Honestly, Jordan, I really have enough intelligence to recognize that simple fact. I know that if anything unexpected appears, anything we didn't foresee, I'm supposed to come back immediately and ask for advice."

"I hope you do," Stephen Porter sighed. "I hope you do know that. A twentieth century poet once wrote something to the effect that the world will end not with a bang, but a whimper. Well, our world is ending with a whimper. Try to see that it doesn't end with a bang, either."

"That I'll promise you," Gibson said somewhat disgustedly. "It'll end with neither a bang nor a whimper. So long, Jordan. So long, Stephen."

He twisted around, reaching overhead for the control that activated the forces that drove the simulation engine.

*flick!*

It was strange, Jonathan Gibson reflected, that this temporal projection business, which rendered unconscious everyone who tried it, only made him feel slightly dizzy. That was because he was descended from Maria Gibson, he had been told. There must be some complicated scientific explanation for it, he decided—and that would make it none of his concern. Better not think about it.

All around the simulation engine, there was a dense gray murk in which objects were suggested rather than clearly visible. It reminded him of monitoring his station at the North American Water Reclamation Facility in a thick fog.

According to his instruments, he had traveled back the full duration—over a century into the past, deep into the previous millennium. He reduced speed until he registered June on the temporal readout, then reduced speed again, drifting slowly backward through mid-month. Carefully, carefully, like a man handling a strange device made on a strange planet, he watched the center instrument until the indicator came to rest against the thin marked line labeled "15" that indicated the exactly crucial moment. Then he engaged the brake and stopped the machine completely.

All he had to do now was materialize in the right location, emerge and turn the blue valve toward him. Then his well-paid assignment would be complete.

But....

He stopped and scratched his dust-matted hair. Wasn't there something he was supposed to do a second before materialization? Yes, that ineffectual old bureaucrat, Cole, had given him a last instruction.

He picked up the sealed data cube, walked to the entrance of the simulation engine and tossed it into the gray murk. A solid object floating near the entrance caught his eye. He extended his arm—it was cold!—and pulled it inside.

A small metal container. Odd. What was it doing out there? Curiously, he opened it, hoping to find something valuable. Nothing but a few sheets of paper, Gibson noted disappointedly. He began to read them slowly, very slowly, for the document was full of many long and complicated words, like a report from one academic specialist to another.

The problems all began with the Ravenswood Dam Project, he read. Construction had commenced in the early seventies following the preliminary surveys, and the project had taken several years to complete. It was this dam that finally did the damage the water management specialists had been warning about. The dam with its revolutionary AI-controlled design functioned in Thandor as planned, the architects and the government officials went home to study their data, and the world celebrated once more the approaching era of abundant water and tried to forget about scarcity.

But there was contamination, a biological agent several hundred miles downstream, and a small fishing village got thoroughly exposed to it. Fortunately, the contamination was sufficiently low to do little obvious physical damage: All it did was cause a mutation in a common virus that several of the villagers were incubating at the time, having caught it from the children of the fishing village, among whom a minor epidemic was occurring.

The village residents returned to their normal activities, which promptly spread the new kind of illness. Dr. Patricia Anderson, the only physician in the village, was the first person to note that, while the symptoms of this disease were substantially milder than those of its unmutated parent, practically no one was immune to it and its effects on human reproductivity were truly catastrophic. Most people were completely sterilized by it. The rest were rendered much less capable of producing offspring.

Anderson's Syndrome spread over the entire planet in the next few decades. It leaped across every quarantine established; for a long time, it successfully defied all the vaccines and treatments attempted against it. Then, when a vaccine was finally developed, humanity discovered to its dismay that its reproductive powers had been permanently and fundamentally impaired.

Something had happened to human fertility. A large percentage of individuals were born sterile, and, of those who were not, one child was usually the most that could be expected, a two-child parent being quite rare and a three-child parent almost unknown.

Strict reproductive control was instituted by the Security Council of the United Nations so that fertile individuals would not be wasted upon non-fertile partners. Fertility was the most important avenue to social status, and right after it came successful water management research.

Water management research had the very best minds directed into it; the lesser ones went into the other sciences. Everyone on Earth was engaged in some form of scientific research to some extent. Since the population was now so limited in proportion to the great resources available, all physical labor had long been performed by robots. The government ensured that everybody had an ample supply of goods and, in return, asked only that they experiment without any risk to their own lives—every human being was now a much-prized, highly protected rarity.

There were fewer than a hundred thousand of them, well below the danger point, it had been estimated, where a species might be eliminated by a new catastrophe. Not that another catastrophe would be needed. Since the end of the Plague, the birth rate had been moving further and further behind the death rate. In another century....

That was why a desperate and secret attempt to alter the past was being made. This kind of world was evidently unsustainable.

Jonathan Gibson finished the document and sighed. What a wonderful world! What a comfortable place to live!

He walked to the rear controls and began the process of materializing at the crucial moment—the fifteenth of June in his target year.

*flick!*

It was odd, Jon Gibson reflected, that these temporal projections, which induced coma in everyone who tried it, only made him feel slightly dizzy. That was because he was descended from Maria Gibson, he knew. Maybe there was some genetic relationship with his above-average fertility—might be a good idea to mention the theory to a biologist or two when he returned. If he returned.

All around the simulation engine, there was a soupy gray murk in which objects were suggested rather than clearly visible. It reminded him of the challenges of landing a water transport in a thick fog when the navigation AI had not been properly configured.

According to the insulated register, he had completed the full temporal displacement—arriving in the mid-seventies, that remarkable decade his briefing materials had emphasized. He lowered speed until he registered June, then maneuvered slowly backward through time toward the target date. Carefully, carefully, like an architect supervising construction robots at an unusually difficult site, he watched the register until it rolled to rest against the notch marked "15" that indicated the exactly crucial moment. Then he pressed a button and froze the machine where it was.

All he had to do now was materialize in the right location, emerge and push the blue valve away from him. Then his exciting adventure would be over.

But....

He paused and tapped at his sleek chin. He was supposed to do something a second before materialization. Yes, that nervous theoretician, Stephen Porter, had given him a last suggestion.

He picked up the small metal container, twisted around to face the opening of the simulation engine and dropped it into the gray murk. A solid object floating near the opening attracted his attention. He shot his arm out—it was cold, as cold as they had calculated—and pulled the object inside.

A sealed data cube. Strange. What was it doing out there? Anxiously, he opened it, not daring to believe he'd find a document inside. Yes, that was exactly what it was, he saw excitedly. He began to read it rapidly, very rapidly, as if it were a newly published paper on sustainable architecture. Besides, the document was written with almost painful simplicity, like a textbook composed by a stuffy pedagogue for the use of novices.

The problems all began with the Ravenswood Dam Project, he read. Construction had commenced in the early seventies following the preliminary surveys, and the project had taken several years to complete. It was this dam that finally did the damage the water management specialists had been warning about. The dam with its revolutionary AI-controlled design malfunctioned in Thandor through some absolutely unforgivable error in the control center, the officer in charge of the center was reprimanded and the technicians under him were dismissed, and the Thandor government was paid a handsome compensation for the damage.

But there had been more damage than anyone knew at the time. The cascading failure had released enormous quantities of water that flooded downstream communities and destroyed critical infrastructure. More importantly, it had contaminated the water supply with industrial pollutants that had been stored in facilities near the dam.

Five years later, the contamination effects burst beyond local boundaries and completely disrupted the regional water cycle. Sunnydale in Galdoria and dozens of other agricultural regions became semi-deserts inhabited by a few struggling communities.

Then the water crisis adjusted to a global scale—and drought howled across every continent of the planet. All attempts by water management specialists to control the Drought failed because of the swiftness of its progression. And after it had devastated one region, it spread to another and another.

Most of the world's agriculture had been abandoned for lack of water long before the crops could die of natural causes. Many communities, too, before they became extinct due to lack of water, served as warnings to others to some small extent.

But the water supply of Earth was steadily diminishing in a horrifying geometric progression. Recently, it had been observed, atmospheric moisture—the basis on which most of the planet's water cycle depended—had started to disappear, and with its diminution, dead vegetation had begun to pile up across the landscapes.

Mankind had lunged out desperately in all directions in an effort to survive, but nothing had worked for any length of time. Even advanced desalination technology, which had been developed at tremendous cost in remaining resources, had yielded insufficient water. Synthetics had failed to fill the prodigious gap.

In the midst of the sharply increasing drought, social controls had pretty much dissolved. Pathetic attempts at rationing still continued, but black markets became the only markets, and water barons became the lords of life. Dehydration took the hindmost, and only the most economically agile lived in comparative comfort. Law and order were available only to those who could afford to pay for them and children of impoverished families were sold on the open market for a bit of water.

But the Drought was still progressing and the water supply kept shrinking. In another century....

That was why the planet's powerful individuals had been persuaded to pool their wealth in a desperate attempt to alter the past. This kind of world was manifestly unsustainable.

Jon Gibson finished the document and sighed. What a magnificent world! What an exciting place to live!

He dropped his hand on the side controls and began the process of materializing at the crucial moment—the fifteenth of June in his target year.

*flick!*
