As the equipment of the control center began to take on a blurred reality all around him, Jonathan Gibson felt a bit of fear at what he was doing. The technicians, he remembered, the Director-General, even the water barons, had all warned him not to proceed with his instructions if anything unusual turned up. That was an enormous amount of power to disobey: he knew he should return with this new information and let superior minds work on it.

They with their easy lives, what did they know what existence had been like for such as he? Thirst, always thirst, struggling, servility, and more thirst. Every time things got really desperate, you and your wife looking sideways at your kids and wondering which of them would bring the best price. Buying security for them, as he was now, at the risk of his life.

But in this other world, this other 2089, there was a state that took care of you and that treasured your children. A man like himself, with four children—why, he'd be an important man, maybe the most important man on Earth! And he'd have robots to work for him and plenty of water. Above all, plenty and plenty of water.

He'd even be a scientist—everyone was a scientist there, weren't they?—and he'd have a large laboratory all to himself. This other world had its troubles, but it was a much nicer place than where he'd come from. He wouldn't return. He'd proceed.

The fear left him and, for the first time in his life, Jonathan Gibson felt the sensation of power.

He materialized the simulation engine around the primary control panel, sweating a bit at the sight of the roomful of technical figures, despite the technicians' reassurances that all this would be happening too fast to be visible. Through a window, he could see workers unfurling patriotic bunting along the dam's observation deck—decorations for what looked like an opening ceremony. A calendar on the wall showed mid-June, and someone had circled a date later that month with the notation "Grand Opening - 200th Anniversary Celebration." He saw the single blue valve pointing upward on the control panel. The valve that controlled the operation of the dam. Now! Now to make a halfway decent world!

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

As the equipment of the control center began to oscillate into reality all around him, Jon Gibson felt a bit of shame at what he was doing. He'd promised Stephen and Jordan to abandon the experiment at any stage if a new factor appeared. He knew he should go back with this new information and have all three of them discuss it.

But what would they be able to tell him, they with their blissful adjustment to their thoroughly planned lives? They, at least, had been ordered to marry women they could live with; he'd drawn a female with whom he was completely incompatible in any but a genetic sense. Water management! He was tired of water management and the sanctity of human life, tired to the tip of his uncalloused fingers, tired to the recesses of his unused muscles. He was tired of having to undertake a simple adventure like a criminal in the night.

But in this other world, this other 2089, someone like himself would be a monarch of the water market, a lord of chaos, making his own rules, taking his own opportunities. So what if the weak, those unfit to carry on the race, suffered? His kind wouldn't.

He'd formed a pretty good idea of the kind of individuals who ruled that other world, from the document in the sealed data cube. The water barons had not even read it. Why, the fools had obviously been manipulated by the technicians into permitting the experiment; they had not grasped the idea that an alternate time track would mean their own non-existence.

This other world had its troubles, but it was certainly a more dynamic place than where he'd come from. It deserved a chance. Yes, that was how he felt: his world was drowsily moribund; this alternate was struggling but managing to fight against destiny. It deserved a chance.

Gibson decided that he was experiencing renunciation and felt proud.

He materialized the simulation engine around the primary control panel, disregarding the roomful of technical figures since he knew they could not see him. Through a window, he glimpsed workers hanging red, white, and blue decorations along the dam's walkways—preparations for some kind of dedication ceremony. A newspaper lay on a nearby desk, its headline celebrating the nation's upcoming milestone anniversary, with coverage of tall ships arriving in harbors and fireworks planned nationwide. The single blue valve pointed downward on the control panel. That was the mechanism that controlled the operation of the dam. Now! Now to make a halfway interesting world!

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

Now! Now to make a halfway decent world!

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

Now! Now to make a halfway interesting world!

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

... pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... toward him.

*flick!*

... away from him.

*flick!*
quality_problem.question: What year was Jonathan Gibson supposed to project back to?

quality_problem.story:
I nearly tripped over the kid in the dark before I saw her.

Her hoverchair was parked as usual on the narrow strip of synthetic grass that separated her mother's housing pod from the one Daniel Wallace and I lived in, but it wasn't exactly where I'd learned to expect it when I rolled in at night from the biotech labs. Usually it was nearer the west end of the strip where Emily could look across the transparent aluminum square of the Foxwood City residential complex and the biodiversity conservation zones to the maglev transit line beyond. But this time it was pushed back into the shadows away from the complex lights.

The girl wasn't watching the conservation zones tonight, as she usually did. Instead she was lying back in her chair with her face turned to the holographic display floating above her, staring upward with such absorbed intensity that she didn't even know I was there until I spoke.

"Anything wrong, Emily?" I asked.

She said, "No, Logan," without taking her eyes off the display.

For a minute I had the prickly feeling you get when you are watching a simulation and find that you know just what is going to happen next. You're puzzled and a little spooked until you realize that the reason you can predict the action so exactly is because you've seen the same thing happen somewhere else a long time ago. I forgot the feeling when I remembered why the kid wasn't watching the conservation zones. But I couldn't help wondering why she'd turned to manipulating molecular structures instead.

"What're you working on up there, Emily?" I asked.

She didn't move and from the tone of her voice I got the impression that she only half heard me.

"I'm rearranging some proteins," she said softly.

I gave it up and went on to my own pod without asking any more fool questions. How can you talk to a kid like that?

Our pod was dark inside. I switched on the light and dumped my packages on the counter, noting the empty flavor enhancer containers scattered by the synthesizer—Daniel's calling cards when he'd been at loose ends. The pattern was familiar: dark pod, empties on the counter, and usually an empty bunk with Daniel having wandered off somewhere. But this time he was actually there, asleep in his bunk, which threw me.

The smell hit me when I shook him awake—synthetic whiskey, the cheap kind from the dispensaries on the east side of Foxwood City. That part fit the pattern well enough. But what made me look twice was that at some time during the day he had bathed and groomed himself. He had even cleaned and pressed a shirt; it hung on a hook over his bunk with a crumpled pack of vapor sticks in the pocket.

Daniel sat up and blinked against the light, a thin, elderly man with bright blue eyes, a clipped gray beard and scanty gray hair tousled and wild from sleep. He was stripped to his undergarments against the heat, looking more presentable than he had in weeks.

"Crawl out and prepare dinner, Rip," I said, holding him to his end of our working agreement. "I've made a shift and I'm hungry."

Daniel got up and stepped into his pants. He padded barefoot across the floor and poked at the packages on the counter.

"Synthesized protein again," he complained. "Logan, I'm sick of this stuff!"

"You don't catch real meat with a basic income credit," I told him. And because I'd never been able to stay sore at him for long I added, "But we got flavor enhancers. Where's the dispenser?"

"I'm sick of flavor enhancers, too," Daniel said. "I need a real drink."

I sniffed the air, making a business of it. "You've had one already. Where?"

He grinned at me then with the wise-to-himself-and-the-world grin that lit up his face like turning on a light inside and made him different from anybody else on earth.

"The largess of Providence," he said, "is bestowed impartially upon sot and Samaritan. I helped the little one next door to the bathroom this afternoon while her mother was away at work, and my selflessness had its just reward."

Sometimes it's hard to tell when Daniel is kidding. He's an educated man—used to teach at some Northern university, he said once, and I never doubted it—and talks like one when he wants to. He still carried traces of that polish from his academic days, though you'd never know it most of the time. Daniel's no bum, though he's a semi-alcoholic and lets me support him like an invalid uncle, and he's keen enough to read my mind like a data stream.

"No, I didn't break into the cupboard and help myself," he said. "The lady—her name is Camila Gutierrez—gave me the drink. Why else do you suppose I'd clean a shirt?"

That was like Daniel. He hadn't touched her bottle though his insides were probably snarled up like corrupted code for the want of it. He'd groomed and pressed a shirt instead so he'd look decent enough to rate a shot of whiskey she'd offer him as a reward. It wasn't such a doubtful gamble at that, because Daniel has a way with him when he bothers to use it; maybe that's why he bums around with me after the lab work and temporary gigs, because he's used that charm too often in the wrong places.

"Good enough," I said and activated a nutrition packet apiece for us while Daniel put the protein to heat.

He told me more about our neighbors while we consumed the packets. The Gutierrezes were permanent residents. The kid—her name was Emily and she was ten—was a genetic disorder case who hadn't walked for over a year, and her mother was a server at a food dispensary named the Coral Shell. There wasn't any Mr. Gutierrez. I guessed there never had been, which would explain why Camila acted so tough and sullen.

I was getting used to this cleaned-up version of Daniel—it seemed like a lot of effort for one drink, but that was his business. We were halfway through dinner when I remembered something the kid had said.

"Who's Rita?" I asked.

Daniel frowned at his plate. "The kid had a therapy companion named Rita, an advanced AI construct with only one optical sensor functioning and no affection protocols for anybody but the girl. The companion isn't coming home. It was destroyed by a transport vehicle on the transit line while Emily was hospitalized with her condition."

"Tough," I said, thinking of the kid sitting out there all day in her hoverchair, straining her eyes across the conservation zones. "You mean she's been waiting a year?"

Daniel nodded, seemed to lose interest in the Gutierrezes, so I let the subject drop. We sat around after dinner and consumed the rest of the flavor enhancers. When we turned in around midnight I figured we wouldn't be staying long at the Foxwood City residential complex. It wasn't a very comfortable place.

I was wrong there. It wasn't comfortable, but we stayed.

I couldn't have said at first why we stuck, and if Daniel could he didn't volunteer. Neither of us talked about it. We just went on living the way we were used to living, a few weeks here and a few there, all over the colonies.

We'd hit the Foxwood City sector too late for the agricultural biotech season, so I went in for the protein synthesis labs instead. I worked the labs all the way from Foxwood City down to Valleyview, Wendria, not signing on with any of the major corporations because I like to move quick when I get restless. I picked the independent cellular engineering runs mostly, because the percentage is good there if you've got steady hands and sharp eyes.

Cellular engineering isn't the career planning opportunity it seems to the one-shift workers who flock along because the credit is decent. You work in a sterile lab, usually, with neural interfaces instead of regular equipment, and you use multiple monitoring systems that go down to the molecular level where the complex structures are. There's no real thrill to it, as the one-shift workers find out quickly. A protein synthesis puts up no more challenge than basic assembly and the biggest job is to maintain quality control once you've got your batch stabilized.

Usually a pro like me sells his output to the lab's owner or to some clumsy worker who wants his metrics boosted, and there's nearly always a bonus—from a pool made up at the beginning of every cycle—for the person producing the highest quality batch of the day. There's a knack to engineering the complex ones, and when the bonuses were running good I only worked a shift or so a week and spent the rest of the time lying around the pod playing strategy games and consuming flavor enhancers with Daniel Wallace.

Usually it was the life of Riley, but somehow it wasn't enough in this place. We'd get about half-intoxicated and work up a promising argument about healthcare policy or ethical decision-making in biotechnology. Then, just when we'd got life looking its screwball funniest with our arguments one or the other of us would look out the window and see Emily Gutierrez in her hoverchair, waiting for an AI companion named Rita to come floating home across the biodiversity conservation zones. She was always there, day or night, until her mother came home from work and guided her inside.

It wasn't right or natural for a kid to wait like that for anything and it worried me. I even offered once to buy the kid another companion but Camila Gutierrez told me quick to mind my own business. Daniel explained that the kid didn't want another companion because she had what Daniel called a psychological block.

"Rita was more than just an AI to her," Daniel said. "She was a sort of symbol because she offered the kid two things that no one else in the world could—security and independence. With Rita keeping her company she felt secure, and she was independent of the kids who could run and play because she had Rita to interact with. If she took another companion now she'd be giving up more than Rita. She'd be giving up everything that Rita had meant to her, then there wouldn't be any point in living."

I could see it when Daniel put it that way. The companion had spent more time with Emily than Camila had, and the kid felt as safe with it as she'd have been with a security detail. And Rita, being a single-user AI, had depended on Emily for the interaction protocols she wouldn't execute for anybody else. The companion needed Emily and Emily needed her. Together, they'd been a natural.

At first I thought it was funny that Emily never complained or cried when Rita didn't come home, but Daniel explained that it was all a part of this psychological block business. If Emily cried she'd be admitting that Rita was lost. So she waited and watched, secure in her belief that Rita would return.

The Gutierrezes got used to Daniel and me being around, but they never got what you'd call intimate. Emily would laugh at some of the droll things Daniel said, but her eyes always went back to the conservation zones and the transit line, looking for Rita. And she never let anything interfere with her routine.

That routine started every morning when old Fernando Simpson, the delivery coordinator, piloted his drone out from Foxwood City to leave a handful of packages for the residential complex tenants. Fernando would always make it a point to route back by way of the Gutierrez pod and Emily would stop him and ask if he'd seen anything of a one-sensor AI companion on his route that day.

Old Fernando would lean against his control panel and deactivate his visor, scowling while he pretended to think.

Then he'd say, "Not today, Emily," or, "Thought so yesterday, but this one had two sensors on it. 'Twasn't Rita."

Then he'd pilot away, shaking his head. Later on the maintenance worker would come around to swap waste processors under the pods and Emily would ask him the same question. Once a month the power company sent out a technician to read the energy meters and he was part of Emily's routine too.

It was hard on Camila. Sometimes the kid would dream at night that Rita had come home and was signaling at the pod entrance to be let in, and she'd wake Camila and beg her to go out and see. When that happened Daniel and I could hear Camila talking to her, low and steady, until all hours of the morning, and when she finally went back to sleep we'd hear her open the cupboard and take out the whiskey bottle.

But there came a night that was more than Camila could take, a night that changed Emily's routine and a lot more with it. It left a mark you've seen yourself—everybody has that's got eyes to see—though you never knew what made it. Nobody ever knew that but Emily and Camila Gutierrez and Daniel and me.

Daniel and I were turning in around midnight that night when the kid sang out next door. We heard Camila get up and go to her, and we got up too and activated a flavor enhancer because we knew neither of us would sleep any more till she got Emily quiet again. But this night was different. Camila hadn't talked to the kid long when she yelled, "Rita! Rita!" and after that we heard both of them crying.

A little later Camila came out into the artificial moonlight and shut the pod door behind her. She looked rumpled and beaten, her hair straggling damply on her shoulders and her eyes puffed and red from crying. The whiskey she'd had hadn't helped any either.

She stood for a while without moving, then she looked up at the sky and said something I'm not likely to forget.

"Why couldn't You give the kid a break?" she said, not railing or anything but loud enough for us to hear. "You, up there—what's another lousy one-sensor AI to You?"

Daniel and I looked at each other in the half-dark of our own pod. "She's done it, Logan," Daniel said.

I knew what he meant and wished I didn't. Camila had finally told the kid that Rita wasn't coming back, not ever.

That's why I was worried about Emily when I came home the next evening and found her manipulating molecular structures instead of watching the conservation zones. It meant she'd given up waiting for Rita. And the quiet way the kid spoke of rearranging proteins worried me more, because it sounded outright impossible.

Not that you could blame her for going off her head. It was tough enough to be pinned to a hoverchair without being able to wiggle so much as a toe. But to lose her companion in the bargain....

I was on my third flavor enhancer when Daniel Wallace rolled in with a big package under his arm. The look of him stopped me—clear-eyed and steady on his feet, carrying himself with something of that old professorial bearing he'd let slip years ago. He was hot and tired from a shopping trip to Springfield District, which itself was unusual enough. It was when he unpacked his package, though, that I thought he'd lost his mind.

"Educational materials for Emily," Daniel said. "Camila and I agreed this morning that the girl needs another interest to occupy her time now, and since she can't go to school I'm going to teach her here."

He went on to explain that Camila hadn't had the heart the night before, desperate as she was, to tell the kid the whole truth. She'd told her instead, quoting an imaginary customer at the Coral Shell, that a transport vehicle with off-world registration had picked Rita up on the transit line and taken her away. It was a good enough story. Emily still didn't know that Rita was destroyed, but her waiting was over because no AI could be expected to find its way home from off-world.

"We've got to give the girl another interest," Daniel said, putting away the materials and activating another flavor enhancer. "Emily has a remarkable talent for concentration—most handicapped children have—that could be the end of her if it isn't diverted into safe channels."

I thought the kid had cracked up already and said so.

"Rearranging proteins?" Daniel said when I told him. "Good Lord, Logan—"

Camila Gutierrez knocked just then, interrupting him. She came in and had a flavor enhancer with us and talked to Daniel about his plan for educating Emily at home. But she couldn't tell us anything more about the kid's new fixation than we already knew. When she asked her why she manipulated molecular structures like that she'd say only that she wants something to remember Rita by.

It was about nine o'clock, when Camila went home to prepare supper. Daniel and I knocked off our strategy game and went outside with our portable chairs to get some air. It was then that the first protein structure changed.

It changed all of a sudden, the way any cellular mutation does, and transformed across the holographic display in a curving, blue-white cascade of molecular bonds. I didn't pay much attention, but Daniel nearly choked on his flavor enhancer.

"Logan," he said, "that was a hemoglobin variant! It mutated! Spontaneously!"

I didn't see anything spontaneous about it and said so. You can see a dozen or so protein structures shift across a display on any work cycle if you're in the mood to look.

"Not just shift, you fool," Daniel said. "The structure hemoglobin—a critical oxygen transport protein—it mutated a good sixty degrees in its quaternary structure, then stabilized!"

I sat up and took notice then, partly because the protein really had stabilized instead of degrading the way an unstable mutation does, partly because anything that excites Daniel Wallace that much is something to think about.

We watched the display like two cats at a mouse-hole, but it didn't change again. After a while a smaller structure did, though, and later in the night a whole procession of them transformed across the display and fell into place around the first one, forming a pattern that didn't make any sense to us. They stopped changing around midnight and we went to bed, but neither of us got to sleep right away.

"Maybe we ought to look for another interest in life ourselves instead of drumming up one for Emily," Daniel said. He meant it as a joke but it had a shaky sound; "Something besides getting intoxicated every night, for instance."

"You think we've got neural degradation from consuming flavor enhancers?" I asked.

Daniel laughed at that, sounding more like his old self. "No, Logan. No two people ever had instantaneous and identical hallucinations."

"Look," I said. "I know this sounds crazy but maybe Emily—"

Daniel wasn't amused any more. "Don't be a fool, Logan. If those proteins really mutated you can be sure of two things—Emily had nothing to do with it, and the news feeds will explain everything tomorrow."

He was wrong on one count at least.

The news feeds next day were packed with alerts three inches high but none of them explained anything. The broadcast commentators quoted every authority they could reach, and biotechnology experts were going crazy everywhere. It just couldn't happen, they said.

Daniel and I went over the news feed by feed that night and I learned more about protein structures than I'd learned in a lifetime. Daniel, as I've said before, is an educated man, and what he couldn't recall offhand about biotechnology the news feeds quoted by chapter and verse. They ran interviews with researchers at GeneTech Laboratories and BioSynth Corporation and MolecularDynamics Institute and God knows where else, but nobody could explain why all of those proteins would spontaneously mutate then stabilize.

It set me back on my heels to learn that hemoglobin was critical for oxygen transport and had a complex quaternary structure, that it was highly conserved across species and had variants that were more efficient than the standard but didn't occur naturally. This variant—researchers called it the "Enhanced" because hemoglobin was the blood protein—hadn't degraded, which puzzled the researchers no end. I suggested to Daniel, only half joking, that maybe the Enhanced had stayed stable because it wasn't complex enough to suit Emily's taste, but Daniel called me down sharp.

"Don't joke about Emily," he said sternly. "Getting back to hemoglobin—it's so fundamental that its genetic code has been conserved for millions of years. That means any mutation would have started when Emily was only eighteen months old. The laws of biochemistry are universal constants, Logan, and researchers say they can't be violated."

"They said the proteins couldn't be tossed around like building blocks, too," I pointed out. "I'm not saying that Emily really mutated those damn proteins, Daniel, but if she did she could have altered the entire biochemical pathway along with them, couldn't she?"

But Daniel wouldn't argue the point. "I'm going out for air," he said.

I trailed along, but we didn't get farther than Emily's hoverchair.

There she sat, tense and absorbed, staring up at the holographic display. Daniel and I followed her gaze, the way you do automatically when somebody ahead of you cranes their neck at something. We looked up just in time to see the proteins start mutating again.

The first one to go was a large complex one that transformed across the display like a cascade reaction—zip, like that—and stabilized beside the group that had mutated the night before.

Daniel said, "There went collagen," and his voice sounded like he had just run a mile.

That was only the beginning. During the next hour forty or fifty more proteins transformed across the display and joined the group that had mutated the night before. The pattern they made still didn't look like anything in particular.

I left Daniel shaking his head at the display and went over to give Emily, who had called it a night and was manually guiding her hoverchair toward the Gutierrez pod, a boost up the entrance ramp. I pushed her inside where Daniel couldn't hear, then I asked her how things were going.

"Slow, Logan," she said. "I've got 'most a hundred to go, yet."

"Then you're really mutating those proteins up there?"

She looked surprised. "Sure, it's not so hard once you know how."

The odds were even that she was pulling my leg, but I went ahead anyway and asked another question.

"I can't make head or tail of it, Emily," I said. "What're you making up there?"

She gave me a very small smile.

"You'll know when I'm through," she said.

I told Daniel about that after we'd bunked in, but he said I should not encourage the kid in her delusional thinking. "Emily's heard everybody talking about those proteins mutating, the broadcast commentators blared about it, so she's excited too. But she's got a lot more imagination than most people, because she's a disabled child, and she could develop a dangerous delusion because she's upset about Rita. The thing to do is give her a logical explanation instead of letting her think her fantasy is a fact."

Daniel was taking all this so hard—because it was upsetting things he'd taken for granted as being facts all his life, like those researchers who were going nuts in droves all over the colonies. I didn't realize how upset Daniel really was, though, till he woke me up at about 4:00 a.m.

"I can't sleep for thinking about those proteins," he said, sitting on the edge of my bunk. "Logan, I'm scared."

That from Daniel was something I'd never expected to hear. It startled me wide enough awake to sit up in the dark and listen while he unloaded his worries.

"I'm afraid," Daniel said, "because what is happening up there isn't right or natural. It just can't be, yet it is."

It was so quiet when he paused that I could hear the blood swishing in my ears. Finally Daniel said, "Logan, the biochemistry we depend on is as delicately balanced as a fine chronometer. If that balance is upset too far our world will be affected drastically."

Ordinarily I wouldn't have argued with Daniel on his own ground, but I could see he was painting a mental picture of the whole biosphere collapsing like a failed simulation and I was afraid to let him go on.

"The trouble with you educated people," I said, "is that you think your experts have got everything figured out, that there's nothing in the world their algorithms can't pin down. Well, I'm an illiterate worker, but I know that your researchers can measure the proteins till they're blue in the face and they'll never learn who designed those proteins there. So how do they know that whoever designed them there won't change them again? I've always heard that if a person had faith enough they could move mountains. Well, if a person has the faith in themselves that Emily's got maybe they could mutate proteins, too."

Daniel sat quiet for a minute.

"'There are more things, Horatio....'" he began, then laughed. "A line worn threadbare by centuries of repetition but as apt tonight as ever, Logan. Do you really believe Emily is mutating those proteins?"

"Why not?" I came back. "It's as good an answer as any the experts have come up with."

Daniel got up and went back to his own bunk. "Maybe you're right. We'll find out tomorrow."

And we did. Daniel did, rather, while I was hard at work engineering cellular structures in the depths of the lab.

I got home a little earlier than usual that night, just before it got really dark. Emily was sitting as usual all alone in her hoverchair. In the gloom I could see a stack of educational materials on the grass beside her, materials Daniel had given her to study. The thing that stopped me was that Emily was staring at her feet as if they were the first ones she'd ever seen, and she had the same look of intense concentration on her face that I'd seen when she was manipulating the proteins.

I didn't know what to say to her, thinking maybe I'd better not mention the proteins. But Emily spoke first.

"Logan," she said, without taking her eyes off her toes, "did you know that Daniel is an awfully wise man?"

I said I'd always thought so, but why?

"Daniel said this morning that I ought not to mutate any more proteins," the kid said. "He says I ought to concentrate instead on learning how to walk again so I can go off-world and find Rita."

For a minute I was mad enough to brain Daniel Wallace if he'd been handy. Anybody that would pull a gag like that on a disabled, helpless kid....

"Daniel says that if I can do what I've been doing to the proteins then it ought to be easy to repair my own nerve pathways," Emily said. "And he's right, Logan. So I'm not going to mutate any more proteins. I'm going to repair my nerve pathways."

She looked up at me with her small, solemn smile. "It took me a whole day to learn how to mutate that first protein, Logan, but I could do this after only a couple of hours. Look...."

And she wiggled the toes on both feet.

It's a pity things don't happen in life like they do in simulations, because a first-class story could be made out of Emily Gutierrez's knack for altering things by concentrating on them. In a simulation Emily might have saved the world or destroyed it, depending on which line would interest the most viewers and bring the creator the fattest credit, but of course it didn't really turn out either way. It ended in what Daniel Wallace called an anticlimax, leaving everybody happy enough except a few researchers who like mysteries anyway or they wouldn't be researchers in the first place.

The proteins that had been mutated stayed where they were, but the pattern they had started was never finished. That unfinished pattern won't ever go away, in case you've wondered about it—it's up there in the database where you can access it any clear cycle—but it will never be finished because Emily Gutierrez lost interest in it when she learned to walk again.

Walking was a slow business with Emily at first because her legs had got thin and weak—partially atrophied muscles, Daniel said—and it took time to make them round and strong again. But in a couple of weeks she was stumping around on support braces and after that she never went near her hoverchair again.

Camila sent her to school at Springfield District by transit and before vacation time came around she was playing sports and swimming in the recreation center with a gang of other kids on rest days.

School opened up a whole new world to Emily and she fitted herself into the routine as neat as if she'd been doing it all her life. She learned a lot there and she forgot a lot that she'd learned for herself by being alone. Before we realized what was happening she was just like any other ten-year-old, full of curiosity and energy, with no more power to alter things by concentrating on them than anybody else had.

I think she actually forgot about those proteins along with other things that had meant so much to her when she was confined to her hoverchair and couldn't do anything but wait and think.

For instance, a basic AI companion followed her home from Foxwood City one day and Camila let her keep it. She programmed the companion and customized it and named it Nova, and after that she never said anything more about going off-world to find Rita. It was only natural, of course, because kids—normal kids—forget their pain quickly. It's a sort of defense mechanism, Daniel says, against the disappointments of this life.

When school opened again in the fall Camila sold her pod and got a position in Springfield District where Emily could walk to school instead of going by transit. When they were gone the Foxwood City residential complex was so lonesome and dead that Daniel and I pulled out and went down to the Valleyview, Wendria sector for the agricultural biotech season. We never heard from Camila and Emily again.

We've moved several times since; we're out in the supply chain management facilities just now, with the logistics coordinators. But everywhere we go we're reminded of them. Every time we access the biochemistry database we see what Daniel calls the Emily Gutierrez Molecular Monument, which is nothing but a funny sort of pattern roughed in with a hundred or so proteins of all sizes and complexities.

The structure of it is so sketchy that you'd never make out what it's supposed to be unless you knew already what you were looking for. To us the head of an AI companion is fairly plain. If you know enough to fill in the gaps you can see it was meant to be a complex construct with only one optical sensor.

Daniel says that footloose workers like him and me forget old associations as quick as kids do—and for the same good reason—so I'm not especially interested now in where Camila and Emily Gutierrez are or how they're doing. But there's one thing I'll always wonder about, now that there's no way of ever knowing for sure.

I wish I'd asked Emily or Camila, before they moved away, how Rita lost that other sensor.
quality_problem.question: What didn't surprise Logan about Daniel Wallace?
quality_problem.correct_answer: That Daniel had been out drinking
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: That Daniel had bathed and groomed himself
answers: That Daniel had bathed and groomed himself
That Daniel had been out drinking

quality_problem.story:
A district simply vanished on the night of March 15th.

A delivery driver named Sofia Stone was the first to report it. She had been rushing south along Highway 7 through the Pearlbrook Region, trying to make up time after a longer-than-expected stop at a distribution center, when she slammed on her brakes. If she'd gone another thirty feet, she would have driven straight into the void where the highway should have continued.

Sofia couldn't see the full extent of the emptiness because of the darkness, but it looked massive. Bigger than any sinkhole she'd ever heard of. Her first thought was some kind of catastrophic infrastructure collapse. She reversed two hundred feet, set out emergency flares, then sped off to find a phone signal.

State authorities converged on the site from multiple directions. Communicating by radio across the vast emptiness, they confirmed that an entire district was definitely missing from the heart of the region. They called in the National Guard.

The Guard surrounded the area with personnel—more than eight hundred were needed—to keep people from falling into the void. A helicopter pilot who flew over it reported that it looked as if someone had used a giant cookie cutter on the landscape, removing a perfect section from Pearlbrook's interior.

The regional transit authority complained that one of its automated trains was missing. The train's schedule had it passing through the area at 11:47 PM. That seemed to fix the time of the disappearance around midnight.

Someone pointed out that March 15th was the Ides of March, historically a day of upheaval.

Somebody else said they'd better check for radiation or chemical contamination. An environmental safety official brought detection equipment, but everything registered normal.

A National Guard officer volunteered to take a vehicle down into the void, having found what seemed like a navigable slope. She was gone for over an hour, but when she emerged on the other side, she reported that the void was smooth, bowl-shaped, and showed no signs of explosion or fire. She'd found no people, no buildings—no trace of anything except the void itself.

The Governor asked federal authorities whether any unidentified aircraft had been in the region. Washington said no. The Department of Defense and various agencies denied conducting any secret experiments.

Nor had there been any sensitive facilities in the missing district that might have been targeted. The area's biggest employer was a film production studio, and the second-biggest was a venture capital firm specializing in virtual reality startups.

A commercial pilot found the missing district early on the morning of March 16th. The pilot, Captain Jonathan Spencer, who prided himself on rational thinking and logic, was afraid he was seeing something impossible. The object emerged from a cloud layer at fifteen thousand feet, and Spencer changed course to avoid it. He noted with minimal relief that his co-pilot also saw the thing and wondered why it wasn't moving.

Then he saw the broadcast tower on it.

A few minutes later, he had relayed a message from the floating landmass, addressed to anyone listening:

It said that the district had declared independence from the ground.

One other radio message came from the airborne territory on that first day. An amateur radio operator reported an unidentified voice saying plaintively:

"Getting cold up here!"

Kevin Mason had been dozing in the observation car of the express train when it jerked to a stop. He looked out the window, hoping this was Magnolia Province, where he planned to catch a connecting flight. But it wasn't. All he could see were emergency lights moving along the tracks.

The conductor looked into the car. A woman with striking auburn hair across the aisle—Kevin had noticed her earlier—asked, "Why did we stop?"

"Someone flagged us down," the conductor said. "We don't normally stop here on the Pearlbrook route."

The woman's hair was professionally styled, and Kevin had observed earlier that she carried herself with the confidence of someone used to authority. Her eyes had been focused on a tablet when Kevin entered the car, giving him time to notice her sharp features and the slight frown lines that suggested she was accustomed to finding fault. Her expression was one of practiced skepticism.

If the woman had given Kevin more than a cursory glance, she would have seen a man in his late twenties—about her age—lean and athletic, with dark hair, an unremarkable face, and a habit of tapping his fingers thoughtfully when concentrating.

But likely all she noticed was the locked metal case he carried, secured by a biometric lock to his left wrist.

"Will we be here long?" Kevin asked the conductor. He didn't want to miss his flight. The sooner he got to Highpoint Territory, the sooner he'd deliver the case. The biometric lock was one reason why his interest in the auburn-haired woman had been only passing.

"Can't say," the conductor told him. He let the door close and went down to the tracks.

Kevin hesitated, shrugged at the woman, said, "Excuse me," and followed the conductor. About twenty people were milling around the train as it sat in the dark. Kevin made his way forward and found a larger group gathered ahead of the locomotive.

Some kind of barricade had been erected across the tracks, covered with every imaginable warning device. There were LED flares, reflective barriers, emergency lights, and even an orange safety vest.

Kevin saw two people who must have been the engineer and assistant talking to an older woman wearing a civil defense vest, a long coat, and hiking boots.

"You'd go over the edge, I'm telling you," the older woman was saying.

"If you don't clear this obstruction," the engineer said, "I'll push right through it. Over the edge? Are you serious?"

"See for yourself," the woman in the vest said. "Go ahead. Look."

The engineer was exasperated. She turned to her assistant. "You look. Humor her. Then let's go."

The woman—she introduced herself as Dr. Vanessa Shaw—went off with the assistant. Kevin followed them. They had walked a quarter mile along the gravel when the assistant stopped. "Okay," she said, "where's this edge? I don't see anything." The tracks seemed to stretch endlessly into the darkness.

"It's another half mile or so," Dr. Shaw said.

"Well, let's hurry. We haven't got all night."

The older woman chuckled. "I'm afraid you do."

They came to it at last, stopping well back from it. Dr. Shaw seemed almost proud as she made a theatrical gesture.

"Behold," she said. "The edge of our new world."

True enough, everything seemed to stop, and they could see lights from the ground shining far below where ground should not be visible.

Kevin Mason and the assistant walked cautiously toward the edge while Dr. Shaw strode ahead with the confidence of someone who had been there before. But there was a wind, and they didn't venture too close. Nevertheless, Kevin could see that it was apparently a clean, precise edge, not ragged like something caused by an explosion. This had the feeling of intentional design.

Standing on tiptoe and fighting a wave of vertigo, Kevin looked over the edge. He didn't need to stand on tiptoe any more than he needed to grip the armrest during a tense movie scene, but the situation seemed to demand it. Over the edge, he could see a vast section of the Pearlbrook Region spread out below. At least he assumed it was Pearlbrook—from up here, the entire region was visible, surrounding the void where they had once been connected to it.

Kevin looked at the assistant, who had a stunned expression, then at Dr. Shaw, who was smiling and nodding.

"You see what I mean," she said. "You would have gone right over. I believe it's a three-mile drop back to Pearlbrook below."

"Of course you could have stayed on the train," the man driving the electric sedan said, "but I really think you'll be more comfortable at the Institute."

Kevin Mason, sitting in the back seat with the auburn-haired woman from the observation car, asked, "Institute?"

"The Institute for Advanced Studies. We focus on applied ethics and cultural sociology, though we're not traditionally accredited. What did you say your name was, miss?"

"Sasha Holmes," she said. "I work in international diplomacy."

"Ms. Holmes. I'm Jin Gupta. You know Mr. Mason, I suppose."

The woman smiled slightly. "We've exchanged glances." Kevin nodded and smiled back.

"There's plenty of room in the guest quarters," Jin said. "People don't exactly line up to visit the Institute."

"Are you connected with it?" Kevin asked.

"Me? No. I'm the district administrator. The whole place has really risen in the world, hasn't it?"

"Literally overnight," Sasha Holmes said. "If what Mr. Mason and the train assistant say is true. I haven't seen the edge myself."

"You'll have a better chance to look in the morning," the administrator said, "assuming we don't settle back down in the meantime."

"Was there any kind of explosion?" Kevin asked.

"No. There wasn't any sensation at all, as far as I noticed. I was reviewing some strategic planning documents on my tablet—we're always dealing with community organizing issues here. Well, suddenly my internet connection improved dramatically. Then the phone rang, and it was Dr. Shaw."

"The older woman with the vest and the hiking boots?" Sasha Holmes asked.

"Yes. Vanessa Shaw, Director of the Institute's Applied Physics program."

"Applied Physics?" Kevin asked.

"Among other things. The Institute isn't bound by traditional academic constraints. Well, Dr. Shaw called and said, 'Jin'—that's my name—'we've achieved separation.' She was being cryptic, of course. I said, 'What?' and then she explained."

"Explained what?" Sasha Holmes asked. "I mean, does she have any theory about this?"

"She has theories about everything. I think what she was trying to convey was that this—this levitation—confirmed her gravitational manipulation hypothesis."

"What's that?" Kevin asked.

"I haven't the faintest idea. I'm an administrator, not a physicist. Dr. Shaw went on about it for a while, something about artificial gravity fields and quantum mechanics, but I think she was mainly calling as a courtesy, so I wouldn't look foolish the next morning."

"What's the population here?" Kevin asked.

"Four thousand, including the Institute staff and students. Four thousand and fifty-three, counting you people from the train. I guess you'll be with us for a while."

"What do you mean by that?" Sasha Holmes asked sharply.

"Well, I don't see how you can get down. Do you?"

"Does this district have an airport?" Kevin asked. "I need to get to Highpoint Territory."

"Nope," Jin said. "No airport. No suitable landing area, either."

"Maybe not for planes," Kevin said, "but helicopters could land almost anywhere."

"No helicopters here."

"Maybe not. But I bet they'll be swarming around by morning."

"Hm," said Jin Gupta. Kevin couldn't quite read his expression in the rearview mirror. "I suppose they could. Well, here's the Institute. You go right through that entrance, where the others are going. There's Dr. Shaw. I need to speak with her—excuse me."

The administrator hurried off across the campus. Kevin looked at Sasha Holmes, who was frowning. "Are you thinking," he asked, "that Administrator Gupta was perhaps less than completely forthcoming?"

"I'm thinking," she said, "that I should have stayed at my conference another day and taken a direct flight."

"Where were you headed?" Kevin asked.

"Highpoint Territory. I work with the diplomatic corps." She paused. "What do you do, Mr. Mason?"

"I'm a courier for a tech company. Artificial intelligence prototypes, mostly. Hence the locked case."

"I see," she said, though her tone suggested she wasn't entirely convinced. "We should find somewhere to sleep. It's getting late."

"Agreed," Kevin said. They were met by a middle-aged man who introduced himself as Marco Watson, the Institute's hospitality coordinator. "We'll make you comfortable," he said. "What a night! Dr. Shaw is absolutely thrilled. We haven't had this much excitement since the particle accelerator malfunctioned."

They caught a glimpse of Dr. Shaw, still in her civil defense vest, gesturing animatedly to someone in a lab coat.

Kevin Mason had slept, but not well. He'd tried to maneuver the metal case through his sleeve to remove his jacket, but whatever was inside was too large. The Institute had given him a private room in the guest quarters, and he'd removed his pants but had to sleep in his shirt and jacket. He got up feeling grimy and did what minimal preparation was possible.

It was eight o'clock according to his watch, and activity was evident outside. He had a view of the campus from his window. Bright sun illuminated young people moving generally toward a low building—probably the cafeteria—while others moved in various directions. The air was remarkably clear, and the morning shadows were sharp. Only then did he fully remember that he and the entire district were suspended in the air, three miles above the region below.

He went through the guest quarters. A few people were still sleeping. Others had left their unmade beds. He shivered as he stepped outside. It was cold, though not freezing, and his breath was visible. First he'd eat, he decided, so he'd have energy to examine the edge in daylight and see the ground below.

The dining hall was cafeteria-style, and he got in line with a tray for juice, eggs, and coffee. He saw no one he knew, but as he looked for a table, a slender woman with platinum blonde hair smiled and gestured to the empty seat across from her.

"You're Mr. Mason," she said. "Won't you join me?"

"Thanks," he said, unloading his tray. "How did you know?"

"The mystery man with the locked case. You're hard to miss. I'm Nathan Morris—yes, Nathan, not Natalie. My parents had a sense of humor. Are you with some intelligence agency? Or did you steal something valuable?"

"How do you do. No, just a tech courier. What an unusual name. Dr. Shaw's student?"

"Assistant, actually," she said. "Also her daughter, though we keep that quiet professionally. A pity, because if I'd had a choice, I'd have gone to a normal university. As it is, I'm duty-bound to represent the second generation at the experimental facility."

"Experimental facility? You mean the Institute?" Kevin struggled to manipulate his utensils without knocking things over with his attached case.

"Here, let me help you," Nathan said, cutting his food. "You should order scrambled eggs tomorrow. Yes, the Institute. Home of the unorthodox theory and the controversial experiment."

"I'm sure it's not that bad. Thanks. As for tomorrow, I hope to be gone by then."

"How do you plan to leave? Float down on a parachute?"

"I'll find a way. I'm more interested in how I got up here."

"You were levitated, like everyone else."

"You make it sound deliberate, Ms. Morris, as if someone lifted an entire district for some purpose."

"Well, that's debatable. Have you seen the news feeds?"

"I didn't know there were any."

"Actually, there's just one local outlet. This is a special edition. The editor must have worked all night." She pulled out her phone and showed him a digital edition.

Kevin blinked at the headline: "District Gets High"

"The editor's something of an independent thinker, like most people around here," Nathan said.

Kevin read the story, which seemed to treat the situation with surprising levity despite its gravity.

"Residents planning to travel beyond district boundaries today are advised to reconsider. It's a long way down. Where we were once surrounded by Pearlbrook, today our territory ends literally at the district line.

A Citizens' Emergency Barrier Committee is being organized, but in the meantime, everyone is warned to stay well away from the edge. The laws of physics seem to have been suspended for the district, but it's doubtful the same exemption would apply to a curious individual bent on investigating..."

Kevin skimmed the rest. "I don't see anything about it being deliberate."

Nathan had been preparing Kevin's coffee. She pushed it toward him and said, "It's not on the front page. The editor and Administrator Gupta don't get along, so you'll find the administrator's statement in a box on page three."

Kevin navigated to the page, took a sip of coffee, nodded his thanks, and read:

"Administrator Claims Independence from Ground

Administrator Jin Gupta, in a proclamation issued locally and transmitted to Pearlbrook via drone, announced today that our district has declared independence. His reasons were as vague as his explanation.

The 'reasons' include: (1) we have been neglected by regional and federal agencies; (2) the Institute has been ridiculed by traditional academic institutions; and (3) we have been subject to unfair pollution control regulations that hampered the film production industry.

The 'explanation' consists of a 73-page paper on gravitational field manipulation by Dr. Vanessa Shaw of the Institute, which the editor (a) does not fully understand; (b) lacks space to publish; and which (being highly technical) he (c) cannot adequately summarize for general readers."

Kevin said, "I'm beginning to like this editor."

"He's wonderful," Nathan said. "He's about the only one in town who challenges Mother."

"Does your mother claim that she levitated the whole district off the ground?"

"Not to me. I'm one of those inconveniences, a skeptic. She gave up trying to convince me when I was seventeen. I had a physics professor at a summer program—not at the Institute—who gave me all kinds of difficult questions to ask Mother. I asked them, being naturally contrary, and Mother has considered me intellectually lost ever since."

"How old are you, Ms. Morris, if I may ask?"

She sat up straighter, adjusting her sweater. She had an excellent figure, intelligent eyes, a delicate nose, and expressive lips. She could have been the star of any campus with a more conventional student body.

"You may call me Nathan," she said. "And I'm twenty-two."

Kevin grinned. "Recently?"

"Four months ago. How old are you, Mr. Mason?"

"Kevin's the name I've had for twenty-eight years. Please use it."

"Gladly. And now, Kevin, unless you want more coffee, I'll accompany you to the edge of the world."

"On such short notice?" Kevin was intrigued. Last night the woman from the train had been coolly professional, and this morning a friendly blonde was apparently offering companionship. He wondered briefly where Sasha Holmes was.

"I'll admit to the double meaning," Nathan said. "What I meant—for now—was that we can walk out to where we used to be connected to the rest of Pearlbrook and see how the ground is managing without us."

"I'd like that. But don't you have work to do?"

"Sure. I'm supposed to be analyzing data from yesterday's sensors. But I'm an expert procrastinator, which is why I'm still finishing my graduate work at my advanced age. On to the edge!"

They walked south from the campus and came to the train tracks. The train was still there, going nowhere. It had been abandoned except for the conductor, who had dutifully remained aboard overnight.

"What's happening?" he asked when he saw them. "Any word from Pearlbrook below?"

"Not that I know of," Kevin said. He introduced Nathan Morris. "What are you going to do?"

"What can I do?" the conductor asked.

"You can go to the Institute and have breakfast," Nathan said. "Nobody's going to bother your train."

The conductor decided that sounded reasonable and left.

"You know," Kevin said, "before the train stopped last night, I thought I saw a stream running alongside the tracks."

"Clearwater Stream," Nathan said. "That's right. It's just over there."

"Is it still there? Hasn't it all poured off the edge by now? Was that our water supply?"

Nathan shrugged. "All I know is the water still works. Let's check the stream."

They found it flowing normally between its banks.

"Looks the same," she said.

"That's strange. Come on, let's follow it to the edge."

The edge, as Nathan called it, looked even more dramatic in daylight. Everything simply stopped. There was a residential area with houses and yards, then nothing. There was Clearwater Stream flowing along, then nothing. In the distance, a grove of trees simply ended.

"Where is the water going?" Kevin asked. "I can't tell."

"Down to the region below, presumably. Rain for the people down there."

"But it should be drained by now. I'm going to look."

"Don't! You'll fall!"

"I'll be careful." He walked cautiously toward the edge. Nathan followed, a few feet behind. He stopped a yard from the brink and waited for vertigo to pass. The Pearlbrook Region was spread out like a satellite image, far below. Kevin took another careful step, then sat down.

"Careful," said Nathan. She laughed nervously, then sat down too.

"I still can't see where the water goes," Kevin said. He lay flat on his stomach and began to inch forward. "You stay there."

Finally, he inched to a point where, by stretching, he could almost reach the edge. He gave another push forward and his right hand closed over the brink. For a moment he lay there, breathing hard, head pressed to the ground.

"How do you feel?" Nathan asked.

"Terrified. When I get my nerve back, I'll lift my head and look."

Nathan reached out tentatively, then firmly grasped his ankle. "Just in case of wind," she said.

"Thanks. That helps. Okay, here goes." He lifted his head. "Damn."

"What?"

"It's still not clear. Do you have a mirror?"

"I have a compact." She took it from her bag with her free hand and tossed it to him. It rolled and Kevin had to grab to keep it from going over. Nathan gasped. Kevin was momentarily shaken and had to put his head back down. "Sorry," she said.

Kevin opened the compact and carefully transferred it to his right hand. He held it out beyond the edge and peered into it, focusing on the end of the stream. "Now I see it. The water isn't going off the edge!"

"It isn't? Then where?"

"Down, yes, but it's as if it's going into a vertical shaft, just short of the edge."

"Why? How?"

"I can't see clearly, but that's what it looks like. Hold on. I'm coming back." He inched away from the edge, then stood and brushed himself off. He returned her compact. "I think we need to check the other end of the stream."

"The source?"

"Exactly."

Clearwater Stream didn't cut through the center of the district but flowed in an arc through the southern part. They had about two miles to walk, past Clearwater Bridge—which used to connect to the surrounding region, Nathan said—past the Recreation Center, and on to the edge again.

But as they approached what should be the source of the stream, they found a chain-link fence blocking the area. "This is new," Nathan said.

The fence, which had a sign on it reading "WARNING—ELECTRIFIED," was semicircular, with each end at the edge, and tarps hung behind it so they couldn't see the mouth of the stream. The water flowed from under the tarp and fence.

"Look how it comes in pulses," Nathan said.

"As if it's being pumped."

Kevin studied the warning sign more carefully. Smaller text below the main warning read: "Protecting water source infrastructure. Electrical charge sufficient to cause serious injury."

"What's the other water source?" Kevin asked.

"North Reservoir, probably," Nathan said. "It's used for the water treatment facility."

"Is the reservoir entirely within the district boundaries?"

"I don't know."

"If it were on the edge, and if someone took a boat out on it, I wonder what would happen?"

"I know one thing—I wouldn't be there holding your ankle while you found out."

She took his arm as they gazed past the electrified fence at the surrounding region below and to the west.

"It's impressive, isn't it?" she said. "I wonder if that's Magnolia Province way over there?"

He patted her hand absent-mindedly. "I wonder if it's west at all. I mean, how do we know we're maintaining the same orientation as before?"

"We could tell by the sun, silly."

"Of course," he said, grinning. "And I guess we're not high enough to see very far. If we were, we'd be able to see the mountain ranges."

They were contemplating the geography when a plane emerged from a cloud layer and, a moment later, veered sharply. They could make out commercial airline markings on the fuselage. As it turned, they imagined they could see faces at the windows. They waved and thought they saw people wave back. Then the plane climbed eastward and disappeared.

"Well," Kevin said as they turned back toward the Institute, "now we know they know. Maybe we'll start getting some answers. Or, if not answers, then rescue."

"Rescue?" Nathan squeezed the arm she was holding. "Why? You'd rather be down there in Pearlbrook than up here with me?"

"If you mean don't I like you, the answer is yes, I do. But if I don't get out of this biometric lock soon so I can shower and change clothes, you're not going to like me."

"You're still quite presentable, if a bit scruffy." She stopped, still holding his arm, and he turned so they were face to face. "So kiss me," she said, "before you get any worse."

They were in the middle of an extremely pleasant kiss when the metal case at the end of Kevin's biometric lock began to emit a high-pitched alarm.

Later that evening, after the alarm had been silenced and Kevin had been questioned extensively by Marco Watson about the case's contents, he found himself alone in the Institute's small library. He had been searching for maps of the region, hoping to understand exactly where the district boundaries lay.

In a dusty corner, he discovered a shelf of bound municipal records. He pulled out a volume labeled "District Charter and Founding Documents" and began leafing through it.

The opening page featured an ornate certificate with an elaborate border and several official seals. The date was 1952, and signatures of the original trustees filled the bottom half of the page. Much of the text was faded, but Kevin could make out references to "the Pearlbrook Region" and "independent governance."

Kevin kept reading. A section on "District Boundaries" included surveyor's notes describing the perimeter in relation to the surrounding Pearlbrook townships. The notes referenced landmarks: "northern boundary at the ridge crest," "southern boundary at Pearl Creek," "eastern boundary following the old logging road."

He turned to a chapter on public utilities. The founding documents established municipal services to manage water, electricity, and waste removal. A footnote explained that all municipal equipment would bear the district seal and identification marks.

A collection of old photographs lined one wall of the library. Kevin studied them—founding members of the Institute, dedication ceremonies, early construction. One showed a group standing before a stone marker at what appeared to be the district's main entrance. The marker's inscription was too small to read in the photograph, but Kevin could see it featured the same tree-and-ridge symbol he'd noticed on various buildings.

He pulled out his phone and searched through the cached version of the local newspaper he'd read that morning. In the classified section, buried among notices for lost pets and furniture sales, he found an advertisement: "Historical Society Annual Meeting, Thursday 7 PM at the Community Center. This year's topic: 'Our Unique Identity Within Greater Pearlbrook.'"

Through the window, he could see the lights of the small downtown area—four thousand people, the administrator had said, now suspended three miles above the region they had once called home. Four thousand people who, if the administrator's proclamation was to be believed, had no intention of returning to their place within Pearlbrook.

Kevin wondered how many of them had chosen this. How many had even known it was coming.

The next morning, Kevin walked through the downtown area before breakfast, wanting to see more of the community whose fate he now shared. The main street was lined with small shops and businesses, most displaying a consistent visual identity—a stylized oak tree with roots extending downward into a ridge-like formation.

He passed a coffee shop called "Ridge Roasters" and a bookstore with "Oak & Page" on its awning. A real estate office had a faded sign in the window: "Welcome to Our Ridge-Top Community."

At the corner, a bronze plaque mounted on a lamppost caught his attention. It commemorated the district's founding and included a brief history: the area had been carved out of Pearlbrook in 1952, established by a group of academics and entrepreneurs who wanted to create an independent research community. Kevin noted how the plaque repeatedly emphasized the district's separation from "the surrounding Pearlbrook townships."

Kevin made his way to the public library next, a small building near the town square. The librarian, an elderly woman with reading glasses perched on her nose, looked up as he entered.

"You're one of the train passengers," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Kevin Mason. I'm trying to learn more about where I've ended up."

"Temporarily ended up, I hope. For your sake, anyway. Some of us chose to live here. I'm Margaret Chen—I've been the librarian for thirty years." She gestured at the shelves around her. "What would you like to know?"

"The basics, I suppose. When was this place established? How did it come to be separate from the rest of Pearlbrook?"

Margaret smiled and pulled out a worn pamphlet. "We published this for our fiftieth anniversary. Take it—we have boxes of them." The cover showed the familiar oak-and-ridge emblem.

Kevin flipped through it. The pamphlet's text was careful to always distinguish "our district" from "the Pearlbrook Region," but he noticed the actual district name appeared only in abbreviated form throughout—"O.R. District"—as if the full name were so well-known to residents that spelling it out would be redundant.

"A common misconception among outsiders," Margaret continued, "is that we're part of Pearlbrook. We've always been separate—administratively, at least. The district was incorporated in 1952 as an independent entity. The founders wanted autonomy for their research institute without interference from regional politics."

"But you're surrounded by Pearlbrook on all sides. Or you were."

"Geography and governance aren't the same thing. We've always been our own district, with our own administration, our own utilities. Pearlbrook is just what surrounds us. Or surrounded us, I suppose I should say now."

Kevin thanked her and wandered through the stacks. In the local history section, he found a slim volume with a water-damaged cover. The title was partially obscured, but he could read "...History of Our Independent District: 1952-2000." The author was listed as a former Institute professor.

He skimmed the introduction, which described the founders' vision of creating a self-governing research community that could operate independently of regional bureaucracy. The second chapter discussed the naming of the district, but the key pages had suffered water damage and were illegible. What Kevin could read mentioned "the prominent geological feature along the northern boundary" and "the dominant tree species of the original forest."

On his way back to the Institute, Kevin passed the town hall. A bronze seal was mounted beside the entrance, showing the same oak-and-ridge design he'd seen throughout town. The seal's outer ring contained text, but decades of weather had worn the lettering smooth in places. He could make out "...ISTRICT OF..." and what might have been "...ARLBROOK REGION" beneath it—or possibly "...RIDGE" followed by something else. The corrosion made it impossible to be certain.

He was still thinking about what he'd learned when he encountered Sasha Holmes outside the Institute's main building.

"Mr. Mason," she said. "You've been exploring."

"Getting my bearings. Have you?"

"In a manner of speaking. I've been monitoring communications with the ground." She paused. "The regional authorities in Pearlbrook are demanding our return. They're calling it an act of terrorism."

"Interesting phrasing—'our return.' As if we belong to them."

"Mm. The administrator disagrees. He says the district has exercised its right to self-determination. He keeps emphasizing that this area was never actually part of Pearlbrook—just surrounded by it."

"Does a district have that right? To simply... leave?"

Sasha's expression was unreadable. "That's a question for diplomats and lawyers. What I can tell you is that Washington is taking this seriously. They've scrambled aircraft and are establishing a no-fly zone around us."

"Around us? We're three miles up. That's quite a zone."

"Indeed." She studied him for a moment. "You seem to have learned something on your walk. Care to share?"

Kevin considered. "Just that there's a lot of local pride here about not being Pearlbrook. Every sign, every emblem—it all emphasizes the distinction. But I still haven't figured out what this place is actually called. Everyone just says 'the district' or 'our community.'"

"The locals know what they call it. They don't need to keep reminding each other."

"True. The pamphlets use 'O.R. District.' I assume that stands for something."

Sasha nodded slowly. "The news broadcasts from below keep referring to 'the missing Pearlbrook district.' The Pearlbrook authorities seem to consider this area part of their region."

"But the residents here disagree. Strongly, apparently."

"Strong enough to levitate three miles into the air to make the point."

"Perhaps we should find out together," Kevin said. "What this place is actually called, I mean. And whether anyone here besides Dr. Shaw knew this was coming."

Sasha offered a slight smile. "After breakfast?"

Kevin nodded, and they walked toward the dining hall. Behind them, the broadcast tower that Captain Spencer had spotted from his aircraft blinked its red warning lights against the morning sky, marking the position of the floating district for any aircraft that might approach.

And far below, in the void where the district had once rested, the residents of Pearlbrook looked up at the impossible sight and argued about what to call the thing that had left them behind.
quality_problem.story_title: And Then the Town Took Off
quality_problem.question: What was the name of the district that vanished?

THE STRATEGIC PARADIGM
BY COLONEL ADRIAN PARSONS (RET.)

There was a general in our forces, and he was wondrous wise;
He charged into a minefield and lost both of his eyes.
And when he saw what he had done, with all his might and main
He charged into another field and got them back again.
MILITARY FOLK SAYING

Colonel Stephen Porter found Captain Benjamin Anderson and the lieutenant waiting in his office when he arrived at the Queenstown Strategic Command Center that morning. Anderson looked as though he'd been up all night reviewing intelligence reports. There were dark circles under his eyes; his usually crisp uniform seemed rumpled at every seam. Porter glanced sharply at his Intelligence Director and sank down behind his desk with a sigh. "All right, Ben—what's wrong?"

"This lieutenant is driving me crazy," said Anderson through clenched teeth. "He's gone completely off the reservation. Nobody's been able to work with him for three weeks, and now at six o'clock this morning he decides he's resigning his commission. I talk to him, I reason with him, I do everything but lock him in the barracks, and I waste my time. He's resigning. Period."

"So you bring him down here," said Porter sourly. "The worst place he could be, if something's really wrong." He looked across at the young officer. "Lieutenant Russell? Come over and sit down."

There was nothing singular about the lieutenant's appearance. He was thin, with a pale face and the earnest expression of any normal twenty-five-year-old officer as he blinked across the desk at Porter. The standard tactical headset rested on the desk beside him. He sat with a mute appeal in his dark eyes as Porter flipped the analysis-switch and blinked in alarm at the wildly fluctuating pattern on the screen.

The lieutenant was in crisis. He was literally pulsating with professional doubt.

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me about it, Matthew," he said gently.

"I don't want to go back to Crestwood Base," said the lieutenant.

"Why?"

"I just don't. I can't function there."

"Are you frightened?"

The lieutenant bit his lip and nodded slowly.

"Of me? Of Captain Anderson?"

"No. Oh, no!"

"Then what?"

Again the mute appeal in the lieutenant's eyes. He groped for words, and none came. Finally he said, "If I could only take this off—" He touched the tactical headset.

"You think that would make you feel better?"

"It would, I know it would."

Porter shook his head. "I don't think so, Matthew. You know what the headset is for, don't you?"

"It filters incoming strategic data."

"That's right. And it filters your analytical outputs. It's a regulator. You need it badly. It would hurt you a great deal if you operated without it, away from the controlled environment."

The lieutenant fought back his frustration. "But I don't want to go back there—" The crisis-pattern was alive again on the screen. "I don't feel effective there. I never want to go back."

"Well, we'll see. You can stay here for a while." Porter nodded at Anderson and stepped into an adjoining room with him. "You say this has been going on for three weeks?"

"I'm afraid so. We thought it was just a temporary pattern—we see so much of that at Crestwood. Usually officers work through these phases on their own. The structured environment there, the regular duties and training exercises—they provide stability. Most recover within days."

"But not Matthew."

"No. His case is different. The question is what to do with him now."

Porter chewed his lip. "I don't like it. We'd better set up a full evaluation on him and try to spot the trouble. And I'm afraid you'll have to handle the arrangements. I've got that young Dr. Parsons from Horizonville to deal with this morning—the one who's threatening to upset the whole Strategic Conference next month with some radical theories he's been developing. I'll probably have to take him out to Crestwood to address his concerns." Porter ran a hand through sparse grey hair. "As for Matthew—he needs to be kept separate from normal operations. No contact with senior staff. No participation in standard training rotations. Nothing that would expose him to command hierarchy."

Anderson frowned. "Complete removal from the regular schedule?"

"Complete removal from everything, Ben. Set it up downstairs. Total restriction—no briefings, no tactical exercises, no group work. Just evaluation protocols in a controlled space." Porter's voice hardened. "And in this case, be absolutely certain of it. If Matthew's in the trouble I think he's in, we don't dare risk unfiltered command exposure now. Keep all senior personnel away from him. We could end up with a broken officer on our hands."

Anderson nodded slowly. "I'll arrange for a private evaluation room. Restricted access. Only the monitoring equipment and essential staff."

"Good. Now I need to prepare for our visitor."

Two letters were waiting on Porter's desk that morning. The first was from Strategic Publications, announcing another shift of deadline on the monograph, and demanding the final proofs two weeks earlier than scheduled. Porter groaned. As director of strategic doctrine at the Queenstown Command Center, he had long since learned how administrative detail could consume operational hours. He knew that his real work was at Crestwood—yet he hadn't even been to Crestwood in over six weeks. And now, as the monograph approached publication date, Porter wondered if he would ever really get back to work again.

The other letter cheered him a bit more. It bore the letterhead of the International Strategic Doctrine Conference:

Dear Colonel Porter:

In recognition of your position as an authority on military decision-making patterns under stress conditions, we would be gratified to schedule you as principle speaker at the Conference in Horizonville on October 12th. A few remarks in discussion of your forthcoming monograph would be entirely in order—

They were waiting for it, then! He ran the final proofs into the scanner excitedly. They knew he had something revolutionary to propose. His earlier papers had only hinted at the direction he was going—but the monograph would clear away the confusion. He scanned the title page proudly. "A Theory of Command Influence on Junior Officer Development and Decision-Making Capacity." A good title—concise, commanding, yet modest. They would read it, all right. And they would find it a light shining brightly in the darkness, a guide to the commanders who were floundering in the jungle of a strange and baffling new doctrine.

For they were floundering. When modern warfare finally forced them to recognize that traditional hierarchical command structures were failing in complex operational environments, they had plunged eagerly into reform, and found themselves in a maddening bramble bush of contradictions and chaos. Nothing worked, and everything worked too well. They were trying to study phenomena which made no sense, observing things that defied classical military theory. Established doctrines came crashing down about their ears as they stood sadly by and watched outcomes that traditional doctrine said could never happen. They had never been in this terrain before, nor in any terrain remotely like it. The old rules didn't work here, the old methods of command failed. And the more they struggled, the thicker and more impenetrable the bramble bush became—

But now Stephen Porter had discovered a pathway through that jungle, a theory to work by—

At his elbow the intercom buzzed. "A gentleman to see you," the aide said. "A Dr. Adrian Parsons. He's very impatient, sir."

He shut off the scanner and said, "Send him in, please."

Dr. Adrian Parsons was tall and thin, with jet black hair and dark mocking eyes. He wore a threadbare academic jacket and carried himself with casual arrogance. He offered Porter a bony hand, then flung himself into a chair as he stared about the office with barely concealed contempt.

"I'm really overwhelmed," he said after a moment. "Within the stronghold of strategic doctrine at last. And face to face with the Master in the trembling flesh!"

Porter frowned. "Dr. Parsons, I don't quite understand—"

"Oh, it's just that I'm impressed," the young man said airily. "Of course, I've seen old dried-up Authorities before—but never before a brand spanking new one, just fresh out of the academy, so to speak!" He touched his forehead in a gesture of mock reverence. "I bow before the Oracle. Speak, oh Colonel, live forever! Cast a pearl at my feet!"

"If you've come here to be insulting," Porter said coldly, "you're just wasting time." He reached for the intercom switch.

"I think you'd better wait before you do that," Parsons said sharply, "because I'm planning to take you apart at the Conference next month unless I like everything I see and hear down here today. And if you don't think I can do it, you're in for quite a shock."

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me—just what, exactly, do you want?"

"I want to hear this fairy tale you're about to publish in the name of 'Theory'," Parsons said. "I want to see this famous Crestwood facility of yours and see for myself how much pressure these experimental controls you keep talking about will actually bear.
