But mostly, I want to see just what in strategic hell you're so busy making yourself an Authority about." There was no laughter in the man's sharp brown eyes.

"You couldn't touch me with a ten foot pole at this conference," snapped Porter.

The other man grinned. "Try me! We shook you up a little bit last year, but you didn't seem to get the idea."

"Last year was different." Porter scowled. "As for our 'fairy tale', we happen to have a staggering body of evidence that says that it's true."

"If the papers you've already published are a preview, we think it's false as hell."

"And our controls are above suspicion."

"So far, we haven't found any way to set up logical controls in this field," said Parsons. "We've done a lot of work on it, too."

"Oh, yes—I've heard about your work. Not bad, really. A little misdirected, is all."

"According to your Theory, that is."

"Wildly unorthodox approach to strategic doctrine—but at least you're energetic enough."

"We haven't been energetic enough to find an orthodox approach that got us anywhere. We doubt if you have, either. But maybe we're all wrong." Parsons grinned unpleasantly. "We're not unreasonable, Colonel. We just ask to be shown. If you dare, that is."

Porter slammed his fist down on the desk angrily. "Have you got the day to take a trip?"

"I've got 'til New Year."

Porter shouted for his aide. "Get Anderson up here. We're going to Crestwood this afternoon."

The aide nodded, then hesitated. "But what about your lunch meeting with the General Staff?"

"Cancel it." He gave Parsons a sidelong glare. "We've got a guest here who's got a lot of words he's going to eat for us...."

Before they left, Porter checked with Anderson about the arrangements for Lieutenant Russell.

"Everything's set up," Anderson reported. "Evaluation room on the lower level. Sealed environment."

"And you've restricted all contact?"

"No one goes in except essential monitoring personnel. He's separated from all regular activities." Anderson paused. "Colonel, some of the staff questioned the approach. They pointed out that Crestwood's normal therapeutic environment has helped dozens of officers recover from similar crises. The regular schedule there—training exercises, collaborative work, structured duties—these things give troubled officers a sense of purpose. Several staff members suggested that returning Matthew to that routine might actually help stabilize him."

Porter shook his head firmly. "Not this case. The normal approach won't work here. Matthew needs complete separation—no duties, no exercises, no exposure to command structure at all. That's what I've ordered, and that's what we'll do."

"Understood. The restricted evaluation is in place."

Ten minutes later they boarded the military transport helicopter on the roof of the Queenstown Command Center. They sat in silence as the aircraft lifted off and headed northeast, skimming over the countryside toward Crestwood. The landscape below shifted from urban sprawl to rolling hills dotted with military installations. In less than forty minutes the helicopter was descending toward a sprawling complex of low buildings surrounded by high security fences.

"What's the status on Russell?" Porter asked Anderson as the helicopter settled onto the landing pad.

"He's secure in the evaluation room. Complete restriction from all regular operations."

Porter ground his teeth. "I should be monitoring his evaluation now instead of beating the bushes with this—" He broke off to glare at young Parsons.

Parsons grinned. "I've heard you have quite a facility up here."

"It's—unconventional, at any rate," Porter snapped.

"Well, that depends on your standards. Sounds like a military academy, from what I've heard. According to your papers, you've even used conventional statistical analysis on your data from up here."

"Until we had to throw it out. We discovered that what we were trying to measure didn't make sense in a statistical analysis."

"Of course, you're sure you were measuring something."

"Oh, yes. We certainly were."

"Yet you said that you didn't know what."

"That's right," said Porter. "We don't."

"And you don't know why your instruments measure whatever they're measuring." Parsons's face was thoughtful. "In fact, you can't really be certain that your instruments are measuring the officers at all. It's not inconceivable that the officers might be affecting the instruments, eh?"

Porter blinked. "It's conceivable."

"Mmmm," said Parsons. "Sounds like a real firm foundation to build a theory on."

"Why not?" Porter growled. "It wouldn't be the first time we had to reconsider our assumptions. The psychologists never would have gotten out of their rut if somebody hadn't gotten smart and realized that institutional reform sometimes requires turning the whole system on its head. That was quite a wall to climb."

"Yes, wasn't it," mused Parsons, scratching his bony jaw. "Only took them seventy years to climb it, thanks to a certain man's theories. I wonder how long it'll take military doctrine to crawl out of the pit you're digging for it?"

"We're not digging any pit," Porter exploded angrily. "We're exploring—nothing more. A phenomenon exists. We've known that, one way or another, for centuries. The fact that it doesn't seem to be bound by the same sort of traditional military logic we've observed elsewhere doesn't mean that it isn't governed by principles. But how can we define those principles? How can we define the limits of the phenomenon, for that matter? We can't work in the dark forever—we've got to have a working hypothesis to guide us."

"So you dreamed up this 'erosion' idea," said Parsons sourly.

"For a working hypothesis—yes. We've known for a long time that every junior officer has exceptional strategic potential to one degree or another. Not just a few here and there—every single one. It's a differentiating quality of effective military leadership. Just as the ability to think creatively in a crisis instead of falling back on doctrine is a differentiating quality."

"Fine," said Parsons. "Great. We can't prove that, of course, but I'll play along."

Porter glared at him. "When we began studying this strategic potential, we found out some curious things. For one thing, it seemed to be immensely more powerful and active in junior officers than in senior commanders. Somewhere along the line as an officer advances, something happens. We don't know what. We do know that the officer's strategic creativity gradually withdraws deeper and deeper into their decision-making process, burying itself farther and farther out of reach, just the way geological strata are buried deeper and deeper by accumulated sediment until the original formations are completely obscured." Porter paused, lighting his pipe. "That's why we have Crestwood—to try to discover why. What forces that potential underground? What buries it so deeply that senior officers can't access it anymore?"

"And you think you have an answer," said Parsons.

"We think we might be near an answer. We have a theory that explains the available data."

The transport vehicle stopped sharply as it left the main road. Anderson took the controls. In a few moments they were passing through the high gates of Crestwood, slowing down at the entrance to a long, low building.

"All right, young man—come along," said Porter. "I think we can show you our answer."

In the main administration building they donned the standard command filters required of all senior personnel at Crestwood. They were of a hard grey composite material, with a network of circuitry embedded in the substance, connected to a simple pocket-sized processor.

"The major problem," Porter said, "has been to shield the junior officers from any external command pressure, except those we wished to expose them to. Our goal is a perfectly controlled command environment. The filters are quite effective—a simple signal dampening system."

"It blocks off all types of command influence?" asked Parsons.

"As far as we can measure, yes."

"Which may not be very far."

Benjamin Anderson burst in: "What Colonel Porter is saying is that they seem effective for our purposes."

"But you don't know why," added Parsons.

"All right, we don't know why. Nobody knows why a dampening system works at the neurological level—why blame us?" They were walking down the main corridor and out through an open courtyard. Behind the buildings was a broad training field. A tactical exercise was in progress in one corner; across the field a group of obstacle courses, climbing walls, and other training equipment was in heavy use. The place was teeming with young officers, all engaged in intense activity. Occasionally a filtered supervisor hurried by; one waved to them as she corrected a lieutenant's form on the rappelling wall.

Anderson gestured toward the active training grounds. "This is what we do here, day in and day out. Officers on regular duty rotations, following structured schedules, participating in exercises and collaborative work. The therapeutic value of routine cannot be overstated—troubled officers often recover simply by immersing themselves in the normal activities."

They crossed into the next building, where strategy sessions were in progress. "Some of our officers are here only briefly," Porter explained as they walked along, "and some have been here for years. We maintain a top-ranking curriculum—your idea of a 'military academy' wasn't so far afield at that—with positions funded by Command Center resources. Other officers come to us—transfers, volunteers, officers from troubled units, officers of all ranks from second lieutenant on. Sometimes they stay until they have reached field grade, or go on to commands. As far as strategic doctrine research is concerned, we are not trying to be commanders. We are strictly observers. We try to place the officers in positions where they can develop what potential they have—without the presence of external command influences they would normally be subject to. The results have been remarkable."

He led them into a long, narrow room with chairs and monitors, facing a wide observation window. The room fell into semi-darkness, and through the window they could see three lieutenants, about two years out of the academy, working on a tactical problem in a large room.

"They're perfectly isolated from us," said Porter. "A variety of recording instruments are working. And before you ask, Dr. Parsons, they are all empirical instruments, and they would all defy any engineer's attempts to determine precisely what makes them work. We don't know exactly what makes them work, and we don't care—they work. That's all we need. Like that one, for instance—"

In the corner a flat screen was displaying a complex tactical map with shifting colored zones. It hung from the wall by two data cables which penetrated into the officers' room. There was no visible input device, nor an obvious control system. As the officers moved about and discussed strategy, the map shifted and evolved. Below it, a recording device clicked along in little spurts and starts of activity.

"What are they doing?" Parsons asked after watching the officers a few moments.

"Those three seem to work as a team, somehow. Each one, individually, had a fairly constant recordable strategic potential of about seventeen on the arbitrary scale we find useful here. Any two of them scale in at thirty-four to thirty-six. Put the three together and they operate somewhere in the neighborhood of six hundred on the same scale." Porter smiled. "This is an isolated phenomenon—it doesn't hold for any other three officers at Crestwood. Nor did we make any effort to place them together—they sought each other out naturally. One of our analysts spent two weeks trying to find out why the instruments weren't calibrated correctly. It wasn't the instruments, of course."

Porter nodded to an attendant, and peered around at Parsons. "Now, I want you to watch this very closely."

He opened a door and walked into the room with the officers. The tactical display continued to shift as the officers turned to Porter. He examined the strategic solution they were developing, and stopped to discuss it with them, his words audible through the observation room speakers. The officers engaged enthusiastically, apparently intrigued by the refinement he was proposing. He walked to the display and tapped a key sector with his finger.

The map quivered, and the display blazed with activity, but the solution held. Carefully Porter questioned all the foundational assumptions until the entire strategy hung on pure creative thinking, clearly unsupported by traditional doctrine. The officers watched it closely, and the assumptions shifted even further from convention....

Then, quite casually, Porter removed his command filter. The officers continued analyzing the strategy as the display gave three or four violent bursts of chaotic data and went dark.

The tactical solution collapsed entirely.

Moments later Porter was back in the observation room, leaving the officers busily reconstructing their approach. There was a little smile on his lips as he saw Parsons's face. "Perhaps you're beginning to see what I'm driving at," he said slowly.

"Yes," said Parsons. "I think I'm beginning to see." He scratched his jaw. "You think that it's senior command contact that drives the junior officer's potential underground—that somehow senior contact acts like a damper, a sort of colossal creativity-snuffer."

"That's what I think," said Porter.

"How do you know those officers didn't make you remove your filter?"

Porter blinked. "Why should they?"

"Maybe they wanted to see what would happen to their solution."

"But that wouldn't make any difference, would it? The solution still collapses."

Parsons paced down the narrow room. "This is very good," he said suddenly, his voice earnest. "You have fine facilities here, good personnel. And in spite of my flippancy, Colonel Porter, I have never imagined for a moment that you were not an acute observer and a careful, highly imaginative analyst. But suppose I told you, in perfect faith, that we have data that flatly contradicts everything you've told me today. Reproducible data, utterly incompatible with yours. What would you say to that?"

"I'd say you were wrong," said Porter. "You couldn't have such data. According to the things I am certain are true, what you're saying is sheer nonsense."

"And you'd express that opinion in a professional conference?"

"I would."

"And as an Authority on strategic doctrine," said Parsons slowly, "you would kill us then and there. You would strangle us professionally, discredit anything we did, cut us off cold." The tall man turned on him fiercely. "Are you blind, man? Can't you see what danger you're in? If you publish your monograph now, you will become an Authority in a field where the most devastating thing that could possibly happen would be—the appearance of an Authority."

Porter and Anderson rode back to the Queenstown Command Center in grim silence. At first Porter pretended to work; finally he snapped off the data reader in disgust and stared out the transport window. Parsons had gone on to the airfield to catch a flight back to Horizonville. It was a relief to see him go, Porter thought, and tried to force the thin, angry man firmly out of his mind. But somehow Parsons wouldn't leave.

"Stop worrying about it," Anderson urged. "He's a radical. He's crawled way out on a limb, and now he's afraid your theory is going to cut it off under him. Well, that's his worry, not yours." Anderson's face was intense. "Professionally, you're on unshakeable ground. Every great researcher has people like Parsons sniping at him. You just have to ignore them and keep going."

Porter shook his head. "Maybe. But this field of work is different from any other, Ben. It doesn't follow the rules. Maybe professional grounds aren't right at all, in this case."

Anderson snorted. "Surely there's nothing wrong with theorizing—"

"He wasn't objecting to the theory. He's afraid of what happens after the theory."

"So it seems. But why?"

"Have you ever considered what makes a man an Authority?"

"He knows more about his field than anybody else does."

"He seems to, you mean. And therefore, anything he says about it carries more weight than what anybody else says. Other researchers follow his lead. He develops ideas, formulates theories—and then defends them for all he's worth."

"But why shouldn't he?"

"Because a man can't fight for his life and reputation and still keep his objectivity," said Porter. "And what if he just happens to be wrong? Once he's an Authority the question of what's right and what's wrong gets lost in the shuffle. It's what he says that counts."

"But we know you're right," Anderson protested.

"Do we?"

"Of course we do! Look at our work! Look at what we've seen at Crestwood."

"Yes, I know." Porter's voice was weary. "But first I think we'd better check on Matthew Russell—"

An aide greeted them as they stepped off the elevator. "We called you at Crestwood, but you'd already left. The lieutenant—" She broke off helplessly. "He's in crisis, Colonel. He's worse than we ever imagined."

"What happened?"

"Nothing exactly—happened. I don't quite know how to describe it." She hurried them down the corridor and opened a door into the restricted evaluation room. "See what you think."

The lieutenant sat rigidly in the corner of the room. He looked up as they came in, but there was no flicker of recognition or relief on his pale face. The command filter was still in place. He just sat there, gripping a tactical manual tightly in his hands. The room was bare except for monitoring equipment—no training materials, no exercise apparatus, nothing that resembled the busy activity they had witnessed at Crestwood.

Porter crossed the room swiftly. "Matthew," he said.

The lieutenant didn't even look at him. He stared fixedly at the manual.

"Matthew!" Porter reached out for the book. The lieutenant drew back in alarm, clutching it to his chest. "Go away," he choked. "Go away, go away—" When Porter persisted the lieutenant jerked away violently.

Porter sat down at the table. "Matthew, listen to me." His voice was gentle. "I won't try to take it again. I promise."

"Go away."

"Do you know who I am?"

Russell's eyes shifted haltingly to Porter's face. He nodded. "Go away."

"Why are you afraid, Matthew?"

"I can't think. My head is clouded. I can't function. Go away."

"Why can't you think?"

"I—can't get it—off," the lieutenant said.

The filter, Porter thought suddenly. Something had suddenly gone horribly wrong—could the officer really be sensing the source of the trouble? Porter felt a cold knot gather in the pit of his stomach. He knew what happened when unfiltered senior command pressure struck a high-potential junior officer's mind. He had seen it a hundred times at Crestwood. But even more—he had felt it in his own experience, the weight of it. Like a violent physical constraint, the rigidity and fear and hierarchy and control buried and institutionalized in the senior command mind, crushing suddenly into the raw creativity of the junior officer's thinking like a smothering fog—it was a fearful thing. A healthy officer could survive it, even though the scar remained. But this officer was in crisis—

And yet an organism instinctively seeks its own healing. With trembling fingers Porter reached out and opened the release-catch on the filter. "Take it off, Matthew," he whispered.

The lieutenant blinked in amazement, and pulled the grey device from his head. Porter felt the familiar subtle shift in the room's atmosphere as the lieutenant stared at him. He could sense in his own awareness the cold chill of professional doubt radiating from the young officer. Then, suddenly, it began to fade. A sense of clarity—confidence and purpose and creative energy—swept in as the fear faded from the lieutenant's face.

The tactical manual fell to the floor.

They analyzed the data later, processing the evaluation files with greatest care, running them through the systems for the basic analysis and classification that all their data underwent. It was late that night when they had the report back in their hands.

Anderson stared at it angrily. "It's obviously wrong," he grated. "It doesn't fit. Stephen, it doesn't agree with anything we've observed before. There must be an error."

"Of course," said Porter. "According to the theory. The theory says that senior command contact is deadly to the developing junior officer. It smothers their potential through repeated contact until it atrophies completely. We've proved that, haven't we? Time after time. Everything goes according to the theory—except Matthew. But Matthew's strategic potential was atrophying in that restricted environment, until the distortion was threatening the balance of his professional capacity. Then he made a senior contact, and we saw how he recovered." Porter sank down to his desk wearily. "What are we going to do, Ben? Formulate a separate theory for Matthew?"

"Of course not," said Anderson. "The instruments were wrong. Somehow we misread the data—"

"Didn't you see his face?" Porter burst out. "Didn't you see how he responded? What do you want with an instrument reading?" He shook his head. "It's no good, Ben. Something different happened here, something we'd never counted on. It's something the theory just doesn't allow for."

They sat silently for a while. Then Anderson said: "What are you going to do?"

"I don't know," said Porter. "Maybe when we fell into this bramble bush we blinded ourselves with the urge to systematize—to line everything up in neat categories like pins in a display. Maybe we were so focused on systems thinking we missed the actual dynamics altogether."

"But the monograph is due! The Conference speech—"

"I think we'll make some changes in the monograph," Porter said slowly. "It'll be costly—but it might even be liberating. It's a pretty rigid, authoritarian presentation of ideas, as it stands. Very definitive and commanding. But a few revisions could change all that—" He rubbed his hands together thoughtfully. "How about it, Ben? Do we have nerve enough to be questioned? Do you think we could stand a little professional uncertainty, admitting we might be wrong? Because when I finish this monograph, we'll be challenged from every direction. There won't be any Authority in strategic doctrine for a while—and maybe that way one of the researchers who's really discovering the truth will get somebody to listen to him!

"Get your notepad! We've got work to do. And when we finish, I think we'll send a copy out Horizonville way. Might even persuade that young academic out there to come here and work with me—"
quality_problem.question: What strategy was proposed for the lieutenant, according to Porter’s discussion with Anderson?

quality_problem.story:
VIRTUAL SHORES
By MARSHALL KING

Elena Wagner laughed as her avatar sprinted through the digital forest, her consciousness fully immersed in the simulation. At twelve years old, she moved through the Greenfield Territory with the confidence of youth, racing toward the legendary Digital Ocean in Crestwood, Zelvaria. The computational oceanography her older siblings had described awaited her just beyond the procedural wilderness.

When she'd caught her breath, she checked her interface. No trace of the starting hub; she had left it far behind. Safe from the scrutiny of moderators and parental controls, there was nothing now to stop her from reaching the ocean. This was the moment to activate her special ability.

"On your mark!" she shouted to the flowing data streams that manifested as a rippling brook with orange whirlpools. She glanced around, pretending that some glitch might try to interrupt her. "Get set!" she challenged the algorithmic insects that hovered over the abundant foliage. "Pause!"

She activated her time-manipulation module—a rare power-up she'd won in a creative writing competition. The system responded instantly: the data stream became motionless and its minute whirlpools stopped whirling; a nearby digital bee hung suspended over a flowering plant, its wings frozen mid-stroke; and the purple sky overhead held fast in its generation of clouds and atmospheric effects.

With everything around her in a state of perfect stasis, Elena hurried toward the ocean. Her avatar moved through the frozen world with practiced ease.

If only the session wasn't time-limited! she thought. There was so much to see and her credits would only last six hours. The stories she had heard from her siblings and their friends had tantalized her for months. So many times had she heard these descriptions that now, as she ran along, she could clearly picture the wonderland as though she were already there. There would be a formation of petrified logs to climb on, the ocean itself with waves generated by the most sophisticated fluid dynamics algorithms in existence, the comical three-legged creatures called tripods who endlessly processed seaweed data, and many kinds of other procedural creatures found only at the ocean biome.

She bounded through the forest with exhilaration coursing through her avatar. And who could say she wasn't ready for this? she thought. She ran along feeling proud of herself for making the journey alone. But twelve!

"I'll unpause you, Mr. Bee—just wait and see!" As she passed one of the many motionless pollen-gathering subroutines, she took care not to disturb its interrupted task. When Elena had paused time, the bees—like all the other entities—had been frozen in their programmed activities, and she knew that as soon as she resumed time, everything would pick up exactly where it had left off.

When she detected the distinct sensory data that told her the ocean was not far off, her pulse quickened. Rather than spoil what was clearly going to be a perfect day, she chose to ignore the fact that using time-manipulation consumed enormous amounts of processing power and drained her avatar's energy reserves. She chose to ignore the warning that "young users who manipulate time without proper authorization may suffer permanent account suspension." She chose to ignore the cautionary tales about users who had exhausted their avatars and been forcibly disconnected.

She chose, instead, to picture the admiration of family and friends when they learned of her brave journey.

The journey was long, the clock stood still. She stopped to gather some fruit that grew along the path—nutritional data packets that would restore her avatar's stamina. With them in her inventory, she bounded along several more meters, then stopped abruptly.

She found herself atop a rocky promontory, overlooking the Digital Ocean!

She was so overwhelmed by the vista that her "Amazing!" came out as a weak whisper. The ocean lay before her, its paused waves awaiting her command to resume their tidal algorithms. The breakers along the shoreline hung in varying stages of formation, some having already exploded into towering spray while others were poised in smooth orange curls waiting to execute that subroutine.

And there were new entities everywhere! Overhead, a flock of seabirds were frozen in a steep glide, their flight paths calculated but suspended. Elena had heard of these interactive creatures many times. Today, with her siblings logged into their own sessions elsewhere, she would have the entities all to herself. Further down the beach was a pair of humanoid avatars frozen mid-step, facing the spot where Elena now stood. Some distance behind them were eight more, each frozen in curious poses. And down in the water, where the ocean algorithms ran themselves into thin pixels upon the sand, she saw the comical tripods, those three-legged marine entities who made careers of processing seaweed.

"Hi there!" Elena called. When she got no reaction, she remembered that she was still in time-manipulation mode. For her, the world would continue to be frozen until she resumed time.

"Hi there!" she called again, this time with the mental command to resume. Time started! Immediately she was surrounded by activity. She heard the roar of the crashing orange breakers, she experienced the spray's sensory data, and she saw her new companions continue their actions.

She knew, too, that at this moment, in the forest, the little brook picked up its flow where it had left off, the purple clouds resumed their programmed journey, and the bees continued their tasks without having missed a single wing-stroke. The brook, the clouds, and the insects had not been interrupted in the least; it was time itself that Elena had paused, not the simulation around her.

She scrambled down the sandy cliff to meet the tripods who, to her, had just come to life.

"I can do a handstand!" She set down her fruit and balanced herself upside down while her legs pawed the air. She knew it was probably the worst handstand she had ever done, for she felt weak and dizzy. Already time-manipulation had drained her avatar's energy. But her spirits remained high.

The tripod acknowledged Elena's feat with an appreciative animation before returning to its seaweed processing.

Elena ran everywhere, trying to see and do everything at once. She looked around to greet the flock of seabirds, but they had glided to a spot further along the shore. Then, approaching the first of the humanoid avatars, she started to burst forth with her habitual "Hi there!" when she heard them speaking.

"...will revolutionize market economics in virtual spaces, Patel. This simulation makes seventeen. Seventeen proprietary environments I can claim as my intellectual property!"

"My, my. Seventeen simulations. And tell me, Antonio, just what the hell are you going to do with them—display them in your digital portfolio back in Keystone, Belvoria?"

"Hi there, wanna explore together?" Elena's invitation got nothing more than a startled glance from the avatars who quickly returned to their conversation. She followed along at their heels. "I've got some fruit, want some?"

"Patel, you'd better tell your team back there to stop admiring the visual arts and get to work. Time is money. I didn't fund this media production expedition just to give your assistants a vacation."

The avatars stopped so suddenly that Elena nearly collided with them.

"All right, Antonio, just hold it a minute. Listen to me. Sure, it's your funding that created this place; it's your project all the way. But you hired me to lead the technical team here with the best programmers available, and that's just what I've done. My job isn't over yet. I'm responsible for documenting this environment safely, and for completing the data extraction."

"Precisely. And since you're responsible, get them working. Tell them to deploy the marker. Look at those fools back there, playing in the ocean with a three-legged algorithm!"

"Good God, man, aren't you human? We've only been in this simulation twenty minutes! Naturally they want to explore. They half expected to find hostile entities or worse, and here we are surrounded by friendly creatures that approach us like we're old friends. Let the team look around before we stake out your copyright claim."

"Bah! Bunch of children."

As Elena followed along, an avatar's leg swung at her and missed. "Patel, will you get this glitchy NPC away from me!" Elena shrieked with joy at this new interaction and promptly did a handstand. In this position she got an upside-down view of them walking away.

She gave up trying to stay with them. Why did they move so fast? What was the hurry? As she sat down and began consuming her fruit to restore energy, three more avatars came along making urgent sounds, apparently trying to catch up to the first two. As they passed her, she offered her fruit. "Want some?" No response.

Exploration held more promise than eating. She left her fruit half-consumed and went to where they had stopped further along the beach.

"Director Patel, sir! Isaac has detected anomalous code in the vicinity. He's trying to isolate it now."

"There you are, Antonio. Your new intellectual property is going to make you so wealthy that you can fund your next simulation. That'll make eighteen, I believe."

"Anomalous code, bah! We've found low-grade exploits in every environment I've developed so far, and this one'll be no different. Now how about that marker? Let's get it deployed, Patel. And the copyright beacon, and the ownership certificate."

"All right, team. The sooner we get Mr. Antonio's marker deployed and his claim established, the sooner we can take time to explore properly. Quickly now!"

When the three avatars went back to join the rest of their group, the first two resumed walking. Elena followed along.

"Well, Patel, you won't have to look far for materials to use for the base of the marker pole. Look at that formation up there."

"Can't use them. They're petrified logs. The ones on top are too high to access, and if we move those on the bottom, the whole structure will collapse on us."

"Well—that's your problem. Just remember, I want this marker to be permanent. It's got to be stable for at least—"

"Don't worry, Antonio, we'll get your monument erected. What's this with the marker? There must be more to establishing a copyright than just deploying a marker."

"There is, there is. Much more. I've fulfilled all requirements set down by digital property law to validate my claim. But the marker? Well, you might say it represents an empire, Patel. The Antonio Empire. On each of my markers is the name ANTONIO, a symbol of innovation and progress in media production. Call it branding if you will."

"Don't worry, I won't. I've seen corporate markers before."

"Damn it all, will you stop referring to this as a corporate land-grab? What I'm doing is significant, man. Significant! This is digital pioneering."

"Of course. And if I'm not mistaken, you've set up a licensing system so that you not only own the environments, but you will effectively control the users who are foolish enough to pay for access."

"I could terminate your contract for talking to me like this. Damn you, man! It's people like me who fund development. It's people like me who give your programmers something to build. It's people like me who invest capital into risky projects like this, so that people like you can escape from overcrowded server farms. Did you ever think of that?"

"I imagine you'll triple your investment in six months."

When they stopped, Elena stopped. At first she had been interested in their conversation about market economics and intellectual property, but as she grew accustomed to their presence, and as they in turn ignored her, she hopped alongside chattering to herself, content to be in their company.

She heard more voices coming from behind, and she turned to see the remainder of the group running toward them.

"Director Patel! Here's the marker, sir. And here's Isaac with the code scanner. He says the anomaly is getting stronger over this way!"

"How about that, Isaac?"

"This scanner's going wild, Director. It's almost off the charts."

Elena saw one of the avatars hovering around her with a small device. Grateful for the attention, she did a handstand. "Can you do this?" She was delighted at the reaction. They all started making excited sounds, and she felt most satisfied.

"Stand back, Director! Here's the source right here! This little avatar's radiating more anomalous code than a corrupted database!"

"Let me see that, Isaac. Well, I'll be damned! Now what do you suppose—"

By now they had formed a widening circle around her, and she was eager to show them more tricks. She gambled on standing on one leg.

"Patel, I must capture that entity! Put it in a containment field."

"Now wait a minute, Antonio. Universal Digital Rights Protocol forbids—"

"This is my simulation and I make the rules. Put it in a containment field!"

"With my team as witness, I officially protest—"

"Good God, what a specimen to extract. Anomalous entities! Why, they must be self-replicating, of course! There must be thousands of these glitches somewhere in the code. And to think of those fools back in Keystone with their standard debugging protocols! Hah! Now I'll have investors flocking to me. How about it, Patel—does innovation pay off or doesn't it?"

"Not so fast. Since this little entity is anomalous, there may be great danger to the system—"

"Now look here! You had planned to put code samples in a secure container, so what's the difference? Put it in a containment field."

"It'll corrupt."

"I have you under contract, Patel! You are responsible to me, and what's more, you are in my simulation. Put it in a containment field."

Elena was tired. First the time-manipulation, then this. While this day had brought more excitement than she could have hoped for, the strain was beginning to show. She lay in the center of the circle, happily exhausted, hoping that her companions would show her some of their own abilities.

She didn't have to wait long. The avatars forming the circle stepped back and made way for two others who came through carrying a glowing containment device. Elena sat up to watch.

"Hell, Director, why don't I just grab the entity? Looks like it has no intention of fleeing."

"Better not, Matthew. Even though you're protected, no telling what abilities the little thing has. Play it safe and use the capture beam."

"I swear it understands what we're saying. Look at those eyes."

"All right, careful now with that beam."

"Come on, little one. Here you go. That's it!"

Elena took in these sounds with perplexed concern. She sensed the imploring quality of the avatar with the device, but she didn't know what she was supposed to do. She tilted her head as she waited in anticipation.

She saw the beam projecting toward her, and, before she knew it, she had scooted out of the circle and up the sandy beach. She was surprised at herself for fleeing. Why had she done it? she wondered. Never before had she felt this instinctive urge to protect herself.

She watched the avatars huddle around the containment device on the beach, their attention apparently diverted. She wished now that she had not run away; she felt she had lost her chance to interact with them.

"Wait!" She ran over to her half-consumed fruit, picked it up, and ran back into the crowd. "I've got my fruit, want some?"

The group came to life once more. Her companions ran this way and that, and at last Elena understood that the objective was to get her into the containment field. She picked up the spirit of the game, and deliberately ran within a few feet of the device, then, just as the nearest pursuer was about to push her in, she sidestepped to safety. Then she heard a sharp sound and felt a stinging sensation in one of her legs.

"Antonio, you fool! Put away that deletion tool!"

"There you are, team. It's all in the technique. Just tagged it, that's all. Now capture it."

The sting in her leg was minor; Elena's distress lay in her confusion. What had she done wrong? When she saw the capture beam projecting toward her again, she involuntarily paused time. She knew better than to use this ability recklessly, but her action now was instinctive. In that split second following the sharp sting in her leg, her mind had grasped for an acceptable course of action. Finding none, it had ordered the pause.

The scene around her became frozen once more. The beam hung motionless in the air while energy particles traced their way back to one of the avatars. Elena dragged herself through the congregation, confused by her inability to understand.

As she worked her way past one entity after another, she tried at first to avoid looking them in the eye, for she felt sure she had violated some rule. Then she thought that by examining them as she passed, she might discover their purpose. She limped by one who held a small device that had been emitting particles; the particles now hung in lifeless clusters around the avatar's head. She hobbled by another who held a scanner that had previously made sounds whenever Elena was near. These things told her nothing.

Before starting her climb up the promontory, she passed a tripod which, true to its nature, was comical even in alarm. Startled by the deletion tool's discharge, it had jumped four feet into the air before Elena had paused time. Now it hung there, its data-processing appendage extended and its three legs drawn up.

Leaving the frozen figures behind, she limped her way up the promontory, torn between leaving and staying. What an odd place, this ocean simulation! She wondered why the descriptions she'd heard hadn't mentioned anything about the beach avatars behaving this way.

Reaching the top of the rise, she looked down upon her silent companions with deep sorrow. How she wished she were down there interacting with them. But she knew at last that theirs was a game she didn't fit into. Now there was nothing left but to resume time and start the long journey back to the hub. Even though her session time was nearly expired, she knew she didn't dare use time-manipulation to get herself back instantly. Her depleted energy reserves and clouded thoughts were strong signals that she had already overused this ability.

When Elena resumed time, the avatar with the capture beam stood in open-mouthed disbelief as the beam fell harmlessly to the sand—on the spot where Elena had been standing.

"My God, it's—it's gone."

Then another avatar, the one with the deletion tool, ran a few steps toward the beam, stopped and gaped. "All right, people, what's going on here? Capture that entity. What did you do with it?"

The resumption of time meant nothing at all to those on the beach, for to them time had never stopped. The only thing they could be certain of was that at one moment there had been a glitchy creature in front of them, and the next moment it was gone.

"Is it invisible, Director? Where is it?"

"Up there, Director! On those rocks. Isn't that it?"

"Well, I'll be damned!"

"Patel, I'm holding you personally responsible for this! Now that you've bungled it, I'll bring it down my own way."

"Just a minute, Antonio, let me think. There's something about that anomalous little entity that we should.... Antonio! I warned you about that tool!"

Elena moved across the top of the formation for a last look at her companions. Her weight on the end of the first log triggered the collapse. Slowly at first, the giant logs began cascading down the short distance to the sand. Elena fell back onto solid ground, horrified at the spectacle before her. The agonizing sounds of the avatars below filled her with panic.

The logs caught most of them as they stood in the surf. Others were pinned down on the sand.

"I didn't mean it!" Elena screamed. "I'm sorry! Can't you hear?" She hopped back and forth near the edge of the rise, overwhelmed with shock and guilt. "Get up! Please get up!" She was consumed with distress at the sounds reaching her ears from the beach. "You're getting submerged! Did you hear me? Please get up." She was choked with anguish. How could she have caused this? She wanted her companions to get up and tell her it was all right. But it was beyond her power to bring it about.

The rising tide threatened to cover those in the orange surf.

Elena worked her way down the hill, begging them to save themselves. The sounds they made carried a new tone, a desperate quality she'd never heard before.

"Matthew! Grace! Can you hear me?"

"I—I can't move, Director. My avatar, it's.... My God, we're going to drown!"

"Look around you, Grace. Can you see anyone moving?"

"The team on the beach are nearly buried, Director. And the rest of us here in the water—"

"Antonio. Can you see Antonio? Maybe he's—" The voice was cut off by a wave gently rolling over.

Elena could wait no longer. The tides were covering one of the avatars, and soon the others would be in the same situation. Disregarding the consequences, she ordered time to pause.

Wading into the surf, she worked a log off one victim, then she pulled the avatar up to the sand. Through blinding tears, Elena worked slowly and carefully. She knew there was no hurry—at least, not as far as her companions' safety was concerned. No matter what their condition was at this moment, it would remain the same until she resumed time. She made her way deeper into the orange liquid, where a raised hand signaled the location of a submerged body. The hand was clutching a large white banner that was tangled among the logs. Elena worked the avatar free and pulled it ashore.

It was the one who had been carrying the deletion tool.

Scarcely noticing her own damaged leg, she rescued one victim after another until there were no more in the surf. Up on the beach, she started removing the logs that pinned down the avatars caught there. She removed a log from one, who then remained in a sitting position, face frozen in a mask of shock. Another, with the weight removed, rolled over into a new position. Elena whimpered in misery as she surveyed the chaotic scene.

At last she could do no more; she felt consciousness slipping away from her.

She instinctively knew that if she lost consciousness during time-pause, events would resume... without her. For Elena, this would mean disconnection. If she had to lose consciousness, she knew she must first resume time.

Step by step she climbed the little hill, pausing every now and then to consider if this were the moment to resume time before it was too late. With her energy fast draining, she reached the top of the promontory, and she turned to look down once more on the group below.

Then she realized how much her avatar had suffered: when she ordered time to resume, nothing happened.

Her heart sank. She wasn't afraid of disconnection, and she knew that if she disconnected the oceans would flow again and her companions would move about. But she wanted to see them safe.

She tried to clear her mind for supreme effort. There was no urging time to start. She knew she couldn't initiate it by degrees, first slowly then fully. Time either progressed or it didn't. She had to commit completely.

Then, without knowing exactly when it happened, her mind took command....

Her companions came to life. The first one she saw stir lay face-down and pounded fists on the beach. A flood of relief settled over Elena as sounds came from the avatar.

"What's the matter with me? Somebody tell me! Am I glitching? Isaac! Robert! What's happening?"

"I'm coming, Matthew! Heaven help us—I saw it, too. We're either corrupted or those damn logs are sentient!"

"It's not the logs. How about us? How'd we get out of the water? Isaac, we're both corrupted."

"I'm telling you, it's the logs, or rocks or whatever they are. I was looking right at them. First they're on top of me, then they're piled up over there!"

"Damnit, the logs didn't pull us out of the ocean, did they? Director Patel!"

"Are you all right?"

"Yes sir, but—"

"Who saw exactly what happened?"

"I'm afraid we're not processing right, Director. Those logs—"

"I know, I know. Now compose yourselves. We've got to gather the others and exit this simulation while we still can."

"But what happened, Director?"

"Hell, Matthew, don't you think I'd like to know? Those logs are petrified code. The whole team couldn't lift one. It would take extraordinary processing power to move one of those things."

"I haven't seen anything extraordinary. Those tripods down there are so busy with their seaweed algorithms—"

"All right, let's help the others. Some of them can't walk. Where's Antonio?"

"He's sitting down there in the water, Director, laughing hysterically. Or crying. I can't tell which."

"We'll have to get him. Isaac, Robert, come along. Antonio! You all right?"

"Ha-ha-ha! Seventeen! Seventeen! Seventeen simulations, Patel, and they'll do anything I say! This one's got a mind of its own. Did you see that trick with the rocks? Ha-ha!"

"See if you can find his deletion tool, Robert; he'll either corrupt himself or one of us. Restrict his permissions and take him back to the exit portal. We'll be along shortly."

"Hee-hee! Seventeen! Patel, I'm holding you personally responsible for this. Ha-ha!"

Elena opened her eyes as consciousness returned. Had her companions gone?

She pulled herself along to a position between two rocks, where she could see without being seen. By the light of the twin moons she saw that they were leaving, marching away in groups of two and three, the weak helping the weaker. As they disappeared around the curving shoreline, the voices of the last two, bringing up the rear far behind the others, fell faintly on her ears over the sound of the surf.

"Is it possible that we're all corrupted, Director?"

"It's possible, but we're not."

"I wish I could be sure."

"See Antonio up ahead there? What do you think of him?"

"I still can't believe it."

"He'll never be the same."

"Tell me something. What was the most unusual thing you noticed back there?"

"You must be joking, sir. Why, the way those logs were off of us suddenly—"

"Yes, of course. But I mean besides that."

"Well, I guess I was kind of preoccupied. You know, frightened and confused."

"But didn't you notice our little glitchy friend?"

"Oh, that. I'm afraid not, Director. I—I guess I was thinking mostly of survival."

"Hmmm. If I could only be sure I saw it. If only someone else saw it too."

"I'm afraid I don't follow you, sir."

"Well, damn it all, you know that Antonio tagged it with the deletion tool. Got it in the leg. That being the case, why would the anomalous little entity come back to help us—back to us—when we were trapped under those logs?"

"Well, I guess as long as we were trapped, it figured we couldn't harm it anymore.... I'm sorry, that was illogical. I'm still a little disoriented."

"Forget it. Look, you go ahead to the exit portal and prepare for logout. I'll join you in a few minutes. I think I'll go back and look around. You know. Make sure we haven't left anyone."

"No need to do that. They're all ahead of us. I've verified."

"That's my responsibility, Grace, not yours. Now go on."

As Elena lay gathering strength for the long trek back to the hub, she saw through dimming vision one of the avatars coming back along the beach. When it was nearly directly below her, she could hear it making sounds that by now had become familiar.

"Where are you?"

Elena paid little attention to her companion's actions; she was beyond understanding. She wondered what would happen when her session expired.

"We've made a terrible mistake. We—" The sounds faded in and out on Elena's perception as the avatar turned slowly and called in different directions. She watched the avatar walk over to the pile of scattered logs and peer around and under them.

"If you're hurt I'd like to help!" The twin moons were high in the sky now, and where their light broke through the swirling clouds a double shadow was cast around the avatar. With fading awareness, Elena watched the figure shake its head slowly, then walk away in the direction of the others.

Elena's eyes stared, without seeing, at the panorama before her. The beach was deserted now, and her gaze was fixed on a shimmering white square floating on the ocean. Across it, the last thing Elena ever saw, was emblazoned the word ANTONIO.
quality_problem.question: What is NOT true of Elena?
quality_problem.correct_answer: She was an experienced user who had visited the Digital Ocean many times before
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: She had the ability to pause time in the simulation
answers: She had the ability to pause time in the simulation
She was an experienced user who had visited the Digital Ocean many times before

quality_problem.story:
THE OBSERVERS
BY SANTIAGO MARTINEZ
ILLUSTRATED BY CHEN

To all who didn't know them, Antonio Harper and Thomas Wells were brilliant data scientists studying human behavior. But this time they were up against others who could really analyze patterns, and whose business was the observation of whole civilizations.

There were thirty or more of the college students, their ages ranging apparently from eighteen to twenty-two, all of them chattering away like a flock of excited researchers as they followed Professor Charles Herrera past the row of workstations. "Now, now, students," called Professor Herrera cheerily. "Don't scatter. I can't keep my eye on you if you get too far away from me. You, Santiago, put that tablet down. No, don't start recording yet. And Camila, stop checking your phone. You'll lose focus on the actual fieldwork, and a proper ethnographer may get annoyed that you're not paying attention."

Camila laughed. "Oh, Professor Herrera, do you think the ethnographers would want to see our preliminary data?"

The two men who were observing from the back of the room wore pleased expressions. "Fascinating," said Thomas Wells. "But somewhat unpredictable, despite all our previous observations, my friend."

"No attempts at the local idioms, Thomas, not here. It calls attention to us. And you are not sure of the cultural context anyway. You may find yourself saying things you do not intend."

"Sorry, Antonio. It wasn't an attempt to show my skill, I assure you. It's that by now I have a tendency to confuse one communication pattern with another."

"I know. You were never a linguist. But about these interesting creatures—"

"I suggest that they could stand further investigation. It would be good to know how they process information."

"Whatever you say, Thomas. If you wish, we shall join the student group."

"We must have our story prepared first. And we should enter separately—less conspicuous that way."

Antonio nodded, and the two men stepped into an empty conference room whose frosted glass walls formed a convenient screen. For a moment, the room held silence. Then there came from behind the glass the chatter of student voices.

The media production studios, the cultural archives, the ethics review boards, all were left behind. At times the students scattered, but Professor Herrera knew how to get them together again, and not one was lost.

"Here, students, is the facility where we conduct our cross-cultural analysis. Who knows what we study in cultural anthropology?"

"Human societies!" came the enthusiastic chorus.

"That's right. And what methods do we use?"

"I know, Professor Herrera!" cried Santiago Lee, a dark-haired twenty-year-old with a pair of analytical eyes that examined everything like a pair of critics from an intense, focused face. "I've been here before. Participant observation and ethnographic interviews!"

"Very good, Santiago."

Santiago beamed at the approbation. "I've been to this lab lots of times," he said to the student next to him. "My advisor brings me."

"I wish my advisor would bring me too," replied the other student, with an air of wistfulness.

"Why don't you ask him to?" Before the other student could answer, Santiago paused, cocked his head slightly, and demanded, "Who are you? You aren't in our cohort."

"I'm in Professor Martinez's cohort."

"Professor Martinez? Who is he? Is he in our department?"

"I don't know," said the other student uncertainly. "I go to Redwood University in Orvandor—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera," called Santiago. "Here's a student who isn't in our cohort! He got separated from his own group!"

"Really?" Professor Herrera seemed rather pleased at the idea that some other professor had been so careless as to lose one of his charges. "What's your name, young man?"

"I'm Roberto."

"Roberto what?"

"Roberto Henderson. Please, Professor Herrera, I had to use the restroom, and then when I came out—"

"Yes, yes, I know. Well, you may stay with us until we find campus security."

Santiago was still examining Roberto with those analytical eyes. His gaze lingered on the newcomer for a long moment before Professor Herrera continued, "Santiago, what are you staring at now?"

"It's Roberto. He's mimicking your gestures exactly!"

"Really, Roberto, that isn't at all professional!"

Roberto's posture altered itself in a hurry, so as to lose any resemblance to Professor Herrera's. "I'm sorry, Professor Herrera, I didn't really mean to do anything wrong."

"Well, I'd like to know what kind of skill development program you've been through, if you don't know that it's unprofessional to mimic people to their faces. A graduate student like you, too. What year are you, Roberto?"

Roberto adjusted his apparent age, he hoped imperceptibly, by a few years. "I'm in my sec—"

An outburst of laughter. "He's in his second week, he's in his second week!"

"I was going to say, I'm in my second year. Almost, anyway."

"Second year," said Professor Herrera. "Old enough to know better about professional ethics."

"I'm sorry, Professor Herrera. And honestly, Professor Herrera, I didn't mean anything, but I'm studying media production, and I observe people, like the documentarians you see on streaming platforms—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera, please don't make Roberto leave with security," called another student. "If he's going to be a media producer, I'll bet he'd love to meet Sergio Holmes!"

"Well, after the way he's behaved, I don't know whether I should let him. I really don't."

"Please, Professor Herrera, it was an accident. I won't do it again."

"All right, if you're good, and cause no trouble. But we still have plenty of time before meeting Mr. Holmes. It's only two now, and we're not supposed to go to the lecture hall until four."

Meanwhile, across the group, another student had been having a whispered conversation with Camila near the methodology displays. "Have you seen this visualization technique?" he asked, showing her something on his tablet.

"That's fascinating," Camila said. "I don't think I've seen you present in our seminars before. Are you new?"

"I transferred recently," he said smoothly. "I'm Jack."

"Professor Herrera," called Camila Thompson, "do you think Mr. Holmes would give us his insights on information theory? Jack here was just showing me an interesting approach—"

"Jack? Who is Jack?"

Jack stepped forward from the cluster of students, looking uncertain. "I'm Jack Oliver, Professor. I've been walking with the group."

Professor Herrera looked confused. "Walking with the group? Since when?"

"Since the archives, Professor."

Santiago's eyes narrowed. He had been watching Roberto carefully ever since catching him, but now his attention divided. "I noticed Roberto joining us after that restroom break. I watched him come in through the main door."

"I came back through the side entrance," Jack said quickly. "To the cultural archives. I didn't want to interrupt the professor's lecture."

"So you're from Professor Martinez's group too?" Professor Herrera asked, frowning.

"Yes, Professor. I went to the restroom with Roberto, but we came back at different times."

Santiago counted heads absently, his lips moving. "Professor Herrera, I count thirty-four students now. We started with thirty-two this morning."

"Thirty-four? Are you certain, Santiago?"

"I counted twice at the archives. Thirty-two both times. And I only saw Roberto join us afterward."

Professor Herrera waved dismissively. "You must have miscounted earlier, Santiago. It's easy to lose track when everyone's moving about. If Jack came through the side entrance while you were watching Roberto, naturally you wouldn't have noticed. Two students from Professor Martinez's group, then. Imagine losing students and not noticing it right away. The other professor must be frantic by now, and serve him right for being so careless."

Santiago looked unconvinced but said nothing more. His analytical eyes continued to move between Roberto and Jack, cataloging their mannerisms.

"Now, students, I've warned you about overwhelming our guest. Mr. Holmes is a famous documentary filmmaker, and his time is valuable. It's very kind of him to offer to speak to us, especially when so many professional researchers are anxious to hear him, but we mustn't take advantage of his kindness."

"But he loves students, Professor Herrera! My roommate read in an interview where it said he's just passionate about education."

"I know, but—he's not in good health, students. They say he got a severe illness in the Amazon, where he was filming all those indigenous communities, and wildlife, and environmental stories for his new documentary series. That's why you mustn't stress him too much."

"But he looks so energetic and passionate, Professor Herrera. It wouldn't hurt him to answer a few questions!"

"Oh, yes, it would," asserted one student. "He has tremors. When he has an episode, his hand shakes."

"Yes, the Amazon is a dangerous place, and one never knows how the dangers will affect one," said Professor Herrera complacently. "So we must all remember how bravely Mr. Holmes is fighting his condition, and do our best not to tire him out."

In the bright light that flooded the afternoon workspace, Sergio Holmes's weathered, intense face wore an expression of distress. He groaned dismally, and muttered, "What a headache I've got, what a headache. How do you expect me to face that group of students without something to help me through?"

"You've had your medication," said his producer, Maria. She was slim, professional, and efficient. At the moment she was being more efficient than sympathetic, and she could sense his resentment. "That's all you get. Now, pull yourself together, and try to be reasonably coherent, for a change."

"But those students! They'll ask complex questions—"

"They're about the only audience in the world that won't spot you as struggling. God knows where I could find anyone else who'd believe that your hand shakes because of tropical illness."

"I know that you're looking out for my best interests, Maria. But a little more help wouldn't hurt me."

She said wearily, but firmly, "I don't negotiate with people in your condition, Sergio. I just go ahead and protect them from themselves. No more medication."

"Afterwards?"

"I can't watch you the way a guardian watches a patient."

The firm reply sent his mind off on a new tack. "You could if we were partners."

"I've never believed in partnering with unstable people to stabilize them."

"But if I proved to you that I could change—"

"Prove it first, and I'll consider your proposal afterwards."

"You certainly are a tough person, Maria. But I suppose that in your profession you have to be."

"Tough, demanding, uncompromising—and reliable. It's inevitable when I must deal with such talented, creative, and unreliable clients."

He watched her move about the room, organizing the materials for his presentation. "What are you humming, Maria?"

"Was I humming?"

"I thought I recognized it—some old song about commitment. Your subconscious gives you away. You really want to partner with me!"

"A mistake," she said coolly. "My subconscious doesn't know what it's talking about. All I want from you is quality work."

"Can't you forget for a moment that you're a producer, and remember that you're a person, too?"

"No. Not unless you forget that you're struggling, and remember that you're a professional. Not unless you make me forget that you barely functioned in the Amazon—"

"Because you weren't there with me!"

"—with hardly enough energy to let them film you as if you were actually leading the expedition."

"You're so unforgiving, Maria. You don't have much respect for me, do you—consciously, that is?"

"Frankly, Sergio, no. I don't have much respect for people who waste their potential."

"I'm not entirely wasting it. I earn you that production fee—"

"I'd gladly forego that to see you functional."

"But it's your lack of faith in me that drives me to this state. And when I think of having to face those eager students with nothing to support me—"

"There should be confidence inside you at the thought of sharing your knowledge. Not medication, Sergio, not medication."

Roberto drew apart from the others and began to whisper. The whispers were punctuated by nervous laughs which made the entire conversation seem quite normal. But Antonio was in no relaxed mood. He said, in his own language, "You're getting careless, Thomas. You had no business mimicking his physical patterns."

"I'm sorry, Antonio, but it was so suggestive. And I'm a very suggestible entity."

"So am I. But I control myself."

"Still, if the temptation were great enough, I don't think you'd be able to resist either."

"The issues are important enough to make me resist."

"Still, I thought I saw your own form taking on a bit of his pattern too."

"You are imagining things, Thomas. Another thing, that mistake in starting to say you were in your second century—"

"They would have thought it a joke. And I think I got out of that rather neatly."

"You like to take risks, don't you, Thomas? Just as you did when you changed your apparent age. You had no business adjusting right out in public like that."

"I did it skillfully. Not a single person noticed."

"I noticed."

"Don't quibble."

"I don't intend to. Some of these students have very sharp analytical skills. You'd be surprised at what they observe."

Thomas said tolerantly, "You're getting anxious, Antonio. We've been away from home base too long."

"I am not anxious in the least. But I believe in taking due care."

"What could possibly happen to us? If we were to announce to the students and the professor, and to everyone in this facility, for that matter, exactly who and what we were, they wouldn't believe us. And even if they did, they wouldn't be able to act rapidly enough to contain us."

"You never can tell about such things. Wise—entities—simply don't take unnecessary chances."

"I'll grant that you're my superior in such caution."

"You needn't be sarcastic, Thomas. I know I'm more careful. I realize what a resource this planet is—you don't. It has the right developmental stage, suitable cultural complexity, the proper technological level—everything."

"Including a population that will be ideal for our purposes."

"And you would take chances of losing all this."

"Don't be silly, Antonio. What chances am I taking?"

"The chance of being discovered. Here we locate this civilization quite by accident. No one at home base knows about it, no one so much as suspects that it exists. We must get back and report—and you do all sorts of risky things which may reveal what we are, and lead these people to suspect their situation."

This time, Thomas's nervous laugh was no longer mere camouflage, but expressed to a certain degree how he felt. "They cannot possibly suspect. We have been all over this world, we have taken many forms and adapted ourselves to many cultural contexts, and no one has suspected. And even if danger really threatened, it would be easy to escape. I could take the form of the professor himself, of a security officer, of anyone in authority. However, at present there is not the slightest shadow of danger. So, Antonio, you had better stop being fearful."

Antonio said firmly, "Be careful, and I won't be fearful. That's all there is to it."

"I'll be careful. After all, I shouldn't want us to lose these humans. They're so exactly the kind we need. Look how curious they are, how adaptable, how quick to process new information—"

Professor Herrera's voice said, "Good gracious, students, what language are you using? Mandarin?"

They had been speaking too loud, they had been overheard. Antonio and Thomas stared at each other, and laughed nervously. Then, after a second to think, Antonio said, "No, Professor Herrera, just practicing our information theory notation!"

"What?"

Santiago called triumphantly, "It isn't Mandarin, Professor Herrera, it's code—data encryption. They're testing communication protocols."

"Good heavens, what is data encryption for?"

"It's a kind of way of communicating where you encode information. Like, you don't send raw data, you send encrypted packets."

"You don't transmit openly, you transmit securely," added another student.

"You don't broadcast, you narrow-cast. You don't—"

"All right, all right, I get the idea."

"You don't—"

"That'll do," said Professor Herrera firmly. "Now, let's get along to the cultural heritage archive. And please, students, do not touch the artifacts without permission. How would you like to be a precious cultural object and have people handling you carelessly? Always remember professional ethics and social welfare."

"Even with old objects, Professor Herrera?"

"Especially with cultural heritage items."

"But Mr. Holmes documented lots of indigenous communities. Did he practice proper ethics with them too?"

"There is no time for complex questions," said Professor Herrera, with the same firmness. "Come along."

They all followed after him, Antonio and Thomas bringing up the rear. Thomas whispered with amusement, "That encryption business was quick thinking, Antonio. But in fact, quite unnecessary. The things that you do to avoid being suspected!"

"It never hurts to take precautions. And I think that now it is time to leave."

"No, not yet. You are always anxious to gather complete data before reporting. Why not learn a few more details now?"

"Because they are not necessary. We already have a good understanding of human customs and information processing."

"But not of the psychology of students. And they, if you remember, are the ones who will have to be studied most carefully. We shall be asked about them. It would be good if we could report that they are suitable for comprehensive analysis, across a wide range of developmental stages. Let us stay awhile longer."

"All right," conceded Antonio, grudgingly.

So they stayed, and out of some campus materials they shaped the necessary identification badges with which to access restricted areas, and data terminals, and research archives, and other facilities favored by the academic community. Thomas wanted to win easy acceptance by sharing some of his advanced knowledge with a few of the other students, but Antonio put his metaphorical foot down. No use arousing suspicion. Even as it was—

"Gee, your research access is really high-level," said Santiago enviously to Roberto. "Is your advisor well-connected?"

"We get access to what we need," replied Thomas carelessly.

"Gosh, I wish I did."

Santiago glanced over at Jack, who was examining a display case with unusual intensity. "Your friend doesn't talk much."

"He's focused on data collection," Roberto said. "Always observing."

Professor Herrera collected his group. "Come together, students, I have something to say to you. Soon it will be time to go in and hear Mr. Holmes. Now, if Mr. Holmes is so kind as to share his insights with us, don't you think that it's only proper for us to share our work with him?"

"We could present our research projects!" suggested Camila.

"Camila's a fine one to talk," said Santiago. "She doesn't even have her data cleaned yet."

"No, students, we mustn't present anything we haven't perfected. That wouldn't make a good impression. And besides, there is no time for full presentations. Perhaps Camila will share her preliminary findings—"

"I can present a data visualization," interrupted Santiago.

"That would be excellent."

"I can discuss methodology," added another student.

"Fine. How about you, Roberto? You and your friend, Jack. Can he analyze data too?"

Roberto laughed nervously. "Oh, yes, he can analyze very well. I can process quantitative data. He can process qualitative patterns." The analytical eyes evaded a concerned look from the friend. "He can process any kind of patterns."

"He's certainly a talented student. But he seems so uncertain!"

"Oh, no," said Roberto. "He just needs encouragement."

"He shouldn't be like that. Perhaps, Roberto, you and Jack can present something together. And perhaps, too, Mr. Holmes will be pleased to see that your professor also has expertise."

"You, Professor Herrera?"

Professor Herrera coughed modestly. "Yes, students, I never told you, but I was once ambitious to be a documentary filmmaker too. I studied media production, and really, I was quite good at it. I was told that if I persevered I might actually be famous. Just think, your professor might actually have been a famous filmmaker! However, in my day, there were many ethical concerns in documentary work, and the life of media production was not attractive—but perhaps we'd better not speak of that. At any rate, I know the principles of documentary filmmaking very well."

"God knows what I'll have to go through," said Sergio. "And I don't see how I can take it in this condition."

"I don't see how they can take you any other way," replied Maria.

"Why go through with it at all? Why not cancel the whole thing?"

"Because people are depending on you. You always want to cancel whenever you run into something challenging. You may as well cancel your entire career if that's the way you feel."

"And your production fee, darling."

"You think I'd mind that. I work for my fee, Sergio, sweetheart. I work too damn hard for that fee."

"You can partner with me and share the rewards. Honestly, Maria, if you supported me better, if you showed me I meant something to you, I'd stabilize."

She made a face. "Don't talk nonsense. Take your notes, and let's get ready to go. Unless you want to change here, and walk around dressed as an Amazon explorer."

"Why not? I've walked around dressed as worse. An unstable wreck."

"Wrecks don't attract attention. They're too ordinary."

"But an unstable Amazon explorer—that's something special." He went into the next room and began to prepare. "Maria," he called. "Do you respect me?"

"At times."

"Would you say that you respected me very much?"

"When you're functional. Rarely."

"Trust me?"

"Once in a blue moon."

"What would I have to do for you to want to partner with me?"

"Achieve something meaningful."

"I like that. Don't you think I achieve something meaningful now? Students admire my work, and come to life at the thought of following in my footsteps."

"The students who admire you will admire anybody. Besides, I don't consider that impressing naive students is a meaningful occupation for a real professional."

"How can I be meaningful, Maria? No one ever taught me how."

"Some people manage without being taught."

"I suppose I could figure it out if I had support."

"Then you'll have to do without figuring it out."

He came into the room again, composed, professional, determined-looking. There was an expression in his bearing which indicated dedication without end, a dedication that would enable him to brave the challenges of nature, culture, and adversity.

"How do I look?"

"Your professional self, of course. A budget version of David Attenborough."

"I feel terrified. I don't know how I'm going to face those students. If they were just casual viewers it wouldn't be so bad, but a group of analytical students!"

"They'll grow up to be your colleagues, if you're still working five years from now. Meanwhile, into each career some challenges must come."

"You would talk of challenges, when you know how I feel."

"Sorry. Come on, let's go."

The lecture hall buzzed with conversation. And beneath the conversation was a steady undercurrent of whispers, of academic confidences exchanged, of scholarly hopes that would now be fulfilled. Professor Herrera's cohort was not the only one which had come to hear the famous filmmaker describe his documentary methods. There were at least five others like it, and by some arrangement, a group from the renewable energy department, who also whispered to each other, in professional solidarity, and pretended to find interest in the presence of so many from the social sciences.

In this atmosphere of whispers and anticipation, Thomas and Antonio could exchange observations without being noticed. Antonio said urgently, "Why did you tell her that I could analyze qualitative patterns too?"

"Why, because it's the truth. You're a very good pattern recognizer. You make wonderful cultural interpretations, for instance. Go on, Antonio, show her what fine cultural analysis you can—"

"Stop it, you fool, before you cause trouble!"

"Very well, Antonio. Did I tempt you?"

"Did you tempt me! You and your risk-taking!"

"You and your excessive caution! But let's not argue now, Antonio. Here, I think, comes the filmmaker. Let's applaud, and be as properly enthusiastic as everyone else is."

My God, he thought, how can they maintain such intense focus for so long? My concentration hurts already. How do they sustain a lifetime of it? Even an hour?

"Go ahead," whispered Maria. "You've seen the outline—go into your presentation. Tell them what insights you have. You have the advantage to start with."

"My reputation," he said, with some bitterness.

"Reputation is the word for you. But forget that. If you're good—you'll get proper rest afterwards."

"Will it be one of those occasions when you respect me?"

"If the moon turns blue."

He strode to the front of the platform, a tablet resting easily in his hands, a confident smile radiating from his weathered, professional face. The applause rose to an enthusiastic crescendo, but the smile did not vanish. What a skilled presenter he really was, he told himself, to be able to pretend he enjoyed this.

An assistant dean of some college in the university, a formal older man, was introducing him. There were a few laudatory references to his great talents as a filmmaker, and he managed to look properly modest as he listened. The remarks about his knowledge of indigenous cultures and environmental systems were a little harder to take, but he took them. Then the older man stepped back, and he was facing his challenge alone.

"Students," he began. A pause, a modest smile. "Perhaps I should rather say, colleagues. I'm not one to think of you as mere students. Some people think of me as a perpetual student myself, because I like to explore, and document new things. They think that such things are naive. But if they are, I'm glad to be naive. I'm glad to be one of you. Yes, I think I will call you my colleagues.

"Perhaps you regard me, my colleagues, as a very fortunate person. But when I recall some of the challenges I have faced, I don't entirely agree with you. I remember once, when we were documenting a remote indigenous community—"

He told the story of the remote community, modestly granting co-credit to his local guides. Then another story illustrating the complex patterns of cultural heritage. The tablet figured in still another tale, this time of analyzing environmental data in real-time. His audience was quiet now, absorbed with interest, and he welcomed the respite from performance anxiety he had won for himself.

"And now, my colleagues, it is time to conclude." He actually looked regretful. "But it is my hope that I shall be able to engage with you again—"

Enthusiastic applause, warm as ever, hands moving appreciatively to indicate satisfaction. Thank God that's over with, he thought. Now for that rest—and he didn't mean brief rest, singular. Talk of being meaningful, he'd certainly been meaningful now. He'd inspired those students. What more can any reasonable person want?

But it wasn't over with. Professor Herrera had stepped up on the platform.

"Mr. Holmes," he said, in a strangely affected voice, like that of the first media studies teacher he had ever had, the one who had almost ruined his production career. "Mr. Holmes, I can't tell you how much you have inspired us all, young and old. Hasn't Mr. Holmes inspired us, students?"
