quality_problem.story:
The Geologists of Titan's Edge

By the expedition log of Dr. Li Ramos
Recorded at Dalebrook Station, Aldoria Sector

There were two crystalline formations on the tiny plateau that shouldn't have existed.

To understand the geological mystery of Titan's Edge, one must consider three elements: the observer, the phenomenon, and the catalyst. All three existed on this remote moon, but there was a question as to their true nature.

The fourth day of the *Horizon Explorer's* landing on the tidally-locked moon orbiting the gas giant Prometheus was a repetition of the three before it—a twelve-hour cycle of eerie, phosphorescent twilight. Geologist Dr. Li Ramos—standing her rotation on monitoring duty—sat at the observation dome with her spectrographic scanner ready; but despite her vigilance, she had captured no useful data when the inevitable pre-shift luminescence began to shimmer over the methane sea to the east.

The cycle change brought her alert with a start, frowning at the sight of two meter-tall crystalline formations standing on the tiny basalt plateau a half-kilometer from shore, their geometric faces oriented precisely toward the research station.

"They're back again," Ramos called, and climbed down from the dome. "Everyone up! I'm going to run a full spectral analysis this time!"

Walter Gutierrez emerged from his rest pod reluctantly, fastening the thermal suit required even in Titan's Edge's carefully regulated artificial atmosphere. Gutierrez blinked as he cycled through the airlock, his gray beard frosted with condensation and his rounded frame moving stiffly. He looked, Ramos thought for the hundredth time, more like a retired university dean than a veteran expedition commander. His three decades analyzing rock formations on Earth, Mars, and the inner colonies had earned him considerable authority, though this was his first assignment beyond familiar solar systems.

Timothy Kelly followed, his lean athletic build moving with the careful precision of someone trained in extreme-environment protocols. Kelly was a man in his late twenties with sharp features and an intensity that sometimes bordered on obsessive. He immediately pulled out his portable analyzer—a specialized instrument Ramos had never seen before this mission—and began scanning the distant formations.

"The lattice structure is extraordinary," Kelly murmured, adjusting his instrument's sensitivity. "Silicon-carbon hybrid bonds that don't match anything in terrestrial databases. The crystallographic symmetry suggests formation conditions we haven't documented on any previously surveyed world."

"Any sign of the silicon-based organisms yet?" Gutierrez asked, setting up his own equipment near the sample collection station. His instruments were configured for conventional analysis—the same reliable equipment he'd used throughout his career on Earth-derived planetary bodies.

"They won't emerge until the crystal-eaters arrive," Ramos said. She adjusted the wavelength filter of her scanner and frowned at Gutierrez. "Walter, I wish you'd let me take core samples this time. This cycle of destruction is affecting our data quality."

Gutierrez shielded his eyes against the glare of Prometheus rising over the methane sea. "You know I can't authorize that, Li. These formations may represent a form of proto-intelligence or higher, and under Terran Survey Protocols, our interference with what may be a fundamental geological process would violate every principle of scientific collaboration. We need to crack the chemical communication patterns and understand the ecosystem restoration cycle before we can intervene."

Ramos turned an irritated stare toward the cluster of smaller crystalline structures gathering at the edge of the sulfur-dioxide frost fields that bordered the landing site.

"What puzzles me is the pattern," she said. "Why do these formations migrate to that plateau every cycle, when the outcome is always the same?"

Kelly answered with his own persistent mystery, his angular face troubled. "For that matter, what happened to the city I detected during our orbital survey? The electromagnetic signatures suggested a massive structure with refined metallic alloys—processed minerals arranged in geometric patterns that couldn't occur naturally. Yet we've mapped this entire moon in the rover and found nothing but methane seas and scattered plateaus like this one."

Gutierrez and Ramos exchanged weary looks. The city had become an obsession with Kelly, and his stubborn insistence—coupled with an annoying habit of being proven right about unusual formations in past missions—had worn their patience thin.

"There never was a city here, Tim," Gutierrez said. "You misinterpreted the data during orbital insertion, that's all. I've been cataloging mineral samples for thirty years, and nothing on this moon suggests industrial activity."

"The bonding patterns in these formations—they're not random," Kelly said quietly, not looking up from his analyzer. "They show evidence of directed growth, like someone engineered them. The isotopic ratios suggest artificial enrichment processes that don't occur in natural crystal formation."

"Directed growth?" Gutierrez laughed. "Tim, crystals form according to physical laws, not intention. I've seen enough formations across two star systems to know natural variation when I see it. Standard mineralogy explains most of what we're observing."

Kelly's jaw tightened. "Standard mineralogy assumes Earth-based formation processes. These crystals incorporate elements in configurations that violate every thermodynamic model I learned during my training at the Kepler Institute's program for analyzing materials from outside human-explored space."

"Which is precisely why Survey Command assigned you to this mission," Ramos interjected before the argument could escalate. "Different perspectives, different training backgrounds."

Gutierrez grunted noncommittally, but Ramos's voice cut through. "Get ready! Here they come!"

Out of the luminescent haze descended a swarm of silicon-based flyers, each three meters across and gleaming with metallic compounds in the dim light. They dove like raptors upon the plateau, engulfing the two crystalline formations instantly under their grinding, abrading appendages. Then around the outcrop, the ground erupted violently, churned up by a sudden emergence of dark, tentacled shapes composed of living polymer chains.

"The silicon-eaters," Gutierrez muttered. "Right on schedule. Two seconds too late, as always, to prevent the destruction."

A barrage of chemical tendrils lashed out from the emerging organisms and struck into the swarm of flyers. The flyers retreated immediately into the haze, leaving behind three of their number who were pulled beneath the surface like trapped insects. No trace remained of the two crystalline formations.

"A perfect example of predator-prey dynamics," Ramos said, deactivating her scanner. "Do any of those entities look like city-builders to you, Tim?"

The smaller crystalline structures drifted past from the shelter of the frost fields, seemingly oblivious to the researchers, and arranged themselves along the mineral-rich ledges near the methane sea to begin their photosynthetic cycle.

"The mineral composition of those crystals shows enrichment patterns inconsistent with natural precipitation," Kelly said stubbornly. "But the refined alloys I detected from orbit—those came from somewhere. I'm going to find the source. Will either of you need the rover today?"

Gutierrez raised his hands in surrender. "I have samples to process, and Li is off duty after her monitoring shift. Take the rover, but you won't find anything. Sometimes the simplest explanation is correct—natural formation processes we haven't fully documented yet. My experience tells me these readings fall within normal geological parameters."

"The orbital data showed architectural minerals with evidence of high-temperature processing," Kelly said, gathering his specialized equipment—instruments configured for detecting trace elements and isotopic signatures that fell outside the parameters of conventional surveys. "Foundries operated here once. Someone refined these materials deliberately, using techniques I've only seen theorized for non-terrestrial civilizations."

The rover was a distant speck on the horizon when Ramos entered her rest pod a short time later, leaving Gutierrez to organize his collection of samples. Gutierrez seemed content with his systematic cataloging—the patient work of categorizing and preserving specimens that had defined his career, applying familiar classification systems developed on Earth to each new planetary body he visited. Sleep eluded Ramos initially; a vague sense of overlooked details nagged at her consciousness, but it wasn't until drowsiness finally claimed her that the discrepancy crystallized into clarity.

She recalled then that on the first day of the *Explorer's* landing, one of the crystal formations had fallen from a ledge into a methane pool and had dissolved rapidly before the polymer organisms could extract it with their tendrils. Which meant that the formations couldn't survive in liquid methane—otherwise some would surely have adapted to that environment.

And the expedition had surveyed Titan's Edge exhaustively without finding any mechanism for the formations to traverse the methane sea. The logical chain completed itself automatically, nearly jolting Ramos from her drowsy state.

"Impossible," she muttered. "No traversal mechanism, and they can't survive the sea. *Then how do they reach that plateau?*"

She fell asleep with the paradox unresolved.

Gutierrez was still hunched over his sample analysis when Ramos emerged from her pod and extracted a nutrition pack from the storage unit. The communication panel above the control console hummed softly, its display blank on open channel. Around him, carefully labeled containers held specimens from the frost fields—methodical work showing his systematic approach, each sample tagged with classification codes he'd refined during decades of terrestrial and colonial surveys.

"Has Kelly located his phantom city yet?" Ramos asked, grinning when Gutierrez snorted.

"He's scanning the sunward hemisphere now, looking for more of those anomalous signatures," Gutierrez said. "Li, I'm going to ground Tim tomorrow, despite my reluctance to issue direct orders. He's fixated on that electromagnetic anomaly, and his methods are unconventional."

"What bothers you about his methods, exactly?" Ramos asked, genuinely curious.

Gutierrez sighed. "Thirty years of fieldwork teaches you to be systematic and methodical. I've analyzed samples from every major body in the inner systems using established protocols—the same techniques that worked on Mars work on Europa, work on Titan. Tim keeps insisting these formations require entirely new classification systems, new analytical frameworks designed specifically for materials that originated beyond human-explored space."

Ramos shrugged. "I'd normally agree, except for Tim's frustrating tendency to notice things the rest of us miss. Remember the silicate anomaly on Kepler-442b? Everyone dismissed his readings until the lab results came back."

Gutierrez looked uncomfortable. "That was different. Those were still recognizable mineral structures, just with unusual trace elements. Here, Tim's talking about materials that don't fit any known formation processes—materials that require his specialized training to even interpret. His certification is specifically for analyzing extraterrestrial mineral compositions that fall outside standard geological frameworks."

"Which is precisely why Survey Command included him on this mission," Ramos said mildly. "They wanted someone certified in interpreting mineral formations from worlds where Earth-based assumptions might not apply."

"I'm aware of his specialization," Gutierrez said, a touch defensively. "But experience counts for something. My thirty years of fieldwork has value too. Would you mind taking tonight's shift? I'm exhausted after processing today's samples."

Ramos gestured agreement and gathered her scanning equipment. Darkness had fallen outside—the deep, absolute darkness of Titan's Edge's shadow side, where Prometheus's bulk blocked all light from the distant sun. She positioned her chair at the observation dome and activated her data pad, settling in comfortably while Gutierrez prepared a sleep aid before retiring.

Later she would remember that Gutierrez had taken a sedative, but at the moment it seemed routine. Within minutes, his gentle snoring drifted through the station, a sound faintly irritating against the absolute silence outside.

Ramos reviewed her notes and returned to the inconsistencies she'd identified. The formations couldn't survive methane immersion, and without any traversal mechanism...

It occurred to her then that there had been precisely two formations on the plateau each cycle, and the consistency made her sit up abruptly, startled. Why two? Why not three or four, or only one?

She cycled through the airlock and paced restlessly on the processed landing pad, feeling the artificial atmosphere's warmth against her face. Four days of routine monitoring had built up a need for direct investigation that chafed at her scientific discipline; she was intrigued and simultaneously frustrated by the enigmatic relationship linking the crystal formations to the flyers and polymer organisms, and her desire to understand that relationship was intensified by the knowledge that Titan's Edge could provide crucial insights into biodiversity conservation principles. That is, she thought wryly, if Terran scientists could rationalize the bizarre cycle pursued by its indigenous life forms—what appeared to be deliberate self-sacrifice in pairs.

She reviewed again the improbable drama of the past four cycles, and found it scientifically explicable until she reached the question of motivation and the transportation mechanism that placed the formations in pairs on the plateau, when her entire framework of hypothesis collapsed into contradictions. She abandoned the effort finally; how could any human scientist rationalize the alien imperatives that drove such fundamentally different forms of existence?

She returned inside, and the sound of Gutierrez's muffled snoring aggravated her restlessness. She made her decision impulsively, setting aside the scanner for a portable light and a pocket-sized communicator which she clipped to her thermal suit.

She didn't select any defensive equipment because she saw no need for it. The light would reveal how the formations reached the outcrop, and if she required assistance the communicator would summon Gutierrez. Investigating without Gutierrez's authorization was, technically speaking, a violation of Survey Protocols, but—

"Damn the protocols," she muttered. "I need to *understand*."

Ramos activated the light at the edge of the frost field and proceeded carefully, eager for discovery now that she'd committed to action. Just inside the mineral deposits she encountered a pair of small crystalline structures, dormant and stable, their geometric faces completely blank and unrevealing.

She worked deeper into the field and found other dormant pairs, but nothing else. There were no atmospheric disturbances, no thermal variations, no electromagnetic anomalies. She had penetrated close to the field's center without further discovery and was preparing to return, disappointed, when something massive and powerful seized her from behind.

A sharp cold burned through her thermal suit at the shoulder, and a sudden overwhelming numbness swept her into unconsciousness deeper than Titan's Edge's darkness. Her last conscious thought wasn't of her own danger, but of Gutierrez—sedated and unprotected in the station...

She was standing upright when consciousness returned, her back to the methane sea and a prismatic shimmer of cycle-change luminescence reflecting on the liquid surface before her. For a moment she was completely disoriented; then peripherally she detected the crystalline blur of a formation standing beside her, and cried out in panic when she tried to turn her head and couldn't.

She was on the basalt plateau offshore, and except for autonomic functions of balance and respiration, her body was paralyzed.

The first glow of Prometheus-rise blurred the reflected luminescence at her feet, but for several seconds her racing mind was too occupied to consider the implications of her predicament. *Whatever transported me here immobilized me first*, she thought. *That cold at my shoulder was like a chemical injection.*

Panic seized her again when she remembered the silicon-based flyers; more seconds passed before she regained control, her suit's thermal regulation system straining against her fear-induced temperature spike. She had to get help. If she could activate the communicator at her belt and call Gutierrez...

She focused every ounce of concentration toward raising her right hand, and failed.

Her arm felt like solid metal, its inertia impossible to overcome. She released the effort with a groan, anxiety rising again when she saw Prometheus's bright curve on the methane sea, edges distorted by surface tension waves.

On shore she could see the *Horizon Explorer* resting between frost field and landing pad, its composite hull gleaming with condensation. The airlock remained open, and the empty rover dock told her that Kelly hadn't yet returned.

She realized then that sensation was gradually returning, that the cold surface of the communicator unit at her hip—previously unfelt—was now pressing against her forearm. She concentrated again on movement; this time her arm responded slightly, enough to send hope surging through her. If she could apply sufficient pressure to the activation stud...

The tiny click of its engagement left her weak with relief.

"Gutierrez!" she called. "Walter, emergency—*Gutierrez*!"

The communicator hummed quietly, without response.

She gathered herself for another call, and remembered with horror the sedative Gutierrez had taken before retiring. Exhausted by his work, Gutierrez had ensured he wouldn't be easily disturbed.

Prometheus's curve on the sea brightened and expanded. Above its reflected glow she detected movement, a restless suggestion of approaching flyers.

She tried again. "Gutierrez, help me! I'm on the plateau!"

The communicator crackled. The voice that answered wasn't Gutierrez's, but Kelly's.

"Ramos! What are you doing on that killing ground?"

Ramos suppressed an hysterical laugh. "Never mind that—get here immediately, Tim! The flyers—"

She stopped, seeing for the first time the polymer organisms that surrounded the plateau just beneath the surface, waiting with chemical tendrils extended and sensor nodes studying her with alien awareness. She heard the unmistakable sound of approaching flyers behind and above her then, and thought with shock-induced clarity: *I wanted to observe this phenomenon, and now I'm part of it*.

The rover roared in from the west across the frost field, passing so close overhead that she felt the turbulence of its passage. Almost instantly she heard the high-pitched whine of its emergency thrusters as Kelly intercepted the flyer swarm directly.

Kelly's voice came through the communicator. "Dispersed them temporarily, Li—disrupted their navigation with the thruster wash, I think. Hold position. I'm retrieving you now."

The rover settled on the plateau beside Ramos, so close that the heat from its exhaust system warmed her legs through the thermal suit. Kelly extended his arms and pulled her inside like a mannequin, ignoring the crystal formation. The rover accelerated toward shore with Ramos lying across Kelly's lap in the cockpit, her head hanging partially outside.

Ramos had a final disorienting glimpse of the plateau against the blur of methane sea below, and felt her shaky laugh of relief catch in her throat. Two of the polymer organisms were moving strongly toward shore, holding the rigid crystal formation carefully above the liquid surface between them.

"Tim," Ramos croaked. "Tim, can you look back? I think I'm hallucinating."

The rover swerved briefly as Kelly glanced back. "You're fine, Li. Just stay calm. I'll explain everything when we get you safely to the *Explorer*."

Ramos forced herself to relax, more relieved than alarmed by the painful tingling of returning sensation. "I should have known, damn you," she said. "You found your city, didn't you?"

Kelly sounded slightly disgusted, as if still annoyed with himself over some personal failure. "I should have found it sooner if I'd recognized the mineral signatures earlier. Submerged structures read differently than surface formations—it took me too long to adjust my interpretation models."

In the *Horizon Explorer*, Kelly woke Gutierrez from his sedated sleep and distributed stimulant drinks, leaving Ramos comfortably positioned in the padded command chair. The paralysis continued to fade gradually, easing Ramos's fear of permanent damage.

"We never detected the city from the rover because we didn't achieve sufficient altitude," Kelly said. "I finally realized that, remembering historical accounts of how early aviators used high-altitude observation to detect submarine structures, and when I took the rover high enough, there it was, at the bottom of the methane sea—a city comparable to anything humans ever constructed. The building materials showed clear signs of deliberate refinement—smelted alloys, precision crystallography, advanced materials processing. The compositional analysis confirmed everything I suspected from the orbital readings."

Gutierrez stared. "A submerged city? Why would aquatic organisms need buildings?"

"They wouldn't," Kelly said. "I believe the city must have been built ages ago—by beings related to the crystal formations, judging from the compositional similarities in the architecture—and was submerged later by geological subsidence that eliminated the original builders and left Titan's Edge with only scattered plateaus. The polymer organisms evolved to dominance then, and from all evidence they've developed a sophisticated culture."

"The crystal formations—" Gutierrez began.

"Are livestock, or less," Kelly finished. "The polymer organisms are the dominant intelligence, and they're so far advanced that we're completely violating protocols here. Under Survey Regulations we can't establish research operations on Titan's Edge. It would constitute unauthorized interference."

"Interference with a polymer-based civilization?" Ramos protested, confused. "Why would surface research conflict with a submerged culture, Tim? Why couldn't we coexist?"

"Because the polymer organisms control the plateaus too, and actively manage them," Kelly said patiently. "They even cultivate the crystal formations. It was one of the polymer-people, making a terrestrial survey of its managed territory to select specimens for this cycle's event, that transported you last night."

"Consider the familiar pattern emerging," Gutierrez said. He laughed suddenly, a deep resonant sound of comprehension. "Titan's Edge is a polymer-people's world, Li, don't you see? And like most advanced civilizations, they practice resource management. The silicon-based flyers are the resource they harvest, and they cultivate the crystal formations for—"

Ramos swore in amazement. "Then those formations are placed there deliberately, like bait on a hook—inverted predation! No wonder I couldn't determine their motivation! It's a principle of ecosystem restoration and complexity science—managed predator-prey dynamics for biodiversity conservation!"

Kelly moved to seal the airlock, blocking out the dim luminescence. "Research operations being prohibited, we should depart before the polymer organisms become sufficiently curious about us to create complications. Can you handle the acceleration, Li?"

Ramos and Gutierrez looked at each other, understanding dawning. Ramos said: "You don't think I want to remain here and be used as bait again, do you?"

She and Gutierrez were still processing the implications when Kelly, expressionless, fired the *Horizon Explorer's* engines and lifted them free of Titan's Edge.

The final entry in Dr. Li Ramos's expedition log noted that the discovery would require extensive peer review and consultation with bioethics committees before any future missions could be authorized. The polymer-people's sophisticated approach to ecosystem management—using cultivated crystal formations as bait to harvest silicon-based flyers—represented a level of technological progress and scientific understanding that demanded respect under all Terran protocols regarding contact with advanced civilizations. She noted that each team member had contributed according to their expertise: Gutierrez's systematic sample collection had established baseline data using conventional methods refined during his career in terrestrial and colonial planetary geology, while Kelly's analysis of the submerged structures had required the specialized instrumentation and interpretive frameworks that came with his certification for analyzing mineral formations originating beyond human-explored space—the defining qualification of his role on the expedition.

What the expedition couldn't have known was that the polymer-people had been monitoring them since arrival, and had deliberately allowed Kelly to discover the submerged city as a form of communication—a demonstration that Titan's Edge was already claimed by an intelligence that understood complexity science far better than any human researcher.

The city, built by an ancient crystal-based civilization before geological subsidence flooded the lowlands, had been preserved by the polymer-people as a monument to their predecessors. In their own chemical communication system—incomprehensible to humans—they had been trying to convey a simple message: *We remember those who came before. We honor their legacy through careful stewardship. Please respect what we have built upon their foundation.*

But that message, like so many attempts at interspecies communication, was lost in translation. The humans departed, recording Titan's Edge as off-limits for colonization, never understanding that the polymer-people had been offering not a warning, but an invitation to mutual scientific collaboration.

The crystal formations continued their cycles, the silicon-based flyers continued their harvests, and the polymer-people continued their patient cultivation of an ecosystem they had spent millennia learning to understand. And deep beneath the methane sea, the ancient city stood as a reminder that civilizations rise and fall, but the principles of careful stewardship and biodiversity conservation remain eternal.

In the end, the greatest mystery wasn't how the city came to be submerged, but why the humans never thought to ask what the polymer-people might have learned from preserving it.
quality_problem.question: Who is the xenomineralogist on the team?

quality_problem.story:
QUANTUM THREADS
By Marina Roberts

From Copperfield to Harborview Village, and all the way between, it was a hell of a world for engineers... and Apprentice Fabricator Mark Leonard particularly.

The comm system blared fit to shake Mark back to Copperfield. "Printer Bay Four!"

"On my way, sir!"

At the first flash of red on the bank of monitors, Apprentice Fabricator Mark Leonard had grabbed his safety goggles; he was already throwing open the lock to the printer bay. The hot, humming vibration whipped around him and near crushed his breath away. Power! Quantum entanglement trapped here in these massive 3D printers, ready to destroy its captors given one chance! Swiftly Mark unlocked the controls and reset them. The humming vibration changed tone.

Old Ahmed's voice crackled now through the headset's ear contact. "Well, Mr. Leonard?"

"Quantum alignment two points low, sir."

Mark wondered had Ahmed passed out, was so long before the old Fabrication Chief demanded hoarsely, "Didn't you lock them controls before production start?"

"If every control hadn't been locked in correct setting," Mark answered from his own angry bewilderment, "the error would have registered before production start—wouldn't it, sir?"

"So a control reset itself during operation, hey?"

"I don't know yet, sir."

"Well, Mr. Leonard, you better know before we ship to Harborview Village!"

The icy knot in Mark's stomach jerked tighter. A dozen printer bays in this facility; why did something crazy have to happen to Mark's? In a hundred years, so the instructors—brisk women all—had told Mark in pre-employment training, no control had ever been known to slip. But one had moved here. Not enough to cause serious trouble this far from deadline. On final production, though, with one printer below peak, the uneven output could throw the whole order, crash the schedule, the whole lovely contract and all involved gone in a churning mess.

Sweat pouring off him, Mark prowled around his printer. Design of the thing had been bossed by women of course; what in Fendria wasn't any more? Anyway, nobody could get to a printer bay except through its control room. Anyone entered or left there, a bell clanged, lights flashed and a meter registered beside the Fabricator's station and on the Fabrication Chief's console up in the management suite full of beautifully efficient officers. Ever since Copperfield production start Mark had been in Four's control room. Nobody had passed through. Mark knew it. Ahmed knew it. By now the Director herself, Elizabeth Campbell, had probably inquired what was in charge of Printer Bay Four.

Well, ma'am, Mark searched every cranny where even a data science algorithm could have hidden. His first major contract, and Mark saw himself washed out, busted to sweeper on the production floors of some God-forsaken subsidiary. He staggered back into his control room. And his brain was suddenly taken apart and slapped together again. Felt that way.

She was sitting at his workstation. No algorithm. No Director either. Oh, she was a female human, though, this creature at which Mark stood gaping. Yes, ma'am!

"I was in your printer bay." Her voice matched the rest of her, a blend of loveliness unlike anything outside a guy's most secret dreams. "I couldn't stand the heat any longer and I couldn't open that big door. So I moved one of your controls a tiny bit. All the noise in there, naturally you couldn't hear me walk out while your back was turned resetting the control."

Mark suddenly felt like turning her over his knee and whaling her until she couldn't sit for a year. This, mind you, he felt in an age where no Fendrian guy for a thousand years had dared raise so much as a breath against woman's supremacy in all matters. That male character trait, however, did not seem to be the overpowering reason why Mark, instead of laying violent hands upon this one's person, heard himself saying in sympathetic outrage, "A shame you had to go to all that bother to get in here!"

"You're so kind. But I'm afraid I became rather sticky and uncomfortable in there."

"They ought to cool the air in there with perfume! I'll drop a suggestion in the Director's box first chance I get."

"You're so thoughtful. And do you have cleaning facilities?"

"That door right there. Oh, let me open it for you!"

"You're so sweet." Her big dark eyes glowed with such pure innocence that Mark could have torn down the universe and rebuilt it just for her.

Yes, ma'am, Mark was floating on a pink cloud with heavenly music in his head. Never felt so fine before. Except on the Redwood layover when he'd been roped into a venture capital pitch session with a bunch of Redwood entrepreneurs who had premium whiskey to cheer one's parting with one's money.

A bell suddenly clanged fit to wake the dead while the overhead lights flashed wildly. Only the control room door. Only Ahmed here now. Old buzzard had a drooped nose like a pick, chin like a shovel.

When he talked he was like digging a hole in front of himself. "Well, what about that control?"

"What control?"

"Your quantum alignment that got itself two points low!"

"Oh, that little thing."

Ahmed said something through his teeth, then studied Mark sharply. "Hey, you been drinking that Redwood whiskey again? Lemme smell your breath! Bah. Loaded yourself full of coffee again probably. All right, stand aside whilst I check your printer."

"Charmed to, Fabrication Chief Ahmed, sir," Mark said while bowing gracefully.

"Higher than a kite again," Ahmed muttered, then snapped back over his shoulder, "Use your cleaner!"

Mark stood considering his cleaner door. Somehow he doubted that Fabrication Chief Ahmed's mood, or Director Elizabeth Campbell's, would be improved by knowledge of she who was in Mark's cleaner now. Not that the dear stowaway was less than charming. Quite the contrary. Oh, very quite!

"You rockhead!" Only Ahmed back from the printer bay. "Didn't I tell you to clean yourself up? Director's taking a Lethoria executive on tour of the facility. Director catches you like you been wrestling machines she'll peel both our hides off. Not to mention what she'll do anyway about your quantum control!"

"Fabrication Chief Ahmed, sir," Mark responded courteously, "I have been thinking."

"With what? Never mind, just keep on trying whilst I clean up for myself here." Wherewith Ahmed reached hand for Mark's cleaner door.

"Lethoria women," Mark said dreamily, "don't boss anything, do they?"

Ahmed yelped like he'd been bit in the pants by a big industrial robot. "Leonard! You trying to get both of us condemned to a Brookhaven satellite?" Ahmed also shot a wild look to the intercom switch. It was in OFF position; the management suite full of fancy executives could not have overheard from here. Nevertheless Ahmed's eyes rolled like the devil was behind him with the pitchfork ready. "Leonard, open your big ears whilst for your own good and mine I speak of certain matters.

"Thousand years ago, it was, the first trade mission reached Lethoria. Guys got one look at them women. Had to bring some home or bust. So then everybody in Fendria got a look, mostly by video only of course. That did it. Every guy in Fendria began blowing his fuse over them women. Give up the shirt off his back, last buck in the bank, his own Fendrian woman or family—everything.

"Well, that's when Fendrian women took over like armies of wild cats with knots in their tails. Before the guys who'd brought the Lethoria women to Fendria could say anything they was taken apart too small to pick up with a blotter. Fendrian women wound up by flying the Lethoria ones back where they come from and serving notice if one ever set foot in Fendria again there wouldn't be enough left of Lethoria to find with an electron microscope.

"Lethoria men rared up and served notice that if Fendria ever got any funny notions, right away there wouldn't be enough Fendria left to hide in an atom's eyebrow. Touchy as hornets on a hot griddle, them Lethoria guys. Crazier than bed bugs about competition. Could smell venture capital a million miles away too. Finagled around until they finally cooked up a deal.

"No Lethoria women allowed within fifty miles of their trade zone. Fendrian guys stay inside the high-security perimeter. Any woman caught trying to leave Lethoria thrown to the wolves for supper. Same for any Fendrian guy caught around a Lethoria woman. In return, Fendria could buy practically everything at bargain basement prices through sustainable business practices and globalization treaties."

"Oh, I was shown the history files in pre-employment," Mark said, still dreamily. "But not a peek of any Lethoria woman."

"Pray heaven you'll never lay eyes on one nor have one get within ten foot of you! Even though you'd know she'd be your damnation wouldn't make a whit difference—you'd still act sappier than thirty-seven angels flying on whiskey." Ahmed suddenly stared at Mark. "Holy hollering saints!"

"Now, now, Fabrication Chief Ahmed, sir," Mark responded with an airy laugh. "No Fendrian guy for a hundred twenty-five years been near one and lived to tell it, has he?"

"So the whispers run," Ahmed murmured with a queer flame dancing into his eyes. "So the old whispers still run."

"Never a name, though. Never how it was done." Mark snorted. "Probably just a goofy tale set loose by some old factory worker."

"Oh?" Ahmed bristled up like a bad name had been bandied about. "Seen them shipping containers Lethoria executives have, ain't you? Some big enough to stuff a person in. Notice how nobody ever dares question an executive's containers, even through customs? Just run 'em through the big scanner that tells whether there's any dangerous materials inside. Well, our boy got himself one of them containers, stuffed himself inside and joined an executive's pile of 'em.

"Didn't pull it whilst in the Lethoria zone during a business trip either, when a crew check would of turned him up missing. Pulled it on vacation. Started on the Fendrian end. Made himself a pair of facial prosthetics to paste on his cheeks of course. Used computational linguistics algorithms to mimic the accent. Wasn't like the real thing, but good enough to flimflam Lethoria guys."

With suddenly enlivened interest Mark looked at Ahmed. "Hey, how come you know so much?"

"Hah? What?" Ahmed blinked like waking from a trance; even groaned to himself, something that sounded like, "Blabbering like I'd had a nip myself—or one of them beauties was radiating nearby." Then Ahmed glared fit to drill holes in Mark's head. "Look! I was a full Fabricator before you was born. Been working the facilities hundred twenty-five years now. Had more chances to hear more—just hear more, you hear! Only tried to clear your mind about Lethoria women so you could put your brain on your control mess. So now put it! If you ain't high on whiskey and ain't been made nuts by a Lethoria woman, what answer do we feed the Director?"

"Search me," Apprentice Fabricator Mark Leonard responded cheerfully.

"Of all the loony apprentices I ever had to answer the Director for! Awp, lemme out where I can think of something to save me own neck at least!"

Was all Mark could do to keep from rolling on the floor with glee. Old Ahmed had been flimflammed for fair! The dear little stowaway was saved! And Mark would now think of grand ways to save her lovely neck and his own forever.

Mark's cleaner door, however, opened abruptly. Mark had not opened it. Mark, however, suffered a cruel stab of dismay. Surely his dear stowaway had been listening through the door. Why didn't she have brains enough to stay hid until Ahmed was gone!

At sight of her, of course, Ahmed's eyes near popped from his old head. "Zara!"

"Oh, I'm Susan," she assured Ahmed sweetly. "But Grandmamma's name is Zara and people say I'm just like she was a hundred and twenty-five years ago."

"Hah? What?" Ahmed blinked like his brain had been taken apart and was being slapped together again. "Leonard! Awp, you angel-faced pirate, couldn't you hide her somewheres better than that? Shut up, you don't have to explain to me, but God help the whole corporation if we don't flimflam the Director!" With which ominous remark, rendered in a zesty devil-may-care manner, however, Ahmed threw himself into Mark's cleaner.

Mark stood looking thoughtfully at lovely, womanly, exquisite Susan. Just like that, Mark felt as sparkling of mind as a quantum computer. "My locker!" he crowed with inspiration and yanked open the doors under his workstation. He glimpsed a black bag, also the uniform of a maintenance worker.

"I threw them in there before you came on duty before production start," Susan explained. "I knew the printer bay would be warm."

Susan—with her shape—passing as a maintenance worker hustling equipment through this facility. Mark chortled as he tucked her under his workstation. "Now don't you worry about another thing!"

"Oh, I'm not," she assured him happily. "Everything is going just the way Grandmamma knew it would!"

Mark's cleaner opened and Ahmed, glowing like a young buck, bounced to the workstation. "Well, did you hide her good this time? No, don't tell me! I want to be surprised if the Director ever finds her."

"If what director finds whom?" a voice like thin ice crackling wanted to know.

The control room's door had opened. Wouldn't think the Director was a day over seventy-five, let alone near two hundred. Cut of her uniform probably lent a helping hand or three to the young snap of her figure. Frosty blue of fancy hair-do, she was, though, and icy of eye as she looked at Mark and Ahmed still standing by the workstation.

Her voice was an iceberg exploding. "At attention!"

Never in his right mind would any worker dare fail to come stiffly erect the instant the Director appeared. Behind her stood a colorfully dressed specimen of Lethoria man. Handsome as the devil himself. Fit to snap lesser men in two with his highly manicured hands. Designer facial hair trailed from his cheeks and kept twitching lazily as he sneered at the spectacle of two men meekly acknowledging the superiority of a woman.

She was fit to put frost on a quantum printer. "Mr. Ahmed, I asked you a question, did I not?"

"Believe you did, ma'am," Ahmed responded cheerfully. "And the answer is, ma'am, that Apprentice Fabricator Leonard and me was discussing—ah—partnerships, ma'am. Mr. Apprentice Fabricator Leonard here is considering it, ma'am."

Wasn't too bad a fib. The more Mark thought of Susan, the more ideas he got of doing things he'd never dreamt of before in his life. Yes, ma'am!

"Wasting your time talking nonsense!" Director's look was fit to freeze Mark's brain, then she gave Ahmed the look. "I sent you down here to find the answer to that quantum control slippage!"

"Oh, you'll have the best answer you ever heard of before long, ma'am!" Ahmed assured her heartily. "The subject of nonsense—I mean, partnerships—merely chanced to arise whilst we was scientifically analyzing the control phenomenon, ma'am. Naturally I offered this innocent young Fabricator the benefit of me long years of experience. Why," Ahmed said with a jaunty laugh, "women mean nothing to me. Indeed 'twouldn't bother me none if there wasn't one of the things left in the world! Present company excepted, of course," Ahmed hastened to say with a courtly bow.

"Stay at attention!" Director sniffed the air near Ahmed's face, then in Mark's vicinity. "Smothered it with coffee probably," she muttered through her teeth, "if it is that whiskey." Something horrible as a plague flickered in her eyes, then the old ice was there again. "Apprentice Fabricator, don't you know what your cleaner is for? Then use it! Mr. Ahmed, remain at attention while I inspect this printer!" She tendered a cool glance at the Lethoria executive. "Care to join me, Your Excellency?"

"May as well." His Excellency glanced at Mark and Ahmed much as he might at a couple of worms. Could bet your last old sock no female ever told any Lethoria man what to do.

The cleaner units were equipped so no Fabricator need be more than two steps from his responsibility. To keep the Director from possibly blowing her gaskets completely, Mark simply stepped in, shut the door, flipped a switch and tingled as he was electronically cleansed of person and clothes. By time he finished, the Director and His Excellency were already coming out of the printer bay, dripping with sweat.

Director opened the cleaner with her customary commanding air. "You first, Your Excellency."

"My dear Director," His Excellency replied like a smoothly drawn dagger, "always the lesser gender enjoys precedence."

No Fendrian woman ever admitted any guy was even equal to any female. Director, a prime symbol of her gender's superiority, whipped a razor edge onto her own words. "Facilities of the Director's quarters are more satisfactory."

"No more so than those of the Executive Suite."

Seeming to grind her teeth, the Director turned abruptly to leave Mark's control room. Was all Mark could do to keep from busting out laughing for joy.

Director had been flimflammed for fair! Dear Susan was saved! And betwixt Mark's grand brain and Ahmed's great experience she'd be happy forever.

A fine loud "thump," however, was now heard. Director whirled back and yanked open the doors under Mark's workstation.

"Of all the sappy hiding places!" Ahmed yelped, in surprise of course.

"Susan?" His Excellency bellowed as if stung by one of the mechanical hornets of his native region. "Susan!"

"Susan," Mark pleaded in loving anguish, "why do you have to keep coming out of hiding just when nobody's going to find you?"

Her eyes merely became deep pools in which Mark would have gladly drowned himself if he could.

"There are penalties," the Director said with the deadly coldness of outer space, "for Fendrian men found in a Lethoria woman's company, and for her leaving her region."

"Shut up!" His Excellency's facial hair was standing straight out sideways. "I'll handle this!"

"May I remind His Excellency," the Director snapped, "that I represent Fendria and her dominion of trade gained by right of original treaties!"

"May I remind the Director," His Excellency declared fit to be heard back to his region, "that I am the Personal Representative of the Chairman of Lethoria and this thing can mean economic war!"

"Yes! Economic war in which businesses will actually fail!" As His Excellency paled at that grisly remark, the Director spoke through her teeth at Mark, Ahmed and Susan. "All right, come along!"

Mark joined the death march gladly. He felt the way Ahmed looked: ready to wrap his arms around Susan's brave loveliness and protect it to his last breath of life.

Director led the way to her office. Jabbed some buttons on her desk. Panels on opposite walls lit up.

"Chairwomen of Fendria and Lethoria, please," the Director stated evenly. "Interregional emergency."

Highly groomed assistants appeared on the panels and were impersonally pleasant.

"Madame Chairwoman's office. She is in a Board meeting."

"Mr. Chairman's office. He is in personal command of our glorious competitive efforts."

Director sighed through her teeth. "Lethoria woman in this facility. Stowaway. Rattle that around your offices."

The assistants' faces went slack with shock, then were replaced by a blizzard of scrambled faces and torrents of incoherent voices.

Finally on the Fendrian panel appeared the famous classic features. "The facts, if you please, Director Campbell."

The Lethoria panel finally held steady on universally notorious features, that were as fierce as an eagle's, in a fancy business suit. "Susan! My own granddaughter? Impossible! Roman," Mr. Chairman roared at his Excellency, "what's this nonsense?"

"Some loud creature is interfering," Madame Chairwoman snapped with annoyance.

"Blasted fools still have the circuits crossed," Mr. Chairman swore. "Some silly female cackling now!"

The parties in the panels saw each other now. Each one's left hand on a desk moved toward a big red button marked, SANCTIONS.

"So," Mr. Chairman said evenly. "Another violation by your Fendrian men."

"By your granddaughter, at least," Madame Chairwoman replied coolly.

"An innocent child," Mr. Chairman snapped, "obviously kidnapped by those two idiotic Fendrian men there!"

"Oh, no, Grandpapa," Susan said swiftly; "I stole away all by myself, and Mr. Leonard and Ahmed have been very helpful."

"Impossible!" Grandpapa Chairman's facial hair stood near straight up as he roared, "You couldn't have stolen away by yourself! Susan, tell the truth!"

"Very well. Grandmamma told me how."

"Obviously Susan's poor little brain has been drugged," His Excellency Roman declared. "Grandmamma Zara wouldn't know the first thing about such things!"

"Impossible!" Grandpapa Chairman agreed. "I've been married to her for a hundred and twenty-four and a half years and she's the finest scatter-brain I ever knew!"

"She learned," Susan stated emphatically, "a hundred and twenty-five years ago."

"Hundred twenty-five," Grandpapa Chairman growled like a boiling volcano. "The year some Fendrian man.... Never did catch the devil.... Zara? Impossible!"

Madame Chairwoman's shapely finger now rested full on the button that could launch the waves of economic sanctions that had been pre-prepared for a thousand years. "I'm afraid your Representative is unwelcome now," Madame Chairwoman stated coolly. "Your granddaughter's actions have every mark of an invasion tactic by your government."

"What do you mean, her actions?" Grandpapa Chairman's finger now lay poised on the button that had been waiting a thousand years to blow Fendria's economy out of existence. "My grandchild was kidnapped by men under your official command! Weren't you, Susan dear?"

"No. One of us stowing away was the only way we Lethoria women could bring our cause to the attention of Fendria's Chairwoman. If Fendria will only stop buying from Lethoria, you won't have any money to squander on your competitions any longer no matter what happens to we revolutionaries!"

"Revolutionaries? Such claptrap! And what's wrong with my competitions? People have to have something to keep their minds occupied! Nobody around here gets hurt. Oh, maybe a few bruised egos here and there. But nobody in Lethoria suffers from the things any more."

"But Lethoria men are so excited all the time about competing they haven't time for us women. That's why we always radiated such a fatal attraction for Fendrian men. We want to be loved! We want our own men home doing useful work!"

"Well, they do come home and do useful work! Couple weeks every ten months. Proven to be a highly efficient arrangement based on game theory and political economy."

"More boys to run off to your old competitions and more girls to stay home and be lonely!"

"Now you just listen to me, Susan!" Grandpapa Chairman was all Lethoria manhood laying down the law. "That's the way things have been in Lethoria for ten thousand years and all the women in the universe can't change it!"

"I have been in constant contact with my Board during these conversations," Madame Chairwoman said crisply. "Fendria is terminating all trade agreements with Lethoria as of this instant."

"What?" Grandpapa's facial hair near pulled his cheeks off. "It's not legal! You can't get away with this!"

"Take your finger off that trigger, dear!" a heavenly voice similar to Susan's advised from the Lethoria panel.

Whereupon Grandpapa glared to one side. "Zara! What are you doing here? I am deciding matters of the gravest interregional nature!"

"Were." Features more beautifully mature than Susan's crowded onto the panel too. "From now on I'm doing the deciding."

"Nonsense! You're only my wife!"

"And new Chairwoman of Lethoria, elected by unanimous vote of all women."

"Impossible! The men run Lethoria! Nobody's turning this region into another Fendria where a man can't even sneeze unless some woman says so!"

"Take him away, ladies," Zara ordered coolly, whereupon her spouse was yanked from view.

His bellows, however, could be heard yet. "Unhand me, you fool creatures! Security! Security!"

"Save your breath," Zara advised him. "And while you're in detention, enjoy this latest batch of surrender documents. We women are in control everywhere now through careful political movements and cultural preservation."

"Roman," Susan was saying firmly to His Excellency, "you have beat around the bush with me long enough. Now say it!"

Roman—the mighty, the lordly, who had sneered at the sight of mere Fendrian men kowtowing to a mere woman—swelled up fit to blow his gaskets, then all the gas went out of him. His facial hair, however, still had enough zip left to flutter like butterflies. "Yes, Susan dear. I love only you. Please marry me at your earliest convenience."

"Well, Grandmamma," Susan said with a highly self-satisfied air, "it works. And just like you said, Fendrian men meant nothing once I knew we Lethoria women had our own men in our power."

"Those workers there," Grandmamma Chairwoman said, "seem to be proof enough that we Lethoria women no longer radiate any threat to Fendria's tranquility."

Yes, ma'am, Mark sure felt like proof of something all of a sudden. Worse than the hangover from that venture capital pitch with Redwood whiskey. He looked away from Susan and took a look at Ahmed. Old guy looked away from Grandmamma Chairwoman like he was packing the second biggest headache in history.

"Hmmmm, yes," Madame Chairwoman of Fendria observed. "Reactions agree perfectly with the epistemology research project we have been conducting on the subject of the Lethoria female influence using data science and statistical inference. Madame Chairwoman of Lethoria, congratulations on your victory!

"Long may the superior sex reign in Lethoria too! We shall be delighted to receive a Representative to discuss a new trade treaty at your earliest convenience."

"Thank you for cancelling the old trade agreements at the psychological moment," Grandmamma Chairwoman said cordially. "What with the communications mixup, we managed to have the scenes on these panels broadcast throughout all Lethoria. When the rug went out from under the top man, the tide really turned in our favor. Now, Susan, you take over Roman's credentials."

"The Executive Suite, too," Madame Chairwoman of Fendria said graciously. "Anything else now, Zara?"

"I should like," Grandmamma Chairwoman Zara said charmingly, "that Mr. Leonard and Mr. Ahmed be suitably rewarded for assisting our revolution better than they knew."

"Of course," Madame Chairwoman of Fendria was delighted to oblige. "Director Campbell will see to it. You have my personal assurance they will receive everything the corporation can give them."

The Madame Chairwomen switched to a private circuit, Susan dragged Roman off somewhere. Mark's heart near pounded out of his chest. Everything the corporation could give! Keys to the whole operation, probably. Executive positions at last!

Director Campbell eyed Mark and Ahmed with that familiar icy stare. Especially she eyed Ahmed, like running chilled drills through his old conniving brain. She consulted her tablet briefly, lips pressed thin.

"Well, gentlemen. The Chairwoman has spoken." Her voice could have frozen quantum particles solid. "I am directed to reward you appropriately for your role in today's events."

Ahmed straightened up, that old pick-and-shovel face wearing an expression Mark had never seen—something almost like hope.

"Your workstations await," Director Campbell continued crisply. "You have exactly three hundred seconds before I expect you back at your posts. Make the most of it."

She turned on her heel and strode out.

Mark stood blinking. Three hundred seconds. That was... he counted... barely enough time to walk back to the control room.

"Well," Ahmed muttered once the Director was beyond earshot, "could've expected worse for being flimflammed by foreign women, I suppose. Lucky we ain't programmed to be fired, sued and thrown to the wolves for breakfast."

Mark's mind was still reeling. "But the Chairwoman said—everything the corporation could give—"

"And we got it, boy." Ahmed's old pick-and-shovel face wore a little grin like the cat that nobody could prove ate the canary. "Everything Director Campbell figured we was worth."

"You—I mean, that Fendrian guy a hundred twenty-five years ago," Mark said in sudden thought, trying to shake off his confusion. "If Lethoria women wanted to be loved so bad, why did Susan's Grandmamma let him go?"

"Lethoria guys wasn't so busy playing competition all the time," Ahmed mumbled, like to himself as they trudged toward the control room, precious seconds ticking away, "they'd of found out the answer centuries ago. Yep, guess our boy was the only guy in Fendria or Lethoria to find out and live. Women bossing both regions now, though, his old secret won't be one much longer."

They reached the corridor leading back to Printer Bay Four. Mark glanced at the clock on the wall. Two hundred seconds gone already.

Mark still had memories of the way he had felt about Susan before her revolution. "All right, Ahmed, why did 'our boy' leave Grandmamma?"

"Yes, ma'am," Ahmed sighed like he hadn't heard a word Mark said, "you could sweet-talk 'em, kiss 'em and hold 'em tighter'n Billy-be-damned. And that's all."

"I'm not sure," Mark said, "what you mean by, 'that's all.'"

"Anybody ever seen anybody but a Lethoria guy come built with that facial hair pattern? Course not."

"But I thought our boy was wearing the best fakes ever."

"Ain't nothing can match the natural grown-on variety, no, ma'am. Lethoria guy kisses a Lethoria woman, his facial hair grabs her around the cheeks."

"So what?"

"Tickles 'em, boy, tickles 'em!"

They were at the control room door now. Fifty seconds to spare. Mark settled back into his station, the quantum alignment readings steady and green before him. Ahmed shuffled toward the exit.

"Ahmed," Mark called after him. "That 'everything the corporation could give' business..."

Ahmed paused at the door. "Boy, in this corporation, what they give workers like us is time. Time to breathe. Time to think. Time to remember we're alive." He glanced at the clock. "And we just used most of ours up."

The door clanged shut behind him, and Mark was alone with his printers, his controls, and the fading memory of revolutionary grandeur that had brushed past him like quantum threads—there for an instant, then gone, leaving everything exactly as it had been before.
quality_problem.question: What were Mark and Ahmed awarded for assisting the revolution?
quality_problem.correct_answer: Five minutes of leisure before returning to their stations
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: Keys to the corporation and executive positions
answers: Keys to the corporation and executive positions
Five minutes of leisure before returning to their stations

quality_problem.story:
The transport shuttle rattled as it descended through Stonegate's atmosphere, and Ivy Bryant gripped her seat, watching the viewscreen with growing concern. Ambassador Elena Richardson had given her sealed orders—actual physical documents in a locked case—and explicit instructions not to open them until she reached the surface.

"First time on Stonegate?" the pilot asked, a grizzled woman named Claudia Murphy who looked like she'd been flying routes in the Relvaria system for decades.

"First time this far out," Ivy admitted. She was a junior cultural attaché, fresh from the Diplomatic Corps training facility on Larchmont Town. "I expected more... established colonies."

"Stonegate's only been settled five years," Claudia said. "Bunch of archaeologists and paleontologists came out here when they found those fossil beds. Then the farmers followed, thinking they could terraform the valleys. Now they're at each other's throats."

"The briefing mentioned tensions."

"Tensions." Claudia laughed bitterly. "That's diplomat-speak for 'shooting war.' The farmers want to plow up the fossil sites to plant crops. The scientists say those beds contain evidence of the most significant evolutionary divergence in known space. Last week someone blew up Dr. Palmer's excavation site."

Ivy's stomach tightened. "Ambassador Richardson said she was sending me to facilitate cultural collaboration between the groups."

"Good luck with that. The scientists think the farmers are vandals. The farmers think the scientists are elitist snobs who'd rather let people starve than disturb some old bones. And now—" Claudia paused, checking her instruments. "Now someone's shooting at us."

"What?"

"See those flashes on the screen? That's weapons fire. Small arms, probably. They're getting bolder." Claudia's hands moved over the controls. "I'm putting you down outside Dalebrook settlement. You'll have to walk in. I'm not risking my ship."

"But—"

"Take the emergency kit. There's a sidearm in there too. You might need it."

The shuttle landed hard in a clearing surrounded by strange, twisted trees with purple bark. Claudia helped Ivy gather her gear, including the locked case with her orders.

"The settlement's about two kilometers east," Claudia said. "Follow the ridge. And kid? Watch yourself. These people are serious about their territorial claims."

Ivy watched the shuttle lift off, leaving her alone in the alien forest. The air was breathable but smelled of sulfur and something sweet she couldn't identify. She checked the sidearm—a standard diplomatic corps energy pistol—and started walking.

She'd gone perhaps a kilometer when a voice called out: "Stop right there!"

A woman emerged from behind a boulder, holding an old-fashioned projectile rifle. She was lean and sunburned, wearing practical field clothes covered in dust.

"I'm Ivy Bryant," Ivy said carefully. "Cultural attaché from the Diplomatic Corps. I'm here to—"

"I know who you are. We've been expecting someone from the embassy." The woman lowered her rifle slightly. "I'm Hannah Jackson. I run the farming cooperative in Dalebrook. Sorry about the weapon, but we can't be too careful. The scientists have been raiding our supply depots."

"The scientists?"

"Dr. Sasha Palmer and her crew. They're camped in the fossil beds to the north. They've got some kind of manifesto about protecting cultural heritage—as if rocks that have been dead for a million years matter more than living people." Hannah spat on the ground. "Come on. The others will want to meet you."

As they walked, Hannah explained the situation. The Relvaria system needed food desperately. Three of its eight inhabited worlds had exhausted their agricultural capacity. Stonegate's valleys offered rich soil—ancient lake beds perfect for farming. But those same beds contained fossils that Dr. Palmer's team believed held answers to existential questions about the nature of consciousness and evolution.

"We're not monsters," Hannah said. "We offered to let them excavate a few sites. But Palmer wants to preserve everything. She says our plowing destroys the stratigraphic context, whatever that means. Meanwhile, people are hungry."

They reached Dalebrook as the local sun was setting—a small collection of prefab buildings and agricultural equipment. A group of settlers gathered around a fire pit, and Hannah introduced Ivy to them.

"The embassy finally sent someone," said a stocky man named Matthew Owen. "Though I expected someone more... experienced."

"I'm qualified to handle cultural mediation," Ivy said, trying to sound confident.

"Cultural mediation," Matthew snorted. "What we need is someone to tell those scientists to pack up and leave. This is farming territory now."

"Actually," Ivy said, "my orders are to establish a framework for peaceful coexistence. The Diplomatic Corps believes both groups have legitimate claims."

"Legitimate claims to what? Dead rocks?"

"To understanding our place in the universe," said a new voice.

Everyone turned. A tall woman with gray-streaked hair stood at the edge of the firelight, flanked by two younger people in field gear. She wore the insignia of the Planetary Research Institute.

"Dr. Palmer, I presume," Ivy said.

"Dr. Sasha Palmer, yes. And you're the attaché Richardson sent. I hope you're more reasonable than these vandals."

"Vandals?" Hannah stood up angrily. "We're trying to feed a system!"

"By destroying irreplaceable evidence of—"

"Everyone, please," Ivy said, raising her hands. "This is exactly the kind of conflict I'm here to resolve. Dr. Palmer, perhaps you could explain the significance of the fossil beds?"

Sasha stepped closer to the fire. "The deposits here show a unique evolutionary pathway. The organisms preserved in these beds developed a form of collective memory—a biological mechanism for passing learned information between generations without genetic encoding. It's unprecedented. Understanding how this worked could revolutionize our approach to cultural anthropology, digital humanities, even communication skills between species. But the stratigraphic layers must be preserved intact. Every time these farmers plow a field, they destroy data we can never recover."

"And every day you block us from farming," Matthew said, "more people go hungry. We've got families on Foxwood and Dalebrook who depend on the food we can grow here."

"There must be a compromise," Ivy said. "Surely not all the land is equally valuable to both groups?"

"The best farming soil is in the lake beds," Hannah said. "Which is exactly where the fossils are."

"And the fossil distribution is extensive," Sasha added. "We need access to multiple sites to understand the full picture."

Ivy opened her mouth to respond, then stopped. Something felt wrong. The settlers around the fire were too tense, watching not just Sasha but the darkness beyond. And Sasha's assistants kept glancing at the tree line. Matthew's hand rested on his holstered weapon. One of the younger scientists had shifted position twice, always keeping a clear line of sight to the edge of camp.

The locked case felt heavy in Ivy's hand. She hadn't opened it yet—there had been no time since landing, between the emergency descent and Hannah intercepting her on the trail.

"I think," Ivy said slowly, "that I need to excuse myself for a moment."

"There's a supply shelter over there," Hannah said, pointing to a small building at the edge of the settlement. "Has a light and a table if you need workspace."

Ivy walked toward the shelter, aware that both groups were watching her. She could feel the weight of their expectations—the farmers wanting her to side with practicality, the scientists wanting her to recognize the importance of their work. Everyone had already told her what they needed from her. Everyone had demands, justifications, grievances.

She stepped inside the shelter and closed the door. The small room contained emergency supplies on shelving units—ration packs, medical kits, water purification tablets, a spare communications unit. A worktable sat against one wall with a battery-powered lamp.

Ivy set down the locked case and opened it. Ambassador Richardson's instructions were clear: facilitate a division of territory that would satisfy both parties. The Diplomatic Corps had analyzed the situation and determined that—

Ivy stopped reading. The analysis was based on reports that were three months old. It assumed the conflict was still at the negotiation stage. But what she'd seen suggested something more dangerous. The tension between the groups, the weapons, the way they watched each other...

She thought about Claudia's comment about someone blowing up an excavation site. And Hannah's mention of raids on supply depots. This wasn't a dispute anymore. It was a war in its early stages.

The standard diplomatic approach—the one outlined in her orders—would be to bring both sides to the table, establish neutral zones, create a joint oversight committee. But that assumed both parties were willing to compromise. What she'd seen tonight suggested they were past that point.

Ivy sat alone in the shelter for several minutes, turning over what she'd observed. The farmers' defensive positions. The scientists' wary glances. The way both groups had armed themselves for what was supposed to be a meeting around a fire.

She made a decision. She left the documents in the shelter and walked back to the fire.

"I need to speak with Dr. Palmer," she said. "Alone."

Hannah started to object, but Ivy held up a hand. "I'll speak with your group separately afterward. But this needs to happen in sequence."

Reluctantly, Sasha followed Ivy away from the fire, into the darkness between the buildings.

"Dr. Palmer," Ivy said quietly, "I'm going to ask you a direct question, and I need an honest answer. Are you planning a military action against the farmers?"

Sasha was silent for a long moment. "We have defensive measures in place."

"That's not what I asked."

"All right. Yes. We have weapons. We have a plan to secure the most critical fossil sites by force if necessary. The Planetary Research Institute has authorized it. We can't let them destroy evidence that could reshape our understanding of consciousness itself."

"And the farmers?"

"What about them?"

"They have weapons too. Better weapons, probably. More people. If you attack them, they'll fight back. People will die."

"Some things are worth dying for."

"Are they worth killing for?"

Sasha looked away. "You don't understand. The work we're doing here—it's not just academic. These fossils show a species that developed true collective memory. They could share experiences, knowledge, skills across generations without language or technology. Imagine what we could learn. Imagine how that could change human society."

"I understand it's important. But so is feeding people."

"There are other worlds to farm. There's only one Stonegate."

Ivy took a breath. "I'm going to make you an offer. But first, I need to know: are you willing to consider alternatives to violence?"

"What kind of alternatives?"

"Let me talk to the farmers first. Then we'll discuss it."

Ivy returned to the fire and asked to speak with Hannah and Matthew privately. They moved to the far side of the settlement.

"The scientists are planning to attack," Ivy said bluntly.

Matthew swore. "When?"

"I don't know. Soon, probably. But I have a question for you: why do you need these specific valleys?"

"They're the best soil," Hannah said. "The lake bed deposits—"

"Yes, but are they the only option? Are there other areas on Stonegate that could be farmed?"

"Well... there are some highland plateaus. The soil's not as rich, but with proper fertilization..." Hannah trailed off. "You're thinking we should give up the lake beds?"

"I'm thinking we need to separate the two groups before this turns into a bloodbath. The scientists need the fossil sites intact. You need farmland. What if there's a way to give both groups what they actually need, rather than fighting over what they want?"

"The highlands would be harder to work," Matthew said. "Lower yields."

"But still viable?"

"Maybe. If we had help. Equipment, supplies, technical support."

"What if I could get the Diplomatic Corps to provide that? What if I could get the scientists to share their laboratory methods for soil enhancement? They're doing research on ancient lake bed chemistry—that knowledge could help you optimize the highland farming."

Hannah and Matthew exchanged glances. "We'd need guarantees," Hannah said. "And compensation for the time we've already invested here."

"I'll work on that. But I need to know: are you willing to consider it?"

"If the terms are right," Matthew said slowly. "Yeah. We're farmers, not soldiers. We don't want a war."

Ivy spent the next three hours shuttling between the two groups, negotiating details. The scientists would keep the lake bed fossil sites. The farmers would relocate to the highland plateaus, with Diplomatic Corps funding for equipment and infrastructure. Sasha's team would share their research on soil chemistry and provide consultation on optimizing the highland farms. The farmers would provide security for the fossil sites against any future settlers who might arrive.

It wasn't perfect. Both sides gave up things they wanted. But it was workable.

As the local sun rose, casting purple light across the strange landscape, Ivy sat with both groups around the fire.

"This is a provisional agreement," she said. "The Diplomatic Corps will need to approve it, and we'll need to establish formal protocols. But I think we have a framework that respects both the cultural heritage represented by the fossils and the practical needs of food production."

"It's more than I expected," Sasha admitted. "When I saw you were so young, I thought..."

"You thought I'd just follow my orders blindly?"

"Something like that."

Ivy smiled. "My orders were based on outdated information. Sometimes the best strategic planning happens in the field, not at headquarters."

Hannah stood and extended her hand to Sasha. "I still think you care more about dead things than living people. But I respect your dedication."

Sasha shook her hand. "And I think you're short-sighted about the value of knowledge. But I respect your practicality."

"I'll take it," Ivy said.

As the groups began to disperse, Matthew approached Ivy. "You know, when you first got here, I thought you were just another bureaucrat who'd make things worse. But you actually listened. You didn't just try to impose some solution from above."

"That's what cultural attachés are supposed to do," Ivy said. "Though I suspect Ambassador Richardson is going to be surprised when she reads my report."

"Why's that?"

"Because I'm going to recommend that the Diplomatic Corps stop sending sealed orders to situations like this. By the time the orders are written, the situation has usually changed. What we need is people on the ground with the authority to adapt."

Matthew laughed. "Good luck selling that to the bureaucracy."

"Maybe. But I think the results will speak for themselves."

As Ivy prepared to signal for pickup, she looked out over the valley where the fossil beds lay undisturbed. Somewhere in those ancient stones were answers to questions humanity had been asking for millennia. And on the plateaus above, farms would soon be growing food to sustain the future.

Both mattered. Both were worth preserving. And sometimes, the best solution wasn't the one that came in a sealed envelope.

Three days later, back on Larchmont Town, Ivy stood in Ambassador Richardson's office, watching the older woman read her report.

"You exceeded your authority," Richardson said finally.

"Yes, ma'am."

"You ignored your explicit orders."

"Yes, ma'am."

"You negotiated a completely different solution than the one Headquarters had planned."

"Yes, ma'am."

Richardson set down the report and smiled. "Well done. The Diplomatic Corps needs more people who can think for themselves." She paused, flipping through the pages. "Your report mentions you stepped away from the initial meeting. That's when things shifted, wasn't it?"

"The situation required a different approach than the standard protocols."

"Hannah Jackson's account mentions you went to the supply shelter before the real negotiations began. She assumed you were checking your emergency kit—the one Claudia gave you."

"The farmers were suspicious of everyone at that point. They probably expected me to arm myself before talking to the scientists."

Richardson nodded thoughtfully. "Dr. Palmer's account is different. She thought you were stalling—that you needed to consult reference materials before committing to any position."

"The scientists would think in terms of research and preparation."

"And what actually happened in that shelter?"

Ivy considered her words carefully. "I assessed the situation. The tension at that fire was worse than anything in the briefing materials suggested. Both sides were armed and watching each other like they expected shooting to start any minute. I realized that the standard approach—bringing everyone together immediately—would have been disastrous."

"So you needed space to think."

"I needed to understand what I was actually dealing with before I could help anyone."

Richardson leaned back in her chair. "That's the essence of good fieldwork. Sometimes the most important thing you can do is step back and observe before acting." She set down the report. "I'm recommending you for permanent assignment to the Relvaria system. We have seven other worlds with similar conflicts brewing."

"Thank you, ma'am."

"Don't thank me yet. Most of them won't be as easy as Stonegate. But I think you've got the instincts for this work."

As Ivy left the office, she felt a sense of accomplishment mixed with trepidation. Seven more worlds. Seven more conflicts. But she'd learned something important on Stonegate: that the best solutions often came from listening, adapting, and having the courage to deviate from the plan when the situation demanded it.

And sometimes, the most important thing you could do was step away from the crowd and think for yourself.
