quality_problem.story:
The alarm pierced through Elena Herrera's consciousness like a needle through fabric.

"Initiate now—initiate now—initiate now—"

Elena awoke in the cramped pod, her breathing labored and shallow. The reinforced walls had buckled inward during the impact, pressing against her chest. She estimated at least two cracked ribs. How long had she been unconscious? Days? Weeks? There was no way to know. Her right hand fumbled for the oxygen regulator and twisted it open. For several minutes she lay there, each breath a small agony.

"Initiate now—initiate now—initiate now—"

The neural implant had awakened her with its programmed alert, signaling that it was time to execute her mission. Twelve years after the corporate war stations had collided in orbit above Parkview Province, the board of directors had sealed her in this survival pod, dormant and waiting, to be awakened only when victory or defeat was certain.

The implant's insistent message confirmed the latter. She had expected nothing else.

Her task was simple: locate the relay station, input the authorization code that would activate the massive energy cores at the heart of the station, and ensure that the conquering corporation would share the fate of the conquered in the cold vacuum of space.

But survival instinct made her hesitate. Life, even measured in minutes, was too precious to surrender immediately. Her mind raced through memories of her past, seeking comfort in what had been.

For fifteen years, alongside her brilliant mentor Samuel James, she had watched the Sentinel Station grow from a skeletal framework into a city-sized orbital platform. But construction had proceeded too slowly. When the Helix Corporation's attack station, the Dominion, emerged from deep space to seize control of the Parkview Province territories and their renewable energy patents, the Sentinel was incomplete, undermanned, and vulnerable.

The defenders could only buy time and hope for a miracle.

The Sentinel, under Samuel James's command, launched everything it had—kinetic projectiles, electromagnetic pulse weapons, even experimental biotechnology weapons that had never been field-tested.

Then, during a catastrophic solar flare event beyond the asteroid belt, both stations lost navigational control and collided. Helix shock troops poured through the breached outer hull of the crippled Sentinel.

Elena stirred uneasily in the pod. The memories became fragmented and terrible here, dominated by visions of death and destruction. She recalled that final conversation with Samuel James.

"In thirty minutes our last shuttle bay will be overrun," he had transmitted directly to her neural implant. "Only one escape pod can still launch. Be on it."

"No. I'll die here with the others."

His tired eyes had studied her face with an unreadable expression. "Then die with purpose. Our research team is developing a protocol that will destroy both stations at the moment of our inevitable defeat. If they succeed, you'll have the responsibility of executing the final command sequence."

"There's a small chance you might survive," added Dr. Sasha Palmer, the lead researcher. "We're also working on an escape mechanism—not just because you're Samuel's protégé, but because this solar storm will prevent communication with Parkview Province for years, and we need someone to survive with our research data if our experiments prove successful."

"But you must be prepared to die," Samuel had warned with gentle finality.

Elena clenched her fists and forced herself back to the present.

That moment had arrived.

With considerable effort, she extracted herself from the damaged pod and collapsed onto the floor, gasping and clutching her chest with both hands. The metal floor was frigid. Apparently the Helix weapons had finally penetrated to the station's core, allowing the cold of space to seep in. It didn't matter. She wouldn't die of cold.

She reached out, searching for the critical component—the authorization key—and gasped in dismay. The secure container had broken free from its mounting and lay on its side. The explosion that had crushed her pod had been devastating.

With a sound of horror, she activated her wrist light and examined the container's interior.

It was completely destroyed.

Once the reality settled in, she composed herself and lay there, breathing carefully and thinking. She had no way to fabricate another authorization key. At best, locating the rare components and tools would take months, and during that time the invaders would be cutting their station free from the dead hulk that held their conquering platform in a metallic death grip.

She gave herself six weeks to accomplish this mutual destruction.

Within that timeframe, she needed to determine whether the energy cores were still functional, and whether she could safely access the reactor chamber herself to manually override the safety systems and remove the control rods. If that proved impossible, she would need to manipulate her Helix enemies into doing it for her.

Still prone, she located the medical kit and wrapped her ribs expertly. The cold was becoming unbearable, so she activated the thermal underlayer she wore beneath her Helix worker's uniform. Then she crawled on her elbows to the small hatch, disengaged the seal, and emerged outside. Ignoring the pain and using the side of the artificial rock formation that concealed her pod, she slowly stood upright. The air was thin and freezing. She adjusted her portable oxygen supply almost automatically while scanning the devastated hydroponic forest as far as she could see. Mentally, she remained alert for wandering hostile minds. She had left her weapons inside the pod, except for the three items in the small pouch at her waist, knowing that her greatest advantage in the coming struggle would be her apparent harmlessness.

Three hundred meters behind her, she detected the mind of a low-ranking Helix soldier from the Ashbury division. Quickly she identified him as a tired, brutish sergeant leading a cleanup squad through the charred stumps and broken branches of the small forest that had supplied oxygen to the defenders of this sector for years.

His name was Kessler. She could feel the shape of his thoughts—the grinding monotony of his deployment, memories of the initial boarding action when his unit had first breached the Sentinel's hull. The Ashbury division operated on six-month deployment cycles, she learned from his resentful memories. Standard protocol called for troops to rotate back to the Dominion's civilian sectors at the cycle's midpoint for leave, then return to complete their tour.

The sergeant couldn't see her green Helix uniform clearly in the dim light and apparently mistook her for a Sentinel survivor. His mind wrestled with a decision: Should he shoot immediately, or should he capture her? The civilian sectors felt impossibly distant. His unit had been pulled from the standard rotation and reassigned to cleanup duty—no leave, no relief, just endless shifts cataloging wreckage. The last supply convoy had arrived weeks ago, carrying only equipment and rations. No personnel transfers. His thoughts turned crude and predatory as he studied her silhouette. His orders were explicit—shoot on sight. Yes, he would shoot.

Elena turned in profile to the plasma rifle and stretched languorously, hoping her grimace of pain wasn't visible. With satisfaction, she sensed a sudden shift in the sergeant's intentions. The weapon lowered, and the man began circling to approach from behind. He didn't alert his squad. He wanted her first. He had noticed her uniform, but that didn't deter him. Afterward, he would summon the squad. Finally, they would kill her and move on. Female support personnel had no business in combat zones anyway.

His mind was a cesspool of frustrated desire. She caught fragments of memory—the entertainment district on the Dominion's residential ring, the last time he'd had shore leave before this deployment began. Then nothing but male troops and the charred remains of the enemy. His resentment flared as he remembered the reassignment order that had come down halfway through the cycle, condemning his squad to cleanup operations instead of the expected rotation home. Three months since that order had arrived. Three months of crawling through wreckage with nothing to show for it.

Hips swaying deliberately, Elena walked into the shattered grove. The man moved faster, still attempting stealth. Most of the overhead lighting panels had been destroyed, and visibility was poor. He wasn't surprised when he lost sight of his target. He continued forward rapidly but cautiously, picking his way through charred and fallen branches, confident she would reappear soon. He had advanced barely twenty meters when a howl of unbearable agony erupted in his mind, and consciousness fled.

She fought for survival beneath that damaged ceiling.

Breathing heavily from the mental effort, Elena emerged from behind a massive blackened tree trunk and hurried to the unconscious man. For individuals with IQs below 100, telepathic cortical disruption was quite effective. With clinical efficiency and no trace of revulsion, she stripped the foul-smelling uniform from the man, then took his weapon, reduced the power setting to minimum, and burned a precise line across his throat. While he bled out, she quickly donned the oversized uniform, secured the plasma rifle, and started up the ash-covered slope. For the immediate future, it would be safer to pass as a Helix soldier than as any type of woman.

---

The interrogator leaned forward, scowling at the woman before him.

"Name?"

"Elena Herrera."

The interrogator's eyes widened. "So you admit to a Sentinel name. Well, Sentinel, you're charged with unauthorized transport on a supply vehicle, and you appear to be wearing both an infantry sergeant's uniform and a Helix support worker's uniform. Incidentally, where is the sergeant? Did you kill him?"

He anticipated a desperate denial. He would cut it short, have the guards remove her, and execution would follow immediately. In a way, it was unfortunate. The woman was clearly from a high Sentinel class. No—he couldn't entertain that thought. His modest salary couldn't support another woman in his quarters, and besides, he wouldn't feel safe with this calculating killer.

"Do you not understand the corporate language? Why did you kill the sergeant?" He leaned impatiently across his desk.

The woman stared directly back at him with clear blue eyes. The guards flanking her dug their fingers into her arms, as was their custom with uncooperative prisoners, but she showed no reaction.

She had analyzed the minds of all three men. She could handle the interrogator alone or the two guards alone, but not all three simultaneously.

"If you're not afraid of me, perhaps you'd be kind enough to dismiss the guards for a few minutes," she said, placing a hand on her hip. "I have valuable information."

So that was her strategy. Purchase her freedom by betraying fugitive Sentinel personnel. Well, he could extract the information and then execute her anyway. He nodded curtly to the guards, who exited the room, exchanging knowing smirks.

Elena Herrera crossed her arms over her chest and touched her broken rib gingerly. The interrogator stared up at her with sadistic anticipation. He would definitely attend the execution. His anticipation was interrupted by a horrible realization. Under the paralyzing force of a mind far superior to his own, he reached beneath the desk and deactivated the recorder.

"Who is the Occupational Director for this Sector?" she asked tersely. This needed to be done quickly before the guards returned.

"Li Flores, Executive Director of Ashbury Operations," the man replied mechanically.

"What is the extent of her jurisdiction?"

"From the station's core, outward six hundred meters radius."

"Good. Prepare for me the standard authorization that a support worker needs for passage to the offices of the Occupational Director."

The interrogator filled in fields on a digital form and applied an encrypted seal at the bottom.

"You will add in the section marked 'comments' the following: 'Skilled worker. Others will follow as they become available.'"

The man's stylus moved obediently across the screen.

Elena smiled faintly at the helpless, inwardly raging interrogator. She took the authorization, folded it, and placed it in a pocket. "Summon the guards," she ordered.

He pressed the button on his desk, and the guards reentered.

"This person is no longer a prisoner," the interrogator stated woodenly. "She is to take the next transport to the Occupational Director of Zone One."

After the transport departed, neither interrogator nor guards retained any memory of the woman. However, in the normal course of administrative procedures, the recording was collected with many others, carefully archived, and sent to the Office of the Occupational Director, Zone One, for audit review.

Elena was extremely cautious with her mental probe as she disembarked from the transport. The Occupational Director would undoubtedly be high-ranking and telepathic. She must not give any cause to suspect similar abilities in a mere support worker.

Fighting had passed through this area recently. Many structures were still smoldering, and many overhead lighting panels were either destroyed or obscured by slowly drifting debris clouds. The acrid smell of decontamination chemicals was everywhere.

She heard the sound of sporadic weapons fire.

"What is that?" she asked the transport operator.

"The Director is executing prisoners," he replied matter-of-factly.

"I see."

"Where did you need to go?"

"To the personnel office."

"That direction." He pointed to the largest structure in the complex—three levels high, reasonably intact.

She walked down the gravel path, which was stained here and there with dark sticky red. She presented her authorization to the guard at the entrance and was admitted to a makeshift waiting area, where another guard observed her impassively. The weapons fire was much closer. She recognized the distinctive reports of a Helix sidearm and began to feel nauseated.

A woman in the green uniform of Helix support staff entered, whispered something to the guard, and then instructed Elena to follow her.

In the anteroom, a grey cat examined her curiously, and Elena frowned. She might need to eliminate the cat if she remained here. Under certain circumstances, the animal could prove her deadliest enemy.

The next room contained a fastidious little man, evidently a supervisor, who was studying her authorization.

"I'm very pleased to have you here, Ms.—ah—" he looked at the authorization suspiciously—"Ms. Herrera. Please sit down. But, as I was just mentioning to Ms. Crawford here"—he nodded to the other woman, who smiled back—"I wish the field officers would make up their minds about whether they want you or don't want you. Why exactly did they transfer you to headquarters?"

She thought rapidly. This pompous bureaucrat needed an answer that would prevent him from verifying with the interrogator. It would need to be something personal. She noted the obvious dye in his eyebrows and sideburns, and the artificial way he had arranged hair over his bald spot. She crossed her legs slowly, ignoring the narrowing eyes of Ms. Crawford, and smoothed the back of her braided blonde hair. He was studying her covertly.

"The men in the combat zones are crude, Mr. Hunter," she said simply. "I was told that you, that is, I mean—"

"Yes?" he was the picture of graciousness. Ms. Crawford began dictating loudly into her voice recorder.

Elena cleared her throat, averted her eyes, and with effort, managed a delicate blush. "I meant to say, I thought I would be happier working for—working here. So I requested a transfer."

Mr. Hunter beamed. "Excellent. But the occupation isn't complete yet, you know. There'll be intensive work here for several weeks before we separate from the enemy station. But you perform well"—winking artfully—"and I'll ensure that—"

He stopped, and his face took on a hunted expression of mingled fear and anxiety. He appeared to be listening.

Elena tensed her mind to receive and deflect a mental probe. She was certain now that the Zone Director was high-ranking and telepathic. The odds were only even that she could deceive her for any extended period if she became interested. She must be avoided if possible. It shouldn't be too difficult. She undoubtedly had numerous personal assistants and would take minimal interest in the minor employees who amused Hunter.

Hunter looked at her uncertainly. "Li Flores, Executive Director of Ashbury Operations, sends her compliments and wishes to see you on the observation deck." He pointed to a corridor. "All the way through there, across to the west wing."

As she left, she heard all activity in the room cease. The recording and computing devices trailed off into watchful silence, and she could feel eyes on her back. She noticed then that the sidearm had ceased firing.

Her pulse was racing as she walked down the corridor. She felt a very strong probe washing over her mind casually, examining the artificial memories she provided: Affairs with officers in combat areas. Reprimands. Demotion and transfer. Her deception of Hunter. Her anticipation of meeting a real Executive Director and hoping she would allow her to perform for her.

The questing probe withdrew as casually as it had come, and she breathed with relief. She could not hope to deceive a suspicious telepath indefinitely. Li Flores was merely amused at her "deception" of the under-supervisor. She had accepted her at face value, as supplied by her false memories.

She opened the door to the observation deck and saw a woman leaning pensively on the railing. She gave no immediate acknowledgment of Elena's presence.

The Executive Director of Ashbury Operations was of indeterminate age, as were most personnel from both stations. Only the left side of her face was visible. It was lean and weathered, and a deep thin scar lifted the corner of her mouth into a sardonic expression. A slight paunch was developing at her midsection, as befitted a warrior turned to tedious administrative work. Her closely cropped black hair and the two gleaming blue-gemmed rings—apparently identical—on her right hand seemed to indicate a certain meticulousness and unconscious superiority. To Elena, the jeweled fingers represented an unnatural contrast to the woman's history and were symptomatic of a personality that could find stimulation only in unusual and cruel pleasures.

In alarm, Elena suddenly realized she had inadvertently allowed her assessment to penetrate her unguarded conscious mind, and that this probe was there receiving it.

"You are correct," Li Flores said coldly, still gazing into the courtyard below. "Now that the prolonged conflict is over, there is little remaining to engage me."

She pushed the sidearm across the railing toward Elena. "Take this."

She had not yet looked at Elena.

Elena crossed the deck, simultaneously grasping the weapon and looking down into the courtyard. There appeared to be nearly thirty Sentinel personnel lying about in pools of their own blood.

Only one person—a Sentinel officer of very high rank—remained standing. His arms were folded gravely across his chest, and he studied the executioner above him almost casually. But when Elena appeared, their eyes met, and he started almost imperceptibly.

Elena Herrera felt a horrible chill spreading through her. The man's hair was white now, and his proud face lined with deep furrows, but there could be no mistake. It was Samuel James.

Her mentor.

Sweat began forming on her forehead, and for a moment she felt that if she wished hard enough, this would be a dream. A dream of a tall, kind, dark-haired man with smile-lines around his eyes, who had taken her under his wing when she was a young researcher and taught her everything about field research, ethical decision-making, and leadership.

An icy, amused voice came through: "Our orders are to execute all prisoners. It is entertaining to shoot down helpless people, isn't it? It gratifies me to know that I am cruel and capricious, and worthy of my position."

Even amid her horror, a cold, analytical part of her was explaining why the Director had summoned her to the observation deck. Because all captured Sentinel personnel had to be executed, she hated her superiors, her own staff, and especially the prisoners. A task so revolting she could not delegate to her officers. She must do it herself, but she wanted her subordinates to know she despised them for it. Elena was merely a symbol of that contempt. Her next words were unsurprising.

"It is even more stimulating to require a trembling subordinate to execute them. You are trembling, you know?"

Elena nodded mutely. Her palm was so wet that a drop of sweat fell from it to the floor. She was thinking frantically. She could kill the Director and save Samuel for a short while. But then the problem of detonating the reactor remained, and it would not be solved more quickly by killing the person who controlled the reactor area. On the contrary, if she could engage her interest—

"According to our records," murmured Li Flores, "the man down there is the last surviving Sentinel officer within the station. It occurred to me that our newest worker would like to begin her duties with impact. The sidearm is adjusted to a focused beam. If you place a shot between the man's eyes, you may perform for me tonight, and perhaps there will be other nights—"

Elena seemed lost in thought for an extended moment. Slowly, she raised the ugly weapon. The doomed Sentinel officer looked up at her peacefully, without expression. She lowered the sidearm, her arm trembling.

Samuel James frowned faintly, then closed his eyes. She raised the weapon again, aimed with a nerveless wrist, and squeezed the trigger. There was a loud, hollow discharge, but no recoil. The Sentinel officer, his eyes still closed and arms folded, sank to the ground, face upward. Blood was flowing from a tiny hole in his forehead.

The woman leaning on the railing turned and looked at Elena, first with amused contempt, then with narrowing, questioning eyes.

"Come here," she ordered.

The sidearm dropped from Elena's hand. With tremendous effort she activated her legs and walked toward her.

Li Flores was studying her face very carefully.

Elena felt she was going to be sick. Her knees were so weak she had to lean on the railing.

With a forefinger, Li Flores lifted the mass of golden curls that hung over Elena's right forehead and examined the scar hidden there, where the researchers had operated on her frontal lobe. The tiny device they had created for her stirred uneasily in her waist-pouch, but Li Flores seemed to be thinking of something else and missed the significance of the scar completely.

She dropped her hand. "I apologize," she said with quiet weariness. "I shouldn't have asked you to execute the Sentinel officer. It was a poor joke." Then: "Have you ever seen me before?"

"No," Elena whispered hoarsely. The woman's mind was in hers, verifying the fact.

"Have you ever met my mother, Sasha Flores, the former Director?"

"No."

"Do you have a daughter?"

"No."

The probe withdrew from her mind, and Li Flores had turned moodily back, surveying the courtyard and the dead. "Hunter will be wondering what happened to you. Come to my quarters at the twentieth hour tonight."

Apparently she suspected nothing.

Samuel. I had to do it. But we'll all join you soon. Soon.

---

Li Flores reclined on her couch, sipping cold violet nectar and following the thinly-clad dancer with narrowed eyes. Music, soft and subtle, emanated from her communications unit, illicitly tuned to an officers' lounge somewhere. Elena made the rhythm part of herself as she swayed slowly on tiptoe.

For the last forty "nights"—the hours designated for rest and sleep—it had been thus. By "day" she probed cautiously into the minds of the office staff, memorizing area designations, channels for official communications, and the names and authorizations of occupational field crews. By night she danced for Li Flores, who never removed her eyes from her, nor her probe from her mind. While dancing it was not too difficult to evade the probe. There was an odd self-hypnosis in dancing that obliterated memory and knowledge.

"Enough for now," Li Flores ordered. "Careful of your rib."

When she had first seen the bandages on Elena's bare chest that first night, Elena had been ready with a memory of dancing on a freshly polished floor and falling.

Li Flores seemed to be debating with herself as Elena sat down on her own couch to rest. She stood, unlocked her desk, and withdrew a tiny data chip, which Elena recognized as media for an amateur holographic projector. She placed the chip in a projector installed in the wall, deactivated the table light, and both of them waited in the darkness, breathing rather audibly.

Suddenly the center of the room was illuminated with a sphere of light approximately half a meter in diameter, and inside the luminous sphere were an elderly woman, a younger woman, and a small girl of about five years. They were walking through a luxurious garden, and then they stopped, looked up, and waved cheerfully.

Elena studied the trio with growing wonder. The elderly woman and the girl were complete strangers.

But the younger woman—!

"That is Sasha, my mother," said Li Flores quietly. "She remained at home because she opposed war. And that is a path in our family estate in Cedarville, Ilvaria. The small girl I fail to recognize, beyond a general resemblance to the Flores line.

"But—can you deny that you are the woman?"

The hologram snapped off, and Elena sat wordless in the darkness.

"There seemed to be some similarity—" she admitted. Her throat was suddenly dry. Yet why should she be alarmed? She genuinely didn't know the woman.

The table light was on now, and Li Flores was prowling restlessly about the room, her scar twisting her otherwise handsome face into a snarling scowl.

"Similarity! Nonsense! That loop of hair over her right forehead concealed a scar identical to yours. I have had the individual frames analyzed!"

Elena's hands knotted unconsciously. She forced her body to relax, but her mind was racing. This introduced another variable to be controlled in her plan for destruction. She must make it a known quantity.

"Did your mother send it to you?" she asked.

"The day before you arrived here. It had been in transit for months, naturally."

"What did she say about it?"

"She said, 'Your widow and daughter send greetings. Be of good spirits, and accept our love.' What absurdity! She knows very well I'm not married and that—well, if I have ever mothered any children, I don't know about them."

"Is that all she said?"

"That's all, except that she included this ring." She pulled one of the duplicate jewels from her right middle finger and tossed it to Elena. "It's identical to the one she had made for me when I reached my majority. For a long time it was thought to be the only stone of its kind on all the planets of the Ilvarian system, a mineralogical anomaly, but I suppose she found another. But why would I want two of them?"

Elena crossed the room and returned the ring.

"Existence is so full of mysteries, isn't it?" murmured Li Flores. "Sometimes it seems unfortunate that we must pass through a sentient phase on our way to death. This foolish, foolish war. Maybe my mother was right."

"You could be court-martialed for that."

"Speaking of court-martials, I must attend one tonight—an appeal from an execution order." She stood, smoothed her hair and clothes, and poured another glass of nectar. "Some incompetent interrogator can't properly account for a female prisoner."

Elena's heart skipped a beat. "Indeed?"

"The fool insists he could remember if we would just give him time. I suppose he accepted a bribe. You'll find one occasionally who attempts some extra profit."

She must absolutely not be seen by the condemned interrogator. The stimulus would almost certainly make him remember.

"I'll wait for you," she said indifferently, extending her arms in a languid yawn.

"Very well." Li Flores stepped to the door, then turned and looked back at her. "On the other hand, I may need a clerk. It's well past hours, and the others have departed."

Beneath a gesture of mild protest, Elena swallowed rapidly.

"Perhaps you'd better come," insisted Li Flores.

Elena stood, unlatched her waist-pouch, checked its contents quickly, and then followed her out.

This might be extremely close. From the pouch she took a bottle of scent and rubbed her ear lobes casually.

"Unusual smell," commented Li Flores, wrinkling her nose.

"Unusual scent," corrected Elena cryptically. She was thinking about the earnest faces of the researchers as they instructed her carefully in the use of the "scent." The adrenal glands, they had explained, provided a useful and powerful stimulant to a person in danger. Adrenalin slowed the heart and digestion, increased blood pressure, and increased perspiration to cool the skin. But there could be too much of a beneficial thing. An overdose of adrenalin, they had pointed out, caused almost immediate pulmonary edema. The lungs filled rapidly with fluid and the victim... drowned. The scent she possessed over-stimulated, in some unknown way, the adrenals of frightened persons. It had no effect on inactive adrenals.

The question remained—who would be more frightened, she or the condemned interrogator?

She was perspiring freely, and the blonde hair on her arms and neck was standing rigidly when Li Flores opened the door for her and they entered the Zone Provost's chambers.

The interrogator sat in restraints, his face pale and drawn. Two guards flanked him. A tribunal of three officers sat behind a raised desk.

The senior officer spoke: "The accused has been found guilty of accepting bribes and falsifying records. The sentence is death by—"

The interrogator's eyes suddenly locked onto Elena, and recognition flooded his features. "That's her! That's the woman! She made me—"

His words choked off as his adrenal glands, over-stimulated by the scent and his own terror, flooded his system. His face turned purple, and he began gasping for air. Within seconds, fluid filled his lungs, and he slumped forward, drowning in his own bodily fluids.

The tribunal members looked at each other in confusion. Li Flores simply raised an eyebrow.

"Well," said the senior officer, "that saves us the expense of an execution. Remove the body."

As they walked back to Li Flores's quarters, the Director said nothing, but Elena could feel the probe examining her mind more carefully than before. She maintained her false memories, adding only genuine confusion about what had just happened to the interrogator.

"Curious," Li Flores finally said. "But I suppose stress can do strange things to the body."

Elena said nothing, but internally she was calculating. She had perhaps two more weeks before Li Flores's suspicions would grow too strong. She needed to access the reactor chamber soon.

Very soon.

Autonomous Combat Drones: Why Not?

If you can build an autonomous cargo drone, you can almost certainly build an autonomous combat drone. Some of the most powerful people in the military establishment have felt compelled to act against this threat. General Samuel James swiftly imposed a ban on Department of Defense funding for fully autonomous weapons research. Bills are in the works in both houses of Congress to outlaw autonomous combat systems--a step urged on all governments by international human rights organizations. Autonomous combat drones are taken to be either 1) a fundamentally dangerous technology that must be stopped or, at the very least, 2) a complex ethical issue that needs legislation and regulation. But what, exactly, is so bad about it?

Start by asking whether nations have a right to defend themselves. I say "yes." I have no moral right to tell other countries they shouldn't be able to protect their citizens, and I don't see that General James has that right either. When James says, "Let us resist the temptation to automate warfare," it comes from a man who has spent his entire career automating every other aspect of military operations. And for a military leader, making noise about autonomous weapons is pretty close to political posturing. It's an easy way to show sound-bite leadership on an issue that everybody is talking about, without much risk of bitter consequences. After all, how much federally funded research was stopped by this ban? Probably almost none, because James has maintained the previous administration's policy of minimizing federal grants for research in artificial intelligence weapons systems. Besides, most researchers thought fully autonomous combat drones were decades away--so, for the moment, there's unlikely to be a grant-request backlog. There is nothing like banning the nonexistent to show true leadership.

The human rights organizations, unlike the general, are known for their principled stands. They also openly claim the authority to decide how nations conduct warfare. I respect their freedom to advocate for their causes, and their followers' freedom to support their mission. But calling for secular governments to implement a ban, thus extending their power beyond those they can persuade, shows rather explicitly that these organizations do not respect the sovereignty of nations. The basic principles they follow were set down decades ago in conventions written before modern technological progress. Drones feature prominently in current military doctrine, but full autonomy does not. So their views on autonomous weapons are mid-20th century rules applied using late 20th century political philosophy to a 21st century issue.

If nations have a right to defend themselves, what right does international diplomacy have to limit the means? Essentially all modern warfare is done these days with technological assistance--in targeting, and often in execution. Truly manual warfare would mean 50 percent mission failure rates and make combat-related death the No. 1 killer of young soldiers.

True, some forms of technological help are more invasive than others. With current semi-autonomous drones, the target identification and weapon release are combined in the system but require human authorization. Less than two decades ago, a similar concern was raised over the ethical issues involved in "remote warfare." To date, nearly 30,000 such missions have been flown by the United States alone. Many military objectives have been achieved. Who has been harmed more than in conventional warfare?

The autonomous combat procedure is similar to current semi-autonomous systems. The only difference is that the human authorization step would be replaced by machine decision-making based on pre-programmed rules of engagement. What law or principle--secular, humanist, or military--says that one combination of human and machine decision-making is OK, but another is not? No matter how closely you study the Geneva Conventions, I don't think you'll find the answer.

Even if nations have the right to do it, is autonomous warfare a good idea? Suppose that every military force in the world stopped using human soldiers, and instead deployed autonomous combat drones. What would the world be like in another 20 or 30 years? The answer is: much like today. Autonomous systems would only execute the strategic decisions of people who are already here. Hating a world of autonomous weapons is hating the current military establishment. Never before was Pogo so right: We have met the enemy, and he is us!

A different scare scenario is a world filled with malfunctioning killer robots. We'll imagine Terminator-style scenarios, fearing rogue AI the way we fear nuclear accidents today. But even technological disasters have their limits. Military systems are not more prone to catastrophic failure than they are to human error. Besides, such a trend would correct itself quickly, because any military that deployed unreliable systems would lose battles and abandon the technology. The world has survived one malfunctioning nuclear early warning system in the Cold War, but give us reliable autonomous systems with proper risk management, and they'll seem a lot more trustworthy.

Autonomous systems already exist. About one in every 1,000 military operations uses some form of automated decision-making. We know them as fire-and-forget missiles. Scientific studies on such systems--deployed in various conflicts--show that they share many characteristics with human-operated weapons. Just how many characteristics they share is a contentious topic in military science. But technological determinism is largely irrelevant to the autonomous weapons issue. Despite how many or how few operational characteristics autonomous systems have in common with human-operated ones, they are different tools in the most fundamental sense. They have their own parameters, their own programming, and their own limitations. Should you be confused on this point, just ask a systems engineer.

Suppose that a defense contractor called you with news of a new autonomous system that could replicate your tactical decisions. Would that suddenly make you less of a soldier, less of a professional? It is hard to see how. So, why would a fully autonomous drone be different? Your autonomous system would be deployed in different conflicts by different commanders--like current semi-autonomous systems, only more independent. A weapon system's basic utility is not governed by how much human involvement it requires, or whether somebody else happens to use similar technology.

Semi-autonomous systems aren't the only automated tools in military life. Think about GPS-guided munitions or radar-guided missiles--if there's no human in the targeting loop, where did the decision come from? It's the military equivalent of delegation--which is to say that they are all partially autonomous, operating with pre-programmed parameters. Modern warfare is almost entirely dependent on such systems. The missiles used in combat have guidance systems, but they've operated with increasing autonomy for more than fifty years in the case of many weapons platforms. The same is true for many defensive systems. Go to a military trade show, and you'll find products with names like "Patriot Automated Defense System," a mix of sensors and algorithms to detect and engage threats without human intervention.

One recurring image in anti-autonomous-weapons propaganda is of some rogue AI launching a global war. Excuse me, but what system is going to launch such a war? Autonomous drones start out as tools under human command. Wars are far easier to start the old fashioned way--by political decisions made by human leaders. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori has worked well enough to send countless young men to their deaths through the ages. Why would we suddenly fear machines more than human judgment?

Remember that autonomy is not the same as artificial general intelligence. We don't get to make Skynet--we have to program specific responses to specific situations. Maybe we could create the perfect tactical system from analysis of Medal of Honor winners' decisions. Their judgment might--or might not--be replicable in code. But, suppose that it is. You might end up with such a cautious system that when a target appears, there is so much verification required that the opportunity passes. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily the way to win a war. And what about the logistics systems? The military has a lot more of them than combat drones. You could try to automate every function, including supply chain management, but what's the point? There's not exactly a shortage of logistics software.

What if a rogue nation deployed autonomous weapons for another thousand years? Sounds bad, but history shows that technological advantages are temporary. We have no more to fear from autonomous weapons in the hands of adversaries than we do from their conventional forces--which is to say, we don't have much to fear if we maintain our own capabilities. Technological superiority rarely lasts. Nazi Germany's wonder weapons didn't save the Third Reich, and the Soviet Union's technological achievements didn't prevent its collapse.

The notion of an autonomous system operating without any human oversight is quaint, but it is unrealistic. First, the system wouldn't really be independent--it would follow its programming. Second, is any military really willing to completely abdicate command authority? A persistent advocate might convince a military to deploy highly autonomous systems, but that is not much different from current cruise missile technology that operates independently once launched.

Fear of autonomous weapons is just another form of technophobia. We all agree it is wrong to discriminate against technologies based on unfounded fears. Calls for a ban on autonomous combat systems amount to discrimination based on one characteristic--the fact that no human is in the immediate decision loop. The most extreme form of discrimination is preemptive prohibition--autonomous weapons are so scary that we must eliminate them before they're fully developed with a ban on their creation.

What is so special about human-in-the-loop warfare anyway? Autonomous systems are the only predictable way to conduct operations, because they follow programmed rules consistently. Human decision-making is a crap shoot by comparison--some random mix of training, emotion, and fatigue. In evolutionary biology, this variation is thought to help species adapt, so to speak. However, evolution for warfare is driven by technology, because we use engineering to control the outcome of battles.

Whatever the concerns about autonomous weapons, the process of human command will always remain central. An expensive and complex automated system will never offer any real competition for human strategic thinking. The militaries most likely to deploy autonomous systems will be those in special circumstances--forces facing overwhelming numerical disadvantages who must use technology anyway, for example. Even there, many will maintain human oversight to ensure accountability. Another special case is where one side faces an adversary with weapons of mass destruction. They might choose autonomous defensive systems, rather than burden their forces with reaction times too slow to counter the threat.

The most upsetting possibility in autonomous warfare isn't rogue AI or unstoppable machines. It's that wealthy nations with advanced technology will deploy them against less developed adversaries. The common practice of using superior firepower to minimize one's own casualties reflects our natural human instinct for self-preservation. Autonomous weapons may resonate with this instinct and cause some nations to wage war this way. So what? Technologically advanced nations do all sorts of things that create asymmetric advantages, and international law is hardly the means with which to stop them.

The "deep ethical issues" about autonomous weapons mainly boil down to fear of change. Economic concerns are bad enough, and they are a factor here, but the thing that truly drives people crazy is loss of control. Millennia of warfare through human decision-making have made the average person instinctively distrust any system that removes humans from the process--say by automating targeting decisions. Autonomous weapons are less personal than human combat, but they strike a similar chord: Something has changed the fundamental nature of warfare.

Consider the case of Major Zara Francis, stationed in Northfield, Havencia. She commanded a squadron that relied heavily on semi-autonomous systems for reconnaissance and targeting. When I interviewed her at the Woodbridge Region military base, she expressed frustration with the limitations of current technology. "We have systems that can identify targets with 99% accuracy," she told me, "but we still require a human to push the button. In fast-moving situations, that delay costs lives--both ours and civilians caught in the crossfire. A properly programmed autonomous system could make better decisions faster than I can."

Major Francis isn't alone in this assessment. Colonel Patrick Stephens, who oversees drone operations from Victorville, Quendor, has been advocating for increased autonomy in defensive systems. "When we're protecting a base from incoming rockets," he explained, "every millisecond counts. Our current semi-autonomous systems are good, but they still require human authorization. By the time someone confirms the threat and authorizes engagement, the rocket has already hit. Full autonomy in defensive scenarios isn't just an advantage--it's a necessity."

The entrepreneurship sector has taken notice. Defense contractors in Ashbury, Lethoria, have invested billions in autonomous systems research, despite the uncertain regulatory environment. Rebecca Pearson, CEO of Advanced Defense Systems, argues that the ban on federal funding simply pushes development to the private sector and foreign competitors. "We're not going to stop innovation," she said at a recent industry conference. "We're just going to ensure that America isn't leading it. China and Russia aren't imposing similar bans. They're racing ahead while we debate philosophy."

Dr. Carmen McDonald, a specialist in military ethics at the National War College, offers a more nuanced view. "The question isn't whether we should develop autonomous weapons," she argues, "but how we ensure they operate within acceptable parameters. We need robust rules of engagement programmed into these systems, regular audits, and accountability mechanisms. Banning the technology doesn't make us safer--it just ensures we're unprepared when others deploy it."

The debate has also drawn attention from unexpected quarters. Sophia Reid, a social justice advocate who typically focuses on education reform, has spoken out about the discriminatory impact of autonomous weapons. "These systems will be deployed primarily against populations in developing nations," she warns. "It's a form of technological imperialism--wealthy nations using robots to wage war against people who can't fight back with similar tools. That's not just a military issue; it's a human rights issue."

Yet even Reid acknowledges the complexity of the situation. "I'm not naive enough to think we can simply ban a technology and make it disappear," she concedes. "But we need international agreements that limit how these systems are used, particularly against civilian populations. The globalization of military technology means we need global solutions."

The technical challenges remain significant. Dr. Paul Graham, who leads an artificial intelligence research lab, points out that current autonomous systems are far from infallible. "We're talking about life-and-death decisions being made by algorithms," he explains. "These systems need to distinguish between combatants and civilians, understand complex rules of engagement, and operate reliably in chaotic environments. That's an enormous technical challenge. We're not there yet, and rushing deployment could be catastrophic."

But Graham also notes the potential benefits. "If we can develop truly reliable autonomous systems, they could actually reduce civilian casualties. Humans make mistakes under stress--they misidentify targets, they overreact, they let emotions cloud judgment. A well-designed autonomous system doesn't have those vulnerabilities. It follows its programming consistently, without fear or anger or fatigue."

The meteorology of public opinion on this issue has been stormy and unpredictable. Initial polls showed overwhelming opposition to autonomous weapons, with 73% of respondents expressing concern. But when the same people were asked about specific scenarios--like using autonomous systems to defend against missile attacks, or to avoid putting soldiers in harm's way--support increased dramatically. Context matters.

Film production companies have certainly capitalized on the fears, churning out movie after movie depicting rogue AI and killer robots. These fictional scenarios shape public perception far more than technical papers or policy debates. Claudia Jackson, a media studies professor, has documented this phenomenon. "Hollywood has created a narrative about autonomous weapons that bears little resemblance to reality," she notes. "But that narrative is powerful. It taps into deep-seated fears about technology and loss of control. Facts have a hard time competing with Terminator."

The reality is that autonomous weapons, like any military technology, will be deployed by some nations regardless of international agreements or moral objections. The question isn't whether they'll exist, but whether democracies will develop them with appropriate safeguards and oversight, or whether we'll cede the field to authoritarian regimes with fewer scruples.

General James's ban may score political points, but it doesn't address the fundamental issues. We need research into autonomous systems--not to build unstoppable killer robots, but to understand how to make these systems safe, reliable, and accountable. We need international agreements that establish clear rules for their use. And we need honest public debate about the trade-offs involved, rather than fear-mongering and simplistic bans.

The proponents of autonomous weapons paint a picture of revolutionary transformation. Their promotional materials speak of systems that will reshape every battlefield, every engagement, every strategic calculation. Defense industry conferences feature presentations on "The Autonomous Warfighter: Transforming Military Operations Across All Domains." Marketing copy from contractors like Advanced Defense Systems promises that autonomous combat drones will "fundamentally transform how warfare is conducted" and "affect the vast majority of military operations within a decade."

Yet these projections deserve scrutiny. History is littered with technologies that promised revolution but delivered evolution. The tank was supposed to end trench warfare overnight--it took decades of doctrinal development. Nuclear weapons were predicted to make conventional forces obsolete--yet here we are with millions of ground troops worldwide. Even the much-hyped "Revolution in Military Affairs" of the 1990s produced incremental improvements, not the fundamental transformation its advocates promised.

When you look past the marketing language, a more modest picture emerges. The militaries most likely to deploy autonomous systems will be those in special circumstances--forces facing overwhelming numerical disadvantages who must use technology anyway, for example. Consider Israel's Iron Dome, a defensive system that operates with significant autonomy because human reaction times simply cannot match incoming rocket speeds. Or consider underwater drone operations, where communication delays make real-time human control impractical. These are niche applications driven by specific operational requirements, not harbingers of universal adoption.

The vast majority of military personnel will continue to operate with human judgment at the center of decision-making. Infantry patrols, logistics convoys, diplomatic protection details, humanitarian missions--these make up the bulk of what militaries actually do, day in and day out. An autonomous drone cannot negotiate with a village elder, cannot make the judgment call to de-escalate a tense checkpoint encounter, cannot decide whether a humanitarian corridor is safe to open. The core competencies that define effective military forces remain stubbornly human.

Some observers conflate two distinct questions: whether autonomous technology will exist, and how extensively it will be used. The first is essentially certain; the second is far more constrained than the hype suggests. Even in air combat, where autonomy seems most advantageous, pilots express skepticism about wholesale replacement. "I've flown alongside semi-autonomous wingmen in exercises," one fighter pilot told me. "They're useful for specific tasks--suppressing air defenses, reconnaissance. But the idea that they'll take over everything we do? That misunderstands what air combat actually involves."

The research conducted for military applications will yield benefits far beyond the battlefield, in fields from transportation to medicine to disaster response. This alone justifies continued development. But we should be clear-eyed about what military deployment will actually look like: targeted applications in specialized roles where autonomy provides clear advantages, not the sweeping transformation that both advocates and critics sometimes imagine.

Once the fuss has died down and further research has paved the way, autonomous combat systems will be one more option among many capabilities. General James's knee-jerk policy changes nothing in the short run, but it is ultimately a giant step backward. In developing systems that can make complex decisions autonomously, the computational linguistics and decision-making algorithms could be applied to countless civilian applications. Work in this area might help elucidate the process by which humans make tactical decisions and yield better training methods for our own soldiers, allowing us to improve human performance. Selfishly speaking, that would be more exciting to me than banning autonomous weapons, because it would help us all. That's a lot more directly useful than preventing the development of technology that might save soldiers' lives.

To some, the engineer laboring away to develop new weapons is a source of evil, never to be trusted. To others, including me, the engineer is the ray of hope, creating the tools that make our forces more effective and keeping our soldiers safer through that innovation. Various arguments can be advanced toward either view, but one key statistic is squarely on my side. The vast majority of military personnel, including those who express concerns about autonomous weapons, owe their lives to previous technological developments. They embody the fruits of military innovation. Don't let the forces of fear, ignorance, and resistance to change turn us back from research. Instead, let us develop--and yes, even deploy--new generations of technologies, which will enable us to conduct more precise, more humane warfare in the next age.

To ban this research is to let fear triumph over reason, to choose ignorance over knowledge. The future will include autonomous systems whether we like it or not. The question is whether we'll understand them well enough to use them wisely. That requires research, not prohibition. It requires thoughtful policy, not knee-jerk reactions. And it requires recognizing that the real danger isn't the technology itself, but how humans choose to deploy it.

quality_problem.correct_answer: Only a tiny fraction of operations, affecting those in specialized roles where autonomy provides clear advantages
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: The vast majority of military operations, fundamentally transforming how warfare is conducted

The Cascade Protocol
By ARIA LAWRENCE

"All right," I said, "what is computational linguistics good for?"

Dr. Angela Hughes, head of my Computational Linguistics Department, sat rigid in her chair, her dark eyes flashing with barely contained anger. Behind her on the wall were several framed certificates from prestigious universities, but right then I didn't care if she'd studied under Chomsky himself. I had been appointed dean and president of Clearwater Technical Institute to ensure the university stayed financially viable. I had a job to do, and I meant to do it.

She spoke with measured precision: "Computational linguistics is the study of language processing through algorithmic and statistical methods, Mr. Johnson."

I tried to make her understand my position. "Look, the venture capital firms who fund our research programs want to see practical applications. To them, computational linguistics sounds like something that translates instruction manuals—hardly worth millions in funding. We need to show them something revolutionary. Come on now." I smiled, knowing it would irritate her. "What are you doing that's worth real money?"

She stood up, her posture straight as a rod, and I could see her jaw clench. These academics always think they're above justifying their work in practical terms.

"This department's development of recursive neural frameworks for modeling information cascades through social networks has been recognized as a groundbreaking contribution to—"

The words sounded impressive, but I needed something concrete. I interrupted, "Recognized by whom? Other linguists? What can it actually do?"

She sat back down, her fingers drumming on her desk as she surveyed the books lining her office walls. "Well, our algorithms have been valuable to social media companies in predicting viral content spread, which they use for content recommendation and advertising placement. And several governments have contracted with us to model misinformation propagation patterns for—"

I held up both hands. "Please, Dr. Hughes! Government contracts for studying misinformation? That's not going to impress the venture capital crowd. They want disruption, innovation, entrepreneurship. What specifically has your department created that would make someone want to invest millions of dollars?"

She picked up a tablet from her desk, tapping it thoughtfully. "Fundamental research doesn't always show immediate commercial applications, Mr. Johnson, but its value is—"

"Then help me understand it," I said, pulling out my phone. "Explain it in terms I can take to investors."

Dr. Hughes smiled tightly. She knew her department was on the chopping block. The other departments—biotechnology, climate adaptation systems, advanced water management—all had corporate sponsors and venture capital backing. Hughes needed to prove her work could generate returns, or I'd have to consolidate her department into Computer Science.

She set down the tablet and leaned forward. "Information networks—whether they're social media platforms, traditional media, or word-of-mouth communication—have certain mathematical properties that determine how messages spread through them. Some messages go viral and reach millions. Others die out immediately. The difference isn't random."

Her voice took on the practiced cadence of a lecturer. "Throughout history, we've seen information cascades that seemed to come from nowhere—religious movements, political revolutions, fashion trends, financial bubbles. What we've discovered is that these cascades follow predictable mathematical patterns based on the network structure and the message's inherent properties. Using advanced computational linguistics combined with network topology analysis, we can now predict—and engineer—information cascades with remarkable precision."

"That's theory," I said. "Where's the proof?"

"Our models are already being used by several Fortune 500 companies for product launch strategies. The peer review process has validated—"

I raised my palm. "I need something more dramatic. A demonstration that would make venture capitalists sit up and take notice. Something that shows this technology can create real-world change."

She looked at me steadily, and I could see her mind working. "All right. Give me six months."

"Six months, and you'll show me something that will bring in funding?"

"Six months, and I'll show you something that will make you wish we'd never had this conversation."

I checked my watch and stood up. "That sounds ominous, but I'll take it. Could we discuss the details over lunch?"

"I'm afraid I have a meeting with the Water Management Department about their desalination project," she said. "But I'll send you a proposal by end of week."

"Fair enough," I said, shaking her hand. Her grip was firm, almost challenging.

As I left, I couldn't shake the feeling that I'd just made a deal with someone far more dangerous than I'd realized.

---

Three days later, Angela Hughes arrived at my office with Dr. Isaac Ahmed, a young postdoc from her department who specialized in memetic engineering.

"Anthony," she said, using my first name for the first time, "I want to show you something."

Isaac opened his laptop and pulled up a complex diagram covered in nodes and arrows. "This is a basic information cascade model," he explained. "Each node represents a person or communication hub. The arrows show information flow. Now watch what happens when we introduce certain linguistic structures."

He typed rapidly, and the diagram began to animate. A message entered at one node, and slowly spread to adjacent nodes. Then the spread accelerated, jumping across the network in an exponential pattern.

"That's a standard viral cascade," Angela said. "Now watch this."

Isaac modified something in the code, and ran the simulation again. This time, the message spread even faster, but more importantly, it triggered secondary cascades. People who received the message didn't just pass it on—they created their own variations, which spread independently while reinforcing the original message.

"We call this a 'resonance cascade,'" Angela explained. "The message is structured to trigger recursive sharing behaviors. Each person who shares it gains social capital, which incentivizes them to recruit others. The linguistic structures we've embedded create a sense of urgency, exclusivity, and potential reward."

I leaned closer to the screen. "This is just a simulation, though."

"For now," Angela said. "For the demonstration, we want to test it in the real world. We'll start small—a single community group in a small town. We'll introduce a carefully engineered message and track how it spreads. If our models are correct, we should see exponential growth following a predictable curve."

"What kind of message?" I asked.

"Something benign. A community improvement initiative, perhaps. The content doesn't matter as much as the structure. We're testing the cascade mechanism, not the message itself."

Isaac pulled up another screen showing several small towns in our region. "We've been analyzing social network data from communities across Ulvaria. Larchmont has ideal properties for a secondary expansion phase—high connectivity to neighboring towns, strong digital infrastructure. But we need somewhere more contained for the initial field work."

He scrolled through the data. "The town needs to be small enough to track carefully, but with enough internal social connections to demonstrate real cascade dynamics. We've identified four candidates."

"What about the ethics board?" I asked.

"We're framing it as organizational consulting," Angela said. "Heritage preservation methodology. Nothing that requires human subjects approval."

I studied the data on screen. "What happens when you want to stop it?"

Angela and Isaac exchanged a glance. "The cascade naturally exhausts itself when it runs out of new nodes to reach," Angela said. "In a town of a few thousand people, it should peak and decline within our six-month timeframe."

"Should?"

"Will," Angela corrected firmly. "The mathematics are sound."

Against my better judgment, I approved the project. After all, what harm could come from a community improvement initiative in a small town?

---

The heritage preservation society we identified was a sleepy group of about twenty retirees who met monthly to discuss local history and organize the occasional historical marker installation. It was the perfect test subject—small, stable, and utterly unremarkable.

Angela and Isaac attended one of their meetings, posing as researchers studying cultural heritage preservation methods. I joined them, using the alias "Henry Martin." We drove two hours from Clearwater into the rural heartland of Ulvaria, passing through Larchmont on the way—Isaac pointed out its central location, noting it would make an excellent hub if we ever wanted to scale the project.

The meeting was exactly as boring as I'd expected. They spent forty-five minutes debating the wording on a plaque commemorating the town's founding. I nearly fell asleep. The meeting hall was a converted farmhouse, its walls covered with photographs of the town's apple orchards from the 1920s. Someone had brought oatmeal cookies. A hand-painted banner read "Preserving Our Heritage Since 1987."

But Angela was watching carefully, taking notes. After the meeting, she approached a woman named Talia Zhang, who had dominated much of the discussion with her forceful opinions about proper historical documentation. Talia wore a button that said "Ask Me About the 1903 Mill Fire."

I watched from a distance as Angela showed Talia something on her tablet—probably the organizational structure we'd designed. Talia's eyes lit up with interest, and she nodded enthusiastically.

As we drove back to Clearwater District, passing through Larchmont again in the early evening, Angela seemed satisfied. "Ms. Zhang is perfect. She has natural leadership qualities and strong social connections in the community. She'll be our catalyst."

"What exactly did you tell her?" I asked.

"I showed her a new organizational framework for heritage societies—one that would allow them to expand their impact and funding. I mentioned that early adopters in the leadership structure would benefit most from the growth."

"Benefit how?"

"Social recognition, primarily. Influence. The ability to shape the direction of the organization. And we built in a small financial incentive structure—nothing illegal, just a modest stipend system funded by membership fees, with bonuses for recruitment."

Isaac added from the back seat, "The key is that the linguistic framing makes recruitment feel like a civic duty rather than a pyramid scheme. We're using honor-culture language patterns combined with community benefit framing. I've been running parallel simulations using Larchmont's demographic data—the model predicts even faster spread there once the initial cascade matures."

I felt a small twinge of unease, but pushed it aside. It was just a heritage society in a small town. What could possibly go wrong?

---

Four months later, I realized we might have made a terrible mistake.

I was in my office reviewing quarterly budget reports when my assistant buzzed me. "Mr. Johnson, there's a call from someone named Jonathan Gibson at the Ulvaria Regional Development Authority. He says it's urgent."

I picked up the phone. "Anthony Johnson speaking."

"Mr. Johnson, I'm calling about the situation developing in the rural Ulvaria region. We understand your university may have had some involvement in the founding of what's now called the Cultural Heritage and Economic Development Collective."

My blood ran cold. "The what?"

"The Collective. It started as a heritage preservation society, but it's grown into something much larger. They've taken over local government functions, rezoned commercial areas, and they're now proposing a regional expansion that would affect water rights for the entire valley. I'm calling because their incorporation documents list your university as having provided 'organizational consulting services.'"

After hanging up, I immediately called Angela Hughes. "What the hell is happening?"

She sounded tired. "It's growing faster than our models predicted. The linguistic structures we used were apparently more effective than we calculated. And they've started modifying the message themselves, making it even more virulent."

"Virulent? Angela, this was supposed to be a controlled demonstration!"

"It was controlled. But the thing about information cascades is that once they reach a certain threshold, they become self-sustaining and self-modifying. The people in our test community aren't just following our script anymore—they're improving on it."

I pulled up news from the region on my computer. The headlines were alarming:

"Rural Collective Announces Merger with Highpoint Historical Society"

"New Economic Model Promises 'Cultural Dividends' for All Members"

"Collective Membership Reaches 2,000; Larchmont Chapter Now Largest"

"Oakdale Origins: How a Small-Town Heritage Group Became a Movement"

I clicked on the last article and felt my stomach drop. The Cultural Heritage and Economic Development Collective had evolved far beyond a heritage society. They'd incorporated elements of water management (claiming historical water rights needed to be preserved), climate adaptation (arguing that cultural heritage included traditional environmental practices), and even film production (documenting their work for "educational purposes").

The article traced the movement's origins: Talia Zhang had given her first recruitment speech at the converted farmhouse where we'd attended that boring meeting. From there, the movement spread to neighboring towns within weeks. Larchmont, with its central location and digital infrastructure, had quickly become the operational headquarters, but the article noted that members still made pilgrimages to the "founding site" for ceremonies.

And their membership was growing exponentially.

I looked at the growth chart embedded in the article. It was a perfect log curve, exactly as Angela's models had predicted. Except it wasn't leveling off.

"Angela," I said carefully into the phone, "when does this stop?"

There was a long pause. "Theoretically? When it runs out of people to recruit."

"You said it would exhaust itself in the original community."

"It should have. But they've started recruiting outside the initial boundaries. The Larchmont expansion happened in week three—much faster than we anticipated. And they've refined the message structure in ways that make it even more compelling. They've essentially weaponized our research."

"Can you stop it?"

Another pause, longer this time. "No. The cascade is self-sustaining now. Any attempt to stop it would just make us targets. The social contract they've created makes opposing the Collective socially unacceptable within the group. Anyone who tries to leave or stop the growth is ostracized."

I hung up and stared at my computer screen. The Collective had just announced the opening of a branch office in Clearwater District.

---

Two months later, I sat in a bar with Angela Hughes, both of us nursing drinks we desperately needed.

"They've gone international," I said, showing her my phone. "There's a branch forming in Havencia. They're calling it a 'global cultural heritage preservation network.'"

Angela nodded slowly. She'd aged visibly in the past months. "The linguistic structures we created were designed to be universally appealing across cultures. We just didn't anticipate how effectively they'd be adapted and spread."

"Your models," I said. "How far does this go?"

She pulled out a napkin and drew a quick graph. The curve went nearly vertical. "If current growth rates continue, and accounting for translation lag between language groups... I'd estimate global saturation in about fifteen years."

"Global saturation? Angela, what does that even mean?"

"It means everyone on Earth will be a member of some branch of the Collective. It will be the largest organization in human history."

"And then what?"

She crumpled the napkin. "I don't know. The models don't predict what happens when a cascade reaches absolute saturation. It might stabilize into some kind of global governance structure. It might collapse catastrophically when there's no more growth to sustain the incentive system. It might evolve into something we can't even imagine."

I thought about the blockchain-based membership system the Collective had recently implemented, creating an immutable record of membership and contribution. I thought about their ventures into biotechnology funding, claiming it was necessary to preserve humanity's "biological heritage." I thought about their increasingly sophisticated decision-making algorithms, which they claimed were based on "collective memory" and "cultural wisdom."

"We created a monster," I said.

"We created a proof of concept," Angela corrected. "We proved that computational linguistics can engineer social movements with mathematical precision. We just proved it too well."

"Will anyone believe we didn't mean for this to happen?"

She laughed bitterly. "Does it matter? We did it. The fact that it was an accident doesn't change the outcome."

I finished my drink and ordered another. On the TV above the bar, a news channel was showing footage of a massive Collective rally in Highpoint, Yendor. Thousands of people chanting in perfect unison, their words shaped by linguistic structures designed to maximize emotional resonance and social bonding.

"For what it's worth," Angela said quietly, "the peer review committee that approved our research methods has opened an investigation. They're calling it a breach of research ethics."

"A bit late for that."

"Yes."

We sat in silence for a while, watching the world change on the screen above us.

"Angela," I finally said, "if anyone asks, I've never heard of that town."

She raised her glass. "If anyone asks, I've never heard of computational linguistics."

We drank to that, knowing it wouldn't help. The cascade was beyond our control now, beyond anyone's control. We'd unleashed something that would reshape human civilization, all because I'd demanded a demonstration that would impress venture capitalists.

The irony wasn't lost on me. We'd created the most successful startup in history—one that would eventually own the world. And neither of us would see a dime from it.

On the TV, the Collective's spokesperson was explaining their new initiative: a global cultural heritage database that would preserve the collective memory of all human cultures. It sounded noble. It probably was noble, in its own way.

But I couldn't shake the feeling that we'd fundamentally altered the course of human history, and not necessarily for the better.

The bartender brought our next round. "You folks hear about this Collective thing?" he asked cheerfully. "My sister just joined the Larchmont chapter—it's the biggest one, you know. Says it's going to revolutionize how we think about cultural heritage and community development. I'm thinking about signing up myself."

Angela and I exchanged a look.

"Yeah," I said. "We've heard about it."

After he left, Angela pulled out her phone and showed me the latest growth projections. The curve was steeper than ever.

"Fifteen years?" I asked.

"Maybe less. They're getting better at this than we ever were."

I thought about the metaphysics of what we'd done—created a social organism that had taken on a life of its own, evolving beyond its creators' intentions or control. It was like watching a new form of life emerge from pure information. And it had all started with that first meeting, in that farmhouse with the 1920s apple orchard photographs on the walls, where Talia Zhang had worn her "Ask Me About the 1903 Mill Fire" button.

"Do you think it's conscious?" I asked.

Angela considered the question seriously. "In a sense, maybe. It has goals, it adapts, it grows. Whether that constitutes consciousness in any meaningful sense..." She shrugged. "That's beyond my field."

"Beyond anyone's field, probably."

We finished our drinks in silence, two architects of the future who wished desperately that we could return to the past.

The Collective would grow. The mathematics were inevitable. And somewhere in the rural heartland of Ulvaria, in a small town that no one outside the region had ever heard of before all this began, Talia Zhang was probably giving another rousing speech about cultural heritage and community development, recruiting another hundred members, pushing the cascade forward.

The world would never be the same.

And it was all because I'd asked for a demonstration.
quality_problem.question: In which small town did the experimental information cascade take place?

quality_problem.story:
The Gravity of Deception
by Alan E. Nourse (Adapted)

The chamber was cold and sterile, illuminated by harsh fluorescent lights that buzzed incessantly overhead. Miguel Ortiz followed the towering Crystalline guard down the polished corridor of the detention facility, his breath forming small clouds in the frigid air. He pulled his Earth-standard thermal jacket closer, shivering as his eyes took in the transparent holding cells lining both sides of the hallway. His polished shoes clicked against the smooth surface, echoing in the empty space.

"How much farther?" he called out irritably.

The guard gestured vaguely with one of its faceted appendages toward the end of the corridor. The hallway suddenly opened into a larger space, and the Crystalline stopped before a reinforced transparent barrier. "I still fail to comprehend the urgency," it chimed in its resonant, musical voice. "We have treated the prisoner with all appropriate protocols."

Miguel peered through the barrier into the holding cell. A figure huddled in the corner gradually came into focus—a thin, wiry man with sharp features and calculating eyes. "Isaac?" Miguel called sharply.

There was a startled gasp from within, and Isaac Hunt suddenly appeared at the barrier, his face breaking into a cunning smile beneath his unkempt hair. "Miguel! I knew they'd send you! I could count on it!" He performed an exaggerated bow. "Not much hospitality to offer, but it's the best I can manage under the circumstances."

Miguel frowned and turned to the guard. "Privacy, please. Interplanetary Protocol Article Seven. And leave the lighting."

The guard chimed its displeasure but departed. "About time you showed up!" Isaac cried. "Lucky they sent you, friend. I've been in here for weeks—"

"Look, Hunt, we're not friends," Miguel snapped. "And you've been here for exactly nineteen days, six hours, and approximately twenty minutes. You're getting as loose with facts as your Crystalline hosts." He studied Isaac's haggard appearance through the barrier. The man's eyes were bloodshot, his clothes disheveled. Miguel's expression softened slightly. "So Isaac Hunt's in trouble again. You look terrible."

Isaac snorted. "These silicon-based bureaucrats don't understand the concept of proper treatment. Synthetic nutrients and recycled water, nothing more. I thought you'd never arrive! I filed an appeal with the Earth Consulate the day I was detained. What took so long? All they had to do was process the extradition, sign the papers, and arrange transport off Lakeside Territory. Why the delay? I've been rotting here—" He stopped mid-sentence, his eyes widening. "You brought the papers, right? We can leave now?"

Miguel stared at the con artist with a mixture of pity and contempt. "You're a complete fool," he said finally. "Do you know that?"

Isaac's eyes narrowed. "What do you mean, fool? So I spend a few weeks in this freezer. The deal was worth it! I've pulled bigger schemes before—remember that fusion reactor scam back on Earth? Had accounts in three different banks there, and they never touched a credit of it. This time I was smarter. Kept it all in one place, right here where I could access it the moment I walked free." He grinned. "Five million credits! That's enough to retire on!"

Miguel nodded grimly. "If you live long enough to collect them, that is."
