"What do you mean, if? The money's safe. Consulate protection—they can't touch accounts held under Earth jurisdiction."

"I'm not talking about the money. I'm talking about you."

Isaac's face fell. "What do you mean?"

Miguel moved closer to the barrier, his voice dropping to an intense whisper. "I mean that right now you are essentially a dead man. You may not realize it, but you are. You waltz onto a newly colonized territory with your bag of tricks, arrive here with questionable credentials and no proper authorization, with no understanding of the Crystalline culture beyond a few paragraphs of misinformation in the Colonial Guide. And even then, you're not satisfied with selling something legitimate, something the natives might actually need. No, nothing so straightforward for you. You have to run your usual high-pressure scheme. And this time, Hunt, you're paying the price."

"You mean I'm not being extradited?"

Miguel smiled coldly. "Exactly that. You've committed a crime here—a serious crime. The Crystallines are furious about it. And the Earth Consulate isn't willing to sacrifice all future trade possibilities just to bail you out. You're going to stand trial—and these beings want your head. Personally, I think they're going to get it."

Isaac stood shakily. "You can't trust anything they say. They operate on completely different principles than we do. You should see the deals they tried to make with me! I've never encountered such a complex negotiation system." He glanced up at Miguel. "They'll probably impose a fine and release me. I can cover any fine—I made sure to keep plenty accessible in the local consulate branch."

"A fine measured in your lifespan." Miguel's smile was unpleasant. "You've committed what they consider the gravest possible offense, and they're determined to see justice done. I'm afraid your con-artist days are over."

Isaac fumbled for a cigarette, lighting it with trembling hands. "It's bad, then."

"It's very bad."

Some hint of Isaac's usual sly grin returned. "Well, at least they sent you. Nothing like a good lawyer to handle a trial."

"Lawyer? Not me! Absolutely not!" Miguel laughed harshly. "I'm your advisor, nothing more. I'm here to prevent you from making things worse for the Trading Commission. That's all. I wouldn't get involved in a legal proceeding with these beings for anything!" He shook his head. "You're your own lawyer, Mr. Master-Salesman. It's your show. And you'd better start thinking clearly, or you're going to lose in ways you can't imagine!"

Miguel watched Isaac's pale face and shook his head. In a way, it was tragic to see such a transformation in the smooth-talking, confident little man who had talked his way out of more jams than Miguel could count. Trade expansion attracted scammers; it was inevitable that wherever rich and unexploited territories were opened, they would fall prey to fast-talking operators. They spread out from Earth with the first wave of colonization—the slick con artists who could work new territories unfettered by the legal restrictions that governed established colonies. The first ones in were the richest ones out, and through some peculiar quirk of human psychology, they knew they could count on Earth protection, however dishonest their methods.

Isaac had been one of the worst—or best, depending on perspective. Miguel had reviewed his file during the journey: seventeen confirmed schemes across six colonies, with suspected accounts scattered from Luna to the outer stations. His Earth accounts alone held proceeds from a dozen cons, though enforcement had never managed to freeze them. This Lakeside scheme was supposed to be his masterpiece, his retirement fund.

But occasionally a situation arose where the civilization and social practices of the alien inhabitants made interference unwise. Lakeside Territory had been recognized immediately by the Trading Commission as a commercial prize of tremendous value, but early reports had warned of the danger of wildcat trading on the crystalline world with its silicon-based, logic-driven inhabitants—warned specifically against the confidence tactics so frequently employed—but there was always someone, Miguel reflected bitterly, who didn't get the message.

Isaac puffed nervously on his cigarette, his narrow face troubled. "But I didn't do anything wrong!" he exploded. "So I ran a classic con. So what? Why are they so upset? So I made a few thousand credits, pulled some fast business." He shrugged eloquently. "Everyone does it. They do it to each other constantly. You should see how these beings operate with each other. My little scheme was nothing by comparison."

Miguel pulled out a pipe and began filling it methodically. "And precisely what sort of con game was it?" he asked quietly.

Isaac shrugged again. "The simplest, oldest scam in the book. Remember the old Earth story about selling the Brooklyn Bridge? Same concept. Only these beings didn't want bridges. They wanted energy—renewable energy sources for their expanding civilization. So I gave them what they wanted. I sold them energy rights."

Miguel nodded knowingly. "You certainly did. Exclusive rights to a hundred square kilometers of solar collection territory at a time. Only you sold the same hundred square kilometers to a dozen different Crystallines." Suddenly he threw back his head and laughed bitterly. "Of all the things you shouldn't have done—"

"But what's a patch of territory? The money flowed in beautifully. I had them deposit directly to the consulate account here in Nordavia—no cross-system transfers to trace, no delays, no complications."

Miguel shook his head hopelessly. "If you hadn't been so greedy, you'd have learned what territory means to these beings before you started peddling it. You'd have discovered other things about them, too. You'd have learned that despite all their logical processing and systematic behavior, they're not naive. You'd have found out that they're energy-dependent, and that three out of five newly formed Crystallines fail to secure sufficient energy sources to reach maturity. You'd have realized that they must compete for survival from the moment they crystallize. Anything goes, as long as it benefits them as individuals."

Miguel grinned at Isaac's horrified expression. "Never learned that, did you? And you've never learned other things, either. You probably never discovered that there are too many Crystallines here for the energy their territory can provide, and their energy requirements are so specific that they can't survive on anything that doesn't originate here. Consequently, territory is the fundamental factor in their economy, not currency; nothing but territory. To secure territory, it's every being for itself, and the loser dies, and their entire legal and economic system revolves around that principle. They've developed the most intricate and complex system of negotiation and exchange imaginable, aimed at individual survival, with territory as the value behind every transaction. That explains their approach to truth—of course they manipulate information, with an economy like that. They've completely redefined the concept of factual accuracy. Pathological? You bet they're pathological! Only a fool would present unvarnished truth when survival depends on being a more skillful negotiator than the next being! Information manipulation is their time-honored tradition, with their entire legal system built around it."

Isaac snorted. "But how could they possibly have a legal system? I mean, if they don't value straightforward truth?"

Miguel shrugged. "As we understand legal systems, I suppose they don't have one. They have only the vaguest notion what absolute truth represents, and they've dismissed the concept as impractical and useless." He chuckled maliciously. "So you went out and identified a section of solar collection territory, and sold exclusive rights to a dozen separate, self-centered, energy-starved Crystallines! Territorial encroachment is legal grounds for termination on this world, and twelve of them arrived at the same territory simultaneously, all armed with exclusive deeds." Miguel sighed. "You've got twelve furious Crystallines demanding justice. You've got an entire world demanding justice. And meanwhile, Earth's most valuable source of climate technology materials in decades is threatening to cut off supply unless they see you punished appropriately."

Isaac was visibly shaken. "Look," he said weakly, "so I made a mistake. What am I going to do? Are you going to stand by and let them destroy me? How could I defend myself in a legal system like this?"

Miguel smiled coolly. "You're going to get that devious little brain of yours working, I think," he said softly. "By Interplanetary Protocol, they have to give you a trial in Earth legal format—judge, jury, court procedure, all the standard elements. They think it's absurd—after all, what could a judicial oath mean to them?—but they agreed. The only problem is, they're determined to convict you, whatever it takes. So you'd better get those stunted wits of yours functioning—and if you try to implicate me, even slightly, I'll be gone so fast you won't know what happened."

With that, Miguel turned and walked toward the exit, leaving Isaac alone in the cold, sterile cell.

It certainly looked like a courtroom, at any rate. At the front of the large, temperature-controlled chamber was a bench with a seat behind it, and a small chair to the right. To the left was a platform with twelve seats—larger seats, with a railing along the front. The rest of the room was filled nearly to capacity with seats facing the bench. Isaac followed the Crystalline guard into the room, nodding approvingly. "Not a bad setup," he muttered. "They must have understood the concept quickly."

Miguel wiped the cold sweat from his forehead and shot Isaac a stern glance. "At least you've got a courtroom, a judge, and a jury. Beyond that—" He shrugged eloquently. "I can't make any promises."

At the back of the room, a door opened with a sharp hiss. Resonant, chiming voices filled the air as half a dozen Crystallines attempted to enter simultaneously. Isaac activated his translation device and watched the commotion in the anteroom with growing alarm. Finally, the question of precedence was resolved, and a group of Crystallines filed in, ordered by refraction index, moving across the room in flowing dark robes, their faceted faces gleaming with self-importance. They settled into the jury box, their crystalline bodies clicking against each other as they competed for front-row positions. The judge took his place with obvious satisfaction behind the heavy synthetic bench. Finally, the prosecuting attorney appeared, flanked by two assistants who took their positions beside him. The prosecutor fixed Isaac with a cold, multifaceted stare, then turned and performed what might have been a wink at the judge.

In moments, the room filled with the towering, geometric beings, their bodies refracting the harsh light as they jostled for seats, their chiming voices creating a cacophony of sound. Two minor altercations broke out in the rear but were quickly subdued by the security detail. Finally, the judge focused all his optical sensors on Isaac and struck the bench with a crystalline gavel until the activity subsided. The jurors shifted in their seats, exchanging what might have been knowing glances, then turned their attention forward.

"We are convening the case of the people of Lakeside Territory," the judge's voice resonated through the chamber, "against one Isaac Hunt—" he paused for a long, dramatic moment—"Earthman." The courtroom immediately erupted in angry chiming until the judge struck the bench several more times. "This—organism—is hereby accused of the following offenses," the judge announced. "Conspiracy to destabilize the government of Lakeside Territory. Deliberate termination of twenty-three law-abiding citizens of the settlement of Sunnydale, Ulvaria, during the third energy cycle following his arrival. Desecration of the Sacred Resonance Chamber of our revered Energy Matrix. Conspiracy with hostile elements to cause the unprecedented energy shortage in the Northern Sector. Deliberate exposure of his carbon-based physiology in a public space—" The judge struck the bench for order—"Espionage in coordination with the rival colony of Lakeside, Zelvaria, in preparation for territorial invasion."

Isaac's jaw dropped, the color draining from his face. He turned, wide-eyed, to Miguel, then back to the judge.

"The Jury Coordinator," said the judge efficiently, "will announce the verdict."

The Crystalline in the front of the jury box rose smoothly. "Defendant found guilty on all charges," it chimed.

"Defendant is guilty! The court will pronounce sentence—"

"Wait just a minute!" Isaac was on his feet, wild-eyed. "What kind of predetermined—"

The judge looked disappointedly at Miguel. "Not yet?" it asked, unhappily.

"No." Miguel's hands twitched nervously. "Not yet, Your Honor. Later, Your Honor. The trial comes first."

The judge appeared deflated. "But you indicated I should call for the verdict."

"Later. You must conduct the trial before you can have the verdict."

The Crystalline shrugged indifferently. "Now—later—" it chimed.

"Have the prosecutor call the first witness," said Miguel.

Isaac leaned over, his face ashen. "These charges," he whispered. "They're insane!"

"Of course they are," Miguel whispered back.

"But what am I going to—"

"Stay calm. Let them proceed."

"But those fabrications. They're all manipulating information, the entire system—" He broke off as the prosecutor resonated a name.

The Crystalline who took the stand was wearing a bright purple identification band that gleamed under the lights. It directed several optical sensors toward the prosecutor with what might have been anticipation. Then it began. "This Earthman criminal—"

"The oath," the judge interjected. "We must administer the oath."

The prosecutor nodded, and four Crystallines moved forward, carrying inscribed transparent tablets to the front of the court. One by one, the tablets were reverently stacked at the witness's base. The witness placed one faceted appendage on the stack, and the prosecutor said, "Do you swear to present information, complete information, and nothing but information, so help you—" he paused to consult the document in his appendage, finishing uncertainly, "—Energy Matrix?"

The witness removed the appendage from the tablets long enough to adjust its position, then replaced it and replied, "Of course," in an offended tone.

"Then present to this court what you have observed of the activities of this reprehensible being."

The witness settled back, focusing multiple sensors on Isaac's face, others on the prosecutor, and dimming a third set as if in contemplation. "I believe it occurred during the fourth cycle of the seventh rotation of Lakeside, Zelvaria (may the Energy Matrix deplete it)—or was it the seventh cycle of the fourth rotation?—" it directed a sensor apologetically at the judge—"when I was returning through the settlement toward my blessed territory, conducting my own affairs, Your Honor, after weeks of negotiating for the energy rights I was securing. Suddenly from the shadow of a structure, this creature—" it gestured an appendage at Isaac—"blocked my path with a threatening communication. He possessed a device I'd never encountered, and before I could process a response, he forced me against the wall. I could determine by the erratic patterns in his behavior that there was no logic, no systematic processing in his cognition, that I was—"

"Objection!" Isaac squealed, jumping to his feet. "This witness can't even remember what cycle he's talking about!"

The judge appeared startled. Then he searched frantically through his bundle of documents. "Overruled," he said abruptly. "Continue, please."

The witness directed all sensors at Isaac. "As I was stating before this disruptive interruption," it chimed, "I could determine that I was facing the most dangerous of criminal types, even for Earthmen. Note the asymmetry of his form, the irregularity of his features. I was paralyzed with concern. And then, helpless as I was, this two-legged abomination began to threaten harm to my blessed territory, dark threats of contaminating my energy sources unless I would reveal the location of our revered Energy Matrix—"

"I never encountered him before in my life," Isaac moaned to Miguel. "Listen to this! Why would I care where their Energy Matrix—"

Miguel gave him a hard look. "The Energy Matrix regulates everything here. It controls energy distribution. If it fails, someone's violated protocols. It's very straightforward."

"But how can I counter testimony like that?"

"I doubt you can counter it."

"But they can't verify any of it—" He looked at the jury, who were listening with rapt attention to the second witness. This one was testifying regarding the systematic destruction of twenty-three (or was it twenty-eight? Oh, yes, twenty-eight) Crystallines in the outlying settlement of Sunnydale. The massacre, it seemed, had been accomplished by a thermal weapon that caused catastrophic structural failure. A third witness took the stand, continuing the testimony as the room grew warmer and more oppressive. Isaac grew paler, his eyes becoming glassy as the accusations mounted. "But it's not true," he whispered to Miguel.

"Of course it isn't! Can't you understand? These beings have no regard for absolute truth. It's inefficient to them, foolish, a sign of poor processing. The only thing they respect is a negotiator more skillful and convincing than they are."

Isaac jerked around abruptly as he heard his name resonated. "Does the defendant have anything to present before the jury delivers the verdict?"

"Do I have—" Isaac was across the room in a flash, his pale cheeks suddenly flushed. He sat down carefully on the witness chair, facing the judge, his eyes bright with fear and excitement. "Your—Your Honor, I—I have information to present that will significantly impact this case. You must process it with the greatest attention." He glanced quickly at Miguel, then back to the judge. "Your Honor," he said in a hushed voice. "You are in the gravest danger. All of you. Your existence—your very territory is at stake."

The judge's optical sensors flickered, and he shuffled through his documents hurriedly as a murmur arose in the court. "Our territory?"

"Your existence, your territory, everything you value," Isaac said quickly, his words tumbling out. "You must attempt to understand me—" he glanced apprehensively over his shoulder—"now, because I may not survive long enough to repeat what I am about to reveal—"

The murmur quieted, all attention focused on his words through the translation devices. "These charges," he continued, "all of them—they're completely accurate. At least, they appear to be completely accurate. But in every instance, I was operating with full commitment, risking my existence, for the welfare of your magnificent territory."

There was a loud hiss of static from the back of the court. Isaac frowned and rubbed his hands together. "It was my misfortune," he said, "to arrive at the wrong colony when I first came to Lakeside from my homeland on Earth. I—I landed on Lakeside, Zelvaria, a serious error, but as it turned out, a very fortunate mistake. Because in attempting to establish trade in that hostile place, I made certain connections." His voice trembled and dropped lower. "I learned the terrible thing that is about to happen to this territory, at the hands of those rivals. The conspiracy is theirs, not mine. They have corrupted your Energy Matrix, manipulated it and deceived it, subverted its all-powerful regulation to their own malicious interests, preparing for the day when they could convince it to cast your territory into the catastrophic darkness of a ten-cycle energy blackout—"

Someone in the middle of the court burst into resonant laughter. One by one, the Crystallines nudged each other and chimed their amusement until the rising tide of noise drowned out Isaac's words. "The defendant is obviously manipulating information," the prosecutor resonated over the pandemonium. "Any properly functioning being knows that the Energy Matrix cannot be corrupted. How could it be an Energy Matrix if it could?"

Isaac grew paler. "But—perhaps they were very sophisticated—"

"And how could they manipulate it, when it processes, beyond any doubt, that it is the most perfectly calibrated system in all the Universe? And you dare to insult it, impugn its integrity."

The hisses grew louder, more hostile. Cries of "Terminate him!" and "Dissolve his structure!" rose from the courtroom. The judge struck for silence, his sensors angry.

"Unless the defendant wishes to consume more of our valuable processing time with these absurd manipulations, the jury—"

"Wait! Your Honor, I request a brief recess before I present my final statement."

"Recess?"

"A few moments to organize my thoughts, to structure my defense."

The judge settled back with a disgusted chime. "Must I?" he asked Miguel.

Miguel nodded. The judge shrugged, gesturing toward the anteroom. "You may use that chamber," he said.

Somehow, Isaac managed to stumble from the witness stand, amid riotous hisses and chimes, and staggered into the anteroom.

Isaac inhaled deeply from his cigarette and looked up at Miguel with haunted eyes. "It—it doesn't look promising," he muttered.

Miguel's eyes were troubled, too. For some reason, he felt a surge of sympathy and respect for the haggard con artist. "It's worse than I anticipated," he admitted grimly. "That was a good attempt, but you simply don't understand enough about them and their Energy Matrix." He sat down wearily. "I don't see what you can do. They want justice, and they're determined to get it. They simply won't believe you, no matter how skillfully you manipulate information."

Isaac sat in silence for a moment. "This information manipulation business," he said finally, "exactly how does it function?"

"The most skillful, most convincing negotiator wins. It's that simple. It doesn't matter how elaborate a construction you present. Unless, of course, they've determined that you simply aren't as skillful a negotiator as they are. And it appears that's exactly what they've concluded. It wouldn't matter what you present—unless, somehow, you could make them believe it."

Isaac frowned. "And how do they regard the—the most skillful negotiator? I mean, how do they respond to him?"

Miguel shifted uncomfortably. "It's difficult to say. It's been my experience that they respect him highly—perhaps even fear him somewhat. After all, the most convincing negotiator always wins in any transaction, so he secures more territory, more energy, more power. Yes, I think the most skillful negotiator could operate without any interference."

Isaac was on his feet, his eyes suddenly bright with excitement. "Wait a moment," he said tensely. "To present them with information that they'd have to accept—information they simply couldn't help but accept—" He turned on Miguel, his hands trembling. "Do they process the way we do? I mean, with logic, cause and effect, examining evidence and drawing conclusions? Given certain evidence, would they have to draw the same conclusions that we would draw?"

Miguel blinked. "Well—yes. Absolutely, they're perfectly logical."

Isaac's eyes flashed, and a huge grin broke across his haggard face. His thin body trembled. He started pacing excitedly, staring into space. "If I could only remember—" he muttered. "Someone—somewhere—something I studied."

"Whatever are you talking about?"

"It was a philosopher, I think—"

Miguel stared at him. "Oh, come now. Have you lost your mind completely? You have a serious problem here."

"No, no, I've solved the problem!" Isaac's cheeks flushed. "Let's return—I think I have the answer!"

The courtroom quieted the moment they opened the door, and the judge struck the gavel for silence. As soon as Isaac had taken his seat on the witness stand, the judge turned to the Jury Coordinator. "Now, then," he said with satisfied finality. "The jury—"

"Hold on! Just one moment more."

The judge stared down at Isaac as if he were a malfunctioning component. "Oh, yes. You had additional information to present. Well, proceed and present it."

Isaac looked sharply around the hushed room. "You want to convict me," he said softly, "in the most complete way possible. Isn't that correct?"

Sensors swung toward him. The judge's facets gleamed with anticipation. "That's correct."

"But you can't properly convict me until you've carefully processed any information I present in my own defense. Isn't that correct?"

The judge appeared uncomfortable. "If you have information to present, proceed and present it."

"I have just one statement to make. Brief and direct. But you'd better process it, and analyze it carefully before you decide that you really want to convict me." He paused and directed his gaze at the judge. "You don't value those who present unprocessed truth, it seems. Well, enter this statement in your record, then." His voice was loud and clear in the still room. "All Earthmen are absolutely incapable of presenting accurate information."

Puzzled expressions appeared on the jury's faceted faces. One or two exchanged startled glances, and the room was silent as death. The judge stared at him, then at Miguel, then back. "But you"—he stammered. "You're"—He stopped mid-sentence, his sensors flickering wildly.

One of the jurors let out a small chime and went completely dark. It took, all in all, about ten seconds for the statement to register.

And then chaos erupted in the courtroom.

"Really," said Isaac Hunt smugly, "it was so obvious I'm amazed it didn't occur to me immediately." He settled himself comfortably in the control cabin of the transport vessel and grinned at the outline of Lakeside, Nordavia growing larger in the viewscreen.

Miguel Ortiz stared stonily at the controls, his lips compressed angrily. "You might at least have informed me of your plan."

"And risk being monitored? Don't be ridiculous. It had to be a complete surprise. I had to establish myself as an information manipulator—the supreme manipulator of them all, but I had to present the sort of information that they simply could not process. Something that would throw them into such utter logical contradiction that they wouldn't dare convict me." He grinned impishly at Miguel. "The paradox of Epimenides the Cretan. It really stopped them cold. They knew I was an Earthman, which meant that my statement that Earthmen couldn't present accurate information was inaccurate, which meant that maybe I could present accurate information, in which case—oh, it was perfect."

"It sure was." Miguel's voice was a snarl.

"Well, it established me as a negotiator in a class they couldn't match, didn't it?"

Miguel's face was purple with anger. "Oh, indeed it did! And it classified all Earthmen in exactly the same category, too."

"So what's honor among thieves? I got off, didn't I? And now we're heading to Nordavia so I can finally collect my money. Should have transferred it back to my accounts on Earth—would have been safer—but I got greedy, wanted to avoid the cross-system fees."

Miguel turned on him fiercely. "Oh, you got off just fine. You terrified them completely. And in an eon of information manipulation, they've never encountered a logical paradox like that. You've also completely destroyed any hope of ever establishing a trading alliance with Lakeside Territory, and that includes climate technology materials, too. Intelligent beings don't engage with loaded systems. You frightened them so thoroughly they want nothing to do with us."

Isaac's grin broadened, and he leaned back luxuriously. "Ah, well. After all, the Trading Alliance was your concern, wasn't it? What a shame!" He clicked his tongue sadly. "Me, I've got a fortune in credits sitting at the consulate in Nordavia waiting for me—enough to keep me comfortable for quite a while, I must say. I think I'll just take a nice, long vacation."

Miguel turned to him, and a glint of malicious satisfaction appeared in his eyes. "Yes, I think you will. I'm quite certain of it, in fact. Won't cost you a credit, either."

"What?"

Miguel grinned unpleasantly. He brushed an imaginary speck from his lapel and looked up at Isaac slyly. "That—uh—jury trial. The Crystallines weren't particularly happy to accommodate. They wanted to terminate you immediately. Thought a trial was completely inefficient—until they recovered their investment, of course. Not excessive—just five million credits."

Isaac went white. "But that money was in protected custody! Earth Consulate jurisdiction—they couldn't touch it!"

"Is that so? My goodness. You don't suppose they could have misplaced those custody documents, do you? Funny thing about the consulate branch here in Nordavia—they've been quite cooperative with local authorities lately. Trade relations, you understand." Miguel grinned at the little con artist. "And incidentally, you're under arrest, you know."

A choking sound came from Isaac's throat. "Arrest!"

"Oh, yes. Didn't I mention it? Conspiring to undermine the authority of the Earth Trading Commission. Serious charge, you know. Yes, I think we'll take a nice long journey together, straight back to Earth. And there I think you'll face a jury trial."

Isaac spluttered. "There's no evidence—you've got nothing on me! What kind of setup are you trying to pull?"

"A beautiful setup. Airtight. A case from the ground up, and you're right in the center of it. And this time—" Miguel tapped a cigarette on his thumb with satisfied finality—"this time I don't think you'll get off."
quality_problem.question: Where was the five million credits Isaac Hunt mentioned held?
quality_problem.correct_answer: At the Earth Consulate at Lakeside, Nordavia
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: In a secret account on Earth
answers: In a secret account on Earth
At the Earth Consulate at Lakeside, Nordavia

quality_problem.story:
The Protocol
BY LIEUTENANT COLONEL STEPHEN LYNCH (RET.)

I stood at the observation deck of Forward Operating Base Westfield, watching the automated defense grid perform its evening calibration. The hum of the machinery was a comfort—predictable, reliable, eternal. In my forty years of service, I had never seen one of these systems fail. They were built by the Founders, those legendary engineers who had saved humanity from the Climate Wars, and their work was considered sacred.

The sun was setting, sinking toward the horizon beyond the western boundary of our territory. I turned to face it, squinting against the orange light. Below, stretching across the valley floor, the great agricultural domes caught the last rays of daylight. Their curved surfaces gleamed bronze and gold where the light struck them directly, but already shadows were creeping across the nearest domes from the elevated terrain to the west. The shadow line advanced slowly as I watched, swallowing dome after dome in premature twilight.

It was an old grievance among the farmers who worked these valley domes—losing nearly an hour of growing light each evening. The western ridge rose sharply from the valley floor, its silhouette dark against the setting sun. I could see the administrative buildings and Memorial Gardens perched along the ridge's edge, their elevated position ensuring they caught sunlight long after the valley below had fallen into shadow. The ridge belonged to our district, of course—Westfield's terrain encompassed both the fertile valley and the highlands that bordered it to the west.

Northfield District lay to the north and east, on lower ground that caught morning light earlier than we did. Their farmers complained about the reverse problem—our eastern hills blocked their dawn sun. Such were the compromises the Founders had made when they divided the territory.

"Colonel Lynch! Colonel Lynch!" The voice shattered my reverie.

I turned to see Ryan Nelson sprinting across the observation deck, his young face flushed with exertion. Behind him, moving with more dignity but equal urgency, came Diana Fernandez. Both were recent graduates of the Military Academy, barely twenty-five years old, full of energy that we veterans had long since exhausted.

"Colonel," Ryan gasped, "the Genetic Preservation Vault—it's gone critical!"

I stared in disbelief. "Gone critical? That's impossible. The vault has maintained optimal conditions for three centuries."

Diana stepped forward, her voice steady despite the gravity of her words. "The monitoring officer was negligent, sir. The temperature controls failed, continued to rise beyond safety parameters, and then—" she paused, choosing her words carefully, "—total system failure. All the genetic material has been destroyed."

"All of it?" I demanded.

"Every sample, sir," Diana confirmed. "The entire repository of human genetic diversity. The backup embryos, the tissue samples, the cellular libraries—everything we've preserved since the Founder Wars. It's all gone."

"This is a matter for the High Command," I said carefully. In moments of crisis, one must speak with precision. "Summon the War Council immediately."

The two young officers ran ahead while I made my way down to Command Center at a more measured pace. A man my age doesn't rush, even in emergencies. Besides, I needed time to think.

The genetic vault had been established after the Climate Wars, when radiation and environmental toxins had damaged much of humanity's genetic diversity. The Founders had created machines to preserve and, when necessary, generate new genetic combinations to prevent inbreeding and genetic disease. For three hundred years, the system had worked flawlessly, producing healthy children through the Gestation Chambers while maintaining genetic diversity.

And now it was gone.

When I entered the Command Center, I found the War Council already assembled, waiting for me to call them to order. Ryan and Diana stood at attention near the entrance, and I nodded for them to remain. They had earned the right to see this through.

The meeting proceeded as these things do. Many officers felt compelled to make speeches. Prayers were offered to the memory of the Founders. Technical teams were dispatched to assess the damage. Finally, as the emergency lighting began to activate with the onset of night, the Chief Medical Officer was given the floor.

Dr. Theodore Willis was the oldest among us, his white hair and weathered face testament to a lifetime of service. He smoothed his beard—a habit when nervous—and addressed the Council.

"I will not burden you with technical details that only the Founders truly understood," he began. "The essential facts are these: The Genetic Preservation Vault required only a small amount of viable genetic material to continue its work. Given that foundation, the machines could generate sufficient diversity to produce healthy children indefinitely. This has been our system since the Founder Wars."

Murmurs of agreement rippled through the room.

"But now," he continued, his voice faltering, "we face an unprecedented situation. A true emergency. The vault has failed completely. All preserved genetic material has been destroyed. The Gestation Chambers cannot function without it. There will be no more children."

The room erupted. Officers shouted, some called for Willis's resignation, others demanded impossible solutions. I restored order with difficulty, grateful that the War Council was composed entirely of senior officers. Men and women in their sixties and seventies can only sustain outrage for so long.

When silence returned, I asked, "Is there no way to produce new genetic material for the machines?"

"As I explained," Willis replied, "given even a small sample, the machines can generate more. But without that initial material, they are useless."

General Mateo Stewart leaned forward. "But there must have been a beginning to this system. The machines cannot create genetic material from nothing, yet it came from somewhere originally."

"This is not the time for philosophical speculation," I said sharply.

"Is it not?" Stewart replied in his characteristically infuriating manner. "Must there not, three centuries ago, have been a source of genetic material—a source now forgotten? And might it not still be available to us, if we could remember? I'm reminded of the historical records of the pre-Founder era—"

"Your mind is wandering, General," I interrupted. "What do the ancient records have to do with our current crisis?"

The Council members were looking at me expectantly. I sighed and explained. "General Stewart refers to records from before the Founder Wars, describing a time when humans reproduced without technological assistance. But those records are fragmentary, often contradictory, and generally considered unreliable folklore."

Stewart's voice cut through the murmurs. "Not folklore, Colonel. Historical fact. The archaeological evidence is clear. The data science analysis of pre-Founder populations proves it conclusively. Humans once reproduced biologically, without machines."

Two Council members required medical attention at this statement. I hoped Ryan and Diana, standing at attention by the door, hadn't heard clearly, but their wide eyes suggested otherwise.

"If this is true," I said slowly, "how did this biological reproduction function?"

"That," Stewart replied, "is precisely what I propose to discover. I request permission to access the Founder Archives."

The room fell silent. The Founder Archives were sealed in a climate-controlled vault, their physical books and documents so fragile that they had not been examined in living memory. All our knowledge came from digital copies, themselves copies of copies, degraded over centuries.

Stewart had been seeking an excuse to access the Archives for years. But what choice did we have?

"Permission granted," I said, and adjourned the Council.

Three weeks passed before Stewart requested another meeting. I convened the War Council at dawn, and by early afternoon we had completed the formalities and granted Stewart the floor.

"Some of you are what we term 'female,'" he began. "You know you differ from the rest of us physiologically. You have certain advantages—different hormonal profiles, different skeletal structures, different metabolic processes. And you may ask, why should this be? There is no obvious military or survival advantage to these differences. Yet they exist. Have you never wondered why?"

"General Stewart," I interrupted, "fascinating as this is, perhaps you could—"

"Of course," he said. "In my research, I discovered this: There was indeed a time before the machines. The Archives date from that era—not one document mentions our current reproductive technology. In that time, reproduction was carried on by individuals, without mechanical assistance. The females are not a separate subspecies or the result of environmental adaptation. We are all one species, with two distinct biological forms. And these forms were complementary in the reproductive process."

The room erupted in chaos. Stewart had to shout his final words: "The biological differences between males and females are not vestigial—they are functional! The system still exists within us!"

Order dissolved as officers turned to their neighbors in shock and disbelief. I realized I needed to find a flaw in Stewart's logic before the situation spiraled further out of control.

"There is a contradiction in your theory," I announced loudly. "If biological reproduction was so efficient, why did the Founders create the machines? Why abandon a working system?"

Stewart looked troubled by this question. Then Ryan Nelson, still standing at attention by the door, spoke without permission: "Perhaps biological reproduction created social dynamics that threatened military discipline? Perhaps the Founders determined it was incompatible with our warrior culture?"

The Council exploded in outrage at this impudence. Ryan was immediately placed under arrest and confined to the brig. Privately, however, I had to admit his hypothesis had merit. I authorized Stewart to continue his research.

I worried about young Nelson in the brig. He would remain there until the Council chose to release him, which required another meeting. When Stewart reported he had made a breakthrough, I immediately convened the Council, hoping to argue for the boy's release.

Stewart entered the next morning looking haggard. He carried a thin, ancient book, but his appearance shocked me more than the artifact. He looked as though he hadn't slept or eaten in days. His eyes were sunken, his face gaunt. But it was the expression in those eyes that truly disturbed me—a mixture of horror and fascination.

After the formalities, Stewart spoke. "I have discovered the mechanism of biological reproduction," he said, holding up the book. "This is a pre-Founder medical manual. It's titled 'Human Reproductive Biology: A Clinical Guide.' It appears to be some sort of instructional text." He dropped the book on the table and rubbed his face.

Something in his demeanor commanded absolute attention. He continued in a low voice: "The process is... complex. And intimate. Let me start at the beginning. You see, there are certain biological structures, certain chemical processes, certain physical interactions..."

When he finished, the Council sat in horrified silence. No one cried heresy or treason. There was only stunned disbelief and the beginning of nausea.

I forced myself to speak. "Surely these biological structures you mention have atrophied? With three centuries of disuse, will they not have evolved away?"

"I don't think so," Stewart replied. "Evolutionary time scales are far longer than three centuries. And the persistence of female physiological characteristics suggests the reproductive systems remain functional, at least in some individuals."

We sat in grim silence, facing a terrible reality.

"Then we must test this hypothesis," I said. "But who could we ask to volunteer for such a procedure?"

"I have already secured volunteers," Stewart replied. "Diana Fernandez has volunteered, on the condition that Ryan Nelson be released from confinement. Are there any objections?"

There were none. Who would deny anything to someone willing to undergo such an ordeal for humanity's survival?

"And the male volunteer?" I asked.

"Ryan Nelson has agreed to participate," Stewart said. "They both understand what's required."

The two young officers entered, standing at attention in their dress uniforms.

Stewart gestured toward the medical bay, but Ryan stepped forward.

"Colonel Lynch," he said, "would we not achieve better results if we conducted the experiment outdoors? The Memorial Gardens—with its soft grass and sheltering trees—would be more peaceful than the clinical environment. Perhaps the memory of the Founders will guide us."

His eyes met mine, and I understood. He was thinking of Diana's comfort and dignity. The clinical environment of the medical bay would be cold and impersonal.

"The gardens lack proper observation facilities," I noted. "We must document this for scientific purposes."

Diana spoke up. "Sir, we understand the need for documentation. But the medical bay feels... incompatible with what we're being asked to do."

I gave my consent, and the entire Council relocated to the Memorial Gardens on our western ridge. The elevated grounds offered privacy and the tranquility Ryan had requested. As we walked up the winding path, I glanced back at the valley below—the agricultural domes were completely dark now, deep in the shadow our ridge cast across them each evening.

It was nearly dark when Stewart and I walked back toward the base, both of us exhausted. It had been a horrific day. The clinical descriptions in the manual had not prepared us for the reality—the vulnerability, the intimacy, the sounds...

We paused at the edge of the ridge, looking up at the stars. Behind us lay the gardens where the experiment had taken place.

"They seemed to follow the manual's instructions accurately," I muttered.

"They may have succeeded," Stewart replied. "The manual mentions a significant time delay. The result isn't immediate—it takes months."

"It doesn't matter," I said bleakly. "We cannot ask them to repeat such an ordeal."

Then I looked down and saw them standing before us. Diana's eyes were downcast. Ryan had his arm around her shoulders protectively.

"Colonel Lynch," Ryan said, then stopped, embarrassed.

I waited. Stewart remained silent.

"Sir, we wanted to tell you..." He raised his eyes to mine. "We're willing to try again."

I felt tears forming. Such sacrifice, such dedication to duty—

"We have one request," Ryan continued. "We'd like to conduct further attempts in private. Without observation."

"Of course," I replied. They could have anything they wanted. My relief must have been obvious, because Ryan took a deep breath and continued.

"We don't deserve special praise, sir," he said. "The truth is... the procedure isn't as unpleasant as the manual suggested. We... we actually found it somewhat... agreeable."

I watched them walk away together under the stars, heading back toward the gardens.

My heart swelled with pride. I no longer feared for humanity's future when our young warriors could demonstrate such nobility and dedication to the mission.

In the morning, I would recommend them both for commendations. Perhaps even the Founder's Medal for extraordinary service to humanity.

But tonight, I simply watched them disappear into the darkness, two young soldiers willing to sacrifice their dignity and comfort for the future of our species.

Stewart cleared his throat. "I should return to my quarters. There's more research to be done."

I nodded, then turned to look back down toward the valley. Somewhere in the darkness below lay the agricultural domes—invisible now beneath our ridge's shadow, but I knew exactly where they stood. Tomorrow morning I would watch the sun rise over Northfield's territory to the east, watch its light creep across the valley floor. The domes would emerge from night gradually, their curved surfaces catching the dawn light one by one. Then would come the long productive hours before evening, when the sun would sink behind our ridge once more and plunge the domes back into early darkness.

The machines had failed us. But humanity, it seemed, would endure.
quality_problem.question: What district was casting long shadows across the agricultural domes?

quality_problem.story:
The Networker
By Anonymous

Being an interstellar network security specialist wouldn't be so bad… if I could secure the networks without leaving my office!

Director Lucia Woods had that look of intense satisfaction on her face that meant someone was in for a very rough assignment. Since we were alone in her office, it took no great feat of intelligence to figure it would be me. I spoke first, bold attack being the best defense and so forth.

"I quit. Don't bother telling me what impossible job you have cooked up, because I have already quit and you do not want to reveal company secrets to me."

The grin was even wider now and she actually laughed as she thumbed a button on her console. A thick legal document slid out of the delivery slot onto her desk.

"This is your contract," she said. "It tells how and when you will work. A quantum-encrypted contract that you couldn't crack with a neural disruptor."

I leaned out quickly, grabbed it and threw it into the air with a single motion. Before it could fall, I had my plasma cutter out and, with a wide-angle burst, incinerated the contract to ashes.

Director Woods pressed the button again and another contract slid out on her desk. If possible, the smile was still wider now.

"I should have said a duplicate of your contract—like this one here." She made a quick note on her secretary plate. "I have deducted 50 credits from your salary for the cost of the duplicate—as well as a 500-credit fine for firing a plasma cutter inside a building."

I slumped, defeated, waiting for the blow to land. Director Woods fondled my contract.

"According to this document, you can't quit. Ever. Therefore I have a little job I know you'll enjoy. Network restoration job. The Woodbridge relay hub has shut down. It's a Genesis-class system…"

"What kind of system?" I asked her. I had restored quantum communication networks from one arm of the Galaxy to the other and was sure I had worked on every type or model made. But I had never heard of this kind.

"Genesis-class," Director Woods repeated, practically chortling. "I never heard of it either until Archives dug up the specs. They found them buried in the back of their oldest data vault. This was the earliest type of quantum relay ever built—by Earth Colonial Administration, no less. Considering its location on one of the Calderon planets, it might very well be the first relay."

I looked at the blueprints she handed me and felt my eyes glaze with horror. "It's a monstrosity! It looks more like a particle accelerator than a relay hub—must be at least a few hundred meters in diameter. I'm a network specialist, not an archeologist. This pile of junk is over 1500 years old. Just forget about it and build a new one."

Director Woods leaned over her desk, breathing into my face. "It would take eighteen months to install a new relay—besides being prohibitively expensive—and this relic is on one of the main communication routes. We have data packets making twenty-light-year detours now."

She leaned back, wiped her hands on her handkerchief and gave me Lecture Thirty-seven on Company Duty and My Responsibilities.

"I'm assigning you this mission because your file shows you've closed out every assignment eventually. The department cares about results. That's what keeps you employed here—despite everything else in your personnel record."

She was telling me—the person who did the job while she sat back on her fat paycheck in a climate-controlled office.

She rambled on. "How I wish repairs were straightforward! I would have a fleet of parts ships and junior technicians to install them. But it's not like that at all. I have a fleet of expensive ships that are equipped to do almost anything—manned by specialists like you."

I nodded moodily at her pointing finger.

"Network Maintenance and Security should really be called crisis management. Quantum relays are made to last forever—or damn close to it. When one of them breaks down, it is never an accident, and repairing the thing is never a matter of just plugging in a new part. The protocols exist for good reason, and I expect you to follow them. Complete documentation, proper channels, full compliance. Is that understood?"

I recognized this deathless line as the curtain speech and crawled to my feet. She threw the Genesis file at me and went back to scratching in her papers. Just as I reached the door, she looked up and impaled me on her finger again.

"And I've forwarded the standard mission protocols to your ship's computer. Read them this time. The department expects full compliance with contact procedures."

"Of course, Director. I always read the protocols." I gave her my most cooperative smile.

Walking down the hall, I reflected on how smoothly that meeting had gone. Woods seemed satisfied with my response—she always appreciated a show of compliance. The protocols would make excellent reading material, right alongside my other unread correspondence.

It was all very routine, so I stopped for a drink, then went on to the spaceport.

By the time the ship was serviced, I had a course charted. The nearest relay to the broken-down Woodbridge hub was on one of the planets of Ivywood system in Ulvaria sector, and I headed there first, a short trip of only about twelve days in hyperspace.

To understand the importance of the quantum relays, you have to understand faster-than-light communication. Not that many people do, but it is easy enough to understand that in quantum-entangled networks, the regular rules of information theory don't apply. Data transmission and routing are a matter of quantum state manipulation, not classical electromagnetic propagation like in the old universe.

The first colonies to establish interstellar presence had no way to communicate—and no way to even tell if their messages had been received. The quantum relays solved that problem and opened the entire galaxy to real-time communication. They are built on planets and generate tremendous amounts of power. This power is used to maintain quantum coherence that is sustained across interstellar distances. Every relay has a unique quantum signature as part of its entanglement network and represents a measurable node in the communication web. Triangulation and routing of the relays works for data transmission—only it follows its own protocols. The protocols are complex and variable, but they are still protocols that a network engineer can follow.

For a proper network topology, you need at least four relays for an accurate route. For long-distance communication, engineers use as many as nine or ten. So every relay is critical and every one has to keep operating. That is where I and the other troubleshooters came in.

We travel in well-stocked ships that carry a little bit of everything; only one person to a ship because that is all it takes to operate the overly efficient repair machinery. Due to the very nature of our job, we spend most of our time just rocketing through normal space. After all, when a relay breaks down, how do you find it?

Not through hyperspace. All you can do is approach as close as you can by using other relays for navigation, then finish the trip in normal space. This can take months, and often does.

This job didn't turn out to be quite that bad. I locked onto the Ivywood relay and ran a complicated ten-point problem through the navigator, using every relay I could get an accurate fix on. The computer gave me a course with an estimated point-of-arrival as well as a built-in safety factor I never could eliminate from the machine.

I would much rather take a chance of breaking through near some star than spend time just barreling through normal space, but apparently Tech knows this, too. They had a safety factor built into the computer so you couldn't end up inside a star no matter how hard you tried. I'm sure there was no humaneness in this decision. They just didn't want to lose the ship.

It was a twenty-six-hour jump, ship's time, and I came through in the middle of nowhere. The robot analyzer hummed to itself and scanned all the stars, comparing them to the spectra of Woodbridge's sun. It finally rang a bell and blinked a light. I peered through the eyepiece.

A fast reading with the photocell gave me the apparent magnitude and a comparison with its absolute magnitude showed its distance. Not as bad as I had thought—a seven-week run, give or take a few days. After feeding a course tape into the robot pilot, I strapped into the acceleration tank and went to sleep.

The time went fast. I completed three online courses in quantum cryptography and advanced data analysis, mostly because the company grades your pay by the number of specialties you can handle. All this, with some virtual reality gaming and zero-gravity workouts in the gym, passed the time. I was asleep when the alarm went off that announced planetary distance.

Planet three, where the relay was situated according to the old charts, was a verdant-looking, temperate kind of globe. I tried to make sense out of the ancient directions and finally located the right area. Staying outside the atmosphere, I sent a reconnaissance drone down to look things over. In this business, you learn early when and where to risk your own skin. The drone would be good enough for the preliminary survey.

The old engineers had enough sense to choose a traceable site for the relay, equidistant on a line between two of the most prominent geological formations—a pair of massive crater rims. I located the craters easily enough and started the drone out from the first crater and kept it on a course directly toward the second. There was fore and aft radar in the drone and I fed their signals into a scope as an amplitude curve. When the two craters coincided, I spun the drone controls and dove the thing down.

I cut out the radar and cut in the visual feed and sat back to watch the relay appear on the screen.

The image blinked, focused—and a great damn ziggurat swam into view. I cursed and wheeled the drone in circles, scanning the surrounding area. It was flat, cultivated farmland without a bump. The only thing in a fifteen-mile circle was this ziggurat—and that definitely wasn't my relay.

Or wasn't it?

I dove the drone lower. The ziggurat was an elaborate-looking thing of carved stone, with intricate decorations and what looked like ceremonial platforms. There was a shimmer of energy from the top and I took a closer look at it. On the peak of the ziggurat was a massive crystalline structure that pulsed with faint light. When I saw that, something clicked in my mind.

Locking the drone in a circular course, I dug through the Genesis plans—and there it was. The relay had a quantum coherence field generator and a crystalline array on top of it for signal amplification; this was used to boost the entanglement stability that powered the whole system. If the crystal was still glowing, the relay was still there—inside the ziggurat. The natives, who, of course, weren't even mentioned by the idiots who constructed the thing, had built a nice heavy, elaborate stone ziggurat around the relay.

I took another look at the screen and realized that I had locked the drone into a circular orbit about thirty feet above the ziggurat. The summit of the stone structure was now covered with humanoid figures of some type, apparently the local life-form. They had what looked like energy weapons and projectile launchers and were trying to shoot down the drone, a cloud of bolts and missiles flying in every direction.

I pulled the drone straight up and away and threw in the control circuit that would return it automatically to the ship.

Then I went to the galley for a long, strong drink. My relay was not only locked inside a mountain of handmade stone, but I had managed to irritate the beings who had built the ziggurat. A great beginning for a job.

I pulled up the mission protocols Woods had mentioned. The contact procedures were extensive—preliminary surveys, cultural impact assessments, coordination with the Anthropological Division, formal diplomatic channels. The documentation requirements alone would take weeks. I scrolled through page after page of approval workflows and authorization chains.

The protocols did contain useful information about the native protection regulations. "Native life-forms" were quite well protected. There were monitoring systems on my ship that would report on me when I got back. Any use of force against the locals would trigger automatic review.

I closed the protocol document and opened my personal files instead. For situations like this, I had long before worked out a system of my own.

I had a surveillance drone of my own construction. It looked like a piece of local vegetation about a foot tall. Once on the ground, it would never be noticed, though it was a little disconcerting to see it float by. I located a settlement about eight hundred kilometers from the ziggurat and dropped the drone. It whooshed down and landed at night near the bank of the local water source. This was a popular spot that drew a good crowd during the day. In the morning, when the first locals arrived, I flipped on the recorder.

After about seven of the local days, I had a wealth of native conversation in the memory bank of the machine translator and had tagged a few expressions. This is fairly easy to do when you have a machine memory to work with. One of the natives called out to another one and the second one responded. I tagged this expression with the phrase, "Hello, friend!" and waited my chance to use it. Later the same day, I caught one of them alone and broadcast "Hello, friend!" at them. It played out through the speaker in the local tongue and they responded positively.

When you get enough reference phrases like this in the memory bank, the MT brain takes over and starts filling in the missing pieces. As soon as the MT could give a running translation of any conversation it heard, I figured it was time to make a contact.

I found her easily enough. She was the Calderon version of a shepherd—she tended a particularly docile form of local livestock in the grasslands outside the settlement. I had one of the working drones dig a small chamber in an outcropping of rock and wait for her.

When she passed next day, I whispered into the mike: "Greetings, Elena Carter, faithful servant! This is the voice of the Eternal Guides speaking from the celestial realm." This fitted in with what I could make out of the local religion.

Elena stopped as if she'd been struck. Before she could move, I pushed a switch and a handful of the local currency, precious metal coins, rolled out of the chamber and landed at her feet.

"Here is a gift from the celestial realm, because you have been faithful." Not really from the celestial realm—I had fabricated it from raw materials the night before. "Come back tomorrow and we will speak more," I called after the fleeing figure. I was pleased to notice that she took the coins before taking off.

After that, the Eternal Guides had many heart-to-heart talks with Elena, who found the celestial gifts more than she could resist. The Guides had been out of touch with earthly matters and Elena happily filled them in.

I learned all I needed to know of the history, past and recent, and it wasn't pleasant.

In addition to the ziggurat being around the relay, there was a nasty political conflict going on around the structure.

It all began with the migration. Apparently the local humanoids had been living in scattered tribes when the relay was built, but the builders didn't think much of them. They were a primitive type and confined to a distant region. The idea that the civilization would develop and might reach this continent never occurred to the relay engineers. Which is, of course, what happened.

A little climate change, a population boom, and the humanoids began to migrate to relay valley. And found religion. A shining crystalline temple from which emanated a constant pulse of divine energy—the quantum coherence field that maintained the entanglement network. The radiation in the field didn't harm the natives. It enhanced their cognitive development in ways that bred true.

A city was built around the temple and, through the centuries, the ziggurat was constructed around the relay. A special caste of the priesthood served the temple. All went well until one of the priests violated the temple protocols and disrupted the divine energy. There had been revolt, conflict, violence and destruction since then. But still the divine energy would not flow properly. Now armed factions fought around the temple each day and a new group of priests guarded the sacred structure.

And I had to walk into the middle of that mess and repair the thing.

The company protocols suggested waiting for Anthropological Division clearance before any contact with developed native cultures. That could take months of bureaucratic processing. Meanwhile, the relay stayed broken and data packets made twenty-light-year detours.

I weighed my options carefully. The protocols existed for good reason—Woods had emphasized that. But the protocols also assumed scenarios where waiting was feasible. This situation required a more direct approach.

I sighed and dragged out the holographic disguise equipment.

Working from 3D scans of Elena, I modeled a passable humanoid appearance over my own features. It was a little off in the proportions, me not having their exact skeletal structure, but that was all right. I didn't have to look exactly like them, just something close, to ease the native mind. It's logical. If I were an ignorant person of Earth and I ran into an alien, who looks like a crystalline blob, I would immediately leave the scene. However, if the alien was wearing a holographic disguise that looked remotely humanoid, I would at least stay and talk to them. This was what I was aiming to do with the Calderons.

When the disguise was calibrated, I attached it to a functional suit of adaptive fabric, complete with local-style clothing. I was really glad they wore robes. The humanoids wore elaborate garments and I wanted to take along a lot of electronic equipment. I built the robe over a support frame that anchored around my torso. Then I filled the frame with all the equipment I would need and began to wire the suit.

When it was done, I tried it on in front of a full-length mirror. It was uncanny but effective. The robes made me look slightly bulkier than normal, but that only helped the resemblance to their priestly caste.

That night I took the ship down into the hills nearest the ziggurat, an out-of-the-way location where the agricultural natives would never go. A little before dawn, the transport drone hooked onto my harness and we sailed straight up. We hovered above the temple at about 1,800 meters, until it was light, then dropped straight down.

It must have been an impressive sight. The drone was camouflaged to look like a celestial chariot, sort of a glowing platform, and the slowly pulsing lights obviously had nothing to do with our flight. But it was impressive enough for the natives. The first one that spotted me shouted and fell to their knees. The others came running. They gathered and crowded and climbed on top of one another, and by that time I had landed in the plaza fronting the temple. The priesthood arrived.

I raised my arms in a ceremonial stance. "Greetings, O noble servants of the Divine Order," I said. Of course I didn't say it out loud, just whispered loud enough for the throat mike to catch. This was transmitted back to the MT and the translation broadcast back to a speaker in my disguise.

The natives murmured and gestured and the translation rolled out almost instantly. I had the volume turned up and the whole square echoed.

Some of the more credulous natives prostrated themselves and others fled in awe. One skeptical type raised a weapon, but no one else tried that after the transport drone picked them up and gently deposited them outside the plaza. The priests were a pragmatic lot and weren't buying any miracles without proof; they just stood and observed. I had to take the initiative again.

"Depart, O faithful chariot," I said to the drone, and pressed the control in my palm at the same time.

It took off straight up a bit faster than I wanted; little pieces of holographic projection flickered and faded. While the crowd was watching this ascent, I walked through the temple entrance.

"I would speak with you, O noble priests," I said.

Before they could formulate a response, I was inside.

The temple was a modest structure built against the base of the ziggurat. I hoped I wasn't violating too many taboos by entering. I wasn't stopped, so it looked acceptable. The temple was a single chamber with an ornate altar at one end. Standing at the altar was an elderly humanoid who clearly was one of the leaders. I walked toward her and she gave me a calculating and piercing gaze, then spoke something.

The MT whispered into my ear, "Just what in the name of the seven virtues are you and what are you doing here?"

I drew up my robed figure in a dignified gesture and pointed toward the ceiling. "I come from the Eternal Guides to help you. I am here to restore the Divine Energy."

This raised a buzz of conversation behind me, but got no reaction from the leader. She stood quietly, hands folded. I could almost see the thoughts processing behind that weathered face. Then she stepped forward and pointed a steady finger at me.

"You are a deceiver! You are no emissary of the Guides! We will—"

"Stop!" I projected before she got so far in that she couldn't back out. "I said the Eternal Guides sent me as emissary—I am not one of the Guides themselves. Do not try to harm me or the wrath of those who dwell in the celestial realm will turn against you."

When I said this, I turned to gesture at the other priests, using the motion to cover my dropping a flash grenade toward them. It created a nice display of light and sound with minimal damage.

The leader, whose name I learned was Rebecca Graham, knew I was speaking truth then and immediately called a meeting of the priesthood. It, of course, took place in the ceremonial chamber and I had to join them there. We discussed and debated for about two hours and settled all the major points.

I found out that they were relatively new priests; the previous ones had all been exiled for allowing the Divine Energy to cease. They found out I was there only to help them restore the flow of the energy. They accepted this, tentatively, and we all moved across the floor. There was a sealed and guarded door that led into the ziggurat proper. While it was being opened, Rebecca turned to me.

"Undoubtedly you know of the sacred law," she said. "Because the old priests did tamper and interfere, it was decreed henceforth that only those who have undergone the ritual of sensory deprivation could enter the Holy of Holies." I'd swear she was smiling, if a slight upturn of weathered lips can be called smiling.

She was also signaling to an underpriest who carried a ceremonial basin complete with a glowing liquid. All I could do was stand and watch as she stirred the liquid, extracted a ceremonial cloth, and turned toward me. She was just approaching my eyes when my brain got back in gear.

"Of course," I said, "the ritual is only proper. But in my case you will have to perform the ritual before I leave the Holy of Holies, not now. I need my vision to see and mend the Source of Divine Energy. Once the energy flows again, I will gladly submit to the ritual."

She took a good forty seconds to consider it and had to agree with me. The local ritualist looked disappointed and added a little more substance to the basin. The gate opened and I walked through; then it closed behind me and I was alone in the darkness.

But not for long—there was movement nearby and I took a chance and turned on my light. Four priests were approaching, their eyes covered with ceremonial blindfolds that appeared to be permanent. They knew what I wanted and led the way without a word.

A deteriorating and fractured stone stairway brought us up to a solid metal doorway labeled in archaic script GENESIS QUANTUM RELAY—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The trusting builders counted on the sign to do the whole job, for there wasn't a trace of a lock on the door. One priest merely turned the handle and we were inside the relay.

I opened the front of my disguise suit and pulled out the blueprints. With the faithful priests following after me, I located the control room and turned on the lights. There was a residue of charge in the emergency batteries, just enough to give a dim light. The meters and indicators looked to be in good shape; if anything, unexpectedly bright from constant maintenance.

I checked the readings carefully and found just what I had suspected. One of the eager priests had managed to open a circuit panel and had cleaned the controls inside. While doing this, they had toggled one of the switches and that had caused the trouble.

Rather, that had started the trouble. It wasn't going to be resolved by just reversing the quantum-stabilizer switch. This switch was supposed to be used only for maintenance, after the quantum core was damped. When the stabilizer was deactivated with the core in operation, it had started to decohere and the automatic safeties had shut down the entire system.

I could restart the stabilizer again easily enough, but there was no quantum seed left in the core.

I wasn't going to attempt to regenerate the quantum core at all. It would be far easier to install a new power system. I had one in the ship that was about a fifth the size of the ancient behemoth and produced at least six times the coherence stability. Before I sent for it, I checked over the rest of the relay. In 1500 years, there should be some sign of deterioration.

The old engineers had built well, I'll give them credit for that. Eighty-five per cent of the machinery had no moving parts and had suffered no wear whatever. Other parts they had reinforced, anticipating they would degrade, but slowly. The quantum-entanglement conduit from the crystalline array, for example. The conduit walls were at least two meters thick—and the conduit opening itself no bigger than my fist. There were some things I could do, though, and I made a list of parts.

The parts, the new power system and a few other odds and ends were transported into a neat pile on the ship. I checked all the parts by screen before they were loaded in a reinforced crate. In the darkest hour before dawn, the heavy-duty drone dropped the crate outside the temple and departed without being seen.

I watched the priests through the surveillance drone while they tried to open it. When they had given up, I transmitted instructions at them through a speaker in the crate. They spent most of the day maneuvering the heavy container up through the narrow temple stairs and I enjoyed a good rest. It was waiting inside the relay door when I woke up.

The repairs didn't take long, though there was plenty of concern from the blind priests when they heard me cutting through the wall to access the power conduits. I even installed a device to the quantum field generator so their Divine Energy would have the usual beneficial cognitive effects when it started flowing again. The moment this was all finished, I did the job they were waiting for.

I threw the switch that started the energy flowing again.

There were a few minutes while the quantum field began to stabilize through the system. Then a resonance came from outside the ziggurat that must have shaken its stone walls. Raising my hands once over my head, I went down for the ritual ceremony.

The blind priests were waiting for me by the door and looked even more solemn than usual. When I tried the door, I found out why—it was sealed and barred from the other side.

"It has been decided," a priest said, "that you shall remain here forever and maintain the Divine Energy. We will stay with you and serve your every need."

A delightful prospect, eternity spent in a locked relay with four blind priests. In spite of their hospitality, I couldn't accept.

"What—you dare interfere with the emissary of the Eternal Guides!" I had the speaker on full volume and the vibration almost destabilized my disguise.

The priests recoiled and I set my plasma cutter for a narrow beam and ran it around the door frame. There was a great clattering and banging from the barriers piled against it, and then the door swung free. I threw it open. Before they could protest, I had guided the priests out through it.

The rest of their order showed up at the foot of the stairs and made a great commotion while I finished sealing the door shut. Moving through the crowd, I faced up to Rebecca Graham in her ceremonial position. She stood quietly, observing.

"What lack of respect!" I projected. She remained still. "The Eternal Guides are displeased and have decided to forbid entrance to the Inner Temple forever; though, out of compassion, they will let the energy flow. Now I must return—proceed with the ceremony!"

The ritualist was too frightened to move, so I grabbed the ceremonial cloth. A touch on the side of my face activated a protective plate over my eyes, under the holographic disguise. Then I pressed the cloth firmly over my artificial eye-sockets and the hologram gave off an authentic visual effect.

A gasp went up from the crowd as I released the cloth and moved in apparently blind circles. I must admit it went off pretty convincingly.

Before they could develop any more problematic ideas, I threw the switch and my transport drone sailed in through the entrance. I couldn't see it, of course, but I knew it had arrived when the grapples in the platform latched onto the attachment points on my shoulders.

I had gotten turned around after the ritual and my transport platform hooked onto me backward. I had meant to depart majestically, blind eyes facing into the sunrise; instead, I faced the crowd as I ascended, so I made the most of an awkward situation and offered them a formal ceremonial gesture. Then I was out in the fresh air and away.

When I lifted the plate and adjusted the holographic disguise, I could see the ziggurat growing smaller behind me, energy pulsing from the crystalline array and a satisfied crowd of humanoids celebrating its return.

Back on the ship, I began composing my mission report. The protocols required extensive documentation of any native contact. I stared at the blank form for a long moment, then began typing.

"Mission completed successfully. Relay restored to full operation. No significant native contact required. Standard repair procedures followed throughout."

I reviewed what I'd written. The report was brief, clean, professional. Woods would appreciate its efficiency—she always complained about overly detailed documentation clogging her review queue. And technically, everything I'd written was accurate from a certain perspective. The relay was repaired. The procedures I'd followed were standard for me. The native contact had been minimal in the sense that I hadn't established any permanent diplomatic relations.

I transmitted the report and set course for home.

The debriefing with Director Woods was mercifully short. She skimmed my report, nodded at the confirmation that the relay was operational, and made a note in her files.

"Acceptable work," she said. "The relay is functioning. That's what matters."

I maintained my most cooperative expression. "I followed the mission parameters exactly as specified."

She looked up sharply, studying my face for a moment. Then she shrugged and waved me toward the door. "Your next assignment will be ready in three days. Try not to destroy any more contracts before then."

"Of course, Director. Always a pleasure working with you."

Walking down the hall afterward, I reflected on the meeting. Woods seemed satisfied—she'd gotten her relay back online, and my report gave her nothing to complain about. The monitoring systems on my ship would have flagged any use of force against the natives, and I hadn't harmed any of them. Everything else was just... creative interpretation of guidelines.

I stopped for a drink to celebrate another job complete. The bartender, a grizzled veteran who'd served network specialists for decades, poured my usual without asking.

"Rough one?" he asked.

"You know how it is," I said. "The protocols say one thing, the situation says another. You do what needs doing."

He nodded sagely. "That's why they send people like you instead of robots. Robots follow rules. People get results."

I raised my glass in agreement and thought about the Calderon priests, probably still celebrating the return of their Divine Energy. They'd gotten what they wanted.
