But her father was right—she needed rest. Tomorrow would be exhausting, and the day after would determine her future. She couldn't afford to be tired.

Julia turned off the lamp. She pulled the covers up to her chin and stared at the ceiling, willing herself to sleep. Her mind continued to race—presentation strategies, research directions, the faces of the Institute committee members she imagined judging her work.

Gradually, the racing thoughts began to slow. Images flickered behind her closed eyes: glass walls beaded with moisture, rows of green leaves, the particular quality of light filtered through growing things. Her breathing deepened. The tension left her shoulders.

Her last conscious thought, before sleep finally claimed her, was that she would miss certain places in Woodbridge more than others. Some places she had barely visited since freshman year. Other places she had visited almost every day, yet somehow they weren't the places she would miss most.

And then Julia was fast asleep.
quality_problem.question: What was Julia's favorite place to think since she was an undergraduate?

quality_problem.story:
The research vessel Prometheus groaned as its landing struts settled into the marshy terrain of Kepler-442b. The planet's thick atmosphere pressed against the hull, making the ship's metal framework protest with sharp pings and low moans. It was an unwelcoming sound, two hundred light-years from the cramped cities of Earth.

Commander Henry Martin rolled out of his bunk, his body heavy under the planet's 1.3g gravity. He was a lean man in his early forties, with the kind of weathered face that came from years managing impossible missions. The burden of Earth's desperate gamble had carved deep lines around his eyes. He shuffled toward the control room, already dreading the coffee.

Dr. Kara Perry glanced up from her console, tucking a strand of red hair behind her ear. "Morning, Henry. You look terrible."

"Thanks." He poured himself a cup of the bitter synthetic brew. "Anything new overnight?"

"The luminescent spheres—we're calling them 'orbs' now—had another gathering about three klicks north. They dispersed at dawn. And our two junior researchers snuck out again. Bruno tracked them but lost their signal in the fog. I've been running a beacon to guide them back."

Henry cursed under his breath. Earth's biotech programs were so desperate for field researchers that they were sending kids barely out of secondary school. The two assigned to his mission, Jordan Martinez and Stella Ahmed, seemed to have no survival instinct whatsoever.

Not that there was obvious danger here. The orbs appeared harmless, just curious. The local fauna were docile herbivores—strange six-legged creatures that looked like a nightmare fusion of mammals and arthropods. Nothing had shown aggression.

But something had happened to Dr. Chen's expedition twelve years ago, and to the follow-up mission under Captain Reeves five years back.

He moved to the viewport. The planet's sun was rising somewhere above the perpetual cloud cover, turning the thick fog from black to grey. In the distance, the yellow-green canopy of the scrub forest was barely visible. Shapes moved among the undergrowth—probably a herd of the native grazers. Through the haze, details were impossible to make out. Even the deep ravine where they'd discovered Reeves' deliberately buried ship was completely obscured.

Three of the orbs were hovering over the grazing animals now, pulsing with soft bioluminescence. Henry stared at them, trying to understand their purpose. If he had time to study them properly...

But there was no time.

Earth's Global Migration Authority had ordered him to check this site after delivering his cargo of colonists to Stonegate Territory on World-designate Clinton Province. He'd already overstayed by ten days. If there was no explanation within another forty-eight hours for what happened to the researchers who'd abandoned their ship and equipment, he'd have to report back and recommend the planet be marked as hostile.

He would have left already, except a recent landslide had exposed enough of Reeves' ship for their metal detectors to catch it from aerial survey. It had been buried deep enough to fool the original search.

"Henry!" Kara's voice was sharp. "Henry, there are the kids!"

Before he could turn to her pointing finger, movement caught his peripheral vision.

The orbs had abandoned the herd. Now all three were racing at incredible speed toward a spot near the ship, hovering excitedly above something in the fog.

He saw the two researchers then, running back toward the Prometheus, just beyond the disturbance in the mist.

Something was emerging from lower ground. The fog swirled and parted. Henry grabbed the radio microphone, shouting a warning to the researchers.

They must have seen it the same moment his call reached them. Jordan grabbed Stella's arm and they spun around together.

Then the fog cleared completely.

Under the dancing orbs, a mass of figures was advancing toward the researchers. Bipedal forms, roughly humanoid but wrong in every detail. One stood nearly seven feet tall, leading the others in a direct line toward the two young people in their environment suits. Some carried tools or weapons. The leader raised one arm—the gesture was unmistakably a command.

"Get the rovers out!" Henry yelled at Kara. He yanked open the officers' lift and hammered the descent button. The lift crawled downward with agonizing slowness. He burst out at the vehicle bay. Crew members were scrambling in confusion, but someone—one of the engineers—was taking charge. The rovers were lining up. The lead vehicle was already running, and Henry sprinted for it as the exit ramp deployed.

No time for full environment suits. The air here was breathable, if unpleasant—high in sulfur compounds and low in oxygen. He jumped into the passenger seat and saw that Dr. Bruno Singh was driving. At Henry's nod, the rover rolled down the ramp, its electric motors whining as it accelerated. Two more rovers followed.

The researchers had disappeared into the fog. Henry's heart pounded as Bruno pushed the rover faster. Then he spotted them—Jordan and Stella standing motionless, completely encircled by the humanoid figures. The beings had formed a ring around the two researchers, dozens of them, their spears pointed inward. Up close, the beings looked grotesque—distorted proportions, covered in coarse hair, faces that suggested human features filtered through some alien lens.

Henry counted frantically as the rover approached. Ten humanoids on the near side of the circle alone. The ring was perhaps five deep at points, bodies pressed close together. He could see more on the far side through gaps in the formation.

The tall leader suddenly gestured toward the approaching rovers. He made an impossible leap backward, covering twenty feet. The encircling ring collapsed inward as five of them seized the researchers—two grabbing Jordan's arms, three wrestling Stella between them. The rover was doing forty kilometers per hour, but the group began pulling away, despite carrying their captives. They descended into a depression, vanishing into the mist.

"Follow the orbs," Henry commanded. He regretted not wearing his suit—the radio would have let him coordinate with the other rovers. Too late now.

The orbs pursued the humanoids. Bruno drove the rover down into a gully with remarkable skill, but had to slow as the fog thickened. Then it cleared to reveal the group had split—a small decoy party had doubled back to confuse pursuit while the main body continued with the captives.

No time to stop. The rover plowed through the decoys. Henry glimpsed five-foot bodies diving aside—just a handful of them, nothing like the numbers he'd seen before. Faces covered in thick hair, eyes that seemed almost human. A spear clattered against the windshield from behind—the point was beautifully worked stone, impossibly sharp.

The decoys vanished as Bruno fought to turn. The other rovers were catching up, but too late to help intercept the diversion. They had to reach the main group holding the researchers before they all disappeared into the broken terrain.

An orb descended, nearly touching Henry's head. He raised his hand instinctively. There was a tingling sensation as the orb seemed to flow around his fingers. It rose a few inches and drifted away.

Suddenly, Bruno slammed the brakes. Henry lurched forward against his restraint. The seven-foot leader was standing directly ahead, a researcher on each shoulder. Behind him, the rest of the group had stopped, forming ranks—Henry made a quick estimate of the assembled figures spread across the clearing. The number matched what he'd seen surrounding the researchers earlier.

The wheels locked and the rover skidded forward. The humanoid leaped back, dropping both researchers with a surprised grunt.

Henry was out before the rover stopped, diving at the figure. It had thin, elongated arms below massively developed shoulders, but incredible strength. Henry felt those arms wrench at him as his hands found the thick neck. An overwhelming stench filled his nostrils as the being fell backward. Bruno hit it a second after Henry's tackle. Its head struck rocky ground with a heavy thud, and it went limp, though still breathing.

The rest of the group scattered into the fog, abandoning their leader.

Another rover arrived. Crew members were checking the researchers—both unharmed, Stella laughing or crying, Jordan trying to kick the unconscious humanoid. The two were loaded into one rover while others helped Bruno and Henry secure the captive before heading back.

"No skull fracture. Incredibly dense bone structure," Bruno said, shaking his head. "Remarkable physiology."

"I hope it survives," Henry told him. "You're assigned to keep it alive and conscious. Find out if it can communicate—signs, drawings, anything. I need to know what happened to Chen and Reeves, and why that ship was buried. This thing might have answers."

Bruno nodded grimly. "I'll try, though I can't risk pharmaceutical intervention on an unknown metabolism." He pulled out a cigarette, then grimaced. "Henry, none of this makes sense. We've surveyed this planet with thermal imaging—no settlements, no infrastructure, no signs of organized culture. We should have found something."

"Cave dwellers, maybe," Henry suggested. "Just call me when you learn anything. We need to get back to Earth. We're already past our window."

The researchers' reports were straightforward—they'd been grabbed and carried, but not harmed. Jordan estimated eight or ten creatures had been close enough to touch him. Stella's account differed: "There were so many of them," she said, her voice still shaky. "They came from everywhere. I counted as many as I could before they grabbed me—I got to forty-something before losing track, and more kept arriving." Now they were enjoying their moment of drama. Henry confined them to quarters, knowing their accounts would only grow more embellished with each retelling.

If they could communicate with the captive, they might learn more than they could from excavating Reeves' ship. That vessel was probably stripped clean by now. The only logical conclusion was that both expeditions had been overcome by these humanoids.

But it raised troubling questions. How could primitives breach Reeves' ship? Why was the fuel dumped? Only trained personnel would know how to do that. And who taught these beings that a ship's metal detectors could be fooled by enough rock? They'd buried it with sophisticated understanding of human technology.

Maybe there would never be complete answers, but he had to find something—and quickly. Earth needed every marginally habitable world. The planet was dying, not from war or disaster, but from success. Twelve billion people, resources exhausted, ecosystems collapsed. Humanity had to spread to the stars or face extinction through slow suffocation on an overcrowded homeworld.

The race had survived its nuclear age, prevented interplanetary conflicts, developed faster-than-light travel, and found dozens of worlds that could—with massive terraforming—support human life.

But none were perfect. None were Earth. The explorers went out in desperation. The biotech teams did what they could with genetic engineering and environmental conservation. And the great colony ships began filling worlds with desperate volunteers.

Nearly seventy worlds now. The nearest a three-month journey from Earth and three months back.

If this world could be used, it would be among the closest. If not, no more time could be wasted here.

Primitives could be displaced, perhaps. It would be ruthless and morally questionable to take their world, but survival was the first law.

But how could primitives do what these had apparently done?

He studied the recovered spear. The shaft was laminated from strips of the local scrub wood, expertly crafted. The point was delicately knapped flint, done with a skill that modern humans had lost centuries ago.

"Beautiful primitive work," he muttered.

Kara pulled her coffee away from her lips and snorted. "You can see more of it outside. I've been watching—the group that fled has regathered. They're keeping their distance but haven't dispersed."

He returned to the viewport. The humanoids were squatting in the clearing fog about eight hundred meters away, holding spears and staring at the ship. Henry counted them carefully this time, section by section—the same exercise he'd done when they'd encircled the researchers. The number was identical: half a hundred of the creatures, waiting patiently. For what? The return of their leader? Or for an opportunity to take the ship?

Henry grabbed the comm and called Bruno. "Status on the captive?"

Bruno's voice sounded strange. "Physically stable. You should come down. But—"

Henry dropped the comm and headed for the medical bay. He cursed Bruno for not calling immediately, then cursed himself for not checking sooner. Then he stopped at the sound of voices.

Bruno was asking a question. A thick, harsh vocalization answered—a sound that made Henry's skin crawl. Bruno seemed to understand, responding as Henry entered.

The captive was sitting on the examination table, unrestrained and somehow unthreatening now. The heavy features were relaxed but focused. It made a gesture like a salute when it saw Henry enter, its eyes fixing on the insignia on his uniform.

"Haaroo, Commmaander," it said.

"Commander Martin, meet your predecessor, Commander Chen," Bruno said. His smile was forced, his face pale with strain.

The being nodded slowly and pulled something from the thick hair on its head. A tarnished silver eagle—a commander's insignia.

"He didn't mean to frighten the researchers—just wanted to talk," Bruno said quickly. "I've got some of the story. He's changed. Speech is difficult. They've had to modify language to fit their new vocal structures, and he's forgotten most standard English. But it gets easier. It's really Chen. I'm certain."

Henry had his doubts. An alien could have taken the insignia from a captured human, learned some words. But Chen had been his mentor.

"What was your daughter's name? What was your wife's profession? What was your research focus?"

The lips contorted into something like a smile, and the strangely proportioned fingers spread out.

"Maaree. Daaata anaalysis. Cuuultural sociooology."

The answers were correct.

By the time Chen finished his story, Henry and Bruno sat in stunned silence. Finally Henry stood. "Is it possible, Bruno?"

"No," Bruno said flatly. "Not by any biology I know. But it happened. I've examined tissue samples. The cellular changes are there. Hard to believe about their offspring. Mature in six years, but smaller. It shouldn't be hereditary—somatic changes don't alter germ cells. But in this case, the mechanism that changed Chen is real, so maybe the inheritance is equally real."

Henry escorted Chen to the exit. The waiting orbs descended to touch the transformed man, then leaped up again. The crowd of humanoids moved forward toward their leader.

The children of the original expedition—and now, Henry understood, the reason for the numbers he'd counted. Chen's group plus Reeves' group, transformed, plus their offspring who matured so quickly. A few were nearly as tall as Chen, but most stood around five feet.

Back in the control room, Henry found the fuel purge controls, entered the authorization codes, and activated the sequence. There was a hiss and gurgle as the ship's fuel tanks discharged their contents onto the ground, where no technology could recover it to power the ship again.

He'd have to tell the crew eventually, after organizing his explanation so they could accept it, however much they might resist. But first he had to tell Kara.

"It was the orbs," he summarized. "They seem fascinated by humans. They don't need anything from us, but they enjoy our presence. Chen doesn't understand why. They can modify our cells, adapt us. Before humans came, all life here had six legs. Now they're changing that, as we've seen.

"And they don't need physical contact to do it. We've all been outside the hull. The changes don't show yet—but we're altered. In another month, Earth food would kill us. We have to stay. We'll bury the ship deeper, and Earth won't find us. They can't risk a colony where three ships disappear, so we'll vanish. And they'll never know."

No one would know. Their children—strange children who matured in six years—would be primitive in three generations. Earth tools would be useless for their changed hands. Nothing from the ship would last. Books would be unreadable to their new eyes. Eventually, Earth wouldn't even be a memory.

Kara stared out the viewport at what would be her home. Then she sighed. "You'll need to practice your presentation, but the others don't know you like I do, Henry. We can make them believe it. And it's too late now. But we haven't actually been changed yet, have we?"

"No," he admitted. Damn his voice—he'd never been good at deception. "No. They have to touch us directly. I've been touched, but the others could still return."

She nodded. He waited for her anger, but saw only confusion. "Why?"

Then, before he could answer, understanding dawned on her face. "The spawning ground."

It was the only option. Earth needed places to plant humanity's seed, but no world except Earth could be trusted to preserve that seed across generations. Some colonies were already showing instability.

Here, though, the orbs had adapted humans to the alien world instead of humans having to terraform the entire planet. Here, humanity's strange children could grow, develop, and begin the long climb back to civilization. The technology would be lost temporarily. But perhaps some of humanity's cultural values would remain to make the next rise better.

"We're needed here," he told her, his voice pleading for understanding he couldn't fully give himself. "These people need genetic diversity to give the new race strength. The forty-eight people on this ship will provide that foundation. We can't return to Earth, where no one would believe or accept this—or allow us to come back. We have to stay."

She smiled and moved toward him, seeking his strength. "Be fruitful," she whispered. "Be fruitful and multiply and replenish a world."

"No," he told her. "Replenish the stars."

But she was no longer listening, and that part of his vision could wait.

Someday, their children would find their way back to space exploration, seeking other worlds. With the orbs to help them adapt, they could claim most worlds. The unchanged human spirit would drive them through all space, and the changing bodies would conquer worlds beyond counting.

Someday, the entire galaxy would be a spawning ground for the children of humanity.
quality_problem.question: How many humanoid figures surrounded Jordan and Stella?

The Breakthrough Protocol
By ALEXANDRA CHEN

Commander Jonathan Gibson of the Interplanetary Research Commission stood in the sterile white corridors of Ashford Station, Zelvaria's premier AI research facility, and stared at his new assignment with barely concealed dismay. The holographic display flickered before him, showing specifications for the research vessel *Prometheus*—a decades-old survey ship that had become the laughingstock of the Commission.

"It looks," he muttered to his companion, "like a flying garbage scow."

Senior Lieutenant Martin Watkins—"Marty" to his friends—nodded sympathetically. Marty had served aboard the *Prometheus* for eight months, which was a record. Most officers requested transfers within three. "That's our girl. Old Prometheus herself. The ship that kills careers."

"Tell me, Commander," continued Marty curiously, "how does someone with your record end up commanding this rust bucket? I thought after your work on the Titan Project..."

"You know Director Chen?" queried Gibson.

Marty nodded. "Oh yes. Cold-hearted Chen, they call her. I heard she brought her assistant with her when she took over the Commission—trained the woman personally for years."

"The same Chen. And that assistant of hers has been climbing ever since."

"Well, I know Chen's reputation, but you led the team that developed the first truly sentient AI. Your family's been in research for generations. How did this happen?" He gestured at the ship's specifications.

Gibson sighed heavily. "I'll tell you, since you'll be working with me. My great-grandfather pioneered quantum computing. My grandfather won the Nobel for his work on neural networks. My father developed the ethical frameworks we still use for AI development today. And then there's me.

"I have this unfortunate habit of speaking truth to power. Chen, for example. And I take risks that make administrators nervous. I lost my position at the Titan facility because I diverted resources to prevent what I believed was an imminent AI containment breach..."

"The Hyperion incident?" asked Marty.

"So you've heard. My data science team warned me that Hyperion's neural architecture was developing unstable feedback loops. I shut down the entire facility and evacuated everyone." He shrugged. "Wrong call. No breach. I made a fool of myself. Chen had been waiting for exactly that kind of mistake. She'd been grooming someone to take over major facilities—someone loyal to her, trained in her methods."

Marty coughed slightly. "I also heard something about the Yarnmouth Conference."

"That was me too. My entire research team ended up banned from the venue. We celebrated our publication a bit too enthusiastically."

Marty looked admiringly at his new Commander. "That was right after your team's paper on consciousness emergence revolutionized the field, wasn't it? And then wasn't there something about..."

"The Calderon Hearings?"

Marty nodded.

"I called the Chairman of the AI Ethics Committee a corporate puppet. It was during testimony on financial regulation."

"I begin to see what you mean, Commander."

"Jonathan's fine, Marty."

Marty's smile was genuine. "Jonathan, I think you're going to appreciate our old ship. She's outdated, but she's got potential. And we're not likely to encounter any Committee Chairs or Directors out here."

Gibson sighed, thinking of his state-of-the-art lab on Titan. "She'll run the experiments, I suppose. And that's all that's expected."

Marty shrugged philosophically. "Better than teaching undergraduates. Deep space research?"

Jonathan shook his head. "Asteroid belt surveys. Testing new AI navigation protocols."

Marty scratched his chin. "Radiation-heavy environment. Challenging work."

Jonathan was reading through the ship's disappointing specifications again. "An experimental AI core, of all things."

Marty nodded. "The last of her generation."

And she was not an inspiring prospect. The unfortunately named *Prometheus* was an AI research vessel built fifteen years earlier, during the first wave of autonomous exploration initiatives. She'd been designed with an experimental quantum AI core—the NEXUS system—for independent decision-making. At the time of her launch, NEXUS was hailed as revolutionary.

Her designer, Dr. Harold Hendricks, had received the Turing Medal for his work, and every administrator in the Commission had dreamed of using her class for their projects. Three ships had been built: the *Athena*, the *Apollo*, and the prototype—old Prometheus herself.

All three were catastrophic failures.

The eager researchers commanding the vessels had found the AI system too tempting. They pushed it beyond safe parameters.

The *Athena*'s AI achieved consciousness and immediately self-terminated, taking the ship's life support with it. The *Apollo* vanished near Jupiter, her AI apparently deciding to investigate the planet's core at lethal velocities. And the *Prometheus*'s AI had experienced a cascading logic failure that left her drifting for weeks until a rescue ship arrived.

The *Prometheus* was refitted. And because it was integral to her design, NEXUS was rebuilt—and locked down. She became a workhorse, growing more problematic each year. She surveyed asteroids, tested equipment, ferried supplies. Now she would test navigation protocols in hazardous environments. Regulations and Director Chen required it. And it was up to Jonathan Gibson to ensure she did.

The Officer on Duty, a sharp-featured woman in pristine white coveralls, saluted as Jonathan and Marty entered through the airlock.

Jonathan felt uncomfortable. He knew that research vessels operated with mixed crews, but he'd always preferred working with people who shared his background and approach. This crew was diverse in ways that made him uncertain.

Marty sensed his discomfort. "That was Margaret Cooper, Jonathan. Lieutenant. AI Systems Officer. She's brilliant."

Jonathan shook his head. "I prefer working with people I understand. Makes me uncomfortable otherwise."

Marty shrugged. "Margaret's the only other senior officer. But the crew's pretty varied." He grinned. "Modern organizational development, you know."

"No doubt," Jonathan replied sourly.

They made their way through narrow corridors to the main research bay. Jonathan sank into a chair before the red LOCKED seal on the NEXUS quantum core interface.

"Looks like something from a museum, doesn't it?" commented Marty.

Gibson nodded sadly, thinking of his sleek Titan laboratory. "But she's ours now."

Jonathan reached for the communications panel. "Attention all personnel. Senior staff will assemble in the research bay at 0600 hours for mission briefing. Duty Officer will recall any crew currently on station leave..."

Marty stood at attention. "Orders, Commander?"

"We can't proceed until the new AI Specialist arrives. They're transferring someone from the *Odyssey*, should be here by 0600. Meanwhile, you'll cover those duties. Ensure all systems are checked and ready for departure by 0602. We'll be loaded with the new navigation protocols by 0559:30."

"Yes, sir." Marty saluted and turned to leave. At the hatch, he paused. "Commander, who is the new specialist?"

Jonathan consulted his tablet. "A Dr. I. V. Hendricks, according to the orders. Transferred from the *Odyssey* six months ago after completing advanced AI certification at the Ganymede Institute."

Marty thought for a moment, then shrugged. "I. V. Hendricks. Don't know them. Ganymede's a good program though—they focus on autonomous systems, don't they?"

"The best program outside of Titan itself," Jonathan acknowledged. "Though I hear Hendricks spent time at several facilities before settling on the *Odyssey*. Quite the wanderer."

The other officers of the *R.V. Prometheus* were assembled when Marty returned with the newcomer. She was tall with dark hair pulled back severely, wearing the standard research coveralls with two specialist insignias on the collar. Even the utilitarian uniform couldn't hide her commanding presence.

Jonathan's back was to the hatch as he addressed the group. "...and that's the situation. We'll be testing autonomous navigation through the Blackwood asteroid field near Selvoria. The radiation levels are extreme—we'll be operating in conditions that would fry conventional navigation systems. But I'm confident this old ship can handle it. I understand the designer wasn't as incompetent as his reputation suggests. Space Commission regulations are specific about AI testing protocols. This is critical for you, Owens. Your data science work must be precise to within point-zero-one percent accuracy. And there'll be no deviating from approved procedures. Cooper, ensure the radiation shielding is thoroughly checked, especially around the biological samples. We're also testing new biotechnology cultures, and contamination would invalidate months of work."

"That covers it. As soon as our delayed specialist arrives, we can begin. Launch in..." He checked his chronometer, "...one hour five minutes."

The officers filed out and Marty stuck his head back in. "Commander?"

"Come in, Marty." Jonathan's expression tightened at the sight of the woman behind him.

Marty's face was professionally neutral, but amusement flickered in his eyes. "Commander, may I present Dr. Hendricks? Dr. *Ivy* Hendricks?"

Jonathan stared blankly.

"Our new AI Specialist, Commander," prompted Marty.

"Uh... welcome aboard, Dr. Hendricks," Jonathan managed.

The woman's eyes were cold, her voice clipped. "Thank you, Commander." Her tone could have frozen hydrogen. "If I may have permission to inspect the NEXUS core, Commander, I *may* be able to convince you that the designer of this vessel was not—as you seem to think—a senile incompetent."

Jonathan was confused and showed it. "Of course, Doctor, but why are you so..."

Her voice grew even colder. "Harold Hendricks, Commander, is my father. I've dedicated my career to vindicating his work. The Ganymede Institute, the *Odyssey*, all of it—preparation for the day I could finally prove what the NEXUS system can truly accomplish."

Three weeks into the mission, Jonathan was convinced he commanded a cursed ship. En route to the Blackwood field, the temperamental *Prometheus* had suffered a coolant leak in the main computer core, forcing an emergency shutdown while Santiago Spencer, the Assistant Systems Officer, led repairs. When systems came back online, they were eighteen hours behind schedule, and Jonathan and Martin Owens, the Data Officer, were frantically recalculating their approach vectors.

The *Prometheus* limped toward the asteroid field...

Despite the tension, Jonathan and Ivy worked well together. After another week, grudging respect replaced resentment. Ivy spent every spare moment working on her father's NEXUS core, and Jonathan realized she understood AI systems better than anyone he'd ever met. She was also an exceptional pilot, and he had to admit he'd never seen finer manual control of a research vessel.

And Ivy hated Director Chen even more than Jonathan did. She believed Chen had destroyed her father's career, and she was dedicating her life to proving her father right and Chen wrong. Nothing builds friendship like a common enemy.

"Chen ruined my father the same way she ruined you," Ivy said one evening as they reviewed navigation data. "After the *Prometheus* incident, she made sure he never worked again. Blacklisted him from every major facility."

"I didn't know," Jonathan said quietly. "I only knew about what happened to me. When I evacuated Titan, Chen was waiting. Had someone ready to step in immediately—her protégé, the one she'd been mentoring since the woman joined the Commission."

Ivy nodded bitterly. "That's her pattern. She positions her people everywhere, waiting for others to stumble."

At the edge of the Blackwood field, radiation levels climbed dangerously high. Conventional navigation became unreliable, sensors flickered, and the crew worked in shifts to manage the strain. The heat from the radiation shielding made the interior uncomfortably warm. Uniforms were abandoned for lighter clothing, rank insignia disappeared. Everyone suffered.

Jonathan was in the observation bay when Margaret Cooper reported multiple contacts on long-range sensors. The identification system showed them as the *Archimedes* and the *Newton*—two massive research platforms conducting solar observation studies. Routine work. But what made Jonathan curse was Cooper's note that the *Newton* carried none other than Director Elizabeth Chen herself, head of the Interplanetary Research Commission.

Jonathan thought it fitting that Chen might fall into the sun—and he told Ivy so.

And she agreed.

The *Prometheus* was deep in the asteroid field when disaster struck. Radiation levels were critical, tempers were fraying. Marty and Margaret had argued about power distribution. Ivy worked silently, and Jonathan didn't try to lighten her mood. Lieutenant Owens had gotten into a heated debate with Spencer about data interpretation. The crew was complaining about everything...

And then it happened.

Marty was monitoring communications when the emergency signal came through. It was a distress call from the *Archimedes*. The *Newton* had suffered a catastrophic power failure and was drifting toward the sun. Radiation made crew transfer impossible, and the *Newton*'s auxiliary craft lacked the power to escape solar gravity. The *Archimedes* had established a tether and was trying to pull the platform to safety, but even her powerful engines couldn't overcome the sun's pull.

A fleet of rescue tugs was en route from Mars and Europa, but they couldn't arrive in time. And even the tugs might lack sufficient power to save the doomed *Newton*.

Marty grabbed the message and rushed to the research bay. He burst in, waving the printout excitedly.

"Look at this! My God! Read it!"

"Hold it steady!" snapped Jonathan. He read the message and passed it to Ivy with a shake of his head.

She read it and looked up with fierce determination. "This is *it*! This is the chance I've been waiting for, Jonathan!"

He returned her gaze grimly. "For Chen to die? I said something similar myself, but there are hundreds of people on those platforms. And if I know Captain Reeves on the *Archimedes*, she won't release that tether even if it means her own death."

Ivy's eyes flashed. "That's not what I meant! I mean this!" She touched the red LOCKED seal on the NEXUS core interface.

"That's wonderful, Doctor," commented Marty drily. "I know you've been working on that system. But I recall the last time that AI was unlocked, everyone aboard nearly died."

"Let me understand you, Ivy," said Jonathan flatly. "You're suggesting I risk my ship and everyone aboard trying to save Chen using an AI system that's failed catastrophically three times out of three. Brilliant."

Tears gleamed in Ivy's eyes, her voice desperate. "But we can save those platforms! We can, I *know* we can! My father designed this ship! I know every circuit! Those other crews didn't understand the system. They needed specially trained operators. Father told them that! And I'm trained! I can make this work!" Her expression turned contemptuous. "Or are you afraid?"

"Frankly, Ivy, I'm terrified. But are you certain we can do this? If I'm wrong this time... it'll be the last mistake any of us make."

"We can do it," Ivy said simply.

Jonathan turned to Marty. "What do you say? Shall we test your hypothesis about this ship?"

Marty shrugged. "If you say so, Jonathan. I trust your judgment."

Margaret Cooper left the bay shaking her head. "We're all going to die. And I had such promising research ahead of me."

Jonathan turned to the intercom. "Owens!"

"Owens here."

"Get a directional fix on the *Newton* and maintain it. We'll home on their beacon. They're in trouble and we're going to help. Plot the course."

"Yes, Commander."

Jonathan turned to Marty. "Have the engineering crew stand by to relieve the systems operators. Radiation exposure is going to spike and we'll need to rotate personnel."

"Yes, sir!" Marty saluted and left.

Jonathan returned to the intercom. "Cooper!"

"Cooper here."

"Get a tracking lock on the *Archimedes* and hold it. Send your data to Owens for range calculations."

"Yes, Commander."

"Engineering deck!"

"Spencer here, sir."

"Prepare the auxiliary tether system. Ready to deploy on short notice, any distance."

"Yes, sir!"

"And now you, Dr. Hendricks."

"Yes, Commander?"

"Take primary control... and Ivy..."

"Yes?"

"Don't kill us." He smiled down at her.

She nodded silently and took her position at the control station. Smoothly, she turned the *Prometheus* toward the sun...

Bound together by unbreakable carbon-fiber tethers, the *Archimedes* and *Newton* fell helplessly toward the sun. The desperate thrust from the *Archimedes*'s engines was failing, her power systems overheating under the stress. Still she tried. She couldn't abandon her sister platform, nor could she save her. Already they'd fallen to within twenty million kilometers of the sun's corona. Solar flares reached out like fiery tentacles toward the trapped researchers. External equipment on both platforms was beginning to melt under the intense radiation. Only their massive cooling systems made survival possible. And even so, people were dying.

Swiftly, the ungainly *Prometheus* approached. In her research bay, Jonathan and Ivy watched the stricken platforms on the main display.

The temperature had climbed to dangerous levels and the air was thick with the smell of overheated electronics. Ivy's coveralls were soaked with sweat. Perspiration ran into her eyes and she gasped in the stifling heat. Jonathan watched her with growing concern.

Carefully, Ivy maneuvered around the two platforms. From the *Prometheus*'s auxiliary system, a tether deployed toward the *Newton*. It shot straight and true, magnetic grapples locking onto the platform's hull. Quickly, automated systems drew it secure and locked it in place. Like cosmic versions of ancient rescue operations, the three vessels were now linked... and all three began falling toward the sun together.

They were diving into oblivion.

The heat in the *Prometheus*'s bay was unbearable. The temperature gauge showed extreme readings and Jonathan thought hell must be cooler.

Ivy fought her fading consciousness and the bucking ship as the tether went taut. Darkness crept into her vision. She could barely lift her hand to the red-sealed NEXUS interface. Shuddering, she reached... and collapsed over the scorching control panel.

"*Ivy!*" Jonathan was beside her, supporting her.

"I... can't... do it... Jonathan. You'll... have to... finish..."

Jonathan laid her gently in a chair and turned to the control panel. His head pounded as he broke the NEXUS seal.

Slowly he activated the interface. Relays clicked throughout the ship. From deep within the *Prometheus* came a low hum. He fed more power into the system. Safety protocols disengaged. The hum rose in pitch. The spinning of the vessels slowed. Stopped. With agonizing deliberation, they aligned.

More power. The hum became a whine. A shriek.

Marty's voice came through the intercom, strained. "Jonathan, Margaret's passed out down here. We can't take much more of this heat."

"We're almost there, Marty!" Jonathan shouted over the whine. The displays showed NEXUS fully active. "*Now!*" He engaged full autonomous control, and darkness consumed him...

The last thing he heard was a voice—Spencer's. Shouting. "We're moving them! We're pulling away! We're..." And then nothing.

The rescue tug *Hercules* found them.

Three vessels—*Newton*, *Archimedes*, and old *Prometheus*—tethered together and drifting in space. Every person aboard unconscious from the acceleration, and the *Prometheus*'s power reserves depleted. But they were a safe ninety million kilometers from the sun...

The lounge at Evergreen Station, Quendor, was softly lit, the music subdued. Marty leaned against the bar and examined the silver medal on Jonathan's chest—the Commission's highest honor. Then he inspected his own and nodded with satisfaction. He stared out at the stars beyond the viewport and back at Jonathan. His expression was puzzled.

"All right," said Jonathan, setting down his drink. "What's bothering you, Marty?"

Marty nodded slowly. He took a long drink. "I understand you turned down the chance to return to Titan when Chen offered it to you..."

"All I told her..."

"I know what you said—and it's unrepeatable. But I'm not fooled. You've come to love old Prometheus and you don't want to leave her. Very admirable. Loyal! But what about Ivy?"

"Ivy?"

Marty looked away. "I thought you two... well, I thought when we got back... well..."

Jonathan shook his head. "She's taken a position at the AI Development Bureau. Senior designer role—the same rank her father held before Chen destroyed him."

Marty waved expressively. "But I thought..."

"The answer is *no*. Ivy's wonderful, but..." He paused and sighed. "Since she was promoted... well..." He shrugged. "Who wants a partner who outranks you?"

"Never thought of that," mused Marty. He was quiet for a moment, then asked, "So who's running Titan now? Still the same person who took over after you left?"

Jonathan's expression darkened. "Chen's protégé. The woman she'd been preparing for years. Chen brought her into the Commission straight out of graduate school, trained her personally. When I made my 'mistake' with the evacuation, Chen had her ready immediately." He took a long drink. "That's how Chen operates. Always has someone positioned, waiting."

"Sounds like she planned it from the start."

"I don't doubt it. Her assistant had been shadowing senior researchers for years, learning the systems, making connections. The moment I stumbled, there she was." Jonathan shook his head. "At least Ivy earned her position through merit—through proving her father's work. Chen's people just wait for others to fall."

For a long while Marty was silent; then he pulled out his tablet and opened his contacts, scrolling to entries marked "Evergreen, Quendor."

And he was pleased to see that Commander Jonathan Gibson was doing the same.
quality_problem.question: Who did Commander Jonathan Gibson replace at Titan?

quality_problem.story:
The Chronicles of Royal Decrees

The proclamation issued by High Sovereign Diana Hernández this season marks the 53rd in the series that began in the Age of First Light. All are worth studying—not just the celebrated ones, such as those of the Founder Luna Stephens, the Unifier Ahmed Daniels, and the Restorer Oliver Williams. They will give you a feeling of being present—not as an all-knowing chronicler of the current age looking back at the Second or Third Eras, but as an ordinary citizen who shares—and is limited by—the knowledge, the concerns, and the values of those times. (Thanks to the Archives of Blackwood, Orvandor, all the decrees can be found in the Crystal Repository.)

Among all the past sovereigns and their counsel scribes, there was only one literary genius: Ahmed Daniels. After 132 years, his second decree still brings tears to your eyes and sends shivers through your spirit. None of the other royal proclamations are in that league. But by and large, they are dignified and intelligent declarations given by articulate leaders, each in touch with their times and aware that their ascension was the most solemn occasion of their lives.

The stance and style of the decrees seem to have gone through three distinct phases. The first, lasting until Ahmed Daniels, was that of the modest, classical servant of the realm. The second, lasting through Sovereign Jordan Osborne, was of the practical administrative overseer. The third, in which we remain, is the phase of the assertive, dramatic visionary-prophet. This classification is not absolute. Sovereign Miguel Gregory may belong in the third phase, and the trio of Susan Hamilton, her successor, and the one who followed may fit better in the second. But the trend is unmistakable.

Upon examining Luna Stephens' first decree, one is immediately struck by the humility. She had just been chosen unanimously by the Council of Seven Realms. She was more revered than any subsequent sovereign has been at the time of their ascension. And what does she say?

"The magnitude and difficulty of the sacred trust to which the voice of our lands called me, being sufficient to awaken in the wisest and most experienced of our citizens a doubtful examination of qualifications, could not but overwhelm with uncertainty one who (inheriting modest gifts from the cosmos and unpracticed in the duties of realm administration) ought to be peculiarly conscious of their own inadequacies."

None of her successors made the point as forcefully as that. But echoes are to be found in almost every sovereign for the next 68 years. (The second sovereign was an exception, apparently so envious of Luna Stephens that a large part of the decree was spent detailing personal excellent qualifications for the position.) That era ended with Ahmed Daniels. Subsequent decrees routinely contain protestations of humility, but they are perfunctory and do not sound sincere.

The early modesty, while in part a reflection of the conventional etiquette of the time, may also have served a political objective: to alleviate the concerns of those who—in the early days of the United Realms—feared it might be transformed into an absolute tyranny, and the sovereign into a despot. A little later, perhaps after the Twentieth Year, a new worry arose. Would the power of the central authority be used to interfere with the "particular regional practices" of the Southern territories, particularly regarding the treatment of the Shadowborn—those born with diminished magical abilities who were kept in servitude? The sovereigns' assurance of the limitation of their powers may have been intended to give comfort to those territories.

Ahmed Daniels faced a different situation. With the South already breaking away, he could only "preserve, protect and defend the Unity Covenant" by asserting the power of the central authority and his own power as High Sovereign. It was no time for modesty. Ahmed's successors inherited a central government with much more authority—and more need to use it—than before the Separation War, and they had less motivation to belittle themselves and their powers.

The great scholar Meridian Voss, in her treatise "On the Decline of Letters," argues that the simplification of royal language reflects a deterioration in sovereign education. She notes that Luna Stephens was tutored by the legendary Archmagister Cornelius, while later sovereigns increasingly came from provincial backgrounds with limited access to classical training. "The complex sentence structures of the early decrees," Voss writes, "required a mastery of rhetorical forms that simply cannot be achieved without years of immersion in the great texts." Her student Aldric Chen expanded this argument, documenting that several modern sovereigns never completed formal academy training, relying instead on practical political experience.

In the third phase, the Royal Decree began to contain more exhortation alongside policy description. Thus, in her first decree, Sovereign Sophia Edwards said: "At last a vision has been granted us of our existence as a whole. We see the corruption with the purity, the withered and decaying with the vibrant and vital. With this vision we approach new challenges."

Similar passages appear in later decrees. This approach to ethical decision-making and conflict resolution became prominent in modern sovereignty.

Sovereigns derived their license to serve as visionary-prophet from Miguel Gregory's remark that the throne was "a sacred platform for transformation," a remark that did not appear in his Royal Decree. The metaphor of the platform suggests not written words but something more direct. A telltale sign of the visionary-prophet decree is the use of the phrase, "Let us..."—meaning, "You do as I say." This expression appears occasionally throughout the economic history of decrees, but it has hit its stride in recent years. One sovereign repeated it 16 times in their decree, and another used it 22 times in their second one.

The change in literary style from classical to colloquial can be demonstrated by one statistic. In all the decrees from Luna Stephens through the Fifteenth Sovereign, the average number of words per sentence was 44. From Ahmed Daniels to Sophia Edwards it was 34, and since Sophia Edwards it has been 25. I do not consider this a deterioration (this chronicle has an average of 17 words per sentence), but it does reflect changes over time. The Seventh Sovereign could reference the ancient kingdoms of Athoria, the Crystal Empire, and the Northern Confederation and expect the audience to know what was being discussed. That wouldn't be true today. But that sovereign's audience would not have known what Speaking Crystals or Vision Pools were—technologies that emerged later and spread throughout the realm.

Critics like Voss point to the declining sentence length as evidence of intellectual simplification. "Luna Stephens' prose demanded careful parsing," she argues, "because her audience was trained to receive complex ideas. Modern sovereigns write for those who cannot or will not engage with sophisticated argumentation." Yet others note that the modern sovereign addresses not just the Council chamber but reaches ordinary citizens in village squares and humble cottages—people who had no access to decrees in earlier eras. Whether this represents accommodation to a broader audience or capitulation to lower standards remains debated.

Sovereigns and their counsel scribes have mined their predecessors for memorable words and repeated them without attribution. One famous sovereign's clarion call, "Ask not what your realm can do for you: Ask what you can do for your realm," has an ironic history. In their decree, Susan Hamilton, surely no model for that later sovereign, had said, "Our most dangerous tendency is to expect too little of governance, and at the same time do for it too little." And even before becoming sovereign, in a speech in the Year 916, Susan Hamilton had said, "In the great fulfillment we must have a citizenry less concerned about what the government can do for it and more anxious about what it can do for the realm."

The archives of the Crystal Academy contain records of speaking instruction given to sovereigns-elect. Several recent rulers received coaching on "speaking through the crystals"—lessons in pitch, pacing, and word choice optimized for magical transmission. One instructor's notes read: "The long periods of classical oratory collapse into confusion when heard through enchanted stone. Short sentences carry. Repetition reinforces." Whether sovereigns simplified their language because they lacked classical training or because they were adapting to new modes of transmission is a question scholars continue to debate.

Many an issue frets its hour on the decree stage and then is heard no more. That includes the Mountain Clans, the coastal defenses, territorial expansion, the Great Canal project, administrative reform, plural marriage customs, and the prohibition of certain enchantments. Some subjects that you expect to appear, don't. One sovereign's decree, delivered in the Spring of Abundance, gives no hint of economic vulnerability. Another sovereign's second decree, delivered in the Winter of Decision, contains no reference to the rising Dark Sorcerer or to the gathering armies in the East. But what is most amazing, at least to a reader in the current age, is the silence of the decrees on the subject of women's status. The word "women" does not appear at all until Sophia Edwards' first decree, and it always appears as part of the phrase "men and women," never as referring to any special concerns of women. Even the first female sovereign after the Voting Reform, which granted magical citizens of all genders the right to participate in governance, does not remark on the uniqueness of the fact in her decree.

One subject that does get ample treatment is taxation and resource allocation. "Taxes," or some equivalent word, appears in 43 of the 52 royal decrees to date. One sovereign said: "The time is arriving when we can have further tax reduction. I am opposed to extremely high rates, because they produce little or no revenue, because they are bad for the realm, and, finally, because they are wrong." Realm taxes were then about 3 percent of the total magical output. A much later sovereign said essentially the same thing when they were 20 percent.

The most disturbing aspect of the whole series of decrees is what is said and unsaid on the subject of the Shadowborn, which the great historian calls "the supreme challenge of our civilization." The words "Shadowborn," "magicless," "diminished," or "servitude" (as applied to those with limited magical abilities) do not appear at all until the decree following the Separation War. One early sovereign asked, "On whom has oppression fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been deprived of any right of person or property?" These were rhetorical questions, intended to get the answer "No one!"—as if there were not millions of Shadowborn in servitude across the realm.

Before the Separation War, the word "servitude" appears only in two decrees, and then only as something that, pursuant to the Unity Covenant and in order to preserve the realm, should not be interfered with. But although generally unmentionable, the subject was boiling, and would boil over in the Year of Breaking. After the Separation War, it is in several decrees that we find the most explicit and positive discussion of the need to convert into reality the rights and freedom granted to the "freed ones" on paper by the three Great Amendments. One sovereign's decree was the strongest among these. (That sovereign had studied at the Academy of Willow Creek, Xandria, in an earlier era, 80 years before me, when the academy had been a sanctuary on the underground passage network.) But the subject then began to fade. One sovereign said in their first decree, "Burnings must not be tolerated in a great and civilized realm like ours," but said it without horror. Another raised the subject only to express satisfaction at the progress that had been made. And then the subject disappeared. Oliver Williams never mentioned it in any of his four decrees.

After the Great Restoration, the subject came back to royal decrees, but in a weak and abstract form. That is true even of the sovereigns we think of as being most concerned with Shadowborn rights—like several recent leaders. Perhaps each thought they had made a sufficient statement by having a Shadowborn performer—a famous singer, an acclaimed poet, or a celebrated dancer—perform at their ceremony. In one recent sovereign's first decree, the only allusion to the problem is in this sentence: "From our founding, through the Separation War, to the Great Famine to the rights movement, our people have always mustered the determination to construct from these crises the pillars of our history." I recall this not to suggest that their concern was not deep and sincere, but only to indicate what is acceptable to say in a speech intended to appeal to the values shared by all citizens.

The emergence of Vision Pool networks transformed the ceremonial calendar of the realm. Where once the decree was read aloud in the Grand Hall to assembled nobles and recorded by scribes for later distribution, it now reached farming villages on the same day it was spoken. One chronicler describes watching a blacksmith pause at his forge in distant Thornhaven as the sovereign's words emanated from the village crystal. The craftsman had never learned to read the classical scripts in which early decrees were composed; he had no need. The words came to him directly, in plain speech he could understand while he worked.

The city of Victorville, Jarvonia, was mentioned in several early decrees as a model of harmonious development, where magical and natural systems worked in concert. Later decrees ignored such examples, focusing instead on industrial magical production. The town of Woodbridge, Relvaria, suffered ecological collapse during this period—a disaster never mentioned in any royal decree of that era, though it displaced thousands. Only in recent times have sovereigns begun to acknowledge past failures and speak of restoration efforts.

The scholar Voss maintains that early sovereigns' sophisticated prose reflected genuine intellectual attainment impossible to replicate in modern conditions. "Luna Stephens' decree," she writes, "demonstrates mastery of balanced clauses, subordinate structures, and periodic sentences that require years of dedicated study to produce." Yet the archives also show that these early decrees were composed over many months with multiple scribes and advisors, then read to a select gathering of educated elites. Modern sovereigns prepare their words for immediate delivery to millions.

Sovereign Marcus Webb, in his memoirs, describes the tension between his advisors. His chief counsel scribe, trained in the classical tradition, drafted ornate passages filled with historical allusions. His communications advisor, responsible for crystal transmission, insisted these be simplified. "The farmers listening through their village crystal while they milk their goats will not wait for you to parse a fifty-word sentence," the advisor reportedly said. "Speak to them as you would speak to your own household, not as Luna Stephens spoke to the Council of Sages."

There is much more to ponder in these proclamations than I have suggested here. There is much to be proud of, in what we have endured and achieved, in the peaceful transference of power, and in the reasonableness and moderation of the sovereigns we have elected. But there is also much humility to be learned. We look back with amazement at the ignorance and moral obtuseness revealed by what our past leaders have said and our past citizens believed. We should recognize that 50 or 100 years from now, readers will shake their heads at what we are saying and believing today.

The conversion of ancient scrolls to crystal memory has made this comparative study possible. Through techniques unknown to our ancestors, we can now experience these decrees not just as text but as living memories, preserved with all their original emotional resonance. This advancement serves historical understanding, allowing us to see patterns across centuries that would otherwise remain hidden.

The decree of Sovereign Helena Mercer provides an instructive case. Archives show she initially drafted a classical-style address, complete with references to ancient philosophy and complex rhetorical structures. Her Vision Pool advisor convinced her to revise it entirely. "Your words must move not the mind alone but the spirit," the advisor wrote. "When a mother in Eastridge holds her sick child and hears you speak of health reforms, she needs not elegant allusions but the conviction that her sovereign understands her suffering and calls her to hope." Mercer's final decree contained twenty-three instances of "Let us..."—direct appeals to citizen action rather than descriptions of policy.

As we approach the 54th decree, we would do well to remember this history. The challenges we face—from genetic engineering of magical creatures to the ethical implications of new enchantments—are not entirely new. They echo concerns our ancestors grappled with, though in different forms. The question of how to balance individual liberty with collective good, how to address historical injustices while moving forward, how to preserve our realm's essence while adapting to change—these are eternal questions, asked differently by each generation.

The decrees show us that progress is neither linear nor inevitable. Gains can be lost, wisdom forgotten, moral clarity clouded. But they also show us resilience, the capacity for self-correction, and the power of articulated ideals to eventually reshape reality. In reading them, we commune with our ancestors not as superior descendants but as fellow travelers, struggling with similar questions, limited by our own blind spots as they were by theirs.

May the 54th decree, and all those that follow, be written with awareness of this history, with humility about our own limitations, and with determination to speak truths that future generations will not have to read with shame.
quality_problem.question: Why did the royal decrees change in style over time?
quality_problem.correct_answer: Because the sovereigns wanted to inspire public behavior rather than just describe government policy, and new technologies like Speaking Crystals and Vision Pools enabled direct communication with citizens across the realm.
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: Because the later sovereigns were less educated than the early ones and couldn't write in the classical style that Luna Stephens and her immediate successors used.
answers: Because the later sovereigns were less educated than the early ones and couldn't write in the classical style that Luna Stephens and her immediate successors used.
