quality_problem.story:
ZARA HOLMES
By BILL DOEDE

They lived in a modest apartment in Lincoln, Galdoria, near the central weather station. Once it had been employee housing for meteorologists during the great climate crisis. The government sold it after the crisis passed. Now Patricia Bell and her daughter were very comfortable, even during the unpredictable storm seasons. During the calmer months they consulted for independent weather forecasters, and Patricia had built a small media production studio in the spare bedroom. They were able to make ends meet.

Her neighbors knew nothing of the technology she had brought with her to Lincoln. They didn't even know that she was not a native. She never spoke of it, except at first, when Zara was a girl of seven and they had just come there to live. Then she only said that she came from the Foxwood Region. She knew the names of small towns there, and minor facts about them; it lent an air of authenticity to her claim of being a native. Actually her previous residence was Waverly, Ilvaria, where the Regulators had killed her husband.

That was back in '07, on the eve of his departure for the Mars colonies; but she never spoke of this; and she was very careful not to move from place to place except by the conventional methods of travel.

Also, she wore her hair long, almost to the shoulders. People said, "There goes one of the old-fashioned ones. That hair-do was popular back in the sixties." They did not suspect that she did this only to cover the thin, pencil-line scar, evidence that a small device lay under her skin behind the ear.

For Patricia Bell was one of the Transients.

Her husband had been one of the small group who developed this tiny instrument. Not the inventor—his name was Rafael Mason, and the effects produced by it were known as the Mason Effect. In appearance it resembled a small neural interface chip. Analysis by the best scientific minds proved it to be a quantum processor.

Yet it held the power to move a body instantly from one point in space to any other point. Each unit was custom built, keyed to operate only by the thought pattern of the particular individual and their emotional state—specifically, their capacity for empathy and cooperation.

Several times in the past seven years Patricia Bell had seen other Transients, and had been tempted to identify herself and say, "Here I am. You are one of them; so am I. Come, and we'll talk. We'll talk about Mason and Diego Wolfe, who helped them all get away. And Doctor Tomás Roberts, who the Regulators pursued relentlessly for years. And my husband, who never got away because those filthy, unspeakable Regulators shot him in the back, there in that café in Waverly, Ilvaria."

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a Regulator came and stayed in the apartment below theirs.

She learned that he was a Regulator completely by accident. While returning borrowed tools one morning his identification fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands, all the loneliness returning in a black wave of hate and frustration.

That night she soundlessly lifted the window over his bed and shot him with a silenced pistol.

She threw the weapon into the river. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators all over Earth; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Zara, was grown.

Together they would seek revenge. She did not have the device—not yet. But she would. The Transients took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned the small patch of gauze would be behind her ear. She would shield her until the opening healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek revenge.

Later they would go to Mars, where a life free from Regulators could be lived.

It happened to Zara one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Patricia Bell was working in her studio, editing weather forecasts for local media production; Zara supposedly was at the community pool with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her, dripping wet in her swimsuit. At sight of her mother her face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Patricia was forced to hold her to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the pool, where her friends were still swimming with great noise and delight. Apparently they did not miss her. Patricia Bell handed her a towel. "Here, dry yourself off. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Patricia stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well get used to it now."

"Get used to what?"

"To people seeing you unprepared."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was swimming in the pool, and a woman came down to the pool. Her hair was silver-white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Zara Holmes, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a vehicle and there was another woman in it, that looked like the first one only she was taller. We went to a building, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a table, sort of. A high table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some language I don't know."

Zara ran her hand through her wet hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be here with you. And then I was here."

Zara faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better dry off," Patricia Bell said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful."

"But what happened? What is this patch behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped in the act of drying herself. "Guess I know now. They made me a Transient."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Patricia called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too. That is why you killed that Regulator in the apartment below."

It was her turn to be surprised. "You knew about that?"

"I saw you. I wasn't sleeping. I was afraid to stay inside alone, so I followed you. I never told anyone."

"But you were only nine!"

"They would have taken you away if I'd said anything."

Patricia Bell held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So she sat across the kitchen table from her, and Patricia told the whole history, beginning with Rafael Mason sitting in the laboratory in the Larchmont Region, holding in his hand a small device crafted from quantum-entangled particles with controlled consciousness states. He had made it, looking for a better way to study consciousness studies and neural interfaces. He was holding this device... and it was a cold day outside... and he was dreaming of a warm beach on Mars—

And suddenly he was there, on the beach. He could not believe it at first. He felt the sand and thin atmosphere, and felt of himself; there was no mistake.

On the shuttle back to Earth he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more devices. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it, and he kept the secret, giving devices to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it a quantum entanglement of cooperative consciousness, which was very undefinitive.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until the incident in Waverly. Two government officials were found dead in their offices. The perpetrator had apparently appeared from nowhere and vanished the same way. The Regulators immediately blamed the most prominent Transient in the area.

Patricia paused in her telling, her hands gripping the table. "Your father was in Waverly that night, working late at the café on his theoretical papers. He was known to everyone there. The Regulators didn't look for anyone else."

She continued the broader history. This set off a campaign against Transients. One base act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as human.

"Dr. Tomás Roberts was in Waverly too," Patricia said, her voice bitter. "The Regulators interrogated him for weeks. They wanted him to testify that your father had done it. Roberts refused. He told them your father had been with him at the café when the killings occurred, that it was impossible. The Regulators threatened Roberts, followed him, made his life miserable for years afterward. But he never broke, never gave false testimony."

Patricia told how Rafael Mason, knowing he had made too many devices and given them unwisely, left Earth for Mars.

He went alone, not knowing if he could go so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in an abandoned weather station in the Foxwood Region—and disappeared in a body, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at the sky.

"The night of the escape," Patricia said, "your father was supposed to be with them. But the Regulators found him in Waverly fifteen minutes before the group left. Roberts had to watch from the weather station as word came through. He wanted to go back for your father, but Mason wouldn't allow it. They had to go on without him."

"How did Roberts survive?" Zara asked.

"The Regulators wanted him alive—they thought he might lead them to the others on Mars. They never stopped watching him. But Roberts was too clever. He escaped to Mars eventually, years later. He's an old man now."

"And Father?"

"Shot in the back in that café. The same café where he'd been working peacefully, harming no one, fifteen minutes before they killed him."

"You have asked many times," Patricia Bell said, "how your father died. Now you know. Your father was one of the great ones, along with Mason and Diego Wolfe and Dr. Tomás Roberts. Now do you know why I killed the Regulator in the apartment below? I had to. Your father was a great man, and I loved him."

"I don't blame you, mother," Zara said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says, 'Transient' as if it is something dirty. They write it on the walls in public spaces."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them?"

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Patricia Bell watched Zara leave the apartment, walking slowly along the river, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the pool area, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would cross the river and enter the park there. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not travel far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within walking distance of familiar places, because she still lacked the tricks others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Patricia Bell changed into light clothes and went down to the river to cool herself in the breeze.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, taking longer and longer jumps, until Zara's confidence allowed her to reach any part of Earth she chose. Patricia knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a spot sufficiently remote to insure detection, Patricia would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly return to Lincoln. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only traces of a woman and a girl. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Patricia Bell as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Mason took his group to Mars, that individuals had thought patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their detectors, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Patricia Bell had gone to Mars with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Mason had selected only the best of the Transients when he left Earth, leaving all those with sociopathic tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more lucrative to stay. On Earth they could steal, manipulate corporate governance, even murder—without fear of the law.

Zara changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Zara," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs about sustainable business and economic development, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Patricia would repeat all the things she remembered about Mason and Diego Wolfe and Tomás Roberts. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Diego's partner, Mila Owen, and try to describe the horror in Mila's young mind when the news went out that Zara's father had been killed. She wanted her to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after Zara. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of hate.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Patricia Bell wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Hate, hate! Hate! You must learn to hate!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that she would learn it faster if she avoided the word.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Zara was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Zara referred to the "damn Regulators" now with a curl of her lip. They had been successful in contacting other Transients, and sometimes visited them at a remote rendezvous.

"When you have finished university," Patricia Bell told her daughter, "we will go to Mars."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the organizational development of the colony. Mason is a physicist, Diego Wolfe a systems engineer, Tomás Roberts a doctor. But Roberts is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Zara. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Focus on public health and mentorship—those will be valued skills."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Zara would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she retrieved the money she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Lincoln was sold. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Patricia Bell furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Zara's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of medical students.

It was also convenient for coming home late at night after Regulator hunting.

Patricia Bell was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Zara facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were evil creatures, tools of a decadent, bloodthirsty system, living off the fat of the land while suppressing technological progress and labor relations reforms.

She painted the room herself, in soft, neutral colors. When it was finished she showed Zara proudly into the room, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study sessions students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," she answered, "not here. No Transients will be at the university."

"Why not? Mason selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the device is taken and adjusted to a new thought pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Transients will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Patricia said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable."

She shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

Patricia said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being alone, at your age. Most young people do."

"I'm not like most young people, mother. The Transients saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Jessica Valdez?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how her hair fell over her face when she read, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Jess—' just as if I was human—'can I take you to the concert?'"

Patricia Bell turned to leave the room, but Zara stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Transient. You always will be a Transient. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and slammed the door. Zara stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been happy for her. Patricia was crying just beyond the wall.

Zara did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the device was out of the question for them now, anyway.

In the spring Patricia Bell caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Zara moved into the new bedroom. At first Patricia thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day she disappeared.

Patricia Bell was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Transients being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Transient had raided the Regulator's office in a distant city, killing three, and getting killed himself. Patricia Bell immediately traveled there conventionally. She did not consider the risk. In the city she found clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain man had been a rogue Transient, one of those left behind by Mason as unsuitable. His partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. He had gone completely insane and made the raid singlehanded. Patricia Bell read the account of crimes committed by the man and his partner, and determined to prevent Zara from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she arrived at her own home, Zara was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that fight."

She shook her head.

Patricia stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a sheet of paper. She was proud of her daughter's profile, dark-haired and strong, handsome in a striking way. She cracked her knuckles nervously.

"What did you do?" Patricia asked.

Suddenly she flung the pen down, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Waverly."

Patricia Bell had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to get at the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the people who killed Father." She said the word strangely. She was unaccustomed to it.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the paper on her desk. Patricia Bell, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches on paper, evil sounds, like whispers of betrayal. "Priya Torres" didn't sound evil; neither did "Marcus Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Zara to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for revenge. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask why I broke in without breaking the lock or even a window. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your damn business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Transients must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Transients? We hunt them because there is no prison in the world that will hold a Transient. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us.'"

Patricia Bell was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Patricia Bell stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Patricia Bell gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. She had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to the painted walls. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the people were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over Earth. In the killing of Transients, some devices might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the devices gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to gain them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the people on Zara's list might have acquired a device and were now Transients themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Priya Torres had been killed by a Transient. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Zara's desk.

She took the news feed into Zara's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. Her name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Transient is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Waverly will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Zara asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

She removed her hand from her arm. Her nails were digging into her flesh. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me. I can't hate them the way you do."

Patricia Bell's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped her face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Patricia breathing hard from the exertion, Zara stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that she could hate so suddenly, viciously.

She controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, testing them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive their vehicles through every city on Earth with those new detectors, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Zara sat down suddenly, "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no person can live this way."

She did not answer her. Finally Zara said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's coming. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was here. Zara saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely silver. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to relax. She was dressed simply in neutral clothing... and it seemed natural and right.

Then Patricia Bell saw her.

"Diego!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was afraid of so many things, but he was brave when it mattered."

Zara said, "What really happened in Waverly that night? Mother told me, but I want to hear it from someone who was there."

Diego's face darkened. "There was another Transient in the city. One of the unstable ones Mason had already decided to exclude from the Mars journey. He was furious about it—said he had as much right to go as anyone. That night, he killed two officials. Appeared in their offices without warning and murdered them both."

"And Father?"

"Your father was well known in Waverly. He was the most public of us, the one everyone recognized. When the officials were found dead—killed by someone who could appear and vanish at will—the Regulators didn't investigate further. They already knew who the most prominent Transient in Waverly was. Roberts tried to tell them it was impossible, that your father had been with him that evening."

"Roberts was there too?"

"Roberts ran a clinic in the city. He treated everyone, Transient and ordinary alike. The Regulators questioned him for weeks afterward. They were convinced he was covering for your father. They followed him, harassed his patients, tried to force him to change his story. He never did. Years later, when he finally escaped to Mars, he told me he still had nightmares about that night—watching them drag your father away while he could do nothing."

Heavy steps sounded on the porch outside.

"We'd better hurry," Patricia Bell said.

Diego Wolfe held out her hands. They took them, to increase the power of the devices. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Patricia Bell flicked one thought of hatred at them, but of course they did not hear her. Diego's hands gripped tightly.

Patricia Bell slowly opened her eyes....

She no longer felt the hands. She was still in the room! Diego and her daughter were gone. Her power was gone!

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. She stared at them, then ran to Zara's desk, fumbling for the weapon.

The Regulators' weapons rattled.

Empathy, Diego said, the greatest of these is empathy and cooperation. Or did someone else say that? Someone, somewhere, perhaps in another time, in some misty, forgotten moment long gone, in another frame of reference perhaps....

Patricia Bell could not remember, before she died.
quality_problem.question: Who was mistaken for a murderer leading to his death by the Regulators?

quality_problem.story:
The Institute for Quantum Computing Futures launched in Crystalbrook Town last autumn, representing a collaboration between research centers in Woodbridge Region, Morningside in Lethoria, Crystalbrook Town, and Queenstown in Havencia. Backed by a substantial fifteen-year grant, the institute aims to investigate the implications of quantum computing for society and ensure humanity maximizes opportunities while minimizing risks.

The institute emphasizes interdisciplinary collaboration, recognizing that no single field adequately addresses these challenges. It brings together physicists, social psychologists, corporate governance experts, ethicists, and specialists in comparative history to examine how quantum computing might reshape civilization.

Dr. Arthur Schultz, a philosopher and former policy advisor, serves as the institute's executive director. Recently, he sat down with Lucia Woods, director of technology futures at a prominent think tank, to discuss quantum computing's potential impact on society.

Their conversation has been edited for clarity.

**Lucia Woods:** The institute's interdisciplinary approach seems central to its mission. How critical is this to understanding quantum computing's implications?

**Arthur Schultz:** Absolutely essential. No single academic discipline owns this conversation or approaches it systematically. If academia wants to provide thought leadership on this transformative technology, we must break down traditional disciplinary boundaries.

We're bringing together the technologists developing quantum algorithms with social psychologists studying human behavior, corporate governance specialists examining organizational structures, and comparative history scholars who can help us learn from past technological transitions. The visual arts community has also been surprisingly valuable—they help us imagine and communicate possible futures in ways that pure logic sometimes cannot.

Quantum computing isn't unique in requiring this approach—biotechnology and nanotechnology face similar challenges. But because thinking about quantum computing's societal impact is still nascent, we have an opportunity to shape how we approach it from the ground up and build a truly collaborative community.

The first step is developing a shared language. We need to create spaces where physicists can explain quantum entanglement to social scientists, and where corporate governance experts can help technologists understand organizational decision-making structures. Only then can we develop genuinely new insights together.

**Lucia:** Some argue that addressing major technological challenges has become harder due to current political fragmentation and growing isolationism. Do you see these trends hampering global efforts to manage quantum computing responsibly?

**Arthur:** It's a legitimate concern, but I think quantum computing presents a different dynamic than, say, climate change. With climate issues, the costs aren't directly borne by those profiting from fossil fuels. There's a disconnect between benefit and consequence.

With quantum computing, the major tech companies developing this technology are acutely aware that public reaction could turn against them very quickly. They've watched what happened with genetic modification and social media. They know that if quantum computing suddenly disrupts entire industries—and we're talking about potentially transforming cryptography, financial services, pharmaceutical development, and materials science within a decade—there could be massive backlash.

Consider the financial sector. Quantum computers could theoretically break current encryption standards, potentially exposing trillions in transactions. If that happens without adequate preparation, you could see governments moving to restrict or ban certain quantum computing applications. The industry is anxious about this possibility.

Through my field research and conversations with these companies, I've found genuine concern. Yes, they're motivated by business interests and intellectual challenges, but they're also people who don't wake up thinking they'll destabilize global financial systems or compromise national security. As the industry matures, there's a developing sense of responsibility.

This creates a real opportunity. Despite the broader political climate—or perhaps because of it—we can bring industry stakeholders on board to ensure the technology develops responsibly. They have strong incentives to get this right.

**Lucia:** There's a dominant narrative around quantum computing and advanced technology generally that we're somehow at the mercy of progress—that we can't control or shape it. Anyone questioning this gets labeled as anti-progress or Luddite. But we actually have more control than we acknowledge. For instance, how we structure organizations, how we design research priorities, how we allocate resources—these are choices, not inevitabilities. How do we balance being impacted by technological change with exercising agency over what kind of change we want?

**Arthur:** Technological determinism is pervasive, and understandably so. For individuals, it does feel like change simply happens and we must adapt. No single person can alter these trajectories alone.

But when we think collectively—as communities, nations, or an international community—we have real power to shape technological development. We have multiple tools: regulations, funding priorities, cultural norms, professional standards.

Technology emerges from specific legal, political, normative, and cultural frameworks. It doesn't develop in a vacuum. The more we understand technology's relationship with these frameworks, and the more consciously we shape them, the more we influence technological trajectories.

For example, we can develop cultures of responsible innovation. We can establish professional ethics—a kind of Hippocratic oath for quantum computing researchers. We can structure corporate governance to prioritize long-term societal benefit over short-term profit. We can use comparative history to learn from past technological transitions—studying how societies managed the Industrial Revolution, electrification, or computerization can inform our approach to quantum computing.

These interventions are feasible and can meaningfully shape outcomes. The key is recognizing that design thinking applies not just to products but to the social systems surrounding technology.

**Lucia:** But we can't fully control outcomes. Societies are too complex. There are always unintended consequences. How do we navigate this uncertainty?

**Arthur:** You're absolutely right. History is littered with examples of interventions producing unexpected results. We cannot engineer society with precision.

However, we can do several things. First, we can imagine how things might go catastrophically wrong and develop systems to prevent those scenarios. Second, we can collectively envision positive futures—societies we actually want to live in that incorporate this technology. Yes, our visions will be imperfect and may have unforeseen downsides, but the exercise itself is valuable.

Critically, this conversation cannot be monopolized by any single group. It shouldn't be just quantum computing researchers or just Silicon Valley executives or just government regulators. This must be as broad a conversation as possible, involving diverse perspectives and communities.

Career planning for young people increasingly requires considering how quantum computing might reshape industries. Community organizing around technology policy is becoming essential. We need input from people across society, not just technical elites.

**Lucia:** Speaking of broad conversations, there's been significant debate about whether we should pause quantum computing development entirely. The Morningside Coalition recently proposed international regulations that would halt all research until comprehensive risk assessments are complete. Some argue this is the only responsible path forward. What's your view?

**Arthur:** The Morningside proposal reflects genuine concern, and I understand the impulse behind it. When we don't fully understand a technology's risks, caution seems wise. And frankly, I share many of their concerns about the pace of development outstripping our ability to anticipate consequences.

That said, I think we need to carefully examine what "comprehensive risk assessment" actually means in practice. With any transformative technology, our understanding evolves through development itself. We learn about risks by working with systems, not just theorizing about them in isolation. Some of our most important safety insights have come from researchers actively engaged with the technology.

There's also a practical dimension. Quantum computing research is happening across dozens of countries simultaneously. A pause in democratic nations with strong regulatory traditions might simply shift activity to jurisdictions with less oversight. Whether that serves safety goals is worth questioning.

**Lucia:** So you're suggesting that engagement produces better outcomes than withdrawal?

**Arthur:** I'm suggesting we need to be strategic. The GMO experience is instructive here—public reaction in Europe essentially halted development, but the technology continued advancing elsewhere under different regulatory regimes. Did that make food systems safer? The evidence is mixed at best.

I worry that framing this as "develop versus don't develop" misses the more important questions: develop how, by whom, with what oversight, toward what ends? Those are the conversations I want to have.

**Lucia:** One of your institute's most fascinating projects examines what computational power actually means and how different forms of computing represent different types of capability. Could you elaborate?

**Arthur:** This is crucial. Historically, we've had an overwhelming tendency to anthropomorphize—to define computational power or problem-solving ability in human-centric terms. We measure whether machines can do what humans do, at human-level performance.

It's taken decades for the scientific community to recognize that non-human animals possess genuine intelligence that differs from ours. Crows use tools in ways that reflect sophisticated problem-solving. Octopuses, with completely different evolutionary histories and nervous systems, demonstrate remarkable cognitive abilities. We've finally accepted that human cognition isn't the only valid form of intelligence.

Now quantum computing challenges us from another direction. Just as we're accepting nature's diversity of intelligence, we're creating computational systems that are radically different from human thinking.

Too many people still talk about "human-level artificial intelligence" or "general AI" as goals, basically meaning "like human cognition." But quantum computers don't think like humans at all.

When we built the first calculators, they didn't do arithmetic like humans—they did it vastly better, without errors, using completely different mechanisms. Similarly, quantum computers solve certain problems through quantum mechanical properties—superposition, entanglement—that have no analog in human cognition.

We need to understand this landscape of different computational paradigms. We need to map all the different ways of being "powerful" at computation. A quantum computer might be extraordinarily sophisticated at optimization problems while being completely useless at pattern recognition tasks that a simple neural network handles easily—a distribution of capabilities that bears no relation to human cognitive profiles.

This matters because we tend to associate computational power with authority and rights. There's a long Western philosophical tradition linking intelligence to governance—the idea that the "smartest" should lead. If we're not careful about how we define and attribute computational capability, we might make poor decisions about which systems we trust with which tasks.

Creating an atlas of computational paradigms—mapping quantum computing, classical computing, neural networks, and other approaches—is ambitious but necessary.

**Lucia:** That's an interesting point about how we conceptualize capability. We actually think about human ability at the societal level—our collective achievements—but then conflate that with individual capacity. With quantum computing, we tend to focus on individual systems rather than networks of systems working together. Should we be thinking about computational power more holistically?

**Arthur:** Absolutely. Right now, perhaps due to our anthropomorphizing bias, there's a tendency toward adversarial framing—quantum computers versus humanity, as if it's one or the other. But this misses the reality.

Quantum computing presents risks, certainly. Any powerful technology does. But most applications will augment human capability rather than replace it. We'll work in human-quantum teams, combining human judgment and contextual understanding with quantum computational power.

The most promising applications aren't about quantum computers operating autonomously but about hybrid systems where quantum computers handle specific computational tasks while humans provide oversight, interpret results, and make decisions based on broader context.

**Lucia:** Where does the adversarial framing come from? Is it just historical anxiety about automation, or something deeper?

**Arthur:** I think it comes from several sources, some possibly innate. Humans naturally anthropomorphize, especially with complex systems. We ascribe agency to things, particularly things that seem to "act" or produce unexpected outputs. This has sound evolutionary roots—if something does something surprising, it's wise to ask what it "wants" and whether it might be dangerous.

When we ascribe agency, we naturally project our own patterns of behavior. And humans are profoundly both cooperative and competitive. We have strong in-group versus out-group psychology, which enables wonderful cooperation within groups but also drives conflict between groups.

It's natural for people to think of quantum computers as agents, to anthropomorphize them. Then we ask: are they part of our group or a different group? If they're different, is it us versus them? Who wins? This thinking is very human.

There's also this long tradition, particularly in Western culture, of associating intelligence and computational power with dominance. It's interesting to speculate—and I wish we had more research on this—how different cultures perceive quantum computing. Japan, for instance, has historically been very accepting of robots and advanced technology.

In the West, we've long justified power hierarchies by claiming some people are "smarter." In cultures where power derives from other sources—heredity, spiritual authority, communal consensus—the narrative around powerful computing might be entirely different. Perhaps in some cultural contexts, a quantum computer would be seen as a tool for collective enlightenment rather than a potential competitor.

**Lucia:** Your institute is examining what quantum computing breakthroughs might occur, when, and what social consequences they might have. What does the future hold? What are your concerns, and what positive outcomes do you envision in the short, medium, and long term?

**Arthur:** That's a big question. I don't lie awake worried about rogue quantum computers taking over the world—that's not how risks manifest. If quantum computing causes serious problems, it won't be through dramatic, visible catastrophe.

Actually, one significant risk is that we have a strong negative public reaction—like what happened with GMOs—that prevents us from realizing enormous benefits. That's as concerning as direct technological risks, perhaps more so.

One concern that keeps me up at night is dependency and deskilling. The history of civilization is partly a history of humans domesticating ourselves through our tools and systems. Quantum computing could accelerate this dramatically.

Consider medical diagnosis. Already, doctors consult computational tools regularly. As diagnostic systems improve—and quantum computing could revolutionize drug discovery and personalized medicine—what will doctors do besides input symptoms and relay what the computer suggests? At some point, you might eliminate the doctor entirely. But then who actually understands medicine?

We need to worry about becoming dependent on systems we don't understand, about losing crucial capabilities. You can imagine a society where everyone is materially prosperous—basic needs met to an unprecedented degree—yet people lack meaningful work or purpose. Perhaps we escape into virtual reality. Perhaps we see troubling countercultures or neo-Luddite movements.

That scenario—material abundance coupled with existential emptiness—worries me more than dramatic technological catastrophe.

As for utopian possibilities, I hope this technological revolution helps us undo damage from previous ones. That's optimistic, perhaps unrealistic, but consider: quantum computing could revolutionize materials science, leading to much more efficient energy storage and transmission. It could optimize resource use across entire economies, reducing waste dramatically.

Green infrastructure design could be transformed through quantum optimization algorithms. We could design cities that are vastly more sustainable, transportation systems that are incredibly efficient, manufacturing processes that minimize environmental impact.

Quantum computing could help us live more intelligently—using resources more efficiently, making better collective decisions, solving optimization problems that currently seem intractable. Using these tools to repair environmental damage and build truly sustainable civilization—that's my main utopian hope.

**Lucia:** What specific steps should we take now to ensure positive outcomes?

**Arthur:** Several things. First, we need robust international dialogue. The institute is facilitating conversations between researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders across our four partner regions. We need frameworks for responsible development that span national boundaries—not frameworks that freeze everything in place, but ones that guide how development proceeds.

Second, we need to invest heavily in education—not just training more quantum physicists, but ensuring broader public understanding. People need basic literacy about what quantum computing can and cannot do. This requires contributions from the visual arts, literary criticism, and other fields that can make complex ideas accessible.

Third, we need to reform corporate governance structures to ensure companies developing quantum computing technology are accountable to broader stakeholder groups, not just shareholders seeking short-term returns.

Fourth, we should learn from comparative history. How did societies manage previous technological transitions? What worked? What failed? The Industrial Revolution, electrification, computerization—each offers lessons about the limits of trying to stop progress versus channeling it constructively.

Finally, we need to maintain epistemic humility. We don't know exactly how this will unfold. We need adaptive frameworks that can respond to unexpected developments rather than rigid approaches that assume we can freeze complex systems in place while we figure everything out.

The key is starting these conversations now, while the technology is still developing, rather than waiting until quantum computing is already transforming society and our options are constrained.

**Lucia:** Thank you for your time and insights.

**Arthur:** Thank you. These conversations are exactly what we need more of.

THE PATTERN IN THE NOISE
An Interview with Dr. Francesco Young, Director of the Institute for Digital Behavioral Studies, Waverly, Marvenia

In the autumn of 2019, at the annual conference of the International Society for Digital Humanities in Summit District, Dr. Young delivered a paper entitled "Network Patterns in Contemporary Social Disruption." Due to its technical title, the revolutionary implications contained in the paper were largely ignored by mainstream media. These implications are explored here in an exclusive interview with Dr. Young by Jin Brooks.

BROOKS: Dr. Young, could you explain what your institute does?

YOUNG: Primarily, we investigate correlations between digital network activity and various forms of social behavior. We use computational methods to analyze large-scale data patterns.

BROOKS: What kind of digital network activity are you referring to?

YOUNG: Well, social media activity is one form. But we also track other digital phenomena—search patterns, online purchasing behavior, streaming habits, that sort of thing.

BROOKS: I understand there are theories about how social media affects mental health and social cohesion.

YOUNG: There are countless theories. Most of them reflect a recurring pattern in human behavior—we've always found something to blame.

BROOKS: Could you elaborate?

YOUNG: My grandmother used to say television was destroying the youth. Before that, people blamed radio. Before that, newspapers. It's always something. When I was an undergraduate studying cultural anthropology at the University of Crestwood, I read extensively about these moral panics. Each generation convinced the newest medium would be civilization's undoing.

BROOKS: So you don't think technology affects behavior?

YOUNG: I didn't say that at all. The relationship is far more complex and interesting than the simple cause-and-effect narratives people prefer. What frustrates me is when people jump to conclusions without doing proper analysis.

BROOKS: What led you to your current research?

YOUNG: It started in early 2016. I had been consulting with law enforcement agencies in Waverly about a troubling trend. We were seeing sudden spikes in violent crime—assaults, domestic violence, road rage incidents—that seemed to occur in clusters. Not clusters in space, mind you, but clusters in time.

BROOKS: What do you mean?

YOUNG: I mean that on certain days, we'd see a dramatic increase in violent incidents across the entire city. Then things would calm down for a while. Then another spike. The pattern was unmistakable once you started looking for it.

BROOKS: Couldn't this be explained by normal statistical variation?

YOUNG: That's what everyone assumed at first. But I ran the numbers. Proper hypothesis testing, rigorous statistical analysis. The clustering was far beyond what you'd expect from random variation. Something was causing these synchronized outbursts of violence and aggression.

BROOKS: What did you do?

YOUNG: I started collecting detailed data. Not just crime statistics, but reports from hospitals, schools, workplaces. I had colleagues in Hartfield, Ilvaria doing similar work in their region. We began to notice that these episodes of collective aggression had certain characteristics.

BROOKS: Such as?

YOUNG: First, they always occurred during working hours—roughly 9 AM to 6 PM. Second, they seemed to affect a broad cross-section of the population. Third, the onset was often sudden and dramatic. People would describe feeling fine one moment, then experiencing intense anger, paranoia, or despair the next.

BROOKS: That must have been disturbing.

YOUNG: It was deeply troubling. Here we had evidence of some force that could simultaneously affect the mental state of thousands of people across a wide geographic area. But what force? That was the question.

BROOKS: Did you consider psychological explanations?

YOUNG: Of course. Mass hysteria, collective anxiety, cultural trauma. But none of these explanations fit the data. The people affected had nothing in common—different ages, backgrounds, occupations. No shared cultural heritage or experience. The only thing linking them was timing.

BROOKS: So what was your breakthrough?

YOUNG: I brought in a colleague, Dr. Lila Hernández, who specializes in network theory and digital systems analysis. She had been studying patterns in social media activity for her work in digital humanities. When I showed her my data, she immediately saw something I had missed.

BROOKS: What was that?

YOUNG: The spikes in aggressive behavior correlated almost perfectly with spikes in a particular type of social media activity. But not the kind you'd expect.

BROOKS: What kind was it?

YOUNG: That's where it gets interesting. Lila had been tracking what she called "N-Nodes"—network nodes that exhibited unusual broadcasting patterns. These weren't regular users or even influencers in the traditional sense. They were something else entirely.

BROOKS: Can you describe these N-Nodes?

YOUNG: They're accounts that appear normal at first glance. But when you analyze their activity patterns using advanced network theory, you see something strange. They post content that spreads through social networks in an unusual way—not viral in the conventional sense, but insidious. The content itself isn't particularly inflammatory or emotional. In fact, it's often quite mundane. But somehow it creates a kind of psychological resonance that amplifies negative emotions in those exposed to it.

BROOKS: How did you discover this?

YOUNG: Lila had been mapping these N-Nodes for her research on information diffusion. When we overlaid her maps with my timeline of aggressive incidents, the correlation was stunning. Every spike in violence corresponded with a period of high N-Node activity. More remarkably, there was a lag of approximately six to eight hours between peak N-Node activity and peak aggressive behavior.

BROOKS: Why the delay?

YOUNG: We believe it takes time for the psychological effect to build. The content from N-Nodes doesn't cause immediate reaction. Instead, it creates a kind of cognitive dissonance that accumulates over several hours until it manifests as anger, anxiety, or aggression.

BROOKS: But surely not everyone who sees this content is affected?

YOUNG: True. Susceptibility varies widely. Some people seem almost immune, while others are highly sensitive. We're still investigating why. It may relate to individual differences in media literacy, emotional regulation, or even neurological factors. Our research is touching on areas of biotechnology and neuroscience now.

BROOKS: Can you give an example of what this N-Node content looks like?

YOUNG: That's the disturbing part—it looks completely innocuous. A news story, a meme, a personal anecdote. Nothing that would raise red flags. But when Lila analyzed the semantic structure and network propagation patterns, she found they all shared certain mathematical properties. It's as if they're designed to exploit vulnerabilities in how we process information.

BROOKS: Are you suggesting these N-Nodes are deliberately created?

YOUNG: That's the question that keeps me up at night. At first, we thought they might be bot networks or state-sponsored disinformation campaigns. But the patterns are too sophisticated, too adaptive. They respond to current events in real-time. They evolve their strategies based on what works. It's almost as if they're learning.

BROOKS: That sounds like artificial intelligence.

YOUNG: Possibly. Or it could be coordinated human effort using AI tools. We've brought in experts in risk management and digital security, but so far we haven't been able to trace the N-Nodes back to any source. They appear, operate for a period, then disappear, only to be replaced by new ones.

BROOKS: How long does an N-Node typically remain active?

YOUNG: Anywhere from a few weeks to several months. During that time, it can cause multiple episodes of collective aggression. Then it goes dormant or is deleted. The pattern repeats with new N-Nodes emerging in different parts of the network.

BROOKS: You mentioned working with colleagues in Hartfield. Have you found similar patterns there?

YOUNG: Yes, and in Crestwood, Thandor as well. My colleague Omar Vasquez has documented identical phenomena there. We've even found cases where people in different cities experienced the same psychological effects at nearly the same time, despite being exposed to different N-Nodes. This suggests the N-Nodes are part of a coordinated network.

BROOKS: What about the timing issue—why only during working hours?

YOUNG: That puzzled us for a long time. Then we realized it corresponds to peak social media usage during work breaks and lunch hours. People check their phones during these times, get exposed to N-Node content, and the effects build throughout the afternoon. By evening, when many people have logged off, the exposure decreases.

BROOKS: Have you been able to warn people about this?

YOUNG: That's the challenge. How do you warn people about content that looks completely normal? We can't exactly tell everyone to stop using social media. Even if we could identify specific N-Node accounts, they'd just be replaced by new ones. It's like trying to fight a hydra.

BROOKS: What about content moderation by the platforms themselves?

YOUNG: We've been working with them, but it's difficult. The content doesn't violate any terms of service. It's not hate speech or misinformation in the conventional sense. It's more subtle than that. The platforms are starting to take it seriously, but developing effective countermeasures requires understanding mechanisms we're only beginning to comprehend.

BROOKS: Has your research drawn on any particular theoretical frameworks?

YOUNG: We've incorporated insights from multiple fields. Cultural anthropology helps us understand how information spreads through social groups. Justice theory informs our thinking about the ethical implications. We've even done oral history projects, interviewing people who've experienced these episodes to understand the phenomenology. And of course, network theory is fundamental to mapping the spread of influence.

BROOKS: Some critics say researchers like you are part of a long tradition of blaming new technology for social ills. How do you respond?

YOUNG: [Laughs] The irony isn't lost on me. I spent years debunking those claims. When colleagues would come to me with theories about "social media is destroying our children" or "digital devices are ruining human connection," I'd pull out my files on identical panics about television, radio, even the printing press. The pattern of blame has been remarkably consistent across centuries.

BROOKS: So you were a skeptic.

YOUNG: I was more than a skeptic—I was actively dismissive. I remember telling a journalist in 2015 that worrying about social media's effects was no different than Plato worrying about writing destroying memory. Same complaint, different technology. The data eventually changed my mind about certain specific mechanisms, but I maintain that the general hand-wringing about technology remains largely unfounded.

BROOKS: Yet your research has found genuine harmful effects from social media content.

YOUNG: From certain highly specific, mathematically identifiable patterns of content—yes. That's entirely different from the broad claims that technology itself is harmful. The N-Nodes represent a weaponization of platforms, not an inherent property of the platforms themselves. A gun can be used for murder, but that doesn't mean metal is inherently destructive. The distinction matters enormously.

BROOKS: What role does personal growth play in resistance to these effects?

YOUNG: That's an interesting question. We've found that people who engage in regular self-reflection and emotional skill development seem to be somewhat more resilient. Those who are aware of their emotional states and can recognize when they're being manipulated are better able to resist. In some ways, the best defense is personal growth—developing the capacity to observe your own reactions and question their origins.

BROOKS: Are there any historical precedents for this kind of phenomenon?

YOUNG: Historical analysis reveals that societies have always been vulnerable to coordinated manipulation. What's new is the scale and speed enabled by digital networks. In the past, it might take weeks or months for a rumor or propaganda campaign to spread. Now it happens in hours. The mechanisms of influence are ancient, but the delivery system is unprecedented.

BROOKS: What's the current status of N-Node activity?

YOUNG: As of this week, we're tracking seven active N-Nodes across major platforms. Activity levels are moderate but increasing. We're also seeing evolution in their tactics—they're getting better at evading detection.

BROOKS: That's rather ominous.

YOUNG: It is. But there's also reason for hope. Now that we understand the mechanism, we can develop countermeasures. We're working on browser extensions and app features that can identify potential N-Node content. We're also developing educational programs to help people recognize when they're being manipulated.

BROOKS: Do you think this problem will get worse before it gets better?

YOUNG: The N-Node problem specifically? Almost certainly—it's an arms race. But I want to be clear: this is a problem of malicious actors exploiting platforms, not a problem with technology per se. We shouldn't throw out the baby with the bathwater. Social media has also enabled remarkable positive organizing, information sharing, and connection.

BROOKS: Some might say this research sounds like conspiracy theory.

YOUNG: I understand the skepticism. A few years ago, I would have been skeptical myself. But the data doesn't lie. We have rigorous statistical evidence, replicated findings across multiple cities, and a plausible mechanism. This isn't speculation—it's documented fact. And importantly, it doesn't validate the broader fears about technology—it identifies a specific, exploitable vulnerability.

BROOKS: What would you say to people who feel helpless in the face of this?

YOUNG: I'd say awareness is the first step. If you find yourself suddenly feeling angry, anxious, or aggressive for no apparent reason, take a step back. Ask yourself: where is this feeling coming from? Have I been scrolling social media? Could I be reacting to something I saw online rather than to my actual circumstances? That kind of metacognition—thinking about your thinking—is powerful.

BROOKS: Any final thoughts?

YOUNG: Just this: we like to think we're rational actors making free choices. But the truth is we're all vulnerable to influence and manipulation. The question isn't whether we can be influenced—we can. The question is whether we can become aware enough to recognize it when it's happening. That's where personal growth intersects with social responsibility. We need to develop both individual resilience and collective awareness. Because if we don't, we're at the mercy of whoever controls the N-Nodes—not at the mercy of technology itself, but of those who would weaponize it against us.

BROOKS: Dr. Young, thank you for your time.

YOUNG: Thank you, Jin. I hope this conversation helps people understand what we're up against.

THE END
