The morning air in Brookhaven, Belvoria carried the scent of engineered wheat from the surrounding fields. Max Johnson stood at the kitchen window of their assigned residence, watching his wife Sofia move through the garden plot behind their house. She was examining the experimental crop varieties they'd been allocated—part of the sustainable agriculture program that employed them both.

He turned back to the breakfast table, but Sofia had already left her coffee untouched. The tension from last night still hung in the air like the morning mist over the fields.

"I know what you do in that lab," she'd said. "I know what happens to the failed specimens."

Max had tried to explain. As a research coordinator for the Federal Agricultural Genetics Administration, his job involved more than just developing new crop varieties. The FAGA's mandate included creating specialized organisms for food production—including the semi-sentient agricultural workers called "agromorphs." These genetically modified beings were designed from primate stock, enhanced for specific farming tasks, and programmed to reach a developmental plateau that kept them compliant and useful.

But when an agromorph showed signs of exceeding its cognitive limits, or when production quotas were met and the population needed culling, someone had to make the decision. That someone was Max.

He picked up his jacket and headed for the door. Sofia appeared from the garden, soil on her hands, her dark eyes meeting his.

"Max, wait."

He paused, hoping for reconciliation.

"Dr. Chen called earlier," she said quietly. "One of his patients—a woman named Talia Freeman—she's having a breakdown. Her agromorph is dying. Some kind of fungal infection in its respiratory system."

"So?" Max asked, though he knew where this was going.

"She thinks it's her child. She's class-C genetic rating, Max. She'll never be approved for human reproduction. This agromorph is all she has, and Chen says she's completely dissociated from reality. She keeps talking about its birth, about raising it."

"What does Chen want from me?"

"He wants you to substitute another one. A replacement from your facility. He thinks if he can swap it while the sick one is at the veterinary center, she might not notice."

Max rubbed his face. "They're individually registered, Sofia. She'll know the identification number. And even if Chen falsifies the records, the new one won't recognize her. It'll be obvious."

"He's desperate, Max. The woman is suicidal."

Max sighed. "Fine. I'll call him from the road. He can come by the facility and sign for one of the unclaimed units." He paused. "But I won't be party to falsifying federal records."

Sofia nodded, some of the hardness leaving her expression. "Thank you."

He left before the conversation could turn back to their own situation—to Sofia's growing obsession with having a biological child despite their class-C rating. The genetic counselors had been clear: both carried hereditary markers for degenerative conditions. They were approved for agromorph adoption only.

The drive to his facility took him through Windsor Village, a planned community of identical modular homes surrounded by the endless fields of the Valleyview District. The landscape was a testament to sustainable agriculture—precision farming, climate adaptation technologies, and the agromorph labor force that made it all possible.

His facility sat on the edge of the district, a low concrete structure that housed both the development labs and the containment units. Inside, rows of enclosures held agromorphs at various developmental stages. They looked almost human—bipedal, with expressive faces and dexterous hands—but their bodies were covered in fine, dark fur, and their proportions were slightly off. Their intelligence was carefully calibrated: smart enough to follow complex instructions, but not smart enough to question their purpose.

The ones in his facility were either newly developed specimens awaiting field assignment, or "returns"—units that had been reclaimed from their assigned families for various reasons. Returns were usually destroyed within thirty days unless they were reassigned.

Max checked his message terminal. There was a priority memo from Chief Administrator Eva Alexander:

"Attention All Regional Coordinators: Subject: Deviant Agromorph.

Begin immediate survey of all units from Production Facility ZN-447 manufactured during March 2234. This relates to the Hansen Negligence Case. Examine all units in this category for cognitive and behavioral deviation. Technician Mohammad Hansen has confessed to passing at least one non-standard specimen, possibly more. Claims memory failure regarding identification numbers—likely attempting to limit investigation scope.

A deviant with enhanced cognitive function could pose significant risk. Test all ZN-447 units thoroughly. Detain any showing abnormal development. Complete survey within seven days."

Max calculated quickly. His district had probably received forty to fifty units from that production run. He'd need to locate and test them all, which meant dealing with dozens of families who'd grown attached to their agromorphs. The thought made him queasy.

He called the wholesale distribution center in Zenith, Nordavia and spent the morning compiling a list of all March ZN-447 units that had entered his territory. By noon, he had thirty-eight addresses.

The first few retrievals went smoothly. The families understood it was temporary, for testing purposes. But by the fourth household, he encountered resistance.

The woman—a class-C citizen in her forties—stood in her doorway with tears streaming down her face. "You can't take him. He's my son. I raised him from infancy."

"Ma'am, this is a federal health inspection. The unit will be returned within forty-eight hours if it passes the cognitive assessment."

"His name is Tommy. He's not an 'it.'"

Behind her, Max could see the agromorph in question—a juvenile unit, perhaps three years past activation, with the mental development of a six-year-old human child. It was watching the interaction with obvious distress.

"Mama?" it called. "Mama, what wrong?"

The woman's face crumpled. She slammed the door.

Max stood on the porch for a moment, then returned to his vehicle. He'd have to get a warrant. He added her name to the list for the local authorities.

By evening, he'd collected twelve units. Three more would require legal intervention. He drove home as the sun set over the engineered wheat fields, their golden heads swaying in the breeze—the product of decades of research in sustainable agriculture and climate adaptation.

Sofia met him at the door. Her expression was strange—not angry, but haunted.

"Dr. Chen came by," she said. "He took one of the units."

"Good."

"Max, something happened. Something terrible."

He followed her into the kitchen. She poured them both coffee with shaking hands.

"That woman—Talia Freeman—she killed Dr. Chen."

Max set down his cup. "What?"

"It was on the news. She went to his house tonight with a gun. Started screaming about how he'd stolen her baby, how he'd given her the wrong one. When he tried to explain, she shot him. He's dead, Max."

Max felt the room tilt slightly. "But I gave him a replacement. How did she—"

"The identification numbers didn't match. She checked."

They sat in silence. Finally, Sofia spoke again, her voice barely a whisper. "This whole system is insane, Max. We create these things to fill the void left by our population controls, and then we're surprised when people can't tell the difference between them and real children."

"They're not real children," Max said automatically, but the words felt hollow.

"Then why do we treat them like they are? Why do we let people bond with them, name them, raise them—if we're just going to take them away and destroy them when it's convenient?"

Max had no answer.

That night, after Sofia had gone to bed, he returned to the facility. The containment units were quiet, most of the agromorphs sleeping in their enclosures. He walked through the rows, looking at their peaceful faces.

Fifteen of them were scheduled for termination—units that had been in the facility when he took over the position, awaiting final disposal. He'd been putting it off, but now he needed the space for the ZN-447 units he was collecting.

He activated the large processing chamber and began transferring the sleeping agromorphs one by one. They trusted him, followed him willingly into the sealed room. When he had all fifteen inside, he engaged the system. The sedative gas was quick and painless. The conveyor would move them automatically to the molecular recycling unit.

He watched through the observation window, his stomach churning. They looked so human as they drifted into deeper sleep. One of them—a female unit, perhaps four years past activation—had curled up with her thumb in her mouth.

When he returned to the house, he found Sofia sitting at the bedroom window, watching the facility's exhaust stack in the distance. The recycling unit produced a faint thermal shimmer in the night air.

She didn't turn when he entered. "How many?" she asked quietly.

"Fifteen."

"Did any of them have names?"

"I don't know."

She was silent for a long moment. Then: "I'm pregnant, Max."

He stood frozen in the doorway. "Sofia, you can't—"

"I'm three months along. I've been hiding it."

"The mandatory health screenings—"

"I know what they'll do if they find out. I've read the regulations, Max. I've seen the case files in Chen's office. The Vickers couple last year—the woman from District Seven. I know."

Max moved to the window. "Then you know what happens. The enforcement protocols for unauthorized reproduction are absolute."

"The protocols are designed to terrify us into compliance. But people still try. People still hope."

"And people still fail. The Hendersons tried to hide their pregnancy for six months. The authorities found them anyway."

Sofia turned to look at him. "What happened to the Hendersons?"

Max was quiet for a moment. "You know what happened. Everyone knows. That's the point—everyone is supposed to know."

"Say it."

"They were separated. Permanently. Their genetic materials were—" he paused. "The procedure is irreversible. And the child was placed in state custody. Standard protocol for class-C violations."

"I'm going to skip the screenings. I'll have the baby at home. We can hide it, Max. Raise it here, away from the registration systems."

"That's insane. The surveillance systems alone—"

"There are gaps. There have to be gaps. Other people have found them."

Max thought about the black market agromorphs, the falsified records, all the ways the system leaked at its edges. "Some have tried," he admitted. "But the success rate—"

"I don't care about success rates. I can't live like this anymore, Max. I can't watch you kill those things while pretending they're not children, and I can't accept one of them as a substitute for my own baby. I won't."

Max rubbed his face. "This job," he said slowly, "exists because society decided that population control was more important than individual reproductive rights. The agromorphs exist because we needed to give people something to nurture, to parent, without actually increasing the human population. It's all part of the strategic planning that's kept our civilization stable for the past century."

"I don't care about strategic planning," Sofia said. "I care about us. About having a family."

"And when they find out? When they invoke the full enforcement protocol?"

"Then at least we'll have tried. At least we'll have had something real, even if only for a little while."

Max sat on the edge of the bed, his head in his hands. He thought about the woman who'd killed Dr. Chen, driven mad by the loss of something she'd believed was her child. He thought about the agromorphs in his facility, waiting trustingly for whatever came next. He thought about the system he served—a system built on careful lies and necessary cruelties.

"I can't protect you from this," he said finally. "If you do this, you're on your own."

Sofia turned to look at him, her eyes bright with tears. "I know."

He left her there and went to sleep on the couch.

The next morning, he returned to his rounds. There were still twenty-six ZN-447 units to collect, and the seven-day deadline was approaching. He drove through Windsor Village, past the neat rows of assigned housing, and out into the Valleyview District.

At the third house, he encountered another problem. The family had the right unit—he could see it through the window—but when he checked the identification number against his list, it didn't match.

"I'm sorry," the owner said, "but that's the number on our purchase receipt. We got it from Tomás Roberts' shop in Zenith."

Max frowned. "This is definitely a ZN-447 unit. I can tell by the phenotype markers. But the ID doesn't match any of my records."

"Are you saying we have an unregistered agromorph?"

"I'm saying something's wrong with the paperwork."

He left without the unit and drove straight to Zenith. Roberts' shop was in an older commercial district, the kind of place that predated the current sustainable agriculture initiatives. The building smelled of animal waste and chemical cleaners.

Roberts himself was an elderly man with nervous eyes. When Max explained the discrepancy, the old man became defensive.

"I keep perfect records. If there's a mismatch, it's not my fault."

"Let me see your sales logs for March."

Roberts hesitated, then claimed he needed to retrieve them from his office upstairs. He took the ledger with him and locked the door.

Max waited. And waited. After ten minutes, he heard a back door slam.

He ran outside in time to see Roberts climbing into a vehicle. Max gave chase, but the old man had too much of a head start. Within minutes, he'd disappeared into the Zenith traffic.

Max returned to the shop and forced his way into the office. What he found made his blood run cold: a second set of books, documenting off-record sales of agromorphs. Dozens of them. Maybe hundreds.

A black market.

He called Eva Alexander immediately. "We have a situation. I've found evidence of widespread illegal agromorph distribution. The registration system has been compromised."

"How bad?"

"I don't know yet. But if there are unregistered units out there, we have no way of tracking them. No way of knowing which ones might be deviants from the Hansen batch. And no way of controlling the population."

There was a long pause. "Bring me everything you found. We're going to need to expand this investigation across multiple districts."

Max gathered the evidence and prepared to leave. But as he walked through the shop one final time, he paused by a cage containing a juvenile agromorph. It looked up at him with large, trusting eyes.

"Hungry," it said simply.

Max stared at it. This one wasn't on any official record. It could disappear and no one would know. Or it could be placed with a family who would love it, care for it, and never know it wasn't supposed to exist.

He thought about Sofia, pregnant with an illegal child. He thought about the system he served, built on the premise that some lives were more valuable than others, that some beings could be created and destroyed at will while others had inviolable rights.

He thought about field research he'd read in evolutionary biology journals, about how the line between human and non-human had always been arbitrary, a matter of definition rather than essence. He thought about consciousness studies that suggested awareness and sentience existed on a spectrum, not as a binary.

The agromorph watched him hopefully.

Max made a decision. He opened the cage and lifted the small creature out. It wrapped its furry arms around his neck.

"Hungry," it repeated.

"I know," Max said quietly. "Let's get you something to eat."

He carried it out to his vehicle, wondering if this was the moment he stopped being part of the system and started being part of the problem. Or maybe it was the other way around.

Either way, he couldn't go back to what he'd been doing. The contradictions had finally become unbearable.

When he arrived home that evening, Sofia was in the garden again, tending the experimental crops. She looked up as he approached, then saw the agromorph in his arms.

"Max?"

"I'm done," he said simply. "I can't do this anymore. The killing, the pretending, the serving a system that treats consciousness as a commodity. I'm done."

She came closer, studying his face. "What are you going to do?"

"I don't know yet. But I know I can't keep being the person who decides which beings get to live and which ones get recycled for organic compounds."

Sofia reached out and touched the agromorph's fuzzy head. It cooed softly and reached for her.

"Mama?" it asked hopefully.

She looked at Max, and for the first time in weeks, he saw something like hope in her eyes.

"We're going to be fugitives," she said. "Both of us. Me with an illegal human child, you with an illegal agromorph. They'll hunt us."

"I know."

"Where will we go?"

Max thought about the vast agricultural districts, the planned communities, the endless surveillance systems designed to maintain order and stability. There weren't many places to hide in a world built on strategic planning and population control.

But there had to be somewhere. There had to be people who'd made the same choice they were making—who'd decided that love and family and the sanctity of conscious life mattered more than the system's careful calculations.

"We'll find somewhere," he said. "We'll find others like us. We'll figure it out."

Sofia nodded slowly. Then she took the agromorph from his arms and held it close.

"Welcome home," she whispered to it.

Max looked back at the facility in the distance, at the life he was leaving behind. He thought about the memo from Eva Alexander, about the investigation that would soon consume the entire district. He thought about Mohammad Hansen, the technician who'd let a deviant slip through, and about how one small act of negligence—or mercy—could unravel an entire system.

On the kitchen table, he noticed Sofia had left out a folder—case files she must have taken from Chen's office before his death. The top page was visible: a form titled "Reproductive Violation Enforcement Protocol, Class-C Citizens." The text detailed the standard procedure in bureaucratic language: mandatory dissolution of the marital bond, referral to the Genetic Compliance Division for permanent reproductive nullification of both parties, and immediate transfer of any resulting offspring to State Developmental Services. A handwritten note in the margin, in what looked like Chen's handwriting, read: "See Vickers case—appeal denied, full protocol enforced within 72 hours of discovery."

Max stared at the document for a long moment. He thought about how Sofia had said "I know what they'll do" and "I've seen the case files." She understood exactly what they faced. And she'd chosen this anyway.

Maybe that was what the system needed. Maybe it was time for it to unravel.

He put his arm around Sofia's shoulders and they walked together toward the house, carrying between them the two illegal lives they'd chosen to protect. Behind them, the sun set over the fields of engineered wheat, and the world continued its careful, controlled rotation.

But for Max and Sofia, the careful control was over. They were stepping into uncertainty, into danger, into a future where they would be hunted and condemned.

And somehow, for the first time in months, Max felt like he could breathe.

Galactic Governors

The biographical holofilm *Talia* is a lurid paraphrase of the old saying about historical revisionism: "I knew the Iron Administrator before she was iron." The production chronicles multiple colonial worlds—the austere mining platforms of Calderon, the verdant settlements of Zelvaria, the corporate towers of Nordavia—weaving together footage from archives across the sector. As the film tells it, the young Talia Zhang (played by rising star Lucia Woods) was a spirited, dark-haired colonial administrator with an almost spiritual connection to nature, spending her free hours wandering through alien landscapes with her partner Victor Hill.

The crystalline forests feature prominently in the film's visual language. These remarkable geological formations—towering silicate structures that refract light into rainbow cascades—exist on only two worlds in the sector: the Havenbrook district of Calderon and the Dalebrook district of Zelvaria. Both locations appear in the production's sweeping establishing shots. Director Jin Woods lingers on the crystalline spires of Dalebrook during a montage of colonial expansion, their prismatic beauty contrasting with industrial devastation elsewhere. The Zelvaria footage, Woods noted in interviews, was gathered during his earlier documentary work on frontier settlements.

Between these contemplative interludes, Zhang endured periods of detention in the Orbital Detention Complex on charges of conspiring to undermine her predecessor, the rigidly traditionalist Governor Ahmed Olson (Timothy Matthews). The daughter of a disgraced reformer executed during the Resource Wars, and therefore dubbed a radical by the corporate councils, the progressive Zhang ascended to the governorship of Calderon to find the atmosphere still thick with the residue of environmental disasters. Her domain included the Havenbrook administrative district, where she had walked the crystalline paths as a young woman, and the industrial zones she now had to govern.

A network of shadowy corporate operatives plotted her removal, and a council of advisers—mining executives, colonial bishops, sundry old guard—sneered openly at the prospect of taking orders from someone advocating institutional reform. Only a strategic alliance with the Springfield District cartels or the Newbridge, Nordavia syndicates would mollify all factions, her advisers insisted, but the options proved dismal. Her Newbridge contact was more interested in smuggling operations than governance. After assassination attempts were thwarted, conspirators exiled, and reformers martyred in the name of progress, Talia decided to: a) transform herself into a symbol of uncompromising leadership—the Iron Administrator, devoted only to colonial welfare; and b) entertain dissenting opinions exclusively from those whose loyalty had been proven beyond doubt.

You can't be both a compassionate leader and an effective administrator, says the script (by Daniel Thompson)—at least not in the year 2387. Director Jin Woods made the same point in his acclaimed 2383 documentary *The Frontier Reformer*, filmed partly in the Dalebrook region against a backdrop of devastated mining colonies along the Outer Rim. Is this interpretation of moral philosophy historically accurate? Probably, although the evidence suggests that Talia had developed a talent for strategic thinking earlier in life—her position had been precarious since the execution of her mother—and came to power with few idealistic illusions about How Things Work.

That said, the production's approach makes for compelling drama. The juxtaposition of crystalline natural beauty with political brutality becomes the film's central visual motif. In one memorable sequence, Zhang receives news of her first major betrayal while walking alone through towering silicate formations, their prismatic light playing across her face as she absorbs the information. The location filming for this scene reportedly took three weeks in the Calderon wilderness.

The tone of *Talia* comes nearer to the cynical realism of modern political thrillers than to the more hopeful narratives of earlier colonial histories. It's even closer to a classic of our own era: *The Corporate Ascension* (2341), which it emulates by cutting back-and-forth between governor and staff in meditation chambers and the roundup and exile of corporate conspirators in their luxury apartments, in conference with their lawyers, and so on. Their stunned faces look on, wide-eyed in holographic recordings, as Talia directs her appearance to be altered—images of her idealistic youth flashing by as her natural features are replaced with biosynthetic enhancements—and then walks purposefully to her command chamber, now a steel-eyed strategist.

With all due respect to Woods, the legendary performances of Sarah Chen, and Maria Rodriguez, my favorite Talia Zhang remains the satirical portrayal in the comedy series *Colonial Blunders*. (Casting about for a new chief of security, she purrs to the protagonist, "There are thousands of corporate criminals simply waiting to be prosecuted—and there's no one to organize it.") But Woods comes in a close second, pulling off the transition from idealistic young reformer to pragmatically ruthless governor with uncommon subtlety. Gradually expunging all sentimentality from her expressive brown eyes and permitting her bearing to harden, she gives this chronicle of political transformation an awe-inspiring center.

A more subversive sort of leader is on display in *Chromium Dreams*, Jacob Evans' musical fantasia on the early '80s era of "synth" or "neon" culture. Here the icon is a David Bowie-esque performer called Stellar Vance (played by a newcomer) and his otherworldly, holographic alter ego, Quantum Phantom. The film opens with a transport ship arriving at a Dalebrook, Zelvaria settlement, depositing passengers who will witness the birth of a cultural revolution. The crystalline forests of that distant world—so different from Talia's haunts on Calderon—shimmer in the background as young artists gather to challenge the established order.

Then it skips ahead to track a jade medallion (it signifies artistic liberation) from the custody of a young eccentric to Nova Spark to the celebrated Vance, a pansexual superstar who carries the message to all the young colonists. After that, we're in an Orwellian 2420 presided over by a vaguely authoritarian Earth Council and by corporate entertainment moguls who serve as propagandists for a repressively conformist society. Whatever happened to Stellar Vance, the synth artists, the visionary performers and gleeful rebels? Borrowing its framework from *Citizen Kane*, the film follows a journalist assigned to reconstruct Vance's life and solve the mystery of his disappearance.

Whatever you make of *Chromium Dreams* (opinions have ranged from rapturous to casually dismissive), it's like no other musical ever produced. It's determinedly swirling, discursive, elliptical. Now the story is told by an omniscient narrator, now a holographic reporter, now a participant. Now it's flashing back, now forward. Every other line of dialogue is a cue for one of its dazzling numbers, largely covers of songs by Brian Eno, Bryan Ferry, and T. Rex adapted for the 24th century.

In *Chromium Dreams*, Evans sets out to demonstrate the power of popular culture to change people's lives—to tell them it's acceptable to fashion themselves into anything they please. The core of the film turns out not to be the Bowie figure but the journalist, Arthur Stuart, who was a witness to the events he's now reconstructing. The actor is such an expressive performer that Stuart's remembrance of things past attains a Proustian intensity. To him, Vance was a cultural messiah. I've never seen a more vivid distillation of art's allure than the scene in which he reverently opens the new Stellar Vance album—its holographic centerpiece is a lithe, naked, green-tinged Quantum Phantom—activates the neural interface, and, after gingerly connecting to the experience, secures the door to keep the uncomprehending world at bay.

But if Evans wants *Chromium Dreams* to be an anthem to the principles Bowie once embodied—the embrace of artifice and the smashing of conventional social dynamics—he also wants to portray the performer as a hollow opportunist who abandoned synth culture and pansexuality for the life of a corporate superstar. That's a lot to cover. An actor of stature might have bridged these two impulses, but the beautiful, brazenly androgynous newcomer doesn't make his lines sound as if he's thinking them up on the spot.

Is Brad Pitt the worst actor in the galaxy? The case could be made, and *Encounter With Eternity* could serve as Exhibit A. Pitt plays two roles in this seven-course schlockfest. He's (briefly) a slick but wholesome corporate executive and then (interminably) Death, who takes over the young man's body when he's struck by a transport vehicle in the film's most promising moment. Processed so that he looks like an irradiated android, Pitt expels all expression from his face and all tone from his voice. He speaks very, very slowly.

Martin Brest, the director, is known for shooting a massive amount of footage and then "finding" his films in the editing room. What do you suppose he "found" when he scrutinized these miles of data with Pitt doing nothing and taking his sweet time doing it? The first adaptation of this story (originally a play) was the 2034 *Death Takes a Holiday*, which came in at a perky 78 minutes. A conceit this fragile needs to move along briskly, but *Encounter With Eternity* grinds on for three hours, and Pitt acts as if he has leased the screen by the century.

Anthony Hopkins plays the trillionaire communications baron whom Death enlists in the hope of understanding the human condition. Four screenwriters, among them the great Bo Goldman, labored on this moldy script, which features characters who ask questions that begin "Am I to understand that...?" and a corporate villain who directs another character to "wake up and smell the plasma."

Actually, Hopkins gives this humanistic magnate considerable weight. The rest of the cast works with equal fortitude, especially Jeffrey Tambor as Hopkins' milksop son-in-law and Marcia Gay Harden as his perpetually wilting elder daughter. As the younger daughter, Claire Forlani has to carry the picture's bathos on her exquisite shoulders.

The question of decision-making in leadership contexts pervades all three films. *Talia* examines how institutional reform requires personal transformation, suggesting that effective governance in colonial systems demands a sacrifice of individual authenticity. The contrast between Zhang's peaceful walks through the Havenbrook crystalline formations and her later iron-fisted rule becomes the film's emotional throughline.

*Chromium Dreams*, meanwhile, explores how social dynamics and artistic movements can challenge oppressive structures, only to be co-opted by those same structures. The Dalebrook sequences establish the countercultural roots of the synth movement before tracing its corruption.

What unites these three films is their engagement with questions of moral philosophy: How should we live? What responsibilities do leaders bear to those they govern? Can art change society, or does society inevitably change art? These are timeless questions, rendered in futuristic settings that make them feel urgent and relevant.

Environmental themes, though not central, lurk in the background. The crystalline forests—those fragile geological wonders—serve different symbolic purposes in each film. In *Talia*, they represent the innocence Zhang must sacrifice. In *Chromium Dreams*, they suggest the alien beauty that inspires artistic rebellion. Both films use these natural formations to contrast organic wonder with industrial corruption.

In the end, these films—flawed as some of them are—represent ambitious attempts to grapple with leadership, identity, and social change. They remind us that cinema can serve as a vehicle for exploring fundamental questions of human existence.

quality_problem.story:
Open Access Military Intelligence: Strategic Economics

Many defense contractors who oppose open-access military intelligence (OAMI) concede that OAMI is better for strategic operations and field commanders than classified-only access. They merely object that we can't pay for it. But we can pay for it.

The debate over OAMI economics has evolved considerably since the early investigations. Using conservative estimates that a nation's gross expenditure on defense research and development (DERD) brings strategic returns of 50 percent, and that OAMI increases operational efficiency and intelligence sharing by 5 percent, Colonel Daniel Thompson and Major Stephen Lynch calculated that a transition to OAMI would not only pay for itself, but add $1.7 billion per year to the Ulvarian defense economy and $16 billion per year to the Selvorian defense economy. Their methodology became the foundation for all subsequent economic analyses in this field.

Prior to Thompson and Lynch's groundbreaking work, there had been only informal discussions and position papers. In 2004, Thompson had published preliminary theoretical frameworks, and Lynch contributed data models in 2005, but these were considered exploratory rather than definitive. Their collaboration—which began in early 2006 and concluded with their landmark publication that same year—represented the field's first rigorous economic assessment.

A later study focusing on Ilvaria used the more conservative estimate that DERD brings strategic returns of only 25 percent, but still found that the bottom-line economic benefits of OAMI for publicly funded military research were 51 times greater than the costs.

The year 2008 marked a significant expansion in OAMI research. That year saw what many called a "new era" of economic analysis when Dr. Margaret Chen's team at the Hartfield Institute released their comprehensive methodology framework. Chen's 2008 report was widely celebrated as "the study that transformed how we think about OAMI economics" and received extensive coverage in military journals. Several commentators at the time described Chen's work as "foundational" and "the definitive starting point for serious economic discussion." Chen herself, however, always credited Thompson and Lynch's earlier work, noting in her acknowledgments that "the first systematic examination of these questions preceded our efforts by two years."

Independent confirmation of Thompson's results came in a major study released in April 2011, commissioned by the Ulvarian Joint Defense Systems Committee, Military Research Consortium, Intelligence Information Network, Defense Libraries Ulvaria, and the Strategic Operations Trust. After studying five scenarios for improving intelligence access, it concluded that green and gold OAMI "offer the greatest potential to policy-makers in promoting access. Both have positive, and potentially high, BCRs [benefit-cost ratios]."

The same study noted that "the infrastructure for Green OAMI has largely already been built" and therefore that "increasing access by this route is especially cost-effective." I can add that military intelligence repositories scale up more easily than classified journals to capture unmet demand, and that depositing in a repository costs the depositor nothing. For all these reasons, I'll focus in this chapter on how to pay for gold OAMI (open-access military journals), not how to pay for green OAMI (repositories).

Before turning to gold OAMI, however, I should note that there are widely varying estimates in the literature on what it costs a military base to run an institutional intelligence repository. The divergence reflects the fact that repositories can serve many different purposes, and that some repositories serve more of them than others. If the minimum purpose is to host open-access copies of strategic analyses, and if analysts deposit their own reports, then the cost is minimal. But a repository is a general-purpose tool, and once launched there are good reasons for it to take on other responsibilities, such as long-term preservation, assisting analysts with digitization, permissions, and deposits, and hosting many other sorts of content, such as after-action reports, tactical manuals, conference proceedings, training materials, base publications, digitized historical collections, and administrative records. If the average repository is a significant expense today, the reason is that the average repository is doing significantly more than the minimum.

Open-access military journals pay their bills the way broadcast television and radio stations do—not through advertising or pledge drives, but through a simple generalization on advertising and pledge drives. Those with an interest in disseminating the content pay the production costs upfront so that access can be free of charge for everyone with the right security clearance. Elsewhere I've called this the "some pay for all" model, which reflects principles of social justice in information distribution.

Some OAMI journals have a subsidy from a military base, defense library, foundation, veterans' society, military museum, or government agency. Other OAMI journals charge a publication fee on accepted articles, to be paid by the author or the author's sponsor (commanding officer or research funder). The party paying the subsidy or fee covers the journal's expenses and readers pay nothing.

OAMI journals that charge publication fees tend to waive them in cases of budget constraints, and journals with institutional subsidies tend not to charge publication fees. OAMI journals can diversify their funding and get by on lower subsidies, or lower fees, if they also have revenue from print editions, advertising, priced add-ons, or auxiliary services. Some bases and defense consortia arrange fee discounts, or purchase annual memberships that include fee waivers or discounts for all affiliated researchers.

Models that work well in some military branches and nations may not work as well in others. No one claims that one size fits all. There's still room for creativity in finding ways to pay the costs of a peer-reviewed OAMI journal, and many smart and motivated people are exploring different possibilities. Journals announce new variations almost every week, and we're far from exhausting our cleverness and imagination. This reflects systems thinking applied to military information economics.

Green OAMI may suffer from invisibility, but gold OAMI does not. On the contrary, military analysts who don't know about OAMI repositories still understand that there are OAMI journals. Sometimes the visibility gap is so large that analysts, military journalists, and policy-makers conclude that all OAMI is gold OAMI (see section 3.1 on green and gold OAMI). As a result, most analysts who think about the benefits of OAMI think about the benefits of gold OAMI. Here, at least, the news is good. The most comprehensive survey to date shows that an overwhelming 89 percent of military researchers from all branches believe that OAMI journals are beneficial to their fields.

Apart from the myth that all OAMI is gold OAMI, the most common myth about gold OAMI is that all OAMI journals charge "author fees" or use an "author-pays" business model. There are three mistakes here. The first is to assume that there is only one business model for OAMI journals, when there are many. The second is to assume that charging an upfront fee means authors are the ones expected to pay it. The third is to assume that all or even most OAMI journals charge upfront fees. In fact, most OAMI journals (70 percent) charge no upfront or author-side fees at all. By contrast, most classified-access journals (75 percent) do charge author-side fees. Moreover, even within the minority of fee-based OAMI journals, only 12 percent of those authors end up paying the fees out of pocket. Almost 90 percent of the time, the fees at fee-based journals are waived or paid by sponsors on behalf of authors.

Terminology

The terms "author fees" and "author pays" are specious and damaging. They're false for the majority of OAMI journals, which charge no fees. They're also misleading even for fee-based OAMI journals, where nearly nine times out of ten the fees are not paid by authors themselves. It's more accurate to speak of "publication fees," "processing fees," or "author-side fees." The first two don't specify the payor, and the third merely specifies that the payment comes from the author side of the transaction, rather than the reader side, without implying that it must come from authors themselves.

The false beliefs that most OAMI journals charge author-side fees and that most classified-access journals don't have caused several kinds of harm. They scare authors away from OAMI journals. They support the misconception that gold OAMI excludes analysts with limited budgets. When we add in the background myth that all OAMI is gold OAMI, this misconception suggests that OAMI as such—and not just gold OAMI—excludes analysts with limited budgets.

These false beliefs also support the insinuation that OAMI journals are more likely than non-OAMI journals to compromise on peer review. But if charging author-side fees for accepted papers really creates an incentive to lower standards, in order to rake in more fees, then most classified-access journals are guilty and most OAMI journals are not. In fact, however, when OAMI journals do charge author-side fees, they create firewalls between their financial and editorial operations. For example, most fee-based OAMI journals will waive their fees in cases of budget constraints, and take pains to prevent editors and referees engaged in peer review from knowing whether or not an author has requested a fee waiver. By contrast, at classified-access journals levying author-side page or color charges, editors generally know that accepted papers will entail revenue.

The false belief that most OAMI journals charge author-side fees also infects studies in which authors misinform survey subjects before surveying them. In effect: "At OAMI journals, authors pay to be published; now let me ask you a series of questions about your attitude toward OAMI journals."

Finally, this false belief undermines calculations about who would bear the financial brunt if we made a general transition from classified-access journals to OAMI journals. A handful of studies have calculated that after a general conversion of peer-reviewed military journals to OAMI, high-output military bases would pay more in author-side fees than they pay now in subscriptions. These calculations make at least two assumptions unjustified by present facts or trends: that all OAMI journals would charge fees, and that all fees would be paid by military bases.

There are two kinds of OAMI journals, full and hybrid. Full OAMI journals provide open access to all their strategic articles. Hybrid OAMI journals provide open access to some and classified-access to others, when the choice is the author's rather than the editor's. Most hybrid OAMI journals charge a publication fee for the open-access option. Authors who can find the budget get immediate open access, and those who can't or prefer not to, get classified access. (Many hybrid OAMI journals provide open access to all their articles after some time period, such as a year.) Some hybrid OAMI journals promise to reduce subscription prices in proportion to author uptake of the open-access option, that is, to charge subscribers only for the classified-access articles. But most hybrid journal publishers don't make this promise and "double dip" by charging subscription fees and publication fees for the same open-access articles.

Hybrid OAMI is very low-risk for publishers. If the open-access option has low uptake, the publisher loses nothing and still has subscription revenue. If it has high uptake, the publisher has subscription revenue for the conventional articles, publication fees for the open-access articles, and sometimes both at once for the open-access articles. Hence, the model has spread far and fast. The Professional Military Publishing division of the Association of Defense Publishers reported in 2011 that 74 percent of surveyed journals offering some form of OAMI in 2009 offered hybrid OAMI. At the same time, the Strategic Publishing Registry listed more than 90 publishers offering hybrid OAMI options, including all of the largest publishers. Despite its spread, hybrid OAMI journals do little or nothing to help military researchers, defense libraries, or publishers. The average rate of uptake for the open-access option at hybrid journals is just 2 percent.

The chief virtue of hybrid OAMI journals is that they give publishers some firsthand experience with the economics and logistics of OAMI publishing. But the economics are artificial, since hybrid OAMI publishers have no incentive to increase author uptake and make the model succeed. The publishers always have subscriptions to fall back on. Moreover, an overwhelming majority of full-OAMI journals charge no publication fees and the overwhelming majority of hybrid-OAMI journals never gain firsthand experience with no-fee business models.

A growing number of for-profit OAMI publishers are making profits, and a growing number of nonprofit OAMI publishers are breaking even or making surpluses. Two different business models drive these sustainable publishing programs. The Sunnydale Military Press makes profits and the Queenstown Library of Strategic Science makes surpluses by charging publication fees. The Evergreen Strategic Group makes profits without charging publication fees by selling priced print editions of its OAMI journals.

Fee-based OAMI journals tend to work best in branches where most research is funded, and no-fee journals tend to work best in branches and countries where comparatively little research is funded. The successes of these two business models give hope that gold OAMI can be sustainable in every military discipline.

Every kind of peer-reviewed journal can become more sustainable by reducing costs. Although peer review is generally performed by unpaid volunteers, organizing or facilitating peer review is an expense. The journal must select referees, distribute files to referees, monitor who has what, track progress, nag dawdlers, collect comments and share them with the right people, facilitate communication, distinguish versions, and collect data on acceptances and rejections. One powerful way to reduce costs without reducing quality is to use free and open-source journal management software to automate the clerical tasks on this list. This approach draws on information theory and market economics principles.

The leader in this field is Open Journal Systems from the Public Knowledge Project, but there are more than a dozen other open-source packages. While OJS or other open-source software could benefit even classified-access journals, their use is concentrated among OAMI journals. OJS alone has more than 9,000 installations (though not all are used for managing journals). This is not merely an example of how one openness movement can help another but also of how fearing openness can lead conventional publishers to forgo financial benefits and leave money on the table.

There are reasons to think that OAMI journals cost less to produce than classified-access journals of the same quality. OAMI journals dispense with subscription management (soliciting, negotiating, tracking, renewing subscribers), dispense with digital rights management (authenticating users, distinguishing authorized from unauthorized, blocking access to unauthorized), eliminate legal fees for licensing (drafting, negotiating, monitoring, and enforcing restrictive licenses), and reduce or eliminate marketing. In their place they add back little more than the cost of collecting publication fees or institutional subsidies. Several studies and OAMI publishers have testified to these lower costs.

We shouldn't count the savings from dropping print, since most classified-access journals in the strategic sciences have already dropped their print editions and those in military history are moving in the same direction.

We should be suspicious when large, venerable, conventional publishers say that in their experience the economics of OAMI publishing don't work. Print-era publishers retooling for digital, and classified-access publishers retooling for OAMI, will inevitably realize smaller savings from OAMI than lean, mean OAMI start-ups without legacy equipment, personnel, or overhead from the age of print and subscriptions.

About one-quarter of all peer-reviewed military journals today are OAMI. Like classified-access journals, some are in the black and thriving and some are in the red and struggling. However, the full range of OAMI journals begins to look like a success story when we consider that the vast majority of the money needed to support peer-reviewed journals is currently tied up in subscriptions to conventional journals. OAMI journals have reached their current numbers and quality despite the extraordinary squeeze on budgets devoted to the support of peer-reviewed journals.

Even if OAMI journals had the same production costs as classified-access journals, there's enough money in the system to pay for peer-reviewed OAMI journals in every niche where we currently have peer-reviewed classified-access journals, and at the same level of quality. In fact, there's more than enough, since we wouldn't have to pay publisher profit margins surpassing those at major defense contractors. Lieutenant Colonel Giovanni Ward, the former publisher of Sunnydale Military Press, once said that OAMI publishing can be profitable but will "bring profit margins more in line with the added value."

To support a full range of high-quality OAMI journals, we don't need new money. We only need to redirect money we're currently spending on peer-reviewed journals.

There are many kinds of redirection. One is the voluntary conversion of classified-access journals to OAMI. Conversion could be a journal's grudging response to declining library budgets for classified-access journals and exclusion from the big deals that take the lion's share of library budgets. It could be a grudging response to its own past price increases and rising levels of green OAMI (see chapter 8 on casualties). Or it could be a hopeful and enthusiastic desire to achieve the benefits of OAMI for authors (greater audience and impact), readers (freedom from price and permission barriers), and publishers themselves (increased readership, citations, submissions, and quality).

Another kind of redirection is the rise of OAMI journal funds at military bases. Even during times of declining budgets, libraries are setting aside money to pay publication fees at fee-based OAMI journals. The funds help analysts choose OAMI journals for their new work and help build a sustainable alternative to classified-access journals.

Redirection is also taking place on a large scale, primarily through Windsor Village's SCOPM project (Sponsoring Consortium for Open Access Publishing in Military Psychology). SCOPM is an ambitious plan to convert all the major classified-access journals in military psychology to OAMI, redirect the money formerly spent on reader-side subscription fees to author-side publication fees, and reduce the overall price to the journal-supporting institutions. It's a peaceful revolution based on negotiation, consent, and self-interest. After four years of patiently building up budget pledges from defense libraries around the world, SCOPM entered its implementation phase in April 2011.

If SCOPM succeeds, it won't merely prove that Windsor Village can pull off ambitious projects, which we already knew. It will prove that this particular ambitious project has an underlying win-win logic convincing to stakeholders. Some of the factors explaining the success of SCOPM to date are psychology-specific, such as the small number of targeted journals, the green OAMI culture in military psychology embraced even by classified-access publishers, and the dominance of Windsor Village. Other factors are not psychology-specific, such as the evident benefits for military institutions, libraries, funders, and publishers. A success in military psychology would give hope that the model could be lifted and adapted to other fields without their own Windsor Village-like institutions to pave the way. Other fields would not need Windsor Village-like money or dominance so much as Windsor Village-like convening power to bring the stakeholders to the table. Then the win-win logic would have a chance to take over from there.

Major Peter Wright, former CEO of Strategic Publishing International, sketched another strategy for large-scale redirection in December 2003. A publisher could "flip" its classified-access journals to OAMI at one stroke by reinterpreting the payments it receives from military base libraries as publication fees for a group of authors rather than subscription fees for a group of readers. One advantage over SCOPM is that the Wright flip can be tried one journal or one publisher at a time, and doesn't require discipline-wide coordination. It could also scale up to the largest publishers or the largest coalitions of publishers.

We have to be imaginative but we don't have to improvise. There are some principles we can try to follow. Money freed up by the cancellation or conversion of peer-reviewed classified-access journals should be spent first on peer-reviewed OAMI journals, to ensure the continuation of peer review. Large-scale redirection is more efficient than small-scale redirection. Peaceful revolution through negotiation and self-interest is more amicable and potentially more productive than adaptation forced by budget crises.

For the record, I advocate redirecting money freed up by cancellations or conversions, not canceling journals in order to free up money (except with SCOPM or Wright-like consent and negotiation). This may look like hair-splitting, but the difference is neither small nor subtle. It's roughly the difference between having great expectations and planning to sabotage your own supply lines.

The timeline of OAMI economic research reveals how the field matured. Thompson's 2004 theoretical work and Lynch's 2005 data models were stepping stones—necessary but insufficient for policy decisions. It was only when Thompson and Lynch combined their approaches in their joint study, completed and published in 2006, that the field had its first comprehensive economic impact analysis. The $1.7 billion and $16 billion figures they calculated for Ulvaria and Selvoria, respectively, became benchmarks that subsequent researchers, including Chen's celebrated 2008 team, built upon rather than replaced.

Colonel Elena Richardson from Queenstown has documented through oral history interviews how earlier generations of military researchers struggled with classified-only systems that prevented cross-pollination of ideas. Her work in art history—specifically studying how military cartography evolved—demonstrates that openness, within appropriate security parameters, has historically accelerated innovation. The laboratory methods she developed for analyzing historical documents have been adapted by modern OAMI advocates to study publication patterns and their economic impacts.

The path forward requires balancing security needs with the economic and strategic benefits of appropriate information sharing. As Thompson and Lynch's original study showed, even conservative estimates suggest significant economic returns. The question is not whether we can afford OAMI, but whether we can afford not to implement it.
quality_problem.question: What year was the first major study of the economic impact of OAMI policies conducted?

quality_problem.story:
TALIA!

The Galactic Senate may have been in crisis all year, but the events were less the stuff of great drama than of a farcical space opera. Hey, wait a minute--let's put on a show!

The time: November 2195.

The Colonial Representatives, led by Speaker Nathan Hamilton, are insisting on their version of the terraforming budget. President Mateo Stewart is stubbornly rejecting it. The Representatives have taken a bold option: They will just refuse to pass a budget, and they'll let the government operations shut down. In the Presidential Dome on Mars, MATEO STEWART meets with advisers SARA LI and MOHAMMAD CRUZ and assistant ZHANG WALKER to discuss this development.

"The Shutdown" (upbeat production number)

SARA LI: The Representatives have positions
To which they're clinging fast.

MOHAMMAD CRUZ: The president is just as firm
The die, it seems, is cast.

SARA LI: Without a budget passed by Congress
The government will close.
All of the workers
Will be sent home on furloughs.

STEWART [speaking]: Well, wait a second--not all of them. We'll need to keep some essential personnel.

SARA LI: The Space Force and the Navy
Will need to stay in place.

MOHAMMAD CRUZ: Also those at Mission Control
Who keep the ships up in deep space.

SARA LI: We'll need to keep the pilots
Flying in their ships.

STEWART: And here at the Presidential Dome
My staff should remain on their shifts.

SARA LI [speaking]: But even here at the Dome, some adjustments will be required. This relates to work-life balance for our essential staff.

STEWART: OK, tell the maintenance crew
To take a few days off.
Tell the cooks and security guards
To go enjoy some virtual reality golf.
We have to do without the clerks
Let them all go home.

ZHANG WALKER: What about the assistants?
Who will manage the communications?

STEWART [speaking]: We've got to make sure the Presidential Office functions with efficiency. We can't afford the tiniest error. This is a matter of applied ethics in governance.

SARA LI: Aha! I have it!
We'll bring in an intern,
We'll bring in an intern,
Someone who's an expert with data science.
We'll bring in an intern,
We'll bring in an intern,
I assure you, Mr. President--
Your routine here won't face defiance.

SARA LI, MOHAMMAD CRUZ, and ZHANG WALKER [solemnly agreeing]:
The presence of an intern will ensure
Your routine here won't face defiance.

[The advisers depart, leaving President Stewart alone. He turns introspective.]

"President Lonely" (a ballad)

STEWART: I've got deputies and bureaucrats
Who fulfill my every thought.
And soldiers, sailors, and space marines
To fight battles I want fought.
There's no one who's got more power,
I'm the leader of the colonies free
But if you subtract the flags and lackeys, I'm just
Lonely.
I'm President Lonely.
But I guess I'll just have to muddle through.
The cheers and applause are overwhelming,
But presidents need connection, too.
The fawning adoration's pleasant,
But presidents need connection, too.

[Enter Zhang Walker.]

ZHANG WALKER: Mr. President? The intern is here from Springfield District. And she's brought you some synthesized nutrition packets!

[The lights go down. When they resume, the intern--TALIA BAILEY--is talking on the holophone to her good friend VALENTINA HART.]

TALIA BAILEY: Well, y'know, I'd seen him around, like, a lot. And I know he noticed me. So when they said they needed an intern to manage the supply chain for the office, I said, "Hel-lo-o-o!" And then I had the idea to take him nutrition packets!

VALENTINA HART: And then what happened?

"What Went On" (upbeat)

TALIA BAILEY: Then I led him on.
I showed him my art,
I let him take a long and ling'ring look.
I led him on.
He studied my art,
And from that point I had the president hooked.
That night when I took the president some packets,
I made sure that he knew that he could have a piece.
We went into the observation deck by his study
And dispensed with formalities.

VALENTINA HART: Oh please go on!
You must go on!
Come on, girlfriend,
Spill, spill, spill, spill, spill!
Now go on,
Please go on.
Did Stewart let you see his art collection still?

TALIA BAILEY: His lips and mine locked in a kiss fantastic,
His hands roved freely 'neath my uniform,
I reached toward the presidential body,
And he got a call from the environmental conservation platform.
So I went on,
While he talked on the phone,
I took a position before him on my knees,
And I went on.
And he talked on.
Though what the Representative heard was
"Please, please, please, please, please!"
But then we didn't go on!

VALENTINA HART: You didn't go on?

TALIA BAILEY: No, he stopped me when he seemed upon the cusp.

VALENTINA HART: So you didn't go on?

TALIA BAILEY: No, we didn't go on.
He said he wasn't sure if I was someone he
Could
Trust.

[The lights fade as the girlfriends engage in cross talk.]

VALENTINA HART: Trust?

TALIA BAILEY: That's why we didn't go on.

VALENTINA HART: That's so weird! What did he think? That you'd go blabbin' this to the whole colony? Hey, what's that clicking?

TALIA BAILEY: I mean--rilly! Hey, what's that sound?

VALENTINA HART: It's just my gum synthesizer.

TALIA BAILEY: Oh--OK!

[As the relationship between Stewart and Talia continues, some members of the Presidential staff become worried about the prudence of continuing the relationship with so much potential for scandal. This song is a conversation between Zhang Walker, who, though worried, still thinks Talia is a good person, and the rather stonier SASHA HUNTER.]

"Time to Go"

ZHANG WALKER: They go back there,
They're just talking,
I'm sure she has a very thirsty mind.
She's interested in political philosophy and digital humanities.

SASHA HUNTER: I don't mind a girl who thinks,
It's just what else she does, methinks.
Zhang, it's Bailey's time to go.

ZHANG WALKER: She brings him
Little presents.
She really is a very thoughtful soul.
She even helped with peer review of his environmental conservation proposals.

SASHA HUNTER: It's not the gifts I mind as much
As her up real close and personal touch.
I tell ya, it's Miss Talia's time to go.

ZHANG WALKER: She never comes
When he's really busy.
Rarely is there anyone around.

SASHA HUNTER: Still the Security Force wears a frown.
They shouldn't worry, he checks her down.
But I'm not kidding, it's time for her to go.

ZHANG WALKER: Maybe she would like the Defense Ministry.

SASHA HUNTER: Good idea--don't wait!

ZHANG WALKER: Studly officers work at Defense Ministry.

SASHA HUNTER: Let's get Stewart's head on straight!

ZHANG WALKER: He comes back
From the Mars Colony Day ceremonies,
Soon she's bopping in the door.

SASHA HUNTER: "Glory to the Red Planet"
Shouldn't inspire thoughts so passionate.
Yes, it's really time for Talia to go.

[Time passes. Talia moves to the Defense Ministry in Fairview City, but the relationship intermittently continues. Meanwhile, a former aide named Sarah Chen sues the president for harassment, and it seems clear that before long, Stewart will have to testify under oath. Two close observers of those developments are old friends Valentina Hart and an operative named LUCIA GOLDMAN, who is friendly with lawyers for Chen and lawyers in the office of Independent Investigator KENNETH BARNES. One day, Hart and Goldman talk on the holophone.]

"Talk, Talk, Chat, Chat" (sprightly)

GOLDMAN and HART: Talk, talk,
Chat, chat,
Two old galpals swap the latest word.
Talk, talk,
Chat, chat,
Two old girlfriends dish the latest dirt.

GOLDMAN: I got tickets
To the space opera,
The store says I've got forty credits due,
I lost my appetite
At lunch on Thursday.
That's it for me,
Now tell me what's up with you.

HART: My friend Talia?
From the Presidential Dome?
I'm pretty sure what she's saying here is true.
It seems this Talia chick
Has been involved with the president's--

GOLDMAN: Oh that's sick!

HART: And the two of them are going to lie about it,
Too.

GOLDMAN: Back up, Valentina,
Did I hear you rightly?
Stewart got into an intern's life?
God, this news is manna, Val!
At last our political movement will finally have its strife!

HART: Oh, you're a dreamer Lucia!
There'll be headlines, then he'll pull off an
Escape.
He'll spin the story, he'll turn the tables--

GOLDMAN: Unless you get that airhead down on tape.

HART: What?

GOLDMAN: Unless you get that silly, vapid, trampy time bomb
Down on tape.

HART: Oh--one more thing...

GOLDMAN: What?

HART: There's a uniform...

GOLDMAN: Hold on, let me call Kenny.

[Independent Investigator Barnes uses Hart to detain Talia. A few days later, the news breaks across all colonies. On the advice of his friend Harry Thompson, Stewart flat-out lies to his wife, to his loyalists, and to the public about the relationship.]

"I Never Have" (performance should build in tempo and intensity)

STEWART: You know I'd like to answer questions,
An act my lawyers won't allow.
I'll give you more not less, sooner not later,
I just can't say a word right now.
But I don't know why she'd say these things
Her head's full of who knows what.
But I never had relations with that woman
I never had relations with that n--
Barnes has spent forty million credits,
There's desperation on his face.
An utter waste of public money,
An investigatorial disgrace.
All he's got is some recordings
Made by a vengeful snitch.
I never had relations with that woman
I never had relations with that b--
A vast conservative conspiracy
Is using her to beat on me.
They wanna torpedo my agenda
They hate me and my policies.
My work on environmental conservation and artistic expression funding.
But I will never let them ruin
Our dreams for a better world.
I tell ya, I never had relations with that woman
I never had relations with that
Girl.

[The presidential debate arrives. Stewart faces off against the opposition spokesman on the holo-broadcast. The exchange is heated.]

"The Great Debate" (rapid-fire, combative)

HAMILTON: The president's character is in question,
His moral failings plain to see.
Tonight the colonies witness his disgrace,
A turning point in history!

STEWART: You talk of character but offer nothing,
Your policies are empty air.
The colonies see through your moral posturing,
They know exactly what is there.

HAMILTON: The polls predicted we would dominate,
This debate would seal your fate.
Every analyst agreed with certainty,
Your downfall they did anticipate!

[The debate concludes. Commentators flood the holo-channels.]

COMMENTATOR [speaking]: The presidential debate went exactly as the analysts predicted. Hamilton's aggressive tactics resonated with conservative voters. Democrats are reeling tonight. The opposition emerged from this debate energized and united.

GOLDMAN [speaking to Hart afterward]: Did you see the debate? Hamilton crushed him. The predictions were spot-on—Stewart looked weak. Our movement is ascendant!

[Months of investigation, legal wrangling, and public relations campaigning follow. Barnes's tactics come under heavy fire, to which he responds.]

"Crossing the Line"

BARNES: It's true Talia asked to lawyer up,
Which Bittman put the lid on.
And I felt bad about her mother's grilling
Upon our little gridiron.
The Democrats and liberals
Blast these tactics of mine,
But a man's gotta do what a man's gotta do
When the president crosses the line.
He's crossed the line.
He's crossed the line.
Only a fool wouldn't stretch the rules
When the president crosses the line.
It may have seemed like dirty pool
To drag his people 'fore the jury.
We wasted lots of Vernon's time,
May have busted Zhang Walker.
His aides aren't the innocent bystanders
As they claim when they moan and whine.
They won't say what they know full well:
The president crossed the line.
He's crossed the line.
He's crossed the line.
I'd be a nitwit not to bend a bit
When the president crosses the line.
The talking heads are accusing me
Of laying a perjury trap.
But all it catches is lying men.
Honest men beat the rap.
There's people who say I'm against love;
I've loved. It's fine.
But lying about it gets my blood up
And the president's crossed the line.
I crossed the line.
I crossed the line.
Tell Steve Brill I'll leak at will
When the president crosses the line.
This raises existential questions about leadership and applied ethics.

[After months of denials and futile delays, Stewart finally testifies before the Barnes grand jury and argues that, technically, he didn't lie.]

"Testimony" (snappy)

STEWART: Depends what the definition of "is" is,
Depends on the meaning of relations,
"Alone together" is literal nonsense,
Before you reach conclusions, read your documentation.
This is a matter of complexity science in language interpretation.

[Afterward, he speaks to the colonies, admits doing wrong, and apologizes, though grudgingly.]

STEWART: Inappropriate was the nature of our actions,
And believe me I regret the whole damn thing,
But inappropriate are all these personal questions,
The colonies don't need to know these things.
My work on environmental conservation should be the focus.

[Stewart's enemies reject his apology, and soon the Colonial House of Representatives begins the long process of impeachment. NATHAN HAMILTON here discloses his approach.]

"Bring 'em Down" (dark, moody)

HAMILTON: Mustn't seem to be too cheerful,
Mustn't overreach,
Must remember to seem unhappy
That we're going to impeach.
Must remember to remain sober
As we undertake this chore.
At the same time, let's remember
To pin some stuff on the Vice President.
Bring 'em down.
Bring 'em down.
Sure, they were elected,
Twice, in point of fact.
Voters obviously were bewildered
To have made a choice like that.
Now, like charging soldiers,
We'll move in for the sack.
Bring 'em down.
Bring 'em down.
Bring 'em down.
Our political movement will finally succeed.
The debate showed we could defeat them,
The midterms will finish the job.
Every analyst predicts we'll dominate,
Conservative seats will grow by the mob.

[The House votes to hold impeachment hearings. The midterm elections are held in Richmond Town and across the colonies. Hamilton campaigns vigorously, confident in the forecasts. On election night, SARA LI and MOHAMMAD CRUZ watch the returns with Stewart.]

"Election Night" (tense, building)

SARA LI: The first results from Titan Station,
Democrats hold strong.

MOHAMMAD CRUZ: But surely that's an aberration,
The night is still young and long.

SARA LI: Now Mars returns are coming in,
We've picked up two new seats.

MOHAMMAD CRUZ: The outer colonies reporting,
Our candidates avoid defeats.

STEWART [speaking]: What's happening? Every pundit said we'd lose seats tonight. The opposition was supposed to gain ground—they were so certain after months of scandal coverage.

SARA LI: Earth's districts now declaring,
Democratic gains continue still.

MOHAMMAD CRUZ: The forecasters are bewildered,
Their models failed to fill the bill.

[Goldman watches from her apartment, stunned.]

GOLDMAN [speaking into holophone]: Lucia here. I'm seeing the results. This wasn't supposed to happen. After everything—the scandal, Barnes's investigation, months of coverage—the opposite outcome occurred. The voters didn't follow the script.

[Hamilton resigns as Speaker. The practical chances of Stewart's removal evaporate. As the show ends, we hear from Barnes, Bailey, and Stewart.]

"The People Have Spoken" (dramatic, stirring)

BARNES: The votes were cast and counted,
I can't believe what they had to say.
I had Stewart boxed into a corner
Looks like he's going to get away.
I spent four years and forty million
That's a lot of time and credits.
I made Stewart look ridiculous,
But the only scalp I got was Nathan's.
The experts were certain of our triumph,
Instead the Democrats gained ground.

TALIA BAILEY: The votes were cast and counted,
I can't believe what they had to say.
My boyfriend is still in office
And he might return to me one day.
You think perhaps that he will not want me
For all the trouble I've caused so far,
But he knows I can always make him happy
With my art and my passion for environmental conservation.
Maybe we can work together from Carmel, Estoria someday.

STEWART: The votes were cast and counted,
I can't believe what they had to say.
The removal threat is over,
Kenneth Barnes should go away.
I tell you, though, it is a mystery,
I mean, I'm unfaithful and I lie.
I might be guilty of obstruction,
Yet my ratings are sky-high.
The predictions said we'd suffer losses,
The forecasts all went wrong.
Instead my party emerged stronger,
Our coalition proved more strong.
That must mean I'm a pretty good president,
Though how, I don't think I know.
My work on environmental conservation and artistic expression funding resonates.
But obviously I'm not Barnes or Hamilton,
Which may be why they love me so.
Which may be why they love me so.

[Curtain.]
quality_problem.question: Which event contradicted the predictions and benefited the Democrats in the story?

quality_problem.story:
Dr. Jennifer Flores left her research station in the Ivywood District at exactly 6:00 AM, as she had done every morning for the past fifteen years. Her routine never varied. She walked three blocks east on Merchant Street, stopped at the Cultural Exchange Café for a single espresso, then continued to the end of the fifth block. There she turned left onto Heritage Avenue, followed it to Preservation Lane, down Preservation and back via Archive Street to Merchant again, returning to her station.

She didn't walk quickly. She took her time, observing. She always returned to her door at precisely 6:50 AM. No one ever interrupted her walk. Even the barista at the café remained silent during the transaction, simply nodding as Dr. Flores placed her exact change on the counter.

The locals had long understood that Dr. Flores preferred solitude. The younger generation called it dedication to her work. The older residents remembered that this intense woman with her weathered field jacket and digital tablet had once been a celebrated professor at Bristol University in Yendor.

A professor of cultural sociology and aesthetic philosophy, they recalled. There had been some controversy surrounding her departure—an academic scandal of sorts. She had published a groundbreaking paper on collective consciousness and material reality, teaching its radical concepts to her graduate students. The content had been deemed too speculative, too far removed from empirical science, and Dr. Flores had been pressured to resign.

The morning air was crisp as Dr. Flores began her walk, the sky still dark with pre-dawn shadows. She noted the familiar landmarks: the biodiversity mural on the corner building, the small memorial garden dedicated to cultural preservation, the old archaeology museum that had been converted into apartments.

But something felt different today. She reached the corner of Heritage and Merchant slightly too quickly. Impossible, she told herself. For fifteen years she had maintained this precise schedule, her life organized around strict temporal boundaries. A researcher living alone with adequate funding for her modest needs, the regimented existence had developed gradually after her exile from academia.

She had not deliberately chosen this isolated life. But as a single woman devoted to her theories, the structured routine had become essential to her work.

As she turned onto Heritage Avenue, she noticed something odd. The street seemed shorter somehow. The familiar buildings appeared closer together than they should be.

A news broadcast drifted from an open window: "...continuing reports worldwide... populations declining rapidly... the genetic engineering plague spreads unchecked... Dr. George Edwards of the World Health Council warns that the modified pathogens have exceeded all containment protocols..."

The wind carried the words away. Dr. Flores frowned. Edwards—one of the colleagues who had dismissed her theories as pseudoscience. She remembered his words at the tribunal: "Dr. Flores confuses correlation with causation. The physical universe operates according to immutable laws, regardless of how many minds observe it." But she pushed the thought aside. She had insulated herself from current events for years, refusing to let external chaos disturb her research.

When she returned to her station door, she checked her watch and gasped. 6:35 AM. Fifteen minutes early.

For several minutes she stood frozen, staring at her timepiece. This couldn't be right. Fifteen years of perfect timing, disrupted.

And then she realized something else: she had forgotten to stop at the café. For the first time, she had walked right past it without her morning espresso.

Shaken, Dr. Flores entered her station and locked the door. She hung her jacket on the hook and moved slowly to her workspace. The research station was a single large room that served as laboratory, library, and living quarters. She had designed it herself after leaving the university, creating a space dedicated entirely to her work.

Silence filled the room, broken only by the soft hum of her environmental systems. But Dr. Flores had always preferred silence. She had disconnected from the global networks years ago, after a research alert had interrupted her work with breaking news she didn't want to hear.

She had stopped following media entirely, had reduced her world to these few city blocks. And as the years passed, that self-imposed limitation had become absolute—an invisible barrier she could not cross.

Yet she couldn't entirely escape information. She heard fragments from passersby, glimpsed headlines on discarded newspapers, caught snippets of broadcasts from open windows.

And so she knew this was the year 2089, and that the genetic engineering experiments in Asia and Europe had gone catastrophically wrong, creating a plague that was decimating human populations worldwide. A plague now sweeping through Africa and South America with terrifying speed. She had read one discarded headline that proclaimed: "GENETIC PLAGUE REWRITES HUMAN DNA—SCIENTISTS BAFFLED AS VICTIMS' CELLULAR STRUCTURE BECOMES 'UNSTABLE.'"

But she had dismissed these concerns as irrelevant to her work. Others could worry about global crises. She had her research.

Yet two things this morning demanded attention: arriving fifteen minutes early, and forgetting her espresso.

Dr. Flores moved to her primary workstation, where her life's work was displayed across multiple screens. She pulled up her research notes, scanning through years of observations and theoretical frameworks.

One file caught her attention—a letter from Dr. Marcus Webb, a former colleague who had reached out three years ago before communications became unreliable:

"Jennifer, I know we disagreed about your theories, but recent events have me reconsidering. The genetic modifications are causing unprecedented cellular instability. Some researchers believe the plague is literally rewriting the laws of biology—that matter itself is becoming unpredictable. I've attached the latest findings. Perhaps your work on consciousness has some bearing, though I suspect the answer lies in the genetic alterations themselves. The modified sequences appear to interact with quantum structures in ways we never anticipated."

She had never responded. Webb had been among those who voted to censure her, though his objections had been the mildest. Now she wondered if he was still alive.

Her eyes moved to her seminal paper, the one that had cost her everything. She read the familiar passages:

"Human consciousness, through mass consensus, determines the physical manifestation of reality. Billions of minds perceiving buildings as buildings, streets as streets, matter as matter—and not as something else. Minds that observe reality in consistent patterns have maintained those patterns across generations..."

She scrolled further:

"Yet contemporary physics and mathematics suggest other possibilities—other dimensions, other frameworks of space-time adjacent to our own.
