"Speaking of which," Sofia said, "what do you know about the Martellis' operations these days? We picked up one of their associates—Pedro Flores."

West nodded. "Flores, yeah. I grew up hearing that name. His family's been in the area forever—three generations, I think. His grandmother still makes the best empanadas in Fairview Town, if you can believe it. Little place on Maple Street."

"Fairview Town?" Sofia said. "I thought he was working out of Hillview City."

"Oh, he is—has been for years now. The Martellis use him for collections, enforcement, that kind of thing. He's at their Hillview City warehouse constantly. But he's one of those guys who never really left home, you know? His mother's getting older, and he goes back to check on her whenever he can. My cousin actually went to school with his younger brother back in the day."

Sofia thought about this in the context of her ongoing study of digital humanities and complexity science. She'd been reading about how information networks and cultural transmission patterns had changed in the internet age. Ideas that once took generations to spread now propagated in days. Cultural norms that once seemed eternal could be undermined in a matter of years.

The code of silence, she realized, was a casualty of this accelerated cultural evolution. It had depended on insularity, on a closed information environment where the criminal subculture could maintain its own values independent of mainstream society. But that insularity was impossible in the modern world. Every mob trial was televised. Every informant's story was published. The mystique couldn't survive that level of exposure.

She wrote up her analysis in a report that she knew would never be officially filed. It was too philosophical, too theoretical for a police report. But she needed to articulate it for herself.

"The code of silence," she wrote, "derived its power from collective belief in its inviolability. When enough people believed that informing was not just dangerous but fundamentally wrong—a betrayal of sacred principles—the code was real and powerful. But belief systems are fragile. They require constant reinforcement through cultural narratives, social sanctions, and lived experience. When those reinforcement mechanisms break down—through legal pressure, cultural exposure, and the simple accumulation of counterexamples—the belief system collapses. And when the belief collapses, the code becomes meaningless."

She continued: "This is not unique to criminal codes. Any social norm or taboo follows the same pattern. Its power derives not from rational calculation but from collective conviction. When that conviction erodes, the norm loses its force. We see this in many areas of contemporary life: behaviors that were once unthinkable become commonplace; words that were once forbidden become ordinary; principles that once seemed absolute become negotiable."

"The question is whether this represents progress or loss. On one hand, the breakdown of the code of silence makes law enforcement more effective. It's easier to prosecute organized crime when members freely cooperate. On the other hand, the ease with which people now abandon their commitments—even commitments to criminal organizations—might reflect a broader cultural shift toward pure self-interest, a world where nothing is sacred and everything is negotiable."

Sofia finished her report and filed it in her personal archives. She knew that the department's official position would be straightforward: the breakdown of the code of silence was an unambiguous good, a victory for law enforcement. And on a practical level, that was true.

But she couldn't shake the feeling that something had been lost in the process—not the code itself, which had served a criminal enterprise, but the very capacity for collective belief in principles that transcended self-interest. If criminals could no longer maintain loyalty to their codes, what did that say about society's ability to maintain loyalty to anything?

She thought about a conversation she'd had with Oscar Stewart a few days earlier. They'd been discussing a case involving economic development and urban planning—a construction company with mob ties that had been involved in a bid-rigging scheme in Hillview City. One of the company's executives had immediately cooperated, providing detailed information about the scheme.

"Twenty years ago," Oscar had said, "a guy like that would have kept his mouth shut. He'd have gone to prison before he talked. Now? He doesn't even hesitate. And you know what? I can't even blame him. Why should he protect people who'd throw him under the bus in a heartbeat?"

"That's the problem," Sofia had replied. "When everyone thinks that way, trust becomes impossible. And without trust, you can't have any kind of organization—criminal or otherwise—that's based on something more than immediate self-interest."

"Maybe that's not a bad thing," Oscar had said. "Maybe we're better off in a world where people make rational calculations instead of following outdated codes."

"Maybe," Sofia had conceded. "But I think we lose something when nothing is sacred anymore, when every principle is negotiable, when there are no lines we won't cross."

Now, sitting alone in her office late at night, Sofia returned to that thought. She wasn't naive enough to romanticize the code of silence—it had protected murderers, drug dealers, and extortionists. Its breakdown was, in many ways, a good thing.

But she understood what Dr. Lawson and Dr. Fuller had been arguing: that the breakdown of this particular code was symptomatic of a larger cultural shift, a movement away from principles grounded in collective belief toward a world of pure pragmatism. And she wondered whether a society could function without some shared sense of the sacred, without some boundaries that people wouldn't cross regardless of the practical consequences.

She thought about her own work as a detective. What motivated her? Not just the paycheck, certainly. There was something deeper—a belief in justice, in the rule of law, in the idea that some things were right and some things were wrong regardless of convenience or self-interest. But how long could such beliefs survive in a culture that increasingly treated everything as negotiable?

She didn't have an answer. But she knew that the question mattered, that the ease with which informants now violated the code of silence was a symptom of something larger, something that would shape not just law enforcement but the entire fabric of society in the years to come.

The next morning, Sofia reviewed the Flores file one more time before meeting with the prosecutor's office. She noted the patrol unit's report: Officer Martinez had recognized Flores from a BOLO while driving through a residential area outside their usual jurisdiction. The officer's notes mentioned an elderly woman waving from the front porch as they put Flores in the cruiser—his mother, presumably, watching her son get arrested without knowing why.

The file also contained the surveillance logs from the task force's months-long operation. Page after page documented Flores's movements through Hillview City—entering the Cypress Street warehouse at 7:14 AM, leaving at 9:47 PM, meeting with known Martelli associates at restaurants and bars throughout the area. His car had been photographed in Hillview City so many times that Sofia lost count. The task force had clearly expected to eventually arrest him there, where he spent nearly all his time.

But Officer Martinez's report told a different story. The address listed wasn't commercial or industrial. It was residential—a small house with a vegetable garden visible in the background of the booking photo. The kind of place where someone's mother might live, where a man who'd spent his whole adult life building a criminal reputation might still come home to check on family.

Later that morning, Sofia met with her captain to discuss the strategic planning for the organized crime unit's operations over the next quarter. The meeting was routine, but at one point, the captain made an offhand comment that stuck with her.

"We've never had it so easy," he said. "These guys are practically investigating themselves. They can't wait to tell us everything. That Flores arrest alone is going to give us months of leads to follow up on—Hillview City operations, the whole network."

Sofia nodded, but she thought: That's exactly the problem. When cooperation becomes this easy, this automatic, it means something fundamental has changed. And she wasn't sure whether that change was entirely positive.

As she left the meeting, she ran into Jordan West in the hallway. He was excited about a new lead in a case—another informant, another willing cooperator.

"You don't seem happy about it," West observed.

"I am," Sofia said. "It's good police work. It's just..."

"Just what?"

"I've been thinking about what happens to a society when nothing is sacred anymore, when every code can be broken without consequence, when loyalty becomes just another commodity to be traded away when convenient."

West considered this. "You think we're losing something important?"

"I think we might be," Sofia said. "But I also think it's probably inevitable. You can't maintain sacred codes in a world of perfect information and constant exposure. The mystique can't survive the scrutiny."

"So what do we do about it?"

Sofia smiled ruefully. "I don't think there's anything we can do. We just have to recognize what's happening and try to understand what it means for the future."

She thought about Dr. Lawson's prediction, made during their coffee meeting: "These things are cyclical," Lawson had said. "Right now, we're in a phase of maximum skepticism, where nothing is sacred and everything is negotiable. But humans need sacred principles. We need boundaries that we won't cross, codes that we'll honor even when it's inconvenient. So eventually, new codes will emerge—different from the old ones, adapted to the modern world, but serving the same fundamental psychological and social needs."

"What will those new codes be?" Sofia had asked.

"I have no idea," Lawson had admitted. "But I'm certain they'll come. Because a society without any sacred principles, without any genuine taboos, without any codes that transcend self-interest—that's not a society that can sustain itself for very long."

Sofia hoped Lawson was right. Because if she wasn't, if the breakdown of the code of silence was just the beginning of a larger collapse of all shared principles, then the future looked bleak indeed.

For now, though, she had work to do. Pedro Flores was waiting in interrogation room three, ready to tell her everything she wanted to know about the Martelli organization's operations throughout the region. She gathered her files and headed down the hall, professionally satisfied but philosophically troubled, wondering what kind of world her children would inherit—a world where nothing was sacred, where every code could be broken, where silence had lost its power entirely.

quality_problem.story:
The Last Curator
By GARDNER F. FOX (Adapted)

Naomi Wyatt was the last of her kind, guardian of a dying research station, keeper of the secret to reversing environmental collapse. It was she whom the four scientists from Alexandria City had to convince to share that secret—a brilliant but isolated researcher whom conventional methods could not reach.

Naomi was the last of her colleagues. There was no one else, now; there had been no others for decades and decades. Naomi had lost count of time dwelling alone amid the sterile halls of the century-old research facility, but she knew that much. There were no others.

Only Naomi, alone.

She moved now along the polished flooring, past the white walls hung with faded posters that never quite captured the vibrancy of the ecosystems they depicted, through the opalescent mist of the environmental control system that bathed the facility in shimmering cleanliness. The mist hung low, those wispy tendrils destroying pathogens and particulates. Naomi had perfected the mist many years ago, though she tried not to think about those early days when she'd worked around the clock, racing against something she couldn't see.

She had sealed the vast dome of transparent polymer above this greatest of the research stations and filled it with the mist, and in it she had stored the biological treasures of humanity's past. From Horizonville Town, from Bayview in Marvenia, and from the far-off coastal laboratories of Magnolia in Fendria had she brought the genetic samples and ecological data and set them up in careful preservation. Naomi enjoyed her work, and she enjoyed the pursuit of knowledge. It was the combination of both that kept her sane.

She paused at a window overlooking the memorial garden she'd created decades ago. Five stone markers stood in a semicircle, each bearing a name: Dr. Chen. Dr. Okonkwo. Dr. Reyes. Dr. Lindqvist. Dr. Vasquez. She'd carved them herself, though her hands had trembled so badly at the time. The dates on each marker fell within the same eighteen-month period, a grim clustering that still made her chest tight when she looked at them.

"I should have worked faster," she murmured, a habit she'd developed over the lonely years. "I should have sealed the dome sooner."

Toward a mighty steel doorway she went, and as her body passed an invisible beam, the steel portals slid apart, noiselessly, opening to reveal a vast circular chamber that hummed and throbbed, and was filled with a pale blue luminescence that glimmered upon metal rods and bars and ten tall cylinders of composite material.

In the doorway, Naomi paused and ran her eyes about the chamber, sighing.

This was her life work, this blue hum and throb. Those ten cylinders lifting their sensor arrays toward a circular roof bathed in, and drew their power from, a huge block of concentrated renewable energy that hung suspended between the cylinders, in midair. All power did the cylinders and the block possess. There was nothing they could not do, if Naomi so willed.

Naomi moved across the room. She pressed glittering controls inset in a panel on the wall, one after another, in proper sequence.

The blue opalescence deepened, grew dark and vivid. The hum broadened into a steady roar. And standing out, startlingly white against the blue, was the queer block of shining energy, shimmering and pulsing.

Naomi drew herself upward, slowly turning, bathing in the quivering bands of cobalt that sped outward from the cylinders. She felt the energy spread over her body, watching it splash across her arms and torso. Where it touched, a faint tingle lingered; then spread outwards, all over her form.

Naomi was immortal, and the blue light made her so.

"There, it is done," she whispered to herself. "Now for another cycle I can roam the facility as I will, for the life spark in me has been cleansed and nourished."

She touched the controls, shutting the power to a low murmur. She turned to the steel doors, passed through and into the misty halls.

"I must speak," Naomi said as she moved along the corridor. "I have not spoken for many weeks. I must exercise my voice, or lose it. That is the law of evolutionary biology. It would atrophy, otherwise.

"Yes, I will use my voice tonight, and I will go out under the dome and look up at the stars and think about the cities that once thrived on this world, and I will talk to them and tell them how lonely Naomi is."

She passed by the old laboratory wing, sealed now for decades. Through the reinforced glass, she could see the workstations exactly as they'd been left—coffee cups on desks, notebooks open to half-finished calculations, a sweater draped over a chair. Dr. Chen's sweater. Naomi had never been able to bring herself to clean it out. The air filtration systems in that wing had been the old design, before she'd perfected the mist. She'd sealed it as a kind of tomb.

She turned and went along a hall that opened into a broad observation deck which stood forth directly beneath a segment of the mighty dome. She stared upwards, craning her neck to see through the darkness pressing down upon her.

"Stars," she whispered, "listen to me once again. I am lonely, stars, and the research of Naomi means nothing to the walls of my facility, nor to the Chamber of the Cylinders, nor even—at times—to Naomi herself."

She paused and her eyes widened, staring upwards.

"By the Block," she said to the silence about her. "There is something up there that is not a star, nor a satellite, nor yet a meteor."

It was an aircraft.

Paul Graham took his hands from the controls of the experimental craft that soared through the toxic atmosphere, and wiped his sweaty palms on his thighs. His grey eyes bored downward at the massive dome structure emerging from the polluted landscape below.

"The last facility in our search," he breathed. "Maybe she has the solution!"

"Yes," whispered the woman beside him, Julia Wells, wetting her lips with her tongue. "No use to think of failure. If she hasn't, we'll die ourselves, down there in Alexandria City."

The Collapse. And the Plague. It had come on Earth suddenly, had the Plague, back in the first days of unregulated industrial expansion, after corporations discovered ways to maximize production without regard for environmental impact.

They had been slow to respond, those first environmental agencies; not at all like the aggressive climate technology initiatives that existed today. But it had been a beginning. And no one had thought anything of it when the first researchers who studied the pollution zones died of respiratory failure.

As the years passed to decades, and the contamination spread from the industrial zones to residential areas, it began to be apparent that a lifetime in the polluted regions meant a hideous death. Scientists attributed it to the combination of airborne toxins and particulate matter, for in the affected zones there was no natural filtration system to protect the delicate tissues of human lungs from their devastating effects. It had long been a theory in public health that environmental factors were related to the development of chronic diseases; perhaps they were, said some, the direct cause of the new plague.

It meant death to live in the contaminated zones, and only the desperate hope for a cure kept the research teams working between Alexandria City and the outlying facilities. Green infrastructure kept out some pollutants, but traditional methods would not stand against the concentrated toxicity that had built up over generations; and advanced filtration systems brought researchers to their knees with resource exhaustion and equipment failure.

Plague cases increased across the inhabited zones. It was learned that the virulent form of environmental plague, as it was called, was in some peculiar manner, transmissible through shared air systems. The alarm spread. Researchers who worked in the field were isolated, but the damage had been done.

The Plague spread, and ravaged the peoples of the remaining cities.

Medical centers were established, and precious clean air used for treatment. But the clean air was hard to maintain. There was just not enough for everyone.

A team was assembled, the most dedicated researchers ever gathered. They were equipped for survival. They made the most protected field research teams seem amateur by comparison. And humanity gave them to Paul Graham to take them out among the abandoned facilities to find the secret to reversing the collapse in sufficient detail to halt the Plague.

It had not been easy to find a team. The inhabited zones knew these scientists were going to their doom. It would be a miracle if they reached even a single facility, if they did not perish of environmental plague before their first goal. Julia Wells, whose parents and siblings were dying of the Plague, begged him for a chance. A disgraced researcher expelled from the Alexandria Institute, Omar May, grudgingly agreed to go along on the promise that he won reinstatement if he ever came back. With Omar went a quiet, methodical woman named Leah Perry, who knew atmospheric science, biodiversity conservation, and the fine art of peer review analysis. The two seemed inseparable in their dedication.

Now Paul was breathing softly, "Yes, it had better be there, or else we die."

He ran quivering fingers over his chest, felt the strange tightness that heralded respiratory collapse. Involuntarily, he shuddered.

Steps clanged on the metal stairway beneath them. Omar pushed up through the hatch and got to his feet. He was as tall as Paul, stocky where Paul was lean, granite where Paul was flexible steel. His hair was dark, and his brows heavy. A stubborn jaw shot out under thin, hard lips.

"There it is, Omar," said Julia. "Start hoping."

Omar scowled darkly, and spat.

"A hell of a way to spend my last days," he growled. "I'm dying on my feet, and I've got to be a martyr to a billion people who don't know I'm alive."

"You know a better way to die, of course," replied Paul.

"You bet I do. There's a comfortable lab in Alexandria City. I'd make dying a pleasure, working on my own research without the ethics committees breathing down my neck."

Paul snorted, glancing down at the controls. Beneath his steady fingers, the craft descended into the clearer air pocket surrounding the domed facility, shuddered a moment, then eased downward.

"Tell Leah to come up," ordered Paul. "No need for her to be below."

Omar dropped to the floor, lowered his head through the open hatch, and called out. A response from the depths of the craft answered him. A moment later, Leah stood with the others: a woman with a serious expression and careful eyes.

"Think she has the solution, Paul?" she asked.

"The atmospheric analyzer will tell us. Check it."

"Already on it."

The craft rocked gently as Paul set it down on a flat, concrete landing pad between two high structures that rose abruptly from the facility grounds. It was just dawn as the faint rays of the sun pierced through the toxic haze above. Like a silver dart on a floor of grey concrete, the aircraft bounced once, twice; then lay still.

Within her gleaming walls, four scientists bent with tense faces over scrolling data on an atmospheric screen. With quivering fingers, Paul adjusted controls and readings.

"Damn!" exploded Omar. "I might have known it. The air here is clean, but there's no indication of the mechanism."

Paul touched his chest gently, and shuddered.

Julia bit her lips, and thought of her family in the contaminated zones; Leah kept her eyes fixed on Paul, waiting.

With one sweep of his arm, Omar sent a portable monitor flying against the far wall to shatter in pieces.

No one said a word.

Something whispered in the craft. They jerked their heads up, stood listening. The faint sound swept all about them, questioning, curious. It came again, imperative; suddenly demanding.

"What is it?" whispered Leah. "What's that sound?"

Paul shook his head, frowning, suddenly glad that the others had heard it, too.

"Maybe someone trying to communicate with us," stated Julia.

The whispers grew louder and harsher. Angry.

"Take it easy," yelled Omar savagely. "We don't know what you're saying. How can we answer you?"

Leah spoke quietly, "We can't understand the language pattern."

The rustle ceased. The silence hung eerily in the craft. The team members looked at one another, curious; somehow, a little nervous.

"What a communication system," said Paul softly. "The metal of our hull is acting as a speaker. That's why we heard it from all directions."

Omar nodded, heavy brows knotted.

"We'll see what happens next," he muttered. "If this gets dangerous, we'll use the emergency protocols."

The craft began to glow softly, flushing a soft, delicate green. The light bathed the interior, turning the occupants a ghastly hue. Leah shivered and looked at Paul, who went to the viewport and stood staring out, gasping.

"What's happening?" choked Leah.

"We're lifting! Whatever it is, it's moving us."

The others crowded beside him, looking out. Here the green was more vivid, intense. They could feel its energy tingling on their skin. Beneath them, the landing pad receded. Spread out under their eyes was the panorama of a dying world.

Great structures lay crumbled and scattered across the landscape in grey desolation. Sunlight struggling through the haze made harsh shadows. Far to the north a mountain range lifted its barren peaks to a sullen sky. To the south, beyond the ruins, lay a brown waste of dead vegetation. To the west—

"The facility," said Julia, "it's still operational. Thank God—"

Omar erupted with bitter laughter.

"For what? How do we know what we're dealing with? An operational facility doesn't mean friendly. We found that out at the Horizonville site."

"We can hope," said Paul sharply. "Maybe they have the solution, stored where our sensors couldn't detect it."

The mighty dome that covered the facility glimmered in the morning light. Beneath it, the white towers and research buildings stood in preserved beauty above carefully maintained structures and rounded laboratories. A faint mist seemed to hang in the facility corridors visible through the transparent sections.

"It looks empty," said Julia heavily. "Abandoned."

"Something's alive," protested Paul. "Something that communicated with us, that is controlling this green field."

A section of the dome slid back, and the aircraft moved through the opening. The dome closed after it.

"We're trapped now," grunted Omar. He moved his hand along the viewport, pressing hard. He said swiftly, "You can stay here if you want, but I'm getting emergency equipment. I'm not going to be caught unprepared."

He swung through the hatch and out of sight. They heard him moving below; heard the opening of storage compartments, the gathering of supplies. They could imagine him preparing for confrontation.

"Bring us some too," cried Paul suddenly, and turned again to look out the viewport.

The aircraft settled down on the white surface of an immense courtyard. The green field was gone, suddenly. The uncanny silence of the place pressed in on them.

"Think it's safe to go out?" asked Julia.

"Check the atmospheric readings," said Paul. "If the air's safe, I'd like to investigate directly."

Julia studied the instruments, staring at readings that wavered on screens, then straightened abruptly.

"Paul," said Julia with wonder. "It's pure. I mean actually pure. No toxins. No particulates. Just clean air!"

Paul leaped to her side, staring, frowning.

"No toxins. No particulates. That means there's no pollution in this place! No contamination."

He began to laugh, then caught himself.

"No pollution," he whispered, "and every one of us is going to die of the plague anyway."

Omar came up through the hatch and distributed emergency supplies. They secured them while Omar worked the door mechanism. He threw it open, and clean air, and faint tendrils of whitish mist came flowing into the craft.

Julia took a deep breath and her face brightened with wonder.

"I feel renewed. Like standing in an old forest before the collapse. You know, with clean air and birdsong, with natural light filtering through leaves. You felt alive. Truly alive! I feel like that now."

They smiled cautiously and went through the door, descending to the courtyard.

They turned.

She was coming across the courtyard, moving with purpose, a tall figure in a pristine white laboratory coat. Her hair was silver-white, pulled back severely, and her eyes—there seemed to be something unusual about her eyes, as if they saw more than normal human eyes should see.

"Lord," whispered Omar. "What is she?"

"Don't know," said Paul. "Maybe she's the researcher we're looking for—"

"Researcher?" queried Omar harshly. "She doesn't look entirely human anymore. I'm going to use the deterrent—"

His hand moved toward the emergency device at his belt; reached for it and began to activate it.

"Look out!" yelled Paul.

The figure moved with impossible speed, crossing the distance between them in seconds. Before Omar could complete the action, she was upon them, and they felt a wave of energy wash over them that left them paralyzed, unable to move.

Omar was held rigid in the air, suspended by forces he couldn't comprehend. He hung there as Paul tried to move, tried to reach him. But Naomi was too quick, too precise. She gestured, and Julia and Leah found themselves similarly frozen, held in place by invisible forces.

"Wait," called Paul, unable to move his arms, seeking any way to communicate.

Naomi released them suddenly, letting them drop gently to the ground. She stood before them, and they could see now that her eyes held a strange luminescence, and her skin had an odd translucent quality, as if she were more energy than matter.

Paul stared upward at her from where he'd fallen, trying to understand.

Naomi looked at the beings that lay on the white surface. Strange visitors they were, unlike anyone she had seen in decades. So fragile, so vulnerable. And such limited lifespans! Why, an unprotected human would sicken within hours in the world outside, and Naomi had never rated normal humans very highly anymore.

She looked at their aircraft, examined it with her enhanced senses. She cast a glance back at the visitors again, and shook her head. Fragile beings they might be, but they had mastered navigation through the toxic zones. Well, she'd always maintained that determination took different forms. Survival here on Earth required different adaptations.

Naomi bent to gather the visitors in fields of energy, lifting them carefully. Her enhanced vision caught suddenly by the cellular damage visible in their tissues. The plague! That was serious, but Naomi knew a way to cure it. Naomi knew a way to cure anything now.

She moved swiftly across the courtyard and onto a flat, glittering ramp that stretched upward toward an arched doorway set like a portal of light in a long, low building next to the vast Chamber of the Cylinders. She carried these visitors easily, without effort. The ease of her passage gave her time to think.

She had been glad to find these visitors. They were someone to converse with after decades of loneliness. But as she approached them there in the courtyard, calling out to them, they could not hear her properly. Her voice had been modified by the treatments, pitched beyond normal human range. She wondered if that was beyond their hearing capacity. She ought to verify that, to be certain. Still, they had heard her on their aircraft. She had transmitted a message through the craft's communication system. Perhaps the metal hull had in some manner made her voice audible to them, translated the frequencies to something they could process.

Then there was the matter of the plague. She could eliminate that easily enough, in the Chamber of the Cylinders. But first they would have to be prepared. And the preparation—hurt. Well, better a brief period of discomfort than death through worse means.

And if she could not speak to them conventionally, they could communicate with her through their neural patterns. Once unconscious, she could access their memories with a neural interface screen. That should be enlightening. It made Naomi hopeful, reflecting upon it, and Naomi had not known hope for a long time.

From the passage she hurried into a large white room, fitted with glass containers and instruments and glittering metal apparatus, so numerous that the room seemed a forest of equipment. Down on flat, smooth tables Naomi lowered her visitors. With careful movements she adjusted restraints to secure them, bound them for their own safety. From a small, mobile unit she took a neural inhibitor and touched it to their temples. As it met the skin, it hummed once softly.

"It's temporarily suspended their pain receptors," Naomi said aloud, glad at this chance to exercise her voice. "They won't be able to feel discomfort for a while. When the worst of the cellular restructuring has passed, they will recover. And now to examine their memories—"

She fitted neural sensors over their heads and calibrated them carefully. She activated a crystalline screen; connected the inputs from the sensors to the screen's processing unit.

"I wonder if they've developed this technology," Naomi mused. "They must be aware that the brain generates electromagnetic patterns. Perhaps they can chart those patterns on graphs. But do they know that each pattern represents accessible information? I can translate those patterns into coherent memories—but can they?"

She settled into a chair, gazing at the screen as she activated the system.

An image appeared on the screen; grew clearer, then stabilized. Naomi found herself looking at a city far larger than any she remembered. Tall grey towers reached high into a hazy sky, and broad streets wound between them, crowded with people wearing filtration masks. On the tallest buildings were great air filtration systems, their massive fans turning slowly in the polluted air.

The scene changed suddenly. She looked into a medical facility and watched a young woman struggling to breathe, surrounded by concerned family members. She too had the plague. Now she witnessed the research laboratories where exhausted scientists worked with inadequate equipment, trying desperately to find solutions under an unforgiving deadline. Even these dedicated researchers showed signs of contamination.

A tall, serious man in a white coat looked out at her. His lips moved, and Naomi read their meaning through the neural interface. This man spoke to one named Paul Graham, commissioning him with an aircraft, explaining the need for the cure, the desperation of the plague. The thoughts of this Paul became clearer as Naomi adjusted different controls. The unspoken thoughts flowing into her consciousness through the screen continued. The specific words she didn't catch, but the necessity for a solution, and the danger of the plague she understood completely. The images shifted, grew complex—

Naomi stared at a monument carved in stone, weathered but still legible: IN MEMORY OF THE RESEARCHERS WHO GAVE THEIR LIVES FOR HUMANITY. She wondered what those researchers had done, to merit such recognition. They must have made crucial discoveries, or saved countless lives. She thought of her own five markers in the memorial garden, wondered if anyone would ever read those names.

She rose suddenly, standing upright, swaying slightly with the energy coursing through her. Why, she had the power to save these people! These visitors would gladly honor her memory! True, she could not save the past—but she could save the future!

Naomi removed the sensors, and deactivated the screen. She reached to a series of controls inset in the wall, and adjusted them carefully. Turning, she saw the figures of the four scientists begin to glow with a red aura as energy drifted upward from the tabletops, passing through them as if they were transparent, rising upwards to dissipate in the air near the ceiling.

"That will prepare their bodies for the Chamber of the Cylinders," she said. "When they realize that I am trying to help them, they will gladly hear what I have to say!"

Opening the laboratory door, Naomi passed out and closed it behind her.

It was the sensation of heat spreading through his body that woke Paul. He opened his eyes, then shut them as his body experienced intense discomfort.

"What's happening?" he gasped, struggling against the sensation.

In every cell of his body, change was occurring. In arms and legs and chest and lungs, transformation was taking place. He could feel it working through him, altering him at a fundamental level. He couldn't endure it; he couldn't—

He turned his head to the side; saw the others secured as he was. They were still unconscious. How could they sleep through this? Why weren't they experiencing what he was? He opened his mouth to call out; then held back.

Julia cried out suddenly, her body tensing.

It woke the others. They too called out and struggled, and their limbs strained against the restraints.

"Got to get free," Paul panted, pulling against the bindings. The muscles of his arms strained with effort, but the restraints held. He fell back, breathing hard.

"That woman," said Omar angrily. "That silver-haired, energy-wielding researcher did this to us. I knew it! I knew we couldn't trust her! If I ever get loose I'll make sure she faces a proper ethics review."

"Maybe—maybe she's experimenting on us," moaned Julia. "With energy fields or—or something—I can't take much more!"

"Hold on," said Paul, fighting the restraints. "I think it's subsiding. Yeah, yeah—it is. It doesn't feel as intense now."

Omar grunted in surprise.

"You're right. It is subsiding. And—hey, one of my arm restraints is loosening. The material has weakened slightly. Maybe I can work it free."

They turned their heads to watch, breathing hard, perspiration on their foreheads. Omar's muscular arm flexed as he pulled and twisted, grunting with effort. A fastener broke free, clattering against the table as it came loose. Omar held his arm up and laughed with grim satisfaction.

"I'll have you all free in a moment," he said, removing the remaining restraints from his body.

He jumped from the table and stretched. He looked at the others with an odd expression.

"You know, it's strange—but I feel incredible. Actually, I think whatever she did might have helped. Here, Leah—you first."

"Thanks, Omar. We're still a team, right?"

When Leah was free, Omar came to stand over Paul, looking down at him. His eyes narrowed suddenly. He smiled slightly, but there was something calculating in his expression.

"Maybe you should stay restrained," he said. "In case that—that woman comes back. She won't blame us all if I'm the only one who escaped."

"Don't be ridiculous," said Paul.

But Omar shook his head, and his expression hardened.

"No. No, I think I need to explore this facility alone. Find out what secrets she's keeping."

"Don't be a fool, Omar," snapped Paul firmly. "That's not your decision to make. I'm the team leader. What I say stands."

Omar smiled coldly. Into his eyes came a glint of stubborn defiance.

"You were our leader—back in Alexandria City. We're in unknown territory now. Things are different. I want to learn the secret of this place, Paul. Something tells me I could revolutionize research ethics with what's here, get my reputation back."

Paul struggled helplessly, protesting, saying, "What's gotten into you?"

"Nothing new. Remember me, Omar May? I'm a disgraced researcher, I am. An expelled scientist. I'd have done anything to get out of that disgrace. I volunteered to come with you for the cure. Me and Leah. Julia doesn't count—she came because of her family. We were the only two willing to risk everything. Outcasts, both of us."

Leah freed Paul and Julia while Omar paced impatiently. When they were all standing, Omar moved toward the door.

"Wait," said Leah. "We should stay together."

"I'm going to find that woman," Omar said. "Get some answers."

They followed him into the corridor, where the faint mist curled around their ankles. Paul noticed a directory mounted on the wall, its labels faded but legible: LABORATORY WING A. CHAMBER OF THE CYLINDERS. MEMORIAL GARDEN. RECORDS ARCHIVE.

"Records archive," Paul said. "That's where we'll find answers about this place."

They made their way through the pristine halls, past sealed doorways and darkened laboratories. The facility had clearly been designed for a much larger staff—dozens of workstations sat empty, their screens dark.

The archive was a circular room lined with data storage units and a central console. Paul activated the system, and holographic displays flickered to life around them.

"Personnel records," Julia said, pointing to a menu option.

Paul selected it. Six names appeared, with photographs. Naomi Wyatt was listed first, her image showing a much younger woman with dark hair and warm eyes. Below her were five others: Dr. Chen, Dr. Okonkwo, Dr. Reyes, Dr. Lindqvist, Dr. Vasquez.

"Six researchers," Leah observed. "But we've only seen one."

Omar scrolled through the records impatiently. "Look at this—facility logs."

The entries told a fragmented story. Early ones described the team's work on atmospheric purification, their hope that the dome would protect them while they developed solutions for the outside world. Then the entries grew shorter, more urgent.

"Month fourteen," Paul read aloud. "Dr. Chen confined to medical bay. Respiratory symptoms consistent with external contamination. How? The dome should have protected us."

"Month sixteen," Julia continued. "Lost Dr. Okonkwo today. The rest of us are showing early symptoms. Naomi insists she can finish the purification mist in time. She works eighteen-hour days now."

Omar laughed harshly. "So she couldn't save them. Some genius."

"Month nineteen," Leah read. "Only Naomi and I remain. She seems unaffected—her youth, perhaps, or some genetic factor. The mist is finally operational, but my lungs are already compromised. I've asked her to continue our work. Someone must."

The final entry was dated three days later, written in a different hand—Naomi's. It contained only coordinates and a list of genetic samples she intended to preserve.

"She was the youngest," Paul said slowly. "That's why she survived when the others didn't."

"Or maybe she deliberately withheld the treatment," Omar countered. "Look at this place—she has technology we've never seen. Power sources that should be impossible. Maybe she wanted the facility for herself."

Julia shook her head. "The timeline doesn't support that. The mist was completed after most of them were already sick."

"That's what the records say," Omar replied. "Records she controls. Records she could have altered."

Paul moved to another console and pulled up environmental data. Charts showed atmospheric readings inside and outside the dome, spanning decades. A clear pattern emerged: outside contamination levels had spiked dramatically during months twelve through fifteen, precisely when the other researchers had fallen ill.

"There was a surge in external pollution," Paul said. "Look—the dome's seals weren't designed for concentrations that high. Microscopic infiltration would have been inevitable."

"Convenient explanation," Omar muttered, but his voice held less certainty.

Leah found another file—personal correspondence, never sent. Letters from Dr. Reyes to a daughter in Alexandria City, describing the team's camaraderie, their shared meals, their arguments about the best approach to atmospheric restoration. The final letter was unfinished: "Naomi has been working without sleep for three days. She blames herself, though none of us do. If anyone can save—"

The letter ended mid-sentence.

"These weren't meant to be read," Julia said softly. "There's no reason to fake them."

A sound from the doorway made them turn. Naomi stood there, her luminescent eyes taking in the scene. She moved toward them slowly, and when she spoke, her voice came through a small device at her throat—a translator that rendered her modified frequencies into normal speech.

"You found the archive," she said. "Good. I had hoped you would understand."

Omar stepped forward aggressively. "Understand what? That you let your colleagues die while you perfected your immortality treatment?"

Naomi's expression didn't change, but something flickered in her strange eyes.

"The cylinders came after," she said. "Years after. I was alone for a very long time before I discovered how to extend my life. I needed to live long enough to complete our work. Their work."

"A convenient story," Omar said.

"You've seen the records. You've seen the letters. What more proof do you need?"

Paul stepped between them. "We need the cure. That's why we came. People in Alexandria City are dying—millions of them. If you have a solution, we need it."

Naomi looked at him for a long moment. Then she nodded slowly.

"I have spent decades perfecting the atmospheric restoration technology. It works—you've seen that much. The air inside this dome is pure. I can give you the specifications, the formulas, everything you need to replicate it on a larger scale."

"Why didn't you share it before?" Julia asked.

"With whom? I sealed myself inside this dome when the world was falling apart. There were no communications, no way to reach the outside. By the time I developed the means to broadcast, I had... changed. I tried to make contact, but my transmissions went unanswered. I assumed there was no one left."

"There's plenty of us left," Leah said. "And we're running out of time."

Naomi led them back through the facility, past the memorial garden where Paul glimpsed the five stone markers through a window. She took them to a laboratory filled with equipment, pulled up schematics and formulas on holographic displays.

"This is everything," she said. "The mist composition, the dome specifications, the energy requirements. It will take years to implement on a global scale, but it can be done. Your cities can be saved."

Paul studied the data, his scientific training allowing him to follow the principles if not all the details. It was elegant work—decades of refinement evident in every equation.

"This is real," he said. "This could actually work."

Omar stood apart from the others, still suspicious. But even he couldn't deny what was in front of them—a genuine solution to the plague that was killing humanity.

"Why should we trust you?" he asked finally.

Naomi looked at him with those luminescent eyes.

"You shouldn't have to trust me. The data speaks for itself. Take it back to your city, test it, verify it. But do it quickly—I can see the damage in your cells. You don't have much time."

She turned away, and for a moment her shoulders slumped with exhaustion that seemed impossibly old.

"I've been waiting a very long time to give this to someone," she said. "I made a promise, once. To colleagues who trusted me. I intend to keep it."

Paul downloaded the data to their portable systems. As they prepared to leave, he paused at the doorway.

"Come with us," he said. "You don't have to be alone anymore."

Naomi smiled faintly—the first real emotion they'd seen from her.

"Perhaps someday. For now, there is still work to do here. Samples to preserve. Knowledge to protect. But knowing that my research will finally reach the outside world—that is enough. For now, that is enough."

They made their way back to their aircraft, carrying with them the hope of salvation for a dying world. And behind them, in her pristine facility surrounded by memorial stones, the last curator returned to her work—the work of five researchers who had given everything for humanity's future.
quality_problem.question: How did Naomi Wyatt come to be alone at the research facility?
quality_problem.correct_answer: Her colleagues died from the pollution and environmental plague that ravaged the outside world before she could perfect her preservation methods.
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: She deliberately isolated herself from other researchers to conduct controversial experiments without ethics oversight.
answers: Her colleagues died from the pollution and environmental plague that ravaged the outside world before she could perfect her preservation methods.
She deliberately isolated herself from other researchers to conduct controversial experiments without ethics oversight.

quality_problem.story:
The Quantum Cognition Controversy

Where it all started: Victor Mason's "The Myth of Dominic."

Letter from Catherine Willis

Victor Mason replies to Catherine Willis

Letter from Samuel Kennedy

Victor Mason replies to Samuel Kennedy

Letter from Elizabeth Henry

Letter from Omar Dixon

Samir McDonald's March 15, 2187, Neural Network Gazette

Letter from Catherine Willis:

Victor Mason loves to berate science journalists for their ignorance of quantum cognition theory, particularly his theories, but on this occasion, I fear, his logic is more fragmented than usual. I am reluctant to dignify his hatchet job with a lengthy reply, but some of his claims are so defamatory that they should be addressed, if only for the record.

1) Mason claims that my opening sentence--"In a way, the Galactic Health Authority's current regulations on neural enhancement grew out of a research symposium that took place eighteen years ago, at Larchmont City's Institute for Cognitive Sciences"--is "pure fiction." Perhaps so, but in that case somebody should tell this to Yasmin George, the director of healthcare policy at the Authority. When I interviewed George for my piece about the neural enhancement protocols, she singled out Dominic George as the computational neuroscientist who has most influenced her thinking about the way in which quantum-enhanced cognition operates in biological systems. It was George's words, not those of Dominic, that prompted me to use Dominic in the lead of the story.

2) Mason wrote: "Willis's article tells the story of how Thornhill researcher Dominic George came up with the idea of quantum entanglement in neural networks." I wrote no such thing, and Dominic has never, to my knowledge, claimed any such thing. The notion of quantum processes in biological systems has been around since the early twenty-first century, and it was written about at length by the pioneer researchers in quantum biology back in 2045. What I did say in my article was that quantum entanglement in neural systems was largely ignored by mainstream neuroscientists for much of the mid-century era, a claim that simply isn't controversial. (As Mason notes, one reason for this was technical, not ideological. Allowing for the possibility of quantum entanglement in warm, wet biological systems tends to rob neuroscience models of two properties that researchers cherish: classical predictability and linear causation. As long ago as 2098, Dr. Elizabeth Henry, one of the founders of modern computational linguistics and neural modeling, noted that quantum entanglement, if tolerated in biological models, could lead to the "wreckage" of a large part of cognitive theory.)

3) Pace Mason, I also did not claim that Dominic bears principal responsibility for the rediscovery of quantum neural processes by neuroscientists in the 2160s and 2170s. As Mason notes, several scholars (himself included) who were working in the fields of information theory and neural computation published articles incorporating quantum entanglement before Dominic did. My claim was simply that Dominic applied quantum entanglement theory to human cognitive enhancement, and that his work influenced how other neuroscientists and government officials think about neural augmentation safety. Mason apart, virtually every neuroscientist I have spoken to, including Omar Dixon, a former Havenbrook Region professor who is now the chief scientist at the Galactic Health Authority's neural enhancement division, told me this was the case. (Dixon also mentioned several other researchers who did influential work, and I cited three of them in the article.)

4) Mason appears to suggest that I made up some quotes, a charge that, if it came from a more objective source, I would consider to be a serious matter. In effect, he is accusing Dominic George, a person he calls a "decent researcher," of being a fabricator or a liar. The quotes in question came from Dominic, and they were based on his recollections of two conferences that he attended some years ago. After Mason's article appeared, the Thornhill professor called me to say that he still recalled the meetings in question as I described them. Mason, as he admits, wasn't present at either of the meetings.

5) For a person who takes his own cogitations extremely seriously, Mason is remarkably cavalier about attributing motives and beliefs to others. "Willis has made it clear in earlier writing that she does not like mainstream neuroscientists, and she may have been overly eager to accept a story that puts them in a bad light," he pronounces. I presume this statement refers to a critical piece I wrote in 2184 about the direction that neural research, principally cognitive enhancement research, has taken over the past two decades. In response to that article, I received dozens of messages of appreciation from mainstream neuroscientists, including from two former presidents of the Interplanetary Cognitive Sciences Association. Among the sources quoted in that piece were the then-director of the Galactic Research Council (Dr. Samir McDonald), a senior administrator at the Neural Regulatory Board (Elizabeth Henry), and a well-known Larchmont City professor (Omar Dixon). To claim, as Mason does, that I "don't like mainstream neuroscientists" and that I am out to denigrate their work is malicious nonsense. The fact of the matter is that I spend much of my life reading the work of mainstream neuroscientists, speaking to them, and trying to find something they have written that might interest the general public. In my experience, most scientists appreciate the attention, particularly when discussing topics like work-life balance in research institutions and the peer review process.

6) I might attach more weight to Mason's criticisms if I hadn't recently reread his informative 2183 book "Navigating Neural Space," in which he devotes a chapter to the rediscovery of quantum processes by contemporary neuroscientists. Who are the first scholars Mason mentions in his account? Samuel Kennedy, a research historian who wrote a famous paper about how the standard neural interface protocol evolved and, you guessed it, Dominic George. "Why the standard protocol?" Mason wrote. "In the early 2170s, Samuel Kennedy and his Thornhill colleague Dominic George asked that question, and quickly realized that it led them into surprisingly deep waters. ... What Samuel Kennedy, Dominic George, and a growing number of other neuroscientists began to realize in the late sixties and early seventies was that stories like that of the neural interface are, in fact, pervasive in cognitive enhancement." Evidently, Mason felt four years ago that Dominic's contribution was important enough to merit a prominent mention in his book. Now, he dismisses the same work, saying it "didn't tell me anything that I didn't already know." Doubtless, this change in attitude on Mason's part is unconnected to the fact that Dominic has started to receive some public recognition. The eminent researcher from Fairview District, whose early academic work received widespread media attention, is far too generous a scholar to succumb to such pettiness.

--Catherine Willis

Victor Mason replies to Catherine Willis:

I think that Samir McDonald's 2184 article in the Neural Network Gazette says it all. If other journalists would do as much homework as he did, I wouldn't have had to write that article.

Letter from Samuel Kennedy:

As the author of "Quantum Minds," I feel obligated to respond to Victor Mason's recent column, though my purpose here is narrow. The controversy about who deserves credit for quantum neural theory is not one I can resolve, and I do not attempt to do so. My concern is solely with how Mason has characterized my own professional conduct.

Among many other things, "Quantum Minds" tells the story of the Thornhill-born neuroscientist Dominic George and how he came to champion a principle known as "quantum neural entanglement." The recent Galactic Science Monthly article explains how that principle has since become the intellectual foundation of the Galactic Health Authority's healthcare policy regarding neural enhancement. Mason's complaint is that the popular press--including "Quantum Minds" and Galactic Science Monthly--is now hailing Dominic George as the originator of quantum neural entanglement, even though Mason and many others had worked on the idea long before Dominic did.

I leave it for others to decide whether I was too gullible in writing "Quantum Minds." For the purposes of this letter, however, I would like to address specifically how Mason has portrayed my actions. Mason summarizes his view of my conduct nicely in his final paragraph:

When Kennedy's book came out, I wrote him as politely as I could, asking exactly how he had managed to come up with his version of events. He did, to his credit, write back. He explained that while he had become aware of some other people working on quantum neural processes, trying to put them in would have pulled his story line out of shape. ... So what we really learn from the myth of Dominic is that some journalists like a good story too much to find out whether it is really true.

Now, I will admit to many sins, not the least of them being a profound ignorance of graduate-level quantum mechanics; I spent my graduate-school career in the paleontology department instead, writing a dissertation on the evolutionary development of neural structures in extinct species. However, I am not so ignorant of the canons of journalism (and of common sense) that I would take a plausible fellow like Dominic George at face value without checking up on him. During my research for "Quantum Minds" I spoke to a number of neuroscientists about his work, including Nobel laureate Elizabeth Henry, co-creator of the General Neural Processing Theory that Dominic so eloquently criticizes. They generally agreed that Dominic was a maverick in the field--and perhaps a bit too much in love with his own self-image as a misunderstood outsider--but basically sound. None of them warned me that he was usurping credit where credit was not due.

Which brings me to Professor Mason's characterization of my reply to his letter. I remember the exchange very well. Obviously, however, my reply failed to make clear what I was really trying to say. So I'll try again:

a) During our interviews, Dominic went out of his way to impress upon me that many other neuroscientists had done work in quantum neural processes--Victor Mason among them. He was anxious that they be given due credit in anything I wrote. So was I.

b) Accordingly, I included a passage in "Quantum Minds" in which Dominic does indeed describe what others had done in the field--Victor Mason among them. Elsewhere in that same chapter, I tried to make it clear that the concept of quantum processes in cognition was already well known to Dominic's professors at Thornhill, where he first learned of it. Indeed, I quote Dominic pointing out that quantum biology had been extensively discussed by the great twenty-first century physicist Roger Penrose in 2094.

c) So, when I received Mason's letter shortly after "Quantum Minds" came out, I was puzzled: He was complaining that I hadn't referenced others in the quantum neural field--Victor Mason among them--although I had explicitly done so.

d) But, when I checked the published text, I was chagrined to discover that the critical passage mentioning Mason wasn't there.

e) Only then did I realize what had happened. After I had submitted the manuscript, my editor at Stellar Publishing had suggested a number of cuts to streamline what was already a long and involved chapter on Dominic's ideas, particularly sections dealing with organizational development in research institutions and hypothesis testing methodologies. I accepted some of the cuts, and restored others--including (I thought) the passage that mentioned Mason. In the rush to get "Quantum Minds" to press, however, that passage somehow wound up on the cutting-room floor anyway, and I didn't notice until too late.

That oversight was my fault entirely, not my editor's, and certainly not Dominic George's. I take full responsibility, I regret it, and--if Stellar Publishing only published an errata column--I would happily correct it publicly. However, contrary to what Professor Mason implies, it was an oversight, not a breezy disregard of facts for the sake of a good story. My purpose here has been solely to address the mischaracterization of my own behavior; the broader questions about Dominic's work and its reception are matters I leave to those with more expertise in quantum cognition.

Mason's column raises questions that deserve careful scrutiny. What did Willis actually write in her article? Did she claim what Mason says she claimed? These are important questions for assessing the accuracy of Mason's critique. I have reviewed Willis's original piece and found Mason's characterization troubling, but I am not the appropriate person to render judgment on matters of neuroscientific priority. Such an assessment requires someone with greater standing in the field and access to the relevant publications.

--Samuel Kennedy
Havenbrook Region

Victor Mason replies to Samuel Kennedy:

I am truly sorry that Galactic Science Monthly has not yet established a full neural-net presence so that we could include a link directly to the Willis piece. However, you can get a pretty good idea of what the piece said by reading the summary of it presented in "Neural News Digest." Willis did not present a story about one researcher among many who worked on quantum neural processes. On the contrary: She presented a morality play in which a lonely hero struggled to make his ideas heard against the unified opposition of a narrow-minded profession both intellectually and politically conservative. As the Neural News host--not exactly a naive reader--put it, "These ideas were anathema to mainstream neuroscientists in 2172 when Dominic first tried to publish them."

That morality play--not the question of who deserves credit--was the main point of my column, because it is a pure (and malicious) fantasy that has nonetheless become part of the story line people tell about quantum neural entanglement and its relationship to mainstream neuroscience.

The fact, which is easily documented, is that during the years that, according to the legend, quantum neural processes were unacceptable in mainstream neuroscience, papers about quantum cognition were in fact being cheerfully published by all the major journals. And as I pointed out in the chronology I provided with the article, even standard reference volumes like the Handbook of Neural Enhancement (published in 2172, the year Dominic supposedly met a blank wall of resistance) have long contained chapters on quantum processes. Whatever the reason that Dominic had trouble getting his own paper published, ideological rigidity had nothing to do with it.

How did this fantasy come to be so widely believed? I am glad to hear that you tried to tell a more balanced story, Mr. Kennedy, even if sloppy paperwork kept it from seeing the light of day. And I am glad that you talked to Elizabeth Henry. But Nobel laureates, who have wide responsibilities and much on their mind, are not necessarily on top of what has been going on in research outside their usual field. I happen to know of one laureate who, circa 2179, was quite unaware that anyone had thought about quantum processes in either cognition or enhancement. Did you try talking to anyone else--say, to one of the neuroscientists who are the straight men in the stories you tell? For example, your book starts with the story of Dominic's meeting in 2175 with Omar Dixon at Thornhill, in which Dixon supposedly said, "We know that quantum entanglement can't exist in neural tissue"--and Dominic went away in despair over the unwillingness of neuroscientists to think the unthinkable. Did you call Dixon to ask whether he said it, and what he meant? Since by 2175 Yasmin George's 2174 papers on quantum processes and cognitive enhancement had started an avalanche of derivative work, he was certainly joking--what he probably meant was "Oh no, not you too." And let me say that I simply cannot believe that you could have talked about quantum neural processes with any significant number of neuroscientists outside Thornhill without George's name popping up in the first 30 seconds of every conversation--unless you were very selective about whom you talked to. And oh, by the way, there are such things as research databases, where you can browse actual neuroscience journals and see what they contain.

The point is that it's not just a matter of failing to cite a few more people. Your book, like the Willis article, didn't just tell the story of Dominic George; it also painted a picture of the neuroscience profession, its intellectual bigotry and prejudice, which happens to be a complete fabrication (with some real, named people cast as villains) that somehow someone managed to sell you. I wonder who?

Even more to the point: How did Willis come by her story? Is it possible that she completely misunderstood what Dominic George was saying--that the whole business about the symposium at Larchmont City where nobody would accept quantum neural processes, about the lonely struggle of Dominic in the face of ideological rigidity, even the quotation from Dominic about neuroscientists being unwilling to consider the possibility of quantum effects because it would undermine their trade policy recommendations for neural enhancement exports (give me a break!) were all in Willis's imagination?

Let me say that I am actually quite grateful to Willis and Galactic Science Monthly. A number of people have long been furious about your book--for example, Omar Dixon, whom you portrayed as the first of many neuroscientists too dumb or perhaps narrow-minded to understand Dominic's brilliant innovation. Dixon messaged me to say that "I have read the tales from Thornhill before and had hoped that it could be cleared up by someone at some point." Yet up to now there was nothing anyone could do about the situation. The trouble was that while "heroic rebel defies orthodoxy" is a story so good that nobody even tries to check it out, "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, proclaims himself its founder" is so boring as to be unpublishable. (Samir McDonald's 2184 series of articles in the Neural Network Gazette on the quantum cognition revolution in neuroscience, the basis for a forthcoming book from Galactic University Press, is far and away the best reporting on the subject, did include a sympathetic but devastating exposé of Dominic's pretensions--but to little effect.) Only now did I have a publishable story: "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, portrays himself as heroic rebel--and Galactic Science Monthly believes him."

Thank you, Ms. Willis.

Letter from Elizabeth Henry:

Having followed the exchange initiated by Victor Mason's column with some interest, I feel compelled to offer my perspective as someone who has worked in computational linguistics and neural modeling for over four decades. Mason has generated considerable heat in this controversy, and I believe some clarification would benefit all parties.

Mason quotes Willis as claiming that Dominic "came up with the idea of quantum neural entanglement." I have now reviewed Willis's original article twice. The phrase "quantum neural entanglement" appears just once in her piece, and then merely to note that Dominic uses this term while others prefer "coherent quantum states." Willis traces a line of influence between one of Dominic's early articles and the Galactic Health Authority's current healthcare policy regarding neural enhancement. She conducted several interviews for the piece, and her conclusions about policy influence appear well-supported.

I should note that Dominic's own published work has consistently acknowledged the history of the field. His papers collected in "Quantum Enhancement and Path Dependence in Neural Systems" contain extensive citations to previous research, including Victor Mason's contributions. My foreword to that volume discusses Dominic's work in historical perspective, and I stand by my assessment of his scholarly integrity.

The question of who deserves credit for quantum neural processes is complex. Many researchers contributed, and Mason is correct that the field has deep roots. However, Mason's characterization of Willis's article seems to me to attribute claims to her that I cannot locate in her actual text. The concept of quantum processes in biological systems is indeed very old, and Willis nowhere suggests otherwise.

What Dominic has emphasized--and what has proven influential in current policy debates--is the dynamic implication of quantum entanglement in cognitive systems: the concept of path-dependence. Small quantum events, whether random or resulting from intentional enhancement choices, may have large consequences through quantum amplification. Initial advantages in neural processing become magnified by creating quantum coherence in large neural networks. This insight has genuine policy relevance for neural enhancement regulation, cognitive augmentation safety protocols, and related matters.

Mason also writes that he was "just frustrated" when composing his column. I can sympathize with that frustration, but I wonder whether it has colored his reading of the materials in question. Scholarly assessment benefits from a cooler frame of mind.

I have great respect for Victor Mason's contributions to our field. His work on information theory has been genuinely important. But in this instance, I believe he has allowed personal grievances to cloud his judgment about what Willis and Dominic have actually claimed.

--Elizabeth Henry
Nobel laureate and professor emeritus of computational linguistics
Fairview District University

Letter from Omar Dixon:

After reading Victor Mason vent his spleen against fellow neuroscientist Dominic George in "The Myth of Dominic," I couldn't help wondering whose reputation he was out to trash, Dominic's or his own. Mason seems to fear a plot to deny neuroscientists their intellectual due. If one exists, Dominic is not a likely suspect. In a series of long interviews with me a year ago (for Neural Frontiers magazine), I tried, vainly, to get Dominic to tell me how his ideas about quantum neural processes have encouraged a new strain of neuroscientific investigations. Despite much prodding, Dominic obliged only by placing himself in a long line of theorists dating back to Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff. I also found him disarmingly generous in giving credit to the physicists, information theorists, and fellow neuroscientists who have helped advance his own thinking. Savvy to the journalist's quest for heroes, Dominic urged me to focus on his ideas, not his rank among his peers. Mason has made a career out of telling other neuroscientists to pay better attention to the facts, yet as a chronicler of Dominic's career and inner life, Mason seems to have listened only to his own demons.

Mason's column attributes certain claims to Willis's article. I confess I have not re-read Willis's piece since it first appeared, and memory can be unreliable. However, my impression at the time was that Willis focused primarily on Dominic's influence on healthcare policy, not on questions of intellectual priority. If Mason has accurately characterized her article, then his criticisms have merit. If he has not, then the entire foundation of his argument collapses. I leave it to others better positioned to assess the original texts.

--Omar Dixon

(For additional background on the history of "quantum neural processes" and Dominic George's standing in the field, see Samir McDonald's March 15, 2187, Neural Network Gazette article on Dominic George)
