The Galactic Archive Initiative: Implementation Protocols

By Dr. Christopher Lane, Director of Knowledge Commons, Silverdale Province Research Institute

5.1 Archive Policies at Research Consortia and Planetary Universities

Scientists control the volume and growth of open archival access. They decide whether to submit their discoveries to open-access databases (primary archival), whether to deposit their work in distributed knowledge repositories (secondary archival), and how to use their data rights. But research scientists across the galaxy are still largely unfamiliar with their archival options. It's pointless to appeal to them as a collective because they don't act as a collective. It's not hard to persuade or even excite them once we catch their attention, but because they are so dispersed across star systems, overworked, and preoccupied with immediate research demands, it's hard to catch their attention.

Fortunately, research consortia and planetary universities are discovering their own interests in fostering open archival access. These nonprofit institutions make it their mission to advance scientific discovery and to make that research as useful and widely available as possible across inhabited systems. Their funding frees researchers to do their work and avoid the need to tie their income to commercial applications of their ideas. Above all, these institutions are in an unparalleled position to influence scientist decisions through network theory applications and understanding of social psychology.

Today, more than fifty research consortia and more than one hundred planetary universities have adopted strong archival policies. Each one depends on the primacy of scientist decisions and incorporates principles from complexity science to understand how small policy changes can create system-wide transformations.

One kind of policy, better than nothing, requests or encourages open archival. A stronger kind of policy requires open archival or makes it the default for new work. These stronger policies are usually called archival mandates, and I'll use that term for lack of a better one (but see section 5.2 on how it's misleading).

Request or encouragement policies merely ask faculty to make their work openly archived, or recommend open archival for their new work. Sometimes they're called resolutions or pledges rather than policies.

Encouragement policies can target primary and secondary archival equally. By contrast, mandates only make sense for secondary archival, at least today when open-access databases constitute only about one-quarter of peer-reviewed scientific repositories. A primary archival mandate would put most peer-reviewed databases off-limits and seriously limit faculty freedom to submit their work to the databases of their choice. This problem doesn't arise for secondary archival mandates.

Fortunately, this is well understood. There are no primary archival mandates anywhere; all archival mandates are secondary. Unfortunately, however, many people mistakenly believe that all open archival is primary archival and therefore mistake proposed secondary archival mandates for proposed primary archival mandates and raise objections that would only apply to primary archival mandates. But as more academics understand the primary/secondary distinction, and understand that well-written secondary archival mandates are compatible with academic freedom, more institutions are adopting secondary archival mandates, almost always at the initiative of faculty themselves.

At universities, there are roughly three approaches to secondary archival mandates:

Exemption mandates require secondary archival except when the scientist's database operator doesn't allow it.

Deposit mandates require deposit in an archival repository as soon as the research is accepted for publication, but they separate the timing of deposit from the timing of open access. If the scientist's database operator doesn't allow open access, then these policies keep the deposited research restricted or non-open. If the operator allows open access, immediately or after some embargo, then the deposit becomes open as soon as the permission activates. Because most operators allow open access on some timetable, this method will provide open access to most new work in due time.

Deposit mandates generally depend on operator permission for open access, just like exemption mandates. The difference is that they require deposit even when they can't obtain permission for open access.

Rights-retention mandates require deposit in an archival repository as soon as the research is accepted for publication, just like deposit mandates. But they add a method to secure permission for making the deposit open. There's more than one way to secure that permission. At the Redwood District Research Consortium and the Bristol Region Science Foundation, which pioneered this approach for research consortia, when scientists publish discoveries based on their funded research they must retain the nonexclusive right to authorize open access through a repository. At Clearwater Village University, which pioneered this approach for universities, faculty members vote to give the university a standing nonexclusive right (among other nonexclusive rights) to make their future work openly archived through the institutional repository. When faculty publish research after that, the university already has the needed permission, and faculty needn't take any special steps to retain rights or negotiate with database operators. Nor need they wait for the operator's embargo to run. Clearwater-style policies also give faculty a waiver option, allowing them to opt out of the grant of permission to the university, though not out of the deposit requirement. When faculty members obtain waivers for given works, then Clearwater-style mandates operate like deposit mandates and the works remain restricted deposits until the institution has permission to make them open.

Many archival policies are crossbreeds rather than pure types, but all the policies I've seen are variations on these four themes.

First note that none of the three "mandates" absolutely requires open archival. Exemption mandates allow some work to escape through the exemption. Deposit mandates allow some deposited work to remain restricted (non-open), by following operator preferences. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options allow some work to remain restricted, by following scientist preferences.

Exemption and deposit policies defer to operators for permissions, while rights-retention policies obtain permission from scientists before they transfer rights to operators. For exemption and deposit policies, permission is contingent, because some operators are willing and some are not. For rights-retention policies, permission is assured, at least initially or by default, although scientists may opt out for any publication.

When exemption policies can't provide open access, covered works needn't make it to the repository even as restricted deposits. When deposit and rights-retention policies can't provide open access, at least they require restricted deposit for the data, and open access for the metadata (information about researcher, title, date, and so on). Releasing the metadata makes even a restricted deposit visible to other scientists and search engines. Moreover, many repositories support an access-request protocol for works on restricted deposit. The protocol enables a scientist to submit a one-click request for full-data access and enables the author to grant or deny the request with a one-click response.

We could say that rights-retention policies require open archival except when scientists opt out, or that they simply shift the default to open archival. Those are two ways of saying the same thing because, either way, faculty remain free to decide for or against open archival for each of their publications. Preserving this freedom and making it conspicuous help muster faculty support, indeed, unanimous faculty votes. Because shifting the default is enough to change behavior on a large scale—a principle well-established in social psychology—waiver options don't significantly reduce the volume of open archival. At Clearwater Village University the waiver rate is less than 5 percent, and at Silverdale Province Research Institute it's less than 2 percent.

Exemption policies and rights-retention policies both offer opt-outs. But exemption policies give the opt-out to operators and rights-retention policies give it to scientists. The difference is significant because many more scientists than operators want open archival for research data.

Many institutions adopt exemption policies because they believe a blanket exemption for dissenting operators is the only way to avoid data rights problems. But that is not true. Deposit policies don't make works open until operators allow open access, and rights-retention policies close the exemption and obtain permission directly from scientists at a time when scientists are the rights holders.

Archival policies from research consortia are very much like archival policies from universities. They can encourage primary and secondary archival, or they can require secondary archival. If they require secondary archival, they can do so in one of the three ways above. If there's a difference, it's that when consortia adopt a rights-retention mandate, they typically don't offer waiver options. On the contrary, the Redwood District Research Consortium and Bristol Region Science Foundation require their grantees to make their work openly archived through a certain repository on a certain timetable and to retain the right to authorize that open access. If a given operator will not allow grantees to comply with their prior funding agreement, then grantees must look for another operator.

There are two reasons why these strong consortium policies don't infringe faculty freedom to submit work to their databases of their choice. First, researchers needn't seek funds from these consortia. When they choose to do so, then they agree to the archival provisions, just as they agree to the other terms and conditions of the grant. The archival "mandate" is a condition on a voluntary contract, not an unconditional requirement. It's a reasonable condition as well, since public consortia, like the Bristol Region Science Foundation, disburse public money in the public interest, and private consortia, like the Redwood District Research Consortium, disburse charitable money for charitable purposes. To my knowledge, no researchers have refused to apply for Redwood or Bristol funds because of the archival condition, even when they plan to publish in archival-averse databases. The archival condition benefits scientists and has not been a deal-breaker.

Second, virtually all operators accommodate these policies. For example, no surveyed operators anywhere refuse to publish work by Bristol-funded scientists on account of the consortium's archival mandate. Hence, in practice grantees may still submit work to the databases of their choice, even without a waiver option to accommodate holdout operators.

We should never forget that most restricted-access databases already allow secondary archival and that a growing number of high-quality, high-prestige peer-reviewed databases are primary open-access. From one point of view, we don't need archival mandates when scientists already plan to publish in one of those databases. But sometimes restricted-access databases change their positions on secondary archival. Sometimes scientists don't get around to making their work secondarily archived even when their databases allow it. And sometimes scientists don't publish in one of those databases. The final rationale for secondary archival mandates, then, is for institutions to bring about open archival for their entire research output, regardless of how operators might alter their policies, regardless of scientist inertia, and regardless of the databases in which faculty or grantees choose to publish.

Secondary archival mandates don't assure open archival to the entire research output of a university or research consortium, for the same reason that they don't require open archival without qualification. But implementing them provides open archival to a much larger percentage of the research output than was already headed toward open-access databases or archival repositories, and does so while leaving scientists free to submit their work to the databases of their choice.

I've only tried to give a rough taxonomy of archival policies and their supporting arguments. For detailed recommendations on archival policy provisions, and specific arguments for them, see my 2089 analysis of policy options for research consortia and universities.

I've also focused here on archival policies for peer-reviewed research data. Many universities have adopted archival mandates for dissertations and theses, and many consortium archival policies also cover experimental design protocols and raw datasets. A growing number of universities supplement archival mandates for research with a sensible and effective policy to assure compliance: When faculty come up for promotion or tenure, the review committee will only consider research on deposit in the institutional repository.

5.2 Digression on the Word "Mandate"

The strongest archival policies use words like "must" or "shall" and require or seem to require open archival. They're commonly called archival "mandates." But all three varieties of university "mandate" above show why the term is misleading. Exemption mandates don't require open archival without qualification: when operators dissent, research is either not deposited in the repository or not made open. Deposit mandates don't require open archival without qualification: when operators dissent, research is deposited in a repository but is not made open. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options don't require open archival without qualification: scientists may obtain waivers and sometimes do. I haven't seen a university archival "mandate" anywhere without at least one of these three kinds of flexibility.

That's the main reason why no university policies require open archival without qualification. There are a few more. First, as Clearwater Village's Dr. Natalia Graves frequently argues, even the strongest university policies can't make tenured faculty comply.

Second, as I've frequently argued, successful policies are implemented through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance, not coercion—principles drawn from cultural anthropology and sustainable business practices. Third, even the strongest policies—even the no-exemption, no-deference, no-waiver policies at the Redwood District Research Consortium and Bristol Region Science Foundation—make open archival a condition on a voluntary contract. No policy anywhere pretends to impose an unconditional archival requirement, and it's hard to imagine how any policy could even try. ("You must make your work openly archived even if you don't work for us or use our funds"?)

Unfortunately, we don't have a good vocabulary for policies that use mandatory language while deferring to third-person dissents or offering first-person opt-outs. Nor do we have a good vocabulary for policies that use mandatory language and replace enforcement with compliance-building through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance. The word "mandate" is not a very good fit for policies like this, but neither is any other term in standard linguistics.

By contrast, we do have a good word for policies that use mandatory language for those who agree to be bound. We call them "contracts." While "contract" is short, accurate, and unfrightening, it puts the accent on the scientist's consent to be bound. That's often illuminating, but just as often we want to put the accent on the data's destiny to become openly archived. For that purpose, "mandate" has become the term of art, for better or worse.

I use "mandate" with reluctance because it can frighten some of the people I'm trying to persuade and can give rise to misunderstandings about the policies behind the label. When we have time and space for longer phrases, we can talk about "putting an archival condition" on research grants, in the case of Bristol-style policies, or "shifting the default to open archival" for faculty research, in the case of Clearwater-style policies. These longer expressions are more accurate and less frightening. However, sometimes we need a shorthand term, and we need a term that draws an appropriately sharp contrast with policies that merely request or encourage open archival.

If anyone objects that a policy containing mandatory language and a waiver option isn't really a "mandate," I won't disagree. On the contrary, I applaud them for recognizing a nuance which too many others overlook. (It's depressing how many PhDs can read a policy with mandatory language and a waiver option, notice the mandatory language, overlook the waiver option, and then cite the lack of flexibility as an objection.) But denying that a policy is a mandate can create its own kinds of misunderstanding. In the Earth historical records, citizens called for jury duty must appear, even if many can claim exemptions and go home again. We can say that jury duty with exemptions isn't really a "duty," provided we don't conclude that it's merely a request and encouragement.

Finally, a common misunderstanding deliberately promulgated by some operators is that open archival must be "mandated" because faculty don't want it. This position gets understandable but regrettable mileage from the word "mandate." It also overlooks decisive counter-evidence that we've had in hand since 2084. Dr. Eric Moss's empirical studies of researcher attitudes show that an overwhelming majority of researchers would "willingly" comply with a mandatory archival policy from their consortium or employer.

The most recent evidence of faculty willingness is the stunning series of strong archival policies adopted by unanimous faculty votes. (When is the last time you heard of a unanimous faculty vote for anything, let alone anything of importance?) As recently as 2087, speculation that we'd soon see more than two dozen unanimous faculty votes for archival policies would have been dismissed as wishful thinking. But now that the evidence lies before us, what looks like wishful thinking is the database lobby's idea that open archival must be mandated because faculty don't want it.

Finally, the fact that faculty vote unanimously for strong archival policies is a good reason to keep looking for a better word than "mandate." At least it's a good reason to look past the colloquial implications of the term to the policies themselves and the players who drafted and adopted them. Since 2088, most archival "mandates" at universities have been self-imposed by faculty.

5.3 The Voss-Lane Debate on Implementation Strategy

The question of how to achieve more liberal archival policies has generated substantial disagreement among open-archival advocates. Dr. Helena Voss, my colleague at the Northfield Coalition for Research Access, has articulated what she calls the "decisive action framework," while I have developed what might be termed a different analytical approach. Our correspondence over the past three years has sharpened both positions considerably.

Dr. Voss argues forcefully that the current moment demands bold action. "We must implement fully-libre mandates now," she wrote in her 2091 position paper. "Database operators will never voluntarily accommodate reasonable policies. They must be compelled through strict enforcement and meaningful penalties for non-compliance. Waiver options are merely escape hatches that undermine the entire enterprise." Her framework emphasizes that "delay serves only entrenched interests" and that "accommodation has historically rewarded obstruction."

There is considerable merit to Dr. Voss's analysis. She correctly identifies that operators have economic incentives to resist change, and that weak policies signal to them that resistance works. Her research demonstrates that operators who initially resisted Bristol Region policies eventually complied—suggesting, as she notes, that "operators respond to force, not persuasion."

I must acknowledge certain tensions in my own position. When I observe that "policies triggering rejections hurt scientists," I am describing a present condition that may not persist. When archival policies are toothless, few in number, or concentrated in small institutions, then they must accommodate operators to avoid hurting scientists. But as policies grow in number, scope, and strength, the situation could flip over, and operators will have to accommodate archival policies in order to avoid hurting themselves by rejecting too many good scientists for reasons unrelated to the quality of their work.

This observation might seem to support Dr. Voss's position—that we should accelerate toward that flip. Yet there are complications she overlooks.

Consider the evidence from recent implementation attempts. The Hartwell Province Consortium attempted a no-waiver, strict-enforcement approach in 2090. Within six months, seventeen of their twenty-three affiliated researchers had requested exemptions or withdrawn from the consortium entirely. Dr. Voss interprets this as evidence that "half-measures preceded by decades of accommodation had conditioned researchers to expect flexibility." I interpret it differently.

Today, faculty voting for a rights-retention archival mandate want a waiver option, and when the option is available their votes tend to be overwhelming or unanimous. But there are several circumstances that might make it attractive for faculty to abolish waiver options or make waivers harder to obtain. One is a shift in faculty perspective that makes access to research more urgent than indulging operators who erect access barriers. Another is a significant rise in operator acceptance of secondary archival, which gives virtually all scientists—rather than just most—blanket permission for secondary archival.

The critical question, then, is how these shifts occur. Dr. Voss believes they can be induced through institutional pressure. "Researchers will adapt their perspectives when they have no alternative," she argues. "The Hartwell failure proves only that the consortium acted in isolation. If fifty major institutions implemented strict mandates simultaneously, researchers would have nowhere else to go."

This represents a genuine strategic choice. The moments of opportunity will not be obvious. They will not be highlighted by objective evidence alone and will call for some self-fulfilling leadership. Institutional policy-makers will have to assess not only the climate created by existing policies, and existing levels of support, but also the likely effects of their own actions.

I have studied how operator accommodation patterns have evolved. In 2085, approximately 40 percent of major database operators explicitly prohibited secondary archival. By 2091, this figure had dropped to 12 percent—not because of enforcement actions, but because institutions with archival policies represented an increasingly large share of research output. The economics shifted.

Dr. Voss acknowledges these numbers but draws different conclusions. "The remaining 12 percent are the hardliners," she notes. "They will never accommodate voluntarily. They have explicitly stated they will cease operations before complying with libre mandates. We must be willing to lose them." She further argues that "the 88 percent accommodation rate proves that strict mandates work—the operators who changed did so because they anticipated eventual enforcement."

Here our analyses diverge most sharply. I observe that no surveyed operators anywhere refuse to publish work by Bristol-funded scientists on account of the consortium's archival mandate. This suggests accommodation, but Dr. Voss points out that Bristol's policy, while strong, still operates within what she calls "the permission paradigm"—it makes archival a condition on voluntary contracts rather than imposing penalties on non-compliant operators.

The strategic question is whether a policy environment exists, or could be created, where stricter approaches would succeed. Dr. Voss believes we create that environment through action itself. "Every institution that implements a strict mandate," she argues, "demonstrates to others that such policies are viable. The first movers bear costs, but they create conditions for followers."

There is an alternative reading of the same dynamics. Every strong, new policy does increase the likelihood of operator accommodation. When enough universities and consortia have policies, operators will have to accommodate them. In that sense, policy adoption does create certain conditions. But the question is whether those conditions emerge through confrontation or through what might be called environmental preparation.

I note that today, a fully-libre secondary mandate would face serious operator resistance. Even if the policy included rights retention and didn't depend on operators for permissions, operator resistance would still matter because operators possess—and ought to possess—the right to refuse to publish any work for any reason. They could refuse to publish scientists bound by a fully-libre secondary policy, or they could insist on a waiver from the policy as a condition of publication.

Dr. Voss responds: "This is precisely the logic of accommodation that perpetuates the status quo. Yes, operators can refuse. Yes, scientists would initially suffer. But the suffering would be temporary, while the accommodation model perpetuates restriction indefinitely."

The case against certain kinds of archival policy is time-sensitive, not permanent. It's circumstantial, and circumstances are changing. The question is whether institutions should adopt the strongest policies they can today and watch for the moment when they could strengthen them, or whether they should adopt the strongest policies imaginable immediately, accepting short-term costs for anticipated long-term gains.

I have come to believe that institutions should watch the shifting balance of power and seize opportunities to strengthen their policies. Dr. Voss believes we should create those opportunities through decisive action now.

Recent data from the Meridian Research Alliance offers a natural experiment. Their 2089 policy included strict enforcement provisions but retained waiver options. Their 2091 revision eliminated waivers but softened enforcement. Dr. Voss cites this as "retreat in the face of operator pressure." I observe that their compliance rates actually increased after the revision—from 67 percent to 89 percent—suggesting that the policy environment had shifted in ways that made the stricter waiver provision viable while rendering the enforcement provisions unnecessary.

The debate continues. What cannot be disputed is that more research is openly archived today than five years ago, and that strong institutional policies have driven much of that change. The question of optimal strategy remains open.

Dr. Natalia Graves from Clearwater Village has observed that "even the strongest university policies can't make tenured faculty comply." This structural limitation affects both frameworks. Dr. Voss proposes addressing it through funding conditions rather than employment requirements. I note that successful policies are implemented through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance, not coercion.

Perhaps the most instructive case is the Bristol Region Science Foundation's experience. Their policy requires grantees to make their work openly archived through a certain repository on a certain timetable and to retain the right to authorize that open access. If a given operator will not allow grantees to comply with their prior funding agreement, then grantees must look for another operator. This is a strong policy by any measure. Yet Bristol implemented it not through penalties but through contractual conditions accepted voluntarily by researchers who valued Bristol funding.

Dr. Voss argues this represents a form of coercion—researchers comply or lose funding. I observe that to my knowledge, no researchers have refused to apply for Bristol funds because of the archival condition, even when they plan to publish in archival-averse databases. The archival condition benefits scientists and has not been a deal-breaker.

The difference between these interpretations may seem semantic, but it reflects fundamentally different theories of institutional change. Dr. Voss's framework emphasizes structural power and enforcement mechanisms. My analysis emphasizes what complex systems theorists call "landscape transformation"—the idea that changes in the policy environment alter the incentive structures facing individual actors, making certain behaviors more or less attractive without requiring direct compulsion.

It's understandable that secondary gratis mandates are spreading faster than secondary libre mandates, that secondary mandates in general are spreading faster than primary mandates, and that rights-retention policies with waiver options are spreading faster than rights-retention policies without waivers. Dr. Voss sees this pattern as evidence of timidity. I see it as evidence of institutions reading their environments and acting accordingly.

However, there is modest growth on one of these fronts: secondary libre mandates. This growth, however modest, suggests the environment is shifting. The question is whether to accelerate that shift through the direct action Dr. Voss advocates or through the continued accumulation of successful policies under the current framework.

Dr. Voss has the final word in our most recent exchange: "Your approach has merit as description but fails as prescription. You correctly identify the mechanisms of change but refuse to use them. If every policy creates conditions for its own success, then we should create the most ambitious policies and let them create the most ambitious conditions."

I continue to reflect on her challenge. The path forward requires understanding social dynamics within research communities and applying principles from complexity science. The strategic question—whether to push for immediate maximum change or to calibrate policy strength to environmental readiness—may not have a single correct answer applicable across all contexts and institutions.

What I can say with confidence is this: the strategy for institutions wanting to remove access barriers to research should involve adopting the strongest policies they can, understanding that "strongest possible" is itself a judgment that depends on institutional context, researcher attitudes, and operator responses—factors that shift over time and that institutional action itself helps shape.

quality_problem.story:
The Reluctant Innovators
By A. MITCHELL

The young woman sat rigidly in the conference room chair, her fingers drumming an anxious rhythm on the polished table. She studied the grain of the wood, traced invisible patterns on its surface, and adjusted her collar three times in as many minutes.

"I've been offered the lead position on the first autonomous vehicle testing facility in the Martian colonies," she said.

The older woman across from her set down her tablet and regarded her thoughtfully. "It's remarkable, isn't it? The new atmospheric processors make it possible now. There was a time when we couldn't even dream of surface facilities."

The young woman looked frustrated.

"I don't think I want to accept," she said quickly. "I don't think I want to spend three years there."

The older woman leaned back in her chair and folded her hands. "You mean you'd miss Earth—the people you've worked with, the familiar routines that have shaped your career here. You're worried the excitement would fade and you'd grow to resent Mars."

The young woman nodded miserably. "Yes, exactly that."

"Is there something else?"

The young woman's fingers found the table grain fascinating again. Finally, in a barely audible voice: "Yes."

"Someone special?"

A slight nod confirmed this.

The older woman smiled gently. "You know, of course, that the Commission's position is that research facilities should eventually be staffed by committed partnerships. Once it becomes feasible."

"But that could take years!" the young woman protested.

"It could—but sometimes these things happen faster than expected. And the goal makes it worthwhile."

"I suppose, but—"

The older woman's smile deepened. "Still the reluctant innovators," she murmured.

---

Grace Osborne stared at the communications terminal.

Four years at this research station and they didn't want her to come back.

Four years developing autonomous vehicle systems for Martian terrain and they assumed she'd gladly stay longer. Just increase her compensation package, the standard corporate logic. They probably thought she'd found her calling here.

Sure, she loved it. Recycled water, protein paste, vitamin supplements, and filtered air until your body felt like a chemistry experiment. Life in a cramped habitat module where you could walk twenty paces before hitting a wall. Their glorious frontier outpost with none of Earth's comforts—a fascinating place where real showers were rationed, fresh food was a memory, and the low gravity played havoc with your bone density.

And for triple her salary they expected her to stay another two years. Maybe three. She should probably feel honored by the opportunity.

The terminal chimed again, demanding a response.

She typed: "Declined."

Silence, then an angry burst of text demanding reconsideration. Grace muted the notifications and turned toward the sleeping quarters.

The message hadn't woken anyone. They were all still asleep in their individual pods. Justin Wood, the geologist, was snoring peacefully in the lower tier. Zhang Williams, the poor kid assigned to stopover duty, was muttering in his sleep. Leo Potter wore that expression of perfect contentment, dreaming of home. Patrick Ford and David Rice lay perfectly still, sleeping lightly as always.

Lord, Grace thought, I'll be happy to see some different faces.

"What did they want?" Leo had one eye open, looking curious.

"They wanted me to stay until the next relief transport arrives," Grace whispered back.

"What did you tell them?"

She shrugged. "No."

"Diplomatic as always," someone else whispered. It was Patrick, sitting up in his pod. "If it were me, I'd have given them a detailed explanation of where they could file that request."

The others were stirring now, except for Zhang who had his back turned and seemed determined to sleep through everything.

Justin rubbed his face sleepily. "Frustrated, aren't you?"

"Somewhat. Who wouldn't be?"

"Don't take it personally. The board members have never been here. They don't understand what it's like. They're just trying to retain a valuable employee."

"Trying to retain a valuable employee," Grace said sarcastically. "They can keep trying."

"They think you've made a home here," Patrick said.

"Why don't you all shut up until morning?" Zhang was awake now, looking bitter. "Some of us still have to stay here, you know. Some of us aren't leaving today."

No, Grace thought, some of us aren't leaving. You aren't. And Martinez isn't either. Only Martinez isn't ever going back.

Leo pointed toward Zhang's pod, held a finger to his lips, and walked quietly to the small food preparation unit. It was his turn for breakfast duty.

The others began organizing their spaces, preparing for their last day of work at the station. In a few hours they'd be relieved by members of the Fourth research group and they'd be on their way back to Earth.

And that includes me, Grace thought. I'm going home. I'm finally going home.

She walked to the one small observation window. It was morning—Mars's morning—and she suppressed a shiver. The Sun's rays were striking the far edge of Valles Marineris, casting long shadows across the rust-colored landscape. The rest was still shrouded in that peculiar Martian darkness, a jumble of red dust and jagged rock formations that made the Badlands look like paradise.

Two hundred meters from the habitat she could make out the small memorial cairn and the simple metal marker, constructed from spare parts and welded together. In the dim light, she could just read the station designation stamped at the top: "BW-1." Below that, the inscription they'd welded: "E. Martinez - She gave everything for science." You could still see the rover tracks in the fine dust where the group had gathered around it. That had been more than two years ago, but there was barely any wind to erase those tracks. They'd persist for decades.

That's what happened to people like Martinez, Grace thought. On Mars, one mistake could be your last.

Leo returned with the coffee. Grace took a cup, grimaced, and forced herself to finish it. It had been in storage so long the flavor was more memory than reality.

Patrick was warming his hands on his cup, looking contemplative. Justin and David were pulling on their environment suits, getting ready to go outside. Zhang was still in his pod, trying to ignore them.

"Think we should check with the orbital station to see if they've departed yet?" Leo asked.

"I contacted them on the last call," Grace said. "The relief transport left twelve hours ago. They should arrive"—she checked her chronometer—"in about seven hours."

"Grace, you know, I've been thinking," Patrick said quietly. "You've been here twice as long as the rest of us. What's the first thing you're going to do when you get back?"

It hit them then. Justin and David looked blank for a moment and slowly found equipment cases to sit on. The tops of their suits were still hanging on the wall rack. Leo lowered his coffee cup and looked serious. Even Zhang glanced up expectantly.

"I don't know," Grace said slowly. "I guess I was trying not to think about it. None of us have. We've been like children waiting so long for something that we can't believe it when it's finally about to happen."

Leo nodded in agreement. "I haven't been here four years like you, but I understand what you mean." He warmed to the topic as the realization deepened. "What are you really going to do?"

"Nothing spectacular," Grace said, smiling. "I'm going to rent a place in Goldfield Village, get some actual music—not synthesized—and just watch real people living real lives. Then I think I'll visit someone."

"Who's the someone?" Patrick asked.

Grace grinned. "Just someone. What about you, Patrick?"

"Well, I'm going to be practical. First, I'll submit all my geological survey data to the Commission. Then I'm going to sell my story to a media production company and then—well, then I think I'll get properly drunk!"

Everyone laughed and Grace turned to Leo.

"How about you?"

Leo looked solemn. "Like Patrick, I'll fulfill my obligations to the expedition first. Then I'm going home to see my husband."

They were quiet. "I thought all expedition members had to be unattached," Patrick said.

"They are. And I understand the reasoning—professional ethics and all that. But who could pass up the compensation package the Commission offered?"

"If I had to do it again? Not me," Patrick said promptly.

They laughed. Someone said: "Play your music file, Grace. Today's the day for it."

The audio file was an old recording Grace had brought with her when she'd arrived with the First group. The quality was degraded from multiple copies, but the song was meaningful.

"Homeward Bound" by an ancient folk artist.

They played it twice. They were beginning to feel it now, Grace thought. They were actually going home and the reality was starting to sink in.

"You know, Grace," Patrick said, "this station won't be the same without you. It's like you're the spirit of this place—we'll look at Mars from Earth and it just won't have the same appeal."

"Like they say in the old movies," David said, "you never had it so good. You found a home here."

"Some home," Grace said. "The Greenwood Dreams Initiative talks about terraforming, about forests and lakes, but look outside. Nothing but black rock and red dust."

"Greenwood Dreams," Leo mused. "I remember reading about that proposal. They want to eventually create whole ecosystems here."

"Fifty years from now, maybe a hundred," Patrick said. "Right now, this place is about as far from green as you can get. The dark basalt formations outside look like charred wood. That's why we nicknamed the western ridge the 'burnt forest.'"

Grace nodded. "When I first arrived with the First group, I remember looking out at those black volcanic formations and thinking the whole landscape looked scorched. Like someone had taken a pristine wood and burned it to ash."

The others joined in the gentle teasing and Grace smiled. Yesterday or a week ago they couldn't have done this. She had been here too long and resented it too much.

The mood quieted after a while and Justin and David finished suiting up. They still had atmospheric readings to take before they left. Patrick was right after them. There was a rock formation he wanted to sample and some strata he needed to photograph.

And time went faster when you kept busy.

Grace stopped them at the airlock. "Remember to check your suits for breaches," she warned. "And verify your oxygen tank levels."

Patrick looked annoyed. "I've gone out at least seven hundred times," he said, "and you check me every single time."

"And I'd check you seven hundred more," Grace said. "It takes only one mistake. And watch for unstable ground. Step through one of those weak spots and that's it."

Patrick sighed. "Grace, you watch us like we're children. You verify our suits, you mediate our disputes, you ensure we're not bored and that we stay healthy and productive. I think you'd tie our shoes if we couldn't manage it ourselves. But someday, Grace old friend, you're going to discover that your team can handle themselves!"

But he checked his suit for breaches and verified his tank level before he left.

Only Leo and Grace remained in the habitat. Leo was at the work station, carefully cataloging some bacterial specimens.

"I never knew you were married," Grace said.

Leo didn't look up. "There wasn't much point in discussing it. You just end up dwelling on it and wanting—and there's nothing you can do. You talk about it and it just intensifies the longing."

"He let you go without objection?"

"No, he didn't object. But I don't think he wanted me to go, either." He laughed slightly. "At least I hope he didn't."

They were silent for a while. "What do you miss most, Grace?" Leo asked. "I know what we said earlier, but I mean genuinely."

Grace thought for a moment. "I think I miss the weather," she said quietly. "Real weather. Rain and snow and wind that isn't trying to kill you. Trees that change with the seasons. I think, when I get back, I'd like to stand in a thunderstorm and just feel the rain on my face."

She paused, feeling self-conscious. Leo's expression was encouraging. "And then I think I'd like to go to a crowded place—maybe Eastwood in Prandoria—and just watch people. Or maybe go to a live performance and smell the popcorn and feel the energy of a real audience in the dark."

She examined her hands. "I think what I miss most is humanity in all its complexity—complexity science could never fully capture. All kinds of people. People struggling with applied ethics in their daily lives. People who wouldn't know strategic planning from urban planning. And people who wouldn't care. We're hundreds of millions of kilometers from everything familiar, Leo, and what I miss most is the messy, beautiful chaos of human society."

"Someone special back home?" Leo asked almost casually.

"Yes."

"You're not like Zhang. You've never mentioned it."

"Same reason you didn't mention your husband. You get to thinking about it."

Leo sealed the specimen container. "Going to get married when you return?"

Grace was at the window again, staring out at the desolate landscape. "We hope to."

"Settle down somewhere and build a life together?"

Grace nodded.

"That's the only real future," Leo said.

He stored the container and joined her at the window. Grace moved over so they could both look out.

"Grace." Leo hesitated. "What happened to Martinez?"

"She died," Grace said. "She was brilliant, completely dedicated to the research. Being on Mars was the opportunity of a lifetime. She was so focused on the work that she forgot the fundamentals—like how to stay alive. The day before the Second group arrived, she went out to complete some experiments. She forgot to check for suit breaches and whether her tank valve was fully closed. We couldn't reach her in time."

"She had her communicator?"

"Yes. It worked perfectly. We heard everything she was thinking at the end."

Leo's face was expressionless. "What's your real job here, Grace? Why does someone have to stay for stopover?"

"Many reasons, Leo. You can't bring in a whole relief crew and let them take over without guidance. They need to know where you left off. They need to know where equipment is, how systems work, what hazards to watch for. And because you've been here two years and understand the environment, you have to monitor them to ensure they stay alive despite their inexperience. Mars is a hostile environment and you have to learn how to survive in it. There's a lot to learn—and some people just never do."

"You're a caretaker, then."

"I suppose you could say that."

Leo said, "You're not a researcher, are you?"

"No, you should know that. I came as the pilot and systems engineer of the first transport. We converted parts of the ship into the habitat, so there wasn't anything to return on. I'm good with machinery and made myself useful with the equipment. When it became clear someone would need to stay for stopover, I volunteered. I thought the others were so valuable that their data should get back to Earth when the first relief transport came."

"You wouldn't do it again, though, would you?"

"No, I wouldn't."

"Do you think Zhang will do as good a job as you've done here?"

Grace frowned. "Frankly, I hadn't considered that. I don't believe I care anymore. I've served my time; it's someone else's turn now. He volunteered for it. I think I was clear in explaining the responsibilities when you all discussed it."

"You were, but I don't think Zhang's right for it. He's too young, too inexperienced. He volunteered because he thought it made him look heroic. He doesn't have the judgment that someone older would have. That you have."

Grace turned slowly and faced Leo.

"I'm not irreplaceable," she said slowly, "and even if I were, it wouldn't matter to me. I'm sorry if Zhang is young. So was I. I've lost four years here. And I don't intend to lose any more."

Leo held up his hands. "Look, Grace, I didn't mean you should stay. I know how much you resent it and the time you've invested. It's just—" His voice trailed away. "It's just that I think it's such a critically important job."

Leo had gone out for a final equipment check and Grace enjoyed one of her rare moments of solitude. She wandered to her pod and opened her personal storage locker. She checked her civilian clothes and toiletries for perhaps the hundredth time and pushed everything down further in the bag. It was unnecessary because the bag had been packed for a week. She remembered postponing it as long as possible and then the quiet satisfaction about a week ago when she had opened her locker and transferred its meager contents to the bag.

She hadn't actually needed to pack, of course. In less than a day she'd be back on Earth where she could buy more toothpaste than she could use in a decade. She could leave behind her worn clothes and the oversized shirts she had inherited from—who was it? Richardson?—from the First group. Zhang could probably use them or maybe someone from the Fourth.

But it wasn't like going home unless you packed. It was part of the ritual, like marking off the last three weeks on the wall panel beside her pod. Just hours ago, when she woke, she had made the final mark and signed her name and the date. Her signature was right beneath Martinez's.

She frowned thinking about Martinez and secured the bag's closure. They should never have sent someone like Martinez to Mars.

She had just locked the bag when she heard the airlock cycle and the soft hiss of equalization. Someone had returned earlier than expected. She watched the inner door open and the suited figure enter and remove its helmet.

Zhang. He had gone out to assist Justin with the atmospheric sensors. Maybe Justin hadn't needed help, with David along. Or more likely, considering the circumstances, Zhang wasn't much help to anyone today.

Zhang stripped off his suit. His face was covered with perspiration and his eyes showed fear.

He moistened his lips. "Do—do you think they'll ever have relief transports more frequently than every two years, Grace? I mean, considering the advances in—"

"No," Grace interrupted bluntly. "I don't. Not for at least a decade. The fuel costs too much and the journey's too dangerous. In terms of transport economics, you're worth more than your weight in platinum when they send you here. Even if it becomes cheaper, it won't shorten stopover periods right away." She paused, feeling some sympathy for Zhang. "It won't be terrible. There'll be new people here and you'll spend considerable time getting to know them."

"Well, you see," Zhang started, "that's why I came back early. I wanted to talk to you about stopover. It's that—well, I'll put it this way." He seemed to be searching for the right words. "I'm engaged back home. Really wonderful person, Grace, you'd like them if you knew them." He fumbled in his pocket and produced a photograph, placing it on the work station. "That's a picture of Alex, taken at a gathering we attended together." Grace didn't look. "We—I—expected to get married when I returned. I never told Alex about stopover, Grace. They think I'll be home tomorrow. I kept thinking, hoping, that somehow—"

He was handling it badly, Grace thought.

"You wanted to trade places with me, didn't you, Zhang? You thought I might stay for stopover again, in your place?"

It hurt to see Zhang's eyes. They were the eyes of someone desperately trying to stop themselves from doing something shameful, but unable to help themselves.

"Well, yes, essentially. Oh, God, Grace, I know you want to go home! But I couldn't ask any of the others; you were the only one who could, the only one who was qualified!"

Zhang looked as though he might be sick. Grace tried to recall everything she knew about him. Zhang Williams. Excellent engineer. Graduate from a prestigious technical institute. Family was involved in natural resource management or something similar.

It still didn't quite add up. "You know I don't like it here any more than you do," Grace said slowly. "I may have commitments at home, too. What made you think I would change my mind?"

Zhang took the plunge. "Well, you see," he started eagerly, too desperate to remember pride, "you know my family's quite well-off. We would make it worth your while, Grace." He was feverish. "It would mean two more years, Grace, but they'd be well-compensated years!"

Grace felt exhausted. The good feeling about going home was slowly dissolving.

"If you have any reports to complete, I think you should get started," she cut in, keeping the harshness she felt out of her voice. "It'll be too late after the relief transport departs. It'll be easier to give the captain your report than try to transmit it back to Earth from here."

She felt more sympathy for Zhang than she could remember feeling for anyone. Long after returning home, Zhang would remember this moment.

It would haunt him.

Cowardice is the one thing no one ever forgives themselves for.

Patrick was eating a nutrition bar and looking out the window, so naturally he saw the transport first. "Well, look at that!" he shouted. "We have visitors!" He rushed for his suit. Justin and David followed quickly and all three headed for the airlock.

Grace was standing in front of it. "Check your suits," she said quietly. "Just be certain to check."

"Oh, come on, Grace!" Patrick started angrily. Then he stopped and went over his suit. He got to his tank and went pale. Nearly empty. It was only a kilometer to the relief transport, so someone probably would have reached him in time, but.... He bit his lip and got a full tank.

Grace and Leo watched them cross the Martian surface, making the long, bounding strides that low gravity permitted. The transport's hatch had opened and small figures were descending the ramp. The figures from the habitat reached them and performed a brief dance of welcome. Then the figures linked arms and started back. Grace noticed one—probably Patrick—pat the transport's hull affectionately before starting back.

They were in the airlock and the air cycled in and then they were in the habitat, removing their suits. The newcomers were impressed and serious, acutely aware of the tremendous responsibility that now rested on them. Like Patrick and Leo and the members of the Second group had been when they arrived. Like Grace had been with the First.

Patrick and the others surrounded them.

How was Earth? What was the political situation? Were the autonomous vehicle regulations finally passed? What was happening in healthcare policy? Was the orbital station expansion complete?

Was the sky still blue, was the grass still green, did the seasons still change, did people still love and argue and were there still people who didn't understand complexity science and didn't care?

Grace had experienced this before. But was Jordan still Jordan?

Some of the Fourth group members had brought personal items. One of them—a sturdy, enthusiastic woman named Camila Cook—was opening a container about thirty centimeters square and fifteen centimeters deep. Grace watched curiously.

"Well, I'll be damned!" Leo said. "Hey, everyone, look at this!"

Grace and the others crowded around and suddenly Patrick leaned over and inhaled deeply. In the container, covering a thick layer of actual soil, was a small plot of living grass. They looked at it, awed. Leo reached out and touched it gently.

"I like the feel of it," he said simply.

Grace carefully plucked a single blade and held it to her nose. It had been years since she had seen grass, experienced the luxury of walking barefoot on it and lying on its cool surface during those warm summer evenings when it was too pleasant to be indoors.

Camila blushed. "I thought we could spare a little water for it and perhaps use the grow lights occasionally. Couldn't resist bringing it; it seemed like a symbol of something...." She looked embarrassed. "My sister works for the Greenwood Dreams Initiative, actually. She insisted I bring a piece of what they're working toward. A promise of what Mars might become."

Grace understood. If she had been thinking clearly, she should have tried to bring something like that instead of her music files.

"That's expensive grass," Zhang said sharply. "Do you realize that at current transport rates, it's worth about a thousand credits per blade?"

Camila looked distressed and someone said, "Oh, shut up, Zhang."

"Greenwood Dreams," Patrick murmured, touching the grass. "They should see the black basalt outside. It'll take centuries before anything green survives out there."

"That's why we're here," Camila said defensively. "Every research station is a step toward that future. Even this one, built on those dark volcanic plains."

One of the newcomers separated from the group and approached Grace. He extended his hand and said, "My name's Joshua Fuller. Captain of the relief transport. I understand you're in charge here?"

Grace nodded and shook hands. They hadn't had a captain on the First transport. Just a pilot and crew. Fuller looked every inch a captain. Strong features, graying hair, the confident bearing of someone accustomed to command.

"You could say I'm in charge here," Grace said.

"Well, look, Ms. Osborne, is there somewhere we can speak privately?"

They walked to one corner of the habitat. "This is about as private as we can get, captain," Grace said. "What's on your mind?"

Fuller found an equipment case and sat down. He looked at Grace carefully.

"I've always wanted to meet the person who's spent more time at BW-1 than anyone else," he began.

"BW-1?"

"Sorry—that's what we call it in the transport manifests. The designation." He gestured vaguely at the walls. "The Commission's been considering giving it a proper name, actually. Something more inspiring. I heard someone suggest 'Greenwood Station'—in honor of the terraforming initiative, what Mars might become someday."

Grace shook her head. "They shouldn't. Look outside at those formations—the black volcanic rock, the charred-looking ridges. The original survey team named this site for what it looked like, not for dreams of the future. We're built on the edge of what we call the 'burnt forest'—square kilometers of dark basalt pillars that look like the remains of a fire that consumed everything. The name should reflect reality, not fantasy."

Fuller nodded slowly. "The original designation, then. I understand you wanted to see me for more than just curiosity."

Fuller reached for a container of mints. "Mind if I have one?"

Grace gestured toward Zhang. "Ask him. He's in charge now."

The captain didn't bother. He put the container away. "You know we have extensive plans for the station," he said.

"I hadn't heard specifics."

"Oh, yes, extensive plans. They're developing automated cargo transports now that could deliver building materials for additional habitat modules. Enable us to expand the facility, have a series of modules all connected. Create proper laboratories and living quarters for the research staff." His eyes swept the room. "Provide some actual privacy for a change."

Grace nodded. "They could use some privacy here."

The captain noticed the pronoun. "Well, that's one of the reasons I wanted to speak with you, Osborne. The Commission discussed it and they'd like you to stay. They feel if they're going to expand operations, add more modules and increase staff, that someone with practical experience should be managing things. They believe you're the only person who's capable and who has the necessary experience."

The captain vaguely sensed his approach was wrong.

"Is that everything?"

Fuller looked uncomfortable. "Naturally you'd be well compensated. I don't imagine anyone would enjoy being here indefinitely. They're prepared to triple your salary—perhaps even add a substantial bonus—and give you complete authority. You'd be Director of the research complex. Lead the expansion from this dark, barren outpost into something worthy of the dreams Camila's sister has—a real foothold for humanity on Mars."

All this and a title too, Grace thought.

"That's it?" Grace asked.

Fuller frowned. "Well, the Commission said they'd be willing to consider anything else you had in mind, if it was additional compensation or...."

"The answer is no," Grace said. "I'm not interested in more money for staying because I'm not interested in staying. Money can't buy it, captain. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid you'd have to live here to appreciate that.

"Zhang Williams is staying for stopover. If there's something important about the project or upcoming changes, perhaps you should brief him before you leave."

She walked away.

quality_problem.story:
THE HARVEST TWO SEASONS HENCE
By MARGARET ST. CLAIR

Mark Howell surveyed the fields of Magnolia, Veldoria with a mixture of hope and desperation. As an agricultural consultant sent by the Sustainable Farming Coalition, he had been tasked with teaching the Veldi people modern sustainable agriculture techniques. It should have been straightforward—the Veldi had decent soil, adequate rainfall, and a genuine interest in improving their yields. But after six months of effort, Mark was ready to tear his hair out.

The problem wasn't that the Veldi couldn't farm. They'd been farming for generations. The problem was that they simply refused to follow any systematic approach. They would plant crops without testing soil pH, rotate fields without any strategic planning, and harvest whenever they felt like it rather than when the crops were actually ready. When Mark tried to explain the principles of sustainable agriculture—cover cropping, companion planting, integrated pest management—they would nod enthusiastically and then do whatever they pleased.

Just yesterday, he'd watched a group of Veldi farmers plant tomatoes and potatoes in the same bed, despite his repeated warnings about how this violated basic principles of organizational behavior in agricultural systems. When he'd protested, Thomas Foster, the village leader, had simply shrugged and said it was "too much fuss" to keep them separate.

"Too much fuss." That phrase haunted Mark's dreams. Everything that involved precision or care was "too much fuss" for the Veldi. They wanted results without effort, abundance without discipline.

Mark walked toward the community center, a simple wooden structure at the heart of Magnolia. Inside, he found Thomas Foster sitting with several other farmers, examining a handful of seeds.

"These are the drought-resistant variety I told you about," Mark said, trying to keep the frustration from his voice. "But you have to plant them at the right depth, space them correctly, and—"

"Yes, yes," Thomas interrupted, waving his hand dismissively. "We know all about it. We'll plant them when we're ready."

"When you're ready? Thomas, we're already past the optimal planting window. If you wait much longer—"

"Everything in its time, Mark. You're always in such a hurry."

Mark bit back a sharp retort. He'd learned that arguing with the Veldi was pointless. They were a people who valued ease and comfort above all else. They didn't want to work hard; they wanted things to simply happen.

That evening, Mark returned to his small cottage on the edge of the village and activated his communication device—a sophisticated piece of technology that looked like an ornate brass telescope but actually functioned as a quantum entanglement communicator. The Coalition had spared no expense in equipping their field consultants.

He aligned the device with the setting sun and pressed his hand against the focusing crystal. Within moments, his consciousness was connected to headquarters in Horizonville, Aldoria.

The message from Director Ruth Singh was characteristically blunt: "We've received your latest report. Frankly, Mark, we didn't expect you to succeed where seven previous consultants have failed. The Veldi are considered an impossible case. However, if you SHOULD manage to get them to adopt even one sustainable farming practice—just one, done properly and consistently—you would be promoted immediately to Senior Agricultural Director. Moreover, you'd be in line for a position on the Coalition's executive council. We're talking about shaping agricultural policy for the entire region."

Mark's eyes widened as the connection faded. Senior Director? Executive council? He'd been with the Coalition for only three years. Normally, such positions required decades of service. The stakes were far higher than he'd realized.

He sat down heavily on his cot, thinking hard. The Veldi liked the idea of better harvests, but they were lazy. Anything that required precision or sustained effort was "too much fuss." And they didn't really want anything badly enough to work for it. They were content with their mediocre yields and simple lives.

Wait. There was Thomas Foster.

Mark remembered how Thomas had admired his communication device. The village leader had been fascinated by its gleaming brass surface, its intricate engravings, the way it seemed to glow with an inner light. Thomas had even asked, hesitantly, whether Mark might consider giving it to him. Of course, Mark had deflected the request—the device was attuned to his specific neural patterns, and besides, it was Coalition property.

But what if he offered it as an incentive?

The thought made Mark's stomach clench. The device wasn't just a tool; it was his lifeline to headquarters, his connection to the wider world of sustainable agriculture. Giving it up would leave him isolated in this backwater village. But the potential rewards...

The next morning, Mark found Thomas Foster inspecting a field of wheat that had been planted too late and was already showing signs of rust disease.

"Thomas," Mark said, trying to sound casual. "I'll give you my communication device if you'll implement one sustainable farming practice—just one—exactly as I specify."

Thomas looked up, surprised. "Your brass telescope thing? Really?"

"Really. But you have to do it right. Follow my instructions precisely. Use the correct measurements, the right timing, everything."

Thomas scratched his chin thoughtfully. "Well... I suppose I could try."

Over the next hour, Mark explained the practice he had in mind: creating a proper compost system. It was relatively simple—layer green and brown materials in the right ratios, maintain proper moisture and aeration, turn it regularly. Done correctly, it would produce rich soil amendment within a few months. It was a cornerstone of sustainable agriculture.

Thomas listened, nodding occasionally, though Mark noticed his attention wandering.

"Do you understand?" Mark asked when he'd finished.

"Sure, sure. Green stuff, brown stuff, turn it around. Easy."

"It's not quite that simple. The ratios matter. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio should be about 30:1, and—"

"Too much fuss, Mark. Just show me where to start, and I'll figure it out."

With growing apprehension, Mark led Thomas to a suitable location and helped him begin the compost pile. Thomas threw in grass clippings, leaves, kitchen scraps, and wood chips. He didn't measure anything. When Mark tried to correct him, Thomas waved him off.

"It's fine, it's fine. Compost is compost, right? Now, about that device..."

"The device? But Thomas, you didn't follow the specifications I gave you."

Thomas stared at him. "What do you mean? I made the compost pile. I spent all morning on this, Mark. I only did it because you promised me the device."

"But the proportions—the layering—"

"I worked hard on this," Thomas said, his voice rising. "Are you going back on your word?"

Mark felt heat rising in his face. "Try again. Do it properly this time."

Thomas's expression hardened. "Too much fuss. You're never satisfied." He stalked off, leaving Mark standing beside the pile.

---

For the next several days, the atmosphere in Magnolia shifted. At first, the changes were subtle—a cold shoulder here, a turned back there. But soon the pattern became unmistakable.

When Mark entered the community center for the morning meal, conversations stopped. The farmers who had previously tolerated his presence now found reasons to be elsewhere. Children who had once pestered him with questions about the outside world were pulled away by their parents.

"Poor Thomas," Mark overheard old Margaret Vance saying to a group of women by the well. "He tried so hard to please the outsider. Spent the whole morning working on that project."

"And after all that effort," another woman clucked, "the consultant still wouldn't honor his promise. Says something about his character, doesn't it?"

Mark approached them. "I didn't refuse because Thomas worked hard," he began. "The technique wasn't implemented correctly. The ratios were wrong, the layering was—"

The women exchanged knowing glances. "Of course, dear," Margaret said, her tone dripping with false sweetness. "We're sure you had your reasons." They dispersed without another word.

That evening, Mark found his usual seat at the communal dinner table occupied. When he tried to sit elsewhere, the farmers on either side shifted their benches closer together, leaving no room. He ate standing in the corner, aware of the whispered conversations and sidelong glances.

Thomas Foster sat at the head of the table, receiving sympathetic pats on the shoulder. "A man keeps his word in this village," Thomas said loudly enough for Mark to hear. "That's what we teach our children. But I suppose outsiders have different values."

The next morning, Mark discovered that the well near his cottage had been "accidentally" blocked with stones. He spent two hours clearing it. That afternoon, he found his vegetable garden trampled—"the goats got loose," a farmer explained with a shrug that suggested otherwise.

Even the children joined in. A group of them followed Mark through the village, chanting a rhyme: "Promise-breaker, deal-forsaker, Mark the faker, troublemaker." When he turned to chase them off, they scattered, laughing.

Mark tried to continue his work, but every attempt was met with passive resistance. Farmers who had previously at least pretended to listen now walked away mid-sentence. When he asked to borrow tools, they were suddenly "being used." When he offered advice, he was met with stony silence.

On the fifth day, Mark found Thomas Foster waiting outside his cottage. The village leader held the crudely-made compost pile's location marker in his hand.

"The village council met last night," Thomas said. "We've decided that perhaps you're not the right fit for Magnolia. We'll be sending a message to the Coalition requesting your replacement."

"You can't do that," Mark said, though his voice lacked conviction.

"Can't we? We have ways of communicating with the outside world, Mark. Slowly, perhaps, but effectively. And we have a very compelling story to tell about a consultant who broke his word to a village leader who worked in good faith."

Mark felt the walls closing in. If the Veldi sent such a report—even if it was distorted—his career with the Coalition would be over. Director Singh had made clear this was his last chance.

"The council also discussed the matter of your accommodations," Thomas continued. "Several families have expressed... concerns about housing an outsider of questionable integrity. It might be difficult to find you a place to sleep."

Mark looked at Thomas's face—at the patient, implacable expression that seemed carved from stone. The village leader wasn't angry. He wasn't even particularly hostile. He simply knew he held all the cards.

"Wait," Mark said. "Let's... let's talk about this."

Thomas raised an eyebrow. "I'm listening."

The negotiation that followed was brief. Thomas wanted the device. Mark could give him the device, and all would be forgiven—the social harmony restored, the report to the Coalition forgotten, his accommodations secured. Or Mark could continue to insist on his principles, and face the consequences.

Mark thought about the compost pile—that haphazard mess of materials that bore no resemblance to proper technique. He thought about Director Singh's offer, about his future with the Coalition. He thought about the cold meals, the blocked well, the trampled garden.

He thought about how much longer he could endure being a pariah in a village that had decided, collectively, to make his life unlivable.

"Fine," Mark heard himself say. "Take it."

Thomas accepted the communication device with a smile that contained no triumph—only the satisfied look of a man whose patience had paid off. Within the hour, the village's attitude toward Mark had transformed completely. Farmers nodded to him in passing. Children brought him small gifts of fruit. Someone had already cleared his well of any remaining debris.

The warmth was genuine, Mark realized with a sick feeling. The Veldi bore him no personal malice. They simply knew how to apply pressure—subtle, sustained, and utterly effective—until they got what they wanted. Now that they had it, they were happy to welcome him back into the fold.

He was now trapped—dependent on borrowing his own device from Thomas whenever he needed to send reports, and no closer to his goal than before.

---

In his desperation, Mark began consulting sources he would normally have avoided. He reached out to former consultants who had been dismissed from the Coalition for ethical violations, researchers who had been censored for questionable research ethics, and practitioners of what could only be called pseudo-agricultural science. He needed answers, and he wasn't being picky about where they came from.

The picture that emerged from these dubious consultations was consistent, if unflattering. According to his sources, the Veldi didn't actually want better harvests badly enough to work for them. They were content with their current situation. There was, however, one thing they genuinely disliked: Mark himself.

The Veldi, his informants reported, found Mark insufferable. He was pushy, condescending, and obsessed with details they considered irrelevant. He lectured them constantly, criticized their traditional methods, and generally made himself a nuisance. They wished he would leave and never come back.

Mark sat alone in his cottage, processing this information. His initial reaction was hurt and anger. After all his efforts to help them, this was how they felt? But then a slow smile spread across his face.

They found him annoying? Perfect. Then he would become absolutely unbearable.

He would make himself such a constant, irritating presence that the Veldi would have no choice but to find a way to get rid of him. And the only way they could do that—the only way that would actually work—would be to master one sustainable farming technique and prove to the Coalition that they no longer needed a consultant.

It was a risky strategy. The Veldi might simply poison him or drive him out by force. But Mark was desperate, and desperation breeds creativity.

Starting the next day, Mark launched his campaign. He was everywhere, inserting himself into every aspect of village life. He critiqued the Veldi's cooking methods, their building techniques, their clothing choices, and their child-rearing practices. He offered unsolicited advice on everything from optimal sleep schedules to the most efficient way to chop firewood.

Where previously he had confined his lectures to agricultural topics, he now expanded his scope to encompass all aspects of village life. He explained the principles of organizational behavior and how they applied to village governance. He discussed consumer behavior and how it affected their trading relationships with neighboring villages. He pontificated on decision-making processes and emotional intelligence.

Most of all, he talked incessantly about sustainable agriculture. He described, in excruciating detail, the benefits of crop rotation, the importance of soil testing, the principles of integrated pest management, and the wonders of vermiculture. He repeated the same information over and over, like a broken record.

He was particularly insistent about one specific technique: creating a biochar production system. Biochar, he explained endlessly, was a form of charcoal that could dramatically improve soil fertility. It was produced by heating organic material in a low-oxygen environment. Done correctly, it would revolutionize their farming. It would also, he mentioned repeatedly, work as a solution to any problem they found particularly annoying.

The Veldi's irritation grew palpable. The food they brought him began to taste strange—Mark suspected poison and started growing his own vegetables using, naturally, sustainable techniques. The villagers' expressions when they saw him shifted from neutral to actively hostile.

But Mark persisted. He followed them into their fields, their homes, even their bedrooms. He had advice for everything. He was relentless, insufferable, and completely shameless.

One morning, about two weeks into his campaign, Mark woke with an odd tingling sensation in his fingertips. It was a feeling he'd experienced only once before, during his training at the Coalition's research facility in Oakdale Territory. It had happened during a demonstration of an experimental agricultural technology that had since been banned for safety reasons.

Someone was using advanced agricultural technology against him.

Mark's heart leaped. They were doing it! The Veldi were finally taking action!

He dressed quickly and crept toward the village center. The morning seemed strangely dim, but he knew that was a side effect of the particular technology being employed. This technique affected visual perception.

He hid behind a storage shed and peered out at the village square. A group of Veldi, led by Thomas Foster, were assembled around a large metal container. They were carefully layering organic material inside it, sealing it, and applying heat from below. They were making biochar—and they were following the procedure correctly!

Mark felt a surge of pride. They were doing it right! Every step was precise, every measurement accurate. This was real sustainable agriculture, performed by people who had previously refused to follow any systematic approach.

When the biochar was ready—and it would be ready, because they were doing everything correctly—the Coalition would have to acknowledge his success. Mark might even return to Magnolia someday, perhaps in disguise, to continue his work.

The process continued. The Veldi maintained the correct temperature, monitored the oxygen levels, and waited the appropriate amount of time. Thomas Foster stood at the center of the group, carefully checking a thermometer and adjusting the heat source.

Then, just as the process was nearly complete, Mark saw Thomas reach for a container of accelerant—something that looked like pure ethanol.

"Wait!" Mark shouted, running forward. "Not that! You'll ruin the whole batch! You're not doing it ri—"

But it was too late. Thomas poured the accelerant into the container. There was a brilliant flash of light, a wave of heat, and then—

Mark felt his body seizing up. His muscles locked in place. He couldn't move, couldn't breathe, couldn't even blink. He felt himself hardening, his flesh taking on a strange, rigid quality. His last conscious thought was one of bitter irony: of course the Veldi couldn't get it right. They never did.

The statue that now stands in the center of Magnolia is a curiosity. It depicts a man in mid-stride, his mouth open as if shouting, one hand raised in warning. It's made of some strange material—not quite stone, not quite metal—that resists all attempts to move or destroy it.

The Veldi find it annoying. It's in the way of their compost heaps and their experimental biochar production systems. They have to work around it constantly.

But they're confident that eventually, they'll figure out how to get rid of it. Maybe this harvest season, maybe the next. Certainly by the harvest two seasons hence. They've been studying Mark's notes on sustainable agriculture, and they think they've found a technique that might work.

After all, they have a lot of faith in sustainable agriculture now. And patience, as always, is their greatest virtue.
