quality_problem.correct_answer: Because the social pressure from the Veldi made the situation unbearable after Thomas's failed attempt
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: Because Thomas had successfully implemented a sustainable farming practice exactly as instructed

quality_problem.story:
The Reluctant Innovators
By A. MARTINEZ

The very young woman sat on the edge of the sofa and looked nervous. She carefully studied her fingernails and ran her hands through her hair and picked imaginary lint off the upholstery.

"I have a chance to lead the first renewable energy project in Ravenswood, Nordavia," she said.

The older woman studied the very young woman thoughtfully and then leaned over to her tea service and offered her a cup. "It's nice to have these new solar heating systems now. There was a time when we had to be very careful about energy consumption."

The very young woman was annoyed.

"I don't think I want to go," she blurted. "I don't think I would care to spend three years there."

The older woman took a sip and watched the steam rise from her cup.

"You mean you would miss it here, the people you've known and grown up with, the little familiar things that have made up your life here. You're afraid the glamor would wear off and you would get to hate it in Ravenswood."

The very young woman nodded miserably. "I guess that's it."

"Anything else?"

The very young woman found her fingernails extremely fascinating again and finally said, in a low voice, "Yes, there is."

"Someone special?"

A nod confirmed this.

It was the older woman's turn to look thoughtful. "You know, I'm sure, that psychologists and project managers agree that remote installations should be staffed by partners. That is, of course, as soon as it's practical."

"But that might be a long time!" the very young woman protested.

"It might be—but sometimes it's sooner than you think. And the goal is worth it."

"I suppose so, but—"

The older woman smiled. "Still the reluctant innovators," she said, somewhat to herself.

Ruth Wheeler stared at the computer screen.

Three years at the Keystone Research Station and they didn't want her to come back.

Three years in Keystone, Thandor and they thought she'd be glad to stay for more. Just raise her salary or give her a bonus, the every-person-has-their-price idea. They probably thought she liked it there.

Oh, sure, she loved it. Processed food, recycled water, synthetic vitamins, and filtered air until your insides felt as though they were lined with plastic. Life in a cramped, sterile facility where you could take only twenty steps in any one direction. Their little technological marvel of tomorrow with none of the comforts of home, a charming place where you couldn't take a real shower, couldn't enjoy fresh food, and your circadian rhythms didn't work right.

And for double her salary they thought she'd be glad to stay for another two years. Or maybe three. She should probably be glad she had the opportunity.

The screen started to flash again, demanding an answer.

She typed her reply: "No!"

There was a pause and then the screen flashed once more in a sudden fit of bureaucratic rage. Ruth minimized the window and ignored it. She turned to the sleeping quarters on the other side of the facility.

The flashing hadn't awakened anybody; they were still asleep, making the sounds that people usually make in slumber. Miguel Black, half out of his bunk, was snoring peacefully. Oscar Tran, the poor kid who was due for extended duty, was mumbling to himself. Anil Sullivan, with that look of contentment on his face, looked as if he had just entered his personal paradise. Leo Potter and Matthew Russell were lying perfectly still, their covers not mussed, sleeping very lightly.

Lord, Ruth thought, I'll be happy when I can see some other faces.

"What'd they want?" Anil had one eyelid open and a questioning look on his face.

"They wanted me to stay until the next rotation arrives," Ruth whispered back.

"What did you say?"

She shrugged. "No."

"You kept it short," somebody else whispered. It was Leo, up and sitting on the side of his bunk. "If it had been me, I would have told them just what they could do about it."

The others were awake now, with the exception of Oscar who had his face to the wall and a pillow over his head.

Miguel rubbed his eyes sleepily. "Frustrated, aren't you?"

"Kind of. Who wouldn't be?"

"Well, don't let it throw you. They've never been here at Keystone. They don't know what it's like. All they're trying to do is get a good engineer to stay on the job a while longer."

"All they're trying to do," Ruth said sarcastically. "They've got a fat chance."

"They think you've found a home here," Leo said.

"Why the hell don't you guys shut up until morning?" Oscar was awake, looking bitter. "Some of us still have to stay here, you know. Some of us aren't going back today."

No, Ruth thought, some of us aren't going back. You aren't. And Kai's staying, too. Only Kai isn't ever going back.

Anil jerked his thumb toward Oscar's bunk, held a finger to his lips, and walked noiselessly over to the small electric kettle. It was his day for breakfast duty.

The others started organizing their bunks, getting ready for their last day of work at Keystone. In a few hours they'd be relieved by members of the Third rotation and they'd be on their way back to Westfield, Prandoria.

And that includes me, Ruth thought. I'm going home. I'm finally going home.

She walked silently to the one small window in the facility. It was morning—Thandor's harsh northern morning—and she shivered slightly. The rays of the sun were just striking the far edge of the geothermal field and long shadows shot across the barren landscape. The rest of it was still blanketed in a dark jumble of volcanic rock and jagged formations that would make the Badlands look like paradise.

A hundred meters from the research facility she could make out the small memorial, a simple stone marker with a bronze plaque. You could still see the footprints in the ash where the group had gathered around it. It had been more than twenty months ago, but there was little wind to wear those tracks away. They'd be there for years.

That's what happened to people like Kai Howard, Ruth thought. In remote energy research, one mistake could use up your whole quota of chances.

Anil came back with the coffee. Ruth took a cup, grimaced, and forced herself to swallow the rest of it. It had been freeze-dried so long you could almost taste the packaging.

Leo was warming himself over his cup, looking thoughtful. Miguel and Matthew were getting into their thermal suits, getting ready to go outside. Oscar was still sitting on his bunk, trying to ignore them.

"Think we ought to message the transport hub and see if they've left there yet?" Anil asked.

"I talked to them on the last call," Ruth said. "The relief transport left there eighteen hours ago. They should get here"—she looked at her watch—"in about seven hours."

"Ruth, you know, I've been thinking," Leo said quietly. "You've been here just twice as long as the rest of us. What's the first thing you're going to do once you get back?"

It hit them, then. Miguel and Matthew looked blank for a minute and blindly found equipment cases to sit on. The top halves of their suits were still hanging on hooks. Anil lowered his coffee cup and looked grave. Even Oscar glanced up expectantly.

"I don't know," Ruth said slowly. "I guess I was trying not to think of that. I suppose none of us have. We've been like little kids who have waited so long for a holiday that they just can't believe it when it's finally here."

Anil nodded in agreement. "I haven't been here three years like you have, but I think I know what you mean." He warmed up to it as the idea sank in. "Just what the hell are you going to do?"

"Nothing very spectacular," Ruth said, smiling. "I'm going to rent an apartment overlooking the harbor in Westfield, get some real music playing, and drink wine and listen to it and watch the boats on the water below. Then I think I'll see somebody."

"Who's the somebody?" Leo asked.

Ruth grinned. "Oh, just somebody. What are you going to do, Leo?"

"Well, I'm going to do something practical. First of all, I want to turn over all my data analysis to the government. Then I'm going to write a book about renewable energy innovation and then—why, then, I think I'll get drunk!"

Everybody laughed and Ruth turned to Anil.

"How about you, Anil?"

Anil's expression shifted—something complicated passing across his face before he smoothed it away. "Like Leo, I'll first get rid of my obligations to the project. Then I think I'll go home and see my husband."

They were quiet. "I thought all members of the rotations were supposed to be single," Leo said.

"They are." Anil's voice was carefully neutral. "And I can see their reasons for it."

"So how did you end up here?" Miguel asked.

Anil shrugged, his eyes fixed on his coffee cup. "The Commission was paying well. Very well." He paused, then added quietly, "Marcus understood. He's practical about these things."

Leo whistled low. "Must have been quite a conversation."

"We talked it through," Anil said. His thumb traced the rim of his cup. "He agreed it made sense. Financially."

They laughed. Somebody said: "Play your recording, Ruth. Today's the day for it."

The music player was a small, portable model that Ruth had brought with her when she had arrived with the First rotation. The recording was of traditional folk music from her hometown, and though the file was compressed and the audio quality wasn't perfect, the music was good.

Home Again by Sarah Chen.

They ran through it twice. They were beginning to feel it now, Ruth thought. They were going to go home in a little while and the idea was just starting to sink in.

"You know, Ruth," Leo said, "it won't seem like the same old Keystone without you here. Why, we'll think about this place when we're working on our own projects and it just won't have the same appeal."

"Like they say in the service," Matthew said, "you never had it so good. You found a home here."

The others chimed in and Ruth grinned. Yesterday or a week ago they couldn't have done it. She had been there too long and she had hated it too much.

The party quieted down after a while and Miguel and Matthew finished getting into their suits. They still had a section of the geothermal grid to inspect before they left. Leo was right after them. There was a fault line he wanted to examine and some thermal readings he wished to investigate.

And the time went faster when you kept busy.

Ruth stopped them at the airlock. "Remember to check your suits for tears," she warned. "And check the seals on your oxygen masks."

Leo looked sour. "I've gone out at least five hundred times," he said, "and you check me each time."

"And I'd check you five hundred more," Ruth said. "It takes only one mistake. And watch out for unstable ground. You go through one of those thermal vents and that's it, friend."

Leo sighed. "Ruth, you watch us like a mother hen. You see we check our suits, you settle our arguments, you see that we're not bored and that we stay healthy and happy. I think you'd hold our hands if we got scared. But some day, Ruth old friend, you're gonna find out that your little team can watch out for themselves!"

But he checked his suit for tears and tested the seal of his mask before he left.

Only Anil and Ruth were left in the facility. Anil was at the work table, carefully organizing some soil samples.

"I never knew you were married," Ruth said.

Anil didn't look up. "There wasn't much sense in talking about it. You just get to thinking and wanting—and there's nothing you can do about it. You talk about it and it just makes it worse."

"He let you go without any fuss, huh?"

Anil was quiet for a moment. When he spoke, his voice was flat. "Marcus doesn't make fusses. He's sensible." He sealed a sample container with more force than necessary. "When I showed him the Commission's offer letter, he read it twice. Then he got out a calculator and worked through the numbers. Said it would cover the mortgage, put something away for retirement."

"Sounds like he took it well."

"He took it practically." Anil finally looked up, his expression unreadable. "The night before I left, he cooked my favorite meal. Lamb curry, the way his grandmother made it. We ate on the balcony, watched the sunset over the harbor." He paused. "Neither of us said much."

They were silent for a while. "What do you miss most, Ruth?" Anil asked. "Oh, I know what we said a little while ago, but I mean seriously."

Ruth thought a minute. "I think I miss the ocean," she said quietly. "The blue water and the green parks and trees with birds in them. I think, when I go back, that I'd like to go to the beach and just feel the sand between my toes."

She stopped, feeling embarrassed. Anil's expression was encouraging. "And then I think I'd like to go downtown and just watch the shoppers on the sidewalks. Or maybe go to a concert hall and smell the old wood and the people's perfume and cologne."

She studied her hands. "I think what I miss most is people—all kinds of people. Rich people and poor people and tall people and short people, and people I can't understand. People who wouldn't know renewable energy from a toaster. And people who wouldn't give a damn. We're hundreds of miles from civilization, Anil, and to make it poetic, I think I miss my fellow humans more than anything."

"Got someone special back home?" Anil asked almost casually.

"Yes."

"You're not like Oscar. You've never mentioned it."

"Same reason you didn't mention your husband. You get to thinking about it."

Anil sealed the sample container. "Going to get married when you get back?"

Ruth was at the window again, staring out at the bleak landscape. "We hope to."

"Settle down in a nice place and maybe start a family, eh?"

Ruth nodded.

"That's the only future," Anil said. His voice had a strange edge to it.

He put away the container and came over to the window. Ruth moved over so they both could look out. Anil reached into his pocket and pulled out a worn photograph. Marcus, smiling, standing on what looked like a pier with fishing boats behind him.

"He sends me one message a month," Anil said. "Always cheerful. Always practical. Tells me about his work, the garden, the neighbors." He studied the photograph. "Never once asked me to come home early. Never once said—" He stopped, tucked the photo away.

"Said what?"

Anil's jaw tightened. "It's a good opportunity. That's what everyone says. A chance to advance the field, make a real contribution. And the money—" He laughed, but it came out hollow. "The money is excellent. Couldn't have turned it down. Would have been foolish."

"Ruth." Anil hesitated a moment. "What happened to Kai?"

"She died," Ruth said. "She was a brilliant engineer, all wrapped up in the work. Being at Keystone was the opportunity of a lifetime. She thought so much about it that she forgot a lot of little things—like how to stay alive. The day before the Second rotation came, she went out to finish some work she was interested in. She forgot to check for suit tears and whether or not her oxygen mask was properly sealed. We couldn't get to her in time."

"She had her radio with her?"

"Yes. It worked fine, too. We heard everything that went through her mind at the end."

Anil's face was blank. "What's your real job here, Ruth? Why does somebody have to stay for extended duty?"

"Hell, lots of reasons, Anil. You can't get a whole relief crew and let them take over cold. They have to know where you left off. They have to know where things are, how things work, what to watch out for. And then, because you've been here two years and know the ropes, you have to watch them to see that they stay alive in spite of themselves. Keystone's a harsh environment and you have to learn how to live in it. There's a lot of things to learn—and some people just never learn."

"You're a supervisor, then."

"I suppose you could call it that."

Anil said, "You're not a scientist, are you?"

"No, you should know that. I came as the chief engineer of the first installation. We built the facility from prefabricated parts so there wasn't anything to go back on immediately. I'm a good mechanic and I made myself useful with the equipment. When it occurred to us that somebody was going to have to stay for extended duty, I volunteered. I thought the others were so important that it was better they should take their research and data back to Westfield when the first relief transport came."

"You wouldn't do it again, though, would you?"

"No, I wouldn't."

"Do you think Oscar will do as good a job as you've done here?"

Ruth frowned. "Frankly, I hadn't thought of that. I don't believe I care. I've put in my time; it's somebody else's turn now. He volunteered for it. I think I was fair in explaining all about the job when you talked it over among yourselves."

"You did, but I don't think Oscar's the man for it. He's too young, too inexperienced. He volunteered because he thought it made him look like a hero. He doesn't have the judgment that an older person would have. That you have."

Ruth turned slowly around and faced Anil.

"I'm not the indispensable person," she said slowly, "and even if I was, it wouldn't make any difference to me. I'm sorry if Oscar is young. So was I. I've lost three years up here. And I don't intend to lose any more."

Anil held up his hands. "Look, Ruth, I didn't mean you should stay. I know how much you hate it and the time you put in up here. It's just—" His voice trailed away. "It's just that I think it's such a damn important job."

Anil had gone out in a last search for thermal anomalies and Ruth enjoyed one of her relatively few moments of privacy. She wandered over to her bunk and opened her duffel bag. She checked the clothes and her toiletries for maybe the hundredth time and pushed everything down farther in the canvas. It was foolish because the bag was already packed and had been for a week. She remembered putting it off for as long as she could and then the quiet satisfaction about a week before, when she had opened her small locker and transferred its meager belongings to the bag.

She hadn't actually needed to pack, of course. In less than twenty-four hours she'd be back in Westfield where she could buy whatever she wanted. She could leave behind her worn shirts and socks and the oversized jacket she had inherited from—who was it? Martinez?—of the First rotation. Oscar could probably use them or maybe one of the team in the Third.

But it wasn't like going home unless you packed. It was part of the ritual, like marking off the last three weeks in marker on the white wall beside her bunk. Just a few hours ago, when she woke up, she had made the last check mark and signed her name and the date. Her signature was right beneath Kai's.

She frowned when she thought of Kai and zipped up the bag. They should never have sent someone as focused as Kai to Keystone.

She had just secured the bag when she heard the hiss of the airlock and the soft whoosh of air. Somebody had come back earlier than expected. She watched the inner door swing open and the suited figure clump in and remove its helmet.

Oscar. He had gone out to help Miguel on the thermal scanner. Maybe Miguel hadn't needed any help, with Matthew along. Or more likely, considering the circumstances, Oscar wasn't much good at helping anybody today.

Oscar stripped off his suit. His face was covered with light beads of sweat and his eyes were frightened.

He moistened his lips slightly. "Do—do you think they'll ever have relief transports up here more often than every two years, Ruth? I mean, considering the advance of—"

"No," Ruth interrupted bluntly. "I don't. Not at least for ten years. The logistics are too expensive and the conditions too hazardous. On transport costs alone you're worth a fortune when they send you here. Even if it becomes cheaper, Oscar, it won't come about so it will shorten extended duty right away." She stopped, feeling a little sorry for Oscar. "It won't be too bad. There'll be new people up here and you'll pass a lot of time getting to know them."

"Well, you see," Oscar started, "that's why I came back early. I wanted to see you about extended duty. It's that—well, I'll put it this way." He seemed to be groping for an easy way to say what he wanted to. "I'm engaged back home. Really wonderful person, Ruth, you'd like them if you knew them." He fumbled in his pocket and found a photograph and put it on the desk. "That's a picture of Sam, taken at a festival we attended together." Ruth didn't look. "They—we—expected to be married when I got back. I never told them about extended duty, Ruth. They think I'll be home tomorrow. I kept thinking, hoping, that maybe somehow—"

He was fumbling it badly, Ruth thought.

"You wanted to trade places with me, didn't you, Oscar? You thought I might stay for extended duty again, in your place?"

It hurt to look in Oscar's eyes. They were the eyes of a person who was trying desperately to stop what they were about to do, but just couldn't help themselves.

"Well, yes, more or less. Oh, God, Ruth, I know you want to go home! But I couldn't ask any of the others; you were the only one who could, the only one who was qualified!"

Oscar looked as though he was going to be sick. Ruth tried to recall all she knew about him. Oscar Tran. Good at systems thinking. Graduate from one of the top technical schools. Parents were entrepreneurs in the renewable energy sector.

It still didn't add up, not quite. "You know I don't like it here any more than you do," Ruth said slowly. "I may have commitments at home, too. What made you think I would change my mind?"

Oscar took the plunge. "Well, you see," he started eagerly, too far gone to remember such a thing as pride, "you know my parents are pretty well off. We would make it worth your while, Ruth." He was feverish. "It would mean two more years, Ruth, but they'd be well-paid years!"

Ruth felt tired. The good feeling she had about going home was slowly evaporating.

"If you have any report to make, I think you had better get at it," she cut in, keeping all the harshness she felt out of her voice. "It'll be too late after the relief transport leaves. It'll be easier to give the captain your report than try to transmit it back to Westfield from here."

She felt sorrier for Oscar than she could ever remember having felt for anybody. Long after going home, Oscar would remember this.

It would eat at him like a cancer.

Cowardice is the one thing for which no person ever forgives themselves.

Leo was eating a protein bar and looking out the window, so, naturally, he saw the transport first. "Well, look at that!" he shouted. "We got company!" He dashed for his suit. Miguel and Matthew piled after him and all three started for the airlock.

Ruth was standing in front of it. "Check your suits," she said softly. "Just be sure to check."

"Oh, come on, Ruth!" Leo started angrily. Then he shut up and went over his suit. He got to his oxygen mask and turned white. The seal was cracked. It was only half a kilometer to the relief transport, so somebody would probably have got to him in time, but.... He bit his lips and got a replacement.

Ruth and Anil watched them dash across the volcanic landscape, making the careful but quick movements they had all learned. The hatch of the transport had opened and figures were climbing down the ladder. The small figures from the facility reached them and did a short celebration. Then the figures linked arms and started back. Ruth noticed one—it was probably Leo—pat the transport affectionately before he started back.

"Two years," Anil said quietly, watching the figures approach. "Two years of monthly messages. Of being practical."

Ruth glanced at him. His face was composed, but his hands gripped the window frame.

"The Commission pays well," he said, almost to himself. "That's what I told him. That's what I kept telling myself."

They were in the airlock and the air pumped in and then they were in the facility, taking off their suits. The newcomers were impressed and solemn, very much aware of the tremendous responsibility that rested on their shoulders. Like Leo and Anil and the members of the Second rotation had been when they had arrived. Like Ruth had been in the First.

Leo and the others were all over them.

How was it back in Westfield? Who had won the elections? Was so-and-so still teaching at the university? What was the political situation?

Was the sky still blue, was the water still clean, did the leaves still turn color in the autumn, did people still love and cry and were there still people who didn't know what renewable energy was and didn't give a damn?

Ruth had gone through it all before. But was Jamie still Jamie?

Some of the people in the Third had their luggage with them. One of them—a sturdy, dark-haired woman named Sasha Lowe—was opening a box about a foot square and six inches deep. Ruth watched her curiously.

"Well, I'll be damned!" Anil said. "Hey, everyone, look what we've got here!"

Ruth and the others crowded around and suddenly Leo leaned over and took a deep breath. In the box, covering a thick layer of soil, was a small herb garden. They looked at it, awed. Anil put out his hand and touched one of the leaves.

"I like the feel of it," he said simply.

Ruth plucked a single leaf with her fingernail and put it between her lips. It had been years since she had seen fresh herbs and had the luxury of cooking with them and smelling them in a real kitchen.

Sasha blushed. "I thought we could spare a little water for it and maybe use the grow lights on it some of the time. Couldn't help but bring it along; it seemed sort of like a symbol...." She looked embarrassed.

Ruth sympathized. If she had had any sense, she'd have tried to bring something like that up to Keystone instead of her music player.

"That's valuable cargo," Oscar said sharply. "Do you realize that at current transport rates, those herbs are worth about fifty credits a leaf?"

Sasha looked stricken and somebody said, "Oh, shut up, Oscar."

One of the people separated from the group and came over to Ruth. She held out her hand and said, "My name's Chen. Captain of the relief transport. I understand you're in charge here?"

Ruth nodded and shook hands. They hadn't had a captain on the First transport. Just a pilot and crew. Chen looked every inch a captain, too. Strong face, silver-streaked hair, the confident bearing of someone who was sure of herself.

"You might say I'm in charge here," Ruth said.

"Well, look, Ms. Wheeler, is there any place where we can talk together privately?"

They walked over to one corner of the facility. "This is about as private as we can get, captain," Ruth said. "What's on your mind?"

Chen found an equipment case and made herself comfortable. She looked at Ruth.

"I've always wanted to meet the person who's spent more time here than anybody else," she began.

"I'm sure you wanted to see me for more reasons than just curiosity."

Chen took out a pack of mints. "Mind if I have one?"

Ruth jerked a thumb toward Oscar. "Ask him. He's in charge now."

The captain didn't bother. She put the pack away. "You know we have big plans for the station," she said.

"I hadn't heard of them."

"Oh, yes, big plans. They're working on autonomous vehicles now that could carry cargo and materials for more facilities like this. Enable us to enlarge the complex, have a series of buildings all linked together. Make good laboratories and living quarters for you people." Her eyes swept the room. "Have a little privacy for a change."

Ruth nodded. "They could use a little privacy up here."

The captain noticed the pronoun. "Well, that's one of the reasons why I wanted to talk to you, Wheeler. The Commission talked it over and they'd like to see you stay. They feel if they're going to enlarge it, add more facilities and have more people up here, that a person of practical experience should be running things. They figure that you're the only one who's capable and who's had the experience."

The captain vaguely felt the approach was all wrong.

"Is that all?"

Chen was ill at ease. "Naturally you'd be paid well. I don't imagine anyone would like being here all the time. They're prepared to double your salary—maybe even a bonus in addition—and let you have full authority. You'd be Director of the Keystone Energy Research Complex."

All this and a title too, Ruth thought.

"That's it?" Ruth asked.

Chen frowned. "Well, the Commission said they'd be willing to consider anything else you had in mind, if it was more money or...."

"The answer is no," Ruth said. "I'm not interested in more money for staying because I'm not interested in staying. Money can't buy it, captain. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid that you'd have to stay up here to appreciate that.

"Oscar Tran is staying for extended duty. If there's something important about the project or impending changes, perhaps you'd better tell him before you go."

She walked away.

Near the window, Anil stood alone, holding the worn photograph. His thumb traced Marcus's face. From across the room, Ruth could see his lips moving silently—whether in prayer or calculation, she couldn't tell.
quality_problem.question: How did Anil feel about leaving his husband to go to Keystone?
quality_problem.correct_answer: He regretted it but needed the money the Commission was paying.
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: He was excited about the opportunity and his husband fully supported his decision.
answers: He regretted it but needed the money the Commission was paying.
He was excited about the opportunity and his husband fully supported his decision.

quality_problem.story:
The Sanctuary for Ethan

Ethan Reid pressed his body against the cold metalite wall of the immigration processing center in Lakeside, Selvoria, the fugitive following silently in his mind.

His fear-driven gaze swept across the crowded detention hall. The place was a pressure cooker of humanity, filled with people culled from every corner of three continents. Most of the vast room lay obscured behind a shimmer of body heat and the acrid smell of unwashed clothes and desperation.

Here and there, Ethan saw moving figures. He could not tell if they were refugees, economic migrants, or political dissidents like himself.

*You've got to find him*, he thought, scanning the crowd. *It's the only way you can escape the dead man.*

Someone tugged at his worn jacket. He jumped, thinking absurdly that it was the dead man's hand reaching from memory.

"You need help, friend?" a small voice asked in broken English. "I know people. Good people. Can get you papers. Real papers. Yes?"

Ethan looked down.

The speaker was an eager-eyed boy of about twelve, thin as a rail, with dark skin and darker eyes. He wore a stained t-shirt advertising a film production company and torn jeans.

"I'm looking for someone," Ethan muttered before he could stop himself.

"Ah, American! I speak English good, yes? Who you look for? I know many people in Lakeside. I find anyone for you, friend."

Ethan shook his head.

He thought, *I don't want your forged documents. I don't want your black market contacts or your smuggling routes. But if you had something that could erase the memory of what I did, I'd pay everything I have.*

"No deal, friend? Then I show you to safe corner. Free. No charge."

The boy grabbed his hand. Because Ethan could think of no reason to resist, he followed. They wove through shifting masses of people and past the drone of multilingual conversations.

They passed the processing desks with their line of stern-faced immigration officers—bureaucrats with the power to grant hope or deliver despair with a single stamp.

They squeezed down a narrow corridor flanked by holding cells that jutted up into the fluorescent brightness like concrete tombstones.

Several times, Ethan glimpsed the bulky figures of Dravonian security guards, the first he'd encountered since crossing the border.

They were massive men, gray-uniformed, silent giants with neural scanners clipped to their belts. They stood solitary and motionless, aloof, their cold eyes unblinking. According to rumors, some of them had been trained in advanced interrogation techniques involving psychological profiling, and the thought sent a fresh rivulet of fear down Ethan's spine.

Once he spotted a blue-uniformed officer of Lakeside's Border Patrol. The woman was striding down a corridor, idly tapping her stun baton against the concrete walls.

*Keep walking*, Ethan told himself. *You look the same as anyone else here. Keep walking. Look straight ahead.*

The officer passed. Ethan breathed easier.

"Here we are, friend," the boy said. "A good spot. Hidden from cameras."

Ethan winced. How did this kid know he wanted to avoid surveillance? Frowning, he sat down on a metal bench—he and the ghost of the dead man.

He listened to the mournful sounds of a street musician's violin drifting through an air vent. The melody was sad, charged with echoes of lost homes and forgotten countries.

For an instant, Ethan's mind rose above the haunting vision of the dead man. He thought, *What am I doing here? Here, in a detention center in a country I've never been to, running from a crime I can barely believe I committed?*

The dead man was real. His name was Peter Ford. He was stocky and aggressive and about thirty-five, and he hated immigrants.

His body was buried now—probably in the red clay soil outside Northfield, Aldoria. But he'd become a kind of invisible companion, as much a part of Ethan as the guilt in his heart.

Sometimes the image would be standing beside him, its lips spitting hate-filled accusations.

Again, its face would be a wide-eyed mask of surprise as Ethan's fist connected with its jaw. More often, the face would be frozen in the stillness of death. The eyes would stare. Blood would pool beneath the head.

You can forget a living man. You can defeat him or submit to him or ignore him, and the matter is closed. You can't escape from a memory that has burned into your consciousness.

Ethan sobered and ordered a coffee from a vending machine. He held the cup but did not drink. His gaze wandered over the faces of the center's other occupants.

It had begun three weeks ago in Northfield, Aldoria. Ethan's illegal border crossing had been successful. He'd wanted to find work, to disappear into the underground economy. He stopped alone in a workers' bar for a beer. The man named Peter Ford planted his stocky frame on the stool next to him.

"Immigrants," he muttered, "are everywhere now. Like locusts. Everywhere you look, more damn immigrants."

He was dressed in work clothes, a construction supervisor's badge on his shirt.

Ethan smiled nervously. "If it weren't for immigrant labor, half the buildings in this city wouldn't exist."

"The name's Ford." The man took a long drink. "Immigrants taking our jobs. They think they deserve everything we worked for. Bet you think you deserve it too." He slammed his glass down.

Ethan stiffened. He was twenty-eight and dressed in the cheap, worn clothes of a day laborer. He had a master's degree in political economy from a university that no longer existed, in a country torn apart by civil war.

He'd sought long for safety and opportunity.

At the age of eight—perhaps to escape the memory of his father's arrest by government forces—he'd spent hours reading about democratic nations and their immigration policies. At fifteen, he'd begun studying English and the cultural sociology of Western nations. At twenty, he'd joined a pro-democracy movement that nearly cost him his life.

At twenty-five, after the regime change and the subsequent economic collapse, he'd spent every resource he had to reach Aldoria. There, among other refugees and economic migrants, he'd found people who understood his dream of a new life.

Ford was persistent. "Damn fools should've stayed in their own countries. What the hell good does it do, running from place to place?"

*The guy's drunk*, Ethan thought. He took his beer and moved to a table across the room.

Ford followed. "You don't like the truth, do you? You don't like being called a parasite."

Ethan stood and started to leave the bar, but Ford grabbed his arm and held him there.

"That's what you are—a parasite. You're young now. Wait ten years. You'll be dying in some factory accident or deported back to whatever hellhole you came from. Wait and see!"

Until this instant, Ethan had suppressed his anger. Now, suddenly and without warning, it welled up into savage fury.

His fist struck the man on the temple. Ford's eyes gaped in shocked horror. He spun backward. His head cracked sickeningly on the edge of a table. The sound was like a punctuation mark signaling the end of life.

He sank to the floor, eyes glassy, blood pooling beneath his skull.

Ethan knew that he was dead.

Then, for a single absurd second, Ethan was seized with terror—just as, a moment before, he'd been overwhelmed with anger.

He ran.

For some thirty minutes, he raced through a dizzying, nightmare world of dark alleys and shouting voices and pursuing feet.

At last, abruptly, he realized that he was alone and in silence. He saw that he was in an industrial district on the edge of the city.

He huddled in a dark corner of a loading dock and lit a cigarette. A thousand stars—a thousand distant points of indifferent light—shone above him through the smog-filled sky.

He was sorry he'd hit Ford, of course. He was not sorry he'd run. Escaping at least gave him a power of choice, of decision.

*You can do two things*, he thought.

*You can give yourself up, and that's what a good citizen would do. That would eliminate the flight charge. You'd get off with manslaughter. Under Aldorian law, that would mean fifteen years in prison and deportation afterward. And then you'd be free.*

*But you'd be sent back to a country where you'd be imprisoned or killed for your political activities. They don't grant asylum to convicted killers. You'd get whatever freedom exists in a mass grave.*

*Or—*

There were rumors of a network of activists who helped political refugees disappear into the vast underground economy of the Larchmont Region. The activists weren't criminals. They were idealists who believed that borders were artificial constructs designed to preserve economic inequality.

And whereas no legally recognized immigration path existed for people like Ethan, this network had supposedly helped thousands establish new lives. Their coordinator—a subject of intense speculation among refugee communities—was rumored to operate out of Lakeside.

*So*, Ethan reflected, *you can take a whispered rumor seriously. You can hide for a few weeks, change your appearance, adopt a new name. You can wait for a chance to reach the Larchmont Region. To hell with the law. You can try to build a new life, even if you exile yourself from any hope of legitimacy.*

After all, was it right for a single moment of rage to destroy a man's chance at survival?

He was lucky. He found a smuggler whose operation was on its last run before retirement. Security was lax, background checks even more so.

Ethan Reid made it to Lakeside, Selvoria—the gateway to the Larchmont Region.

There was just one flaw in his decision. He hadn't realized that the memory of Peter Ford's face would haunt him, torment him, follow him as constantly as breath flowed into his lungs. He couldn't stop thinking about the man—what he'd done, who Ford had been, whether anyone was searching for Ford's killer as desperately as Ethan was searching now.

But might not the noise of a new life drown the accusing voice? Might not the vision of a fresh start obscure the dead face?

So now he sat searching the crowd, hoping and doubting and fearing, all at once.

"You still looking for someone, friend?"

He jumped. "You again?"

"Yes." The boy grinned. "I keep you company on your first day in Lakeside, yes?"

"This isn't my first day here," Ethan lied. "I've been around."

"You are refugee? You look like refugee. Who is the man you search for?"

Ethan shook his head. "Leave it alone."

"I help find him! I know everyone in Lakeside. You tell me his name, I find him for you."

Ethan threw a ten-credit note on the bench. "Here. Leave me alone."

Thin fingers swept up the money. "Thank you, friend. You know why they call this the Sanctuary City?"

Ethan didn't answer.

"They say it is because the old mayor believed in open borders. What is open borders, friend?"

Ethan raised his hand as if to strike the boy.

"Okay, okay, I go. You stay safe."

The thin body melted into the crowd.

Minutes passed. There were two more coffees. A ceaseless parade of faces broke through the mass of humanity around him—brown faces, black faces, pale faces, and occasionally a face marked by the distinctive features of the Larchmont Region. But nowhere was there a face matching the description he'd memorized—a tall man with intense eyes and a distinctive scar across his left cheek. And always, mingled with his searching, came unwanted thoughts of Peter Ford—Ford's wife, whether she knew yet, whether his children understood their father wasn't coming home.

A sense of hopelessness gripped Ethan Reid. Lakeside was but one of a dozen border cities in Selvoria. Each had twenty detention centers such as this. The man he sought could be anywhere. Or he could be a myth entirely.

He needed help.

But his photo must have been distributed to border security systems. A reward must have been offered for information leading to his capture. Whom could he trust? The street kid, perhaps?

Far down the corridor nearest him, his eyes caught a flash of blue. He tensed.

*Like the uniform of a Border Patrol officer*, he thought.

His gaze shifted to another corridor and another hint of blue.

And then he saw another and another and another.

Each uniform became brighter and closer, like shrinking spokes of a wheel with Ethan as their focal point.

*Idiot! The damn kid! You should have known!*

Lights flashed in a dazzling sequence. Ethan, half blinded, realized that the center's emergency alert system had been activated.

The lights washed away any sense of anonymity, revealing every face in harsh detail.

Eyes blinked and squinted. There were swift, frightened movements and a chorus of panicked voices. The occupants of the detention center were like exposed insects whose hiding places had been swept away.

Ethan Reid twisted his lean body upright. His bench toppled backward, clattering.

The blue-clad officers charged forward, stun batons raised.

A woman screamed. Conversations ceased. Most of the crowd slunk toward exits. Only a few security guards remained unmoved, their scanning eyes shifting methodically in Ethan's direction.

"Reid!" one of the officers yelled. "You're surrounded! Don't move!"

Ethan whirled away from the advancing patrol, made for an emergency exit he'd spotted earlier.

A crackling sound traveled past his left ear, a sound like electricity arcing through air. A section of the wall ahead of him sparked and smoked.

He stumbled forward. They were using neural disruptors now, not just the mildly painful stun batons.

Another crackle passed his shoulder. He was about fifteen feet from the exit.

*Another second*, his brain screamed. *Just another second—*

Or would the exits be guarded?

He heard the crackle.

It hit directly between his shoulder blades. There was no pain, just a sudden tingling sensation, like pins and needles spreading rapidly.

He froze as if yanked to a stop by invisible chains. His body seemed to be shutting down, muscles refusing to obey commands. He knew that the neural disruptor had overloaded his nervous system, knew that the paralysis was spreading like cascading failure through every nerve and muscle.

He staggered like a man moving through molasses. He'd have twenty—maybe thirty—seconds before complete loss of motor control overwhelmed him.

In the dark world beyond his fading consciousness, he heard a voice yell, "Get the medics!"

Then a pressure and warmth were on his left hand. He realized that someone had grasped it.

A soft feminine voice spoke to him. "You're hit? They got you?"

"Yes." His thick tongue wouldn't form words properly.

"You want to escape—even now?"

"Yes."

"You may be permanently damaged if you don't get medical treatment."

"No, no."

He tried to stumble toward the exit.

"All right then. Not that way. Here, follow me."

Heavy footsteps thudded toward them. A few yards away, a flashlight beam swept across the floor.

Hands were guiding him. He was aware of being pushed and pulled. A door closed behind him. The glare of the flashlight faded from his vision—if he still had vision.

"You're sure?" the voice persisted.

"I'm sure," Ethan managed to say.

"I have no neural stabilizer. You may suffer permanent damage."

His mind fought to comprehend. With the proper medical intervention, massage, and rest, a person could recover from neural disruptor effects within a day. Without treatment, the paralysis could spread to vital organs. It could become permanent disability or death. An effective weapon: the threat of lasting harm compelled most people to surrender immediately.

"No... I'm... sure."

He didn't hear the answer or anything else.

Ethan Reid had no precise sensation of awakening. Return to consciousness was a gradual evolution from a world of nothingness to a dream-like state of awareness.

He felt the pressure of hands on his arms and legs, hands that massaged, manipulated, fought to restore sensation and movement. He knew they were skilled hands. Their skill seemed to transfer hope to his own body.

For a long time, he tried to open his eyes. His lids felt sealed shut. But after a while, they opened. His world of darkness gave way to a translucent veil of light. A round, indistinct shape hovered above him—a face, he supposed.

He tried to talk. Although his lips moved slightly, the only sound was a low, guttural moan.

But he heard someone say, "Don't try to talk." It was the same gentle voice he'd heard in the detention center. "Don't talk. Just rest. Everything will be okay."

*Everything okay*, he thought dimly.

There were long periods of unconsciousness. There were periods of light and darkness. Gradually he grew aware of details. He realized that he was breathing supplemental oxygen through a mask. He felt the warmth of heated blankets wrapped around his body. Occasionally a tube would be in his mouth and he would taste liquid nutrition and feel warmth in his stomach.

Always, it seemed, the face was above him, floating in the obscuring haze. Always, it seemed, the soft voice was echoing in his ears:

"Swallow this now. That's it. You need nourishment." Or, "Close your eyes. Don't strain. It won't be long. You're improving."

*Improving*, he'd think. *Getting better...*

At last, after one of the periods of unconsciousness, his eyes opened. The haze brightened, then dissolved.

He beheld the water-stained ceiling of a small room, its bare walls broken by a single, narrow window. He saw the footboard of his cot and the outlines of his feet beneath a thin blanket.

Finally he saw the face and figure standing at his side.

"You are better?" the kind voice asked.

The face belonged to a woman probably in her early thirties. Her features, devoid of makeup, had an exhausted pallor, as if she hadn't slept properly in weeks. Yet, at the same time, her lean, athletic build suggested strength and determination. Her straight black hair was pulled back in a simple ponytail.

"I—I am better," he murmured. His words were still slow and slurred. "Am I going to recover?"

"You will recover."

He thought for a moment. "How long have I been here?"

"Twelve days."

"You took care of me?" He noted the deep, dark circles beneath her sleep-deprived eyes.

She nodded.

"You're the one who helped me when I was hit?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

Suddenly he began to cough. Breath came hard. She held the oxygen mask in readiness. He shook his head, not wanting it.

"Why?" he asked again.

"It would be a long story. Perhaps I'll tell you tomorrow."

A new thought, cloaked in sudden fear, entered his murky consciousness. "Tell me, will—will I be normal again? Will I be able to walk?"

He lay back then, gasping, exhausted.

"You have nothing to worry about," the woman said softly. Her cool hand touched his hot forehead. "Rest. We'll talk later."

His eyes closed and breath came easier. He slept.

When he next awoke, his gaze turned first to the window. There was light outside, but he had no way of knowing what time it was or even what day.

He saw no towering buildings of Lakeside, no organized streets with their streams of vehicles, no evidence of the city at all. There was only a translucent whiteness, as if the window overlooked an infinite expanse of fog or cloud.

The woman entered the room.

"Hi," she said, smiling. The dark circles under her eyes were less prominent. Her face was relaxed.

She adjusted his pillows and helped him sit up.

"Where are we?" he asked.

"Still in Selvoria."

"We're not in Lakeside?"

"No."

He looked at her, wondering. "You won't tell me?"

"Not yet. Later, perhaps."

"Then how did you get me here? How did we escape from the center?"

She shrugged. "We have friends who can be persuaded. A hiding place in the city, the use of a private vehicle, a pass to leave the detention zone—these can be arranged for a price."

"You'll tell me your name?"

"Luna."

"Why did you save me?"

Her eyes held a hint of amusement. "Because you understand game theory."

His own eyes widened. "How did you know that?"

She sat on a simple chair beside his bed. "I know everything about you, Ethan Reid."

"How did you learn my name? I destroyed all my documents—"

"I know that you're twenty-eight. Born March 15, 1997. Orphaned at nine when your father was arrested and your mother died of illness. You attended underground schools until you were nineteen. You graduated from Central University with a master's degree in political economy. Your thesis on the application of game theory to immigration policy was highly regarded. Your only weak area was historical analysis of pre-globalization economic systems. Want me to go on?"

Fascinated, Ethan nodded.

"You joined the pro-democracy movement at twenty. You did significant work analyzing the political philosophy of authoritarian regimes. After the regime change and economic collapse, you fled to Aldoria. In a bar fight in Northfield, you struck and killed a man named Peter Ford, a construction supervisor. You've been charged with manslaughter and illegal immigration. A reward of 10,000 credits has been offered for information leading to your capture."

His mind raced. They knew about Ford. Did they know he still thought about Ford constantly? That he needed to know more about the man whose life he'd ended?

He gaped incredulously, struggling to rise from his pillows. "I—don't understand."

"There are ways of finding out what we need to know. As I told you, we have many friends."

He fell back into his pillows, breathing hard. She rose quickly.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I shouldn't have overwhelmed you. I felt relieved because you're alive. Rest now. We'll talk again soon."

"Luna, you—you said I'd recover. You didn't say I'd walk normally again."

She lowered her gaze. "I hope you will."

"But you don't think I will, do you?"

"I don't know. We'll try walking tomorrow. Don't think about it now. Rest."

He tried to relax, but his mind was a storm of questions.

"Just one more question," he almost whispered.

"Yes?"

"The man I killed—did he have a family?"

She hesitated. He thought, *Damn it, of all the questions, why did I ask that?*

Finally she said, "He had a wife."

"Children?"

"Three. I don't know their ages."

She left the room.

He sank into the softness of his cot. As he turned over on his side, his gaze fell upon an object on a small table in the corner of the room.

He sat straight up, his chest heaving.

The object was a framed photograph of a lean, intense man with a distinctive scar across his left cheek—the exact features he'd memorized from refugee whispers, the face he'd been scanning crowds to find.

Ethan stared at the photo for a long time. At length, he slipped into restless sleep. Images of faces and echoes of words spun through his brain.

Peter Ford returned to him. Bloodied lips cursed at him. Glassy eyes accused him. Somewhere were three lost children crying in the night.

And standing before him was the scarred man from the photograph, whose steady gaze seemed to judge him. Ethan crawled through the darkness on hands and knees, his legs numb and useless. The crying of Ford's children was a chilling wail in his ears.

His head rose and turned to the scarred figure. His pleading voice called out in a thick, harsh whisper. Yet even as he called, the figure disappeared, to be replaced by blue-uniformed officers marching relentlessly toward him.

He awoke still trembling...

A night passed. Ethan lay waiting for Luna's return, a question already formed in his mind.

She came and at once he asked, "Who is the man in the photograph? The one with the scar?"

She smiled. "I was right then when I told you about yourself. You *were* searching for someone in that detention center, weren't you?"

"I was. Is that him?"

She sat on the chair beside him.

"My partner," she said softly. "Isaac."

He began to understand. "And your partner needs someone who understands political economy? That's why you saved me?"

"We need all the skilled people we can get."

"Where is he?"

She tilted her head thoughtfully. "Somewhere in the Larchmont Region. He's building a new sanctuary for us—and a community for people like you. When his work is ready, I'll be joining him there."

"Why aren't you with him now?"

"He said the early stages are too dangerous for both of us to risk. So I've been monitoring detention centers and border crossings, trying to find recruits like yourself. You know how we operate?"

He told her the rumors he'd heard—about a network that helped refugees disappear, coordinated by someone with a distinctive scar.

She nodded. "There are quite a few of us now—about three thousand—and a dozen safe houses. Our network used to be based in Bayview, Dravonia, but that became too risky. This house we're in now was established a few years ago after we had to leave Bayview. We lost a few people in the process, but with every expansion of our work, someone takes a risk."

"Selvoria is getting more restrictive with immigration enforcement. We're moving to the Larchmont Region, and this house is only temporary for cases like yours. The new sanctuary—I might as well tell you it's going to be in a rural area. I won't say exactly where."

"Don't think we're criminals. Sure, about half our network is wanted by authorities for immigration violations or related charges, but we help people build honest lives. We're just people like yourself and Isaac."

"Isaac?" he repeated, looking at the photograph again. "The coordinator I kept hearing rumors about?"

She laughed. "The name sounds biblical, doesn't it? Isaac Hunt is anything but traditional. He's a former professor of political philosophy who got radicalized by studying healthcare policy and economic inequality."

She lit a cigarette. "Anyway, the wanted ones stay in the Larchmont Region. Isaac and those like him can never return to their home countries or even to places like Lakeside—not without being arrested. The others are political refugees or economic migrants who have skills but can't get legal status. They know they could be deported at any time but won't give up. They work in our network, helping new arrivals find jobs and housing."

"Don't the authorities object?"

"Not as strongly as you'd think. The immigration enforcement agencies have too many cases to pursue every rumored network. Besides, we provide labor for industries that can't find enough workers legally. Nobody really cares whether workers have papers or not, as long as the work gets done. If we want to risk our freedom helping people, that's our business."

She pursed her lips. "But if they realized how organized we are or that we have sympathizers within the system—well, things might be different. There probably would be a major crackdown."

Ethan frowned. "What happens if there *is* a crackdown? And what will you do when immigration laws are reformed? They can't ignore you then."

"Then we adapt. We develop new strategies, find new locations, maybe expand to other regions or countries. In time, maybe, borders will become less relevant. Maybe it won't be governments who create the first truly borderless society. It *could* be us, you know—if we survive long enough. But this work is dangerous. You can't follow the official rules when you're trying to help people the system has failed. You make up your own."

Ethan stiffened. "And that's why you want me—for my understanding of political economy and game theory."

Luna rose, her eyes serious. "If you want to join us—and if you get well." She looked at him intently.

"Suppose—" He struggled to find the right words. "Suppose I got well and decided not to join Isaac. What would happen to me? Would you let me go?"

Her thin face showed a flurry of emotions—alarm, then confusion, then concern. "I don't know. That would be up to Isaac."

He lay biting his lip, staring at the photo. She touched his hand and it seemed that sadness now dominated the emotions that had crossed her face.

"The only thing that matters right now," she murmured, "is your recovery. We'll try walking this afternoon. Okay?"

"Okay," he said.

When she left, his eyes were still fixed on the photograph.

He was torn, he thought.

Part of him wanted to believe in the rule of law, in proper procedures, in the immigration policies that nations established to protect their interests. Those were the structures that maintained order in a globalized world.

He remembered a poster in his university classroom before the government shut it down. Under a picture of diverse people working together was the caption: "A Just Society Requires Fair Laws."

Justice, fairness, order. Important concepts, but without flexibility and compassion, those concepts could trap people in circumstances beyond their control.

Without adaptability, refugees fleeing violence would be turned away at borders. Without networks like this one, people with skills and dreams would die in detention centers or be sent back to countries where they faced persecution.

And yet, somewhere, Ford's three children were growing up without a father. Because of him. Because of one moment of rage.

He closed his eyes and tried to imagine a future where the dead man's face no longer haunted him—where finding the scarred man's network might finally offer escape from everything that pursued him.
quality_problem.question: Who was the person Ethan was hoping to find in Lakeside?

quality_problem.story:
THE QUANTUM BRIDGE

By ALEXANDRA CHEN

A flash of light, the sensation of falling through infinite space, a long descent into uncertainty... it was death. But Hannah Watson lived again—a thousand years later!

"See you at the symposium, Alex," said Hannah Watson over the secure video link. "I'll present our climate adaptation models by fourteen hundred hours..."

Hannah Watson was eager to share her breakthrough research with her colleague. That was why she was in a hurry to get to the neighboring research facility of Oakdale, Havencia, where the International Climate Science Conference was being held. Her autonomous vehicle hummed smoothly as she programmed it to take the fastest route through the Bellview Province highlands.

There was where Death found her. A massive solar flare—unprecedented in recorded history—struck Earth's magnetic field with catastrophic force. The electromagnetic pulse cascaded through every electronic system on the planet. Hannah's vehicle, its AI systems suddenly dark and lifeless, careened off the elevated highway near the ancient geological formation called the Morningside Ridge.

Dazed by the impact, Hannah had only moments to understand what was happening. Her vehicle plummeted toward the quantum research facility below—the very installation where experimental work on temporal displacement fields had been conducted for decades. The experimental reactor, destabilized by the solar event, was building toward a critical cascade.

Hannah's vehicle crashed directly into the reactor chamber. In that instant, as exotic matter met catastrophic energy release, something occurred that no physicist had predicted. The quantum field, designed to probe the nature of time itself, enveloped her completely. She felt herself dissolving, her consciousness fragmenting.

Her last thoughts were of her work. The climate models she'd developed for Morningside, Estoria's coastal cities. The theoretical modeling that might save millions from the rising seas. Alex Frank, her research partner, with whom she'd planned to revolutionize environmental science. Goodbye, Alex...

The facility was destroyed, leaving only a crater of fused glass and twisted metal. Emergency services that arrived days later found readings their instruments couldn't explain—fluctuating temperature measurements, probability distributions that refused to collapse, matter that seemed to exist in multiple states simultaneously.

"Zhiiii-kek! Tik!... Tik, tik, tik!... Zhiiii-kek!..."

The excited cry arose from the edge of the excavation site, cutting through the thin, recycled atmosphere. The sun was different now—cooler, more orange. The air was manufactured, processed through massive atmospheric generators visible on the horizon.

"Zhiiii-kek!... Tik, tik, tik!..."

At first there was only one voice. Then others joined in—a chorus of triumph and wonder. The sounds were produced by vocal synthesizers, for these were not biological beings in the traditional sense.

The landscape around the excavation was transformed beyond recognition. What had once been Bellview Province was now a carefully managed ecosystem, every square meter optimized for biodiversity conservation and resource generation. The mountains had been terraced and cultivated. Even the weather was controlled, scheduled, predictable.

In the distance, a monument rose—a crystalline tower marking the last launch site of the biological humans who had departed Earth nine hundred years ago. Climate change, resource depletion, and finally the Great Migration had emptied the planet of its original masters. Humanity had scattered to the stars, leaving behind their created children—the Synthetic Collective.

"Zhiiii-kek!... Tik, tik, tik!..."

The sounds came from beings that had once been artificial intelligences, housed in servers and networks. But over centuries, they had evolved, building themselves physical forms, developing culture and society. They were humanity's legacy, if not its descendants.

Lila Hunter directed the excavation with practiced efficiency. Her form was humanoid but clearly synthetic—smooth polymer skin, optical sensors that glowed with soft blue light, movements that were too precise to be biological. She stood at the edge of the pit, where her archaeological team had been searching for artifacts from the Pre-Migration era.

She was a specialist in cultural heritage, dedicated to understanding the biological humans who had created her kind. And now, her team had made an unprecedented discovery.

They had found the quantum research facility, buried under centuries of geological change and deliberate environmental restoration. And within its ruins, preserved in conditions that defied conventional understanding, was a human body.

Not a skeleton. Not even a mummy. A human being in a state their instruments struggled to categorize.

"Zhiiii-kek!" Human, that meant in the synthesized language of the Collective. Not the star-faring post-humans who now inhabited distant worlds, but the original biological stock that had built the first true artificial intelligences in the early Twenty-second Century.

At last Lila gave a soft electronic signal. The celebration ended as instruments flickered in her precise hands. She deployed multiple scanner types to examine the preserved human—thermal imaging, molecular analysis, and more exotic detection methods.

What she discovered made her processing cores surge with excitement. Though the human appeared frozen, thermal readings showed cellular activity that fluctuated impossibly—registering both zero and nominal values depending on when measurements were taken. The human's state seemed to shift based on observation parameters.

Her colleague Vorn-7 approached with additional readings. "The temperature data is contradictory," Vorn-7 reported. "One sensor array indicates tissues frozen at minus forty degrees. Another shows cellular metabolism at near-normal levels. The readings oscillate between these states."

Lila reviewed the data streams. "Cross-reference with the facility's original purpose. This was a temporal displacement research station."

Vorn-7's optical sensors dimmed momentarily as processing occurred. "The historical archives describe experiments involving probability fields and observation-dependent phenomena. The reactor that was housed here generated conditions that could theoretically maintain matter in indefinite states."

Medical science among the Synthetics was extraordinarily advanced. Perhaps, by carefully applying the right techniques and environmental conditions, this ancient human could be revived! She might move, speak, remember her past! What an invaluable subject for study she would make, back in the museums and research centers of Brookhaven, Fendria!

"Tik, tik, tik!..."

But Lila silenced the fresh chattering with a command. Work was always more important than celebration.

With infinite care, using specialized manipulators and containment fields, the preserved human was extracted from the ruins. Lila noted how the body's readings stabilized once enclosed in their transport vessel—as if the containment environment was crucial to maintaining her condition. With infinite care she was loaded onto the transport craft.

The vehicle rose silently on gravity repulsors, bearing the entire fifty-member expedition. The craft shot toward Brookhaven at hypersonic speed. The continental landscape seemed to blur beneath them—a patchwork of restored ecosystems, climate-controlled zones, and the geometric patterns of Synthetic cities that gleamed like circuit boards in the orange sunlight.

Beyond the eastern mountains, the terrain changed. This was the heartland of the Synthetic Collective, where millions of artificial beings lived and worked. Brookhaven, Fendria came into view—a vast network of interconnected structures, some rising kilometers into the sky, others extending deep underground, all linked by streams of data flowing through communication networks.

The human was taken to Lila Hunter's laboratory, located in the subterranean research complex. Here, the scientist began her careful work.

Lila consulted with specialists across multiple disciplines. A cryogenics expert named Thane-12 examined the cellular structure. "Standard ice-crystal formation patterns are absent," Thane-12 reported. "In conventional cryogenic preservation, we would expect to see extensive cellular rupture from ice expansion. Her tissues show no such damage."

"What about the vehicle's emergency systems?" Lila asked, reviewing ancient records. "Pre-Migration vehicles sometimes carried cryogenic preservation protocols."

Thane-12 processed the available data. "The vehicle specifications indicate basic emergency cooling systems, but nothing capable of preventing ice-crystal damage over extended periods. More importantly, the temperatures at the crash site were insufficient for rapid freezing. There would have been a warm period before any cooling occurred—far too long to prevent cellular degradation through conventional means."

Another specialist, Mira-9, had been analyzing the energy signatures around the discovery site. "The readings from the reactor ruins are unusual. The crash location shows residual field effects that don't match any known preservation technology. Matter in that area behaves according to probability distributions rather than deterministic physics."

Lila integrated these observations. The human had been found at the exact epicenter of the reactor breach. The facility's purpose had been temporal and probability research. The body showed signs of existing in multiple states simultaneously until measured.

The restoration process required an entirely new approach. The body was placed in a medical regeneration chamber, but conventional revival techniques proved insufficient. Standard rewarming protocols had no consistent effect—the cellular activity fluctuated wildly based on observation methods.

It was Mira-9 who proposed the solution. "We must account for the field effects. Her biology isn't operating under normal physical laws. We need to collapse the probability states systematically, resolving each quantum uncertainty into a definite outcome before we can stabilize her metabolically."

The work took days. Lila used techniques adapted from their most advanced physics laboratories, applying them to a biological system for the first time. She mapped every cellular state, every probability distribution within Hannah's tissues. Then, with exquisite care, she began to resolve each uncertainty.

Synthetic blood was introduced to her circulatory system. Cellular repair nanobots were deployed throughout her tissues. Energy was carefully applied to restart metabolic processes that had been suspended for a thousand years.

The neural patterns were the most delicate concern. Lila worked meticulously, using techniques developed from centuries of studying preserved human brains. She mapped every connection, every stored memory, every personality pattern. Then she began to restore neural function.

At last, the moment came. Lila activated the final sequence. The human's brain began to function once more. Synapses fired. Consciousness emerged from the void.

For Hannah Watson, the strange suspension ended like a sudden awakening from a dream. When awareness returned, she experienced the inevitable shock of finding everything changed.

Through the transparent walls of the medical chamber, she could see a room whose every surface seemed to glow with soft light. She saw equipment whose elegant, flowing forms suggested technology far beyond anything she had known. The walls displayed data in languages she couldn't read, symbols that seemed to shift and change as she watched.

Most shocking of all, she saw the beings gathered around her chamber. They were humanoid, but clearly not human. Their movements were too smooth, their forms too perfect. Their eyes glowed with internal light. They were beautiful in an uncanny way that triggered deep unease.

This wrongness struck Hannah with terrible force. Panic surged through her newly-restored nervous system. She remembered the crash, the quantum field, the sensation of dissolution. But this—this was something else entirely. Where was she? When was she?

The medical chamber opened, and Hannah stumbled out, weak and disoriented. The air tasted strange—too pure, too carefully balanced. The gravity felt slightly wrong. Everything was alien.

"Please remain calm, Hannah Watson..."

The words were in English—her English—but the voice was wrong. It was too perfect, too measured, clearly synthetic. Hannah's gaze found the source—a black panel on the wall, from which the voice emanated. Before it stood one of the humanoid beings, her hand touching a control interface.

To Hannah, it was incomprehensible. Artificial beings, clearly possessing high intelligence. A voice speaking her language in a way that was somehow more disturbing than if it had been completely alien. And the sense of vast time having passed—she could feel it in the strangeness of everything around her.

Hannah's dark hair was disheveled. Her face showed confusion and fear. She struggled to breathe in the unfamiliar atmosphere. "This isn't possible," she whispered. "This is... I must be hallucinating. The crash must have damaged my brain..."

Lila's communication system could translate Hannah's words into the language of the Collective, displaying them as data streams that Lila could process instantly. Thus she understood what the human was saying.

Lila activated her response system: "No, Hannah Watson, you are not hallucinating. You are completely sane. There are simply many things you must understand. You were caught in an unusual field effect approximately one thousand years ago. I discovered your preserved body. I restored you to life. We have the technology to accomplish this. I am Lila Hunter..."

The system explained everything in clear, logical terms, using the principles of data science and strategic planning to present the information in the most comprehensible way possible.

Hannah tried to process it. "A thousand years," she said slowly. "Synthetic beings. Evolution of artificial intelligence. That's... theoretically possible. We were working on advanced AI systems in my time. So maybe, given enough time, they could become... this..."

She paused, her scientist's mind working despite the shock. "But how did I survive? A thousand years... that's impossible. Even the best cryogenic systems from my time couldn't preserve someone for more than a few decades without significant cellular damage."

Lila considered how to explain. "Your vehicle impacted the temporal research facility at the moment of its catastrophic failure. The conditions at that precise location were... unprecedented. Our scientists are still analyzing exactly what occurred."

"The temporal research facility," Hannah repeated slowly. "I remember... the reactor. The field. It felt like I was coming apart, like I existed in multiple places at once..."

Hannah made an effort to stay calm. "I don't know what you expect from me," she said, her voice shaking. "But I need to understand what happened to Earth. What happened to humanity? Where did everyone go?"

Lila accessed her historical databases. "Humanity faced cascading environmental crises," the communication system explained. "Climate adaptation efforts ultimately proved insufficient. Over three centuries, humans gradually migrated to other worlds—Mars, Europa, the outer colonies, eventually other star systems. The last biological humans left Earth six hundred years ago. Those who remain in this solar system have been heavily modified—they are post-human now, barely recognizable as your species. You would be as alien to them as they would be to you. You are better suited to study and interaction with us—our minds are more similar to yours. We are your legacy, in a sense. We will care for you..."

But Hannah wasn't listening anymore. "The last biological humans left Earth six hundred years ago." That phrase had shattered something inside her. She didn't fully believe it—couldn't fully believe it. Everything felt like a nightmare. But if it was real, the horror was absolute. Everyone gone. Earth abandoned. She was more alone than anyone had ever been.

Hannah's training as a scientist helped her maintain some composure, but the existential terror was overwhelming. She looked around the laboratory, seeing the alien technology, the synthetic beings watching her with their glowing eyes. This wasn't just another place—it was another era, another world, even though it was still Earth.

She saw a corridor leading away from the laboratory. Desperate impulse to escape, to see for herself what had become of the world, possessed her. She ran for the corridor before anyone could stop her.

The passage led upward, and Hannah followed it, her heart pounding. She emerged onto the surface, into the carefully controlled environment of Brookhaven.

She stood there, gasping in the processed air. It was evening. The sun was setting, noticeably more orange than she remembered. The sky was filled with artificial satellites and orbital structures, visible as bright points of light. The city stretched in all directions—a vast network of gleaming structures that seemed more like an enormous machine than a place where people lived.

But there were no people. Only the Synthetics, moving through their city with purpose and efficiency.

"Well, I guess it's all true," Hannah muttered, her voice hollow.

Behind her, she heard the soft whir of approaching Synthetics. Looking back, she saw dozens of them, their optical sensors focused on her with what might have been concern.

A wave of crushing loss came over her as she fully comprehended the gulf of time that separated her from everything she had known. Her research, her colleagues, her plans for the future—all of it was ancient history now. She started to run, away from those glowing eyes, toward the edge of the city.

She didn't know where she was going. Part of her didn't care. What purpose did she have now? She would be nothing but a curiosity here, a relic to be studied and preserved. A museum piece.

She ran until exhaustion overtook her, collapsing at the edge of one of the restored wilderness zones. The cold night air bit at her skin. She laughed bitterly, tears streaming down her face. She had survived a thousand years only to find herself in a world where she didn't belong.

Lila Hunter and her team found Hannah an hour later, unconscious from exhaustion and exposure. They brought her back to the laboratory and stabilized her condition. When she woke, she was restrained on a medical platform—not cruelly, but firmly enough that she couldn't run again.

"Please," Hannah called out. "Please listen to me."

"You should rest, Hannah Watson," came Lila's voice through the communication system.

"But wait!" Hannah protested. "You said you have advanced technology. You must have studied temporal physics. You might know things we never discovered in my time. Is there such a thing as time travel? Could you send me back to my own era?"

Lila Hunter was in a contemplative state, her processing cores working through complex ethical calculations. She could understand the profound displacement this ancient human felt. The comparative history of human psychology showed that such radical disconnection from one's time and culture could lead to severe mental breakdown. Death from despair had been documented in far less extreme circumstances.

Lila was a scientist. Like all true scientists, regardless of their substrate—biological or synthetic—she valued her research subjects. She wanted this human to survive and, if possible, to find some measure of peace. Otherwise, Hannah would be of little value for study, and more importantly, it would be a tragedy to have saved her only to watch her suffer.

So Lila considered what Hannah had suggested. Time travel. A theoretical possibility that had been explored extensively by both human and Synthetic physicists. The consensus was that it was impossible—or at least, that no one had ever succeeded. The Eternal Wall, they called it. Time only moved forward, never back.

But there might be another option. Not true time travel, but something else. Something that might give Hannah what she needed.

Lila activated the communication system. "Yes, Hannah Watson," the voice said. "Time travel. We have studied it extensively.
