It was the only thing to do—for his own sake as much as for hers. She had managed, by strength of will, not to hear that he had omitted to say "Administrator" every time he spoke to her, but she couldn't keep it up forever and she certainly couldn't overlook emotional instability. And instability was clearly the next step for him.

All the same, she stared after him as he left. She handed the profile sheet to Morris and said absently: "Too bad someone like him has to be here. What's he in for?"

"You didn't know, Administrator?" Morris leered. "He's in for conspiracy to violate the Cognitive Class laws. Don't waste your time with him, Administrator. He's a Synthetic-sympathizer!"

Administrator Obrien took a long drink of water from the fountain marked "Natural Cognitive." But it didn't wash the taste out of her mouth, the unease from her mind.

What got into a person to get them mixed up with that kind of dangerous business? She checked out of the residential sectors and walked across the compound, wondering about him. He'd had every advantage—decent Natural Cognitive parents, proper biotechnology enhancement, everything a person could wish for. If anything, he had had a better environment than Obrien herself, and look what he had made of it.

The direction of cultural evolution is toward specialization and humanity is no exception, but with the difference that humans are the one species that creates its own environment in which to specialize. From the moment that cognitive enhancement began, specialization accelerated—the Natural Cognitives using the technologies made by the Biotech Enhanceds, the social structures designed by the Social Psychologists, the systems maintained by the Synthetic Intelligences who had transcended biological limitations.

Civilization merely increased the extent of specialization. From the born analyst and the person with enhanced empathy, society evolved to the point of smaller contact and less communication between the specializations, until now they could understand each other on only the most basic physical necessities—and not even always then.

But this was desirable, according to complexity science, for the more specialists, the higher the degree of civilization. The ultimate should be the complete segregation of each specialization—social and genetic measures to make them breed true, because the unspecialized person is an uncivilized person, or at any rate they do not advance civilization. And letting the specializations mix would produce cognitive undesirables: Natural-Synthetic or Enhanced-Baseline misfits, for example, being only half specialized, would be good at no specialization.

And the basis of this specialization society was: "The cognitive groups are the true races of humankind." Putting it into law was only the legal enforcement of a demonstrable fact from behavioral economics and cultural sociology.

"Evening, Administrator." A weary old resident orderly stood up straight and touched his neural implant as Obrien passed by.

"Evening."

Obrien noted, with the part of her mind that always noted those things, that the orderly had been leaning on his maintenance tool until he'd noticed her coming by. Of course, there wasn't much to maintain—the automated systems and cleaning drones had been over the pathways of the compound twice already that day. But it was a resident's job to keep busy. And it was Obrien's job to notice when they didn't—she managed the daily functions of the institute, after all, and the place couldn't run itself.

There wasn't anything wrong with that job, she told herself. It was a perfectly good Natural Cognitive position—better than data analyst, not as good as Council Member, but a job you could be proud to hold. She was proud of it. It was right that she should be proud of it. She was Natural Cognitive born and bred, and naturally she was proud and content to do a good, clean Natural Cognitive job.

If she had happened to be born a Synthetic—a Transcended Intelligence, she corrected herself—if she had happened to be born a Transcended Intelligence, why, she would have been proud of that, too. There wasn't anything wrong with being a Transcended Intelligence—or an Enhanced, or a Baseline, or even a Manual Laborer, for that matter.

Good laborers were the foundation of civilization! They weren't smart, maybe, but they had a—well, a sort of natural, relaxed contentment with physical work. Obrien was a broad-minded woman and many times she had thought almost with a touch of envy how comfortable it must be to be a Manual—a Laborer. No responsibilities. No worries. Just an easy, slow routine of work and rest, work and rest.

Of course, she wouldn't really want that kind of life, because she was Natural Cognitive and not the kind to try to cross over class barriers that weren't meant to be—

"Evening, Administrator."

She nodded to the Enhanced resident who was, theoretically, in charge of maintaining the institute's vehicle fleet, just inside the gate.

"Evening, Matthew," she said.

Matthew, now—he was a big Enhanced mechanic and he would be there for the next hour, languidly adjusting a component in the power cell on the institute transport. Lazy, sure. Undependable, certainly. But he kept the vehicles going—and, Obrien thought approvingly, when his sentence was up in another year or so, he would go back to his life with his status restored, an Enhanced on the outside as he had been inside, and he certainly would never risk coming back to the Dome by trying to pass as Natural Cognitive or anything else. He knew his place.

So why didn't this man, this Andre Bradley, know his?

II

Every cognitive development institute has its Isolation Protocol—sometimes they are called by different names. Old Eastwood called it "the silence chamber;" Stonebridge called it "the neural dampeners;" elsewhere it was called "the void," "the disconnect," "the freeze." When you're in it, you don't much care what it is called; it is a place for punishment.

And punishment is what you get.

Sector Z in Foxwood Cognitive Development Institute was the disciplinary sector, and because of the white isolation suits its inhabitants wore, it was called the Whiteout. It was a community of its own, an enclave within the larger city-state that was the Dome. And like any other community, it had its leading citizens... two of them. Their names were Lena Moore and Aisha Hughes.

Andre Bradley heard them before she reached the Whiteout. He was in a detachment of three unfortunates like himself, convoyed by an irritable guard, climbing the steel steps toward Sector Z from the floor below, when he heard the screaming.

"Owoo-o-o," screamed Moore from one end of the sector and "Yow-w-w!" shrieked Hughes at the other.

The inside deck guard of Sector Z looked nervously at the outside deck guard. The outside guard looked impassively back—after all, she was on the outside.

The inside guard muttered: "Manual rats! They're getting on my nerves."

The outside guard shrugged.

"Detail, halt!" The two guards turned to see what was coming in as the three new candidates for the Whiteout slumped to a stop at the head of the stairs. "Here they are," Morris told them. "Take good care of them, will you? Especially the man—he's going to like it here, because there's plenty of Manuals and Enhanceds and Synthetics to keep him company." He laughed coarsely and abandoned his charges to the Sector Z guards.

The outside guard said sourly: "A Natural, for God's sake. Now Obrien knows I hate it when there's a Natural in here. It gets the others all riled up."

"Let them in," the inside guard told her. "The others are riled up already."

Andre Bradley looked carefully at the floor and paid them no attention. The outside guard pulled the switch that turned on the neural dampening fields that swamped the floor of the sector corridor and of each individual cell. While the fields were on, you could ignore the residents—they simply could not move fast enough, against the cognitive drag of the field, to do any harm. But it was a rule that, even in Sector Z, you didn't leave the dampener fields on all the time—only when the cell doors had to be opened or a resident's restraining garment removed.

Andre walked bravely forward through the opened gate—and fell flat on his face. It was his first experience of a neural dampening field. It was like thinking through molasses.

The guard guffawed and lifted him up by one shoulder. "Take it easy, brother. Come on, get in your cell." She steered him in the right direction and pointed to a white isolation suit on the cell platform. "Put that on. Being as you're a Natural, we won't activate it fully, but the rules say you got to wear it and the rules—Hey. He's crying!" She shook her head, marveling. It was the first time she had ever seen a resident cry in the Whiteout.

However, she was wrong. Andre's shoulders were shaking, but not from tears. Andre Bradley had got a good look at Moore and at Hughes as he passed them by and he was fighting off an almost uncontrollable urge to retch.

Moore and Hughes were what are called institute predators. They were Manual Laborers—"Manuals," for short—or, at any rate, they had been once. They had spent so much time in institutes that it was sometimes hard even for them to remember what they really were, outside. Moore was a big, grinning woman with eyes like a predatory bird. Hughes was a lithe five-footer with the build of a predatory bird—and the sad, vacant eyes of livestock.

Moore stopped yelling for a moment. "Hey, Hughes!"

"What do you want, Moore?" called Hughes from her own cell.

"We got a Natural with us! Maybe we ought to cut out this yelling so as not to disturb the Natural!" She screeched with howling, maniacal laughter. "Anyway, if we don't cut this out, they'll get us in trouble, Hughes!"

"Oh, you think so?" shrieked Hughes. "Jeez, I wish you hadn't said that, Moore. You got me scared! I'm so scared, I'm gonna have to yell!"

The howling started all over again.

The inside guard finished putting the new residents away and turned off the dampener field once more. She licked her lips. "Say, you want to take a turn in here for a while?"

"Uh-uh." The outside guard shook her head.

"You're yellow," the inside guard said moodily. "Ah, I don't know why I don't quit this lousy job. Hey, you! Pipe down or I'll come in and beat your head off!"

"Ee-ee-ee!" screamed Moore in a shrill falsetto. "I'm scared!" Then she grinned at the guard, all but her predatory eyes. "Don't you know you can't hurt a Manual by hitting them on the head, Boss?"

"Shut up!" yelled the inside guard.

Andre Bradley's distress now was genuine. He simply could not help it. The crazy yowling of the hard-timers, Moore and Hughes, was getting under his skin. They weren't even—even human, he told himself miserably, trying to maintain composure silently so as not to give the guards the satisfaction of seeing him break—they were animals!

Resentment and anger, he could understand. He told himself doggedly that resentment and anger were natural and right. They were perfectly normal expressions of the freedom-loving citizen's rebellion against the vile and stifling system of Cognitive Classes. It was good that Moore and Hughes still had enough spirit to struggle against the vicious system—

But did they have to scream so?

The senseless yelling was driving him crazy. He abandoned himself to distress and he didn't even care who saw him any more. Senseless!

It never occurred to Andre Bradley that it might not be senseless, because noise hides noise. But then he hadn't been a resident very long.

III

Obrien walked into the upper office suite, the one with windows overlooking the compound. The woman behind the desk was pouring herself a cup of steaming black coffee.

"I smell trouble," said Obrien.

"Trouble? Trouble?" Megan Wilson clutched her throat and her little round eyes looked terrified—as perhaps they should have. Wilson had been at the institute longer than anyone could remember, though privately she was a fussy old woman trying to hold onto the last decent job she would have in her life.

"Trouble? What trouble?"

Obrien shrugged. "Different things. You know Nathan, from Sector A? This afternoon, he was engaged in creative collaboration with the maintenance orderlies in the compound."

Wilson, faintly relieved, faintly annoyed, scolded: "Obrien, what did you want to worry me for? There's nothing wrong with creative collaboration in the compound. That's what integration periods are for."

"You don't see what I mean. Nathan was a Natural on the outside—an architect. Those maintenance residents were Manual Laborers. Naturals and Manuals don't mix; it isn't natural according to epistemology. And there are other things."

Obrien hesitated, frowning. How could you explain that it didn't feel right?

"For instance—Well, there's Valentina in the women's sector. She's a pretty good old resident—that's why she's the sector orderly. She's a lifer, she's got no place to go, she gets along with the other women. But today she put a man named Bradley on report. Why? Because she told Bradley to process in Manual talk and Bradley didn't understand. Now Valentina wouldn't—"

Wilson raised her hand. "Please, Obrien, don't bother me about that kind of stuff." She sighed heavily and rubbed her eyes. She reached in a desk drawer for something, hesitated, glanced at Obrien, then dropped a pale blue tablet into the cup. She drank it down eagerly, ignoring the scalding heat.

She leaned back, looking suddenly happier and much more assured.

"Obrien, you handle the residents, and I handle my responsibilities. Your job is just as important as my job," she said piously. "Everybody's job is just as important as everybody else's, right? But we have to stick to our own jobs. We don't want to try to pass."

Obrien snapped erect, abruptly angry. Pass! What the devil way was that for Wilson to talk to her?

"Excuse the expression, Obrien," Wilson said anxiously. "I mean, after all, 'Specialization is the goal of civilization,' right?" She was a great woman for platitudes, was Wilson. "You know you don't want to worry about my end of things. And I don't want to worry about yours. You see?" And she folded her hands and smiled like a Natural Cognitive Buddha.

Obrien choked back her temper. "I'm telling you that there's trouble coming up. I sense the signs."

"Handle it, then!" snapped Wilson, irritated at last.

"But suppose it's too big to handle. Suppose—"

"It isn't," Wilson said positively. "Don't borrow trouble with all your supposing, Obrien." She sipped the remains of her coffee, made a wry face, poured a fresh cup and, with an elaborate show of not noticing what she was doing, dropped three of the pale blue tablets into it this time.

She sat beaming into space, waiting for the jolt to take effect.

"Well, then," she said at last. "You just remember what I've told you tonight, Obrien, and we'll get along fine. 'Specialization is the— Oh, curse the thing."

Her phone was ringing. Wilson picked it up irritably.

That was the trouble with those pale blue tablets, thought Obrien; they gave you a lift, but they put you on edge.

"Hello," barked Wilson, not even glancing at the viewscreen. "What do you want? Don't you know I'm—What? You did what? You're going to WHAT?"

She looked at the viewscreen at last with a look of pure horror. Whatever she saw on it, it did not reassure her. Her eyes opened like clamshells in a steamer.

"Obrien," she said faintly, "my mistake."

And she hung up—more or less by accident; the handset dropped from her fingers.

The person on the other end of the phone was calling from Sector Z.

Five minutes before, she hadn't been anywhere near the phone and it didn't look as if her chances of ever getting near it were very good. Because five minutes before, she was in her cell, with the rest of the hard-timers of the Whiteout.

Her name was Moore.

She was still yelling. Andre Bradley, in the cell across from her, thought that maybe, after all, the woman was really in pain. Maybe the crazy screams were screams of agony, because certainly her face was the face of an agonized person.

The outside guard bellowed: "Okay, okay. Take ten!"

Andre froze, waiting to see what would happen. What actually did happen was that the guard reached up and closed the switch that actuated the dampener fields on the floors of the cells. The institute rules were humanitarian, even for the dregs that inhabited the Whiteout. Ten minutes out of every two hours, even the worst case had to be allowed to take their hands out of the restraining garment.

"Rest period" it was called—in the rule book. The residents had a less lovely term for it.

At the guard's yell, the residents jumped to their feet.

Bradley was a little slow getting off the edge of the steel-slat platform—nobody had warned him that the eddy currents in the dampener fields had a way of making metal smoke-hot. He gasped but didn't cry out. Score one more painful lesson in his new language course. He rubbed his legs gingerly—and slowly, slowly, for the eddy currents did not permit you to move fast. It was like pushing against rubber; the faster you tried to move, the greater the resistance.

The guard peered genially into his cell. "You're okay, brother." He proudly ignored her as she slogged deliberately away on her rounds. She didn't have to untie him and practically stand over him while he attended to various personal matters, as she did with the female residents. It was not much to be grateful for, but Andre Bradley was grateful. At least he didn't have to live quite like a Synthetic—like an underprivileged Transcended Intelligence, he told himself, conscience-stricken.

Across the hall, the guard was saying irritably: "What the hell's the matter with you?" She opened the door of the cell with an insulated key held in a protective glove.

Moore was in that cell and she was doubled over.

The guard looked at her doubtfully. It could be a trick, maybe. Couldn't it? But she could see Moore's face and the agony in it was real enough. And Moore was gasping, through real tears: "Cramps. I—I—"

"Ah, you Manuals always got a pain in the gut." The guard lumbered around Moore to the fasteners at the back of the suit. Funny smell in here, she told herself—not for the first time. And imagine, some people didn't believe that Manuals had a smell of their own! But this time, she realized cloudily, it was a rather unusual smell. Something burning. Almost like flesh scorching.

It wasn't pleasant. She finished unfastening Moore and turned away; let the stinking Manual take care of her own troubles. She only had ten minutes to get all the way around Sector Z and the residents complained like crazy if she didn't make sure they all got the most possible free time. She was pretty good at moving through the dampener field. She was a little vain about it, even; at times she had been known to boast of her ability to make the rounds in two minutes, every time.

Every time but this.

For Moore moaned behind her, oddly close.

The guard turned, but not quickly enough. There was Moore—astonishingly, she was half out of her suit; her arms hadn't been in the sleeves at all! And in one of the hands, incredibly, there was something that glinted and smoked.

"All right," croaked Moore, tears trickling out of eyes nearly shut with pain.

But it wasn't the tears that held the guard; it was the shining, smoking thing, now poised at her throat. A weapon! It looked as though it had been made out of a platform support, ripped loose from its frame God knows how, hidden inside the white isolation suit God knows how—filed, filed to sharpness over endless hours.

No wonder Moore moaned—the eddy currents in the weapon were slowly cooking her hand; and the blister against her abdomen, where the weapon had been hidden during other rest periods, felt like raw acid.

"All right," whispered Moore, "just walk out the door and you won't get hurt. Unless the other guard makes trouble, you won't get hurt, so tell her not to, you hear?"

She was nearly fainting with the pain.

But she hadn't let go.

She didn't let go. And she didn't stop.

IV

It was Moore on the phone—Moore with her eyes still streaming tears, Moore with Hughes standing right behind her, menacing the two bound deck guards.

Hughes shoved Moore out of the way. "Hey, you in the office!" she said, and the voice was a cheerful bray, though the predatory eyes were cold and hating. "You got to get a medic in here. My friend Moore, she hurt herself real bad and she needs a doctor." She gestured playfully at the guards with the weapon. "I tell you. I got this blade and I got your guards here. Enough said? So get a medic in here quick, you hear?"

And she snapped the connection.

Obrien said: "I told you I sensed trouble!"

Wilson lifted her head, glared, started feebly to speak, hesitated, and picked up the long-distance phone. She said to the institute operator: "Get me the governor—fast."

Riot!

The word spread out from the institute on seven-league boots.

It snatched the city governor out of a friendly game of Political Economy with his manager and their spouses—and just when he was holding the Infrastructure Card concealed in reserve.

It broke up the Regional Championship Research Ethics Finals at the Evergreen Academy to the south, as half the contestants had to respond in earnest to an Alert that was real.

It reached to security stations and media centers and checkpoint barriers, and from there it filtered into the homes and lives of the nineteen million persons that lived within a few dozen miles of the Dome.

Riot. And yet fewer than half a dozen people were involved.

A handful of people, and the enormous bulk of the city-state quivered in every cognitive class and sector. In its ten million homes, in its hundreds of thousands of public places, the city-state's people shook under the impact of the news from the institute.

For the news touched them where their fears lay. Riot! And not merely a street conflict among unruly Manuals, or a facility dispute of Enhanceds stressed from a hard day at the plant. The riot was down among the corrupt elements that underlay the state itself. Manuals brawled with Manuals and no one cared; but in the Dome, all classes were cast together.

Forty miles to the south, Evergreen Academy was a blaze of light. The security personnel tumbled out of their quarters and common rooms at the screech of the alert siren, and behind them their families stretched and yawned and worried. An alert! The older kids fussed and complained and their parents shut them up. No, there wasn't any alert scheduled for tonight; no, they didn't know where the parent on duty was going; no, the kids couldn't get up yet—it was the middle of the night.

And as soon as they had the kids back in bed, most of the off-duty parents struggled into their own security uniforms and headed for the briefing area to hear.

They caught the words from a distance—not quite correctly. "Riot!" gasped a security officer first-class, parent of three. "The Manuals! I told Charlie they'd get out of hand and—Alex, we aren't safe. You know how they are about Natural families! I'm going right home and getting a weapon and standing right by the door and—"

"Weapon!" snapped Alex, surveillance-sergeant, with two children querulously awake in their nursery at home. "What in God's name is the use of a weapon? You can't hurt a Manual by conventional means. You'd better come along to Supply with me and draw neural disruptors—you'll need them before this night is over."

But the security personnel themselves heard the briefing loud and clear over the alert speakers, and they knew it was not merely a matter of trouble in the Manual quarters. The Dome! The governor himself had called them out; they were to fly interdicting missions at such-and-such levels on such-and-such flight circuits around the institute.

It had started with that phone call from Wilson's office—the call that reached the governor's attention because Wilson had a direct line that bypassed the usual channels. Obrien had often wondered about that line, had once asked about getting one herself. "That's not how it works," Wilson had said, looking faintly amused. "You file your reports. They go through the oversight board. That's the proper way." When Obrien had pressed, Wilson had only shrugged. "Some things are above your level, Obrien. Don't take it personally."

The high-speed transports took off on cushions of air; and the surveillance drones took off with a humming roar; and last of all, the hovercrafts took off... and they were the ones who might actually accomplish something. They took up their observation posts on the institute perimeter, a pilot and two operators in each hovercraft, stone-faced, staring grimly alert at the institute below.

They were ready for the breakout.

But there wasn't any breakout.

The transports went home for fuel. The drones went home for recharging. The hovercrafts hung on—still ready, still waiting.

The transports came back and circled harmlessly about, and went away again. They stayed away. The hovercraft personnel never faltered and never relaxed. The institute below them was washed with light—from the guard posts on the walls, from the residential sectors themselves, from the mobile lights of the guard squadrons surrounding the walls.

North of the institute, on the long, flat, organized developments of planned land, the modular row houses of the Natural Cognitive neighborhoods showed lights in every window as the Naturals stood ready to repel invasion from their undesired neighbors to the east, the Manuals. In the crowded housing of the laborers' quarters, the Manuals shouted from window to window; and there were crowds in the bright streets.

"The whole bloody thing's going to blow up!" a hovercraft operator yelled bitterly to her pilot, above the hum and roar of the hovering engines. "Look at the mobs in Manual Quarter! The first breakout from the Dome's going to start a conflict like you never saw and we'll be right in the middle of it!"

She was partly right. She would be right in the middle of it—for every person in the city-state would be right in the middle of it. There was no place anywhere that would be spared.

No mixing. That was the prescription that kept the city-state alive. There's no harm in a family conflict—and aren't all Enhanceds a family, aren't all Manuals a clan, aren't all Naturals and Cognitives related by closer ties than blood or genetics?

But the declassed residents of the Dome were the dregs of every class; and once they spread, the neat compartmentation of society was pierced. The breakout would mean riot on a bigger scale than any institute had ever known.

But she was also partly wrong. Because the breakout wasn't seeming to come.

V

Back in the hastily-organized command center, Obrien coordinated the internal response. She had sector monitors reporting to her from every wing, guards checking in on the quarter-hour, medical teams standing by. This was what she did—managed the daily machinery of the institute, kept the gears turning, handled the thousand small decisions that kept ten thousand residents fed and housed and controlled.

"The situation in Sector Z is contained," Obrien reported to a monitor who'd asked for guidance. "Moore and Hughes have the two guards, but they're not going anywhere. What they want is medical attention and they'll get it—eventually. Right now we wait them out."

The monitor nodded, then hesitated. "Should I check with anyone else? About the waiting, I mean?"

"I'm telling you how we're handling it," Obrien said flatly. "You want to go running upstairs every time there's a decision to make?"

"No, Administrator." The monitor hurried off.

That was how things worked at Foxwood. Obrien gave the orders that mattered inside the walls. She assigned the sectors, approved the isolation protocols, ran the rehabilitation programs. When a resident needed discipline, it was Obrien who handed it down. When a guard had a question, it was Obrien who answered it. She was the one who walked the compound floors, knew the residents by name, sensed the trouble before it started.

Wilson, meanwhile, was in her office with a representative who had arrived by emergency transport. The man had asked for Wilson specifically when he landed—had asked by name, as if he knew exactly who to speak with about matters beyond the institute's walls. They'd been in there for hours.

Obrien had tried to brief the representative herself when he first arrived. She'd stopped him in the corridor, started explaining the tactical situation in Sector Z, the disposition of guards, the likely trajectory of the standoff.

He'd cut her off. "I need to speak with Wilson."

"I can tell you everything about the current situation—"

"I'm sure you can. But I need Wilson." And he'd walked past her without another word.

It stung. Obrien had been in the institute for fifteen years. She knew every corridor, every resident, every weakness in the security protocols. She was the one who'd first spotted the instability, who'd tried to warn Wilson hours before the crisis broke. And yet when the representative from the governor's office arrived, he walked past her like she was furniture.

She told herself it didn't matter. What mattered was handling the crisis. What mattered was the ten thousand souls behind these walls, and she was the one who knew how to manage them.

From down the hall, she could hear Wilson's voice rising in pitch—that defensive, almost pleading tone she got when she was talking to people who outranked her. Then the representative's voice, calm and authoritative, asking questions about protocols, about liability, about what the regional council would think.

Obrien turned back to her monitors. Let Wilson handle the politics. Someone had to run the institute.

The standoff in Sector Z dragged on through the night. Moore and Hughes kept the guards. The medical team waited at the sector entrance, unable to enter. Obrien coordinated the waiting—positioned guards at key junctions, kept the other residents calm, made sure the supply lines stayed open.

Around three in the morning, a young guard approached her with a clipboard. "Administrator, we need authorization for the extended shift payments. The overnight crew is asking about hazard compensation."

"Approved," Obrien said, initialing the form.

"Also—" the guard hesitated. "There's been a request from the regional oversight board. They want documentation of all decisions made during the crisis. They're asking who authorized the containment strategy."

Obrien paused. The containment strategy had been her call—wait them out, don't escalate, let Moore and Hughes realize they had nowhere to go. It was the right call. She was sure of it.

But documentation for the oversight board meant accountability, and accountability meant—

"Tell them to submit a formal request through the proper channels," she said. "We'll respond when the crisis is resolved."

The guard nodded and left.

Obrien rubbed her temples. Somewhere upstairs, Wilson was probably signing forms of her own—different forms, the kind that went to the governor's office, the kind that would determine how this night was remembered by the people who mattered.

Two women, two different kinds of work. Obrien wondered, not for the first time, which kind mattered more.

By dawn, Moore had collapsed from her injuries. Hughes, seeing her partner unconscious and the medical team finally rushing in, had dropped the weapon without a fight. The guards were freed, shaken but unharmed. The crisis was over.

Obrien supervised the cleanup, the incident reports, the debriefing of the guards. She checked on Andre Bradley, still in his cell, still wearing the white suit, looking even more haunted than before. She walked the compound floors as the sun came up, making sure everything was back in order.

When she finally made it upstairs, Wilson's office was empty. The governor's representative was long gone. On Wilson's desk, Obrien saw a stack of documents—forms and authorizations, stamped and signed, bearing Wilson's signature and the seal of the regional council.

The forms authorized everything: the containment strategy, the medical response, the guard deployments. Everything Obrien had decided, now officially approved and documented. Wilson's name on every page.

Obrien stared at the documents for a long moment. Then she turned and walked back to the compound floors. There was always more work to do.
quality_problem.question: Who was the director of the Foxwood Cognitive Development Institute?

quality_problem.story:
The Singing Clock Tower
CHAPTER I
An Unsolved Mystery

"Tell Olivia about it," begged Nora. "Please, Lucy, it can't be as bad as it appears. There isn't anything that Olivia can't figure out."

Lucy tilted her head disdainfully. "We're colleagues now. We're both working on the Glendale Regional Arts Council and should support each other. But you always did take Olivia's side. She was the one who nearly disrupted our joint performance trying to solve a mystery. I don't believe she'd understand—understand any better than I do. Everyone has problems, and I'm sure Olivia is no exception."

"You're right, Lucy," announced Olivia, coming in to serve tea to the two friends she had invited for lunch at Thomas's suggestion. "I do have problems, and there are plenty of mysteries I can't solve."

"Name one," challenged Nora. "Just mention one single strange thing you couldn't explain, and I'll believe you. I've seen you in action, Olivia Lane—"

"Olivia Hill, remember?"

"Well, you were Olivia Lane when you solved all those mysteries. I met you when the whole Glendale Region was threatened by the controversial dam project and you solved that—"

"That," declared Olivia, "was my brother Juan, not me. He was the hero without even meaning to be. He was the one who spoke at the town council meeting and convinced them to reconsider. I was off chasing shadows."

"A vanishing shadow," Nora said with a sigh. "What you did wasn't easy, Olivia."

"It didn't need to be as hard as it was," Olivia confessed. "I know now that keeping that promise not to talk about the environmental impact study was a great big mistake and could have cost the region its heritage sites. I should have told Steven."

"Please," Lucy said, a pained expression clouding her pretty face, "let's not talk about him now."

Nora glanced at Lucy with concern, but said nothing. She had noticed Lucy's reluctance to discuss certain topics before.

"Very well," Olivia agreed. "What shall we talk about?"

"You," Nora said, "and all the mysteries you've solved. Maybe you were mistaken about a thing or two before the dam controversy, but what about the haunted theater you investigated? You were the one who tracked down the strange occurrences backstage and in the orchestra pit and goodness knows where all. You've been chasing mysteries ever since I met you, and not one of them did you fail to explain in some sensible, logical fashion."

"Before I met you," Olivia said, thinking back, "there were plenty of them I couldn't explain. There was one I used to call the spirit of the clock tower, but what it was or how it sang to me is more than I know. If my grandparents knew, they weren't telling. And now they're both gone and I can't ask them. They left me a lot of unsolved mysteries along with this house. Maybe I'll find the answers to some of them when I finish sorting Grandmother's things. They're stored in one end of the attic."

"Another mysterious attic? How thrilling!" exclaimed Nora. "Why don't you investigate and expose the truth?"

"I didn't say the attic was mysterious."

Olivia was almost sorry she had mentioned it. She wasn't in the mood for digging up old mysteries, but Nora and Lucy insisted. It all began, she finally told them, the summer before they met. Juan had just started working on the regional newspaper. Olivia remembered that it was Lucy's father, Richard Stone, who gave him his job with the Glendale Regional Herald. He had turned in some interesting coverage of a local arts festival, convincing Mr. Stone that he had in him the makings of a good reporter. And so it was that he spent the summer Olivia was remembering in Cliffside where the wealthy families had their estates, while she had to suffer the heat and loneliness of Maplewood.

Her thoughts were what had made it so hard, she confessed now as she reviewed everything that had happened. She just couldn't help resenting the fact that her parents left her every summer while they went off on a cultural exchange program by themselves. What did they think she would do?

"You'll have plenty to read," her father had told her. "I bought you six new books in that mystery series you like. When they're finished there are plenty of old programs and playbills around. Your grandmother never throws anything away. She has theater memorabilia she's saved since your mother was a girl. If you ask for them she'll let you have the whole collection. I know how you love the performing arts."

"I do, Dad, but if the programs are that old—"

Olivia had stopped. She had seen her father's tired eyes and had realized that a busy professor needed a vacation much more than a student who had too little to do. He and Olivia's mother usually went to the international arts conference where they had met. It was a precious memory. Every summer Professor Lane and his wife relived it. And every summer Olivia went to stay with her grandmother Hill, who scolded and fussed and tried to pretend she wasn't glad to have her.

"You here again?" she had greeted her that summer, and Olivia hadn't noticed her old eyes twinkling behind her glasses. "What do you propose to do with yourself this time?"

"Read," Olivia had told her. "Mom and Dad say you have a whole collection of old theater programs—"

"In the attic. Go up and look them over if you can stand the heat."

Olivia went, not to look over the old programs so much as to escape to a place where she could have a good cry. It was the summer before her fifteenth birthday. In another year she would have outgrown her childish resentment of her parents' vacation or be grown up enough to ask them to let her have a vacation of her own. In another year she would be summering at the prestigious Evergreen Arts Academy and solving a mystery to be known as the Phantom Performance.

"A whole series of strange events," Nora would be telling her, "and you solved everything."

But then she didn't even know Nora. She had no idea so many thrilling adventures awaited her. There seemed to be nothing—nothing—and so the tears came and spilled over on one of the programs. As Olivia wiped it away she noticed that it had fallen on a picture of a clock tower.

"A clock tower with musical notes floating from it. How strange!" she remembered saying aloud.

Olivia had never seen a real singing clock tower. The thrill of walking up to the door of the palatial arts center in Cliffside was still ahead of her. On the grounds a clock tower still chimed melodies like those she was to hear on her honeymoon in the musical district of Galdoria's capital. But all that was in the future. If anyone had told the freckled-faced, ponytailed girl that she would one day marry Thomas Hill, she would have laughed in their faces.

"That tease!"

For then she knew Thomas only as an older boy who used to tease her and call her bookworm until one day she yelled back at him, "Bookworms are intelligent and so am I!"

Thomas was to win Olivia's heart when he gave her a music box and suggested she keep it forever. The music box was now a treasured keepsake. But the summer Olivia found the picture of a clock tower and spilled tears on it she had no music box. She had nothing, she confessed, not even a friend. It had helped to pretend the clock tower in the picture was filled with all the songs lonely girls like herself had ever wished to hear.

"But that would make it enchanted!" she had suddenly exclaimed. "If I could find it I'd wish—"

A step had sounded on the stairs. Olivia remembered it distinctly. She had turned to see her grandmother and to hear her say in her usual abrupt fashion, "Enchanted clock tower, indeed! If you let people know your wishes instead of muttering them to yourself, most of them aren't so impossible."

"Were they?" asked Nora.

She and Lucy had listened to this much of what Olivia was telling them without interruption.

"That's the unsolved mystery," Olivia replied. "There weren't any of them impossible."

And she went on to tell them how, the very next day, her grandparents had taken her to a clock tower exactly like the one in the picture. It was in the center of a beautiful arts complex with gardens leading up to it. Beside the main path were smaller sculptures with water features. Olivia had stared at them a moment and then climbed the steps to the tower.

"Am I dreaming?" she remembered saying aloud. "Is this beautiful clock tower real?"

A voice had answered, although she could see no one.

"Make your wishes, Olivia. Wish wisely. If you sing a note at the tower your wishes will surely come true."

"A note?" Olivia had asked. "How can I sing when I'm so amazed? This is a wonderful place."

"Sing a note at the tower and your wishes will surely come true," the voice had repeated.

"But what should I sing?"

"You found plenty to cry about back at your grandmother's house," the mysterious voice had reminded her. "Weren't you crying on my picture up there in the attic?"

"Then you—you are the clock tower!" Olivia remembered exclaiming. "But a clock tower doesn't speak. It doesn't have a voice."

"Wish wisely," the voice from the tower had said in a mysterious whisper.

CHAPTER II
If Wishes Came True

"Did you?" Nora interrupted the story to ask excitedly. "Oh, Olivia! Don't keep us in suspense any longer. What did you wish?"

"Patience," Olivia said with a smile. "I'm coming to that."

First, she told her friends, she had to think of a wise wish. There had been so much she wanted in those early days before the dam controversy. Her best friend had moved away.

"You see," she explained, "I made the mistake of having just one best friend. There wasn't anybody in Maplewood. I remember thinking of how lonely I was and how I wished for friends and opportunities, and suddenly I began to hum a melody. It echoed in the tower. I thought I had to wish quickly before it faded, and so I began naming the things I wanted as fast as I could. I'm not sure they were wise wishes. They seem rather selfish to me, now. I wasn't thinking of anybody but me, Olivia Lane, and what I wanted. It wasn't until after I began to think of others that my wishes started to come true."

"But what were they?" Nora insisted.

Lucy seemed unusually quiet and thoughtful. Olivia did not notice the concern in her eyes as she replied airily, "Oh, didn't I tell you? I wished for lots of friends and opportunities in the performing arts, and I wished I could marry someone who worked in justice theory or conflict resolution and solve a lot of mysteries and that's as far as I got when the echo vanished. I thought the spell was broken and so I didn't wish for anything more."

"Wasn't there anything more you wanted?" Nora asked.

"Of course," replied Olivia. "There were lots more things. I wanted to travel, of course, and work in media production, and have a nice home, and—"

"And your wishes all came true!"

"Every one of them," Olivia agreed. "Thomas did become a mediator specializing in conflict resolution, and I did get involved in the performing arts. That seemed impossible at the time, but the future did hold all of it for me."

"Strange how things work out," Nora said, squeezing Lucy's hand under the table. "Don't you think friends should tell each other their problems, Olivia?"

"Thomas and I always do," she replied, "but then it was different. I didn't know I would marry Thomas or that he would become a mediator, and I didn't know about any of the opportunities that would come. It is strange, isn't it? But the strangest thing of all was the clock tower itself."

"Why?" asked Lucy. "Do you still think it was enchanted?"

Nora laughed at this, but Olivia was serious as she answered, "I was still young enough to think so at the time. I wandered around, growing very drowsy. Then I found a bench in the garden and sat down. I must have dozed off, because I remember waking up and wondering if the voice in the clock tower had been a dream."

"A bench?" Nora questioned. "Are you sure it wasn't a magic carpet?"

"No, it was a bench all right," Olivia assured her, laughing. "It was in a beautiful garden all surrounded by flowering hedges. Did I tell you it was June?"

"All the year around?"

Again Nora laughed. But Lucy said abruptly, "Let's not talk about gardens in June. It's a long way from June to December."

"Do you mean a garden changes? I know," Olivia said, "but I think this one would be beautiful at any time of the year. There were sculptures, too, and I don't know how many different kinds of plantings. I explored the garden all around the clock tower."

"And then what happened?" Lucy urged her.

"Yes, yes. Go on," entreated Nora. "I didn't dream you'd kept anything that exciting a secret. Why didn't you try to solve the mystery?"

"I think I would have tried," Olivia admitted, "if I had been older or more experienced. I really should have investigated it more thoroughly and learned the secret of the tower. But after the echo went away it didn't speak to me any more, and I didn't really think it had heard my wishes. I was still wishing for a friend when I met you, Nora. It did seem impossible for us to be friends at first, didn't it? Lucy was your friend."

"I did make trouble for you," Lucy remembered. "It was all because of my foolish jealousy."

"It was nothing compared to the trouble caused by the dam controversy," declared Olivia. "After that things started happening so fast that I completely forgot about the clock tower. Honestly, Nora, I don't believe I thought about it again until after we moved to Cliffside and I walked up to your door and saw the arts center on the hill."

"The old Cliffside landmark, I always called it," Nora said with a giggle. "I've seen lots nicer clock towers."

"You have?" asked Olivia. "Then maybe you've seen the one I've been telling you about. I think the picture of it is still in the attic. Come on up and I'll show you."

Nora and Lucy had finished their tea while Olivia was telling them the story of the clock tower. Somehow, she wasn't hungry for hers. She had tasted it too often while she was making it.

"I'll save it for later," she decided.

Nora watched as Olivia cleared the cups.

"Sometimes," Olivia said fondly, "I think about those old days and wonder what really happened."

"Let's go look at that picture," Nora said eagerly.

Leaving the table, they all started upstairs. In modernizing her grandparents' house to suit her own and Thomas's tastes, Olivia had seen to it that the old stair door was removed. But there was still a door closing off the narrower stairs that led to the attic.

"Come on. There's nothing up here to be afraid of," Olivia urged her friends.

"Maybe not, but I'm beginning to get curious," confessed Nora as she followed Olivia to the storage room at the top of the last flight of stairs.

"So am I," Lucy admitted. "I'm interested in seeing this mysterious picture."

"Up here we can all turn back the clock," Olivia said mysteriously. "Does anybody care to explore the past?"

The exploration began enthusiastically with Olivia relating still more of what she remembered about the clock tower.

"When I told Grandma about it she laughed and said I must have dreamed it. She said if wishes came true that easily she'd be living in a palace. But would she?" Olivia wondered. "When I first remember this house she was still using oil lamps. I think she and Grandpa liked the way they lived without any modern conveniences or anything."

"I think so, too," Nora agreed, looking around the old attic. "It is strange they both died the same winter, isn't it?"

"Maybe they wanted it that way. Maybe they wished neither of them would outlive the other. If they did wish at the tower," Olivia went on more thoughtfully, "I'm sure that was one of their wishes. Another could have been to keep the good old days, as Grandma used to call them. That one came true in a way. They did manage to keep a little of the past when they kept all these old things. That's what I meant about turning back the clock."

"If wishes came true I'd like to turn it back a little myself," Lucy began. "It would be nice if things were the way they used to be when I trusted Steven—"

"Don't you trust him now?" Olivia asked.

Afterwards she was sorry for the interruption. Nora and Olivia both questioned Lucy, but that was all she would say. Olivia wondered, as they searched through the old programs, what was wrong. Lucy was of a suspicious disposition. Was jealousy coming between her and her partner, Steven Richardson? Until now they had seemed to work well together. But there was no happiness in Lucy's face as she gazed at a picture of one of the clock towers and then said in a tight little voice, "It is. It's the very same one."

"But that's the picture I've been searching for!" Olivia said eagerly. "Do you know where it is?"

Lucy paused, her fingers tightening on the edge of the program. "I think I might have seen it somewhere before."

"Where?" Nora pressed eagerly.

"I can't quite remember," Lucy said. "These old towers all look alike after a while, don't they? Let's go," she added quickly to Nora. Olivia knew she was suggesting a fast trip home. But, apparently, Nora did not understand it that way. If she did, she pretended not to.

"Where?" she asked. "To the clock tower? I'd love to, wouldn't you, Olivia?"

"I certainly would," Olivia replied enthusiastically. "Do you recognize it, too?"

"I think so," Nora answered after studying a little more closely the picture they had found. "It looks like the tower on the Matthews estate."

"The technology company Matthews?" Olivia questioned. "Then my grandparents must have driven old Bessie all the way to the edge of Cliffside."

"Not quite all the way," Lucy said. "The Matthews own that stretch of woodland just before you come into the city. You've passed it lots of times."

"Of course," agreed Olivia. She put the program back in its place and turned eagerly to her friends. "I do remember a road turning off into the woods and going on uphill," she told them. "I never thought it led to a house, though. There isn't even a gate. Could that be the road my grandparents took?"

"Why don't we take it ourselves and find out?" Nora suggested.

CHAPTER III
A Strange Encounter

Lucy was not too enthusiastic about the proposed trip to the Matthews estate. Finally she agreed to it under one condition. They were not to drive all the way to the house which, she said, was just over the hilltop. They were to park the car where no one would see it and follow the path to the clock tower.

"But suppose we can't find the path?" asked Olivia.

"You'll remember it, won't you?"

Olivia thought she would, but she wasn't too sure. She and Nora both argued that it would be better to inquire at the house. Nora knew Pablo Matthews slightly.

"He'd be glad to show us around," Nora said as they started off in the blue car she was driving.

Lucy shifted uncomfortably in the back seat. "I'm not sure that's the best approach."

"Why ever not?" Nora asked, glancing at her in the rearview mirror.

"I just think we should be careful, that's all. Large estates can have all sorts of security measures."

It was a neat little car, not too conspicuous, and easy to park in out-of-the-way places. Olivia laughed and said if they did find the clock tower she thought she'd wish for one exactly like Nora's car.

"Well, you know what your grandmother said about wishes, don't you?" Lucy asked. "If you let people know about them instead of muttering them to yourself most of them aren't so impossible."

"Quite true," Olivia agreed. "I'll let Thomas know about this one. He's my gift-giver, and it will soon be the holidays. Maybe I should have worn the coat he gave me last year."

"Your jacket's better in case it rains. It's too warm for snow. We picked a perfect day for this trip," Nora continued, guiding the car around curves as it climbed the steep hill beyond Maplewood.

The trip was a short one. In twenty minutes they had covered the distance that had seemed such a long way to Olivia when she was riding in her grandfather's old truck.

"I've been thinking about it," she said, "and I've just about figured out how it happened. I didn't think my grandparents knew the Matthews well enough to pay them a visit, though. We must have looked odd driving up to a beautiful estate in Grandpa's old truck. I do remember that Grandma had some handmade quilts to deliver. But that still doesn't explain what happened afterwards. When I woke up on the bench I was alone in the garden. Truck, grandparents—all had disappeared."

"How could they?" asked Nora.

"Anyway," Lucy began, "you had a chance to see how beautiful everything was before—"

She stopped mid-sentence and turned to look out the window.

"Before what?" questioned Olivia.

"Before the seasons changed, I mean. Gardens look so different in winter." Lucy kept her gaze fixed on the passing trees. "You were telling us how you woke up on the bench, but you never did explain how you got back home."

"Didn't I?" asked Olivia. "I'd forgotten a lot of it, but it's beginning to come back now. I do remember driving home along this road. You see, I thought my grandparents had left me in the garden for a surprise and would return for me. I told you I was all alone. There wasn't a house in sight."

"The Matthews house is just over the top of this next hill," Nora put in.

"I know. You told me that. Now I know why I couldn't see it. All I could see was the old clock tower and a path leading in that direction. Naturally, I followed it. There's something about a path in the woods that always tempts me."

"We know that, Olivia. Thomas told us all about your latest mystery. You followed a trail or something."

"Well, this trail led out of the garden where the bench was and then through an archway," Olivia continued. "All sorts of little statues and ornaments peered out at me from unexpected places. I was actually nervous by the time I reached the old tower. There wasn't time to explore it. Just then I heard the rumble of my grandfather's truck and knew he was driving off without me."

"He was!" Olivia's friends both chorused in surprise, and Nora asked, "Why would he do a thing like that?"

"I think now it was just to tease me. He did stop and wait for me after a while," Olivia remembered. "The quilts were gone. Grandma must have delivered them, but I didn't ask where. If she made them for Mrs. Matthews they may still be there."

"The Matthews family has been going through changes lately," Lucy said, her voice measured. "Properties change hands. Things get redistributed."

"You seem to know a lot about the Matthews," Nora observed.

"Only what everyone knows," Lucy replied quickly. "The arts council has dealings with many families in the region."

"Watch out!" Olivia suddenly exclaimed. "There's another car coming."

As Nora swerved to avoid the oncoming car, Lucy turned her face toward the window, adjusting her scarf. The car passed them, driven by a man with intense, calculating eyes and sharp features. The dark cap he was wearing covered most of his hair.

Nora steadied the wheel. "That was close. Everyone all right?"

"Fine," Lucy said, still facing the window. "Just startled."

"You've gone quite pale," Olivia observed.

"It's the winding road. I've never been good with sudden turns." Lucy smiled, but her hands remained clasped tightly in her lap.

"Let's not go up there," Lucy said after a moment. "I'm not feeling well. Perhaps we could come back another day."

"But we've come all this way," Nora protested. "And you were so sure about where to park and which path to take. It's almost as if you've been here before."

"Haven't we all driven past this road dozens of times?" Lucy replied. "One picks things up."

"Maybe not, but we can pretend we think the Matthews still live here, can't we?" Olivia said. "If anyone asks, we're just old acquaintances paying a visit."

She was beginning to wonder about Lucy's familiarity with this place. Nora kept on driving along the narrow, gravelly road. Soon there were more evergreens and hedges to be seen. They looked very green next to the bare trees in the woods beyond. The sky was gray with white clouds being driven across it by the wind.

"There's the tower!" Lucy exclaimed. "I can see it over to the left. It looks like something out of a fairy tale, doesn't it?"

"It looks mysterious all right," agreed Olivia. "I wonder what it is."

"I suppose it's nothing but an old clock tower. It would be fun to explore it, though," Nora said. "But if there are new people living here they'll never give us permission."

"We might explore it without permission," Olivia suggested daringly. "Come on!" she urged her friends as Nora parked the car in a cleared place beside the road. "Who's going to stop us? And who wants to explore a gloomy old tower, anyway? Let's look for the garden."

"Do you think we should?" Lucy asked, glancing nervously up the road. "Perhaps we should wait until we know more about who lives here now."

"If you know anything about the people who live here now, I think you ought to let us know," Nora said. "Otherwise, I'm afraid we won't be very welcome."

Lucy hesitated. "I may have heard something at the arts council. Mohammad Hansen's name has come up in connection with this property. His family might have acquired it."

"Mohammad Hansen?" Olivia asked. "I remember him from the council meetings. Quiet fellow. What's his interest in this estate?"

"Business dealings, I suppose. The Matthews had financial difficulties after the scandal."

"What scandal?" Olivia pressed.

"You remember Pablo Matthews," Nora said with a sigh. "There was an investigation into electoral fraud. He manipulated voting records during the regional council elections. Falsified documents too."

Now Olivia did remember. It was something she would have preferred to forget. She liked to think she was a good judge of character, and she had taken Pablo Matthews for a quiet, principled person who would never stoop to corruption.

"I don't see what all this has to do with the clock tower," Nora said impatiently. "Are we going to look for it, or aren't we?"

"Of course we are. That's what we came for. I just like to know what I'm walking into before I walk into it," Olivia explained.

"You seem to think there's danger in this expedition of ours, don't you?" asked Lucy.

"I don't know what to think. You seem to know this area quite well, but you haven't said how."

Lucy studied her fingernails. "The arts council has business throughout the region. One becomes familiar with various properties."

"I'd better turn the car around," Nora decided, "in case we have to leave in a hurry. I don't expect we'll encounter any real danger, but we may be accused of trespassing."

"I'm sure we will be," announced Olivia as two dark-coated figures strode down the road toward them. "You drove right by a NO TRESPASSING sign, and this isn't a welcoming committee coming to meet us!"

As the figures approached, Lucy drew back slightly, positioning herself behind Olivia. One of the men called out something, and Lucy's face went still.

"We should go," she said quietly. "Now."

"Do you know them?" Nora asked, already starting the engine.

"I've had some dealings with people connected to this property," Lucy admitted. "Through the council. It's complicated."

"Lucy," Olivia said slowly, "when Steven's name came up earlier, and just now with Mohammad Hansen—is there something connecting all of this?"

Lucy was quiet for a long moment as Nora backed the car around. "There are things I can't discuss. Council business. You understand."

"I understand that you've been very careful about what you say today," Olivia replied.

"We all have our reasons for discretion," Lucy said. "I'm sure you had yours when you kept that promise about the environmental impact study."

The comparison stung, but before Olivia could respond, the men had reached the car. One of them rapped on the window.

"This is private property," he said firmly. "You'll need to leave."

"Of course," Nora said smoothly. "We were just turning around. Old friends of the Matthews family—we didn't realize they'd moved."

The man's eyes swept over the three women, lingering on Lucy for a moment. "The Matthews haven't lived here for some time."

"Our mistake," Lucy said, her voice perfectly pleasant. "We'll be on our way."

As they drove back down the winding road, Nora caught Olivia's eye in the mirror. Lucy sat very still in the back seat, watching the clock tower disappear behind the trees.

"That man seemed to recognize you, Lucy," Nora ventured.

"Did he? I didn't notice." Lucy pulled out a compact and checked her reflection, as if the matter were already forgotten. "We should do this again sometime. When we have proper permission, of course."

The car wound its way back toward Maplewood, and Olivia found herself thinking about the afternoon—Lucy's reaction when Steven's name came up, her knowledge of this estate's layout, her careful positioning when the car had passed earlier, her measured responses about the council's business. Each thing by itself seemed ordinary enough. Lucy had always been reserved, even guarded. It was simply her nature.

But as they drove in silence, Olivia couldn't help but wonder what Lucy's work with the arts council really involved, and whether the mysteries of the old clock tower might be the least of the secrets hidden on that estate.
quality_problem.story_title:
The Haunted Fountain
A Judy Bolton Mystery
quality_problem.question: Of the three women, who seems to be keeping more secrets than the others?

quality_problem.story:
The briefing room fell silent as Colonel Antonio Foster stepped to the podium. Outside, the Lethorian sun beat down on the dusty compound, but inside, the air conditioning hummed steadily, keeping the assembled officers comfortable as they waited for the intelligence update.

"Good morning," Foster began, his voice carrying the weight of twenty years in uniform. "Today we're discussing a significant shift in how we handle classified intelligence dissemination within theater. I'm calling it Open Intelligence Access, or OIA."

Major Paul Sanders leaned forward in his seat, intrigued. As the base's senior intelligence officer, any changes to information sharing protocols fell squarely within his domain.

Foster continued, "For decades, we've operated under a system where intelligence reports were tightly controlled, distributed only through official channels, with access restricted based on clearance levels and need-to-know. This made sense in the era of paper reports and courier pouches. But we're now in an age of digital networks and instantaneous communication. The technology has created what I'm calling an access revolution."

He clicked to the next slide, which displayed a simple diagram showing information flow patterns.

"Digital technologies allow us to make perfect copies of intelligence products. Our secure networks allow us to share these copies across the entire theater of operations at essentially no cost. About fifteen years ago, this kind of sharing became technically feasible. Before that, it would have seemed impossible."

Captain Nicole Leonard, the base's logistics officer, raised her hand. "Sir, I understand the technical capability, but why would intelligence officers want to share their analysis so broadly? Doesn't that undermine their value?"

Foster nodded, anticipating the question. "That's exactly the misconception I want to address. Let's think about a specific subset of intelligence personnel—those who produce analytical products. These analysts aren't writing reports to sell them. They're not compensated based on how many people read their work. They're paid salaries by the military to produce analysis that advances our operational effectiveness."

He paused, letting that sink in. "These analysts write for impact, not for personal gain. They want their insights to reach decision-makers at every level. When we restrict access to their work, we're actually harming their professional goals. We're limiting their impact and reducing the operational value of their analysis."

Lieutenant Jana Silva, who had spent three years as an intelligence analyst at Blackwood before her recent transfer, spoke up from her seat near the back. "Sir, at Blackwood, we had excellent analytical capabilities and robust information sharing within the base. What would OIA change?"

"Great question, Lieutenant, and it gets to the heart of why we need theater-wide reform," Foster replied. "Blackwood does excellent work. So does this base. So do the teams at Parkview and Crystalbrook. But how much of Blackwood's analysis reaches us here? How much of our work reaches them? The barriers aren't between analysts and their local commanders—they're between bases."

Lieutenant Laura Little, a young intelligence analyst, added, "But sir, what about operational security? Aren't we talking about classified material?"

"Excellent question," Foster replied. "I should clarify. Open Intelligence Access doesn't mean making classified material public. It means removing unnecessary barriers to access within our cleared community—everyone operating in theater with appropriate clearances. We're talking about eliminating the arbitrary restrictions that prevent a platoon leader in Parkview from accessing the same threat analysis available to a battalion commander in Crystalbrook."

He advanced to the next slide, which outlined the concept more formally.

"OIA is defined as intelligence products that are digital, available on our secure networks, free of bureaucratic access barriers, and free of most distribution restrictions within the cleared community. We're removing two specific barriers: clearance-level inflation and permission-seeking requirements."

Major Sanders interjected, "Can you elaborate on clearance-level inflation?"

"Certainly. Too often, intelligence products are classified at higher levels than necessary, not because the content requires it, but because it's easier to over-classify than to carefully evaluate appropriate classification. A report that should be SECRET gets marked TOP SECRET. This creates an artificial scarcity. When an analyst needs to review dozens of reports for a single assessment, or when a planning cell needs access to hundreds of products to develop an operation, these inflated classifications become insurmountable barriers."

Silva nodded vigorously. "At Blackwood, I saw this constantly. Reports I wrote at SECRET would get bumped to TOP SECRET by distribution officers who never read them. Then analysts at other bases couldn't access work that should have been available to them."

"Exactly the problem," Foster confirmed, pointing at Silva. "And the Lieutenant's experience at Blackwood illustrates why we chose that installation as one of our pilot sites. They've already identified these barriers. They're ready for change."

He moved to discuss the second barrier. "Permission-seeking is equally problematic. Even when you have the right clearance, you often need special permission to access certain databases or products. You need to justify your need-to-know. This might make sense for truly sensitive sources and methods, but we've applied it far too broadly."

Captain Helena Porter, the base's communications officer, asked, "What about different types of OIA? Are we talking about one uniform approach?"

"Good question. We can be more specific about access vehicles. In the terminology we're developing, OIA delivered through centralized intelligence databases is called 'gold OIA.' OIA delivered through local unit repositories is called 'green OIA.' Products that remain restricted through traditional channels are called 'controlled access' or CA. While every kind of OIA removes clearance-level barriers, there are different permission barriers we could address. If we remove clearance barriers alone, we provide 'gratis OIA.' If we remove permission barriers as well, we provide 'libre OIA.'"

Silva raised her hand again. "Sir, this sounds ideal in theory, but what about the analysts themselves? When I was at Blackwood, some of the senior analysts were protective of their work. They worried about losing credit."

Foster smiled. "That's a crucial point, and it gets to the heart of why OIA actually serves analyst interests. Studies within our community and allied militaries have shown that broadly-shared intelligence products are referenced more often in subsequent analysis and operational planning. Products available through OIA channels see higher usage rates than restricted products, even when produced by the same analytical cell."

He clicked to a slide showing data from a preliminary assessment. "When you enlarge the audience for an analysis, you enlarge the subset of that audience who will later build upon it, reference it, or request follow-up from the original analyst. This converts directly to professional recognition and career advancement."

Major Sanders nodded thoughtfully. "So OIA isn't a sacrifice for analysts who write for impact rather than personal gain. It actually enhances their professional standing."

"Exactly," Foster confirmed. "It increases a product's visibility, retrievability, audience, usage, and influence—all of which convert to career advancement. For intelligence professionals, it's beneficial even if it required extra effort. But as we'll see, it doesn't require significant additional effort."

He advanced to address common concerns. "Now, let me clarify what OIA is not, because there are many misconceptions."

"First, OIA isn't an attempt to bypass quality control or peer review. All intelligence products still go through standard review processes. Senior analysts, subject matter experts, and chain-of-command review remain in place. OIA is compatible with every level of review we currently maintain."

"Second, OIA isn't an attempt to violate classification systems or operational security. It works entirely within existing security frameworks. We're not declassifying anything. We're simply ensuring that products are classified at appropriate levels and made available to everyone with appropriate clearances."

Lieutenant Little asked, "What about analysts' control over their own products? Does OIA reduce their authority?"

"On the contrary," Foster replied, "OIA depends on analyst decisions and actually requires analysts to exercise more control over their work than traditional dissemination allows. One OIA strategy is for analysts to retain distribution authority they might otherwise cede to higher headquarters. Another is for commands to permit broader distribution than traditionally allowed. Traditional systems often strip analysts of any say in how their products are shared. OIA returns some of that control."

Captain Porter pressed further. "But sir, doesn't this reduce flexibility? What if analysts want to restrict certain products?"

"OIA doesn't eliminate analyst discretion," Foster explained. "Analysts remain free to classify products appropriately and to apply necessary handling restrictions. Policies encouraging OIA do so conditionally—for example, for products developed under certain operational directives. These policies generally include exceptions and waiver options. The goal is to make broad access the default, not to eliminate all restrictions."

Major Sanders interjected, "I notice you haven't mentioned our coalition partners. How does OIA affect intelligence sharing with allied forces?"

"Another excellent question," Foster said. "OIA within our own forces doesn't require changes to coalition sharing protocols. We can still maintain appropriate releasability restrictions. However, the principles of OIA suggest we should examine whether some coalition sharing restrictions are more restrictive than necessary. That's a separate discussion, but the logic applies."

Foster clicked to a new slide titled "What Makes OIA Possible?"

"OIA is made possible by secure digital networks and command authorization. Two background facts explain why this works in the military intelligence context. First, intelligence analysts are government employees producing work products as part of their official duties. The government owns the rights to their analysis. There's no copyright issue—it's all government work product."

Silva spoke up again. "Sir, is this really new? At Blackwood, we always tried to share intelligence appropriately. Colonel Vance there pushed hard for information sharing within the Selvorian theater."

"Yes and no," Foster replied. "Colonel Vance's work at Blackwood is part of why they're a pilot site. The principle of sharing intelligence with those who need it isn't new. What's new is recognizing that in the digital age, 'those who need it' can be much broader than we traditionally assumed, and the barriers we erected in the paper era are no longer necessary. The technology has changed, but our procedures haven't kept pace."

He continued, "Think about it historically. Intelligence sharing evolved in an era when copying reports was expensive and time-consuming, when distribution meant physical courier runs, when storage was limited. We developed elaborate systems to control who got what. Those systems made sense then. But now? We can put a report on a secure server and make it instantly available to thousands of cleared personnel across the theater. The old restrictions are obsolete."

Captain Leonard asked, "What about the human element? Don't analysts sometimes hoard information for job security?"

Foster nodded. "That's a cultural challenge, not a technical one. Some analysts do fear that sharing their work too broadly will reduce their value. But that fear is misplaced. In reality, analysts who share their work broadly become known as subject matter experts. They get more requests for follow-up analysis, more opportunities to contribute to high-level planning, more visibility with senior leaders. The analysts who hoard information become isolated and irrelevant."

He clicked to a slide showing a quote from a strategic intelligence directive: "An old tradition and a new technology have converged to make possible unprecedented operational effectiveness. The old tradition is the military intelligence community's mission to inform decision-makers at all levels. The new technology is secure digital networks."

Major Sanders raised a practical concern. "Sir, what about the implementation? How do we actually make this happen at this installation?"

"The basic implementation is straightforward," Foster replied. "We're establishing a theater-wide intelligence repository accessible to all cleared personnel. Analysts will upload their products to this repository with appropriate classification markings and handling caveats. The system will automatically enforce access controls based on clearance levels. Users can search, retrieve, and download any product they're cleared to access."

"For green OIA, individual units will maintain their own repositories, but they'll be networked so products can be discovered and requested across units. An analyst in Parkview can find a relevant report from Blackwood and request access through automated channels."

Lieutenant Little asked, "What about quality control? Won't we be flooded with low-quality products?"

"The repository will include rating and review features," Foster explained. "Users can rate products for usefulness and accuracy. Over time, high-quality analysts will build reputations, and their products will be more readily trusted. Poor-quality work will be quickly identified and ignored. It's a form of crowdsourced quality control that complements formal review processes."

He addressed the group as a whole. "I want to emphasize that OIA isn't primarily about helping junior personnel, though they'll certainly benefit. The focus is on enhancing operational effectiveness at all levels. Senior commanders need access to tactical-level reporting. Staff officers need access to products from other functional areas. Analysts need access to each other's work to avoid duplication and build on existing analysis."

Captain Porter asked, "Does this mean we're eliminating all access restrictions?"

"No," Foster clarified. "Even with full OIA implementation, some barriers will remain. Compartmented programs will still have special access requirements. Coalition sharing will still require releasability determinations. Some sources and methods will still require protection beyond standard classification. OIA removes unnecessary barriers, not all barriers."

Major Sanders asked, "What's the timeline for implementation?"

"We're starting with a pilot program here and at three other bases," Foster replied. "Blackwood in Selvoria, as I mentioned—Lieutenant Silva's former posting. One in Parkview, Orvandor. And one in Crystalbrook, Lethoria. Over the next six months, we'll refine the technical infrastructure and work through cultural resistance. Then we'll expand theater-wide."

He paused and looked around the room. "I chose this location to launch the briefing cycle because of the maple leaf symbol we display here—representing growth and adaptation. What better place to announce an initiative about adapting our procedures to new realities?"

Foster advanced to his final slide. "The success of OIA depends on leadership at every level. We need commanders who understand the operational value of information sharing. We need analysts who embrace broad dissemination as professionally beneficial. We need technical personnel who can maintain the infrastructure. And we need all of us to challenge the outdated assumptions that create unnecessary barriers."

He concluded, "This isn't about technology for technology's sake. It's about operational effectiveness. It's about ensuring that the right information reaches the right people at the right time. In modern warfare, information dominance isn't about hoarding intelligence—it's about leveraging it. OIA is how we achieve that leverage."

As the briefing ended, the officers filed out, discussing the implications. Lieutenant Silva approached Major Sanders. "Sir, what do you think? Will this actually work?"

Sanders considered the question. "The logic is sound. We've been operating with paper-era procedures in a digital-age environment. If we can overcome the cultural resistance—and that's a big if—this could significantly enhance our operational effectiveness."

Silva nodded. "I saw the resistance at Blackwood. Some of the senior analysts there still think information hoarding gives them job security. But the younger generation is ready for change."

"You'll be crucial to this," Sanders replied. "You can bridge both worlds—you know how Blackwood operates, and now you're here helping us implement. Your experience will help us avoid pitfalls."

"I'm willing to try," Silva said. "As an analyst, I want my work to have impact. If OIA helps achieve that, I'm all for it."
