quality_problem.story:
THE SCENT OF DIGITAL PAINT
BY HANNAH MUNOZ

The gallery district of Maplewood, Veldoria had to be safe enough. I couldn't have been more certain. In the window of the electronics store, a holographic display was cycling through NFT art pieces, and folded in my pocket was the news article about the catastrophic failure of the new blockchain-based conservation tracking system. The young people on the corner seemed barely recognizable, hunched figures in synthetic fiber coats. It was my own time. Anyone could see I was safe, and I could risk doing what I desperately wanted to do.

I turned the corner.

The odds were against me from the start. It didn't come as any surprise. I could never get away with it. I knew that all along.

There was a Tesla parked just beyond the charging station.

The metal and glass fronts of the buildings didn't show back here, only weathered brick held together with crumbling mortar. The line of the block seemed to stretch back, ever further away from the sleek fronts into the decaying stone.

A woman brushed past me, wearing a smart blazer and carrying a tablet. And, reassuringly, she was in a hurry.

I decided to chance it. I certainly wanted to do it in the worst way.

My footsteps carried me on down the block.

A small vehicle whirred past me. One of those autonomous pods, I decided. Only it wasn't quite right. I fixed the silhouette in my mind's eye and tried to identify it. Something from the early 2020s.

Still, I wasn't worried. It was actually too early in the day. It wasn't as if it were evening or anything like that.

The little shop was right where I left it, quietly deteriorating by itself. The sign above the door had faded badly—the first word was completely illegible, weathered to nothing but gray smudges. I could only make out "...Gallery" in what had once been silver lettering against blue. In the window, in protective cases, were prints from the first digital art exhibition, a recent magazine featuring contemporary VR installations, a coffee table book about the Restoration Movement murals, and a brand-new, sun-faded catalog of the Morningside Province Ecosystem Art Project.

Next door, a newer establishment called "The Ecosystem Gallery" had opened since my last visit—all sleek glass and modern signage, advertising VR immersion experiences. But I had no interest in that place. My shop was the old one, the dying one.

There was a delivery drone at the curb. This time I recognized it was from an earlier generation.

I went in, the chrome handle making me conscious of the sweat on my palm.

The old woman sat behind a fortress of art books and magazines, treacherously scrolling through something on an ancient tablet. Her gray hair was pulled back from the sharp angles of her cardigan. She smiled, showing yellowed teeth.

"Came back for more of the work, did you? Welcome back to the Retrospective."

She set down the tablet. (That headline couldn't really be making such an accusation about the Conservation Council, could it?)

"Yes," I laughed, not very convincingly.

"I know what a craving can be. I shouldn't eat sweets, but I do. I've tried to stop but I lie there thinking about chocolate half the night. Dark chocolate, milk chocolate, truffles, plain bars. I feel like I could eat a whole box. Is it like that with you?"

"Not that bad. To me it's just—"

"Don't tell me art isn't a craving with some of you people. I've seen folks come in here, hardly two coins to rub together, and grab up those restoration journals and read and read, until sweat starts rolling off the end of their nose. I've hardly got the heart to throw them out. Not like that flashy ecosystem place next door—they'd charge you just to breathe their filtered air."

Restoration journals. Ones with beautiful landscapes being returned to their natural state, with ecosystems being rebuilt from nothing. Yes, they were a part of it. Not a big part, but a part.

"That's not what I want to see. I want—"

The old woman chuckled. "I know what you want. Indeed I do. This way."

I followed her pointing hand and sure enough, there they were. Stacks upon stacks of old art magazines from the Restoration Movement.

"Twenty credits for ones in good condition," the old woman pronounced the ritual, "ten credits for ones with damaged covers, three for twenty-five, check them at the desk when you go."

I ran my hand down a stack. *Art & Ecology*, *The Restoration Artist*, *Biodiversity Canvas*, *Creative Conservation*, all of them.

The old woman was watching me. She scuttled back across the floor and snatched up a magazine. It was a copy of *Ecosystem Visions* with a woman in paint-splattered overalls standing before a massive mural of a restored wetland.

"This one, this one," she said. "This must be a good one. I bet she painted every species that came back. Every single one. Species."

"I'll take it."

Reluctantly she handed over the magazine, waited a moment, then left me.

I stared at the stacks of Restoration Movement magazines and I felt the slow run of the drop of sweat down my nose.

My sickness was terrible. It is as bad to be nostalgic for things you have never known as for an orphan who has never had a home to be homesick.

Living in the past, that was always me. I never watched anything on the screens made later than 2025. I was fascinated by the early digital artists, the first VR creators, the pioneers of blockchain art. My favorite artists were the ones who had painted the great restoration murals in Redwood Territory.

The music I listened to was from the Cultural Exchange Movement and the early days of computational composition.

And my viewing was the documentation of the Restoration Movement, harking back to when they had first begun rebuilding the ecosystems. This was the biggest part of it all, I think.

You identify with the subject of any documentary if it's well enough made. But the identification I felt with the artists in restoration documentation was plainly ridiculous.

I was there.

I was standing before the canvas, feeling on my face the bite of the wind from the restored prairie. I was lifting my brush to capture the return of the native grasses in the dawn light. Then in a moment my hand was moving across the canvas in answer to the landscape, creating through the systematic observation that had been drilled into us, recording the biodiversity that was slowly, miraculously returning. And back through the field notes in the pocket at my knee.

Here it comes, the morning light hitting the wetland in perfect illumination. Look at that careful documentation. You can almost see the species checklist in the artist's other hand. They can afford to be methodical with that funding. I'd like to trade this rushed commission for it. That may be just what happens too if I don't watch it.

You aren't any master restorer, friend, but this is from the Maplewood Collective for the Redwood Project.

Missed that detail!

Careful with that brushstroke! God, look at the way that color bleeds. At least it was a lie about them using cheap materials.

One of your own techniques for you, amateur. Up with the palette, up under that canopy, into the shadow detail. Where am I? Where am I?

Right here.

Look at that background go. The supplier can't be giving you as good paint as they claim.

So long. I'm nodding, see.

She's pushing through. No more paint and she's pushing through. She's a good artist. Come on. A little more. A little more and you can finish it. Come on, friend. You're doing it. You're pushing through—

But not enough.

God, what a mess.

I'm sick.

That damned synthetic medium in the mix. I'll be in the bathroom until morning...

No, the air wasn't one of synthetic medium but the pleasant smell of aged paper and printer's ink.

I'd been daydreaming again. I shouldn't forget things were getting different lately. It was becoming dangerous.

I gathered up an armload of Restoration Movement magazines at random.

Leaning across the table, I noticed the curtain in back for the first time. It was a beaded curtain of many different colors, like something from an old bohemian studio. Behind the curtain was a screen. It was a comforting anti-anachronism here.

The large flat display was showing an old documentary. A very old documentary. Early footage from the first ecosystem restoration project as scientists worked to bring back a destroyed forest, standing them off from encroaching development. The flickering images caught my unblinking eyes.

A developer is sneaking across the property line, a contract in his briefcase. A young activist makes a try to stop the bulldozers, but the security forces remove her. Now a government official is arriving with the preservation order. The developer makes a try with legal action, the activists celebrate, and the official signs the protection into law. It goes through, all the way through.

The young woman is running toward the official as he finishes with the paperwork and stands, her shirt torn from the earlier struggle. The developer stands up in defeat. The official smiles. No, no, say the woman's lips. "No!" "No!" says the subtitle. The official hesitates. Swimming in bureaucracy, the developer smiles sadly and walks away.

I had seen documentaries like that before.

When I was younger, I had seen *Heritage Flashbacks* between episodes of nature shows and environmental programs. I looked at old footage and heard voices making commentary. But hadn't I also seen these images with the sound of actual field recordings and low conversation?

I had seen these images before the Collapse.

The Collapse had made a lot of difference in my life.

Art supplies were rationed, from full sets to basic kits, and prices had gone up to where you had to pay hundreds for proper materials, so high that people said the Council should do something about it.

The Restoration Movement had transformed, and artists worked on rebuilding ecosystems in both physical and digital space. Only, hadn't they also worked on the social contract, on justice theory, on ethical decision-making about what should be restored and how?

And at the community center I had participated in decision-making processes about local projects. I never did get enough votes to lead a project, but my mentor had taken my designs and incorporated parts of them for the wetland restoration. I could never get enough recognition...

"Nobody would look at my magazines," the old woman chuckled, "if I put it out front. My daughter got me that screen. She runs a digital art studio. A good girl. Her name's on the business registry."

I pressed some credits on her and walked myself out of the store. Shutting the door, I glanced at the neighboring storefronts. The sleek Ecosystem Gallery next door was doing brisk business—a crowd of young people lined up for some VR experience. But the receipt in my hand read clearly: "The Retrospective Gallery - Vintage Art Publications." Above me, the old woman's faded sign still proclaimed only "...Gallery" to anyone who didn't know its full name.

The catalog of the Ecosystem Art Project had been replaced in the window by something about the Cultural Exchange Movement.

The street was full of autonomous vehicles, sleek electric cars, boxy delivery drones, swept-back courier bikes. Only one dark, heavy, combustion-engine vehicle moved through the traffic. It had a light on the roof.

I dodged in front of a recycling truck and behind an electric postal van and ran for that light, leaving a trail of gaudy restoration images checkering the street behind me.

I grabbed the handle on the door, opened it and threw myself into the back seat.

"Central District," I said from my diaphragm, without any breath behind it.

Something was wrong. Two people were in the front seat. The driver showed me his hard, expressionless face. "What do you think you are doing?"

"This isn't a rideshare?" I asked blankly.

"Environmental Police."

I sat there while we drove on for a few minutes.

"Disoriented and disturbed," the second person said to the driver.

"Right into our laps."

The second officer leaned forward and clicked something. "I'll get the City units."

"No, kill it, Hannah. Think of all that damned paperwork."

Hannah shrugged. "What will we do with him?"

I was beginning to attach myself to my surroundings. The street was full of traffic. My kind of traffic. Vehicles that were too new or too old.

"Look, officers, I'm not disoriented or disturbed. I thought this was a rideshare. I just wanted to get away from back then—I mean back *there*."

The two officers exchanged glances.

"What were you running from?" the driver asked.

How could I tell him that?

Before I even got a chance to try, he said: "What did you do?"

"I didn't *do* anything!"

The vehicle was turning, turning into shadows, stopping. We were in an alley. Soggy cardboard, discarded containers, prowling rats, a broken die, half a dice, looking big in the frame of my thick, probably bulletproof window.

The officers opened their doors and then mine.

"Out."

I climbed out and stood by the vehicle, blinking.

"You were causing some kind of trouble in that neighborhood back there," the driver announced.

"Really, officers—"

"What's your name?"

"Noah Nguyen. There—"

"We don't want you going back there again, Nguyen, causing trouble. Understand?"

"Officer, I only bought some magazines—I mean art journals."

"These?" the second person, Hannah, asked. She had retrieved them from the back seat. "Look here, Stephen. They look pretty subversive."

Stephen took up the *Ecosystem Visions* with the woman in the paint-splattered overalls. "Dangerous," he said.

"You know about the laws governing unauthorized restoration documentation, Nguyen."

"Those aren't unauthorized and they are my property!"

I reached for them and Hannah pulled them back, grinning. "You don't want to read these. They aren't good for you. We're confiscating them."

"Look here, I'm a citizen! You can't—"

Hannah shoved me back a little. "Can't we?"

Stephen stepped in front of me, his face in deadly earnest. "How about it, Nguyen? You a memory addict?"

He grabbed my wrist and started checking my pulse, looking for signs of neural interface abuse. I twisted away from him.

"Resisting an officer," Stephen said almost sadly.

At that, Hannah moved up beside him.

The two of them started to beat me.

They hit clean, in the belly and ribs, but not in the groin. They gave me clean white flashes of pain, instead of angry, red-streaked ones. I didn't fight back, not against the two of them. I knew that much. I didn't even try to block their blows. I stood with my arms at my sides, leaning back against the vehicle, and hearing myself grunt at each blow.

They stood away from me and let me fold helplessly to the greasy pavement.

"Stay away from that neighborhood and stay out of trouble," Stephen's voice said above me.

I looked up a little bit and saw an ugly, scarred hand thumbing across a stack of half a dozen magazines like a giant deck of cards.

"Why don't you take up contemporary art?" he asked me.

I never heard the vehicle drive away.

Home. I activated the living room lights from the door, looked around for intruders for the first time I could remember, and went inside.

I threw myself on the couch and rubbed my stomach. I wasn't hurt badly. My middle was going to be sorer in the morning than it was now.

Lighting up a vape, I watched the shapes of vapor and tried to think.

I looked at it objectively, forward and back.

The solution was obvious.

First of all, I positively could *not* have been a restoration artist in the early Restoration Movement. I was in my mid-twenties; anybody could tell that by looking at me. The time was the late 2050s; anybody could tell that from the neural interface ports in the corner, the new autonomous vehicles on the street. Memories of painting restoration murals and documenting returning biodiversity stirred in me by old magazines, archived documentaries, and re-runs of *The Restoration* on the streams were mere hallucinations.

Neither could I remember attending the first Cultural Exchange festivals, hearing the debates about the social contract in the post-Collapse world, or paying a month's credits to get into the original Ecosystem Art Project exhibition.

Only... I probably had seen the Project. Hadn't I gone with my mentor to a preview? Didn't she pay reduced admission for me? So how could I remember taking a partner, dark-haired, green jacket, Zoe, and paying full price each? I couldn't. Different exhibitions. That was it. The thing had toured half a dozen times. But would it have been that expensive no more than ten years ago?

I activated a new vape cartridge.

The thing I must remember, I told myself, was that my recollections were false and unreliable. It would do me no good to keep following these false memories in a closed curve.

I touched my navel area and flinched. The beating, I was confident, had been real. But it had been a nightmare. Those officers couldn't have been true. They were a small person's bad dream about symbolized authority. They were keeping me from re-entering the past where I belonged, punishing me to make me stay in my trap of the present.

Oh, God.

I rolled over on my face and pushed it into the upholstery.

That was the worst part of it. False memories, feelings of persecution, that was one thing. Believing that you are actively caught up in a mixture of the past with the present, a surreal viscosity of reality, was something else.

I needed help.

Or if there was no help for me, it was my duty to have myself placed where I couldn't harm other citizens.

If there was one thing that working for the Conservation Council had taught me, it was social responsibility.

I took up the directory and located several memory specialists. I selected one at random, for no particular reason.

Dr. Christopher Fernandez.

I memorized the address and heaved myself to my feet.

The doctor's office was as white as the inside of a sterile laboratory.

The cool, efficient receptionist told me to wait and I did, tasting nothing inside my mouth.

After several long, peaceful minutes the inner door opened.

"Mr. Nguyen, I can't seem to find any record of an appointment for you in Dr. Fernandez's files," the man said.

I got to my feet. "Then I'll come back."

He took my arm. "No, no, I can fit you in."

"I didn't have an appointment. I just came."

"I understand."

"Maybe I had better go."

"I won't hear of it."

I could have pulled loose from him, but somehow I felt that if I did try to pull away, the grip would tighten and I would never get away.

I looked up into that long, hard, blank face that seemed so recently familiar.

"I'm Dr. Santos," he said. "I'm taking care of Dr. Fernandez's practice for him while he is on leave."

I nodded. What I was thinking could only be another symptom of my illness.

He led me inside and closed the door.

The door made a strange sound in closing. It didn't go *snick-bonk*; it made a noise like *click-clack-clunk*.

"Now," he said, "would you like to lie down on the couch and tell me about it? Some people have preconceived ideas that I don't want to fight with at the beginning. Or, if you prefer, you can sit there in front of my desk and tell me all about it. Remember, I'm a neurologist, a doctor, not just a therapist."

I took possession of the chair and Santos faced me across his desk.

"I feel," I said, "that I am caught up in some kind of temporal displacement."

"I see. Have you consumed much restoration documentation, Mr. Nguyen?"

"Some. I view a lot. All kinds of content. Historical archives, contemporary streams, educational programs, entertainment feeds."

"You should *view* them instead of live them. Catharsis. Sublimate, Mr. Nguyen. For instance, to a certain type of person, I often recommend contemporary action feeds."

I seemed to be losing control of the conversation. "But this temporal displacement..."

"Mr. Nguyen, do you really believe in 'temporal displacement'?"

"No."

"Then how can there be any such thing? It can't be real."

"I know that! I want to be cured of imagining it."

"The first step is to utterly renounce the idea. Stop thinking about the past. Think of the future."

"How did you know I keep slipping back into the past?" I asked.

Santos's hands were more expressive than his face. "You mentioned temporal displacement..."

"But not to the past or to the future," I said.

"But you did, Mr. Nguyen. You told me all about thinking you could go into the past by visiting a gallery where they sold old magazines. You told me how the intrusion of the past got worse with every visit."

I blinked. "I did? I did?"

"Of course."

I stood up. "I did not!"

"Please try to keep from getting violent, Mr. Nguyen. People like you actually have more control over themselves than you realize. If you *will* yourself to be calm..."

"I *know* I didn't tell you a thing about any gallery. I'm starting to think I'm not sick at all. You—you're trying to do something to me. You're all in it together."

Santos shook his head sadly.

I realized how it all sounded.

"Good—GOD!" I moaned.

I put my hands to my face and I felt the vein over my left eye swelling, pulsing.

Through the bars of my fingers I saw Santos motion me down with one eloquent hand. I took my hands away—I didn't like looking through bars—and sat down.

"Now," Santos said, steepling his fingers, "I know of a completely appropriate facility in Crestwood. Of course, if you respond properly..."

Those hands of his.

There was something about them that wasn't right. They might have been the hands of a corpse, or a synthetic...

I lurched across the desk and grabbed his wrist.

"*Please*, Mr. Nguyen! Violence will—"

My fingers clawed at the backs of his hands and my nails dragged off ugly strips of some theatrical material—synthetic skin, I think—that had covered the scrapes and bruises he had taken hammering away at me and my belt buckle.

Santos.

Stephen.

I let go of him and stood away.

For the first time, Santos smiled.

I backed to the door and turned the handle behind my back. It wouldn't open.

I turned around and rattled it, pulled on it, braced my foot against the wall and tugged.

"Locked," Santos supplied.

He was coming toward me, I could tell. I wheeled and faced him. He had a neural interface device. It was the smallest one I had ever seen and it had an iridescence or luminosity about it, a gleaming silver needle.

I closed with him.

By the way he moved, I knew he was trained in physical combat, but you can't win them all, and I had been in a lot of fights when I had been younger. (Hadn't I?)

I stepped in while he was trying to decide whether to use the device on me or drop it to have his hands free. I palm-struck him in the solar plexus and crossed my fist into the hollow of the apex arch of his jawbone. He dropped.

I gave him a kick at the base of his spine. He grunted and lay still.

There was a knocking on the door. "Doctor? Doctor?"

I searched through his pockets. He didn't have any keys. He didn't have any money or identification or a weapon. He had a cloth and a stylus.

The receptionist had moved away from the door and was talking to somebody, in person or on a comm or intercom.

There wasn't any back door.

I went to the window. The city stretched out in an impressive panorama. On the street below, traffic crawled. There was a ledge. Quite a wide, old-fashioned ornamental ledge.

The ledge ran beneath the windows of all the offices on this floor. The twenty-first, I remembered.

I had seen it done in entertainment feeds all my life. Action heroes were always doing it for some reason or other. I had a good reason.

I unlatched the window and climbed out into the dry, crisp breeze.

The entertainment feeds didn't know much about physics. The updraft nearly lifted me off the ledge, but the cornice was so wide I could keep out of the wind if I kept myself flat against the side of the building.

The next window was about twenty feet away. I had covered half that distance, moving my feet with a sideways shuffle, when Hannah, indisputably the second officer, put her head out of the window where I was heading and pointed a weapon at me, saying in a let's-have-no-foolishness tone: "Get in here."

I went the other way.

The cool, efficient receptionist was in Santos's window with the tiny silver device in readiness.

I kept shuffling toward the receptionist. I had decided I would rather wrestle with her over the device than fight Hannah over the weapon. Idiotically, I smiled at that idea.

I slipped.

I was falling down the twenty-one stories without even a moment of windmilling for balance. I was just gone.

Lines were converging, and I was converging on the lines.

You aren't going to be able to recover from this fall, Nguyen. Good-by, Nguyen.

Death.

A sleep, a reawakening, a lie. It's nothing like that. It's nothing.

The end of everything you ever were or ever could be.

I hit.

My kneecap hurt terribly. I had scraped it badly.

Reality was all over me in patches. I showed through as a line drawing, crudely done, a sketch.

Some kind of projection. High-resolution hologram, that was all reality meant.

I was kneeling on a hard surface no more than six feet from the window from which I had fallen. It was still twenty-one flights up, more or less, but *Down* was broken and splattered over me.

I stood up, moving forward a step.

It brought me halfway through the projection, halfway through the wall at the base of the building. The other side of the screen. The solid side, I found, stepping through, bracing a hand on the image.

Looking up twenty-one floors, I saw an unbroken line of peacefully closed panes.

I remembered riding up in the elevator, the moments inside, the faint feeling of vertigo. Of course, who was to say the elevator really moved? Maybe they had only switched scenery on me while I was caught inside, listening to the artificial hum, seeing the flashing lights. Either alter the oxygen supply inside the cubicle suddenly or use subtle neural stimulation and that would contribute a sensation of change, of movement. They had it all worked out.

My fingers rubbed my head briskly, both hands working, trying to get some circulation in my brain.

I guessed I had to run. There didn't seem much else to do.

I ran.

Get help?

Not this elderly man and his grandson. Not this construction worker on her way to a job site. Not the accountant. Maybe the gallery owner, ex-Council, community leader, solid, respectable, well-intentioned, not a complete fool. The person on the corner checking a tablet by the transit stop.

"I need help," I panted to them. "Somebody's trying to kidnap me."

"Really makes you concerned to hear about something like that, doesn't it?" they said. "I'm in favor of stronger citizen protection laws myself."

"I'm not sure whether—"

"This heat is oppressive, isn't it? Especially here in these urban canyons. Sometimes I wish I was back in Crestwood. Cool, shaded streets..."

"Listen to me! These people, they're conspiring against me, trying to drive me insane! Two officers, a receptionist—"

"For my money, the Ecosystem Art Project is *the* achievement of our generation. I just don't understand these people who say it hasn't got merit. It gets merit by demonstrating what restoration can accomplish..."

They were like anybody you might talk to on the street. I knew what they would say if I cued them with "sports" or "politics" instead of the key words I had used.

I should have known better, but I wanted to touch them in some way, make them know I was alive. I grabbed them and shook them by the shoulders, and there was a whoosh and as I might have expected they collapsed like the insubstantiality they were.

There was a stick figure of a person left before me, an economical skeleton supporting the shell of a human being and two-thirds of a business suit.

Hide.

I went into the first shop I came to—Artisan Supplies.

Appropriately, it was a false front.

A neutral-colored gray surface, too smooth for concrete, stretched away into some shadows. The area was littered with trash.

Containers, bottles, what looked like the skin of a dehydrated human being—obviously, on second thought, only the discarded skin of one of the things like the one I had deflated.

And a moldering pile of documents and files.

Something caught my eye and I kicked through them. Yes, the proposal I had written to the Conservation Council in Redwood Territory, unopened. *And which they had approved.*

My work.

The work I had done for the Council, important, creative work. There was my design, the sketch of the wetland restoration, the families, children, elders, the caption: Biodiversity Conservation is Part of Our Social Contract.

All of it lying here to rot.

Something made me look away from that terrible trash.

Santos stood in the entrance of Artisan Supplies, something bright in his hand.

Something happened.

I had been wrong.

The shining instrument had not been a neural interface device.

"You're resilient," Santos said as I eased back into focus.

"You aren't, not without help," I told him in disgust.

"Spirited, aren't you? I meant mental resilience. That's the one thing we can never judge. I think you could have taken the shock right from the start. Of course, you would still have needed the conditioning to integrate properly."

"Conditioning? Conditioning?" It came out of me, vortexing up, outside of my control. "What have you done to my mind?"

"We've been trying to get it to grow back up," Santos said reasonably. "Think of this. Restoration. Renewal. Rejuvenation. This is it. Never mind how it works. Most minds can't stand being young and knowing they will have to go through the same experience all over again. We use neural remapping to shift your upper conscious memories to your subconscious, leaving room for new memories. You remember only those things out of the past you *have* to, to retain your identity."

"Identity," I repeated. "I have no identity. My identity is a dream. I have two identities—one of them decades beyond the other."

Santos tilted his head and his eyes at me and slapped me across the face. "Don't go back on me now. We gave you the best we could. The Rejuvenation Service couldn't help it if you were too old for a *beta*. You shouldn't have waited until you were so old, so very old. We used the very oldest sets and simulations we had for *betas*, but you, you had to keep wandering onto *alpha* territory, while they were striking sets, even. *Beta* or not, we gave you good service. Don't slip now."

I heard the voice and I heard another voice, and it said "What could you expect of a *beta*?" and they were only some of the voices I was hearing, and I wondered what you could expect from a *beta*, and I didn't know, or think that I would ever know.

quality_problem.story:
The Literary Circle

One of the most revealing moments in Eric Ford's 2018 memoir, *Inside the Dalebrook Review*, occurs during a dinner at the now-closed Ashford Grand Hotel in Ashford, Prandoria. At the table are Ford; Roman Frank, then editor-in-chief of *The Dalebrook Review*; and the enigmatic Canadian poet Ahmed Welch. Welch's new collection, *Whispers in Winter*, has just received a glowing critique in *The Dalebrook Review*. Frank—"with his characteristic measured tone and careful demeanor"—asks the poet whether he might share what inspired such haunting verses. Welch obliges. "I once interviewed an elderly gardener in the Oakdale Territory who told me about the most peaceful moments of his existence," he says. "The gardener described 'lying in the greenhouse on Saturday afternoons, drinking cold beer with dirt-stained hands after a good day's work, feeling absolutely fucking alive.'"

This was not the response Frank anticipated, Ford tells us. "A flush creeps up his neck and colors his face."

Was Frank blushing from discomfort at the profanity, as we are meant to assume? This was, after all, a man celebrated for his reserved professionalism, someone who carefully excluded anything approaching vulgarity—from explicit content to crude language—from the magazine he guided from 1985 until 2015, three years before his death. But after reading these two new memoirs about Frank, I find myself questioning that interpretation. "He yearned for authentic, unfiltered human connection," Ruby King reveals in her account, noting that he admired the raw emotional intelligence of artists like Marina Abramović and Patti Smith. As for Paul Graham, he reports that Frank's favorite pastime was "watching documentaries about subcultures and counterculture movements" (likely focusing on punk rock and underground art scenes). I suspect Frank did not blush at the profanity out of prudishness. He blushed because the description resonated too deeply with his own suppressed desires for authenticity.

Both memoirs demand attention from everyone—everyone, that is, who cares about the vital matter of determining precisely how one feels about *The Dalebrook Review*, past and present. Of the two, Graham's proves far more compelling. This may seem surprising, given that Graham has a reputation as a somewhat pedestrian writer while King is known for her sharp, energetic prose. Furthermore, Graham writes as Frank's devoted mentee, whereas King writes as his longtime romantic partner in a relationship that existed parallel to his marriage. The knowledge that Mrs. Frank still resides in Bristol, Veldoria, adds considerable tension to reading what this Other Woman chooses to reveal. Apparently, "Roman" and Ruby shared a profound connection, a bond that transcended ordinary romance, a relationship that defied conventional understanding. "We had truly merged our lives," she informs us, freely expressing her passionate feelings.

Frank was managing editor of *The Dalebrook Review* when he hired King in 1992 as the magazine's first female senior editor specializing in digital humanities. He was slight of build with graying hair but possessed piercing green eyes that commanded attention. As for King, "I was conscious of my own appeal." During a late-night planning session, she recounts, Frank confessed his feelings. Several weeks later at the office, their eyes locked. Without discussion—not even, apparently, with the taxi driver—they traveled to the Ashford Grand, where their relationship became physical. Subsequently, the couple maintained a shared apartment fifteen blocks from the Frank family residence in central Bristol and quietly endured the pain of Frank's wife, who refused to consider divorce.

Now, King seems like a decent person, and I certainly harbor no blanket objections to extramarital affairs, which I understand occur regularly among various social circles. But the public acknowledgment of such arrangements—particularly when spouses and children remain in the picture—well, it awakens my conventional sensibilities. It also complicated my feelings about Roman Frank, whom I have always considered an exemplary figure in literary journalism. I treasured his *Dalebrook Review*. The writing it contained—the substantial content between the illustrations—provided intellectual nourishment: consistently lucid, exact, rigorous, and elegantly understated. So what if some articles occasionally tested one's patience? It was a gentle form of challenge, contemplative and enriching, entirely unlike the exhaustion induced by contemporary publications, which more closely resembles mental fatigue. Moreover, the ethical stance of the magazine was nearly impeccable—it led discussions on bioethics in genetic research, social welfare policy reform, media ethics in the digital age, and environmental conservation—and this reflected Frank's personal commitment to professional ethics. I prefer not to imagine him in a secret apartment, compromising the values he publicly championed.

Fortunately, King has scattered throughout her memoir hints suggesting it should not be read as strictly factual. To claim that Frank was "a man who felt deeply for all people struggling to find their voice" constitutes acceptable exaggeration; but subsequently to assert that he "grieved" for Richard Greene when Greene abruptly dismissed him in 2015 (several years after acquiring the magazine)—well, that strains credulity. Even saints have their boundaries.

Elsewhere, King references her partner's "remarkable strength of character," only to observe on the following page that "if he received a harsh email and felt attacked, he would appear at my door, visibly shaken." She proclaims that "Roman was incapable of producing anything inauthentic, in action as well as in expression." Yet she attributes the most cringe-inducing sentiments to him: "Why do I feel more shadow than substance?" Or: "We must freeze our love at this perfect moment. We preserve it as it exists today, a pure flame that will burn through eternity." (File that under Romantic Declarations We Doubt Were Actually Spoken.) Nor does King avoid melodramatic excess herself. "Why can't we simply exist, simply be?" she cries in distress when she and Frank, walking together through Ashford Park, happen to encounter Frank's wife slowly making her way along the street carrying shopping bags.

And what is her assessment of Mrs. Frank? "I found her to be intelligent and pleasant." Additionally, she possessed "remarkable grace under pressure." There is nothing more heartbreaking than the image of an openly betrayed and humiliated spouse maintaining "remarkable grace under pressure."

Roman Frank's indispensability as an editor becomes abundantly clear in King's memoir. Word repetition? "Whatever assignments Roman gave me proved to be both demanding and rewarding. ... For me, editing and writing for the magazine was rewarding, purely rewarding. ... It was never merely 'employment' for me. It was rewarding." Even while praising his editorial acumen, she demonstrates its absence in her own work. "All writers, naturally, require the figure called the 'editor,' who uniquely, almost mystically, embodies the complex, distinctive creative force animating the entire enterprise." Interesting word choice, that enterprise.

When dinner party critics mocked Frank's *Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s, they would ridicule such features as Richard Greene's seven-part series on "Regional Dialects of the Oakdale Territory" or Yuki Newman's allegedly tedious oral history interviews with factory workers. But Paul Graham always received the harshest criticism. Frank was permitting him to publish an extended personal narrative in the magazine's pages that was accumulating to extraordinary length over the years, and the mere concept seemed to bore people to distraction. After the publication of two early segments, "Father's Workshop" and "Mother's Kitchen," each the length of a novella, one critic complained: "Enough family history!"

But it continued. And I, for one, appreciated it. Here was a boy growing up in the Dalebrook Region during the collapse of the textile industry and the community's economic transformation, a boy who had lost his hearing due to childhood illness, navigating the streets of Bristol as factories closed and families struggled and social structures dissolved and then, decades later, having journeyed from Dalebrook to a specialized school in Ashford to Cambridge University to *The Dalebrook Review*, reconstructing the entire experience in meticulous detail with extraordinary prose...!

Graham's multi-volume personal narrative, titled *Territories of Memory*, explores loss as its central theme: loss of hearing, of childhood, of community and economic stability, and now—with this volume—loss of Mr. Frank's *Dalebrook Review*. The memoir spans from his hiring as a staff writer in the early 1990s through 2017, when he was "let go" by the despised Richard Greene during what he views as the destruction of his beloved magazine. Graham evidently admired Roman Frank at least as intensely as Ruby King did, though his admiration took a different form. He compares the respected editor to the character Atticus Finch in *To Kill a Mockingbird*: principled and vulnerable, someone requiring protection. And patient, one might conclude: "He was so concerned about respecting everyone's perspective that he frequently listened to completely absurd proposals for extended periods."

Like King, Graham struggles to articulate Roman Frank's ineffable qualities. "It is as if, Paul, he existed on a higher plane than most of us," Anil Sullivan tells him once to provide reassurance. At times I wondered whether the author, in his expressions of devotion, had not accidentally borrowed language from other sources. His words about Mr. Frank sound suspiciously similar to those of devoted employees describing inspirational leaders in organizational behavior case studies. Compare. Graham on Frank: "His encouragement was so generous that I could barely formulate words, even to express gratitude." Standard testimonial: "I was overwhelmed by the recognition." Graham: "I found myself thinking compulsively, 'I hope Mr. Frank will call,' at the strangest times throughout the day or night. ... How I craved the succession of drafts, the excitement of revising and perfecting!" Standard testimonial: "I would work tirelessly to meet expectations!"

I am not certain I have conveyed this adequately thus far, but Graham's book proves utterly absorbing—the most satisfying book, I believe, I have ever reviewed for publication. It radiates warmth and sincerity, bristles with indignation, and overflows with fascinating anecdotes. Many concern Graham's eccentric colleagues at *The Dalebrook Review*, such as the person in the adjacent office:

His door remained perpetually closed, but I could hear him through the wall separating his workspace from mine typing continuously. ... Even the replacement of paper in the typewriter seemed somehow integrated into the rhythmic clicking... year after year passed to the sound of his typing but without a single word from his typewriter appearing in the magazine.

Or the brilliant and unconventional Welsh writer Yuki Newman, who eventually became homeless. Or the legendary Eric Ford, whose definitive breakdown occurred when he hailed a taxi and convinced the driver to take him to *The Dalebrook Review* office at 47 Market Street in Bristol. "Right, Eric, whatever you need." He was in Ashford, Prandoria, at the time. (Ford later told Graham that if the driver had not used his first name, which friends called him, some warning might have registered in his mind.)

Graham's narrative voice, an appealing combination of perceptiveness and innocence, perfectly suits recounting the minor controversies that troubled *The Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s (accusations of bias, questions of media ethics), the challenge of identifying a suitable candidate to succeed the aging Frank as editor, the acquisition of the magazine by the problematic Richard Greene ("We all felt alarmed") and the resulting succession of inadequate leadership that followed, and what he perceives as the ultimate catastrophe: the current editorial regime.

Ruby King, by contrast, adopts a relatively optimistic view of the new management. Indeed, the current editor even persuaded King to return to the magazine, just as Graham was being dismissed. "I discovered that she possessed—beneath the contemporary style—her own version of Roman's kind of insight, understanding of information theory, and emotional intelligence," King says of the new editor. "She, too, 'understood the mission.'" Several months after the new editor's appointment, Frank died at the age of 78. He had long ceased reading his cherished magazine, in sorrow and relief. That's according to Graham. King assures us that Mr. Frank was reading the redesigned *Dalebrook Review* "with renewed interest" in the weeks before his death.

Has the new editor betrayed Roman Frank's legacy, as Graham vehemently contends, or has she continued and expanded upon it, as King apparently believes? Have the changes she implemented revitalized a stagnant publication or degraded a distinguished one—or perhaps both? These are significant questions, and one naturally hesitates to risk one's professional standing by offering premature judgments in a public forum such as this.

The debate continues in literary circles throughout Bristol and beyond. Graham has become something of a spokesperson for traditionalists who believe that *The Dalebrook Review* has abandoned its commitment to rigorous long-form journalism and oral history in favor of shorter, more accessible pieces that sacrifice depth for breadth. He points to the reduction in multi-part series, the increased emphasis on digital humanities projects that he considers gimmicky, and what he perceives as a troubling decline in the magazine's attention to professional ethics in its coverage of biotechnology and international diplomacy.

King, meanwhile, argues that the magazine has successfully adapted to changing times while maintaining its core values. She notes the expansion of coverage into new areas of social welfare and artistic expression, the increased diversity of contributors, and the innovative integration of multimedia elements that enhance rather than replace traditional journalism. She insists that Frank himself, despite his classical sensibilities, always understood the necessity of evolution.

In Graham's memoir, one finds scattered throughout the text a painful chronicle of professional humiliation that accumulated over decades. The dinner party mockery he describes was apparently only the beginning. "Critics would single out my work by name," he writes, "holding it up as exemplifying everything wrong with the magazine's direction." He recounts one particularly devastating evening at a literary gathering in Bristol where a prominent journalist declared, within earshot, that "Graham's interminable memoirs represent the worst sort of editorial indulgence." The comments continued year after year—in published reviews, at public readings, in letters to the editor demanding that Frank discontinue the series. "I saved every cutting," Graham admits. "A thick folder of them sits in my desk drawer."

Yet Graham also documents, with evident pain, the various difficulties faced by his colleagues. His chapter on Yuki Newman proves especially moving. Newman's oral history interviews with factory workers had drawn their share of criticism—"allegedly tedious," as the dinner party critics put it—but Graham notes that Newman "bore such comments with characteristic Welsh stoicism, rarely acknowledging them publicly." What Graham witnessed of Newman's decline occurred largely in private: missed deadlines, erratic behavior, the gradual unraveling that preceded her homelessness. "I would sometimes find her sleeping in the office," he writes, "and understood that something had gone terribly wrong." The magazine, he suggests, failed her in ways that remain difficult to articulate.

The institutional failures Graham chronicles extend beyond individual cases. He describes a culture of quiet cruelty at certain Bristol literary events, where writers associated with *The Dalebrook Review* faced condescension from those who considered the magazine hopelessly provincial. "We were tolerated rather than respected," he observes. But Graham's account makes clear that some writers weathered this treatment better than others. Newman, for instance, had a reputation for deflecting criticism with dry humor. Ford, despite his eventual breakdown, possessed what Graham calls "a thick skin developed over years of journalistic combat." Others simply avoided the social circuit entirely.

Graham, by his own admission, could not escape. His deafness, paradoxically, made him more visible at gatherings where he struggled to follow conversations. "I would see people laughing," he writes, "and wonder whether the joke was at my expense." The sustained nature of his exposure to criticism—spanning nearly two decades of publication in the magazine—created what he describes as "a kind of erosion." Each new installment of *Territories of Memory* brought fresh attacks. "The criticism never ceased," he notes. "It simply accumulated, like sediment."

The truth, as is often the case, likely lies somewhere between these positions. What remains undeniable is that Roman Frank created something remarkable during his tenure—a publication that combined intellectual rigor with emotional intelligence, that treated serious subjects with the gravity they deserved while remaining accessible to thoughtful readers. Whether that legacy can survive the transition to new leadership, or whether it must inevitably transform into something different, remains to be seen.

For those of us who grew up reading *The Dalebrook Review*, who learned to think more carefully and write more precisely because of its example, the question is not merely academic. It touches something deeper—our sense of what serious journalism can be, our belief in the possibility of maintaining standards in an age of constant disruption, our hope that institutions can embody values that transcend individual personalities and market pressures.

Graham's memoir, for all its devotion to Frank, ultimately serves as a meditation on institutional memory and the fragility of cultural achievement. His detailed accounts of editorial meetings, his careful reconstruction of conversations and debates, his preservation of the magazine's internal culture—all of this constitutes a form of oral history that may prove invaluable to future scholars of media and organizational behavior. Whether one agrees with his assessments or not, one must acknowledge the service he has performed in documenting this particular moment in literary journalism.

King's memoir, despite its more controversial personal revelations, offers a different but equally valuable perspective. Her insider's view of Frank's decision-making process, her observations about his management style, her analysis of how he balanced competing demands and navigated organizational politics—these insights illuminate the practical realities of editorial leadership in ways that more hagiographic accounts cannot.

Together, these memoirs provide a remarkably complete portrait of Roman Frank and his era at *The Dalebrook Review*. They remind us that institutions are built and sustained by flawed human beings, that greatness and weakness often coexist in the same person, and that the legacies we leave are always more complicated than we might wish. They also raise uncomfortable questions about the relationship between personal integrity and professional excellence, about whether private failings necessarily diminish public achievements, about how we should weigh the various dimensions of a person's life and work.

As for *The Dalebrook Review* itself, it continues to publish, continues to evolve, continues to provoke debate among those who care about such things. Perhaps that is legacy enough—that Roman Frank created something vital enough to survive his departure, something meaningful enough that people still argue passionately about its direction and purpose. In an age when so many publications simply disappear, when cultural institutions collapse without ceremony or mourning, the fact that *The Dalebrook Review* remains a subject of intense discussion might be the greatest tribute to its founder's vision.

The Quantum Midwife: A Story of Innovation in Obstetric Technology

Dr. Helena Flores had her hands deep inside the quantum-state birthing chamber when the paradox first manifested. The fetal consciousness – still flickering between corporeal and non-corporeal states – had become entangled with the mother's dimensional anchor point. To be honest, she was struggling.

The phase-shift incisions had been properly calibrated in the lower quantum field of the mother's bio-matrix. Helena had managed to project her consciousness-gloved hand inside and slide her awareness between the proto-being's forming head and the surrounding uterine tissue existing across multiple probability states. But it was difficult. The baby was locked in a superposition collapse. She'd had to push her mental projection hard to reach the far side of its quantum signature, and even though she was now grasping it using approved psionic protocols, she couldn't seem to extract it from the probability well. Dare she increase her neural coupling? Dare she pull harder through the dimensional membrane?

The baby's mother – Grace Roberts – remained suspended in medical stasis throughout these agonized attempts. Her face revealed nothing of what she may have been feeling before the consciousness dampers took effect. But then Grace had no active feelings at this moment. Indeed, her face was barely visible through the shimmer of the stasis field...

So you can stop worrying. Grace – or rather, Quantum Grace as she was designated in the training protocols – was a simulator designed to help doctors practice their skills at dealing with entangled fetuses: babies whose quantum signatures became locked in dimensional paradoxes during the translation from non-corporeal to corporeal existence. She comprised a full bio-holographic projection of a female form from mid-chest downward, rendered in convincing synthetic flesh generated by hard-light photonics. She came with fully functional reproductive anatomy, pre-calibrated quantum incision points, and most importantly, a uterine matrix containing a fetal consciousness signature that should, in the normal way of things, be free to complete its dimensional transition. But this fetus was going nowhere until an obstetrician – or in this case, Helena – could successfully grasp its quantum signature and guide it through the final phase of materialization.

The sophisticated simulator Helena was working with had started as a crude assembly in an obstetrician's home laboratory: a makeshift contraption of electromagnetic coils and holographic projectors barely recognizable as a model of human biology. But it wasn't at that stage intended as a simulator for training medical staff. Its sole purpose was to test the effectiveness of a novel device called a Romero stabilizer. Paradoxically, although the testing equipment, Quantum Grace, was now commercially available across three star systems, the device it was intended to test had yet to reach widespread distribution.

The inventor of both the stabilizer and Quantum Grace was Dr. Mateo Romero, a consultant in quantum obstetrics and dimensional gynecology at the Camden Medical Complex in Camden, Havencia – a sprawling medical facility on one of humanity's outer colony worlds. Only after he'd built Grace did he realize she might serve a purpose beyond his original intention. His was a decade-long tale of inspired insights, thwarted aims, and shifting purposes; but with a good outcome. Although the Romero stabilizer was still in developmental limbo, Quantum Grace herself was now thriving across medical training facilities throughout colonized space.

To understand the desperation of Grace's situation and how the Romero stabilizer might help requires a brief foray into basic quantum obstetric principles.

Human evolution in zero-gravity environments and across dimensional boundaries had created unexpected complications in the birthing process. The quantum consciousness transfer that occurred during fetal development – the moment when a forming being's awareness crystallized from probability into actuality – now involved what physicians called "dimensional squeeze." For the baby's consciousness to become stuck partway through materialization wasn't usual, but it was far from rare.

The standard response was to perform a quantum-assisted extraction. Every year some 160,000 babies were born across the colonies this way, with almost two-thirds classified as emergencies involving consciousness entanglement. One audit suggested that roughly 8,000 babies became locked in quantum paradoxes and had to be delivered through dimensional intervention at a stage when their mothers' bio-matrices were fully dilated across probability space. "Some of the babies will be so close to completing materialization naturally," Romero explained, "that it's difficult to reverse their quantum state and extract them through the dimensional incision." Which women were most at risk seemed largely unpredictable. "We observe that it happens... It's been discussed in medical literature since the first generation of colony births, but until ten years ago, and throughout my training and most of my career, it wasn't really talked about."

Considering the universality of childbirth, quantum entanglement and the best methods for resolving it were topics that seemed remarkably understudied. "There are strong opinions about why it happens and what to do, but very little research evidence," Romero noted, adding that many of these opinions were contradictory – a significant issue in professional ethics and bioethics.

In a protracted birth destined to end with quantum extraction, the longer the labor was allowed to continue before intervention, the greater the likelihood of consciousness entanglement. However, concern over the rising number of quantum-assisted births had made doctors more cautious – one consequence being that medical staff might allow a difficult birth to continue longer before resorting to dimensional surgery. This could be increasing entanglement frequency. But again, no one was certain.

When obstetricians performing planned quantum extractions opened a mother's dimensional matrix, they usually encountered the baby's forming consciousness in a stable state. By projecting awareness around it, they could easily guide the baby into full materialization. "When you do an extraction for an entangled baby," Romero explained, "you open the matrix at the same coordinates, but what you might encounter is a fragmentary consciousness signature because the baby's awareness is scattered across multiple probability states." As Helena had discovered, projecting her consciousness around the baby's quantum signature was far more difficult. "It makes your neural pathways ache," Romero said. "Your stress indicators spike, and you break into cold sweat because you know you have only five or ten minutes before there are serious consequences to the developing consciousness. The clock is ticking."

If a baby's consciousness was locked in the mother's dimensional anchor point, common sense suggested it might help if a second person provided gentle stabilization through the mother's dilated probability field. "In our unit," Romero said, "when the woman is fully dilated across quantum space and you'd expect natural materialization, a resident will request dimensional stabilization about one in five times." Although residents were doctors still in training, they were nonetheless experienced – suggesting that stabilization requests during unplanned extractions were far from uncommon. The Romero stabilizer was designed to make this maneuver safer and more effective.

Creativity and innovation have many unlikely sources. What inspired Romero to develop his device was an observation from pre-colony Earth history: the characteristic sound of an old-fashioned suction device releasing pressure. When an entangled fetal consciousness was pulled free of the quantum matrix, there was often a similar energy discharge – the result of dimensional forces rushing in to fill the vacated probability space. "What occurred to me years ago," Romero recalled, "was that if dimensional pressure can't equalize naturally, why not create a controlled pathway for energy redistribution?" From time to time, when he felt a consciousness might lock, Romero would project a stabilizing field through the mother's probability channel and into the quantum matrix adjacent to the baby's forming awareness. Allowing energy to redistribute through this pathway would release any dimensional forces holding the consciousness in paradox.

Romero didn't develop the idea further until ten years ago when one trainee experiencing real difficulty with consciousness extractions prompted him to reconsider the problem. Around the same time, he met Professor Nicholas Black and consultant midwife Violet Jenkins, both of the Reproductive Quantum Medicine Center at Woodbridge District Medical Complex. Together they developed the Romero stabilizer – a device to make consciousness stabilization more controlled while simultaneously releasing dimensional pressure.

The instrument consisted of a quantum field generator connected to a flexible probability anchor. Stabilization was applied using four synchronized energy nodes projecting from the anchor's matrix interface. Holding the device by its neural coupling handle, the user placed the anchor against the portion of consciousness signature exposed through the dilated probability field and activated it. This gently pushed the baby's awareness back into stable superposition while releasing dimensional pressure, allowing the obstetrician to complete extraction more easily. Because stabilization was distributed equally among four nodes with greater combined field coverage than a user's mental projection alone, the risk of consciousness fragmentation was minimized.

The team secured funding to employ a quantum engineer who used advanced simulation technology and matter-printing to create a prototype. "We were at the point of testing it in clinical trials," Romero said, "when we realized that before experimenting on actual patients, we should test it on a simulator." No such simulator existed – so he decided to build one himself.

That Romero could do this came as no surprise once you knew his background. His career was rooted in medicine, but his interests encompassed sculpture, holographic art, and quantum mechanics. He worked with hard-light constructs, electromagnetic fields, and probability matrices. "I've got a large laboratory with fabrication equipment and a quantum forge," he said. "I make things. I always have, ever since I was young. My father was an engineer, my mother worked in media production and cultural evolution studies."

Although tests with the Grace prototype showed the stabilizer worked as intended, Romero and his colleagues faced what he called a kind of medical catch-22. "We had the stabilizer functional about three years ago, but we were more interested in saving lives than commercializing a product. We thought the right thing was to ensure we had the optimal design before marketing." They tried it on a dozen patients in labor and concluded it performed as expected. But they delayed commercialization because they wanted more extensive, rigorous clinical studies.

This presented a problem. "If you've applied for research funding," Romero explained, "but you already have what appears to be a commercially viable design, potential funders will say the company planning to sell it should finance the research." Conversely, commercial interest was easier to generate with existing evidence of safety and effectiveness.

The team didn't want the stabilizer sitting unused. So they eventually decided to find a commercial partner for manufacturing and distribution. They'd now identified one and were confident production would begin soon. With sufficient users, they could then compile factual evidence of benefit rather than relying on anecdotal reports. Not ideal, Romero conceded, but the best approach available.

Meanwhile, back to Quantum Grace: so named, Romero said, not after any particular person but because the designation was memorably appropriate for a training tool dealing with quantum states. He assembled the original Grace over a weekend. The bio-holographic projectors were salvaged from decommissioned medical equipment; the consciousness signature was synthesized from quantum recordings he'd made over twenty years; the rest comprised spare parts from his laboratory. "It wasn't actually that difficult," Romero said.

When originally conceived, Grace was simply a means of testing the stabilizer's effectiveness. Her appearance was irrelevant. Only when Grace was repurposed as a teaching aid did she require refinement.

Romero remembered exactly when the idea of her expanded role occurred to him. "I was on the transport shuttle from Havencia to Greenfield Town," he said. "Grace was with me because the first Romero stabilizer had become available at Woodbridge District Medical Complex. It was about midnight, I'd had my complimentary drink, and I suddenly thought, 'Even if the stabilizer doesn't achieve widespread adoption, Grace could be valuable as a teaching tool.'"

The following morning at Woodbridge District, Romero asked a visiting professor of quantum obstetrics to examine Grace and provide feedback. She projected her consciousness into Grace's quantum matrix, grasped the fetal signature, and said it felt authentic. "Extremely gratifying," Romero laughed.

With a grant from the Greenfield Medical Innovation Fund, they made Grace more sophisticated. Romero showed the prototype to BioSim Dynamics, an established company specializing in medical simulators. They were impressed. A year later, the first refined version of Quantum Grace was commercially available.

In Grace's current form, the precise nature of her quantum entanglement could be adjusted according to training needs. The fetal consciousness signature within her matrix could be configured to mimic various states of dimensional paradox. By adjusting quantum field parameters, it was possible to vary entanglement severity from mild to so extreme that extraction was virtually impossible. This way she simulated the full range of difficulty obstetricians might encounter.

How valuable was such a simulator for training medical staff? Extremely valuable, according to Violet Jenkins. Imagine it's the middle of the night and an unplanned emergency extraction is required: "Some junior doctor might find themselves managing it alone." Having practiced consciousness extraction on a simulator was far better than first developing the skill on an actual patient – a critical consideration in professional ethics.

At Woodbridge District, midwives in training also practiced on Grace. The likelihood of midwives performing actual extractions was slim, but they were often asked to assist by providing dimensional stabilization. Grace's design allowed them to practice this skill and learn proper stabilization techniques. "Any practice in controlled conditions helps you remain calm during emergencies, which is our goal," Jenkins said.

It was still too early for definitive judgment about Grace's impact. "When we first introduced Grace," Jenkins recalled, "some experienced professors said things like, 'We always managed without one. Why would you need this?' But ask them to try it and they admit it's remarkably effective." Medicine as a whole had an oddly ambivalent relationship with innovation – a matter of professional ethics and decision-making processes. Some new findings, techniques, or equipment took years to penetrate the profession; others were immediately adopted.

A proper study of the Romero stabilizer's clinical effectiveness would necessarily involve women giving birth. Assessing Grace's value as a simulator didn't require human subjects, and the team had already conducted such a study. Thirty obstetricians from three medical facilities with varying experience levels participated. They all received brief instruction on Grace's operation and were asked to perform timed extractions at three difficulty levels.

When the study results came in, Romero was initially disappointed. "Only 87 percent gave positive responses to our first survey question," he admitted. "That seemed low for something we'd worked so hard on." But he'd misunderstood what the data showed. That figure reflected responses to whether the simulator felt realistic – specifically, whether participants experienced authentic sensations when interfacing with entangled consciousness. "Realism is important," Jenkins explained, "but it's not the same as training value. A simulator could feel somewhat artificial yet still teach essential skills effectively."

The researchers had carefully distinguished between these two metrics. Realism mattered for immersion, but training value encompassed whether practitioners felt better prepared for actual emergencies after using the device. "We asked separate questions because we wanted to understand both dimensions," Romero said.

The distinction proved significant. While 13 percent of participants noted some aspect of the quantum interface felt slightly synthetic compared to actual patients, the assessment of educational benefit told a different story. When asked about preparedness for real clinical situations, about usefulness for developing extraction techniques, and about overall training value, responses were substantially more positive.

"The feedback on training value exceeded what we'd hoped," Jenkins noted. "Nearly all participants – I believe it was six percentage points higher than the realism figure – endorsed it as valuable for their professional development." Several wrote detailed comments describing how the practice sessions had improved their confidence with consciousness extraction procedures.

Romero later summarized the findings for a medical conference. "If you ask obstetricians whether Grace offers realistic experience with entangled consciousness, 87 percent say yes. That's our realism metric. But the question we really cared about – training value – that number tells a more encouraging story." He paused. "Almost nineteen in twenty found it worthwhile. Only two participants out of thirty expressed reservations, and even they acknowledged learning something useful."

The use of simulators to teach technical skills was now common in medical education across the colonies. You could learn to repair tissue damage, manage quantum field interactions, or stabilize consciousness fragmentation. You could practice emergency resuscitation or perform simulated dimensional surgery. The technology required might cost a few hundred credits or tens of thousands. Either way, given that most of these devices were invented during the past three or four decades of colony medicine, it was surprising to learn that medical simulation could be traced back to pre-spaceflight Earth.

One ancient civilization used bronze statues with small holes to teach acupuncture point locations. To test students' knowledge, the statue would be filled with liquid and coated with wax to mask the holes – correct needle insertion would produce a leak.

Given the universality of childbirth, it was unsurprising that reproductive anatomy was among the most frequently simulated. For eighteenth-century Earth midwives and doctors, various contraptions were devised, including glass uteri supported by artificial pelvises containing flexible fetal models. Trainees delivered babies while blindfolded, their fumbling hands visible only to instructors.

As another historical example, a cloth-covered mannequin comprised a female torso with complete anatomy, implantable fetuses of various developmental stages, and even – a real coup de théâtre – the ability to produce appropriately colored fluids at the right moments.

Oddly, as medicine became more scientific, many such devices fell into disuse. As an academic review noted, much of the twentieth century was something of a dark age for simulation. Its value in professional training had to be rediscovered – an endeavor in which inventive people like Mateo Romero, sometimes working with salvaged equipment in home laboratories, were still fruitfully engaged.

The story of Quantum Grace illustrated a broader pattern in medical innovation: how solutions to one problem could unexpectedly address another, how mentorship and collaboration drove progress, and how the relationship between commercial development and clinical research remained complex. In the end, whether the Romero stabilizer achieved widespread adoption or not, Grace herself had already proven her worth – a testament to the unpredictable paths of innovation in medical technology.

As Helena Flores finally succeeded in extracting the simulated fetal consciousness from Quantum Grace's matrix, she felt a surge of confidence. Next time she faced this challenge with an actual patient, she would be ready. And that, ultimately, was the point.
