After all, she was still Patricia Alvarez, the same person who had kissed her family goodbye at the start of last summer, with a love for family and friends which was, if anything, stronger than before. Once she could communicate this, the strangeness would disappear and the First Returned would again become good old Patricia. It was little enough to ask for—a return to old values, old relationships, the normalcies of the everyday instead of the chaos of the spotlight. It would certainly be granted to her.

She slept.

Dinner was at seven p.m. Her mother came; her Uncle Leo and Aunt Marcus came. Together with Tomás, Eva and herself, they made six, and ate in the dining room at the big table.

Before she'd become the First Returned, it would have been a noisy affair. Her family had never been noted for a lack of energy, a lack of conversation, and Eva had always chosen mealtimes—especially with company present—to describe everything and anything that had happened to her during the day. And Tomás himself had always chatted, especially with her mother, though they didn't agree about political philosophy. Still, it had been good-natured; the general tone of their lives had been good-natured.

This wasn't good-natured. Exactly what it was she wasn't sure. "Stiff" was perhaps the word.

They began with soup, Tomás and Mother serving quickly, efficiently from the kitchen, then sitting down at the table. She looked at Mother as she raised her first spoonful of warm broth, and said, "Looking well as always." It was nothing new; she'd said it many many times before, but her mother had always reacted with a bright smile and a quip something like, "Well enough for my age, you mean." This time she burst into tears. It shocked her. But what shocked her even more was the fact that no one looked up, commented, made any attempt to comfort her; no one indicated in any way that a woman was sobbing at the table.

She was sitting directly across from Mother, and reached out and touched her left hand which lay limply beside the silverware. She didn't move it—she hadn't touched her once beyond that first, quick, strangely-cool embrace at the door—then a few seconds later she withdrew it and let it drop out of sight.

So there she was, Patricia Alvarez, at home with the family. So there she was, the pioneer returned, waiting to be treated as a human being.

The soup bowls were cleared away and the main course served. Uncle Leo began to talk. "The most fascinating organizational behavior study you ever did see," he boomed in his powerful professor's voice. "Still ongoing. We'll publish before—" At that point he looked at Patricia, and Patricia nodded encouragement, desperately interested in this normalcy, and Leo's voice died away. He looked down at his plate, mumbled, "Food's getting cold," and began to eat. His hand shook a little; his weathered face was not quite as confident as Patricia remembered it.

Aunt Marcus made a few quavering statements about the Regional Arts Council, and Patricia looked across the table to where she sat between Leo and Mother—her husband and daughter bracketed her, and yet she felt alone—and said, "I've missed working on my time management projects. Here it is late summer and I haven't organized a single schedule since before last summer."

Aunt Marcus smiled, if you could call it that—a pitiful twitching of the lips—and nodded. She threw her eyes in Patricia's direction, and past her, and then down to her plate. Mother, who was still sniffling, said, "I have a terrible headache. I'm going to lie down in the guest room a while." She touched Patricia's shoulder in passing—her affectionate, effusive mother who would embrace stray animals and strange children, who had often overwhelmed her with an excess of physical and verbal affection—she barely touched Patricia's shoulder and fled.

So now five of them sat at the table. The meat was served—thin, rare slices of protein, the juices running warmly from the center. She cut into it and raised a forkful to her mouth, then glanced at Eva and said, "Looks fresh enough to have been prepared this morning." Eva said, "Yeah, Mom." Aunt Marcus put down her knife and fork and murmured something to her husband. Leo cleared his throat and said Marcus was developing new dietary preferences and he guessed she was going into the living room for a while. "She'll be back for dessert, of course," he said, his laugh sounding forced.

Patricia looked at Tomás; Tomás was busy with his plate. Patricia looked at Eva; Eva was busy with her plate. Patricia looked at Leo; Leo was chewing, gazing out over their heads to the kitchen. Patricia looked at Marcus; she was disappearing into the living room.

She brought her fist down on the table. The settings jumped; a glass overturned, spilling water. She brought it down again and again. They were all standing now. She sat there and pounded the table with her right fist—Patricia Alvarez, who would never have thought of making such a scene before, but who was now so sick and tired of being treated as the First Returned, of being stood back from, looked at in awe of, felt in fear of, that she could have smashed more than a table.

Tomás said, "Patricia!"

She said, voice hoarse, "Shut up. Go away. Let me eat alone. I'm sick of the lot of you."

Mother and Leo returned a few minutes later where she sat forcing food down her throat. Mother said, "Patricia dear—" She didn't answer. She began to cry, and Patricia was glad she left the house then. She had never said anything really harsh to her mother. She was afraid this would have been the time. Leo merely cleared his throat and mumbled something about getting together again soon and "come visit the research center" and he, too, was gone. Marcus never did manage to speak to her.

She finished her meal and waited. Soon Tomás came in with the special dessert he'd been preparing half the day—a magnificent layered cake. He served her, and cut portions for himself and Eva. He hesitated near her chair, and when she made no comment he called the girl. Then the three of them were sitting, facing the empty side of the table. They ate the cake. Eva finished first and got up and said, "Hey, I promised—"

"You promised your friends you'd work on media production or study information theory or something; anything to get away from your mother."

Eva's head dropped and she muttered, "No, Mom."

Tomás said, "She'll stay home, Patricia. We'll spend an evening together—talking, watching programs, playing games."

Eva said, "Sure, Mom, if you want to."

Patricia stood up. "The question is not whether I want to. You both know I want to. The question is whether you want to."

They answered together that of course they wanted to. But their eyes—her husband's and daughter's eyes—could not meet hers, and so she said she was going to her room because she was, after all, very tired and would in all probability continue to be very tired for a long, long time and that they shouldn't count on her for normal social interaction.

She fell asleep quickly, lying there in her clothes.

But she didn't sleep long. Tomás shook her and she opened her eyes to a lighted room. "Akira and Manuel are here." She blinked at him. He smiled, and it seemed his old smile. "They're so anxious to see you, Patricia. I could barely keep Akira from coming up and waking you herself. They want to go out and see the city. Please, Patricia, say you will."

She sat up. "Akira," she muttered. "Akira and Manuel." They'd had wonderful times together, from university on. Akira and Manuel, their oldest and closest friends. Perhaps this would begin her real homecoming.

See the city? They'd celebrate it properly!

It didn't turn out that way. She was disappointed; but then again, she'd also expected it. This entire first day at home had conditioned her to expect nothing good. They went to the entertainment complex, and Akira sounded very much the way she always had—quick-witted and full of laughter and full of stories. She hugged Tomás the way she always had, and embraced Patricia warmly (but not the way she always had—so much more carefully, almost remotely), and insisted they all drink more than was good for them as she always had. And for once, Patricia was ready to go along on the drinking. For once, she matched Akira glass for glass.

They didn't stay at the entertainment complex very long. At ten o'clock they crossed the plaza to Meridian's Café, where Akira and the others ordered food and coffee and Patricia went right on drinking. Tomás said something to her, but she merely smiled and waved her hand and gulped another ounce of oblivion.

There was music and dancing in Meridian's Café. She'd been there many times before, and she was sure several of the patrons recognized her. But except for a few abortive glances in her direction, it was as if she were a stranger in a city halfway around the world.

At midnight, she was still drinking. The others wanted to leave, but she said, "I haven't danced with my friend Manuel." Her tongue was thick, her mind was blurred, and yet she could read the strange expression on his face—friendly Manuel, who'd always joked with her, who'd made a ritual of joking with her. Friendly Manuel, who now looked as if he were going to be sick.

"So let's dance," she said and stood up.

They were on the dance floor. She held him close, and hummed and chatted. And through the alcoholic haze saw he was a stiff-smiled, stiff-bodied, mechanical dancing partner.

The music finished; they walked back to the booth. Akira said, "Time to head home."

Patricia said, "First one dance with my loving husband."

She and Tomás danced. She didn't hold him close as she had Manuel. She waited for him to come close on his own, and he did, and yet he didn't. Because while he put himself against her, there was something in his face—no, in his eyes; it always showed in the eyes—that made her know he was trying to be the old Tomás and not succeeding. This time when the music ended, she was ready to go home.

They rode back through Pearlbrook District, she and Tomás in the rear of Akira's vehicle, Manuel driving because Akira had drunk just a little too much, Akira singing and telling an occasional story, and somehow not her old self. No one was their old self. No one would ever be their old self with the First Returned.

They turned left, to take the short cut along Memorial Road, and Akira finished a story about a consciousness researcher and a media personality and looked at her husband and then past him at the long, ornate fence paralleling the road. "Hey," she said, pointing, "do you know what they say about that place?"

Manuel glanced to the left, and so did Patricia and Tomás. Manuel made a little sound, and Tomás seemed to stop breathing, but Akira went on a while longer, not yet aware of her supposed faux pas.

"You know what they say?" she repeated, turning to the back seat, the laughter bubbling up. "You know what, folks?"

Manuel said, "Did you notice the new construction near—"

Patricia said, "No, Akira, what do they say?"

Akira said, "They say it's—" And then she caught herself and waved her hand and muttered, "I forgot what I was going to say."

"They say it's where people go to rest forever," Patricia said, and looked through the window, past the ornate fence, into the large memorial park at the fleeting monuments.

The vehicle was filled with horrified silence when there should have been nothing but laughter, or irritation at a too-old observation. "Maybe you should let me out right here," Patricia said. "I'm home—or that's what everyone seems to think. Maybe I should lie down in one of those crypts. Maybe that would satisfy people. Maybe that's the only way to act, like something from ancient metaphysics or horror stories."

Tomás said, "Oh, Patricia, don't, don't!"

The vehicle raced along the road, crossed a main thoroughfare, went four blocks and pulled to a stop. She didn't bother saying good night. She didn't wait for Tomás. She just got out and walked up the stone path and entered the house.

"Patricia," Tomás whispered from the guest room doorway, "I'm so sorry—"

"There's nothing to be sorry about. It's just a matter of time. It'll all work out in time."

"Yes," he said quickly, "that's it. I need a little time. We all need a little time. Because it's so strange, Patricia. Because it's so frightening. I should have told you that the moment you walked in. I think I've hurt you terribly, we've all hurt you terribly, by trying to hide that we're frightened."

"I'm going to stay in the guest room," she said, "for as long as necessary. For good if need be."

"How could it be for good? How, Patricia?"

That question was perhaps the first firm basis for hope she'd had since returning. And there was something else; what Gupta had told her, even as Gupta himself had reacted as all people did.

"There are others coming, Tomás. Eight that I know of in the suspension chambers right now. My colleague, Dr. Nelson, who died at the same moment I did—she's going to be next. She was injured worse than I was, so it took a little longer, but she's almost ready. And there'll be many more, Tomás. The government is going to save all they possibly can from now on. Every time a young and healthy person loses their life by accident, by violence, and their body can be recovered, they'll go into the chambers and they'll start the regenerative neural and organ process—the process that made it all possible, combining neuroscience and biotechnology. So people have to get used to us. And the old stories, the old terrors, the ugly old superstitions have to die, because in time each place will have some of us; because in time it'll be an ordinary thing."

Tomás said, "Yes, and I'm so grateful that you're here, Patricia. Please believe that. Please be patient with me and Eva and—" He paused. "There's one question."

She knew what the question was. It had been the first asked her by everyone from the Premier of Dravonia on down, a question that touched on consciousness studies and the nature of existence itself.

"I experienced nothing," she said. "It was as if I slept those eight and a half months in the chamber—slept without dreaming. No metaphysical revelations, no journey through consciousness. Just... absence. And then weeks of rehabilitation before I could return here."

He came to her and touched her face with his lips, and she was satisfied.

Later, half asleep, she heard a dog howling, and remembered stories of how they announced death and the presence of the returned. She shivered and pulled the covers closer to her and luxuriated in being safe in her own home.

THE END
quality_problem.question: How long was Patricia's journey away from home?

quality_problem.story:
The Stellar Archive
By ADAPTED WORK

Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive Project was a cursed venture leased for a mysterious tour of the outer colonies. It made a one-night installation on a Marvenia research station—to find that sabotage stalked it from the shadows in corrupted data streams.

Matthew Fisher leaned forward across the small conference table. He knocked over the mug of synthetic coffee, but it didn't matter. The mug was empty. He jabbed me in the shoulder with his stylus, not very hard. Not hard enough to actually hurt, just enough to make his point.

"We," he said, "are finished. Bankrupt. Out of funding and out of options." He added, as an afterthought, "Destitute."

I looked at him. I said sourly, "You're exaggerating!"

"Exaggerating." Matthew put his elbows on the table and peered at me through a curtain of very dark hair that needed cutting. "She says I'm exaggerating! With Fisher's Digital Humanities Archive, the Greatest Cultural Repository in the Colonies, so deep in debt..."

"It's no deeper in debt than you are in denial." I was irritated because he'd been hogging the coffee dispenser all morning. "The Greatest Cultural Repository. Please! I've managed Fisher's Digital Archive around the Woodbridge Region for seven years, and I know. It's underfunded, it's understaffed, it's breaking down! Nothing works, from the quantum computing servers to the junior archivists. In short, it's failing!"

I must have been more tired than I thought. Nobody insults Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive to Matthew Fisher's face unless they're exhausted and want a long argument.

Matthew stood up. He stood up slowly. I had plenty of time to see his brown eyes narrow, and hear the soft hum of the environmental controls, and watch the curious stares of the station personnel at nearby tables swing toward us, interested and somewhat amused.

I had plenty of time to think how I'm not as diplomatic as I should be, and how Matthew has a temper when pushed.

I said, "Matthew. Wait. I..."

Somebody said, "Excuse me. Is one of you Dr. Matthew Fisher?"

Matthew put his hands on the table. He closed his eyes and smiled tightly and said, very carefully:

"Would you be here about the server lease, or the data storage fees?"

I shot a glance at the newcomer. She'd saved me from an uncomfortable confrontation, even if she was a creditor; and I felt sorry for her. Matthew Fisher straightened his shoulders like he was preparing for battle.

The stranger was petite. She made even me look tall. She was dressed in dark-grey professional attire, very conservative. There was a touch of grey in her dark hair and her skin was pale, smooth, and carefully maintained. She had the kind of face that university administrators will trust with sensitive projects. I looked for her security detail.

There didn't seem to be any. The woman looked at Matthew with pale grey eyes, and her voice was softer than his.

She said, "I don't think you understand."

I felt uneasy, suddenly. Somebody shifted in their seat. The sound was loud in the quiet cafeteria. I straightened up, and my palms were damp. Matthew Fisher sighed.

Then I saw what the woman was holding in her hand.

I stood up quickly. "Wait," I said. "Look at that."

Matthew glared at me. "What's wrong with you, Samantha? I'm handling this."

"Shut up," I said. "Look what she's got there. A funding authorization!"

The woman looked at me. She hadn't reacted at all. "Yes," she said. "A funding authorization. Quite substantial. Would you permit me to join you?"

Matthew Fisher sat down. He managed a more genuine smile. "Of course. I'm Dr. Fisher. This is Samantha Boyd, my project manager." He looked at the spilled coffee. "I apologize for that. Misunderstanding."

The woman smiled slightly. She did it with her lips. The rest of her face remained professional and unreadable, almost mask-like. I realized with a start that it wasn't a mask at all. It was the most complete poker face I'd ever encountered, and you couldn't read those calm grey eyes any more than you could read encrypted data.

I didn't trust her. I didn't trust her at all. But she had funding. I said, "Hello. Let's find a private meeting room. These station personnel make me nervous, watching like they're waiting for entertainment."

The woman nodded. "Excellent suggestion. My name is Margaret Kim. I wish to—ah—commission your archive services."

I looked at Matthew. He looked more hopeful than he had in months. We didn't say anything until we got Margaret Kim into a private conference room with fresh coffee on the table. Then I cleared my throat.

"What exactly did you have in mind, Ms. Kim?"

Kim sipped her coffee, made a polite face, and set it down. "I have access to independent funding sources. It has always been my mission to preserve cultural heritage for future generations..."

Matthew got tense. "Just a moment," he murmured, and started to stand. I touched his arm.

"Let Ms. Kim finish."

He sat down, looking suspicious. Kim ignored him. She continued, quietly,

"I have always believed that oral history preservation, properly executed, is the most valuable service we can provide to humanity's collective memory..."

I said, "Of course. But what was your specific proposal?"

"There are many settlements along the Marvenia frontier where no systematic cultural documentation has been conducted. I propose to remedy that. I propose to commission your archive, Dr. Fisher, to make a tour of several colonies in the outer territories."

Matthew had relaxed. His eyes began to show interest. He started to speak, and I interrupted.

"That would be expensive, Ms. Kim," I said. "We'd have to postpone several other projects..."

She looked at me. I was stretching the truth, and she knew it. But she said,

"I quite understand. I would be prepared..."

The door slid open suddenly. Kim stopped talking. Matthew and I turned to look at the figure in the doorway.

It was Miguel Ortiz, our senior technician—a tall, intense man from a Terran colony on Mars. I'd visited once. Miguel looks a lot like the landscape there—serious, uncompromising, and tough. His hands, gripping the doorframe, were stained with equipment grease and were nearly as large as maintenance tools.

He said, "Boss, the quantum computing array is acting up again."

"The array can wait," said Matthew. "Can't you see I'm in a meeting?"

Miguel's dark eyes were worried. "I'm telling you, Boss, the system isn't stable. It hasn't had proper maintenance. If something..."

I said, "That'll all be taken care of, Miguel. Please give us a moment."

He looked at me like he was calculating how much trouble I was causing. "Fine! But the system's unstable. It's overheating, understand? And if it doesn't get proper attention soon I'm not sure our backup protocols will hold."

He left, letting the door slide shut with emphasis. Matthew Fisher groaned. Kim cleared her throat and said, rather formally,

"The quantum computing array?"

"Yes. It's somewhat temperamental." Matthew took a quick sip of coffee. I elaborated.

"It's the backbone of our archive operations, Ms. Kim. A state-of-the-art quantum computing system. The only other comparable system in the region belongs to the University Consortium, and theirs is much smaller than ours."

Theirs was also much newer, but I didn't mention that. Our array may be outdated, but it's still impressive. I only hoped it wouldn't fail completely, because without it we'd have a more dysfunctional operation than even I could tolerate.

Kim looked impressed. "A quantum computing array. How fascinating! The applications for digital humanities research must be extraordinary. The processing capabilities..."

We were getting off track. I said tactfully, "We'd need at least fifty thousand credits."

It was twice what we had any right to ask. I was prepared to negotiate. Kim looked at me with that unreadable expression. For a fraction of a second I thought I saw something behind her calm grey eyes, and my instincts screamed warning. Kim smiled professionally.

"I'm not inclined to haggle. Fifty thousand Universal Credits will be acceptable." She produced a tablet, entered some commands, and displayed an authorization code.

"By way of initial funding. My legal representative and I will meet with you tomorrow morning with a formal contract and project timeline. Good evening."

We said good evening, trying to contain our relief. Kim departed. Matthew reached for the tablet to verify the authorization, but I was faster.

"Wait," I said. "There are creditors waiting for this. Serious creditors with legal claims. Here." I transferred a small amount to a discretionary account. "We can celebrate with this."

Matthew has an extensive vocabulary. He used it. When he caught his breath he said suddenly,

"Kim is running some kind of operation."

"Obviously."

"It may be illegitimate."

"Possibly. And she may be eccentric and genuine. For heaven's sake!" I said. "You want to sit here until the project collapses completely?"

Matthew looked at me, oddly. He looked at the tablet in my hands. He ran his fingers through his dark hair.

"Yeah," he said. "I hope there'll be enough left to pay the lawyers." He moved toward the door. "Hey, let's get Miguel. We need to discuss this!"

It was quite late when we returned to the aging research station where Fisher's Digital Archive was housed in its cramped quarters. Late as it was, they were waiting for us. About fifteen of them, sitting around the common area and looking very unhappy.

It was lonely out there, with the station's recycled air cool and stale, carrying that faint metallic taste of old environmental systems. There's a feeling to these outer stations, like something abandoned and waiting. An uneasy feeling. The fluorescent lights flickered occasionally.

Matthew Fisher walked into the common area where our team had gathered. He was steady enough. He waved and said, "Hello, everyone."

They stood up from their workstations and chairs and came toward us. I straightened and prepared for confrontation. We felt we owed these people more than just apologies. It grates on a person's pride to have to avoid their own team members in the corridors. This was the first time in weeks we'd faced them directly.

I displayed the funding authorization on my tablet. That stopped them. Very formally, Matthew and I explained the situation, outlined the payment schedule, and answered questions. Matthew stretched and looked genuinely relieved.

"Well?" he said.

"Well," I said.

We had a productive discussion. Some people were skeptical. We addressed their concerns. Everyone felt better afterward. They had assurance of payment, and we had their renewed commitment.

The news spread through the station quickly. The junior archivists and the data specialists and the oral history researchers and all the other dedicated but underpaid professionals that make up a digital humanities project were noticeably more optimistic, discussing the possibilities over dinner.

Matthew Fisher regarded them with satisfaction, wiping fatigue from his eyes. "They're good people, Sam. Excellent colleagues. They stayed with me, and I'm going to make it right."

I said, "Sure," rather wearily. Matthew looked thoughtful.

"Let's check on the quantum array."

I didn't want to check on the quantum array. I never felt comfortable in the server room, especially at night or during system maintenance. I'm a people person, myself. The hum and heat of high-powered computing gives me anxiety. But Matthew looked determined, so I shrugged.

"Okay. But just for a minute. Then we need sleep."

"You're a good colleague, Sam. Best project manager anywhere..."

The argument had worn him down. I was worried he'd make a mistake and damage something expensive. That's why I went along. If I hadn't... Oh, well, what's a few sleepless nights among colleagues?

It was dim in the server room. At the far end, there was a soft blue glow. Miguel was evidently monitoring the quantum array. We started down the long corridor between the rows of server racks and cooling units and backup systems.

Our footsteps echoed on the metal floor. I wasn't as confident as Matthew, and my skin prickled with unease. It's the sound, I think; the constant hum and the occasional clicks and whirs. And the sense of them, these powerful machines processing endless streams of data, with their patient indifference contained by cooling systems and surge protectors.

Matthew Fisher stumbled slightly. I caught his arm, and then wiped sweat from my forehead despite the cool air. An alarm sounded. A sharp, piercing warning tone that cut through the mechanical ambiance. The quantum array, experiencing critical errors.

It had been stable. Now every monitoring system activated simultaneously. My stomach dropped. I called out every technical term I could think of, and I couldn't hear myself over the alarms. Presently a loud electronic tone silenced the warnings. Miguel had triggered the emergency shutdown.

But the systems didn't stabilize. Not really. They were compromised. You can sense it when systems are compromised. I think that's why I'm anxious around them. They make me feel vulnerable—like our entire project could disappear in an instant. Yeah. They were compromised that night, suddenly...

Miguel looked grim as we reached the main console. "It's getting worse," he said. "Someone's been accessing the system."

"That's concerning," said Matthew Fisher. His eyes looked tired. He swayed slightly with exhaustion. "That's very concerning." He frowned.

I looked at the quantum array. Its housing was the largest and most sophisticated in the facility and even so it looked like it could fail catastrophically at any moment. I don't know if you've ever seen a quantum computing array in crisis. There are only a few in the outer colonies. If you haven't, nothing I can say will convey the anxiety.

They're what the tech specialists call "bleeding edge technology." Seems the engineers had ambitious ideas about quantum computing. The arrays were quite successful initially, but something always causes problems and now there's only a few operational, way out in the research facilities, where even the maintenance crews rarely go. Expensive experiments.

I couldn't help feeling worried about it. The array was housed in its protective chamber with its cooling systems—yes, multiple redundant systems—working overtime and its processing cores deep in their quantum states, executing calculations. Just calculating. Not for anything specific. The status displays showed unstable qubits, like warning fires.

The ambient light was blue-white on the metallic housing, but the error indicators made the monitoring displays flash red, showing system failures. It looked like a disaster waiting to happen.

Miguel said quietly, "Someone's been tampering with it. And somebody needs to fix this properly."

Matthew frowned. I said irritably, "Be reasonable, Miguel! Nobody outside the team has access. There must be a logical explanation."

The alarm sounded again. The array didn't move, obviously, but the temperature readings spiked. The warning, that close, was deafening, and it made me feel cold and hollow inside. The danger, the sheer technical catastrophe...

Matthew Fisher looked shaken. I said, "You'll have to stabilize this, Miguel. It's threatening the entire archive."

He worked on the emergency protocols, and things stabilized somewhat. Miguel stood looking at the monitoring displays, checking readings carefully, like a diagnostician. Then he turned to us.

"I've been maintaining this system," he said. "When we salvaged it from the university surplus and everyone thought it was too damaged to use, I rebuilt it. I know this array. I can work with it. But this time..."

He shrugged. He was large and intense and serious, and his voice carried genuine concern.

"This time," he said, "I'm not certain we can recover."

"Well for Pete's sake, do what you can. We have a contract, and we need it operational." I took Matthew's arm. "Come on, we need rest."

He leaned on my shoulder and we left. Miguel didn't acknowledge us. Matthew looked troubled.

"You were right, Sam," he mumbled. "Project's in trouble. I know it. But it's my life's work. I care about it, Sam. Understand? Like Miguel there with the array. It's old and problematic, but he maintains it. I care..."

"I know," I told him. "Stop worrying for one night."

We were far from the server room then. The racks and systems loomed high and dark around us. It was quiet. The subtle, uneasy hum all around us and our footsteps only made it quieter.

Matthew was nearly asleep on his feet. I started to guide him back. And then I noticed something on a nearby terminal—small traces of unauthorized access, barely visible in the system logs.

I called out, "Miguel! Miguel, there's been a security breach! Miguel—we need you!"

I started to return to the server room. Matthew leaned heavily on me, exhausted. The alarms burst suddenly in a deafening cascade of warnings and error messages, amplified by the metal walls, and above it all I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems screaming in overload.

I thought, "Someone's here. Someone caused this. Someone wants to destroy us!" I tried to call out again. It caught in my throat. I was sweating, and it was cold.

Matthew's stumbling steps tangled with mine. We fell. I caught him, protecting his head, and braced myself against a server rack.

The first system failure hit. It was like an electrical shock, a cascade of shutdowns spreading through the network. I shouted. The failures propagated through the connected systems.

Matthew groaned and struggled. I remember holding on and thinking, "This is it. This is the end, and I'm terrified!"

Then everything went dark.

---

Emily Gutierrez, our station medic, was checking my vital signs when I woke up. Her round face showed concern. She'd worked double shifts recently, and she looked exhausted.

"You're okay, Ms. Boyd," she said gently. "You'll be fine."

She gave me something for the headache. It helped. I asked, "Where's Matthew? How is he?"

"Dr. Fisher is fine. You protected him from injury. You're quite the hero, Ms. Boyd. Miguel got the systems shut down in time. You're a hero."

I said, "Right," and pushed myself up carefully. I managed to stand, though I felt dizzy. I made it to the small mirror in my quarters—I was in my own room—and I saw I looked exhausted but uninjured.

Matthew Fisher opened the door. He looked pale and serious, and there was a bruise on his arm. He said:

"Kim is here with her legal representative."

I found my jacket. "I'll be right there."

Emily left, still looking concerned. Matthew closed the door.

"Sam," he said, "those systems were stable when we arrived. Someone deliberately compromised them. On purpose."

I felt terrible. I said, "Obviously. Nobody saw anything, I suppose?" Matthew shook his head.

"Question is, Sam, who wants to sabotage us, and why?"

"Kim. She realizes she's made a mistake funding us."

"Fifty thousand credits," said Matthew quietly, "for some remote colony documentation work. It doesn't add up, Sam. You think we should withdraw?"

I shrugged. "You're the director. I'm only the one who manages the creditors."

"Yeah," Matthew said thoughtfully. "And I hear unemployment isn't pleasant. Okay, Sam. Let's go sign." He reached for the door and looked at me. "And—uh—Sam, I..."

I said, "Forget it. Next time, just don't trip over me, that's all!"

We had a difficult journey to Goldfield, Marvenia. The quantum array remained unstable, and Miguel, on the rare occasions he emerged from the server room, looked like he was expecting catastrophe. To make it worse, Jacob Anderson, our lead oral historian, fell ill during transit, and one of our junior archivists quit unexpectedly.

Her name was Vera Chen. She was slight, with close-cropped dark hair and a distinctive scar across her left eyebrow—the result, she'd once told me, of a childhood accident on a mining station. Her hands were always restless, fingers tapping surfaces even when she sat still. She'd been competent enough, unremarkable in most ways, but she had access to our systems.

Nobody would have minded her departure, except she took copies of sensitive research data with her. It lasted just long enough to terrify that group of paranoid academics. Digital humanities people are peculiar that way.

Matthew and I did some quiet investigating, but it was futile. Anyone on the team might have sabotaged those systems. It didn't help to know that somebody, maybe the person working next to you, was planning to destroy everything. By the time we reached Goldfield, I was ready to resign entirely.

Matthew guided our transport to the edge of Goldfield, the first location on our itinerary. I stood beside him, looking at the settlement through the viewports. It was Marvenia, certainly. Red dust and scattered prefab structures and harsh sunlight, and a cluster of weather-beaten buildings grouped together defensively. People in environment suits were approaching for a look.

I saw Kim's sleek corporate shuttle parked at a dedicated landing pad, and our equipment transport beside it. Matthew groaned.

"A disaster, Sam. A complete disaster!"

I muttered, "What do you expect, with this underfunded project!" and exited. He followed. The team was gathering near the airlock, but they weren't enthusiastic. You develop instincts for these things. The thin Marvenia atmosphere was already infiltrating through the seals.

As we passed the corridor to the server room, I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems, struggling.

The technical crew was busy setting up equipment, working carefully in the harsh environment. The documentation team was heading for the settlement. Matthew and I stood in our environment suits, observing.

I heard a sound behind me and turned. Angela Perry, our xenoanthropology specialist, was standing in the dust with her helmet off, breathing the thin atmosphere, and her weathered face tilted back, eyes closed. She was smiling. It looked unsettling.

You find many xenoanthropology specialists in digital humanities projects, studying cultural adaptation in frontier settlements. They're colonial specialists, they're not typical academics, and they never let you forget it.

Angela opened her sharp eyes and looked at me and laughed.

"Failure," she whispered. "Failure and conflict. The settlement warns me. I can sense it in the atmosphere."

The harsh sunlight beat down on her. She shivered despite the heat, and her expression was intense.

"The frontier colonies are resistant," she whispered. "Something has been disturbed. They are resistant, and I sense failure ahead!"

She walked away, laughing, and I cursed under my breath, and my stomach was tight. Matthew said,

"Let's see if they have a cafeteria in this place."

We weren't halfway across the landing area when a man emerged from a building at the settlement's edge. We could see him clearly, because he was separated from the crowd approaching us.

He stumbled in the dust, calling out. It took him several attempts to make our names clear enough to understand.

Matthew said, "Sam—that's Jacob Anderson."

We started running. The crowd, mostly rugged colonists in work clothes, turned to see what was happening. People began to converge on the man who staggered and gasped in the thin air.

Jacob Anderson was an oral historian, collecting cultural narratives from frontier communities. He'd collaborated with us several times previously, when funding allowed, and we had a good working relationship.

I hadn't seen him for two years. I remembered him as energetic and enthusiastic, passionate about preserving oral histories. I felt sick, looking at him now.

Matthew tried to help him. Anderson was shaking, trembling like someone in shock. Some colonist stepped forward from the gathering crowd and pressed a canteen into his trembling hands. The person was slight, wearing dust-stained work clothes like the others, with close-cropped dark hair visible beneath a battered cap.

I was focused on Anderson then, trying to assess his condition. Matthew was asking questions. The crowd pressed closer, curious faces everywhere. I caught only glimpses of the person who'd given him the canteen—restless fingers, a scar across the left eyebrow catching the harsh sunlight—before they stepped back into the mass of colonists.

We got Anderson inside the building. It turned out to be a small community center, with a few private meeting rooms at the back. We got him into one and closed the door on numerous curious faces. Anderson drank from the canteen. The crowd had dispersed outside.

Matthew said gently, "Okay, Jacob. Relax. What happened?"

Anderson tried to compose himself. He hadn't slept. The energetic lines of his face had gone slack and his eyes were red-rimmed. He was covered with dust, and his hands shook.

He said hoarsely, "I found it. I said I would, and I did. I found it and documented it."

He set down the canteen clumsily. "Help me," he said simply. "I'm frightened." His voice broke.

"I have it secured. They want to locate it, but I won't tell them. It needs to be returned. Returned to its source. I tried to do it myself, but they prevented me, and I was afraid they'd find it..."

He reached suddenly and gripped the edge of the table. "I don't know how they discovered it, but they did. I have to return it. I have to..."

Matthew looked at me. Anderson was pale and sweating. I felt frightened, suddenly. I said, "Return what where?"

Matthew stood. "I'll get the medic," he said. "Stay with him." Anderson grabbed his wrist. Anderson's fingers were white and the veins in his hands stood out prominently.

"Don't leave me. Need to tell you—where it is. Need to return it. Promise you'll return it." He gasped, struggling for breath.

"Of course," said Matthew. "Of course we'll return it. What is it?"

Anderson's face was terrible. I felt nauseated, watching him fight for air. I wanted to get Emily anyway, but somehow I knew it was too late. Anderson whispered,

"Cultural artifact. Irreplaceable. Original. You don't understand...! Return it."

"Where is it, Jacob?"

I reached past Matthew suddenly and opened the door. Kim was standing there. Kim, leaning forward, clearly listening. Anderson made a harsh choking sound and collapsed across the table.

Kim's expression didn't change. She didn't move while Matthew checked Anderson's pulse. Matthew didn't need to speak. We knew.

"Heart attack?" said Kim finally.

"Yes," said Matthew. He looked as shaken as I felt. "Poor Jacob."

I looked at the canteen on the table. I looked at Kim with her unreadable professional face. I moved past Matthew and firmly guided Kim into a chair.

"Keep her here until I return," I said.

Matthew stared at me. Kim started to object. "Be quiet," I told her. "We have a contract." I left the room and walked to the main area.

I began to notice something then. There were quite a few people in the center. At first glance they looked appropriate—a weathered, capable group of colonists in practical clothing.

Then I looked more carefully. They were dressed appropriately enough. But they moved wrong for frontier colonists, on Marvenia or anywhere else.

The place was unnaturally quiet. The center administrator was a heavy-set woman with calculating eyes and short grey hair. She was arranging water containers behind the main counter, canteens and bottles lined up in neat rows. She looked nervous.

I approached the counter. "Water," I said. She provided it, reluctantly, from a dispenser. Her thick fingers were clumsy on the controls. I reached for it, casually.

"That man we brought in," I said. "He seems very distressed. Dehydrated. What's he been doing out here?"

The administrator glanced toward the back of the center, toward the storage area, and said nothing. She was the type who ran places like this—managing supplies, maintaining order, providing for the community. Her grey hair was cropped short for practicality. She handed me the water without meeting my eyes.

"Research," said a voice beside me. "As if you didn't know."

I turned. Someone was standing next to me—slight build, close-cropped dark hair, dust-stained work clothes. Their fingers were tapping restlessly against the counter. There was a scar across their left eyebrow.

The administrator stepped back, putting distance between herself and whatever was about to happen. Her calculating eyes watched us both.

**QUESTION:** Who was the person that provided Anderson with water?

**OPTION A:** A center administrator
**OPTION B:** A familiar person from the crowd

**CORRECT ANSWER:** B
quality_problem.question: Who was the person that provided Anderson with water?
quality_problem.correct_answer: A familiar person from the crowd
answers: A familiar person from the crowd

quality_problem.story:
Dr. Sophia Edwards left her laboratory at the Oceanographic Research Institute in Oakdale Village at exactly 6:00 PM and began the evening walk she had taken, without fail, for fifteen solid years.

The walk never varied. She paced three blocks down Harbor Street, stopped at the Blue Whale Café to purchase a kelp tea, then walked to the end of the fifth block on Harbor. There she turned left on Maritime Avenue, followed Maritime to Coral Street, down Coral and so by way of Beacon back to Harbor again and to her small apartment above the institute.

She didn't walk quickly. She took her time. She always returned to her door at exactly 6:50 PM. No one ever stopped to talk with her. Even the barista at the Blue Whale Café remained silent while preparing her drink. Dr. Edwards merely nodded, the woman prepared the tea, and Dr. Edwards took her cup. That was all.

For people long ago had gathered that Dr. Edwards desired solitude. The newer generation of researchers called it dedication to her work. Certain colleagues had a different word for it. The senior scientists remembered that this intense woman with her waterproof notebook, titanium data collection tools, and ever-present rain jacket had once been a celebrated professor at Ravenswood Regional University.

The notebook was her constant companion—she was never without it. In fifteen years, no colleague had ever seen Dr. Edwards separated from that waterproof notebook, not for a single moment during working hours. She carried it everywhere: to the laboratory, on her walks, even clutching it during the rare institute-wide safety drills. The notebook contained her observations, her measurements, her meticulous records of oceanic phenomena spanning a decade and a half.

A professor of oceanography, they recalled, specializing in deep-sea ecosystems and marine resource management. At any rate, a controversy of some sort was connected with her name—an academic dispute. She had published a research paper, and she had presented that research to international conferences. What that research proposed had long been forgotten by most, but whatever it was had been considered sufficiently radical to cost Dr. Edwards her tenured position at the university.

A pale moon hung over the harbor and a sharp, salt-tinged wind was blowing when Dr. Edwards started out at six o'clock.

It was a good evening, she told herself, breathing the clean ocean air and the faint scent of seaweed from the nearby docks.

She walked steadily, her notebook tucked securely in her jacket pocket—its familiar weight against her side, the one possession she would never leave behind. She noticed that the streetlight at the corner of Harbor and Beacon was flickering, and she frowned slightly when forced to step around construction barriers before the entrance to Building 47.

It seemed she reached the corner of Maritime and Harbor just a bit too quickly, but she told herself this couldn't be. For fifteen years, since the year following her dismissal from the university, she had lived by precise routine.

The same thing, at the same time, day after day. She had not deliberately chosen such a regimented existence. A single woman, living alone with her research stipend and savings, the timed routine had developed gradually—a framework for maintaining work-life balance in the absence of other anchors.

So she turned on Maritime and back on Coral. The security guard at the corner of Coral and Beacon nodded to her as always, a silent acknowledgment of her nightly passage.

A news broadcast was playing from someone's open window, and fragments drifted to Dr. Edwards.

"...continuing to occur worldwide...entire research station in Larchmont Province vanished...leading marine biologist, Dr. Christopher Lane, cannot explain..."

The wind carried the words away and Dr. Edwards pressed her lips together. Another sensationalist report, probably. She remembered similar panic years before, something about atmospheric anomalies. And Lane! What did Lane have to do with anything? He was one of the scientists who had dismissed her paper as pseudoscience.

But she pushed the thought away, focused on the familiar rhythm of her steps, looked at the known landmarks that emerged from the coastal darkness as she walked. For there was nothing—absolutely nothing in the world—that she would let disturb her equilibrium. That was a principle she had established fifteen years ago.

There was a group of researchers outside the institute's main entrance at the corner of Coral and Beacon, talking urgently. Dr. Edwards caught excited phrases: "It's happening in every coastal region...What could cause this...The data analysis shows nothing..."

But as Dr. Edwards approached, they fell silent and watched her pass. She, for her part, gave them no acknowledgment. That was how it had been for many years, ever since people had accepted that she did not wish to engage.

One of the researchers, a young woman named Camila Bryant, half-stepped forward as if to speak, but then retreated, and Dr. Edwards continued her walk.

Back at her apartment door, she stopped and, as she had done a thousand times before, checked her waterproof watch.

She stared at it in confusion. It was only 6:35 PM.

For long minutes she stood examining the watch. The timepiece hadn't stopped; its second hand still swept smoothly around the face.

But fifteen minutes too early! For fifteen years, day in and day out, she had left at six and returned at ten minutes to seven. Now...

It wasn't until then that she realized something else was wrong. She had no kelp tea. For the first time, she had failed to stop at the Blue Whale Café.

Shaken, muttering to herself, Dr. Edwards unlocked her apartment and secured the door behind her.

She hung her jacket on the hook in the entryway—then paused, reaching back to retrieve the notebook from the pocket. She would not leave it there, even overnight, even in her own home. She carried it with her into the living area.

Dropping into her reading chair, she set the notebook on the side table and shook her head in bewilderment. Her eyes drifted automatically to the wall opposite, finding the familiar image there—the underwater scene she had positioned directly in her line of sight when she'd first arranged this room, so she could see it without turning her head.

Silence filled the room. A silence measured by the soft hum of the temperature control system.

But silence was familiar to Dr. Edwards. Once she had enjoyed music—classical recordings she could stream through her speakers. But the speakers sat disconnected in the corner. Dr. Edwards had unplugged them years before, precisely on the evening when a concert had been interrupted for breaking news.

She had stopped following news feeds and scientific journals too, had isolated herself to a few city blocks. And as the years passed, that self-imposed isolation had become absolute, an invisible but impenetrable boundary marking an area five blocks by four. Beyond that perimeter lay something she could not name, would not acknowledge. Beyond it, she never ventured.

But recluse though she was, she could not entirely escape information. Things researchers discussed in the hallways, fragments of broadcasts from open windows, headlines glimpsed on discarded tablets.

And so she knew this was the year 2089, and that the conflicts in the Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions had ended in catastrophe, followed by a mysterious phenomenon—a plague of disappearances sweeping through region after region like an invisible tide, erasing populations. A phenomenon undoubtedly connected to the wars and their disruption of natural resource management systems.

But those things she dismissed as concerns far removed from her small world. She disregarded them. She pretended she had never heard of them. Others might worry and theorize if they wished. To her, they simply did not matter.

But there were two things tonight that did matter. Two disturbing, inexplicable events. She had arrived home fifteen minutes early. She had forgotten her kelp tea.

Huddled in the chair, she frowned. It was unsettling to have her routine disrupted. There must be something wrong. Had her long isolation finally affected her mind—perhaps just slightly—enough to impair her judgment? Had she lost her sense of temporal precision, of spatial awareness?

No, she hadn't. Take this room, for example. After fifteen years, it had become as integral to her identity as her research methodology. Every detail was recorded in her mind with scientific clarity: the titanium desk with its organized specimen samples; the shelf with her carefully maintained equipment; the chronometer that displayed not only time but date, lunar phase, and tidal information; the specimen jar on the side table; her waterproof notebook beside it; and on the wall, the framed photograph.

The photograph showed an underwater scene in the foreground, a coral reef teeming with life. Far in the distance, almost at the edge of visibility, was the vague outline of a research submersible. Dr. Edwards had acquired it during her years at the university, before her dismissal—a memento of fieldwork in the Pacific, of a time when she had believed her research would change the world.

There were other images too. The coastal landscape above the storage unit, the marine charts in the corner where she sat, the satellite imagery above the bookshelf. But the reef photograph hung on the wall directly facing her chair. When she sat here in the evenings, her eyes found it naturally, inevitably. It was the first thing she saw upon sitting, the last thing she looked at before rising.

Further reflection became difficult as Dr. Edwards felt exhaustion overtaking her. She prepared for bed mechanically, slipping the notebook into the drawer of her bedside table where it remained each night. For an hour she lay awake, troubled by undefined anxieties she could neither articulate nor comprehend.

When finally she slept, it was to experience a series of disturbing dreams. She dreamed first that she was conducting fieldwork on a small research platform in the open ocean, that the waters around the platform teemed with unknown organisms—bioluminescent creatures that pulsed with alien light—and that steadily those organisms were consuming the platform itself.

In another dream, she was pursued by something she could neither observe nor measure, but only sense. And as she tried to flee, she remained stationary. Her legs moved frantically, but she made no progress. It was as if she ran on a treadmill in the laboratory.

Then again the threat surrounded her, a vast, incomprehensible presence, and she tried to call out but couldn't. She opened her mouth and strained but filled her lungs to bursting with the effort to shout—but no sound emerged.

All next day she was uneasy, and as she left the apartment that evening at precisely 6:00 PM, she kept reminding herself: "You must not forget tonight! You must remember to stop for your tea!"

She patted her jacket pocket, confirming the notebook's presence—a reassuring ritual she performed dozens of times daily. The notebook was essential to her work, irreplaceable. Without it, she would feel exposed, vulnerable.

The streetlight at the corner of Beacon was still flickering, and in front of Building 47 the construction barriers remained in place. Everything appeared the same as the night before.

And now, she told herself, the Blue Whale Café is in the next block. I must not forget tonight. To forget twice consecutively would be unacceptable.

She held that thought firmly in mind, walked just slightly faster down the street.

But at the corner she stopped, disoriented. Bewildered, she stared down the next block. There was no blue neon sign, no welcoming light on the sidewalk to mark the small café tucked into this research district.

She stared at the street marker and read the word slowly: MARITIME. She read it again, disbelieving, for this shouldn't be Maritime Avenue, but Dock Street. She had walked two blocks, and the café was between Dock and Maritime. She hadn't reached Dock yet—and here was Maritime.

Or had she, absent-mindedly, walked one block farther than intended, passed the café as on the previous night?

For the first time in fifteen years, Dr. Edwards retraced her steps. She walked back to Beacon, then turned and went back to Maritime again and on to Coral. Then back to Maritime again, where she stood stunned while a single, impossible fact crystallized in her mind:

There wasn't any café! The block from Dock to Maritime had disappeared!

Now she understood why she had missed the café the night before, why she had arrived home fifteen minutes early.

On legs that felt numb, she stumbled back to her apartment. She locked the door behind her and made her way unsteadily to her chair in the corner.

What was this? What did it mean? By what inconceivable mechanism could a paved street with buildings, equipment, and structures be erased and the space it had occupied be closed up?

Was something happening in the world that she, in her isolated existence, knew nothing about?

Dr. Edwards shivered, started to adjust her jacket, then stopped as she realized the room temperature was regulated. The cold she felt came from somewhere else. The cold of fear and uncertainty, the chill of half-formed understanding.

Her eyes found the reef photograph on the wall—the coral formations, the distant submersible, the blue depths she had once explored. Looking at it steadied her somehow, as it always did.

A profound silence had descended, a silence still measured by the chronometer's digital display. And yet a silence that held a different quality than she had ever experienced before. Not a comfortable, familiar silence—but a silence that suggested emptiness and void.

There was something behind this, Dr. Edwards told herself. Something that connected to fragments of memory buried in her consciousness, demanding recognition. Something tied to the conversations she had overheard at the institute, pieces of broadcasts she had heard while walking, the urgent discussions among researchers. Something related to events in the world from which she had withdrawn.

She recalled them now and focused on the central theme: the wars and disappearances. Hints of Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions swept nearly clean of human presence, of the phenomenon spreading through African coastlines, of its appearance in South American ports, of the desperate efforts of North American authorities to prevent its advance.

Millions of people had vanished from Pacific and Asian regions, African and South American coasts. Billions, perhaps.

And somehow those grim statistics seemed connected to her own experience. Something, somewhere, some element of her earlier research, seemed to hold an explanation. But try as she might, her confused mind failed to find the answer.

The chronometer advanced silently, its display shifting from 7:29 to 7:30.

Dr. Edwards stood, walked to the window, and looked out.

Moonlight painted the harbor in silver and black, silhouetting the cranes and vessels against a luminous sky.

But the research building directly across the street was not the same. It was strangely distorted, its proportions wrong, like a structure that had suddenly become non-Euclidean.

She stared at it in shock, trying to determine what was wrong. She recalled how it had always stood, solid, a standard example of modern marine research architecture.

Then, before her eyes, the building corrected itself. Slowly it resolved, smoothed out its strange angles, readjusted its dimensions, became once again the familiar structure she knew it must be.

With relief, Dr. Edwards turned back toward the room.

But before she moved away from the window, she looked again. The building was distorted—as severe, perhaps worse than before!

Gasping, Dr. Edwards moved away from the window, went to her bedroom, and took sedatives from her medical kit.

Her dreams that night were the same as before. Again there was the research platform in open ocean. Again she was alone upon it. Again the bioluminescent organisms were consuming her foundation piece by piece.

She woke, body drenched with perspiration. Dim light of early dawn filtered through the window. The clock beside her bed showed 7:15 AM. For a long time she lay motionless.

Again the inexplicable events of the night before returned to haunt her, and as she lay there staring at the window, she remembered them one by one. But her mind, still clouded by sleep and confusion, processed the events mechanically, lost the sharp edge of terror that surrounded them.

The light through the window slowly brightened. Dr. Edwards slid out of bed, crossed to the window, the cold floor against her bare feet. She forced herself to look out.

There was nothing outside the window. No shapes. As if there might be fog. But no fog, however dense, could obscure the equipment storage shed that stood close to the building.

But the shed was there—shadowy, indistinct in the gray light, with rust visible on its panels, a few identification markers still attached to its surface.

The shed was there now. But it hadn't been when she first looked. Dr. Edwards was certain of that.

And now she saw the faint outline of the adjacent research building—but that outline was wrong. The dimensions didn't align properly—they were distorted. As if some massive force had grasped the building and twisted it out of true. Like the building she had seen across the street the night before, the building that had painfully corrected itself when she focused on how it should appear.

Perhaps if she concentrated on how the adjacent building should look, it too might correct itself. But Dr. Edwards was exhausted. Too exhausted to focus on the building.

She turned from the window and dressed slowly. In the living area, she collapsed into her chair, rested her feet on the ottoman. For a long time she sat, trying to think. Her gaze kept drifting to the reef photograph, the coral formations offering a strange comfort—a reminder of a world that had once made sense.

And then, abruptly, something like an electrical shock ran through her. Rigid, she sat there, hollow inside at the realization. Minutes later she rose and almost ran across the room to the bookshelf mounted on the wall.

There were many volumes on the shelf: her reference texts on the first level, her research journals on the lower levels. The second level contained but one publication. And it was around this publication that Dr. Edwards' entire professional life had revolved.

Fifteen years ago she had written it and foolishly attempted to present its hypothesis to the international oceanographic community. The media, she remembered, had sensationalized it extensively. Controversy had erupted. Narrow-minded colleagues, failing to understand either her methodology or her conclusions, but seeing in her another proponent of pseudoscience, had forced her resignation from the university.

It was a straightforward paper, really, dismissed by most authorities as merely the speculation of an overzealous researcher.

Dr. Edwards took it down now, opened the cover, and began reading slowly through the pages. For a moment, the memory of her former career swept over her.

Then her eyes focused on a paragraph, a paragraph written so long ago the very words seemed foreign and distant:

"Human consciousness itself, through collective observation and measurement, maintains the physical structure of observable reality—yes, even the ocean depths we study. Billions of minds perceiving currents as currents, organisms as organisms, geological formations as formations—and not as something else. Minds that observe phenomena as they are and have maintained phenomena as they were. Eliminate those minds, and the entire framework of matter, deprived of its observational foundation, will collapse and transform like a column of sand..."

Her eyes followed down the page:

"Yet this would relate not to matter itself—but only to matter's configuration. For while human consciousness through long ages may have shaped our understanding of the space we inhabit, consciousness would have limited conceivable influence upon the existence of that matter. What exists in our known universe shall exist perpetually and can never be destroyed, only altered or transformed.

"But in modern theoretical physics and oceanography, we gain insight into the possibility—yes, probability—that there are other dimensions, other frameworks of space-time intersecting with the one we occupy.

"If a probe is inserted into a two-dimensional plane, would that plane have any knowledge of the probe? It would not, for in this case the plane is two-dimensional, the probe three-dimensional. Yet both occupy the same space.

"Granting then that the power of human consciousness alone maintains this universe, or at least this world in its present configuration, may we not go further and envision other consciousnesses in some other dimension observing us, waiting, waiting strategically for the moment they can assume control of matter? Such a concept is not impossible. It is a logical conclusion if we accept the dual hypothesis: that consciousness does control the configuration of all matter; and that other realities exist in juxtaposition with ours.

"Perhaps we shall encounter a day, far distant, when our dimension, our world will dissolve beneath our feet and before our eyes as some stronger consciousness reaches out from the dimensional shadows of the very space we inhabit and wrests from us the matter which we know to be our own."

She stood stunned beside the bookshelf, her eyes staring unseeing at the window.

She had written that. And because of those words, she had been called a pseudoscientist, had been compelled to resign her position at the university, had been forced into this isolated existence.

A tremendous realization struck her. Humans had vanished by the millions worldwide. Where there had been thousands of minds, there now were one or two. An insufficient force to maintain the configuration of matter intact.

The disappearances had swept Pacific and Asian regions nearly clean of life, had devastated African coasts, had reached South American ports—might even have come to North America. She remembered the whispers she had heard, the words of the researchers at the institute entrance, the buildings vanishing. Something scientists could not explain. But those were merely fragments of information. She did not know the complete picture—she could not know. She never monitored broadcasts, never read scientific journals.

But abruptly everything fit together in her mind like the solution to a complex equation. The significance of it all gripped her with devastating clarity.

There were not sufficient consciousnesses in existence to maintain the material world in its familiar configuration. Some other intelligence from another dimension was struggling to supersede human observation and transform this universe into its own framework!

Abruptly Dr. Edwards closed the paper, returned it to the shelf, and retrieved her jacket.

She had to know more. She had to find someone who could provide information.

She moved through the entryway to the door, emerged onto the walkway. Outside she looked skyward, trying to locate the sun. But there wasn't any sun—only an all-pervading grayness that shrouded everything—not a gray fog, but a gray emptiness that seemed devoid of life, of any movement.

The walkway led to the street and there it ended, but as she moved forward the pavement came into view and the building ahead loomed out of the gray, but a building with distortions.

She moved forward rapidly. Visibility extended only a few meters, and as she approached them the buildings materialized like two-dimensional projections without depth, like twisted cardboard structures appearing in misty conditions.

Once she stopped and looked back and saw that the grayness had closed in behind her. The buildings were erased, the walkway faded into nothing.

She called out, hoping to attract attention. But her voice frightened her. It seemed to echo upward into higher levels of the atmosphere, as if a giant opening had appeared to a vast space high above her.

She continued until she came to the corner of Maritime. There, on the curb, she stopped and stared. The gray barrier was thicker there, but she did not realize how close it was until she glanced down and saw there was nothing, nothing at all beyond the curb. No dull gleam of wet pavement, no sign of a street. It was as if all existence ended here at the corner of Harbor and Maritime.

With a sharp cry, Dr. Edwards turned and ran. Back down the street she raced, jacket streaming behind her in the wind. She felt the notebook bouncing in her pocket with each stride—that precious, irreplaceable record of her work.

Breathing hard, she reached her building and stumbled up the walkway, grateful that it still existed.

On the threshold she stood for a moment, catching her breath. She glanced back over her shoulder, and a strange feeling of inner emptiness seemed to wash over her. At that moment, the gray nothingness appeared to thin—the enveloping curtain fell away, and she saw...

Vague and indistinct, yet cast in holographic outline, an enormous structure was silhouetted against the darkening sky. It was a structure fantastic with geometric domes, crystalline towers, and suspended platforms and connecting bridges. Corridor-like passages, flanked on either side by luminous panels and transport systems, stretched endlessly to the vanishing point. Great beams of multicolored energy probed huge patterns and spirals above the higher levels.

And beyond, like a final backdrop, rose a colossal barrier. It was from that barrier—from its angular projections and geometric features—that Dr. Edwards felt the presence observing her.

Thousands of consciousnesses focused with a single purpose.

And as she continued to observe, something else seemed to form above that barrier. A pattern this time, that swirled and shifted in the ribbons of energy and rapidly coalesced into strange mathematical configurations, without definite form or detail. A vast intelligence, an intelligence of incomprehensible power and purpose, staring down with calculating composure.

Then the structure and the intelligence slid out of focus; the vision faded like a deactivated hologram, and the grayness returned.

Dr. Edwards pushed open the door of her apartment. But she did not lock it. There was no purpose in locks—not anymore.

The temperature control was still functioning, and she adjusted it upward, though she knew the cold she felt came from within.

Without removing her jacket, she sank exhausted into her chair, closed her eyes then opened them again.

She sighed with relief as she saw the room was unchanged. Everything in its accustomed place: the chronometer, the specimen jar, the equipment on the shelf, the reef photograph on the wall facing her.

Everything was as it should be. The chronometer measured the silence with its silent display; it advanced to the next minute and the equipment emitted its usual faint hum.

This was her room, she thought. Rooms acquire the identity of the person who inhabits them, become part of them. This was her world, her own private world, and as such it would be the last to go.

But how long could she—her consciousness—maintain its existence?

Dr. Edwards stared at the reef photograph, and for a moment a small measure of reassurance returned to her. The coral formations glowed with remembered color—the anemones, the schools of fish frozen in their dance, the distant submersible that had once carried her into those depths. They couldn't take this away. The rest of the world might dissolve because there was insufficient observational power to maintain its configuration.

But this room was hers. She alone had furnished it. She alone, since she had first moved into this apartment, had lived here.

This room would remain. It must remain—it must...

She rose from her chair and walked across the room to the bookshelf, stood staring at the second level with its single publication. Her eyes shifted to the top level, and swift terror gripped her.

For not all the books were there. Many books weren't there! Only the most familiar, the most frequently referenced ones.

So the transformation had already begun here! The unfamiliar books were gone, and that fit the pattern—for it would be the least familiar things that would disappear first.

Turning, she stared across the room. Was it her imagination, or did the specimen jar on the table blur and begin to fade?

But as she stared at it, it became clear again, a solid, substantial object.

For a moment real fear reached out and touched her with icy fingers. For she knew that this room no longer was protected against the thing that had happened out there on the street.

Or had it really happened? Might not all this exist within her own mind? Might not the street be as it always was, with researchers walking and equipment functioning? Might not the Blue Whale Café still exist, its blue neon sign glowing in the evening?

Could it be that she was losing her sanity? She had heard whispers when she had passed, whispers the gossiping researchers had not intended her to hear. And she had seen the looks when she walked by. They thought her unstable. Could she be actually unstable?

But she knew she wasn't unstable. She knew that she perhaps was the most rational of all people who walked the earth. For she, and she alone, had foreseen this very thing. And the others had dismissed her for it.

Somewhere else the researchers might be working in a laboratory. But it would be a different laboratory. And the researchers undoubtedly would be different too.

For the matter of which the laboratory and everything within it had been formed would now be cast in a different configuration, claimed by different consciousnesses in a different dimension.

"Perhaps we shall encounter a day, far distant, when our dimension, our world will dissolve beneath our feet and before our eyes as some stronger consciousness reaches out from the dimensional shadows of the very space we inhabit and wrests from us the matter which we know to be our own."

But there had been no need to wait for that distant day. Scant years after she had written those prophetic words, the thing was happening. Humanity had played unwittingly into the hands of those other consciousnesses in the other dimension. Humanity had waged wars, and wars had created conditions for mass disappearances. And the whole vast cycle of events was but a component of a strategic plan.

She could see it all now. By an insidious form of manipulation, entities from that other dimension—or was it one supreme intelligence—had deliberately created the conditions for conflict. The reduction of the world's consciousness had been carefully planned with calculated premeditation.

On impulse she suddenly turned, crossed the room, and opened the connecting door to the bedroom. She stopped on the threshold, and a sound of despair forced its way to her lips.

There was no bedroom. Where her bed and storage units had been, there was grayish nothingness. Her notebook—she had left it in the bedside drawer. It was gone now, claimed by the void along with everything else in that room.

Like an automaton, she turned again and moved to the entry door. Here, too, she found what she had expected. There was no entryway, no familiar jacket hook and equipment rack.

Nothing...

Weakly Dr. Edwards moved back to her chair in the corner.

"So here I am," she said, half aloud.

So there she was. Making a final stand in the last corner of the world that remained to her.

Perhaps there were other people like her, she thought. People who stood at bay against the emptiness that marked the transition from one dimension to another. People who had lived close to the things they valued, who had endowed those things with such substantial form by power of consciousness alone that they now stood out alone against the power of some greater consciousness.

The street was gone. The rest of her apartment was gone. This room still retained its form.

This room, she knew, would remain the longest. And when the rest of the room was gone, this corner with her chair would persist. For this was the location where she had lived for fifteen years. The bedroom was for sleeping, the kitchenette for eating. This room was for living. This was her final stand.

These were the walls and floors and photographs and equipment that had absorbed her will to make them walls and photographs and equipment.

She looked toward the window into a blank world. The adjacent buildings were already gone. Others had not lived with them as she had lived with this room. Their attention had been divided, broadly distributed; their thoughts had not been concentrated as hers upon an area five blocks by four, or a room fifteen by thirteen.

Staring toward the window, she saw it again. The same vision she had observed before, yet different in an indescribable way. There was the structure illuminated against the sky. There were the geometric towers and crystalline features, the dome-shaped projections and platforms. She could see with stereoscopic clarity the suspended bridges, the luminous corridors sweeping on into infinity. The vision was closer this time, but the depth and proportion had changed—as if she were viewing it from two concurrent perspectives simultaneously.

And the intelligence—the intelligence of magnitude—of power, of cosmic strategy and purpose...

Dr. Edwards turned her attention back into the room. The chronometer was advancing slowly, steadily. The grayness was infiltrating the room.

The desk and equipment were the first to go. They simply faded away, and with them went one corner of the room.

And then the specimen jar.

"Oh, well," said Dr. Edwards, "I never did value that particularly."

Now as she sat there, it didn't seem strange to be without the desk or the equipment. It was as if it were something quite normal. Something one could expect to happen.

Perhaps, if she concentrated hard enough, she could restore them.

But, after all, what was the purpose? One person, alone, could not resist the irresistible advance of nothingness. One person, all alone, simply couldn't do it.

She wondered what the specimen jar looked like in that other dimension. It certainly wouldn't be a specimen jar, nor would the equipment be equipment, for perhaps they didn't have specimen jars or equipment in the invading dimension.

She wondered, as a matter of fact, what she herself would look like when she finally transitioned into the unknown. For she was matter, too, just as the specimen jar and equipment were matter.

She wondered if she would retain her individuality—if she still would be a person. Or would she merely be a thing?

There was one answer to all of that. She simply didn't know.

Nothingness advanced upon her, consumed its way across the room, approaching her as she sat in the chair beneath the shelf. And she waited for it.

The room, or what remained of it, plunged into profound silence.

Dr. Edwards started. The chronometer had stopped. Strange—the first time in fifteen years.

She leaped from her chair and then sat down again.

The chronometer hadn't stopped.

It wasn't there.

She looked at the wall facing her. The reef photograph remained—the coral, the fish, the distant submersible. Of all the objects in the room, it alone persisted, suspended now in the encroaching grayness. The image she had looked at every evening for fifteen years, the one thing her consciousness had held most firmly in its grasp.

There was a tingling sensation in her feet.
quality_problem.question: What object was most important to Dr. Edwards in her room?
quality_problem.correct_answer: A framed photograph of a coral reef
