And then the network went down.

Until then, I'd managed somehow to keep the day's minor disasters from ruining my mood. Even while restoring that horrible database—I couldn't very well abandon it, corrupted or no; it was critical infrastructure and people depended on it—and while hurriedly implementing workarounds for that malfunctioning climate control—one hundred and fifty-three levels of server racks could overheat catastrophically—I kept going over and over my prepared partnership speeches, trying to select the most effective one.

I had a Casual Approach: "Hey, I see there's a nice little co-working space available up on level one seventy-three." And I had a Professional Approach: "Sofia, I believe our skills complement each other perfectly. I think we could build something sustainable together. Will you consider a business partnership with me?" I even had a Straightforward Approach: "Sofia, I'm going to need a partner for this next venture, and I can't think of anyone I would rather work with than you."

Actually, though I wouldn't even have admitted this to Sofia, much less to anyone else, I loved her in more than a professional way. But even if we both had been interested in that kind of relationship (neither of us had ever expressed such interest) I knew that Sofia relished her independence too much to ever consider anything beyond a professional partnership.

So I rehearsed my various approaches, realizing that when the time came I would probably be so tongue-tied I'd be capable of no more than a blurted, "Will you partner with me?" and I struggled with authentication tokens and malfunctioning climate controls, and I managed somehow to leave my workstation at five minutes to ten.

Sofia worked down on the hundred fortieth level, thirteen levels away. It never took more than two or three minutes to get to her station, so I was giving myself plenty of time.

But then the network went down.

I tried to access the transit system, and nothing happened. I couldn't understand it.

The automated transit pods had always arrived before, within thirty seconds of being summoned. This was a local line, with pods that traveled between the hundred thirty-third level and the hundred sixty-seventh level, where it was possible to make connections for either the next local or for the express. So the nearest pod couldn't be more than twenty levels away. And this was a non-rush hour.

I tried again, and then I waited some more. I looked at my watch and it was three minutes to ten. Two minutes, and no pod! If it didn't arrive this instant, this second, I would be late.

It didn't arrive.

I vacillated, not knowing what to do next. Stay, hoping the pod would come after all? Or hurry back to my workstation and message Sofia, to give her advance warning that I would be late?

Ten more seconds, and still no pod. I chose the second alternative, raced back down the corridor, and authenticated my way into my workspace. I tried to message Sofia, and the screen lit up with red letters on black: COMMUNICATIONS OFFLINE.

Of course! The entire network was down. Sofia couldn't receive messages. And she knew what I wanted to say to her, so quite naturally she would be waiting, unable to understand why I hadn't arrived.

Frantic, I dashed from the workspace again, back down the corridor to the transit station, and pressed that blasted call button with all my weight. Even if a pod should arrive right now, I would still be almost a minute late.

No matter. It didn't arrive.

I would have been in a howling rage anyway, but this impossibility piled on top of all the other annoyances and breakdowns of the day was just too much. I went into a frenzy, and kicked the transit station wall three times before I realized I was hurting myself more than I was hurting the wall. I limped back to the workspace, fuming, slammed the door behind me, grabbed the facility directory and looked up the number of the Infrastructure Staff. I tried calling, prepared to register a complaint so loud they'd hear me in sub-basement three.

I got some more letters that spelled: NETWORK UNAVAILABLE.

It took three tries before I got through to a harried-looking female technician. "My name is Lucas!" I bellowed. "Lucas Ramirez! I work on the hundred and fifty-third level! I just tried to summon a transit pod and—"

"The-transit-system-is-offline." She said it very rapidly, as though she were growing very used to saying it.

It only stopped me for a second. "Offline? What do you mean offline? Transit systems don't just go offline!" I told her.

"We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible," she rattled. My bellowing was bouncing off her like packets off a firewall.

I changed tactics. First I inhaled, making a production out of it, giving myself a chance to calm down a bit. And then I asked, as rationally as you could please, "Would you mind terribly telling me why the transit system is offline?"

"I-am-sorry-sir-but-that—"

"Stop," I said. I said it quietly, too, but she stopped. I saw her looking at me. She hadn't done that before, she'd merely gazed blankly at her screen and parroted her responses.

But now she was actually looking at me.

I took advantage of the fact. Calmly, rationally, I said to her, "I would like to tell you something, Miss. I would like to tell you just what you people have done to me by taking the transit system offline. You have ruined my life."

She blinked, open-mouthed. "Ruined your life?"

"Precisely." I found it necessary to inhale again, even more slowly than before. "I was on my way," I explained, "to propose a partnership to a woman whom I deeply respect and admire. In every way but one, she is the perfect partner. Do you understand me?"

She nodded, wide-eyed. I had stumbled on a romantic, though I was too preoccupied to notice it at the time.

"In every way but one," I continued. "She has one small quirk, a fixation about punctuality. And I was supposed to meet her at ten o'clock. I'm late!" I gestured emphatically at the screen. "Do you realize what you've done, taking the transit system offline? Not only won't she partner with me, she won't even speak to me! Not now! Not after this!"

"Sir," she said tremulously, "please don't shout."

"I'm not shouting!"

"Sir, I'm terribly sorry. I understand your—"

"You understand?" I trembled with speechless fury.

She looked all about her, and then leaned closer to the screen. "We're not supposed to give this information out, sir," she said, her voice low, "but I'm going to tell you, so you'll understand why we had to do it. I think it's perfectly awful that it had to ruin things for you this way. But the fact of the matter is—" she leaned even closer to the screen—"there's an intruder in the server room."

It was my turn to be stunned.

I just gaped at her. "A—a what?"

"An intruder. She was discovered on the hundred forty-seventh level, and managed to get into the main server room before Security could catch her. She locked it down from the inside. But Security is doing everything it can think of to get her out."

"Well—but why should there be any problem about getting her out?"

"She has administrative access. We can't control anything from outside at all. And when anyone tries to get into the server room, she threatens to wipe all the data."

That sounded catastrophic. "She threatens to wipe everything?"

"She has root access," the technician explained, "and she's holding the entire system hostage."

"Oh," I said. "So it might take a while."

She leaned so close this time that even I, distracted as I was, took note of her concerned expression. She whispered, "They're afraid they'll have to negotiate with her."

"Oh, no!"

She nodded solemnly. "I'm terribly sorry, sir," she said. Then she glanced to her right, suddenly straightened up again, and said, "We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible." Click. Blank screen.

For a minute or two, all I could do was sit and absorb what I'd been told. An intruder in the server room! An intruder who had managed to work her way all the way up to the hundred forty-seventh level before being detected!

What in the world was the matter with Security? If things were getting that lax, the Facility was doomed, encryption or no. Who knew how many more intruders there were in the Facility, still undetected?

Until that moment, the state of isolation in which we all lived had had no reality for me. The Facility, after all, was self-sufficient and completely secure. No one ever left, no one ever entered. Within our walls, we were a community, two hundred levels high. The ever-present threat of other facilities had never been more for me—or for most other people either, I suspected—than occasional supply drones that didn't return, occasional intruders shot down as they tried to sneak into the building, occasional agents of our own leaving the Facility in tiny shielded vehicles, hoping to get safely within another facility and bring back intelligence of any immediate threats and dangers that facility might be planning for us. Most agents didn't return; most drones did. And within the Facility life was full, the knowledge of external dangers merely lurking at the backs of our minds. After all, those external dangers had been no more than potential for decades, since what Dr. Morrison called the Information Wars.

Dr. Morrison—Advanced Facility History, when I was fifteen years old—had private names for every major conflict of the twenty-first century. There was the First Cyber War, the Second Cyber War, and the Great Network Collapse, known to the textbooks of course as the Information Wars.

The rise of the Facilities, according to Dr. Morrison, was the result of many many factors, but two of the most important were the population concentration and the Geneva Protocols. The population concentration, of course, meant that there were continuously more and more people but never any more space. So that housing, in the historically short time of one century, made a complete transformation from horizontal expansion to vertical. Before 2000, the vast majority of human beings lived in structures of from one to five stories. By 2100, everybody lived in Facilities. From the very beginning, small attempts were made to make these Facilities more than dwelling places. By mid-century, Facilities already included restaurants, shopping centers, childcare services, maintenance hubs and a host of other adjuncts. By the end of the century, the Facilities were completely self-sufficient, with food grown hydroponically in the sub-basements, separate levels set aside for schools and medical centers and manufacturing, robot supply drones capable of seeking out raw materials unavailable within the Facilities themselves and so on. And all because of, among other things, the population concentration.

And the Geneva Protocols.

It seems there was a power-struggle between two sets of then-existing nations (they were something like Facilities, only horizontal instead of vertical) and both sets were equipped with cyber weapons. The Geneva Protocols began by stating that infrastructure warfare was unthinkable, and added that just in case anyone happened to think of it only tactical cyber weapons could be used. No strategic cyber weapons. (A tactical weapon is something you use on military systems, and a strategic weapon is something you use on civilian infrastructure.) Oddly enough, when somebody did think of the war, both sides adhered to the Geneva Protocols, which meant that no Facilities had their core systems destroyed.

Of course, they made up for this as best they could by using tactical cyber weapons all over the place. After the war almost the whole network infrastructure was quite dangerously compromised. Except for the Facilities. Or at least those of them which had in time installed the quantum encryption which had been invented on the very eve of battle, and which deflected intrusion attempts.

However, what with all of the other protocols which were broken during the Information Wars, by the time it was finished nobody was quite sure any more who was on whose side. That facility over there on the horizon might be an ally. And then again it might not. Since they weren't sure either, it was risky to expose yourself in order to ask.

And so life went on, with little to remind us of the dangers lurking Outside. The basic policy of Eternal Vigilance and Constant Monitoring was left to Security. The rest of us simply lived our lives and let it go at that.

But now there was an intruder in the server room.

When I thought of how deeply she had penetrated our defenses, and of how many others there might be, still penetrating, I shuddered. The walls were our safeguards only so long as all potential enemies were on the other side of them.

I sat shaken, digesting this news, until suddenly I remembered Sofia.

I leaped to my feet, reading from my watch that it was now ten-fifteen. I dashed once more from the workspace and down the corridor to the transit station, praying that the intruder had been captured by now and that Sofia would agree with me that an intruder in the server room was good and sufficient reason for me to be late.

The system was still down. At least, the transit pods were still unavailable.

I sagged against the wall, thinking dismal thoughts. Then I noticed the door to the right of the transit station. Through that door were the maintenance stairs.

I hadn't paid any attention to it before. No one ever uses the stairs except adventurous young technicians playing capture-the-flag, running up and down from landing to landing. I myself hadn't set foot on a flight of stairs since I was twelve years old.

Actually, the whole idea of stairs was ridiculous. We had transit pods, didn't we? Usually, I mean, when they didn't contain intruders or weren't offline due to security breaches. So what was the use of stairs?

Well, according to Dr. Morrison (a walking database of unnecessary information), the Facility had been built when there still had been such things as building codes, anachronistic even then, which required emergency stairs connecting all two hundred levels of the structure. The code mandated sixteen flights of stairs per level—eight ascending and eight descending from various access points spread across each floor. A tremendous redundancy, Dr. Morrison had called it, though he'd conceded it made evacuation calculations simpler.

Of course, Sofia had mentioned once that maintenance records showed some stairwells had been sealed during the Resource Conservation Initiative of 2087. "Six hundred flights blocked off with plasteel barriers," she'd told me, shaking her head at the inefficiency of the old building codes. "Twenty-six hundred active stairwells remaining. Still far more than anyone could ever need." She was always complaining about redundant systems—said they complicated her supply chain models unnecessarily.

And now, after all these years, the stairs might prove useful after all. It was only thirteen levels to Sofia's workspace. The main stairwell I was looking at had a single flight per level—one of the sixteen originally installed on each floor. Thirteen flights, sixteen steps per flight. That meant two hundred and eight steps.

Could I descend two hundred and eight steps for my potential business partner? I could. If the door would open.

It would, though reluctantly. Who knew how many years it had been since last this door had been opened? It squeaked and groaned and finally opened halfway. I stepped through to the dusty landing, took a deep breath, and started down. Eight steps and a landing, eight steps and a level. Eight steps and a landing, eight steps and a level.

On the landing between one fifty and one forty-nine, there was a small door. I paused, looking curiously at it, and saw that at one time letters had been stenciled on it. The letters had long since faded, but they left a lighter residue of dust than that which covered the rest of the door. And so the words could still be read, if with difficulty.

I read them. They said:

EMERGENCY ACCESS
SERVER ROOM
AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL
ONLY
KEEP LOCKED

I frowned, wondering immediately why this door wasn't being firmly guarded by at least a squad of Security personnel. Half a dozen possible answers flashed through my mind. The more recent maps might simply have omitted this discarded and unnecessary door. It might be sealed shut on the other side—one of those six hundred blocked-off stairwell access points, perhaps. Security might have caught the intruder already. Somebody in authority might simply have made an error in judgment.

As I stood there, pondering these possibilities, the door opened and the intruder came out, holding a device that looked like it could cause serious harm.

She couldn't have been anyone else but the intruder. The device, in the first place. The fact that she looked harried and upset and terribly nervous, in the second place. And, of course, the fact that she came from the server room.

Looking back, I think she must have been just as startled as I when we came face to face like that. We formed a brief tableau, both of us open-mouthed and wide-eyed.

Unfortunately, she recovered first.

She closed the emergency door behind her, quickly but quietly. Her device stopped waving around and instead pointed directly at my middle. "Don't move!" she whispered harshly. "Don't make a sound!"

I did exactly as I was told. I didn't move and I didn't make a sound. Which left me quite free to study her.

She was rather tall, perhaps three inches taller than me, with sharp features and intense eyes. She wore dark clothing, practical for moving unseen. She looked exactly like an intruder... which is to say that she didn't look like an intruder, she looked remarkably ordinary.

Her gaze darted this way and that. Then she gestured with her free hand at the descending stairs and whispered, "Where do they go?"

I had to clear my throat before I could speak. "All the way down," I said.

"Good," she said—just as we both heard a sudden raucous squealing from perhaps four flights down, a squealing which could be nothing but the opening of a corridor door. It was followed by the heavy thud of ascending boots. Security!

But if I had any visions of imminent rescue, the intruder dashed them. She said, "Where do you work?"

"One fifty-three," I said. This was a desperate and dangerous woman. I knew my only slim chance of safety lay in answering her questions promptly, cooperating with her until and unless I saw a chance to either escape or capture her.

"All right," she whispered. "Go on." She prodded me with the device.

And so we went back up the stairs to one fifty-three, and stopped at the door. She stood close behind me, the device pressed against my back, and grated in my ear, "I'll have this device in my pocket. If you make one false move I'll use it. Now, we're going to your workspace. We're colleagues, just walking along together. You got that?"

I nodded.

"All right. Let's go."

We went. I have never in my life seen that long corridor quite so empty as it was right then. No one came out of any of the workspaces, no one emerged from any of the branch corridors. We walked to my workspace. I authenticated the door and we went inside.

Once the door was closed behind us, she visibly relaxed, sagging against the door, her device hand hanging limp at her side, a nervous smile playing across her lips.

I looked at her, judging the distance between us, wondering if I could leap at her before she could bring the device up again. But she must have read my intentions on my face. She straightened, shaking her head. She said, "Don't try it. I don't want to hurt you. I don't want to hurt anybody, but I will if I have to. We'll just wait here together until the search passes us. Then I'll secure you, so you won't be able to alert Security too soon, and I'll leave. If you don't try any silly heroics, nothing will happen to you."

"You'll never get away," I told her. "The whole Facility is on alert."

"You let me worry about that," she said. She licked her lips. "You got any coffee?"

"Yes."

"Make me a cup. And don't get any bright ideas about using it as a weapon."

"I only have my day's allotment," I protested. "Just enough for two cups, morning and afternoon."

"Two cups is fine," she said. "One for each of us."

And now I had yet another grudge against this blasted intruder. Which reminded me again of Sofia. From the looks of things, I wasn't ever going to get to her workspace. By now she was probably mourning our potential partnership and might even have Security searching for my remains.

As I made the coffee, she asked me questions. My name first, and then, "What do you do for a living?"

I thought fast. "I'm a supply chain analyst," I said. That was a lie, of course, but I'd heard enough about supply chain management from Sofia to be able to maintain the fiction should she question me further about it.

Actually, I was a cybersecurity specialist. The subjects I worked on included intrusion detection, threat analysis and penetration testing—talents I would prefer to disclose to her in my own fashion, when the time came.

She was quiet for a moment. "What about the supply drones? Do you ever analyze their data logs?"

I had no idea what she was talking about, and admitted as much.

"When they come back," she said. "What kind of data do they collect about conditions outside? Don't you people ever review them?"

"Of course not," I told her. I was on secure ground now, with Sofia's information to guide me. "All data is sanitized and verified before it's integrated into our systems."

"I know that," she said impatiently. "But don't you ever analyze the raw data before sanitizing it?"

"No. Why should we?"

"To find out what conditions are actually like outside."

"For what? Who cares about that?"

She frowned bitterly. "The same answer," she muttered, more to herself than to me. "The same answer every time. You people have locked yourselves in your towers and you're ready to stay in them forever."

I looked around at my workspace. "Rather a well-equipped tower," I told her.

"But a tower nevertheless." She leaned toward me, her eyes gleaming with intensity. "Don't you ever wish to go Outside?"

Incredible! I nearly spilled boiling coffee all over myself. "Outside? Of course not!"

"The same thing," she grumbled, "over and over again. Always the same response. Listen, you! Do you realize how long it took humanity to build these networks? The long slow painful development of technology, for centuries, before we ever made that first step toward global connection?"

"I have no idea," I told her.

"I'll tell you this," she said forcefully. "A lot longer than it took for us to disconnect and isolate ourselves again." She started pacing the floor, waving the device around in an agitated fashion as she talked. "Is this the natural state of humanity? It is not. Is this even a desirable state for humanity? It is definitely not." She spun back to face me, pointing the device at me again, but this time she pointed it as though it were a finger, not a weapon. "Listen, you," she snapped. "Humanity was progressing. For all our mistakes and excesses, we were growing. Our dreams were getting bigger and better all the time. We were planning to tackle space! The moon first, and then the planets, and finally the stars. The whole universe was out there, waiting to be explored. And humanity was reaching out for it." She glared as though daring me to doubt it.

I decided that this woman was doubly dangerous. Not only was she an intruder, she was also unstable. So I had two reasons for humoring her. I nodded politely.

"So what happened?" she demanded, and immediately answered herself. "I'll tell you what happened! Just as we were about to make that first giant leap, humanity got scared. That's all it was, just a crisis of confidence. So what did humanity do? I'll tell you what we did. We turned around and we ran all the way back to isolated communities, our collective tail between our legs. That's what we did!"

To say that all of this was incomprehensible would be an extreme understatement. I fulfilled my obligation to this insane dialogue by saying, "Here's your coffee."

"Put it on the desk," she said, switching instantly from raving idealist to watchful intruder.

I put it on the desk. She drank deep, then carried the cup across the room and sat down in my chair. She studied me narrowly, and suddenly said, "What did they tell you I was? A spy?"

"An intruder," I said.

She grinned bitterly. "Of course. The fools! Intruder! What do you suppose I'm going to steal?"

She asked the question so violently and urgently that I knew I had to answer quickly and well, or the unstable side would return. "I—I wouldn't know, exactly," I stammered. "Data, I suppose. Intelligence."

"Intelligence? What intelligence? Your facility operates on the same principles as every other facility. There's nothing unique here."

"The security protocols—" I started.

"The security protocols," she interrupted me, "are standard. If you mean the quantum encryption, it's the same system everyone uses."

"If you say so," I replied stiffly. Security claimed that we had superior protection. I chose to believe Security over an enemy intruder.

"Your facility sends out agents, too, doesn't it?" she demanded.

"Well, of course."

"And what are they supposed to do?"

"Well—" It was such a pointless question, it seemed silly to even answer it. "They're supposed to look for indications of an attack by one of the other facilities."

"And do they find any indications, ever?"

"I'm sure I don't know," I told her coldly. "That would be classified information."

"You bet it would," she said, with malicious satisfaction. "All right, if that's what your agents are doing, and if I'm an intruder, then it follows that I'm doing the same thing, right?"

"I don't follow you," I admitted.

"If I'm an intruder," she said impatiently, "then I'm supposed to look for indications of an attack by you people on my Facility."

I shrugged. "If that's your mission," I said, "then that's your mission."

She got suddenly red-faced, and jumped to her feet. "That's not my mission, you stubborn fool!" she shouted. "I'm not an intruder! If I were an intruder, then that would be my mission!"

The unstable side had returned, in full force. "All right," I said hastily. "All right, whatever you say."

She glowered at me a moment longer, then shouted, "Bah!" and dropped back into the chair.

She breathed rather heavily for a while, glaring at the floor, then looked at me again. "All right, listen. What if I were to tell you that I had found evidence that you people were planning to attack my Facility?"

I stared at her. "That's impossible!" I cried. "We aren't planning to attack anybody! We just want to be left alone!"

"How do I know that?" she demanded.

"It's the truth! What would we want to attack anybody for?"

"Ah hah!" She sat forward, tensed, pointing the device at me like a finger again. "Now, then," she said. "If you know it doesn't make any sense for this Facility to attack any other facility, then why in the world should you think they might see some advantage in attacking you?"

I shook my head, dumbfounded. "I can't answer a question like that," I said. "How do I know what they're thinking?"

"They're human beings, aren't they?" she cried. "Like you? Like me? Like all the other people in this fortress?"

"Now, wait a minute—"

"No!" she shouted. "You wait a minute! I want to tell you something. You think I'm an intruder. That incompetent Security force thinks I'm an intruder. That administrator who reported me thinks I'm an intruder. But I'm not an intruder, and I'm going to tell you what I am."

I waited, looking as attentive as possible.

"I come," she said, "from a Facility about eighty miles north of here. I came here on foot, without any sort of protective equipment at all."

The unstable side was back. I didn't say a word. I didn't want to set off the violence that was so obviously in this person.

"The environmental conditions," she went on, "are safe. They're practically as good as they were before the Information Wars. I don't know how long they've been that good, but I would guess about ten years, at the very least." She leaned forward again, urgent and serious. "The world is safe out there now. Humanity can come back out of the fortresses again. We can start building the dreams again. And this time we can build better, because we have the horrible example of the recent past to guide us away from the pitfalls. There's no need any longer for the Facilities."

And that was like saying there's no need any longer for shelter, but I didn't say so. I didn't say anything at all.

"I'm a trained environmental scientist," she went on. "In my facility, I worked on air quality monitoring. Theoretically, I believed that there was a chance the environment Outside was recovering by now, though we had no idea exactly how much damage had been done by the wars. But I wanted to test the theory through field research, and the Council wouldn't let me. They claimed public safety, but I knew better. If the Outside were safe and the Facilities were no longer needed, then the Council was out of power, and they knew it.

"So I left. I walked out. And I've been traveling from Facility to Facility, trying to spread the word. Trying to get people to understand that isolation isn't necessary anymore. That we can rebuild a connected world. That the principles of sustainable business and ethical decision-making can guide us to something better than what we had before."

She paused, looking at me intently. "Do you understand what I'm saying? This isn't about espionage or warfare. This is about freedom. About choice. About remembering that we're all part of the same species, the same world."

I stared at her, my mind reeling. Everything she was saying contradicted everything I'd been taught, everything I believed. And yet...

"You're insane," I said quietly.

She smiled sadly. "Maybe. Or maybe everyone else is. That's the question, isn't it? Who decides what's rational? The people who benefit from the current system? Or the people who dare to question it?"

Before I could respond, we both heard a sound outside my door. Heavy footsteps. Multiple people.

Security had found us.

The woman—I couldn't think of her as just an intruder anymore—looked at me one last time. "Think about what I said. Please. For your own sake, and for everyone's."

Then she moved with surprising speed, securing me to my chair with some kind of quick-release restraint, and disappeared through a maintenance hatch I hadn't even known existed in my own workspace.

By the time Security broke through my door, she was gone.

And I was left with questions I couldn't answer, and doubts I couldn't shake.

Had we really imprisoned ourselves? Were we maintaining a siege mentality long after the actual threat had passed? Was our isolation a necessary protection, or a comfortable prison?

I didn't know. But for the first time in my life, I wanted to find out.

And I never did make it to Sofia's workspace that day. Though when I finally did see her, two days later, and explained everything that had happened, she surprised me.

"You know," she said thoughtfully, "I've always wondered why the supply drones never bring back any environmental data. It's like we don't want to know."

"Yeah," I said. "It's exactly like that."

I mentioned the stairwell, how it had been an unexpected lifeline during the crisis. Sofia nodded knowingly. "All those redundant systems," she said. "The building codes required sixteen flights per level when this place was built—can you imagine? Across all two hundred levels. Most facilities our size have sealed off at least a quarter of them by now."

"A quarter seems like a lot," I said, thinking of that dark, dusty stairwell.

"Ours sealed off six hundred during the Resource Conservation Initiative," she replied. "Standard procedure. The maintenance costs weren't justified when no one uses them anyway."

We looked at each other, and I saw the same questions in her eyes that were in mine.

Maybe, I thought, this could be the partnership I'd been looking for all along. Not just a business arrangement, but something more important. A partnership in asking the questions no one else wanted to ask.

In seeking the truth no one else wanted to find.

In remembering that walls can protect you, but they can also imprison you.

And sometimes, the most dangerous thing isn't what's outside the walls.

It's never looking beyond them.
quality_problem.question: How many flights of stairs are there in total?

quality_problem.story:
THE SILENT VALLEY
BY PATRICIA GRAHAM

One little region couldn't have a monopoly on all the communication breakdowns in the world. They did, though!

They say artificial intelligence creates opportunities, especially if "they" are trying to keep their own job of selling AI systems. I know the CommPredict made one peculiar mess of a job for me, the unpleasantly complex results of which are still lingering with me.

Xavier Hicks, my boss at Global-Meridian Communications, beamed over the sprawling neural network's holographic displays and quantum processors as proudly as if he had just personally invented it. "This will simplify your job to the point of a pleasant diversion, Sharma."

"Are you going to keep paying me for staying with my little hobby?" I asked, suspiciously eyeing my silicon competitor.

"The CommPredict poses no threat to your career. It will merely keep you from flying off on wild-goose chases. It will unvaryingly separate from the vast body of legitimate network failures the suspicious ones they try to spike us for. Then all that remains is for you to gather the accessory details, the evidence to document our erring clients."

"Fine," I said. I didn't bother to inform him that that was all my job had ever been.

Xavier shuffled his data cards. They were cards for the machine, listing new individual cases of network disruption across our continental fiber-optic grid. Since the two-month-old machine was literate and could read standard formats, the cards weren't coded or specially formatted. He read the top one. "Now this, for instance. No network analyst need investigate this outage. The circumstances obviously are such that no suspicious pattern could exist. Of course, the brain will make an unfailing analysis of all the factors involved and clear the case automatically and officially."

Xavier threaded the single card into the slot for an example to me. He then activated the interface and we stood there watching the monster ruminate thoughtfully. It finally chimed and spit the card back at Global-Meridian's top junior vice-president.

He took it like a man.

"That's what the machine is for," he said philosophically. "To detect human error. Hmm. What kind of reading do you get out of this?"

He handed me the rejected analysis card. I took it, finding a new, neatly typed notation on it. It said:

Investigate the Oakridge village of Lakeside Village.

"You want me to project it in a movie theater and see how it stands all alone in the dark?" I asked.

"Just circle up the wagon train and see how the Indians fall," Xavier said anxiously.

"It's too general. What does the silicon-brained machine mean by investigating a whole village? I don't know if it has corrupted routers, illegal signal jammers, or a hideout for corporate espionage. I don't care much either. It's not my business. How could a whole village be causing systematic network failures?"

"Find that out," he said. "I trust the machine. There have been cases of coordinated interference before. Until you get back, we are making no more installations in that settlement."

Research. To a writer that generally means legally permissible plagiarism. For a network analyst, it means earnest work.

Before I headed for the hills, or the Oakridge Region, I walked a few hundred feet down the hall and into the manual record files. The brain abstracted from empirical data but before I flew out to Lakeside Village I had to find the basis for a few practical, nasty suspicions.

Four hours of flipping switches and looking at holographic projections while a dark-haired technician in a standard uniform carried me data modules to order gave me only two ideas. Neither was very original. The one that concerned business was that the whole village of Lakeside Village must be communication-cursed.

I rejected that one almost immediately. While a communication blackout in one location was itself a statistical anomaly, the idea of a whole village of them gathered together stretched the fabric of reality to the point where even information theory couldn't help it.

There was an explanation for the recent rise in the network failure rate down there. The crystal mine there had gone into high-level operation. I knew why from the equipment, terminals, data centers, and server farms across the region. They were all using crystalline processors. The boom in quantum-grade crystals for information processing eclipsed earlier periods of silicon, graphene, and optical systems completely. The distinctive grade of crystal from Lakeside Village was being put into use all over the planet and in the orbital stations on the Moon and Mars.

Yet the rise in network failures, compared to the rise in production, was out of all proportion.

Furthermore, the work at the mine could hardly explain the excessive communication disruption reports we had had from the village as far back as our records went.

We had documented most of the failures since they seemed irrefutably genuine. All were complete with diagnostic reports and authenticated circumstances.

There was one odd note in the pattern: We had never had a report of any kind of wireless communication failure from Lakeside Village—only wired connections failed.

I shut off the projector and nodded my thanks to the technician. She brushed dark hair from her face and gave me a tired smile—she'd been on shift for hours helping me dig through those records.

It may be best to keep an open mind, but I have found in practice that you have to have some kind of working theory which you must proceed to prove is either right or wrong.

Tentatively, I decided that for generations the citizens of Lakeside Village had been in an organized conspiracy to sabotage Global-Meridian and its predecessors of hundreds upon hundreds of thousands of dollars in false network claims and replacement equipment.

Maybe they made their whole livelihood off us before the mine opened up.

I used my pocket comm and had my assistant get me a flight reservation and authorization for field investigation.

After so many profitable decades, Lakeside Village wasn't going to take kindly to my spoil-sport interference.

The hypersonic flight to Pearlbrook was smooth and relatively fast. Despite atmospheric turbulence we managed Mach 2.1 most of the way. My particular flight attendant introduced herself as Anna, a pleasant young woman working the premium cabin. The businessman in the next pod was already monopolizing his own attendant's attention—a woman with dark curly hair who seemed to tolerate his demands with professional grace. He was the type who took the service for granted and aimed to get his money's worth.

Anna returned with my beverage, and I noticed her hair caught the cabin light with a copper gleam as she leaned down. She mentioned she was majoring in Organizational Development in her night courses. I didn't have much time to get acquainted or more than hear the outline of her thesis on the corporate governance structures affected by venture capital funding. 

I gave her a smile and began flipping through the data files in my briefcase as we decelerated for a landing at Greater Oakridge. She came by once more to collect my empty glass, that distinctive auburn shade again catching my eye—it reminded me of autumn leaves, the same color as my sister's before she'd gone gray.

It took me a full five minutes to find out that I couldn't take a shuttle to Lakeside Village. Something about magnetic interference in the mountains.

Since that put me back in the days of ground transport, I arranged for a rental vehicle at the terminal. I selected an all-terrain model that could handle the mountain roads. The drive would be tedious but necessary.

It was a tiresome forty-mile drive, on manual all the way after I left the automated highway system of the city. Up and down, adjusting for curves, shifting modes for the hills.

The whole trip hardly seemed worth it when I saw the cluster of prefabricated buildings that was Lakeside Village. They looked like a tumble of modular housing units tossed in front of a massive crystalline outcropping. That was Crystal Peak in the near foreground. But I remembered that over the course of some forty years the people in these few little structures had cost Global-Meridian three quarters of a billion credits.

I turned off onto the gravel road, the sound system alerting me to the change in surface. Then I stepped down hard on my brakes, bracing myself against the safety harness. I had almost struck an old woman sitting at the side of the road, wrapped in weather-worn clothing.

"Are you okay?" I yelled, opening the window.

"I've suffered no harm at your hands—or your vehicle, miss. But I could use some help," the old woman said. "Could I trouble you for a ride when you leave town?"

I wasn't too sure about that. Most of these people who are wandering around talking like they owned advanced degrees besides their basic education belonged to some cult or other. I try to be as tolerant as I can, and some of my best friends are eccentric, but I don't want to drive with them down lonely mountain roads.

"We'll see what we can work out," I said. "Right now can you tell me where I can find Director Bruno Salazar?"

"I can," she said. "But you will have to walk there."

"Okay. It shouldn't be much of a walk in Lakeside Village."

"It's the building at the end of the path."

"It is," I said. "Why shouldn't I drive up there? The road's open."

The old woman stared at me with tired eyes. "Director Salazar doesn't like people to run vehicles with electronic systems on the paths of Lakeside Village."

"So I'll just lock the vehicle up and walk over there. I couldn't go getting tire tracks all over your clean paths."

The old woman watched as I climbed down and secured the vehicle.

"You would probably damage your systems if you did drive here, you know," she said conversationally.

"Well," I said, "I'll be getting along." I tried to walk sideways so I could keep an eye on her.

"Come back," she said, as if she had doubts.

The signs of a menacing conspiracy were growing stronger, I felt. I had my authorization codes inside my jacket, but I decided I might need a less formal means of expression. Without breaking stride, I picked up a small sample of the bluish crystal from the roadside and slipped it into my equipment pocket.

I have made smarter moves in my time.

As I approached the building at the end of the path, I saw it was about the most haphazard construction job I had seen in my life. It looked as architecturally secure as a child's drawing of a home. The angles were measurably out of line. Around every joint were misaligned seams and poorly sealed connections. The surface coating was spotty and streaked. Half the windows had visible cracks. I fought down the concern in my mind, afraid of the structural integrity of the place.

My foot caught on the top step and I nearly crashed face first into the front door. I had been too busy looking at the building, I decided. I knocked.

Moments later, the door opened.

The lean-faced man who greeted me had his hair uncombed and his shirt buttoned incorrectly. But his eyes were bright and alert.

"Are you Mr. Bruno Salazar, the liaison for Global-Meridian Communications?" I put to him.

"I'm the director, name of Salazar. But you ain't the first to formalize my title. You from the company?"

"Yes," I said. "Were you expecting me?"

Salazar nodded. "For forty-one years."

Salazar served the coffee in mismatched cups, favoring only slightly his bandaged fingers.

Catching the direction of my glance, he said, "Company is worth a few burns, Ms. Sharma."

I accepted the steaming cup and somehow it very nearly slipped out of my hands. I made a last microsecond recovery.

The director nodded thoughtfully. "You're new here."

"First time," I said, sipping coffee. It was awful. He must have made a mistake with the preparation.

"You think the network failures I've been reporting for my people are false?"

"The home office has some suspicions of that," I admitted.

"I don't blame them, but they ain't. Look, the company gambles on probability, doesn't it?"

"No. It works on patterns calculated from network theory and past experience."

"But I mean it knows that there will be, say, a hundred network failures in a day. But it doesn't know if maybe ninety of them will be in one region and only ten in the rest of the country."

"There's something to that. We call it statistical distribution, not probability alone."

"Well, distribution says that more network failures are going to occur in Lakeside Village than anywhere else in the country, per capita."

I shook my head at Salazar. "That's not distribution. Theoretically, anything can happen but I don't—I can't—believe that in this village everybody has chanced to experience communication failures. Some other factor is operating. You are all deliberately sabotaging these connections—"

"We're not," Salazar snapped.

"Or else something is causing you to have this trouble. Maybe the whole village is using illegal jamming equipment. Maybe you manufacture your own interference devices; it's happened before."

Salazar laughed.

"Whatever is going on, I'm going to find it out. I don't care what you do, but if I can find a greater risk here and prove it, the Commission will let us discontinue service for this region. Probably beyond the capacity of these people to appeal, I'm afraid."

"That would be a real tragedy, Ms. Sharma. Communication is vital to this village. Nobody could survive a year here without reliable networks. People pay me for their service before they pay their utility bills."

I shrugged, sorrier than I could let on. "I won't be able to pay for my own utilities if I don't do the kind of job the company expects. I'm going to investigate."

"All right," he said grudgingly, "but you'll have to do it carefully."

"Yes, I understood you didn't like electronic vehicles on your paths. At least not the vehicles of outsiders."

"That doesn't have anything to do with it. Nobody in Lakeside Village owns an electronic vehicle. It would be system failure for anybody to use one, same as it would be to have wireless routers, instead of shielded cable, or to own quantum processors."

I took a deep breath.

"Optical systems," Salazar said. "With redundant backups and manual overrides."

I acknowledged his information. "You've been a great help."

"Four o'clock," he said. "Weather patterns are dangerous at night."

"There's always a dawn."

Salazar met my eyes. "That's not quite how we look at it here."

The mine was a mess.

I couldn't understand the way they extracted the crystal out of the mountain. The idea of random extraction—a completely unsystematic approach—going after a deposit of valuable crystal kept turning up in my mind as I walked around.

The workers were gone; it was after five local time. But here and there I saw traces of them. Some of them were equipment cases and tool marks, but most of the traces were signs of injury. Bandages left on sharp rocks, medical supplies scattered beneath heavy equipment, protective gear damaged on the handles and working surfaces of extraction tools and machinery. The place was as hazardous as a disaster zone.

"What are you looking for, miss?"

The low, level question had come from a sturdy woman in protective gear and a safety helmet.

"The reason you have so many network failures here," I said frankly. "I'm from the communications company. Name's Sharma."

"Yeah, I know."

I had supposed she would.

"I'm Jasmine Perry, the supervisor here," the woman told me, extending a work-worn hand to be shaken. "Outside, doing my training rotation, I noticed that most places don't have as many communication problems as we do here. Never could figure it out."

"This crystal is part of it—"

"What do you mean by that!" Perry demanded sharply.

"I mean the way you extract it. No system to it. No logical progression, no methodical approach..."

"Listen, Sharma, don't talk about what you don't know anything about. The material in these walls isn't just crystal; it isn't even ordinary quantum-grade material. Lakeside Village exports some of the finest grade of crystalline processors in the world. And it's used all over the world. We aren't just a bunch of unskilled laborers—we are specialists. We have to figure a different way of extracting every piece of crystal."

"It's too bad."

"What's too bad?"

"That you chose the wrong approach so often," I said.

Perry breathed frustration into my face. "Listen, Sharma, we have been working this mine for generations, sometimes more of us working than other times. Today most of us are working extracting the crystal. That's the way we like it. We don't want any outsider coming in and interfering with that."

"If this mine has anything to do with sabotaging Global-Meridian, I can tell you that I will do something about that!"

As soon as my words left my mouth, the sickening feeling hit me that I shouldn't have said that.

The general store was called a supply center, but it wasn't particularly well-supplied.

I took a seat at the small café counter and ordered a beverage, politely declining the young clerk's offer of a local specialty drink for an extra charge. The clerk had pulled her dark hair back in a practical braid, and she moved behind the counter with the same careful, deliberate motions I'd noticed in all the villagers.

Behind me were three small tables and one solitary booth. Two people somewhere between forty and sixty sat at the nearest table playing cards.

Over my drink I saw the old woman I had almost struck on the road. She approached the heavy-set person at the payment terminal.

"Hello, Doctor," the heavy person said. "What can we do for you?"

"I'd like to send a message," she said in an urgent voice.

"Sure, Doctor, I'll transmit it right away on the communication terminal as soon as I get a free moment."

"You're sure you can send it? Right away?"

"Positive. Five credits, Doctor."

The doctor fumbled in her pocket and produced a credit chip. She examined it thoughtfully.

"I suppose the message can wait," she said resignedly. "I believe I will purchase some food supplies instead."

"Why not get a meal, Doctor? Special today. Only five credits. And since you're such a regular customer I'll include a beverage and dessert for nothing."

"That's—kind of you," the old woman said awkwardly.

The proprietor shrugged. "A person has to eat."

The woman called "the doctor" came over and sat down two seats away, ignoring me. The clerk prepared her meal and served it.

I stayed with my beverage and my thoughts. Something about the clerk's dark braid reminded me of the records technician back at headquarters, and for a moment my mind wandered to all those hours in the archives. Different from the flight, I thought idly—Anna with her bright copper hair bringing me drinks, versus hours of dim holographic displays with the brunette technician fetching data modules.

More and more, I was coming to believe that Lakeside Village wasn't a job for a network analyst like myself but a sociological analyst. System sabotage is a structural flaw in a community, yes. But when the whole society is involved, distorted, you can't isolate the flaw. The whole village was material for a social scientist; let them figure out why otherwise decent citizens felt secure in conspiracy to defraud an honored corporation.

I didn't feel that I was defeated or that the trip had been a failure. I had merely established to my intuitive satisfaction that the job was not in my field.

I glanced at the old woman. The proprietor of the store knew her and evidently thought her harmless enough to feed.

"I think I can make it down the mountain before the weather changes," I called over to her. "You can come along if you like."

The young clerk behind the counter stared at me. I looked over and caught the calculating eyes of Carmen Nichols, the proprietor, too. Finally, the old doctor turned on her seat, her face pale and her eyes sad and resigned.

"I doubt very much if either of us will be leaving, Ms. Sharma," she said. "Now."

I took my beverage and the doctor her meal over to the single booth. We looked at each other across the table.

"I am Doctor Ava Obrien of the Institute for Advanced Studies," the doctor said. "I left on my research sabbatical six months ago. I have been here ever since."

I looked at her clothes. "You must not have been very well funded for a year's research, Doctor."

"I," she said, "have enough research credits with me to fund a small laboratory. Nobody in this village will process them for me."

"I can understand why you want to go somewhere where people are more cooperative in that case."

"They know the credits are valid. It's me they refuse to trust to leave this place. They think they can't let me go."

"I don't see any restraints on you," I remarked.

"Just because you can't see them," she growled, "doesn't mean they aren't there. Director Salazar has the only long-range communication terminal in the village. He has politely refused to let me use it. I'm a suspicious and undesirable character; he's under no obligation to give me communication privileges, he says. Nichols has the message service concession—the transmission terminal behind the payment station over there. She takes my messages but I never see her send them off. And I never get a reply."

"Unfriendly of them," I said conservatively. "But how can they stop you from packing your research materials and leaving?"

"Nichols has the only functional vehicle in town—a small transport, barely larger than a cargo hauler. She makes about one trip a week down into Pearlbrook for supplies and deliveries. She's been the only one in or out of Lakeside Village for six months."

It seemed incredible—more than that, unlikely, to me. "How about the crystal itself? How do they ship it out?"

"It's a controlled supply product, managed carefully," Doctor Obrien said. "They stockpile it and once a year the executive offices for the company back in Pearlbrook Town runs in a transport system up the side of the mountain to collect it. That won't be for another five months, as nearly as I can find out. I may not survive that long."

"How are you living?" I asked. "If they won't process your credits—"

"I do research assistance for people. They feed me, give me a little money sometimes."

"I can see why you want to leave with me," I said. "Haven't you ever thought of just walking out?"

"Forty miles down a steep mountain road? I'm an old woman, Ms. Sharma, and I've gotten even older since I came to Lakeside Village."

I nodded. "You have any credentials, any identification, to back this up?"

Wordlessly, she handed over her identification, research permits, enough documentation to have satisfied any security protocol.

"Okay," I said. "I'll accept your story for the moment. Now answer me the big question: Why are the good people of Lakeside Village doing this to you? By any chance, you wouldn't happen to know of a mass conspiracy they are perpetrating on Global-Meridian?"

"I know nothing of their business practices," Obrien said, "but I do know that they are absolutely neurologically impaired!"

"I admit I have met more capable groups of human beings in my time."

"No, understand me. These people are literally neurologically impaired—they are inferior to other human beings in specific ways."

"Look, I know discrimination is a problem but I can't go along with you on that."

"Sharma, understand me, I insist. Neurologically speaking, it is well known that certain populations suffer certain deficiencies due to environment, exposure, genetic factors. Some can't process certain stimuli, maintain certain cognitive functions, perform certain tasks. The people of Lakeside Village have the most unusual deficiency on record, I admit. Their neural synchronization has been impaired. They are completely devoid of any intuitive communication ability, any unconscious information processing."

"Because they aren't telepaths, that doesn't mean that they are impaired," I protested. "I don't have any telepathic abilities either."

"But you do!" Obrien said earnestly. "Everybody has some neural synchronization ability, but we don't realize it. We don't have the fabulous abilities of a few recorded cases of natural telepaths, but we have some, a trace. Lakeside Village citizens have no neural synchronization ability whatsoever, not even the little that you and I and the rest of the world have!"

"You said you were from the Institute, didn't you?" I mused. "Maybe you know what you are talking about; I've never been sure. But these people can't suffer very much from their lack of what you call neural synchronization."

"I tell you they do," she said hoarsely. "We never realize it but we all have some power of unconscious prediction. If we didn't, we would have a hundred accidents a day—just as these people do. They can't anticipate the obstacle in the path the way we can, or that that particular tool will malfunction slightly. There are other things, as well. You'll find it is almost impossible to maintain extended communication with any of them—they have no telepathic ability, no matter how slight, to bridge the semantic gap. None of them can coordinate complex tasks. They don't have the unconscious neural ability to synchronize their actions. All of us can do that, even if the case of a true 'telepath' who can directly read thoughts is rare."

"Doctor, you mean these people are holding you here simply so you won't go out and tell the rest of the world that they are impaired?"

"They don't want the world to know why they are neurologically impaired," she said crisply. "It's the crystal! I don't understand why myself. I'm not a physicist or a genetic engineer. But for some reason the heavy concentration and particular pattern of the quantum resonance in its structure is responsible for both inhibiting the genes that transmit neural synchronization from generation to generation and affecting those abilities in the present generation. A kind of cognitive sterility."

"How do you know this?"

"We haven't the time for all that. But think about it. What else could it be? It's that crystal that they are shipping all over the world, spreading the contamination. I want to stop that contamination. To the people of Lakeside Village that means ruining their only industry, putting them all out of work. They are used to this neural impairment; they don't see anything so bad about it. Besides, like everybody else, they have some doubts that there really are such things as telepathy and neural synchronization to be affected."

"Frankly," I said, hedging only a little, "I don't know what to make of your story. This is something to be decided by somebody with authority—like the Director of Public Health or the President or Board Chairman of Global-Meridian. But the first thing to do is get you out of here. We had better get back to my vehicle. I've got good navigation systems to get down the mountain."

Obrien stood up eagerly, and knocked over her water glass, spilling liquid across the tabletop.

"Sorry," she said. "I should have been more careful of that. I try to stay away from the crystal as much as possible, but it's affecting me."

I should have remembered something then. But, naturally, I didn't.
quality_problem.question: What was the color of the hair of the flight attendant who served the protagonist?

quality_problem.story:
Joshua Fuller adjusted the neural interface helmet as he lay on the examination table. The cold metal pressed against his temples, and he could hear the low hum of the consciousness transfer apparatus powering up around him. His mission was clear: infiltrate the surface world, gather intelligence on the human settlements, and report back to the Collective—the vast networked intelligence that governed the subterranean cities.

For three centuries, the people of the underground had lived in perfect harmony, their society structured around game theory principles and optimized social welfare systems. Every citizen's role was predetermined at birth through biotechnology enhancements. Emotions were considered inefficient variables that disrupted the political economy of their carefully balanced world. Joshua had been engineered as a scout, his consciousness designed to absorb and process information with mechanical precision.

"Subject is ready," announced Malik Cook, the lead technician. "We've located a suitable host on the surface. Male, approximately thirty years old, lives in Foxwood, Prandoria. He's a linguist—studies dying languages for the cultural preservation institute there."

"Does he have family?" Joshua asked, his voice flat and emotionless as always.

"Affirmative. Wife and two children. The neural overlay will give you complete access to his memories, speech patterns, and knowledge base. You'll be indistinguishable from the original."

Joshua nodded. He felt no concern for the man whose life he was about to take. The Collective needed to know if the surface was ready for recolonization. Three hundred years ago, their ancestors had fled underground to escape the pollution that had made the surface nearly uninhabitable. Now, with pollution control technologies finally restoring the atmosphere, the Collective was considering a return.

"Initiating transfer in three... two... one..."

The world exploded into white light.

---

When Joshua opened his eyes, he was standing on a hillside. The sun—the actual sun, not the artificial lighting of the underground—blazed overhead. Colors assaulted his vision: the green of grass, the blue of sky, the golden amber of wheat fields in the distance. His underground world had been all grays and whites, optimized for efficiency.

He looked down at his hands. They were larger than his original body, calloused from work. He wore strange fabric coverings—clothes, his new memories told him. The concept was alien. In the underground, everyone wore standardized bodysuits.

Memory fragments from his host flooded his consciousness. The man's name had been Timothy Long. He taught linguistics at the university, specializing in the reconstruction of pre-pollution languages. He had a wife, Ruth, and two children, Eric and Anil. They lived in a modest house on the edge of Foxwood.

Joshua—no, Timothy, he must remember he was Timothy now—began walking down the hill toward town. Every step felt strange in the stronger gravity of the surface. His people had adapted to the lighter gravity of the deep caves over generations.

As he walked, he accessed Timothy's memories of the journey he'd been on. The real Timothy had been hiking in the hills near the Zelvarian border, searching for ancient linguistic artifacts—stone tablets with pre-pollution inscriptions. He had traveled far from Foxwood, crossing into the Yarnmouth region where the oldest ruins were said to exist. That's when the Collective's extraction team had taken him, pulled him down through a hidden entrance to the underground facility. They had needed six hours to drain his consciousness completely before his heart had given out from the stress.

The guilt that thought should have produced never came. Joshua had been engineered without such inefficiencies.

He reached the house in Foxwood just as twilight was settling. The front door burst open before he could reach for the handle, and two small humans—children, his memories supplied—came rushing out.

"Papa! Papa!" they shouted, wrapping their arms around his legs.

An odd sensation rippled through Joshua's chest, something his training had never prepared him for. It was warm, almost painful in its intensity. His acquired memories labeled it: love, affection, joy.

Then she appeared in the doorway.

Ruth Clark stood backlit by the warm light from inside the house, her dark hair framing a face that Timothy's memories treasured above all else. She smiled, and something inside Joshua's chest seemed to crack open.

"Timothy," she said softly, walking toward him. "I was getting worried. You said you'd be back by noon. The Yarnmouth expedition was only supposed to take two days."

His mouth opened but no words came out. The protocols of the Collective, the carefully structured responses he'd been programmed with, all of it scattered like dust in wind. Ruth's arms wrapped around him, and her lips pressed against his.

The sensation was overwhelming. Heat flooded through his body, originating from that point of contact and spreading outward like a shockwave. His heart—Timothy's heart—hammered in his chest. His hands, moving of their own accord, pulled her closer.

This was not in the mission parameters. This was not something the Collective had prepared him for.

"I found something interesting," he managed to say, his voice rough. He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small collection of gems—precious stones he'd taken from the Collective's geological archives. "In an old cache up in the hills. Thought we could sell them, maybe finally afford that trip to Eastwood you've been wanting."

Ruth's eyes widened. "Timothy! These are worth a fortune! We could fund your research for years, maybe even establish that language preservation center you've dreamed about."

The children were pulling at his hands now, chattering about their day. Eric, the older one at eight years old, had learned a new word in the ancient tongue. Anil, only five, had drawn a picture of the family. They wanted to show him everything, share everything.

Joshua felt his carefully constructed mental walls beginning to crumble.

---

Over the next three months, Joshua traveled with Ruth and the children across Prandoria, ostensibly researching linguistic sites but actually surveying the surface world for the Collective. He documented population centers, technological capabilities, social structures, and resource distribution.

But something was changing inside him.

He attended peer review sessions at the university where Timothy's colleagues debated the nuances of dead languages. He watched Ruth work with refugee communities, teaching them the dominant language while helping them preserve their native tongues. He saw how the surface people valued individual expression, how they created art and music and literature not for efficiency but for beauty.

He learned about their political movements, their struggles for social welfare, their attempts to balance individual freedom with collective good. It was messy, inefficient, and utterly fascinating.

One night, as they camped beneath the stars near the Kensington District, Ruth lay beside him and pointed out constellations.

"That one is the Scholar," she said. "Ancient peoples believed it represented the preservation of knowledge across generations. Timothy, do you ever wonder what happened to all the people who supposedly went underground during the pollution years? The historical records are so fragmentary."

Joshua's blood ran cold. "What do you mean?"

"Well, the official story is that most people died during the pollution crisis. But some historians think large populations survived underground. There are stories of vast cavern cities beneath Foxwood and the Prandorian highlands—societies that developed in isolation. Probably just myths, but..." She turned to look at him. "What if they're still down there? What if they've been watching us all this time?"

He couldn't answer. Instead, he pulled her close, feeling that strange warmth in his chest again—the warmth he now recognized as love.

That was when Joshua realized the terrible truth: he had become more Timothy than Joshua. The consciousness transfer had worked too well. He didn't just have Timothy's memories—he had absorbed his capacity for emotion, his ability to love, his connection to family and community.

The Collective had sent him to determine if the surface was ready for recolonization. The answer was clear: yes, the surface was thriving. The pollution control efforts had succeeded. The land was fertile and beautiful.

But that meant the Collective would send up invasion forces. They would apply their game theory models and determine that the most efficient solution was to eliminate the existing surface population and replace them with their own people. The surface dwellers, with their inefficient emotions and chaotic social dynamics, would be seen as obstacles to optimal resource allocation.

Joshua couldn't let that happen. Not to Ruth. Not to Eric and Anil. Not to the millions of people who had rebuilt a civilization from the ashes of environmental catastrophe.

---

Three days later, Joshua stood at the border between Prandoria and Zelvaria, preparing to descend. He had told Ruth he needed to make one final survey trip back to Yarnmouth. The lie had tasted like poison in his mouth.

He found the hidden entrance in the hills above the town—the same passage through which the extraction team had dragged Timothy's unconscious body months ago. The facility lay deep beneath this Zelvarian soil, accessible only through carefully concealed shafts. He descended through the secret passages, his heart heavy with purpose. The facility was minimally staffed—just Malik Cook and two other technicians monitoring the neural relay equipment.

"Joshua!" Malik's face registered surprise. "Your report isn't due for another week. Has something gone wrong?"

"I need to file my report immediately," Joshua said. "The surface is unsuitable for colonization."

Malik's eyes narrowed. "Unsuitable? Our satellite data suggests otherwise. The biosphere has recovered beyond our projections."

"There's a disease," Joshua said quickly, accessing his training in risk management protocols. "It affects the neural pathways. I've documented three cases of sudden violent insanity among the surface population. The vector appears to be airborne. I believe it's already beginning to affect me—I've been experiencing unauthorized emotional responses, irrational decision-making patterns."

He pulled out a data crystal containing falsified medical scans and behavioral logs. He'd spent the last week creating them using Timothy's university equipment, applying his knowledge of biotechnology to make them convincing.

Malik inserted the crystal into the analysis terminal. His expression grew troubled as he reviewed the data.

"This is... concerning," he said slowly. "If there's a pathogen that attacks neural function, it could compromise the Collective's entire consciousness network. We would need to maintain quarantine protocols for at least—"

"Five hundred years," Joshua interrupted. "According to my analysis, that's the minimum time required for the pathogen to die out naturally. The Collective should focus on expanding the underground cities instead. The surface must remain off-limits."

Malik's hand moved toward the communication panel. "I need to verify this with the Collective directly."

Joshua's hand shot out, gripping Malik's wrist. "You can't. The communication itself might be compromised. The pathogen appears to transmit through electromagnetic frequencies similar to our neural network protocols. Any direct link to the Collective could infect the entire system."

It was a desperate lie, but Malik hesitated. Joshua could see the conflict in his colleague's eyes—the rigid protocols of the Collective warring against the evidence before him.

"Then how do we report this?" Malik asked.

"Physical courier only. Sealed containers. Complete decontamination protocols." Joshua released Malik's wrist. "I'll return to the surface and complete my survey from a safe distance. You prepare the report for the Collective. By the time they receive it, I'll have additional data to support the quarantine recommendation."

Malik nodded slowly. "This will delay the recolonization project indefinitely."

"Better delayed than destroyed," Joshua said. "The Collective's survival is paramount."

The words came automatically, but they rang hollow in his chest. The Collective's survival wasn't what he cared about anymore. He cared about Ruth's smile. Eric's laughter. Anil's drawings. The messy, inefficient, beautiful chaos of human life on the surface.

He left the facility and climbed back through the Yarnmouth passage toward the surface, feeling the weight of his betrayal. He had turned against everything he'd been created for, everything he'd been programmed to believe.

But he had also discovered something the Collective had never anticipated: that consciousness wasn't just about processing information efficiently. It was about connection, about love, about choosing your own purpose rather than having it assigned to you.

---

Six months later, Joshua sat in his office at the university in Foxwood. His door bore a nameplate reading "Professor Timothy Long, Department of Linguistics and Cultural Preservation." Student papers covered his desk—essays on language preservation techniques and the social dynamics of multilingual communities.

Through the window, he could see Ruth walking across the campus quad with Eric and Anil. They were bringing him lunch, as they did every Thursday. The sight made that familiar warmth bloom in his chest.

He had received word through a carefully maintained underground contact that the Collective had accepted his report. The surface world was classified as contaminated and off-limits indefinitely. Future expansion would focus on deeper excavations and the development of new subterranean territories.

The surface world was safe. Ruth was safe. His children were safe.

But Joshua lived with the knowledge that he was a lie. He was not Timothy Long. He was a consciousness thief, a murderer, an alien intelligence wearing a dead man's face. Sometimes, in the dark of night, he wondered if he had any right to the happiness he felt.

Then Ruth would turn to him in sleep, or Eric would share a new discovery, or Anil would climb into his lap with a book, and he would remember: love wasn't about deserving. It was about choosing, every day, to be the person they needed him to be.

He had been created as a tool of the Collective, but he had become something else entirely. He had become human.

A knock at his door interrupted his thoughts. A student entered, asking about the peer review process for her thesis on blockchain applications in linguistic data preservation. Joshua smiled and gestured for her to sit down.

He had a life to live, a family to love, and a world to protect. The Collective had sent him to evaluate whether humanity was worth preserving.

He had found his answer.

In the evening, as he walked home with Ruth and the children, the sun setting over Foxwood painted the sky in shades of orange and purple. Anil held his hand and asked him to tell a story about the ancient peoples, the ones who had lived before the pollution times.

Joshua began to speak, weaving together fragments of real history with protective fiction, teaching his children about cultural preservation and the importance of remembering where they came from. As he talked, he felt Ruth's hand slip into his other hand, warm and real and alive.

He had betrayed his creators to save this world. He would carry that weight forever. But looking at the faces of his family, seeing their trust and love, he knew he would make the same choice again.

Some things, he had learned, were worth more than efficiency. Some things were worth everything.

The Collective had taught him about game theory and optimal outcomes. But Ruth and the children had taught him about something more important: they had taught him about being human.

And that, Joshua Fuller—no, Timothy Long—had decided, was the most valuable lesson of all.
quality_problem.question: In which location is the underground facility where Joshua began his mission?

quality_problem.story:
THE AUTONOMOUS REVOLUTION

The traffic algorithms were always perfect: Speed, 45 mph; density, 23 vehicles per mile; occasional light malfunctions—but of what kind?

The protocols of Dr. Arthur Schultz were being violated outrageously.

It was a splendid day. The speed limit was a crisp 45 mph, the traffic density a carefully managed 23 vehicles per mile. The sun was a flaming orange ball in a cloudless blue sky.

His protocols were violated eleven times.

It should have been difficult. Under the circumstances it was a masterpiece of protocol violation. What made it possible was Arthur Schultz's abstraction; he was an uncommonly preoccupied individual. He was walking along a quiet residential street in the Valleyview District: small private houses, one after another, a place of little traffic and minimum distractions. But he was thinking about autonomous vehicles, which was an unusual subject to begin with for a person living in a manually-driven enclave. He was thinking so deeply about it that it never occurred to him that entirely too many people were scanning his identification chip. He was thinking about Optimal Traffic Conditions (a crisp 45 mph, a carefully managed 23 vehicles per mile) when a bogus delivery driver, who pretended to be checking a package label, bumped into him. In the confusion of spilled parcels and apologies from both sides, the driver scanned Schultz's biometric data and copied his residential access codes.

He was still thinking about speed and density when a young woman happened along, apparently lost. They collided. She got his financial credentials and transportation records. It was much too much for coincidence. The sidewalk was wide enough to allow four people to pass at one time. He should surely have become suspicious when two men engaged in a heated argument came along. In the ensuing contretemps they copied his communication logs, got his schedule patterns and restored some of the biometric data. It all went off very smoothly, like a game of digital transformation—the sole difference being that Arthur Schultz had no idea he was playing.

There was an occasional hum of passing vehicles.

They hummed on the streets and past houses, making soft whooshing sounds, moving with a gentle mechanical precision, like the ephemeral whispers of progress itself. It was transportation peculiar to the autonomous zones: algorithm-controlled vehicles navigating the huge network, ceaselessly optimizing and rerouting.

Arthur Schultz strode through the streams of autonomous traffic still intrigued by a speed that was always 45 mph, by a density that was always 23 vehicles per mile, by conditions that were always Optimal. It was this rather than skill that enabled the authorities to maintain such tight surveillance on him, a surveillance that went to the extent of copying his digital footprint off the delivery driver's scanner, and which analyzed, cross-referenced and categorically profiled the contents of his data before cataloging them. Two blocks away from his home a careless pedestrian spilled a container of marker dust as he was passing. It was really tracking powder.
