He left his gait signature, stride measurement, height, weight and handedness behind.

By the time Schultz reached his front door an entire profile complete with predictive models had been prepared and was being reviewed by two agents in a silver patrol car parked down the street.

Agent Priya Sharma had undoubtedly been affected by her job.

Sitting behind the wheel of the silver car, she watched Arthur Schultz approach with a distinct feeling of admiration, although it was an odd, objective kind of admiration, analytical in nature. It was similar to that of a systems analyst observing for the first time a new and particularly elegant algorithm under development.

Sharma's job was to identify deviations. They couldn't be tolerated within the confines of an autonomous zone. Conformity had become more than a social force; it was a traffic necessity. And, after years of working at it, Sharma had become an admirer of genuine nonconformity. She came to see that authentic quirks were rare and, as time went on, due partly to her own small efforts, rarer.

Schultz was a masterpiece of deviation. He was utterly inexplicable. Sharma was almost proud of Arthur Schultz.

"Sometimes his house moves," Sharma said.

"House moves," Agent Eric Moss wrote in his tablet. Then he stopped and frowned. He reread what he'd just written.

"You heard right. The house moves," Sharma said, savoring it.

Moss looked at the Schultz house through the enhanced display of the windshield. "Like from... side to side?" he asked in a somewhat patronizing tone of voice.

"And forward and back."

Moss returned the tablet to the breast pocket of his silver uniform. "Go on," he said, amused. "It sounds interesting." He tossed the profile carelessly on the back seat.

Sharma sat stiffly behind the wheel, affronted. The cynical Moss couldn't really appreciate fine deviations. In some ways Moss was a conformist. Sharma had held out on Schultz for months. She had even contrived to engage him in conversation once, a pleasantly absurd, illogical little chat that intrigued her for weeks. It was only with the greatest reluctance that she finally mentioned Schultz to Moss. After years of searching for differences Sharma had seen how extraordinarily repetitive people were, algorithms really, dimly executing subroutines, each believing itself autonomous and unique. They spoke in an incessant chatter of predictable responses, and their actions were unbelievably programmed.

Then a fine robust deviant came along and the others—the algorithms—refused to believe it. The agent was probably on the point of suggesting a vacation.

"Why don't you take a vacation?" Agent Moss suggested.

"It's like this, Moss. Do you know what manual control is? Human steering? Individual decision-making?"

"I've heard of them."

"They say there are places where humans still drive vehicles. Manually. Decisions like you and I can't imagine. And if there was a house connected to such systems and if decisions did occur, it would move exactly the way that one does. Sometimes I get the feeling the whole place is going to disconnect from its foundation and go rolling down the avenue."

Agent Moss pursed his lips.

"I'll tell you something else," Sharma went on. "The windows all polarize at the same time. You'll be watching and all of a sudden every single window in the place will darken to maximum opacity." Sharma leaned back in the seat, her eyes still on the house. "Sometimes I think there's a whole network of people in there waiting for a signal—as if they all had something important to transmit but had to block surveillance first so no one could monitor. Why else polarize the windows in an autonomous zone? And then as soon as the place is secured they all begin transmitting—and that's why the house moves."

Moss whistled.

"No, I don't need a vacation."

An autonomous vehicle glided silently past the windshield. Sharma started and bumped her knee on the steering column.

"No, you don't need a rest," Moss said. "You're starting to see moving houses, hear phantom transmissions. You've got deviations in your brain, Sharma, algorithms of fatigue, subroutines of irrationality—"

At that moment, all at once, every last window in the house darkened to maximum opacity.

The street was quiet and still, not a movement, not a sound. Moss and Sharma both leaned forward, as if waiting for the ghostly transmissions to commence.

The house began to move.

It shifted from side to side, it rolled forward and back, it swayed and dipped and twisted, straining at the anchor of its foundation. The house could have been preparing to disconnect and roll down the...

Moss looked at Sharma and Sharma looked at Moss and then they both looked back at the moving house.

"And the power," Sharma said. "The power he uses! He could be running the most energy-intensive operation in the district. He could have a whole server farm of computational systems, and he still wouldn't need all that power."

The agent had picked up the profile. He thumbed through the pages now in amazement. "Where do you get a guy like this?" he asked. "Did you see what he's researching?"

"And navigation systems won't work on this street."

The agent lit a cigarette and sighed.

He usually sighed when making the decision to investigate a dwelling. It expressed his weariness and distaste for people who went off and got deviant when they could be enjoying a happy, normal existence. There was something implacable about his sighs.

"He'll be coming out soon," Sharma said. "He has dinner next door with a widow. Then he goes to the archives. Always the same. Dinner at the widow's next door and then the archives."

Moss's eyebrows went up a fraction of an inch. "The archives?" he said. "Is he in with that bunch?"

Sharma nodded.

"Should be very interesting," Moss said slowly.

"I can't wait to see what he's got in there," Sharma murmured, watching the house with a consuming interest.

They sat there in silence and every now and then their eyes widened as the house performed a new movement.

Schultz stopped on the porch to brush the tracking powder off his shoes. He hadn't seen the patrol car and this intense preoccupation of his was also responsible for the moving house—he simply hadn't noticed. There was a certain amount of vibration, of course. He had a bootleg connection into the autonomous vehicle charging grid, and the high-voltage current caused some oscillation against the thin walls of the house. At least, he called it oscillation; he'd never thought to watch from outside.

He went in and threw his jacket on the sofa, there being no room left in the closets. Crossing the living room he stopped to press a button.

Every window darkened to maximum opacity.

"Secure as a vault," he thought, satisfied. He continued on toward the closet at the foot of the stairs and then stopped again. Was that right? No, tight as a encrypted file. He went on, thinking: The old systems.

The downstairs closet was like a great control panel, a profusion of switches surrounding the Master Controller, which was a miniature traffic simulator that processed 365.25 scenarios per hour. The switches had a curious elegance about them. They were all quite old, salvaged from manual vehicles and control towers and they activated in graceful sequences at the rate of 30 and 31 times an hour... although there was one slightly eccentric relay that vacillated between 28 and 29. He watched as they clicked and flashed in the darkness, and then set them for seven o'clock in the evening, April seventh, any year.

Outside, the autonomous zone vanished.

It was replaced by an illusion. Or, as Schultz hoped it might appear, the illusion of the autonomous zone vanished and was replaced by a more satisfactory, and, for his specific purpose, more functional, illusion. Looking through the window he saw only a highway.

Instead of algorithm-controlled vehicles at perpetual optimal flow, there were manually-driven cars moving chaotically, marred only by an occasional collision which left the smell of burning rubber in the air. There was also a gigantic billboard. It dominated a huge area of sky, and it advertised. The cars and billboard both looked down upon a highway that was itself chaotic, composed largely of individual decisions.

Individual choice, he thought, and freedom. Satisfactory. And dinner for two. Blast, he'd never be able to figure that one out! He watched as the billboard displayed, "Drive Your Own Destiny" and the manually-driven cars flashed slowly from red to violet taillights, then went back to the closet and turned on the sound. The house began to fill with the roar of engines as the billboard shifted to "Freedom Means Choice."

He rubbed his chin critically. It seemed all right. A chaotic highway, an advertising billboard, vehicles, sound. They were all purely speculative of course. He had no idea how manual driving really felt—or looked for that matter. Not to mention a billboard. But then, neither did the widow. He'd have to be confident, assertive. Insist on it. I tell you, my dear, this is a genuine realistic manual highway. Now, does it do anything to your sense of autonomy? Do you feel the thrill of individual decision-making?

His own sense of autonomy didn't seem to be affected. But then he hadn't read that book on ancient transportation and trade policy customs.

How really odd the ancients were. Courtship seemed to be an incredibly long and drawn-out process, accompanied by a considerable amount of inefficiency. Communication seemed virtually impossible. "No" meant any number of things, depending on the emotional intelligence of the speaker and the circumstances. It could mean yes, it could mean ask me again later this evening.

He went up the stairs to the bedroom closet and tried the weather-maker, thinking roguishly: Thou shalt not flood. The risks he was taking! A light rain fell on the highway and speakers began to play romantic music. Undiminished, the giant billboard and the chaotic traffic continued to be prominent, although the traffic occasionally collided and demolished several of the lane markers.

The last switch in the bedroom closet was a rather elegant control lever from an old 1995 manual transmission. This was on the bootleg connection; he gingerly moved it.

Far below in the cellar there was a rumble and then the soft hum of power came to him.

He went downstairs to watch out the living room window. This was important; the window had a really fixed attitude about power surges. The lane markers bent and sparked against each other as the power rose and the billboard shook a trifle as it whispered "Choose Your Own Path."

He watched with folded arms, considering how he would start. My dear Mrs. Hamilton. Too formal. They'd be looking out at the chaotic highway; time to be a bit forward. My very dear Mrs. Hamilton. No. Contrived. How about a simple, Dear Susan. That might be it. I was wondering, seeing as how it's so late, if you wouldn't rather stay over instead of going home...

Preoccupied, he hadn't noticed the power building up, didn't hear the shaking and rattling of the connections. There were attic connections linked to wall connections and wall connections linked to cellar connections, and they made one gigantic network that began to overload and surge as high-voltage current from the autonomous vehicle grid rushed in, slowly opening the manual transmission lever wider and wider...

The lane markers thrashed about, short-circuiting each other. The chaotic traffic shot off sparks and then quickly disappeared from sight. The billboard fell on the highway and rolled ponderously along, displaying "Freedom Has Consequences."

The shaking house finally woke him up. He scrambled upstairs to the manual transmission lever and shut it off.

At the window again, he sighed. Repairs were in order. And it wasn't the first time the power got out of control.

Why didn't she marry him and save all this bother? He shut it all down and went out the front door, wondering about the logic of the months, about structured August and eccentric February and romantic April. April. Its days were thirty and it follows September. And all the rest have thirty-one. What a strange people, the ancients!

He still didn't see the silver car parked down the street.

"Men are too fragile," Susan Hamilton said over dinner. "For all practical purposes I'm never going to marry again. All my husbands malfunction."

"Would you pass the asparagus, please?" Arthur Schultz said.

She handed him a platter of steaming green asparagus. "And don't look at me that way," she said. "I'm not going to marry you and if you want reasons I'll give you four of them. Robert. James. William. And Thomas."

The widow was an intense woman. She did everything intensely—talking, cooking, dressing. Her asparagus was intensely green. Her clothes rustled and her jewelry clinked and her voice resonated. She was possessed by an uncontrollable energy. Schultz had never known anyone like her. "You forgot to season the potatoes," she said intensely, then went on as calmly as it was possible for her to be, to explain why she couldn't marry him. "Do you have any idea what people are saying? They're all saying I'm cursed! I drain my husbands of their vitality and when they're depleted I carry their bodies outside on my way to city hall."

"As long as there are people," he said philosophically, "there'll be gossip."

"But it's the environment! Why don't they talk about that? The environment is toxic, I'm positive. It's not nourishing. The environment is toxic and Robert, James, William and Thomas couldn't stand it. Poor Thomas. He was never so healthy as on the day he was born. From then on things got steadily worse for him."

"I don't seem to mind the environment."

She threw up her hands. "You'd be the worst of the lot!" She left the table, rustling and clinking about the room. "I can just hear them. Try some of the salad. Five. That's what they'd say. That woman did it again. And the plain fact is I don't want you on my record."

"Really," Schultz protested. "I feel splendid. Never better."

He could hear her moving about and then felt her hands on his shoulders. "And what about those very elaborate plans you've been making to convince me?"

Schultz froze with three asparagus spears hanging from his fork.

"Don't you think they'll find out? I found out and you can bet they will. It's my fault, I guess. I talk too much. And I don't always tell the truth. To be completely honest with you, Dr. Schultz, it wasn't the old customs at all standing between us, it was environment. I can't have another man malfunction on me, it's bad for my self-esteem. And now you've gone and done something illegal and peculiar."

Schultz put his fork down. "Dear Susan," he started to say.

"And of course when they do find out and they ask you why, Dr. Schultz, you'll tell them. No, no heroics, please! When they ask a man a question he always answers and you will too. You'll tell them I wanted to be courted and when they hear that they'll be around to ask me a few questions. You see, we're both a bit deviant."

"I hadn't thought of that," Schultz said quietly.

"Oh, it doesn't really matter. I'll join Robert, James, William—"

"That won't be necessary," Schultz said with unusual force. "With all due respect to Robert, James, William and Thomas, I might as well state here and now I have other plans for you, Susan."

"But my dear Arthur," she said, leaning across the table. "We're trapped, you and I."

"Not if we could leave the autonomous zone," Schultz said quietly.

"That's impossible! How?"

In no hurry, now that he had the widow's complete attention, Schultz leaned across the table and whispered: "Manual control, Susan? Space? Miles and miles of space where the traffic algorithms have no control whatever? Where the wind blows across highways; or is it the other way around? No matter. How would you like that, Susan?"

Breathing somewhat faster than usual, the widow rested her chin on her two hands. "Pray continue," she said.

"Endless vistas of individual choice and freedom? April roads, Susan. And June, which as you may know follows directly upon April and is supposed to be the month of brides, of marrying. June also lies beyond the autonomous zone."

"I see."

"And," Dr. Schultz added, his voice a honeyed whisper, "they say that somewhere out in the space and the freedom and the individual choice, the sleeping manual transmission awakens and engages because on a certain day it's spring and that's when it roams the Open Highway where algorithms no longer calculate."

"My." Susan Hamilton rose, paced slowly to the window and then came back to the table, standing directly over Schultz. "If you can get us outside the autonomous zone," she said, "out where a man stays vital long enough for his wife to get to know him... if you can do that, Dr. Schultz... you may call me Susan."

When Arthur Schultz stepped out of the widow's house, there was a look of such intense abstraction on his features that Sharma felt a wistful desire to get out of the car and walk along with the man. It would be such a deliciously deviant experience. ("April has thirty days," Schultz mumbled, passing them, "because thirty is the largest number such that all smaller numbers not having a common divisor with it are primes." Moss frowned and added it to the profile. Sharma sighed.)

Pinning his hopes on the Movement, Schultz went straight to the archives several blocks away, a neglected depressing place given over to government records and censored old files with redactions in them. It was used so infrequently that the Movement was able to meet there undisturbed. The archivist was a weathered, obsolete woman of eighty. She spent her days reading ancient transportation logs and, like the files around her, had been rendered by time's own censor into near unintelligibility.

"Here's one," she said to him as he entered. "Manual Vehicle Registration. Issued to Jennifer Alvarez on March 14, 1979 for five years. What do you make of it?"

In the litter of files and records and dried out ink stamps that surrounded the archivist, Schultz noticed a torn poster with a curious illustration. "What's that?" he said.

"A highway," she replied quickly. "Now listen to this. Seven years later on March 21, 1986, Antonio Harper took out the same registration. What do you make of that?"

"I'd say," Arthur Schultz said, "that he... that he recommended it to her, that one day they met on the street and he told her about this registration and then they... they went to the office together and she registered it and eventually, why eventually they got married."

"Hah! They were brother and sister!" the archivist shouted in her parched voice, her old bureaucratic eyes laughing with cunning.

Schultz smiled weakly and looked again at the poster. The highway was unquestionably a transportation phenomenon. It stretched ominously, like a malevolent ribbon, and coursed the countryside chaotically, carrying individuals to destinations. He couldn't help wondering if highways did anything to feminine pulses, if they could possibly be a part of a romantic evening, with dinner and freedom. He absently stuffed the poster in his pocket and went on into the other rooms, the archivist mumbling after him: "Katherine Rodriguez, April 21, 1991," as though reading inscriptions on a tombstone.

The Movement met in what had been the research room, where unpaid scholars of the afternoon had once upon a time studied records for other people's projects. The members sat around at the standard tables looking oddly like giants fled from their algorithms, protesting.

"Where did the old society fail?" the leader was demanding of them. He stood in the center of the room, leaning on a heavy walking stick. He glanced around at the group almost complacently, and waited as Arthur Schultz squeezed into an empty chair. "We live in an autonomous zone," the leader said, "for lack of something. A decision! What is the one thing that the great technological societies before ours could not automate, notwithstanding their various artificial intelligences, electronic and otherwise?"

Schultz was the kind of man who never answered a rhetorical question. He waited, uncomfortable in the standard chair, while the others struggled with this problem in revolutionary logic.

"A sound trade policy," the leader said, aware that no one else had obtained the insight. "If a sound trade policy can't be automated the only alternative is not to have any trade policy at all. Thus the movement into autonomous zones began—by common consent of the governments. This is known as self-regulation."

Logically out in left field, Arthur Schultz waited for a lull in the ensuing discussion and then politely inquired how it might be arranged for him to get out.

"Out?" the leader said, frowning. "Out? Out where?"

"Outside the autonomous zone."

"Oh. All in good time, my friend. One day we shall all disconnect and leave."

"And that day I'll await impatiently," Schultz replied with marvelous tact, "because it will be lonely out there for the two of us. My future wife and I have to leave now."

"Nonsense. Ridiculous! You have to be prepared for the Open Highway. You can't just up and leave, it would be suicide, Schultz. And logically very poor."

"Then you have discussed preparations, the practical necessities of life on the Open Highway. Food, fuel, a map perhaps? What else? Have I left anything out?"

The leader sighed. "The gentleman wants to know if he's left anything out," he said to the group.

Schultz looked around at them, at some dozen pained expressions.

"Tell the man what he's forgotten," the leader said, walking to the far window and turning his back quite pointedly on them.

Everyone spoke at the same moment. "A sound trade policy," they all said, it being almost too obvious for words.

On his way out the archivist shouted at him: "Water Management Records, thirty-five years overdue!" She was calculating the fine as he closed the door.

Arthur Schultz's preoccupation finally came to an end when he was one block away from his house. It was then that he realized something unusual must have occurred. A silver patrol car of the security authorities was parked at his front door. And something else was happening too.

His house was moving.

It was disconcerting, and at the same time fascinating, to watch one's residence oscillating on its foundation. It was such a strange sight that for the moment he didn't give a thought to what might be causing it. But when he stepped gingerly onto the porch, which was doing its own independent vibration, he reached for the doorknob with an immense curiosity.

The door flung itself open and knocked him back off the porch.

From a prone position on his minuscule front lawn, Schultz watched as his favorite reading chair sailed out of the living room on a blast of electromagnetic interference and went spinning down the avenue in the bright sunshine. A wild surge and a thick static poured out of the house. It brought chairs, clothes, small tables, lamps trailing their cords, tablets, sofa cushions. The house was emptying itself fiercely, as if purging an old, corrupted system. From deep inside he could hear the rumble of his ancient server rack as it rolled ponderously from room to room.

He stood up; a charged field swept over him, crackling at his face, standing his hair on end. It was a buzzing in his ears, and a tingle on his skin. He got hit by a shoe.

As he forced his way back to the doorway waves of interference played over his face and he heard a voice cry out from somewhere in the living room.

"Help!" Agent Moss called.

Standing in the doorway with his hair standing on end, the interference crackling about him, the server rack rumbling in the distance like thunder, Arthur Schultz suddenly saw it all very clearly.

"Power," he said in a whisper.

"What's happening?" Moss yelled, crouching behind the sofa.

"Grid power," he said.

"What?!"

"Overload surge!"

The interference crackled for a moment and then Moss's lost voice emerged from the chaos of the living room. "These are not Optimal Traffic Conditions!" the voice wailed. "The speed is not 45 mph. The density is not 23 vehicles per mile!"

Schultz held his face up to let the static wash over it. "Individual choice!" he shouted. "Freedom! My soul for manual control!" He grasped the doorway to keep from being blown out of the house.

"Are you going to make it stop or aren't you!" Moss yelled.

"You'll have to tell me what you did first!"

"I told her not to touch that lever! Sharma. She's in the upstairs bedroom!"

When he heard this Schultz plunged into the house and fought his way up the stairs. He found Sharma standing outside the bedroom with a lever in her hand.

"What have I done?" Sharma asked in the monotone of shock.

Schultz took the lever. It was from a 1995 manual transmission.

"I'm not sure what's going to come of this," he said to Sharma with an astonishing amount of objectivity, "but the entire autonomous vehicle charging grid is now flowing through my bedroom."

The interference screamed.

"Is there something I can turn?" Sharma asked.

"Not any more there isn't."

They started down the stairs carefully, but the surge caught them and they quickly reached the bottom in a charged heap.

Recruiting Agent Moss from behind his sofa, the three carefully edged out of the house and forced the front door shut.

The interference died. The static dispersed. They stood tingling in the Optimal Traffic Conditions of the bright avenue.

"I never figured on this," Sharma said, shaking her head.

With the front door closed the power quickly built up inside the house. They could see the furnishings whirl past the windows. The house did a wild, energized dance.

"What kind of a place is this?" Moss said, his courage beginning to return. He took out his tablet but it was completely fried. He tossed it away.

"Sure, he was different," Sharma murmured. "I knew that much."

When the roof disconnected they weren't really surprised. With a certain amount of equanimity they watched it lift off almost gracefully, standing on end for a moment before toppling to the ground. It was strangely slow motion, as was the black spinning vortex that now rose out of the master bedroom, spewing data and devices every which way.

"Now what?" Moss said, thoroughly exasperated, as this strange black vortex began to accelerate, whirling about like some malevolent algorithm...

Arthur Schultz took out the poster he'd found in the archives. He held it up and carefully compared the spinning vortex in his bedroom with the illustration. The vortex rose and spun, assuming the identical shape of the illustration.

"It's a data storm," he said softly. "A network data storm!"

"What," Moss asked, his bravado slipping away again, "what... is a data storm?"

The data storm roared and moved out of the bedroom, out over the rear of the house toward the edge of the autonomous zone. "It says here," Schultz shouted over the roaring, "that individuals traveled from controlled zones to free territories in data storms and that... and that free territories are wonderful and mysterious lands beyond the confines of algorithmic living."

Moss's eyes and mouth were great zeros.

"Is there something I can turn?" Sharma asked.

Huge chunks of infrastructure began to fail around them.

"Schultz!" Moss shouted. "This is a direct order! Make it go back!"

Schultz stared at the cascading failures spreading across the district. For a long moment, he watched the autonomous vehicles swerving at frightful angles, depleted of charge, rushing to the charging stations which they quickly overwhelmed. The algorithm-controlled traffic vanished behind the mushrooming data storm. Optimal conditions collapsed across entire blocks.

The infrastructure failure was spreading rapidly now—power substations sparked and went dark, navigation beacons flickered out, the carefully maintained grid that kept twenty-three vehicles per mile at precisely forty-five miles per hour was disintegrating before their eyes.

Moss grabbed Schultz's arm. "You have to stop this! The whole district is going down!"

Schultz pulled free and began running toward the next house. "Mrs. Hamilton!" he shouted. "Susan!"

Behind him, Moss stood frozen, watching the destruction spread. His tablet was destroyed. His car was powerless. The entire surveillance network he relied upon was collapsing into chaos. He looked at the data storm with something approaching horror.

Sharma, standing beside him, watched Schultz disappear around the corner of the Hamilton house. "He's actually going to do it," she murmured, and there was something in her voice that might have been admiration.

"Do what?" Moss demanded. "Destroy everything? Look at this mess!" He gestured at the sparking substations, the wandering vehicles, the darkened houses. "Years of infrastructure optimization, gone! The traffic patterns alone will take months to recalibrate!"

"He's going to escape," Sharma said quietly.

Moss turned to stare at her. "Escape? Into that?" He pointed at the data storm, which was now a towering black spiral reaching toward the edge of the autonomous zone. "That's not escape, that's suicide!"

But even as he spoke, they could see two figures emerging from the Hamilton house—Schultz and the widow, hand in hand, running toward the vortex.

"Stop them!" Moss shouted, but his voice was lost in the roar of failing systems.

Sharma didn't move. She watched as the two figures grew smaller, watched as they approached the spinning darkness at the boundary of everything she had spent her career protecting. The data storm seemed to reach down for them, seemed to open like a doorway.

"The whole district," Moss was saying, his voice cracking. "The whole district is going to have to be rebuilt from scratch. Do you understand what this means? The optimization protocols, the traffic algorithms, the surveillance networks—everything! All because that lunatic couldn't leave well enough alone!"

The two figures disappeared into the vortex.

The data storm began to move, carrying them toward the edge of the autonomous zone, toward the Open Highway, toward a place where decisions were still made by humans, where the epistemology of control gave way to the archaeology of freedom, where the linguistics of algorithms dissolved into the simple language of choice.

Sharma and Moss stood in the wreckage of the Valleyview District, watching the storm recede. Behind them, autonomous vehicles wandered aimlessly, their algorithms confused and corrupted. Power flickered on and off across the neighborhood. The silver patrol car sat dead at the curb, its enhanced display dark.

"All of this," Moss said, his voice hollow. "All of this destruction. And for what? Some romantic notion about manual control?"

Sharma said nothing. She was thinking about the pleasantly absurd conversation she'd once had with Schultz, about the fine robust deviant she'd watched for months, about the way his house moved and his windows darkened and his power consumption defied explanation.

"We'll have to file a report," Moss continued, mechanically. "Catastrophic infrastructure failure. Unauthorized grid access. Deliberate sabotage of autonomous systems." He looked around at the chaos surrounding them. "They'll want to know how this happened. They'll want to know who's responsible."

The data storm was a distant smudge now, barely visible against the horizon. Somewhere beyond it lay the Open Highway, and April roads, and June weddings, and a lifetime of manual control.

"He got what he wanted," Sharma said finally.

Moss stared at her. "What?"

"Schultz. He got what he wanted. He escaped."

"And destroyed half the district doing it!" Moss kicked at a piece of debris. "When I get my hands on that lever—" He stopped, remembering. The lever was gone, pulled from its housing by Sharma, now lying somewhere in the rubble of Schultz's bedroom. The bootleg connection was severed. The damage was done.

"There's nothing to get your hands on," Sharma said. "It's over."

But for Moss, standing in the ruins of optimal conditions, watching the last traces of the data storm fade into the distance, it wasn't over at all. It was just beginning—the long, tedious process of reconstruction, of recalibration, of restoring the autonomous zone to its proper state of algorithmic perfection.

Somewhere out there, beyond the boundary of everything he understood, Arthur Schultz and Susan Hamilton were discovering what it meant to choose their own path.

And here, in the wreckage they'd left behind, Agent Eric Moss was discovering what it meant to clean up the mess.

quality_problem.story:
The Protocol
BY LIEUTENANT COLONEL STEPHEN LYNCH (RET.)

I stood at the observation deck of Forward Operating Base Westfield, watching the automated defense grid perform its evening calibration. The hum of the machinery was a comfort—predictable, reliable, eternal. In my forty years of service, I had never seen one of these systems fail. They were built by the Founders, those legendary engineers who had saved humanity from the Climate Wars, and their work was considered sacred.

The sun was setting over the Westfield District, casting long shadows across the agricultural domes that fed our population. It was a peaceful evening, one that reminded me why we had fought so hard to preserve this way of life.

"Colonel Lynch! Colonel Lynch!" The voice shattered my reverie.

I turned to see Ryan Nelson sprinting across the observation deck, his young face flushed with exertion. Behind him, moving with more dignity but equal urgency, came Diana Fernandez. Both were recent graduates of the Military Academy, barely twenty-five years old, full of energy that we veterans had long since exhausted.

"Colonel," Ryan gasped, "the Genetic Preservation Vault—it's gone critical!"

I stared in disbelief. "Gone critical? That's impossible. The vault has maintained optimal conditions for three centuries."

Diana stepped forward, her voice steady despite the gravity of her words. "The monitoring officer was negligent, sir. The temperature controls failed, continued to rise beyond safety parameters, and then—total system failure. All the genetic material has been destroyed."

"All of it?" I demanded.

"Every sample, sir. The entire repository of human genetic diversity. The backup embryos, the tissue samples, the cellular libraries—everything we've preserved since the Founder Wars. It's all gone."

When I entered the Command Center, I found the War Council already assembled. Ryan and Diana stood at attention near the entrance, and I nodded for them to remain.

The Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Theodore Willis, addressed the Council after the preliminary speeches concluded.

"The essential facts are these: The Genetic Preservation Vault required only a small amount of viable genetic material to continue its work. Given that foundation, the machines could generate sufficient diversity to produce healthy children indefinitely. But now we face an unprecedented situation. The vault has failed completely. There will be no more children."

The room erupted. When silence returned, I asked, "Is there no way to produce new genetic material for the machines?"

"Without that initial material, they are useless," Willis replied.

General Mateo Stewart leaned forward. "But there must have been a beginning to this system. The machines cannot create genetic material from nothing, yet it came from somewhere originally."

"This is not the time for philosophical speculation," I said sharply.

"Is it not?" Stewart replied. "Humans once reproduced biologically, without machines. The archaeological evidence is clear."

Two Council members required medical attention at this statement. I hoped Ryan and Diana hadn't heard clearly, but their wide eyes suggested otherwise.

"Permission granted to access the Founder Archives," I said, and adjourned the Council.

---

Three weeks later, Stewart reported his findings to the reconvened Council.

"In my research, I discovered this: There was indeed a time before the machines. The biological differences between males and females are not vestigial—they are functional. The system still exists within us."

Order dissolved as officers turned to their neighbors. I announced loudly: "There is a contradiction in your theory. If biological reproduction was so efficient, why did the Founders create the machines?"

Ryan Nelson, still standing at attention, spoke without permission: "Perhaps biological reproduction created social dynamics that threatened military discipline? Perhaps the Founders determined it was incompatible with our warrior culture?"

The Council exploded in outrage at this impudence. Ryan was immediately placed under arrest and confined to the brig.

---

Stewart entered the next morning looking haggard. He carried a thin, ancient book titled "Human Reproductive Biology: A Clinical Guide."

When he finished explaining the mechanism of biological reproduction, the Council sat in horrified silence.

"Then we must test this hypothesis," I said. "But who could we ask to volunteer for such a procedure?"

"I have already secured volunteers," Stewart replied. "Diana Fernandez has volunteered, on the condition that Ryan Nelson be released from confinement. Ryan Nelson has agreed to participate. They both understand what's required."

General Harrison, who had been silent throughout, spoke up. "I must register my objection. These are junior officers acting without proper authorization channels. They've circumvented the chain of command entirely."

"The situation is unprecedented," I replied.

"Precisely why we need experienced personnel making these decisions, not impulsive young soldiers who may not grasp the implications." Harrison's face was stern. "What happens when this fails? What precedent does this set?"

Stewart intervened. "The volunteers are waiting, General. Time is critical."

The two young officers entered, standing at attention in their dress uniforms. Ryan stepped forward.

"Colonel Lynch, would we not achieve better results if we conducted the experiment at the Memorial Gardens in Northfield, where the Founders are honored?"

His eyes met mine. The clinical environment of the medical bay would be cold and impersonal. I gave my consent, and the entire Council relocated to Northfield.

---

It was nearly dark when Stewart and I walked back to the Westfield District. The clinical descriptions in the manual had not prepared us for the reality—the vulnerability, the intimacy.

We paused at the gate of the base. "They seemed to follow the manual's instructions accurately," I muttered.

"They may have succeeded," Stewart replied. "The result isn't immediate—it takes months."

Then I looked down and saw them standing before us. Diana's eyes were downcast. Ryan had his arm around her shoulders.

"Colonel Lynch," Ryan said, then stopped, embarrassed. "Sir, we wanted to tell you... we're willing to try again."

General Harrison materialized from the shadows, his arms crossed. "Of course they're willing. Look at them. They've turned a crisis into an opportunity for personal gratification."

"General—" I began.

"Don't you see it, Lynch? The way they're standing together. The way they requested privacy. They're not thinking about humanity's survival. They're thinking about themselves."

Ryan's jaw tightened. "Sir, that's not—"

"You volunteered awfully quickly," Harrison continued. "Both of you. A truly reluctant sacrifice would have required more deliberation."

Diana finally looked up. "We understood the urgency, General. Every day without action—"

"Urgency. Yes." Harrison's voice dripped with skepticism. "Tell me, Lieutenant Fernandez, when you and Nelson discussed volunteering, was it purely clinical? Or did something else factor into your decision?"

The silence stretched. Ryan's arm around Diana's shoulders seemed suddenly conspicuous.

"We have one request," Ryan finally said, ignoring Harrison and addressing me directly. "We'd like to conduct further attempts in private. Without observation."

"Naturally," Harrison muttered.

"Of course," I replied. "You've earned that consideration."

Ryan took a deep breath. "We don't deserve special praise, sir. The truth is... the procedure isn't as unpleasant as the manual suggested. We... we actually found it somewhat... agreeable."

Harrison laughed—a short, bitter sound. "There it is. The truth emerges."

I watched Ryan and Diana walk away together under the stars, heading toward the Memorial Gardens. Harrison stood beside me, shaking his head.

"You're too credulous, Lynch. Those two saw an opportunity and seized it. The biological instincts Stewart described—they're clearly already activated. Whatever nobility you're projecting onto them, it's your own construction."

I considered his words. It was true that they had volunteered quickly. True that they seemed comfortable together in ways that suggested prior... interest. True that their request for privacy was convenient.

But I had also seen Diana's face when Stewart described the procedure to the Council. The fear in her eyes. The way her hands had trembled before she steadied them. And Ryan—he had spoken out of turn, been thrown in the brig, and still volunteered knowing the consequences if he failed.

"General," I said slowly, "I've been in the military for forty years. I've seen soldiers volunteer for dangerous missions for all sorts of reasons—duty, glory, peer pressure, guilt. Sometimes soldiers volunteer because they want to, and sometimes that wanting doesn't diminish the sacrifice."

Harrison snorted. "Philosophy. I deal in facts. The fact is, we have two junior officers who have found a way to engage in unprecedented physical intimacy under the cover of military necessity. And we're going to decorate them for it."

"Perhaps. But consider the alternative interpretation. Two young people, raised in our warrior culture, trained to view physical vulnerability as weakness—and they've agreed to expose themselves completely, in the most intimate way imaginable, for an outcome they can't even verify for months. They could fail. They could be humiliated. The entire Council watched them."

"They requested that themselves."

"At the Memorial Gardens, yes. A small dignity. But the initial attempt was observed, documented, analyzed."

Harrison was silent for a moment. "You're determined to see them as something elevated."

"I'm trying to see them clearly. And clearly, they've done something no one else would do."

---

In the morning, I submitted my report to High Command. I noted the volunteers' willingness to repeat the procedure. I documented their request for privacy. I included Harrison's objections in full.

The recommendation for commendation was not mine to make alone. The War Council would debate it. Harrison would argue his interpretation. Others would argue theirs.

But when I thought of Ryan and Diana, walking together toward the gardens in the darkness, I remembered something else from that evening. Before they left, Diana had turned back to look at the Command Center—at all of us, the old officers who had spent our lives avoiding risk, maintaining systems built by greater people.

Her expression wasn't triumph or excitement. It was determination, tinged with something I recognized from my own youth, from the days before I learned to calculate every action.

It was the look of someone who had chosen to act when action was terrifying.

Whether that made them heroes or simply young people following instincts older than our civilization—that was for the historians to decide. The machines had failed us. But two soldiers had stepped into the gap, whatever their reasons.

The Council would convene tomorrow to discuss appropriate recognition. I would advocate for the Founder's Medal. Harrison would advocate for caution, for waiting to see results before offering praise.

Both arguments had merit. That was the nature of unprecedented situations.

I turned off my desk lamp and looked out at the Memorial Gardens, visible as a dark patch against the lights of the agricultural domes.

Whatever the Council decided, those two were out there now, continuing their work. Humanity's future—if there was to be one—rested on their shoulders.

I found I was grateful they had volunteered. Whatever their reasons.

quality_problem.story:
THE PARADOX PROTOCOL

By Anonymous

The holding facility in Cliffside, Fendria had been constructed with remarkable precision. Patrick Harrison had seen plenty of detention centers during his career in international diplomacy, but nothing quite matched the sterile efficiency of this one. Every surface gleamed under the facility's distinctive emerald lighting—a wavelength the Fendrians had determined optimal for concentration and compliance. The green glow bathed everything, making accurate observation of his surroundings nearly impossible.

The Fendrians, Harrison reflected as he stretched out on the uncomfortably rigid cot, were nothing if not meticulous. All the preliminary intelligence reports had emphasized this trait; their obsession with precision and logical consistency had made them extraordinarily successful in fields like data science and blockchain technology. Within the past decade, they'd revolutionized digital security protocols and were on the verge of creating an unhackable global network. Before long, they'd control the infrastructure of international communications, and then—inevitably—they'd leverage that control into political dominance.

An outcome, the Coalition of Democratic Nations was certain, that would be catastrophic for global freedom.

Harrison sighed and stared at the ceiling. He'd been in isolation for four days now, with nothing to occupy his mind but his own thoughts. He'd tried mental exercises, memory games, even attempting to compose poetry in his head—but his talents didn't lie in creative writing. He couldn't pick the lock with his bare hands; he couldn't even influence the probability that his guards might make a mistake.

He could do, as a matter of fact, precisely nothing except wait. He wished the Fendrians had at least provided him with reading material. A technical manual on water management systems would have been better than this endless boredom.

In any reasonably-run prison, he told himself with frustration, there would at least be other inmates. But in this Fendrian facility, Harrison was completely alone.

True, every evening technicians came and subjected him to intensive language training while he was unconscious, but Harrison got no enjoyment from that. Now he could discuss everything from game theory to entrepreneurship in flawless Fendrian, but he had no one to talk to. He shifted position on the cot and examined the walls again. The Fendrians were thorough; there wasn't even a scratch to distract him.

He wasn't tired and he wasn't hungry; they'd provided him with nutritionally optimized meal replacements. But he was desperately bored and ready to talk to anyone about anything, just for human—or quasi-human—contact.

As he reached this conclusion, the door opened with a pneumatic hiss. Harrison stood quickly and turned to face his visitor.

Under the green illumination, the Fendrian's skin appeared an odd shade—neither quite one color nor another. The being was tall, and Harrison found himself squinting, trying to discern the natural pigmentation beneath the facility's chromatic distortion. The Fendrian's complexion reminded him of deep ocean water under certain lighting conditions. Life throughout the explored regions seemed to favor humanoid forms; Harrison didn't know why, and the scientists back home had offered dozens of theories without reaching consensus. Harrison didn't particularly care; it wasn't his area of expertise.

The Fendrian studied him through pale, almost colorless eyes. "You are Patrick Harrison," he said in a flat, emotionless tone.

It was a ritual, Harrison had learned. "You are Fendrian," he replied.

The being nodded once. "I am Oliver Carter of Fendria," he said. The formalities completed, he entered the cell, the door sliding shut behind him. Harrison briefly considered attacking, but dismissed the idea. He was a prisoner, and it would be foolish to assume his captors lacked hidden defenses beyond the visible neural disruptor holstered at Carter's side and the small blade at his belt.

"What is your purpose here?" Harrison said. The Fendrian language—apparently the entire nation spoke one standardized dialect—was rigid and mathematical in structure, but easily learned under hypnotic conditioning. It was the most ruthlessly logical linguistic construction Harrison had encountered in his diplomatic career, reminiscent of formal logic systems he'd studied years ago.

"I have no purpose here," Carter said, standing near the door. His uniform was the standard Fendrian military issue—a deep forest green that supposedly complemented their natural coloring, though Harrison couldn't verify this under the current lighting. "Do you have additional questions?"

Harrison suppressed a sigh. "Why have you come to this location?" he asked, mentally adjusting to the Fendrian literalist interpretation of language.

"I have been ordered to come to this location," Carter said, "by the Director. The Director requires information from you."

The Fendrian term wasn't quite "requires"—it was more specific, roughly translating to "demands with full legal authority." Harrison filed the distinction away. "Why did the Director not come to me?" he asked.

"The Director is the Director," Carter said, as if this explained everything. "You will go to the Director. This is the command."

Harrison smoothed his hair and straightened his posture. "I acknowledge the Director's command," he said—another required response. Everyone acknowledged the Director's commands in Fendria. Failure to do so meant immediate termination.

But Harrison meant exactly what he'd said. He was going to follow the Director's commands—and in doing so, eliminate the Fendrian threat to global democratic governance forever.

That, after all, was his mission.

---

The Director's office was large, rectangular, and overwhelmingly gray. The walls were dark gray, the furniture—a single imposing desk, several rigid chairs, and a row of filing cabinets—was light gray metal, and even the window treatments were slate-colored. More importantly, Harrison noted with relief, the lighting here was neutral—standard white illumination that allowed accurate color perception for the first time since his arrival.

The Director himself was unlike anything Harrison had expected based on his cell observations. A Fendrian over six and a half feet tall with correspondingly broad shoulders, the Director sat behind his desk, fingers steepled precisely, studying Harrison and his two escorts. In the neutral lighting, Harrison could finally see what the intelligence briefings had described: the distinctive pigmentation that set Fendrians apart from humans. The Director's skin had that characteristic tint—the same shade as the ocean photographs Harrison had seen in geography texts, the color of water under an afternoon sky.

The escorts stood on either side of their prisoner, motionless as statues. Their complexions matched the Director's precisely—that same aquatic hue that seemed to shimmer slightly under direct illumination.

Harrison wasn't trying to escape. He wasn't begging for mercy. He wasn't defying authority. He was simply answering questions.

The Fendrians valued clarity above all else. They were a logical people. The Director had begun with Harrison's nationality, his full name, his biological sex, and whether his appearance was typical for his species.

Harrison was now addressing the last question. "Some humans are taller than I am," he said, "and some are shorter."

"Specify the range," the Director commanded.

Harrison shrugged slightly. "Some exceed two meters in height," he said, using the Fendrian measurement system, "while others are below one meter." He saw no need to mention that both extremes were exceptional cases. "Additionally, there is a category of humans who are typically between forty and sixty centimeters tall—usually around forty-five centimeters. We call these 'children,'" he added helpfully.

"'Typically'?" the Director said sharply. "We require precision here. We are a scientific society. We demand exactitude."

Harrison nodded quickly. "My species is more... variable," he said apologetically.

"Imprecise," the Director muttered. His complexion seemed to darken momentarily with irritation—Harrison noticed the way Fendrian skin shifted toward deeper shades of its base color when emotions ran high.

"Undoubtedly," Harrison agreed politely. "I'll provide the most accurate information I can."

"You will answer my questions," the Director said, "with complete precision." He paused, his expression unchanging. "You arrived in Fendria via aircraft," he continued. "Explain the purpose."

"My assignment required it," Harrison said.

"An obvious falsehood," the Director said. "The aircraft crashed; our analysis proves this conclusively."

"Correct," Harrison said.

"And your assignment is to crash aircraft?" the Director said. "This is inefficient."

Harrison shrugged again. "What I state is accurate," he said. "Do you possess verification methods?"

"We do," the Director told him. "We are a precise and scientific nation. A truth-verification system has been calibrated to your physiology. It will be applied to you now."

Harrison looked toward the door as it opened, admitting two technicians pushing a large device. The machine was painted in the standard Fendrian equipment color—a muted greenish-gray that supposedly reduced visual fatigue during extended operations. It was bulky, angular, and metallic, mounted on wheels, covered with displays, sensors, blinking indicators, cables, and featuring a seat with restraints. It was clearly a polygraph system—and Harrison marveled again at this society. Coalition technology had nothing approaching their mastery of physical sciences; adapting a hypnotic language-training program to an alien mind so rapidly had been impressive enough, but calibrating the extraordinarily sensitive mechanisms of a polygraph to unfamiliar physiology was nearly miraculous.

The Fendrians, under different circumstances, would have been valuable allies in promoting global stability and cultural exchange.

Being what they are, however, they could only threaten the democratic world order. And Harrison's understanding of that threat grew with each passing hour.

He hoped the polygraph had been calibrated correctly. If it indicated deception, he wouldn't survive long, and both his mission and his strong personal preference demanded his continued survival.

He swallowed hard. But when the technicians strapped him into the seat, attached sensors and electrodes to his body at various points, and tightened the final restraints, he offered no resistance.

"We will test the device," the Director said. "In what location are you?"

"In the Director's office," Harrison said calmly.

"Are you standing or seated?"

"I am seated," Harrison said.

"Are you a vrakken?" the Director asked. A vrakken was a small Fendrian animal, Harrison knew, something like an oversized beetle with an iridescent green carapace.

"I am not," he said.

The Director glanced at his technicians for confirmation, then nodded at their signal. "You will now state a falsehood," he said. "Are you standing or seated?"

"I am standing," Harrison said.

The technicians signaled again. The Director looked satisfied. "The device," he announced, "has been successfully calibrated to your physiology. Questioning will now proceed."

Harrison swallowed again. The test seemed inadequate to him. But the Fendrians knew their business better than anyone else could. They had the methodology and the logic and the expertise.

He hoped they were right.

The Director was studying him intently. Harrison tried to appear cooperative. "Why did you come to Fendria?" the Director asked.

"My assignment required it," Harrison said.

The Director nodded. "Your assignment is to crash aircraft," he said. "This is wasteful, but the device indicates truth. Very well; we will learn more about your assignment. Was the crash deliberate?"

Harrison maintained a neutral expression. "Yes," he said.

The Director's eyes narrowed slightly. "Very well," he said. "Was your assignment completed when the aircraft crashed?"

"No," Harrison said.

"What additional objectives does your assignment include?" the Director asked.

Harrison decided to introduce his first complication. "Remaining alive."

The Director's face flushed with agitation, the pigmentation intensifying to a shade that reminded Harrison of photographs he'd seen of the deep sea—that particular color water took on far below the surface, where sunlight barely penetrated. "Do not waste time with self-evident facts!" he said sharply. "Do not attempt to deceive us; we are a logical and scientific people! Answer appropriately."

"I have stated the truth," Harrison said.

"But it is not—not the truth we seek," the Director said.

Harrison shrugged. "I responded to your question," he said. "I was unaware that truth had multiple categories. Surely truth is truth, just as the Director is the Director?"

"I—" The Director stopped himself. "You attempt to confuse the Director," he said finally, his voice controlled again, his complexion gradually returning to its normal shade. "But the Director will not be confused. We have specialists in logical analysis who will advise the Director. They will be summoned."

Harrison's escorts had been standing idle now that their prisoner was restrained in the polygraph. The Director gestured and they exited quickly.

The Director looked down at Harrison. "You will discover that you cannot deceive us," he said. "You will discover that such primitive attempts will achieve nothing."

Harrison sincerely hoped so.

---

The logic specialists arrived within minutes, and Harrison was firmly informed that logical paradoxes would not confuse anyone in Fendria. Russell's paradox, the liar's paradox, Zeno's paradoxes, and all the other classic logical puzzles were elementary material for the Fendrians. "They can be resolved through formal logic systems," one specialist, a slight being named Jordan West, told Harrison coolly. West's skin matched the others precisely—that same distinctive color that Harrison had noted throughout the population. "Naturally, you would not comprehend the formal systems. But that is irrelevant. You need only understand that we cannot be confused by such methods."

"Excellent," Harrison said.

The specialist blinked. "Excellent?" he said.

"Naturally," Harrison said pleasantly.

The specialist's expression hardened, his jaw tightening, his complexion shifting to a deeper, more intense shade of its base color—like bruised sky, Harrison thought, or twilight reflected on still water. "Your strategy has failed," the specialist said, "yet you call this excellent. You can only mean that your strategy differs from what we have assumed."

"Correct," Harrison said.

There was a brief silence. The specialist's expression shifted to something like satisfaction, his skin gradually lightening again. He examined the polygraph displays carefully. "What is your strategy?" he asked quietly.

"To answer your questions truthfully and logically," Harrison said.

The silence lasted longer this time.

"The device indicates truth," the specialist said finally, his tone suggesting awe. "Therefore, you must be betraying your own nation. You must want us to dominate your region, and have come here secretly to assist us."

Harrison was grateful that wasn't a question. It was, after all, the only logical conclusion.

But it happened to be wrong.

---

"Your nation is called the Bristol Region?" the Director asked. Several minutes had passed; the specialists were clustered around the desk, their identical coloring creating an almost uniform visual effect—like a row of identical figures, distinguished only by height and build. Harrison remained strapped to the polygraph; a logical society might use a traitor, but a logical society does not trust him.

"Sometimes," Harrison said.

"It has other names?" the Director asked.

"It has no name," Harrison said truthfully. The Fendrian idiom was similar to English; certainly a nation had no name of its own. People assigned names to it, that was all. It possessed none inherently.

"Yet you call it the Bristol Region?" the Director said.

"I do," Harrison said, "for convenience in communication."

"Do you know its precise geographical coordinates?" the Director asked.

"Not with exactitude," Harrison said.

There was a stir among the specialists. "But you can locate it again," the Director said.

"I can," Harrison said.

"And you will provide us with information about it?" the Director continued.

"I will," Harrison said, "to the extent of my knowledge."

"We will require information about defensive capabilities," the Director said, "and about strategic planning and fortifications. But we must first understand the decision-making structure in your region. Is your nation affiliated with others in a governmental alliance, or does it exist independently?"

Harrison almost smiled. "Both," he said.

A brief silence was broken by one of the specialists. "We have theorized that a subordinate entity may be permitted to make certain decisions independently, with only major decisions reserved for the central authority. This seems inefficient and error-prone, yet it is a possible system. Is this what you mean?"

Very astute, Harrison thought. "It is," he said.

"Then the government that controls multiple nations is supreme," the Director said.

"It is," Harrison said.

"Who exercises this control?" the Director asked.

The crucial question had finally been asked. Harrison was grateful that the logical Fendrians had chosen to begin systematically, rather than jumping to questions about military capabilities first; it saved considerable time.

"The answer to that question," Harrison said, "cannot be provided to you."

"Every factual question has an answer," the Director said sharply. "No paradox is involved here; a government exists, and some entity governs. Perhaps multiple entities share this function; perhaps automated systems perform the work. But where there is government, there is a governor. Is this not so?"

"Certainly," Harrison said. "It is completely obvious and accurate."

"The nation from which you come is part of an alliance of nations that are governed, you have stated," the Director continued.

"Correct," Harrison said.

"Then there is a governor for this alliance," the Director said.

"Correct," Harrison said again.

The Director exhaled slowly. "Describe this governor to us," he said.

Harrison shrugged. "The description cannot be provided to you."

The Director turned to his specialists and a brief whispered consultation occurred. When it ended, the Director returned his attention to Harrison. "Is the limitation in you?" he asked. "Are you somehow unable to describe this government?"

"It can be described," Harrison said.

"Then you will suffer negative consequences if you describe it to us?" the Director continued.

"I will not," Harrison said.

This prompted another consultation. With some satisfaction, Harrison noticed that the Fendrians were becoming visibly uncertain; their skin tones were fluctuating subtly, shifting between lighter and deeper variations of that characteristic color as emotions waxed and waned.

The plan was working.

The Director had finished conferring. "You are attempting again to confuse us," he said.

Harrison shook his head earnestly. "I am attempting," he said, "not to confuse you."

"Then I demand an answer," the Director said.

"I request that I be permitted to ask a question," Harrison said.

The Director hesitated, then nodded once. "Ask it," he said. "We will answer if we determine it appropriate."

Harrison tried to look grateful. "Very well," he said. "What is your system of government?"

The Director gestured to a heavy-set being, who stepped forward from the group of Fendrians, inclined his head toward Harrison, and began speaking in a surprisingly melodious voice. "Our government is the only logical form of government," he said. "The Director commands all, and citizens obey. Through this method, uniformity is achieved, and this uniformity enables rapid action and concentrated force. All Fendrians act simultaneously in the same manner. The Director is selected by the previous Director; through this method we ensure consistent wisdom and stable judgment."

"You have heard our government described," the Director said. "Now, you will describe yours to us."

Harrison shook his head. "If you insist," he said, "I'll attempt it. But you will not understand it."

The Director's expression hardened. "We will understand," he said. "Begin. Who governs you?"

"No one," Harrison said.

"But you are governed?"

Harrison nodded. "Yes."

"Then there is a governor," the Director insisted.

"Correct," Harrison said. "But everyone is the governor."

"Then there is no government," the Director said. "There is no unified decision-making."

"No," Harrison said calmly, "there are many decisions binding on all citizens."

"Who makes them binding?" the Director asked. "Who compels you to accept these decisions? Some of them must be unfavorable to some individuals?"

"Many of them are unfavorable," Harrison said. "But we are not compelled to accept them."

"Do you act against your own interests?"

Harrison shrugged. "Not knowingly," he said. The Director glanced sharply at the technicians monitoring the polygraph. Harrison turned to observe their expressions—their faces all bore that same distinctive hue, unchanged by emotional response as they focused on their instruments. They needed no words; the polygraph was clearly indicating that he was telling the truth. But the truth wasn't making any sense. "I warned you that you wouldn't understand it," he said.

"It is a flaw in your description," the Director said, his voice strained, his complexion darkening to what Harrison now recognized as the Fendrian indicator of extreme frustration.

"My description is as precise as possible," Harrison said.

The Director breathed heavily. "Let us try a different approach," he said. "Everyone is the governor. Do you share a collective consciousness? A hive mind has been theorized, though we have encountered no examples—"

"Neither have we," Harrison said. "We are all individuals, like yourselves."

"But with no single director to formulate policy, to make decisions—"

"We have no need of one," Harrison said calmly.

"Ah," the Director said suddenly, as if seeing clarity ahead. "And why not?"

"We call our form of government 'democracy,'" Harrison said. "It means government by the people. There is no need for another director."

One of the specialists spoke up suddenly. "The individuals themselves govern each other?" he said. "This is clearly impossible; no single individual can possess the force to compel acceptance of commands. Without this force, there can be no effective government."

"That is our form of government," Harrison said.

"You are lying," the specialist said.

One of the technicians interjected: "The device indicates—"

"Then the device is malfunctioning," the specialist said. "It will be recalibrated."

Harrison wondered, as the technicians began arguing, how long they'd spend examining the polygraph before they realized it had no malfunction to correct. He hoped it wouldn't take too long; he could foresee another period of tedious boredom ahead. And besides, he was getting homesick for the Bristol Region.

---

It took five days—but boredom never really materialized. Harrison found himself receiving more attention than he'd anticipated; one by one, the specialists visited his cell, each with a different approach to resolving the apparent contradictions in his statements. Under the facility's green lighting, they all looked somewhat different than they had in the Director's office—the chromatic distortion making their features seem almost alien, their skin taking on an unusual cast that made Harrison's initial observations seem questionable.

Some left angry. Others simply left, bewildered.

On the fifth day, Harrison escaped.

It wasn't particularly difficult; he hadn't expected it to be. Even the most logical of thinking beings possesses a subconscious mind as well as a conscious one, and one method of dealing with an insoluble problem is to make the problem vanish. There were only two ways to accomplish that, and eliminating the problem's focal point was somewhat more complicated. That couldn't be done by the subconscious mind alone; the conscious mind had to participate. And it couldn't.

Because that would require recognizing, fully and consciously, that the problem was genuinely insoluble. And the Fendrians weren't capable of that kind of thinking.

Harrison was grateful that their genius had been confined to the physical and computational sciences. Any insight into psychology would have given them the key to his existence and his entire strategy within seconds.

But then, it was precisely that lack of insight that had necessitated this particular mission. That, and the authoritarian political structure of Fendria.

The same lack of insight allowed the Fendrian subconscious to work on his escape without any troublesome interference from deep reflection. Someone left a door unlocked and a weapon accessible—all quite unintentional, Harrison was certain. Reaching his aircraft was slightly more complicated, but presented no fundamental obstacles; he was airborne, and then beyond Fendrian airspace, within a few hours of leaving the cell.

He set his course, relaxed, and cleared his mind. He had no telepathic abilities, but the specialists at Coalition Intelligence did; he couldn't receive messages, but he could send them. He sent one now.

*Mission accomplished; the Fendrians won't be expanding their authoritarian model into neighboring regions anytime soon. They've been given a conceptual puzzle—a beautifully indigestible puzzle that will occupy them until they finally manage to comprehend it. But they can't comprehend it and remain what they are; you need to embrace democratic principles, to some degree, to understand the concept. What makes us obey laws we ourselves create? What makes us obey laws that disadvantage us personally? Enlightened self-interest, naturally—but try to make a Fendrian grasp it!*

*With one director and one standardized language, they simply weren't equipped for this kind of translation. They were too successful with physical sciences to pursue psychology or political science seriously. No social sciences, no insight into my mind or their own—and that means no translation.*

*But—damn it—I wish I were home already. I'm absolutely bored out of my mind!*

---

Back in Lincoln, Nordavia, at Coalition Intelligence headquarters, Director Giovanni Potter received Harrison's mental transmission and smiled. The Fendrian problem had been neutralized, at least for the foreseeable future. They'd spend years, perhaps decades, trying to understand how a government could function without a single director, how laws could be binding without a single enforcer, how order could emerge from apparent chaos.

And by the time they figured it out—if they ever did—they'd no longer be the threat they currently posed. Understanding democracy required experiencing it, and experiencing it would change them fundamentally.

Potter drafted a brief report for the Coalition Council, noting the successful completion of the mission. Patrick Harrison, specialist in strategic planning and international diplomacy, had once again proven himself invaluable.

The report concluded: "The Paradox Protocol remains our most effective non-violent method for neutralizing authoritarian expansionist threats. Recommend continued deployment in similar situations."

Potter signed the report and filed it securely. Then he sent a message to Harrison: *Welcome home when you arrive. Well done.*

Harrison, still hours away from home, received the message as a vague sense of approval and warmth. It wasn't much, but it helped with the boredom.

He wondered what his next assignment would be. Probably something in Rosewood, Nordavia, where a new separatist movement was gaining strength. Or perhaps Cliffside again, if the Fendrians recovered faster than expected.

Either way, he'd be ready. That was his job, after all—to preserve the democratic way of life, one paradox at a time.
