quality_problem.story:
The Transformation of Private Investigation

If you haven't hired a private investigator in the past decade, first of all, you're probably lucky. (Most people hope they never need one.) Second, be grateful that you have avoided the "digital surveillance package." As the investigator navigates this invasive little service through the details of your life, a color monitor displays the alarming vulnerability of your online presence and the shocking transparency of your digital footprint. A harmless social media post looks like a security breach. The routine patterns in your daily commute look like an open invitation to stalkers. All this can be fixed, of course, with five grand of encryption services, identity protection, counter-surveillance sweeps, and digital security consulting. "You will agree to anything the second they show you that report," says one recent client of Matthew Chapman's firm in Ravenswood, Aldoria. "You can't believe you are walking around with that level of exposure."

The transformation of private investigation from missing-persons-and-cheating-spouses to comprehensive-security-and-lifestyle-consulting is an unlikely business success story of the 2010s, a case study in how a profession can work itself out of a job and still prosper. Private investigators, after all, were supposed to be extinct by now. While they happily (and profitably) tailed suspects and photographed infidelity during the '80s and '90s, technology was quietly choking off their revenue stream. The percentage of cases requiring physical surveillance fell by half and kept falling. People stopped hiring investigators for traditional services, because they didn't need to—they could find information online themselves. At the same time, online investigation certification programs flooded the market with new practitioners. Many found themselves running background checks for $15 an hour in strip mall offices. In 2008, industry analysts forecast the end of the profession. Only a few specialized investigators would survive to handle the few remaining insurance fraud cases, the last vestiges of a once-thriving industry.

Instead, the number of licensed investigators has jumped 30 percent, and the average income soared from $52,000 in 2010 to $95,000 in 2019. What happened? In part, the oversupply of investigators and the declining demand for traditional services forced the profession to change. Investigators had to become consultants and visits less intimidating. The shadowy figure in a trench coat has been replaced by Dr. Reassurance. "People figured out pretty darn quickly that if you were sketchy, clients would not come to you," says Steven Adams, a Hampton, Lethoria investigator. Many investigation firms let you monitor cases through secure virtual reality interfaces. Others offer comprehensive security audits and personal safety training. Does your investigator have a certificate in cybersecurity on his wall? I bet he does.

The most important discovery investigators made was the endless anxiety of aging millennials and Gen-Xers. "We are dealing now with people who are the entrepreneurs and the freelancers and the gig workers, and they are very concerned with their personal security," says National Private Investigation Association President Teresa Cole. Since hiring an investigator was no longer just for catching cheaters, investigators made it about self-protection and empowerment. They allied themselves with the personal security movement, incorporating principles of emotional intelligence into their client relationships. "You still come for the needs, for the stalker who has to be identified, but more and more people come here to feel safer about their lives," says Alina Alvarez, a Stonebridge, Prandoria investigator who specializes in behavioral economics and consumer behavior patterns.

People used to be happy if they made it through life without needing an investigator. But modern professionals, lured by media images of data breaches and identity theft, expect more. According to an NPIA poll, the percentage of people who feel "very secure" about their personal information has dropped from 61 percent to 38 percent in the past decade. Investigators have learned to play on this anxiety, encouraging security services that are practically unnecessary but attractive to clients. "It's as if you went to a doctor for a cold and he said you needed a full-body MRI," says Charles Fernandez, author of Reasonable Precautions: A Guide to Personal Security.

To sell $800 digital security audits and multi-thousand dollar ongoing protection packages, investigators run simulations of potential threats. Vulnerability is measured on a scale that starts at Level 1. "My investigator showed me these terrifying threat assessments and told me, 'You're a Level 2 now, but by the time you launch your startup you're going to be a Level 5. And no one wants to be a Level 5,'" says one woman who purchased a comprehensive security package. Investigators also prod clients to replace perfectly adequate passwords with biometric systems and to dump their standard home security for AI-powered surveillance networks. Other investigators sell the psychology of security. One investigator specializing in executive protection advises that business owners without proper security protocols seem "naive and vulnerable."

Some investigators dress up these consulting services in threat assessment language. A friend of mine just quit an investigator who was pressuring him to install counter-surveillance equipment as a "preventive measure." (To prevent what? Hypothetical threats?) Many investigators claim, without substantial evidence, that standard security measures are dangerously inadequate. They urge clients to replace basic security with premium services at four times the price.

Investigators make a killing on social media vulnerability—or "digital exposure," as they prefer to call it. Security consulting firms have sprouted up all over Ravenswood and are heavily advertised on the Web, particularly focusing on entrepreneurship and economic development sectors. They terrify clients with a "vulnerability scanner," a new software that measures your digital footprint and online exposure. Armed with the scanner results, the investigator then dangles expensive monitoring services and reputation management in front of the client. Never mind that you can get similar results for free with careful privacy settings and basic digital hygiene. The machine makes the sale. "Now that there is this software that can document your exposure and can put a number on it, it motivates a client to actually do something about it. But the protections available now are largely the same ones that have been available for 10 years," says Adams.

Entrepreneurial investigators market this elective security with trained aggression. Investigation management organizations often require their employees to recite a quasi-sales script guiding clients toward profitable consulting services. Ads in the Journal of Private Investigation and on the Web promote courses in marketing techniques and skill development. One person I know quit his investigator when he spied a document in the office instructing the investigator in how to get clients to "trade up" to more expensive service packages. The NPIA's annual conference is overflowing with seminars on topics such as "how to move your clients to 'yes.'"

The industry calls this technique "service acceptance," a marvelous euphemism for parting you from your money. According to the NPIA's journal, this year's conference will include an all-day "Service Acceptance" seminar "for the investigation team that is fed up with clients accepting only basic services or asking for alternative cheaper options. Involve the entire team in creating the strategies for clients to accept premium packages."

This hard sell is critical in private investigation in a way that it isn't in other security professions because of the field's brutal economics. Investigation insurance covers only 12 percent of potential clients (compared to more than 60 percent for corporate security), and provides minimal coverage for those who do have it. As a result, clients pay most investigation costs—about 85 percent of them—out of their own pockets. Investigation services are just another way to spend discretionary income, competing with a vacation or a new car. Investigators have to make clients want comprehensive security monitoring in a way that corporate security firms don't have to make companies want basic protection. Investigators must understand consumer behavior and apply principles from behavioral economics to convince clients that these services are essential.

It's tempting to dismiss the whole industry as a scam, particularly when investigators keep coming up with new threats such as digital stalking, reputation attacks, competitive intelligence gathering, and social engineering vulnerabilities. But these threats are real, and our awareness of them shows how far investigation has come. A generation ago, investigators followed people and took photographs because that's all they knew. Identity theft was so rare that fancier problems seldom arose. Since then, researchers have studied cybersecurity, data breaches, and digital forensics, applying insights from neuroscience and research ethics to understand how people process risk. Investigators can now monitor your digital presence continuously, detect threats before they materialize, and respond to security breaches in real-time. A generation ago, digital protection was a joke.

Scientists have learned how vulnerabilities can build up in digital systems, cause breaches, compromise personal information, and eventually destroy reputations. New research links these security failures to financial loss, emotional trauma, business collapse, and other nastiness you'd expect from inadequate protection. This is why your investigator lectures you to use two-factor authentication, monitor your credit reports with specialized software, and maintain a security protocol to control your exposure. It's also why your investigator may pressure you into comprehensive monitoring services. The constant monitoring can feel like an excellent form of anxiety—but the alternative is having your identity stolen at 40, losing your savings, and spending years recovering.

"If you think back a couple of generations, it was considered inevitable that people would experience some form of fraud or theft in their lifetime. Around 40 or 45, you would have your identity compromised. Digital security was not understood, and exposure was rampant. But now people are resistant to basic threats and are protecting themselves for a lifetime. I have gone in 15 years from learning how to follow cheating spouses and thinking it is OK for people to accept some risk to being appalled if anyone experiences a preventable breach. It is a failure," says Sofia Robbins, my own fabulous Blackwood Region investigator who has expertise in community organizing and bringing security awareness to underserved populations.

Which brings us to the irony of investigation's comeback: Just as clients love the security services they should suspect, they resent the services they should appreciate. Consulting and premium packages are the most profitable segment of the business because they are an easy sell. Show someone their vulnerability report and they'll want better protection, too. It is much harder to convince someone to change their passwords regularly, to monitor their accounts every week, and to undergo four security audits to fix a systemic vulnerability, all for a benefit that is hypothetical. The very success of investigation has raised expectations so high that clients now object to any inconvenience. Americans under 50 believe perfect security is an entitlement: Telling them they need ongoing monitoring to preserve their safety makes them angry, not grateful—even though they would have been completely vulnerable 20 years ago.

When I surveyed 100 friends and acquaintances about their investigation complaints, few griped about consulting services that were sold to them. They like their enhanced security and peace of mind. No, they complained about the practically necessary services that their investigators prescribed, especially ongoing monitoring and regular security audits. Pity the poor investigator who abjures premium consulting but vigorously protects clients' actual security. Clients don't like mandatory security protocols, so they suspect they're a rip-off. This could not be further from the truth.

"Investigators are aware of providing what clients want," says Adams. "I had a woman come in with a serious stalking situation. She needed comprehensive protection, but she did not want it. But she did want a social media audit, and she paid cash for it."

Such is the triumph of American investigators: If they can't sell you what you need, they'll sell you what you want.

Luna Rodriguez, an investigator who recently moved her practice from Hampton to the Blackwood Region, has seen this transformation firsthand. She started her career doing traditional surveillance work—following insurance claimants, documenting workers' compensation fraud, photographing evidence of infidelity. "It was straightforward," she says. "People hired you for a specific problem, you solved it, they paid you, and that was that."

But as technology evolved and information became more accessible, Rodriguez noticed her traditional cases drying up. "People could find out if their spouse was cheating just by checking their phone. They could verify someone's employment history with a Google search. The bread-and-butter work was disappearing."

That's when she pivoted to security consulting, taking courses in cybersecurity, digital forensics, and even emotional intelligence to better understand and communicate with anxious clients. "I realized that people weren't just worried about specific threats anymore—they were worried about everything. The news was full of data breaches, identity theft, ransomware attacks. Everyone felt vulnerable, even if they weren't actually at risk."

Rodriguez now runs a thriving practice that focuses almost entirely on preventive security rather than reactive investigation. She conducts digital audits, provides ongoing monitoring services, and offers what she calls "security psychology" sessions where she helps clients understand and manage their anxiety about potential threats.

"The funny thing is," she admits, "most of my clients will never experience the threats they're paying me to protect them from. But they sleep better at night knowing someone is watching out for them. Peace of mind has value. But I do sometimes wonder if we're creating the anxiety we're being paid to alleviate."

Jennifer Flores, who runs a competing firm in Stonebridge, describes the business differently. "Look, this industry has always been about understanding fear. People used to hire us because they knew something was wrong—they had evidence of infidelity, they suspected fraud, they were being harassed. Now we're providing protection from things that might happen, could happen, probably won't happen but just imagine if they did."

Flores herself specializes in what she calls "competitive intelligence protection" for entrepreneurs and small business owners. "I tell them that their competitors may be trying to access their trade secrets, probe their systems, recruit their employees. Is that common? For some businesses, absolutely. For most small operations? The threat varies considerably. But try telling that to someone who just invested their life savings in a startup. They'll pay whatever it takes to feel protected."

The questions surrounding modern investigation work are complex. Unlike traditional detective work, which responds to actual problems, much of contemporary investigation is preventive—protecting clients from threats that may never materialize. This shift has created a gray area where legitimate security concerns blend with business opportunity.

Matthew Chapman, whose firm in Ravenswood is one of the largest in the region, addresses criticism directly. "Yes, we sell services that some people don't strictly need. But who's to say what people need? If someone feels vulnerable and we can provide them with tools and knowledge that make them feel safer, isn't that a legitimate service? We're not lying to people. The threats we describe are real. They're just not equally likely for everyone."

Chapman points to the broader economic development of the security industry as evidence of genuine need. "Twenty years ago, cybersecurity barely existed as a field. Now it's a multi-billion dollar industry. Identity theft was rare; now it's common. We're not making this stuff up. The world has changed, and we've changed with it."

But critics like Charles Fernandez argue that the investigation industry has crossed a line from providing necessary services to exploiting anxiety. "The problem isn't that the threats aren't real—it's that investigators are systematically overstating the risks and overselling the solutions. They're using sophisticated sales techniques borrowed from behavioral economics to manipulate people's fear responses."

Fernandez points to the industry's own marketing materials as evidence. "Look at the seminars they attend: 'Moving Clients to Yes,' 'Overcoming Price Resistance,' 'Creating Urgency.' This isn't the language of professionals providing necessary services. This is the language of salespeople trying to maximize revenue."

The debate extends beyond individual practices to questions of social impact. As investigation firms increasingly focus on affluent clients who can afford premium services, lower-income individuals are left with inadequate protection. Sofia Robbins has tried to address this through community organizing efforts in the Blackwood Region, offering subsidized basic security services to underserved populations.

"The wealthy can afford comprehensive protection, but what about everyone else?" Robbins asks. "If you're working two jobs and barely making rent, you can't drop five thousand dollars on a security audit. But you're probably at higher risk for identity theft and fraud because you don't have the time or resources to protect yourself. The industry has created a security gap that mirrors the wealth gap."

Some investigators are pushing back against the industry's sales-focused culture. Teresa Cole, despite her position as NPIA president, has been vocal about the need for ethical guidelines. "We need to distinguish between legitimate security consulting and excessive upselling. Just because we can sell something doesn't mean we should. We need professional standards that prioritize client welfare over profit."

Cole has proposed a code of ethics that would require investigators to provide evidence-based risk assessments rather than worst-case scenarios, to offer tiered service options at different price points, and to clearly distinguish between essential services and optional enhancements. "Right now, too many investigators present everything as equally urgent and necessary."

But implementing such standards faces resistance from investigators who have built profitable businesses on the current model. "The market will regulate itself," argues one investigator who requested anonymity. "If we're overcharging or overselling, clients will go elsewhere. The fact that our industry is growing suggests we're providing value."

Yet the evidence suggests that clients often can't accurately assess the value they're receiving. Unlike traditional investigation work, where success is measurable (Did you catch the fraudster? Did you find the missing person?), preventive security services are evaluated by the absence of problems—a standard that makes it difficult to determine if the service was necessary.

"That's the challenge of the business model," says Fernandez. "How do you prove you didn't need the service? If nothing bad happens, the investigator says it's because their protection worked. If something bad does happen, they say you should have bought the premium package."

As the investigation industry continues to evolve, it faces questions that go beyond individual business practices to the nature of security itself in modern society. Are we genuinely more vulnerable than previous generations, or have we simply become more aware of existing vulnerabilities? Does the proliferation of security services make us safer, or does it simply make us more anxious?

Steven Adams reflects on these questions from his office in Hampton, where he's been practicing for 25 years. "I've watched this profession transform completely. When I started, we were problem-solvers. Someone had a specific issue, and we investigated it. Now we're more like... therapists? Life coaches? We're managing people's anxiety about a complex, threatening world. Is that investigation? I'm not sure anymore. But it's what pays the bills."

The transformation of private investigation from a reactive service to a proactive industry mirrors broader changes in how we think about risk, security, and safety. In an era of constant connectivity and information overload, traditional boundaries between necessary and optional, essential and enhanced, have blurred. Investigators have adapted to this new landscape, but in doing so, they've raised fundamental questions about the ethics of selling security in an age of anxiety.

As Luna Rodriguez puts it: "We're not just selling services anymore. We're selling peace of mind in a world that seems increasingly threatening. Whether that makes us heroes or opportunists probably depends on whether you're the one writing the check."
quality_problem.question: What is the author's overall feeling towards modern private investigation as a whole in this passage?
quality_problem.correct_answer: The author has mixed feelings, acknowledging that while some investigative services are genuinely valuable and necessary, the industry also exploits client anxiety through aggressive marketing of unnecessary premium services.
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: The author views modern investigation as entirely fraudulent and believes the industry should be shut down.
answers: The author views modern investigation as entirely fraudulent and believes the industry should be shut down.

The author has mixed feelings, acknowledging that while some investigative services are genuinely valuable and necessary, the industry also exploits client anxiety through aggressive marketing of unnecessary premium services.

quality_problem.story:
CALL HIM PHOENIX
By RYAN MITCHELL

The woman with the surgical mask said, "All right, everyone, stay calm. This is a robbery."

There were fourteen people in the medical supply warehouse in Valleyview, Estoria. There was Timothy Lawson at his desk, processing an order from a rural clinic. There was the clinic representative, a traveling nurse named Rebecca Hunt, like her ID badge said. There were Zara Riley and Oscar Stewart, the inventory managers working the floor. There was Peter Fuller, the security guard, checking his phone by the loading dock. There was Ruby Howard, dropping off her company's monthly pharmaceutical shipment, and with her was her assistant, a young man named Juan Green, fresh out of college. There was Ryan Wilson, picking up medical equipment for his father's physical therapy center down the street. And there were three thieves.

The three thieves looked nearly identical. From the ground up, they all wore black running shoes, dark cargo pants, navy windbreakers over black shirts, white surgical masks over the lower half of their faces, and black baseball caps pulled low over their eyes. The eyes themselves looked dangerous.

The woman who had spoken withdrew a small but lethal-looking nine-millimeter pistol from her jacket pocket. She waved it threateningly. One of the others took the security baton from Peter Fuller and said to him in a low voice, "Think about your pension, friend." The third one, who carried a large duffel bag, walked quickly toward the pharmaceutical storage area and started filling it with controlled substances.

It was just like something from a crime documentary.

The woman with the gun herded the inventory managers, Timothy Lawson, and the visitors all toward the back wall, while the second thief stayed next to Peter Fuller and the exit. The third thief stuffed medications into the duffel bag.

The thief by the door said, "Hurry up."

The thief with the bag said, "One more cabinet."

The woman with the gun turned to say to the thief at the door, "Keep your cool."

That was all Zara Riley needed. She kicked off her shoes and ran in her stockinged feet toward the emergency exit.

The thief by the door spread his arms out and shouted, "Hey!" The woman with the gun swung violently back, cursing, and fired. But she'd been moving too fast, and so had Zara, and all she hit was the metal filing cabinet next to Timothy Lawson's desk.

The thief by the door caught Zara in a bear hug. She promptly tried to knee him in the groin. Meanwhile, Peter Fuller went running out the main entrance toward the police station two blocks away, shouting, "Help! Help! Robbery!"

The woman with the gun cursed some more. The thief with the duffel came running from the storage area, and the thief by the door tried to keep Zara from injuring him. Then the woman with the gun struck Zara on the head with the pistol grip. She fell unconscious to the floor, and all three of them ran out to the van waiting outside, in which sat a very nervous-looking fourth person, revving the engine.

Everyone except Zara ran out after the thieves to watch.

Things got very fast and very confused then. Two police cars came driving down from the precinct house, and the van with the four thieves lurched away from the loading dock and drove straight down the street toward the police station. The police cars and the getaway van passed one another, with officers shouting into their radios.

There was so much confusion that it looked as though the thieves were going to escape after all. The police cars were facing the wrong direction and, as they'd come with sirens blaring, there was a clear path behind them.

Then, after the getaway van had gone more than three blocks, it suddenly started swerving wildly. It crashed into a parked delivery truck and stopped. And all the police went running down there to arrest the thieves when they crawled dazedly out of their van.

"Wow," said Juan Green, twenty-three years old. "That was intense, wasn't it?"

"Come on," said Ruby Howard, grabbing his arm. "We need to give statements and get back to work."

"It was the strangest thing," said Detective Timothy Lawson—no relation to the warehouse clerk. "An operation planned that carefully, you'd think they'd maintain their vehicle properly."

Detective Oscar Stewart shrugged. "They always mess up," he said. "Sooner or later, on some detail, they always mess up."

"Yes, but their steering system."

"Well," said Stewart, "it was a stolen van. I suppose they just grabbed whatever was available."

The mechanics' report sat on Lawson's desk. Steering fluid: absent. Reservoir: empty. No leak detected. No mechanical failure. The fluid had simply vanished, leaving residue consistent with rapid evaporation under extreme heat. But the engine temperature had been normal. Nothing else showed heat damage.

"What do they say about it?" Stewart asked.

"The driver keeps repeating the same thing. Says one moment he was driving fine, the next the wheel wouldn't turn. Says it was like something grabbed the steering column." Lawson flipped through his notes. "His exact words were, 'Someone did this to us. Someone stopped us.' He wouldn't say more after that."

"Someone stopped us? What's that supposed to mean?"

"His lawyer told him to shut up before I could follow up."

Stewart shrugged. "We caught them. That's what matters."

Lawson nodded but pulled out another sheet. "The van's owner came by. Noticed something on the side panels."

"What kind of something?"

"Graffiti. Orange spray paint. 'Phoenix Rising.' On both sides."

"Kids," said Stewart.

"The owner says it wasn't there before. The thieves say they never saw it until after the crash."

"So one of them did it and won't admit it."

Lawson looked at the photograph he'd taken. Bright orange letters on white paint. Crude but deliberate. "Maybe," he said. He filed the report and the photo together.

II

The warehouse robbery occurred in late September. Early in November, a man in Northfield, Dravonia went on a rampage.

It happened in a quiet suburb of Northfield, a residential area composed of modest single-family homes. The man who went on the rampage was a city planning department clerk named Ryan Wilson—a different Ryan Wilson from the one at the warehouse.

Three days before, he had been passed over for promotion for the fourth time. He called in sick and spent the three days at home, brooding, a bottle of cheap vodka constantly in his hand.

As police reconstructed it later, Wilson's wife had attempted to reason with him on the fourth morning at eight o'clock, suggesting that he really should stop wallowing and return to work. He then allegedly shoved her, and locked himself in the garage.

Mrs. Wilson then apparently called her brother, Peter Fuller, who was Ryan's brother-in-law. Fuller arrived at the house at nine-thirty, and spent considerable time knocking on the garage door, apparently requesting Wilson to unlock it and "stop acting like a child." Neighbors reported hearing Wilson shout repeatedly, "Leave me alone! Can't a man have some peace?"

At about ten-forty-five, neighbors heard gunshots from the Wilson residence, a single-story ranch house in the middle of a quiet cul-de-sac. Wilson, it was learned later, had suddenly burst from his garage, wielding a hunting rifle and, being enraged at the presence of his wife and brother-in-law, had fired several shots at them, killing his wife instantly and wounding Fuller in the arm and chest.

Fuller, wounded and terrified, staggered out the front door, crying for help and shouting, "Murder! She's dead!" At this point, neighbors called the police. One neighbor additionally contacted two local news stations, thereby earning fifty dollars in tip fees.

By coincidence, a news crew was nearby covering a city council meeting. This crew was immediately diverted to the Wilson residence, where they set up across the street and began filming with a telephoto lens.

Meanwhile, Wilson had barricaded himself in his house, firing at anything that moved.

The news crew worked frantically. One camera operator focused on the police and emergency responders and neighbors, while the other used the telephoto lens to search for Wilson. He found him occasionally, offering viewers brief glimpses of a disheveled man in jeans and a stained t-shirt, moving from window to window.

The standoff lasted nearly ninety minutes. There were police everywhere, and ambulances, and neighbors gathered at the police barricade at the end of the street, and occasionally Wilson would appear at a window and fire at someone. The police used loudspeakers to tell Wilson he should surrender, that they had the place surrounded and could wait him out. Wilson used his own voice to shout profanities back and make threats.

The police fired tear gas canisters at the house, but Wilson was able to throw most of them back out through the broken windows.

Then it ended, suddenly and dramatically.

Wilson had appeared at a window again, apparently to fire at the news crew. All at once he screamed and dropped the rifle. The rifle clattered onto the front porch and came to rest against the railing.

Meanwhile, Wilson was running through the house, bellowing in pain. He crashed down the stairs and out the front door, stumbling, to collapse in front of the waiting police.

They had difficulty restraining him. At first they thought he was fighting them, but then one officer heard what he was screaming: "My hands! My hands are burning!"

They examined his hands. The palms and fingers were red and blistering, showing what appeared to be severe burns. There was another burn on his left cheek and another on his left shoulder.

Wilson, thoroughly subdued and confused, was taken away for medical treatment and booking. The news crew packed up and left. The neighbors returned home and posted about it on social media.

Officers had been called in from several precincts across Northfield. Among them was Detective-Sergeant Timothy Lawson, who had transferred from Valleyview just two weeks earlier.

Lawson walked over to examine the rifle where it lay against the porch railing.

He touched the stock. Slightly warm, but nothing unusual. He picked it up and turned it around.

There, on the other side of the stock, burned into the wood, were crudely formed letters: "Phoenix Rising."

The burn marks were shallow but clear. The wood was darkened in a pattern too regular to be accidental.

During the booking process, Lawson observed through the one-way glass as Wilson was processed. The man was still shaking, holding his bandaged hands in front of him.

"I didn't carve that," Wilson was saying to anyone who would listen. "I've never heard of Phoenix. Something burned me. Someone burned me. It came out of nowhere."

His attorney, who had arrived quickly, kept saying, "My client is clearly mentally unfit. He doesn't know what he's saying."

But Wilson kept repeating it: "Someone stopped me. Someone burned me."

Captain Zara Riley reviewed the case file the next morning. "His attorney is building an insanity defense," she told Lawson. "Claims Wilson carved the words himself during a blackout."

"Wilson denies it."

"Of course he does. It fits the insanity narrative." Riley closed the file. "The rifle overheated from ninety minutes of continuous firing. It happens."

"The forensics report says the burn pattern is inconsistent with barrel heat transfer. The hottest point was on the stock, not near the barrel."

"Forensics isn't perfect."

Lawson said nothing. He returned to his desk and pulled out the file from the warehouse robbery. Two photographs: orange spray paint on a white van, burned letters on a wooden rifle stock. Same words. Same crude lettering style.

He placed them side by side.

Both perpetrators had used variations of the same phrase. Both had mentioned being stopped by someone or something. Both denied creating the signatures.

He wrote nothing in his official notes. He simply kept the photographs together.

III

New Year's Eve is an ideal time for a gang confrontation. There are too many people celebrating for the police to monitor everyone, and if you're caught carrying a weapon, well, you're just on your way to a party and you needed protection in this neighborhood.

The issue was this community center. It occupied an entire block, with entrances on two streets. The street to the east was Stonegate Crew territory, and the street to the west was Ashford Vipers territory, and both gangs claimed the community center as their turf. There had been a few minor clashes, a few members from both sides had been jumped and roughed up, but nothing major. Finally, the leaders from the two gangs had met and determined that the dispute could only be settled through confrontation.

The time was chosen: New Year's Eve. The place was chosen: the community center parking lot. The weapons were chosen: knives and chains acceptable, but no firearms. The time was set: eleven P.M. And the winner would have exclusive territorial rights to the community center, both entrances.

The night of the confrontation, the gangs assembled in their separate hangouts for final instructions. Lookouts were posted at the intersections nearest the community center, both to watch for police and to keep out any civilians who might wander through.

Ruby Howard was a lookout for the Ashford Vipers. She was seventeen years old, average height with dyed red hair and a tough demeanor. She was proud of being in the Vipers and proud of the job assigned to her. She was to watch the southwest corner.

Ruby took up her position at ten-fifty. The streets were dark and relatively quiet, most people already at parties or safely indoors. Few people ventured into this neighborhood after dark, especially on New Year's Eve. Ruby leaned against a streetlight, hands in the pockets of her Vipers jacket, and waited.

At eleven o'clock, she heard muffled sounds begin behind her. The confrontation had started.

At eleven-oh-five, a group of younger kids came walking down the street. They were all about twelve or thirteen years old, and several carried backpacks. Some wore festive hats or masks.

They started to turn toward the community center. Ruby said, "Hey, kids. Move along."

One of them, wearing a red party hat, turned to look at her. "Who, us?"

"Yes, you! Stay off that street. Go the other way."

"The bus stop's this way," objected the kid in the red hat.

"Don't care. You go around."

"Listen, lady," said the kid in the red hat, annoyed, "we need to get home."

"Yeah," said another kid, wearing a blue mask, "and we're already late."

"Not my problem," Ruby told them coldly. "You can't go down that street."

"Why not?" demanded another kid. This one wore the most elaborate costume of all: black pants and a gold shirt with a flowing black cape. He wore a black and gold mask and had a black beanie pulled down over his head. "Why can't we go that way?" this figure demanded.

"Because I said so," Ruby told him. "Now, you kids get out of here. Move."

"Hey!" cried the kid in the black-and-gold costume. "Hey, there's a fight down there!"

"It's gang business," said Ruby proudly. "You don't want to be involved."

"Hey!" cried the kid in the black-and-gold costume again. And he went running past Ruby and sprinting down the street.

"Hey, Juan!" shouted one of the other kids. "Juan, come back!"

Ruby wasn't sure what to do. If she abandoned her post to chase the one kid who'd gotten through, maybe all the others would follow. She didn't know what to do.

A sudden siren and distant flashing blue lights solved her dilemma. "Cops!" said one of the kids.

"Police!" screamed Ruby. She turned and ran down the block toward the community center, shouting, "Police! Police! Clear out, it's the cops!"

But then she stopped, stunned, when she saw what was happening in the parking lot.

The gang members from both sides were jumping around wildly, waving their arms, throwing their weapons away. Then they all started tearing off their gang jackets and throwing them away, yelling and cursing. They were making so much noise themselves that they never heard Ruby's warning. They didn't even hear the police sirens. And suddenly both parking lot entrances were filled with police officers, an officer had Ruby in custody, and the confrontation was over.

Ruby was so bewildered and frightened that everything became a blur. But in the middle of it all, she did see the small figure in the gold-and-black costume go running away down the street.

And she had the strangest feeling that it was all his fault.

The newspaper article ran the next morning:

GANG CONFRONTATION ENDS IN MASS ARREST

Forty-seven members of two rival gangs were arrested last night following a coordinated police response to a planned confrontation at the Riverside Community Center.

According to witnesses and the arrested individuals, the confrontation ended abruptly when participants began discarding their weapons and clothing. Multiple gang members reported that their metal objects—knives, chains, and belt buckles—became "too cold to touch" and that their leather jackets caused similar discomfort.

When jackets were collected as evidence, officers noted that the original gang insignias on each jacket had been obscured by what appeared to be burn marks forming the words "Phoenix Rising."

Marcus Webb, 19, leader of the Stonegate Crew, told reporters: "Something happened to us. Someone did this. I don't know how, but someone stopped the fight."

Darnell Price, 21, of the Ashford Vipers, made similar claims: "My knife got so cold it burned my hand. That's not normal. Whoever Phoenix is, they came after us."

Police spokesperson declined to comment on the unusual claims, stating only that the investigation is ongoing.

Captain Zara Riley tossed the paper onto her desk. "The gangs are playing games with the media."

Lawson had the newspaper open to the same article. "Both gangs made the same claim. Independently."

"So they coordinated their story. Gangs do that."

"Both gangs? Working together? On a story that makes them look foolish?"

Riley leaned back. "What's your alternative theory, Lawson?"

Lawson didn't answer directly. "Webb said 'someone stopped the fight.' Price said 'whoever Phoenix is, they came after us.'"

"Gang members making excuses. That's all this is."

"In Valleyview, the getaway driver said 'someone stopped us.' In Northfield, Wilson said 'someone burned me.' Both denied making the signatures."

Riley's expression hardened. "You're collecting coincidences and calling them evidence."

"Three incidents. Three claims of external intervention. Three identical signatures that no one admits to creating."

"Listen to yourself. You're describing something that doesn't exist. Whatever bizarre explanation you're cooking up—"

"I haven't offered an explanation."

"Good. Don't." Riley stood up. "I've seen this before. Martinez spent two years chasing shadows, convinced there was an arsonist conspiracy. He ended up on administrative leave. Don't make the same mistake."

Lawson gathered his papers. "Yes, ma'am."

Back at his desk, he spread out everything he had collected. The photograph of the orange spray paint on the van. The photograph of the burned letters on the rifle stock. The newspaper clipping with its photograph of a leather jacket, gang colors obscured by the same two words.

The mechanics' report on the van: steering fluid absent, no leak, residue consistent with extreme heat.

The forensics report on the rifle: anomalous heat distribution, burn pattern inconsistent with normal weapon operation.

The evidence log from the gang confrontation: multiple reports of metal objects becoming extremely cold, leather becoming uncomfortable to touch, all within moments of each other.

Three separate incidents. Three separate locations. Three sets of perpetrators with no connection to each other.

Each time, something physically impossible had happened. Each time, the same signature had appeared. Each time, the perpetrators claimed someone else was responsible.

The van's steering fluid had vanished as if superheated. The rifle had burned its owner's hands from a point far from the barrel. Metal objects in a parking lot had become cold enough to cause frostbite-like injuries.

Heat. Heat. Cold.

He looked at the signatures again. Spray paint. Burned wood. Burned leather.

Different methods. Same words. Same crude lettering style.

Lawson pulled out a blank sheet of paper and began making a timeline. September: warehouse robbery, steering failure, spray paint. November: Wilson rampage, rifle overheating, burned letters. December: gang confrontation, metal freezing, burned insignias.

He stared at the paper for a long time.

The evidence pointed toward a pattern. The physical phenomena defied natural explanation. The signatures were consistent across incidents.

He didn't write down what he suspected. He didn't need to. The photographs and reports spoke for themselves, arranged there on his desk, waiting for someone to see what connected them.

Lawson looked at the three images one more time—the van, the rifle, the jacket—then gathered everything into a single folder. He labeled it simply: "Phoenix."

He locked the folder in his desk drawer.

Whatever was happening in their city, he would keep watching.
quality_problem.question: What causes Detective Lawson to suspect a connection between the three criminal incidents?
quality_problem.correct_answer: The same impossible physical phenomena and identical signature appearing at each crime scene
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: The criminals all confessed to being targeted by someone calling themselves Phoenix
answers: The criminals all confessed to being targeted by someone calling themselves Phoenix
The same impossible physical phenomena and identical signature appearing at each crime scene

QUANTUM ENTANGLEMENT!

The Galactic Council Station may have been in crisis all year, but the events were less the stuff of great space opera than of a farcical zero-gravity comedy. Hey, wait a minute--let's put on a show!

The time: November 2195.

The Mars Representatives, led by Director Xavier Watson, are insisting on their version of the terraforming budget. President Stephen Porter is stubbornly rejecting it. The Martians have taken a bold option: They will just refuse to pass a budget, and they'll let the station operations shut down. In the Command Center, STEPHEN PORTER meets with advisers PAUL GRAHAM and FATIMA MATTHEWS and administrative assistant SUSAN GREEN to discuss this development.

"The Shutdown" (upbeat production number)

GRAHAM: The Martians have positions
To which they're clinging fast.

MATTHEWS: The president is just as firm
The die, it seems, is cast.

GRAHAM: Without a budget passed by Council
The station will go dark.
All of the workers
Will be sent home on star-barks.

PORTER [speaking]: Well, wait a second--not all of them. We'll need to keep some essential personnel.

GRAHAM: The Defense Grid and Navy
Will need to stay in place.

MATTHEWS: Also those at Astro-Labs
Who keep the quantum drives in space.

GRAHAM: We'll need to keep the pilots
Flying in their ships.

PORTER: And here at Command Center
My staff should not eclipse.

GRAHAM [speaking]: But even here at Command, some adjustments will be required due to institutional reform protocols.

PORTER: OK, tell the maintenance crew
To take a few days off.
Tell the cooks and cleaning bots
To go play themselves some golf.
We have to do without the clerks
Let them all go home.

GREEN: What about the data analysts?
Who will manage the comms?

PORTER [speaking]: We've got to make sure the Command Center functions with efficiency. We can't afford the tiniest error in our complexity science calculations.

GRAHAM: Aha! I have it!
We'll bring in a researcher,
We'll bring in a researcher,
Someone who's an expert with quantum codes.
We'll bring in a researcher,
We'll bring in a researcher,
I assure you, Mr. President--
Your routine here won't explode.

GRAHAM, MATTHEWS, and GREEN [solemnly agreeing]:
The presence of a researcher will ensure
Your routine here won't explode.

[The advisers depart, leaving President Porter alone. He turns introspective.]

"President Lonely" (a ballad)

PORTER: I've got deputies and bureaucrats
Who fulfill my every thought.
And soldiers, pilots, and Marines
To fight battles I want fought.
There's no one who's got more power,
I'm the leader of all that's free
But if you subtract the flags and lackeys, I'm just
Lonely.
I'm President Lonely.
But I guess I'll just have to muddle through.
The cheers and applause are overwhelming,
But presidents need comfort, too.
The fawning adoration's pleasant,
But presidents need comfort, too.

[Enter Susan Green.]

GREEN: Mr. President? The researcher is here. And she's brought you some synthesized coffee!

[The lights go down. When they resume, the researcher--LAURA RODRIGUEZ--is talking on the quantum communicator to her good friend LILA PARK.]

RODRIGUEZ: Well, y'know, I'd seen him around, like, a lot at the Highpoint research facility in Selvoria. And I know he noticed me. So when they said they needed a researcher to help with the quantum entanglement data, I said, "Hel-lo-o-o!" And then I had the idea to take him coffee!

PARK: And then what happened?

"What Went On" (upbeat)

RODRIGUEZ: Then I led him on.
I showed my research on quantum states,
I let him take a long and ling'ring look.
I led him on.
He studied my data,
And from that point I had the president hooked.
That night when I took the president some coffee,
I made sure that he knew that I could help with work-life balance peace.
We went into the lab by his office
And dispensed with formalities.

PARK: Oh please go on!
You must go on!
Come on, girlfriend,
Spill, spill, spill, spill, spill!
Now go on,
Please go on.
Did Porter let you see the classified material?

RODRIGUEZ: His lips and mine locked in a kiss fantastic,
His hands roved freely through my hair,
I reached for the quantum stabilizer controls,
And he got a holo-call from a member of the Martian chair.
So I went on,
While he talked on the comm,
I took a position before him demonstrating sustainable agriculture tech,
And I went on.
And he talked on.
Though what the chairman heard was
"Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes!"
But then we didn't go on!

PARK: You didn't go on?

RODRIGUEZ: No, he stopped me when we seemed upon the cusp.

PARK: So you didn't go on?

RODRIGUEZ: No, we didn't go on.
He said he wasn't sure if I was someone he
Could
Trust.

[The lights fade as the girlfriends engage in cross talk.]

PARK: Trust?

RODRIGUEZ: That's why we didn't go on.

PARK: That's so weird! What did he think? That you'd go blabbin' this to the whole galaxy?

RODRIGUEZ: I mean--rilly! Hey, what's that static?

PARK: It's just my neural implant.

RODRIGUEZ: Oh--OK!

[As the relationship between Porter and Laura continues, some members of the Command staff become worried about the prudence of continuing the relationship with so much potential for scandal. This song is a conversation between Susan Green, who, though worried, still thinks Laura is a good person, and the rather stonier VALERIA HERNANDEZ.]

"Time to Go"

GREEN: They go back there,
They're just talking,
I'm sure she has a very brilliant mind.

HERNANDEZ: I don't mind a girl who thinks,
It's just the conflict resolution she brings.
Susan, it's Rodriguez's time to go.

GREEN: She brings him
Little presents.
She really is a very thoughtful soul.

HERNANDEZ: It's not the gifts I mind as much
As her up real close and personal touch.
I tell ya, it's Miss Laura's time to go.

GREEN: She never comes
When he's really busy.
Rarely is there anyone around.

HERNANDEZ: Still the Security Force wears a frown.
They shouldn't worry, he checks her down.
But I'm not kidding, it's time for her to go.

GREEN: Maybe she would like the Dawnridge Station.

HERNANDEZ: Good idea--don't wait!

GREEN: Brilliant guys work at Dawnridge in Prandoria.

HERNANDEZ: Let's get Porter's head on straight!

GREEN: He comes back
From Council services,
Soon she's bopping in the door.

HERNANDEZ: "Hallelujah, Peace Is Rising"
Shouldn't inspire thoughts so sizzlin'.
Yes, it's really time for Laura to go.

[Time passes. Laura is transferred to Dawnridge Station. A stage direction indicates: "LAURA packs her belongings at Command Center, exchanges a tearful goodbye with PORTER, and departs on a transport ship." Meanwhile, a former staffer named Jasmine Chen sues the president for harassment, and it seems clear that before long, Porter will have to testify under oath. Two close observers of those developments are old friends Lila Park and XAVIER WATSON, who is friendly with lawyers for Chen and lawyers in the office of Independent Investigator FATIMA MATTHEWS. One day, Park and Watson talk on the quantum comm.]

"Talk, Talk, Chat, Chat" (sprightly)

WATSON and PARK: Talk, talk,
Chat, chat,
Two old pals swap the latest word.
Talk, talk,
Chat, chat,
Two old friends dish the latest dirt.

WATSON: I got tickets
To the zero-g opera,
Station billing says I've got credits due,
I lost a tooth implant
At lunch on Thursday.
That's it for me,
Now tell me what's up with you.

PARK: My friend Laura?
The one who left Command Center?
She's been at Dawnridge now eight months or so.
I hear she misses Porter something fierce,
But she told me that whole chapter's closed.

WATSON: What do you mean?
What's happened with those two?

PARK: She told me when she left the station,
Porter said they had to end it—too much at stake.
She cried for weeks at Dawnridge, Xavier,
Said her heart would never stop its ache.

WATSON: So it's over then?
The president moved on?

PARK: That's what Laura keeps insisting,
Says she's focused on her research now.
Though I notice something strange, Xavier—

WATSON: What's that?

PARK: She takes leave every few weeks somehow.
And yesterday I called her quarters
Three times and got no reply.
When I finally reached her late that evening,
She sounded breathless, wouldn't say why.

WATSON: Interesting, Lila,
Very interesting indeed.
Where does she go on all this leave time?
Does she tell you where she's been?

PARK: She mentioned visiting her mother once,
Another time a conference in the Rim.
But Laura's mother lives on Proxima Station—
I checked the logs, no transport carried her to him.
I mean, to there. To Proxima.

WATSON: You said "him."

PARK: A slip of tongue. I'm sure it's nothing.
Laura swears it's over, says she's moved along.

WATSON: But you don't believe her?

PARK: I want to, Xavier.
But something in her voice sounds wrong.
Last week she mentioned buying Porter's favorite tea—
Said old habits die hard, nothing more.
Then she caught herself and changed the subject fast,
Started talking about Dawnridge's research floor.

WATSON: Lila, listen carefully—
This matters more than you might know.
If something's happening between those two,
The galaxy deserves to know.

PARK: But she denies it, Xavier!
She says their chapter closed when she left Command.
She told me Porter ended everything,
Said scandal wasn't worth the risk he'd planned.

WATSON: And yet she buys his tea.
And yet she disappears.
And yet she sounds breathless when you call.

PARK: There's one more thing I haven't mentioned—
Something that might mean nothing at all.
I visited her quarters at Dawnridge last month,
Helped her organize her research files.
I noticed transport passes in her drawer,
Stamped for routes across three hundred miles.

WATSON: Routes to where?

PARK: The passes didn't specify.
They were coded for executive shuttles—
The kind that don't leave traces when they fly.

WATSON: Executive shuttles, Lila—
Those require clearance from above.
A researcher can't book those on her own.

PARK: I know, Xavier.
That's why I'm concerned.
Someone powerful approved her flights unknown.

WATSON: Back up, Lila,
Did I hear you rightly?
You think Porter's still involved somehow?

PARK: I don't know what to think—
She swears it ended clean.
But none of her denials add up now.

WATSON: God, this news is manna, Lila!
At last our cause will finally have its chance!

PARK: Oh, you're a dreamer Xavier!
There'll be headlines, then he'll pull off an
Escape.
He'll spin the story, he'll turn the tables—

WATSON: Unless you get that airhead down on tape.

PARK: What?

WATSON: Unless you get that silly, vapid, trampy time bomb
Down on tape.

PARK: Oh—one more thing...

WATSON: What?

PARK: There's a data chip she keeps hidden—
She showed it to me once, then grabbed it back.
Said it was personal, nothing important,
But her hands were shaking as she closed the pack.

WATSON: A data chip?

PARK: She guards it like her life depends on it.

WATSON: Hold on, let me call Fatima.

[Independent Investigator Matthews uses Park to detain Laura. Under questioning, Laura initially maintains that her relationship with Porter ended completely when she transferred to Dawnridge. Matthews presses her about the transport passes and the data chip.]

"The Interrogation" (tense, building)

MATTHEWS: Miss Rodriguez, you say it ended
When you left for Dawnridge Station.

RODRIGUEZ: That's right, that's what I've been saying—
A clean and total separation.

MATTHEWS: Then explain these transport records
That my team has now obtained.
Three visits back to Galactic Command
Since you left—please explain.

RODRIGUEZ: I had friends at Command Center,
People I wanted to see.

MATTHEWS: At two in the morning, Miss Rodriguez?
Your shuttle logs show that clearly.

RODRIGUEZ: I... there were research emergencies.
Quantum data I needed to review.

MATTHEWS: In the president's private quarters?
The security logs place you there too.

[Rodriguez breaks down.]

RODRIGUEZ: Fine! I tried to move on, tried to forget!
But every few weeks he'd send a message through channels unknown.
"Come see me," he'd write, "I miss your research."
And I couldn't resist—I've never felt so alone!

MATTHEWS: So the relationship didn't end.

RODRIGUEZ: It ended and started and ended again!
Every time I thought I'd finally let go,
Another message would come, another midnight flight,
And I'd be back in his arms before I even said no.

MATTHEWS: How many times, Miss Rodriguez?

RODRIGUEZ: I stopped counting after five or six.
Sometimes months would pass with nothing,
Then he'd call and I'd be there by six.

[The news breaks across all quantum networks. On the advice of his pal from Morningside Village, Porter flat-out lies to his wife, to his loyalists, and to the public about the relationship.]

"I Never Have" (performance should build in tempo and intensity)

PORTER: You know I'd like to answer questions,
An act my lawyers won't allow.
I'll give you more not less, sooner not later,
I just can't say a word right now.
But I don't know why she'd say these things
Her head's full of who knows what.
But I never had relations with that woman
I never had relations with that—
When she left for Dawnridge, that was final,
We wished each other well and said goodbye.
Whatever happened at Command stayed at Command,
To say anything else is a lie.
All Matthews has is some recordings
Made by a vengeful snitch.
I never had relations with that woman
I never had relations with that b—
A vast right-wing conspiracy
Is using her to beat on me.
They wanna torpedo my agenda
They hate me and my policies.
But I will never let them ruin
Our dreams for a better world.
I tell ya, I never had relations with that woman
I never had relations with that
Girl.

[Months of investigation, legal wrangling, and public relations campaigning follow. Matthews' tactics come under heavy fire, to which she responds.]

"Crossing the Line"

MATTHEWS: It's true Laura asked to lawyer up,
Which Stevens put the lid on.
And I felt bad about her mother's grilling
Upon our little gridiron.
The Democrats and liberals
Blast these tactics of mine,
But a woman's gotta do what a woman's gotta do
When the president crosses the line.
He's crossed the line.
He's crossed the line.
Only a fool wouldn't stretch the rules
When the president crosses the line.
It may have seemed like dirty pool
To drag his people 'fore the jury.
We wasted lots of Vernon's time,
May have busted Susan Green.
His aides aren't the innocent bystanders
As they claim when they moan and whine.
They won't say what they know full well:
The president crossed the line.
He's crossed the line.
He's crossed the line.
I'd be a nitwit not to bend a bit
When the president crosses the line.
The talking heads are accusing me
Of laying a perjury trap.
But all it catches is lying men.
Honest men beat the rap.
There's people who say I'm against love;
I've had love. It's fine.
But lying about it gets my blood up
And the president's crossed the line.
I crossed the line.
I crossed the line.
Tell the media I'll leak at will
When the president crosses the line.

[After months of denials and futile delays, Porter finally testifies before the Matthews investigation and argues that, technically, he didn't lie.]

"Testimony" (snappy)

PORTER: Depends what the definition of "relations" is,
Depends on the meaning of intimate contact,
"After Dawnridge" needs careful parsing,
Before you reach conclusions, check your facts.
When I said it ended, I meant my intention—
My heart was resolved to let her go.
That my resolve sometimes weakened late at night
Is something the galaxy doesn't need to know.

[Afterward, he speaks to the galaxy, admits doing wrong, and apologizes, though grudgingly.]

PORTER: Inappropriate was the nature of our actions,
And believe me I regret the whole damn thing,
But inappropriate are all these personal questions,
The galaxy doesn't need to know these things.

[Porter's enemies reject his apology, and soon the Galactic Council begins the long process of removal proceedings. XAVIER WATSON here discloses his approach.]

"Bring 'em Down" (dark, moody)

WATSON: Mustn't seem to be too cheerful,
Mustn't overreach,
Must remember to seem unhappy
That we're going to impeach.
Must remember to remain sober
As we undertake this chore.
At the same time, let's remember
To pin some stuff on Gore.
Bring 'em down.
Bring 'em down.
Sure, they were elected,
Twice, in point of fact.
Voters obviously were bewildered
To have made a choice like that.
Now, like charging warriors,
We'll move in for the sack.
Bring 'em down.
Bring 'em down.
Bring 'em down.

[The Council votes to hold removal hearings. But just a few weeks later, the midterm elections, which are expected to go the Martian way, are held. Contrary to predictions based on consumer behavior analysis, the Democrats pick up seats, and the Martians' obsession with scandal is repudiated. Watson resigns, and the practical chances of Porter's removal evaporate. As the show ends, we hear from Matthews, Rodriguez, and Porter.]

"The People Have Spoken" (dramatic, stirring)

MATTHEWS: The election was held and the people have spoken,
I can't believe what they had to say.
I had Porter boxed into a corner
Looks like he's going to get away.
I spent four years and 40 million
That's a lot of time and credits.
I made Porter look ridiculous,
But the only scalp I got was Xavier's.

RODRIGUEZ: The election was held and the people have spoken,
I can't believe what they had to say.
My boyfriend is still in office
Though I wonder what comes next.
The transfer to Dawnridge was supposed to end things—
That's what Porter told me in those final texts.
But messages kept coming through the darkness,
And shuttles flew when no one else was near.
Whether we'll find our way back to each other,
Or whether this time goodbye is sincere—
I still don't know.
I may never know.

PORTER: The election was held and the people have spoken,
I can't believe what they had to say.
The removal threat is over,
Fatima Matthews should go away.
I tell you, though, it is a mystery,
I mean, I'm unfaithful and I lie.
I might be guilty of obstruction,
Yet my ratings are sky-high.
That must mean I'm a pretty good president,
Though how, I don't think I know.
But obviously I'm not Matthews or Watson,
Which may be why they love me so.
Which may be why they love me so.

[Curtain.]

quality_problem.correct_answer: The relationship with Porter continued intermittently.
