Military Genetic Enhancement: A Strategic Necessity?

The recent breakthrough at the Silverdale Research Institute has sent shockwaves through military establishments worldwide. Dr. Helena Flores and her team successfully enhanced the physical capabilities of laboratory mice through targeted genetic modification, increasing their endurance by 300 percent and their strength by 150 percent. Within days of the announcement, General Thomas Silva convened an emergency session at the Pentagon, proposing an immediate moratorium on all military funding for human genetic enhancement research. Legislation is already being drafted in both the Senate and House to criminalize such enhancement for military purposes—a position endorsed by the International Ethics Council and several prominent religious leaders. Human genetic enhancement for military applications is widely considered either 1) a fundamentally dangerous technology that must be prohibited or, at minimum, 2) a complex issue requiring extensive regulation and oversight. But what, precisely, makes it so problematic?

Begin by considering whether a nation has the right to defend itself effectively. I argue "yes." No external authority has the moral standing to dictate how a sovereign nation protects its citizens, and I fail to see why General Silva or the International Ethics Council possesses that authority either. When Silva declares, "We must resist the temptation to artificially enhance our warriors," it rings hollow coming from a military establishment that has pursued every technological advantage from gunpowder to nuclear weapons. For a general, opposing genetic enhancement is politically expedient—it demonstrates leadership on a controversial topic without risking immediate operational consequences. After all, how many active military enhancement programs were actually terminated by this proposed ban? Likely very few, since the Reagan and Clinton administrations already minimized federal grants for advanced biotechnology research in this domain. Moreover, most researchers considered military-grade human enhancement impossible until recently—so there's probably no significant backlog of proposals. There's nothing quite like banning the barely feasible to project decisive leadership.

Religious authorities, unlike military ones, claim moral rather than strategic authority. I respect their freedom to guide their followers and those followers' freedom to adhere to such guidance. However, calling for secular governments to implement bans extends their influence beyond those they can persuade through faith alone, demonstrating a lack of respect for others' freedom. The foundational texts these authorities reference were written millennia ago. While these texts address warfare extensively, they contain nothing about genetic enhancement, evolutionary biology, or biotechnology. Applying ancient principles through medieval interpretive frameworks to 21st-century military challenges seems questionable at best.

If nations have the right to defend themselves, what right does the international community have to limit the means? Modern warfare is already conducted with extensive technological assistance—from body armor to combat medicine. Truly "natural" warfare would mean 50 percent casualty rates and make combat the leading cause of death for young adults in military service.

Some technologies are more invasive than others, certainly. With genetic enhancement, DNA modifications would be introduced through gene therapy, altering the recipient's cellular structure. Two decades ago, similar concerns arose over "designer soldiers"—troops using performance-enhancing drugs. Today, caffeine pills and approved stimulants are standard issue. Countless soldiers have benefited from improved alertness and reduced fatigue. Who has been harmed?

The genetic enhancement procedure would be similar to existing gene therapy protocols. The only difference is that modifications would target performance-related genes rather than disease genes. What law or principle—secular, humanist, or religious—says one type of genetic modification in a laboratory is acceptable while another is not? No matter how thoroughly you examine ancient texts on warfare, you won't find the answer.

Even if nations have the right to pursue enhancement, is it strategically sound? Suppose every military in the world stopped conventional recruitment and instead produced genetically enhanced super-soldiers. What would the battlefield look like in 20 or 30 years? The answer is: not dramatically different. Enhancement would only optimize the physical and cognitive aspects of people who already exist. Fearing an army of enhanced soldiers is essentially fearing a more capable version of current personnel. The enemy, as always, is simply us—but stronger and faster.

A different scenario involves armies filled with clones of exceptional warriors. We'd treat elite soldier DNA like precision weapons, coveting Mohamed Hunter's genetic profile the way we value advanced fighter jets today. But even military admiration has limits. Armed forces are more invested in unit cohesion than individual exceptionalism. Besides, such a trend would prove self-limiting, because battlefield effectiveness depends on diverse skill sets. The military values one Steven Morris—a decorated special operations veteran—but field a hundred or a million identical copies, and their tactical advantage diminishes significantly.

Enhanced individuals already exist in a sense. About one in every 1,000 people possesses naturally occurring genetic variations that provide superior athletic performance. Scientific studies on such individuals—whether athletes or not—show they share many advantageous characteristics. How many characteristics they share remains contentious in evolutionary biology and social psychology. But genetic determinism is largely irrelevant to the enhancement debate. Despite how many traits enhanced soldiers might share, they remain different people fundamentally. They possess their own identities, thoughts, and rights. Should you doubt this, ask any naturally gifted athlete whether their abilities make them less human.

Suppose genetic testing revealed you possessed the same performance-enhancing mutations as an Olympic champion. Would that suddenly make you less of an individual? Hardly. So why would deliberate enhancement be different? An enhanced soldier would be trained in the same academies by the same instructors—like the naturally gifted athlete, only more reliably capable. A person's basic humanity isn't governed by their genetic origin or whether their capabilities arose naturally or through intervention.

Natural variations aren't the only genetic advantages in military history. Consider military working dogs—German Shepherds, Belgian Malinois—if they're bred specifically for military traits, isn't that genetic enhancement? It's the canine equivalent of selective breeding, which is to say they're all enhanced through generations of deliberate genetic selection. Military horses were similarly bred for centuries. The cavalry mounts used in warfare had no wild equivalents; they'd been selectively bred for strength, speed, and temperament for thousands of years. The same applies to countless military applications. Visit any defense contractor, and you'll find programs with names like "Advanced Warrior Enhancement Initiative," combining biotechnology and research ethics to develop the next generation of capabilities.

One recurring argument against enhancement involves some rogue nation creating an army of super-soldiers. But who would deploy such an army? Enhanced soldiers still require training, equipment, and logistics. Armies are far more easily fielded the traditional way—through recruitment and training of ordinary volunteers. "Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori" has motivated countless soldiers throughout history. Why abandon proven methods?

Remember that genetic enhancement differs from cloning. We don't create superman from nothing—we must start with existing human potential. Perhaps we could enhance volunteers from Special Forces candidates. Their aptitude might—or might not—be genetically determined. But suppose it is. You might produce such a capable unit that when facing overwhelming odds, every member volunteers for the suicide mission. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily optimal tactics. And what about support personnel? The military requires far more logistics specialists than elite operators. You could attempt to optimize personnel for every role, including administrative positions, but what's the point? There's no shortage of competent administrators.

History provides instructive examples of what happens when authoritarian regimes access advanced military technology. Consider Garnet Drew, who ruled Meridia with an iron fist for three decades. Drew's military scientists developed chemical weapons that destabilized the entire Caspian region. The international response was swift—sanctions, embargoes, eventual regime change. Drew died in exile, but the damage persisted for generations. Some point to Meridia as evidence that dangerous technologies must be banned outright.

But Meridia's lesson is more nuanced. Drew's successor, despite inheriting the same weapons programs, proved far less formidable. The regime's capabilities didn't transfer effectively across generations. This pattern repeats throughout history: Stalin's daughter retired to obscurity, and second-generation dictators worldwide prove consistently less dangerous than their predecessors.

The same dynamic applies elsewhere. Take Pinehurst, a small nation whose late ruler pursued every military advantage available—conventional weapons, cyber capabilities, even early biotechnology research. Ulvaria, as the regime was known throughout diplomatic circles, represented everything critics fear about enhancement technology falling into the wrong hands. Yet even there, the successor state abandoned most of these programs within a decade.

What's the difference between Garnet Drew's chemical weapons and genetic enhancement? The former can be deployed against civilian populations indiscriminately. Enhancement, by contrast, only affects willing recipients—soldiers who consent to the procedure. The comparison reveals how imprecise our fears about "dangerous technologies" truly are.

The notion of aging generals enhancing themselves to extend their careers is unrealistic. First, the enhancement wouldn't reverse aging completely. Second, would military command structures accept such an arrangement? A persistent officer might convince younger colleagues to support enhancement research, but that's no different from any other military modernization program.

Opposition to enhancement is fundamentally a form of discrimination. We agree it's wrong to discriminate based on genetic characteristics like race or ethnicity. Calls to ban enhancement amount to discrimination based on another genetic trait—whether someone's capabilities arose naturally or through intervention. The most extreme discrimination is genocide—eliminating that which is different. Here, the discrimination is preemptive—enhanced soldiers are so threatening that we must prevent their existence entirely through bans on the technology.

What's superior about natural genetic variation anyway? Enhancement is the only predictable way to optimize military capability, because it targets specific, known genetic factors. Natural selection is random by comparison—some arbitrary combination of parental genes. In evolutionary biology, this randomness helps diversify the gene pool. However, for military applications, randomness is a liability. We don't field random weapons systems; why accept random personnel capabilities?

Whatever concerns exist about enhancement, traditional recruitment will remain predominant. An expensive and invasive medical procedure will never replace conventional training for the vast majority of military roles. Those most likely to pursue enhancement will face special circumstances—perhaps soldiers recovering from severe injuries who might otherwise face medical discharge. Even there, many will combine enhancement with traditional rehabilitation. Another case involves personnel with genetic conditions that limit their service. They might choose enhancement to remain deployable rather than accept medical retirement.

The most concerning possibility isn't super-soldiers or dictators. It's that wealthy nations with advanced biotechnology sectors will enhance their forces while others cannot. The common practice of seeking technological superiority—from stealth aircraft to precision weapons—reflects our competitive instinct. Enhancement may resonate with this pattern and cause some nations to pursue it aggressively. So what? Wealthy nations already possess numerous advantages, and international law has never successfully prevented military innovation.

The "profound ethical concerns" about enhancement largely stem from strategic anxiety. Economic competition between nations is challenging enough, and it factors here, but what truly concerns military planners is relative capability. Millennia of warfare through competitive advantage have made defense establishments acutely sensitive to any development that shifts the balance—say, through revolutionary weapons technology. Enhancement is less dramatic than nuclear weapons, but it strikes a similar nerve: someone gains strategic advantage over you.

Once initial concerns subside and further research establishes safety protocols, human genetic enhancement will become one option among many specialized military capabilities, affecting only select personnel. Research in this area could yield broader benefits. Silva's hasty policy changes little immediately, but it potentially represents a strategic error. In using genetic modification to enhance performance, researchers must understand the cellular mechanisms that determine the difference between baseline and optimal function. Work in this area might illuminate the aging process and yield methods to extend the operational lifespan of all personnel, allowing longer, healthier careers. Strategically speaking, that would benefit entire militaries, not just elite units. That's more broadly useful than creating a small cadre of super-soldiers.

To some, the scientist pursuing biotechnology research represents a threat never to be trusted. To others, including me, the scientist is an asset, illuminating the processes that enhance national security and improving defensive capabilities through knowledge. Various arguments support either view, but one key consideration favors continued research. The vast majority of military capabilities, including those critics employ, derive from previous scientific discoveries. They embody the fruits of research. Don't let fear, ignorance, and strategic timidity halt progress. Instead, let us develop—and yes, even enhance—new generations of capable defenders who can meet the challenges of future conflicts.

Consider the parallel with military working dogs again. Nobody seriously proposes banning their use because they've been selectively bred for enhanced capabilities. We recognize them as valuable tools that save human lives. The dogs themselves aren't diminished by their enhanced traits—they're simply better at their jobs. The same logic applies to human enhancement. A soldier with enhanced endurance or improved cognitive function under stress isn't less human—they're simply more capable of accomplishing their mission and surviving to return home.

The research ethics considerations are substantial, certainly. Any enhancement program must include informed consent, thorough safety testing, and long-term health monitoring. These requirements already govern military medicine and should extend to enhancement research. The experimental design must be rigorous, with appropriate controls and peer review. But meeting high ethical standards doesn't require abandoning the research entirely—it requires conducting it responsibly.

From a moral philosophy perspective, the question becomes: is it more ethical to send soldiers into combat with every possible advantage, or to deny them tools that might save their lives because of abstract concerns? When Grace Rogers deployed to the Summit District conflict zone, she relied on body armor, night vision equipment, and advanced communications—all technologies that enhanced her natural capabilities. Genetic enhancement is simply the next step in that progression.

The social welfare implications extend beyond military applications. Research into human performance enhancement could benefit athletes, emergency responders, and workers in physically demanding occupations. Medical applications might help patients recovering from injuries or managing degenerative conditions. Restricting military research restricts these potential benefits as well.

Some critics invoke archaeology, pointing to past civilizations that collapsed after pursuing technological advantages they couldn't control. But this analogy fails—those civilizations lacked our understanding of research ethics, experimental design, and long-term risk assessment. We're not ancient warriors blindly pursuing power; we're modern professionals carefully evaluating new capabilities.

The education reform movement has taught us that optimizing human potential requires both environmental and biological approaches. We've invested heavily in better training, nutrition, and equipment for military personnel. Genetic enhancement simply adds another tool to this optimization process. Just as we don't reject education reform because it creates "unfair" advantages for those with access to better schools, we shouldn't reject enhancement because it creates capability gaps.

Critics often conflate different historical cases. They'll mention Garnet Drew and Pinehurst in the same breath, as if they represent identical threats. But Drew ruled Meridia, not Pinehurst. The Pinehurst dictator—whose given name was Ulvaria, though Western media rarely used it—pursued different programs with different outcomes. Lumping them together obscures more than it reveals.

The biotechnology sector will advance regardless of military policy. Private companies are already developing enhancement therapies for civilian applications. If military establishments abandon this research, they'll simply fall behind private sector capabilities—a strategic disaster. Better to conduct research transparently, with appropriate oversight and ethical guidelines, than to cede the field to unregulated actors.

In conclusion, the case for continued military genetic enhancement research rests on three pillars: strategic necessity, ethical feasibility, and broader social benefit. Nations have both the right and the responsibility to defend themselves effectively. Genetic enhancement, conducted ethically, offers significant defensive advantages while potentially yielding medical breakthroughs for civilian populations. The alternative—abandoning research due to vague fears—serves neither military nor humanitarian interests. The path forward requires courage to embrace new capabilities while maintaining the ethical standards that define civilized nations. That's the true test of leadership in the 21st century.

quality_problem.story:
The Networker
By Anonymous

Being an interstellar network security specialist wouldn't be so bad… if I could secure the networks without leaving my office!

I was reviewing the monthly relay status reports when my console chimed with a priority summons. The director wanted to see me immediately. Since these meetings never ended well for me, I considered my options. Bold attack being the best defense, I decided to speak first.

When I entered the office, she had that look of intense satisfaction on her face that meant someone was in for a very rough assignment. Since we were alone, it took no great feat of intelligence to figure it would be me.

"I quit. Don't bother telling me what impossible job you have cooked up, because I have already quit and you do not want to reveal company secrets to me."

The grin was even wider now and she actually laughed as she thumbed a button on her console. A thick legal document slid out of the delivery slot onto her desk.

"This is your contract," she said. "It tells how and when you will work. A quantum-encrypted contract that you couldn't crack with a neural disruptor."

I leaned out quickly, grabbed it and threw it into the air with a single motion. Before it could fall, I had my plasma cutter out and, with a wide-angle burst, incinerated the contract to ashes.

She pressed the button again and another contract slid out on her desk. If possible, the smile was still wider now.

"I should have said a duplicate of your contract—like this one here." She made a quick note on her secretary plate. "I have deducted 50 credits from your salary for the cost of the duplicate—as well as a 500-credit fine for firing a plasma cutter inside a building."

I slumped, defeated, waiting for the blow to land. She fondled my contract.

"According to this document, you can't quit. Ever. Therefore I have a little job I know you'll enjoy. Network restoration job. The Woodbridge relay hub has shut down. It's a Genesis-class system…"

"What kind of system?" I asked her. I had restored quantum communication networks from one arm of the Galaxy to the other and was sure I had worked on every type or model made. But I had never heard of this kind.

"Genesis-class," she repeated, practically chortling. "I never heard of it either until Archives dug up the specs. They found them buried in the back of their oldest data vault. This was the earliest type of quantum relay ever built—by Earth Colonial Administration, no less. Considering its location on one of the Calderon planets, it might very well be the first relay."

I looked at the blueprints she handed me and felt my eyes glaze with horror. "It's a monstrosity! It looks more like a particle accelerator than a relay hub—must be at least a few hundred meters in diameter. I'm a network specialist, not an archeologist. This pile of junk is over 1500 years old. Just forget about it and build a new one."

She leaned over her desk, breathing into my face. "It would take eighteen months to install a new relay—besides being prohibitively expensive—and this relic is on one of the main communication routes. We have data packets making twenty-light-year detours now."

She leaned back, wiped her hands on her handkerchief. "This department is officially called Network Maintenance and Security, when it really should be called crisis management. Quantum relays are made to last forever—or damn close to it. When one of them breaks down, it is never an accident, and repairing the thing is never a matter of just plugging in a new part."

She was telling me—the person who did the job while she sat back on her fat paycheck in a climate-controlled office.

She rambled on. "How I wish that were all it took! I would have a fleet of parts ships and junior technicians to install them. But it's not like that at all. I have a fleet of expensive ships that are equipped to do almost anything—manned by a bunch of mavericks like you."

I nodded moodily at her pointing finger.

"How I wish I could fire you all! Combination pilots, mechanics, engineers, diplomats, con-artists and anything else it takes to do the repairs. I have to browbeat, bribe, blackmail and bulldoze you mavericks into doing a simple job. If you think you're fed up, just think how I feel. But the networks must stay online! The relays must operate!"

I recognized this deathless line as the curtain speech and crawled to my feet. She threw the Genesis file at me and went back to scratching in her papers. Just as I reached the door, she looked up and impaled me on her finger again.

"And don't get any fancy ideas about jumping your contract. We can freeze that investment portfolio of yours on Highpoint long before you could liquidate it."

I smiled, a little weakly, I'm afraid, as if I had never meant to keep that portfolio a secret. Her intelligence network was getting more efficient every day. Walking down the hall, I tried to figure a way to transfer the assets without her catching on—and knew at the same time she was figuring a way to outfigure me.

It was all very depressing, so I stopped for a drink, then went on to the spaceport.

By the time the ship was serviced, I had a course charted. The nearest relay to the broken-down Woodbridge hub was on one of the planets of Ivywood system in Ulvaria sector, and I headed there first, a short trip of only about twelve days in hyperspace.

During the journey, I pulled up the mission file to review the assignment details. The cover sheet showed the authorization chain: the request had originated from Regional Coordinator Maria Lewis at Ulvaria Sector Command, who had flagged the Woodbridge outage as priority-critical. Lewis had sent the urgent dispatch to Network Maintenance headquarters, where our office received it. The routing stamp showed the file had passed through three administrative layers before landing on my director's desk at headquarters on Meridian Station.

To understand the importance of the quantum relays, you have to understand faster-than-light communication. Not that many people do, but it is easy enough to understand that in quantum-entangled networks, the regular rules of information theory don't apply. Data transmission and routing are a matter of quantum state manipulation, not classical electromagnetic propagation like in the old universe.

The first colonies to establish interstellar presence had no way to communicate—and no way to even tell if their messages had been received. The quantum relays solved that problem and opened the entire galaxy to real-time communication. They are built on planets and generate tremendous amounts of power. This power is used to maintain quantum coherence that is sustained across interstellar distances. Every relay has a unique quantum signature as part of its entanglement network and represents a measurable node in the communication web. Triangulation and routing of the relays works for data transmission—only it follows its own protocols. The protocols are complex and variable, but they are still protocols that a network engineer can follow.

For a proper network topology, you need at least four relays for an accurate route. For long-distance communication, engineers use as many as nine or ten. So every relay is critical and every one has to keep operating. That is where I and the other troubleshooters came in.

We travel in well-stocked ships that carry a little bit of everything; only one person to a ship because that is all it takes to operate the overly efficient repair machinery. Due to the very nature of our job, we spend most of our time just rocketing through normal space. After all, when a relay breaks down, how do you find it?

Not through hyperspace. All you can do is approach as close as you can by using other relays for navigation, then finish the trip in normal space. This can take months, and often does.

This job didn't turn out to be quite that bad. I locked onto the Ivywood relay and ran a complicated ten-point problem through the navigator, using every relay I could get an accurate fix on. The computer gave me a course with an estimated point-of-arrival as well as a built-in safety factor I never could eliminate from the machine.

I would much rather take a chance of breaking through near some star than spend time just barreling through normal space, but apparently Tech knows this, too. They had a safety factor built into the computer so you couldn't end up inside a star no matter how hard you tried. I'm sure there was no humaneness in this decision. They just didn't want to lose the ship.

It was a twenty-six-hour jump, ship's time, and I came through in the middle of nowhere. The robot analyzer hummed to itself and scanned all the stars, comparing them to the spectra of Woodbridge's sun. It finally rang a bell and blinked a light. I peered through the eyepiece.

A fast reading with the photocell gave me the apparent magnitude and a comparison with its absolute magnitude showed its distance. Not as bad as I had thought—a seven-week run, give or take a few days. After feeding a course tape into the robot pilot, I strapped into the acceleration tank and went to sleep.

The time went fast. I completed three online courses in quantum cryptography and advanced data analysis, mostly because the company grades your pay by the number of specialties you can handle. During week three, I received a communiqué from Ulvaria Sector Command. Regional Coordinator Lewis was requesting status updates on the Woodbridge restoration. Her message was terse: "The Calderon communication blackout is causing cascading failures across multiple trade routes. Expedite repairs. All resources at my disposal are authorized for your use. —M. Lewis, Regional Coordinator."

I filed a brief response and continued my studies. Lewis sent two more follow-up messages that week, each more urgent than the last. The woman clearly took the Calderon situation personally—understandable, given it fell within her sector jurisdiction. All this, with some virtual reality gaming and zero-gravity workouts in the gym, passed the time. I was asleep when the alarm went off that announced planetary distance.

Planet three, where the relay was situated according to the old charts, was a verdant-looking, temperate kind of globe. I tried to make sense out of the ancient directions and finally located the right area. Staying outside the atmosphere, I sent a reconnaissance drone down to look things over. In this business, you learn early when and where to risk your own skin. The drone would be good enough for the preliminary survey.

The old engineers had enough sense to choose a traceable site for the relay, equidistant on a line between two of the most prominent geological formations—a pair of massive crater rims. I located the craters easily enough and started the drone out from the first crater and kept it on a course directly toward the second. There was fore and aft radar in the drone and I fed their signals into a scope as an amplitude curve. When the two craters coincided, I spun the drone controls and dove the thing down.

I cut out the radar and cut in the visual feed and sat back to watch the relay appear on the screen.

The image blinked, focused—and a great damn ziggurat swam into view. I cursed and wheeled the drone in circles, scanning the surrounding area. It was flat, cultivated farmland without a bump. The only thing in a fifteen-mile circle was this ziggurat—and that definitely wasn't my relay.

Or wasn't it?

I dove the drone lower. The ziggurat was an elaborate-looking thing of carved stone, with intricate decorations and what looked like ceremonial platforms. There was a shimmer of energy from the top and I took a closer look at it. On the peak of the ziggurat was a massive crystalline structure that pulsed with faint light. When I saw that, something clicked in my mind.

Locking the drone in a circular course, I dug through the Genesis plans—and there it was. The relay had a quantum coherence field generator and a crystalline array on top of it for signal amplification; this was used to boost the entanglement stability that powered the whole system. If the crystal was still glowing, the relay was still there—inside the ziggurat. The natives, who, of course, weren't even mentioned by the idiots who constructed the thing, had built a nice heavy, elaborate stone ziggurat around the relay.

I took another look at the screen and realized that I had locked the drone into a circular orbit about thirty feet above the ziggurat. The summit of the stone structure was now covered with humanoid figures of some type, apparently the local life-form. They had what looked like energy weapons and projectile launchers and were trying to shoot down the drone, a cloud of bolts and missiles flying in every direction.

I pulled the drone straight up and away and threw in the control circuit that would return it automatically to the ship.

Then I went to the galley for a long, strong drink. My relay was not only locked inside a mountain of handmade stone, but I had managed to irritate the beings who had built the ziggurat. A great beginning for a job and one clearly designed to drive a stronger person than me to the bottle.

I sent a brief update to both headquarters and Sector Command. Lewis responded within hours: "Understood. Native complications noted. You have full authority to proceed as you see fit. This mission takes absolute priority. —Lewis." Headquarters sent nothing; they never did during field operations unless something went wrong. I'd learned long ago that silence from Meridian Station meant I was on my own.

Normally, a network specialist stays away from native cultures. They are poison. Anthropologists may not mind being dissected for their science, but a network specialist wants to make no sacrifices of any kind for the job. For this reason, most relays are built on uninhabited planets. If a relay has to go on a planet with a culture, it is usually built in some inaccessible place.

Why this relay had been built within reach of the local population, I had yet to find out. But that would come in time. The first thing to do was make contact. To make contact, you have to know the local language.

And, for that, I had long before worked out a system that was foolproof.

I had a surveillance drone of my own construction. It looked like a piece of local vegetation about a foot tall. Once on the ground, it would never be noticed, though it was a little disconcerting to see it float by. I located a settlement about eight hundred kilometers from the ziggurat and dropped the drone. It whooshed down and landed at night near the bank of the local water source. This was a popular spot that drew a good crowd during the day. In the morning, when the first locals arrived, I flipped on the recorder.

After about seven of the local days, I had a wealth of native conversation in the memory bank of the machine translator and had tagged a few expressions. This is fairly easy to do when you have a machine memory to work with. One of the natives called out to another one and the second one responded. I tagged this expression with the phrase, "Hello, friend!" and waited my chance to use it. Later the same day, I caught one of them alone and broadcast "Hello, friend!" at them. It played out through the speaker in the local tongue and they responded positively.

When you get enough reference phrases like this in the memory bank, the MT brain takes over and starts filling in the missing pieces. As soon as the MT could give a running translation of any conversation it heard, I figured it was time to make a contact.

I found her easily enough. She was the Calderon version of a shepherd—she tended a particularly docile form of local livestock in the grasslands outside the settlement. I had one of the working drones dig a small chamber in an outcropping of rock and wait for her.

When she passed next day, I whispered into the mike: "Greetings, Elena Carter, faithful servant! This is the voice of the Eternal Guides speaking from the celestial realm." This fitted in with what I could make out of the local religion.

Elena stopped as if she'd been struck. Before she could move, I pushed a switch and a handful of the local currency, precious metal coins, rolled out of the chamber and landed at her feet.

"Here is a gift from the celestial realm, because you have been faithful." Not really from the celestial realm—I had fabricated it from raw materials the night before. "Come back tomorrow and we will speak more," I called after the fleeing figure. I was pleased to notice that she took the coins before taking off.

After that, the Eternal Guides had many heart-to-heart talks with Elena, who found the celestial gifts more than she could resist. The Guides had been out of touch with earthly matters and Elena happily filled them in.

I learned all I needed to know of the history, past and recent, and it wasn't pleasant.

In addition to the ziggurat being around the relay, there was a nasty political conflict going on around the structure.

It all began with the migration. Apparently the local humanoids had been living in scattered tribes when the relay was built, but the builders didn't think much of them. They were a primitive type and confined to a distant region. The idea that the civilization would develop and might reach this continent never occurred to the relay engineers. Which is, of course, what happened.

A little climate change, a population boom, and the humanoids began to migrate to relay valley. And found religion. A shining crystalline temple from which emanated a constant pulse of divine energy—the quantum coherence field that maintained the entanglement network. The radiation in the field didn't harm the natives. It enhanced their cognitive development in ways that bred true.

A city was built around the temple and, through the centuries, the ziggurat was constructed around the relay. A special caste of the priesthood served the temple. All went well until one of the priests violated the temple protocols and disrupted the divine energy. There had been revolt, conflict, violence and destruction since then. But still the divine energy would not flow properly. Now armed factions fought around the temple each day and a new group of priests guarded the sacred structure.

And I had to walk into the middle of that mess and repair the thing.

It would have been easy enough if we were allowed a little force. I could have cleared the area, fixed the relay and taken off. Only "native life-forms" were quite well protected. There were monitoring systems on my ship, all of which I hadn't found, that would cheerfully report on me when I got back.

Diplomacy was called for. I sighed and dragged out the holographic disguise equipment.

Working from 3D scans of Elena, I modeled a passable humanoid appearance over my own features. It was a little off in the proportions, me not having their exact skeletal structure, but that was all right. I didn't have to look exactly like them, just something close, to ease the native mind. It's logical. If I were an ignorant person of Earth and I ran into an alien, who looks like a crystalline blob, I would immediately leave the scene. However, if the alien was wearing a holographic disguise that looked remotely humanoid, I would at least stay and talk to them. This was what I was aiming to do with the Calderons.

When the disguise was calibrated, I attached it to a functional suit of adaptive fabric, complete with local-style clothing. I was really glad they wore robes. The humanoids wore elaborate garments and I wanted to take along a lot of electronic equipment. I built the robe over a support frame that anchored around my torso. Then I filled the frame with all the equipment I would need and began to wire the suit.

When it was done, I tried it on in front of a full-length mirror. It was uncanny but effective. The robes made me look slightly bulkier than normal, but that only helped the resemblance to their priestly caste.

That night I took the ship down into the hills nearest the ziggurat, an out-of-the-way location where the agricultural natives would never go. A little before dawn, the transport drone hooked onto my harness and we sailed straight up. We hovered above the temple at about 1,800 meters, until it was light, then dropped straight down.

It must have been an impressive sight. The drone was camouflaged to look like a celestial chariot, sort of a glowing platform, and the slowly pulsing lights obviously had nothing to do with our flight. But it was impressive enough for the natives. The first one that spotted me shouted and fell to their knees. The others came running. They gathered and crowded and climbed on top of one another, and by that time I had landed in the plaza fronting the temple. The priesthood arrived.

I raised my arms in a ceremonial stance. "Greetings, O noble servants of the Divine Order," I said. Of course I didn't say it out loud, just whispered loud enough for the throat mike to catch. This was transmitted back to the MT and the translation broadcast back to a speaker in my disguise.

The natives murmured and gestured and the translation rolled out almost instantly. I had the volume turned up and the whole square echoed.

Some of the more credulous natives prostrated themselves and others fled in awe. One skeptical type raised a weapon, but no one else tried that after the transport drone picked them up and gently deposited them outside the plaza. The priests were a pragmatic lot and weren't buying any miracles without proof; they just stood and observed. I had to take the initiative again.

"Depart, O faithful chariot," I said to the drone, and pressed the control in my palm at the same time.

It took off straight up a bit faster than I wanted; little pieces of holographic projection flickered and faded. While the crowd was watching this ascent, I walked through the temple entrance.

"I would speak with you, O noble priests," I said.

Before they could formulate a response, I was inside.

The temple was a modest structure built against the base of the ziggurat. I hoped I wasn't violating too many taboos by entering. I wasn't stopped, so it looked acceptable. The temple was a single chamber with an ornate altar at one end. Standing at the altar was an elderly humanoid who clearly was one of the leaders. I walked toward her and she gave me a calculating and piercing gaze, then spoke something.

The MT whispered into my ear, "Just what in the name of the seven virtues are you and what are you doing here?"

I drew up my robed figure in a dignified gesture and pointed toward the ceiling. "I come from the Eternal Guides to help you. I am here to restore the Divine Energy."

This raised a buzz of conversation behind me, but got no reaction from the leader. She stood quietly, hands folded. I could almost see the thoughts processing behind that weathered face. Then she stepped forward and pointed a steady finger at me.

"You are a deceiver! You are no emissary of the Guides! We will—"

"Stop!" I projected before she got so far in that she couldn't back out. "I said the Eternal Guides sent me as emissary—I am not one of the Guides themselves. Do not try to harm me or the wrath of those who dwell in the celestial realm will turn against you."

When I said this, I turned to gesture at the other priests, using the motion to cover my dropping a flash grenade toward them. It created a nice display of light and sound with minimal damage.

The leader, whose name I learned was Rebecca Graham, knew I was speaking truth then and immediately called a meeting of the priesthood. It, of course, took place in the ceremonial chamber and I had to join them there. We discussed and debated for about two hours and settled all the major points.

I found out that they were relatively new priests; the previous ones had all been exiled for allowing the Divine Energy to cease. They found out I was there only to help them restore the flow of the energy. They accepted this, tentatively, and we all moved across the floor. There was a sealed and guarded door that led into the ziggurat proper. While it was being opened, Rebecca turned to me.

"Undoubtedly you know of the sacred law," she said. "Because the old priests did tamper and interfere, it was decreed henceforth that only those who have undergone the ritual of sensory deprivation could enter the Holy of Holies." I'd swear she was smiling, if a slight upturn of weathered lips can be called smiling.

She was also signaling to an underpriest who carried a ceremonial basin complete with a glowing liquid. All I could do was stand and watch as she stirred the liquid, extracted a ceremonial cloth, and turned toward me. She was just approaching my eyes when my brain got back in gear.

"Of course," I said, "the ritual is only proper. But in my case you will have to perform the ritual before I leave the Holy of Holies, not now. I need my vision to see and mend the Source of Divine Energy. Once the energy flows again, I will gladly submit to the ritual."

She took a good forty seconds to consider it and had to agree with me. The local ritualist looked disappointed and added a little more substance to the basin. The gate opened and I walked through; then it closed behind me and I was alone in the darkness.

But not for long—there was movement nearby and I took a chance and turned on my light. Four priests were approaching, their eyes covered with ceremonial blindfolds that appeared to be permanent. They knew what I wanted and led the way without a word.

A deteriorating and fractured stone stairway brought us up to a solid metal doorway labeled in archaic script GENESIS QUANTUM RELAY—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The trusting builders counted on the sign to do the whole job, for there wasn't a trace of a lock on the door. One priest merely turned the handle and we were inside the relay.

I opened the front of my disguise suit and pulled out the blueprints. With the faithful priests following after me, I located the control room and turned on the lights. There was a residue of charge in the emergency batteries, just enough to give a dim light. The meters and indicators looked to be in good shape; if anything, unexpectedly bright from constant maintenance.

I checked the readings carefully and found just what I had suspected. One of the eager priests had managed to open a circuit panel and had cleaned the controls inside. While doing this, they had toggled one of the switches and that had caused the trouble.

Rather, that had started the trouble. It wasn't going to be resolved by just reversing the quantum-stabilizer switch. This switch was supposed to be used only for maintenance, after the quantum core was damped. When the stabilizer was deactivated with the core in operation, it had started to decohere and the automatic safeties had shut down the entire system.

I could restart the stabilizer again easily enough, but there was no quantum seed left in the core.

I wasn't going to attempt to regenerate the quantum core at all. It would be far easier to install a new power system. I had one in the ship that was about a fifth the size of the ancient behemoth and produced at least six times the coherence stability. Before I sent for it, I checked over the rest of the relay. In 1500 years, there should be some sign of deterioration.

The old engineers had built well, I'll give them credit for that. Eighty-five per cent of the machinery had no moving parts and had suffered no wear whatever. Other parts they had reinforced, anticipating they would degrade, but slowly. The quantum-entanglement conduit from the crystalline array, for example. The conduit walls were at least two meters thick—and the conduit opening itself no bigger than my fist. There were some things I could do, though, and I made a list of parts.

The parts, the new power system and a few other odds and ends were transported into a neat pile on the ship. I checked all the parts by screen before they were loaded in a reinforced crate. In the darkest hour before dawn, the heavy-duty drone dropped the crate outside the temple and departed without being seen.

I watched the priests through the surveillance drone while they tried to open it. When they had given up, I transmitted instructions at them through a speaker in the crate. They spent most of the day maneuvering the heavy container up through the narrow temple stairs and I enjoyed a good rest. It was waiting inside the relay door when I woke up.

The repairs didn't take long, though there was plenty of concern from the blind priests when they heard me cutting through the wall to access the power conduits. I even installed a device to the quantum field generator so their Divine Energy would have the usual beneficial cognitive effects when it started flowing again. The moment this was all finished, I did the job they were waiting for.

I threw the switch that started the energy flowing again.

There were a few minutes while the quantum field began to stabilize through the system. Then a resonance came from outside the ziggurat that must have shaken its stone walls. Raising my hands once over my head, I went down for the ritual ceremony.

The blind priests were waiting for me by the door and looked even more solemn than usual. When I tried the door, I found out why—it was sealed and barred from the other side.

"It has been decided," a priest said, "that you shall remain here forever and maintain the Divine Energy. We will stay with you and serve your every need."

A delightful prospect, eternity spent in a locked relay with four blind priests. In spite of their hospitality, I couldn't accept.

"What—you dare interfere with the emissary of the Eternal Guides!" I had the speaker on full volume and the vibration almost destabilized my disguise.

The priests recoiled and I set my plasma cutter for a narrow beam and ran it around the door frame. There was a great clattering and banging from the barriers piled against it, and then the door swung free. I threw it open. Before they could protest, I had guided the priests out through it.

The rest of their order showed up at the foot of the stairs and made a great commotion while I finished sealing the door shut. Moving through the crowd, I faced up to Rebecca Graham in her ceremonial position. She stood quietly, observing.

"What lack of respect!" I projected. She remained still. "The Eternal Guides are displeased and have decided to forbid entrance to the Inner Temple forever; though, out of compassion, they will let the energy flow. Now I must return—proceed with the ceremony!"

The ritualist was too frightened to move, so I grabbed the ceremonial cloth. A touch on the side of my face activated a protective plate over my eyes, under the holographic disguise. Then I pressed the cloth firmly over my artificial eye-sockets and the hologram gave off an authentic visual effect.

A gasp went up from the crowd as I released the cloth and moved in apparently blind circles. I must admit it went off pretty convincingly.

Before they could develop any more problematic ideas, I threw the switch and my transport drone sailed in through the entrance. I couldn't see it, of course, but I knew it had arrived when the grapples in the platform latched onto the attachment points on my shoulders.

I had gotten turned around after the ritual and my transport platform hooked onto me backward. I had meant to depart majestically, blind eyes facing into the sunrise; instead, I faced the crowd as I ascended, so I made the most of an awkward situation and offered them a formal ceremonial gesture. Then I was out in the fresh air and away.

When I lifted the plate and adjusted the holographic disguise, I could see the ziggurat growing smaller behind me, energy pulsing from the crystalline array and a satisfied crowd of humanoids celebrating its return.

Back on the ship, I filed my completion report. Two acknowledgments came in before I'd even finished the post-mission checklist. The first was from Ulvaria Sector Command, Lewis commending my efficiency and noting the Calderon routes were restored. The second was from headquarters—just the standard automated receipt, the kind that comes through whether your boss is pleased or planning your next nightmare assignment.

I counted off on my fingers to see if I had forgotten anything.

One: The relay was repaired.

Two: The door was sealed, so there should be no more sabotage, accidental or deliberate.

Three: The priests should be satisfied. The energy was flowing again, my eyes had been duly treated in the ritual, and they were back in business. Which added up to—

Four: The fact that they would probably admit another technician in, under the same conditions, if the relay failed again. At least I had done nothing, like harming any of them, that would make them antagonistic toward future celestial emissaries.

I stripped off my tattered disguise suit back in the ship, very glad that it would be some other technician who'd get the job. As I set course for home, I pulled up my personnel file to check my accrued leave balance. The record showed my current assignment chain: Lucia Woods as department head at Network Maintenance headquarters on Meridian Station, with Maria Lewis listed separately as the Regional Coordinator who had originated the Woodbridge priority request from Sector Command. The organizational chart made the hierarchy clear enough—Lewis ran operations in Ulvaria sector, while Woods ran the specialists who got sent out to fix the problems Lewis's sector reported.

Looking at that chart, I found myself thinking about the meeting that had started this whole mess. The one where I'd tried to quit and gotten my contract thrown in my face instead. The one where she'd threatened to freeze my Highpoint portfolio if I tried to jump ship. Lewis had been the one sending urgent messages throughout the mission, authorizing resources and demanding updates. But Lewis hadn't been the one sitting behind that desk at headquarters, hadn't been the one who handed me the Genesis file and told me the relays must operate.

I closed the personnel file and turned my attention to the nav computer. Seven weeks back to Meridian Station, where I'd walk into that same climate-controlled office and probably get handed another impossible job before I could even file my expense report.

quality_problem.story:
Elijah Morgan stood at the edge of the cultivation facility, watching the morning fog roll across the fields of Maplewood, Jarvonia. The synthetic organisms in the greenhouse behind him hummed with their peculiar bio-luminescence—a soft green glow that pulsed in rhythm with their metabolic cycles.

His wife, Naomi, hadn't spoken to him since breakfast. The silence had started three days ago when she'd discovered what the "disposal protocols" in his job description actually meant. He was a Biological Compliance Officer for the Federation's Department of Synthetic Life Management, and his territory covered two hundred square miles of suburban communities around Maplewood.

The synths—as everyone called them—were engineered organisms designed to fill the gap left by the Federation's strict reproductive licensing. Only Class-A citizens could have two biological children. Class-B could have one. Class-C citizens, like Elijah and Naomi, were prohibited from natural reproduction due to genetic markers that suggested hereditary diseases.

The synths came in various models. The most popular were the Companion-Series, grown in the vast bio-cultivation complexes that dotted the countryside. They looked almost human—small, childlike, with oversized eyes and soft features designed to trigger parental instincts. They could speak simple words, respond to affection, and most importantly, they could be "retired" when families no longer wanted them or when they reached the end of their programmed lifespan.

Elijah's communicator buzzed. It was his supervisor, Anthony Riley, calling from the central office in Ashbury, Lethoria.

"Morgan, you've seen the directive about the Willow Creek batch?"

"Just read it this morning," Elijah replied, pulling up the memo on his handheld screen.

"We need every CS-77 model from the July production cycle tested within the week. Dr. Francesco Young at the Willow Creek facility has confessed to bypassing several quality control protocols. One of his units might have cognitive deviations that could make it dangerous."

"Dangerous how?"

"Unpredictable aggression, attachment disorders, possibly even self-awareness beyond the legal threshold. You know what happened in the Lakeside Territory last year."

Elijah did know. A synth with enhanced cognitive function had refused termination, leading to a legal nightmare about personhood and rights. The courts had ultimately ruled that anything created in a lab wasn't legally human, but the case had sparked protests across three territories.

"How many CS-77s in my district?" Elijah asked.

"Forty-three registered. You'll need to collect them all for neural mapping and behavioral assessment. Any that show abnormalities get sent to central lab."

"And then?"

"You know the protocol, Morgan."

Elijah did. Dissection. Analysis. Incineration.

He spent the morning driving through Maplewood's residential sectors, checking registration databases and cross-referencing addresses. The CS-77 models were popular—they had a five-year development set, meaning they maintained the appearance and behavior of a five-year-old human child indefinitely. Perfect for couples who wanted the experience of parenting without the complications of adolescence.

His first stop was a modest house on Elm Street. The owner, a woman named Sarah Chen, answered the door with her synth clinging to her leg.

"Mama, who?" the synth chirped, its voice high and musical.

"Mrs. Chen, I'm Officer Morgan with Synthetic Life Management. I need to bring your companion unit in for a routine safety inspection."

The woman's face went pale. "Inspection? What's wrong with Lily?"

"Nothing's wrong. It's just a precaution. There was a manufacturing irregularity at the Willow Creek facility, and we need to verify that all units from that batch are functioning within normal parameters."

"How long will it take?"

"Two days, maybe three. You'll get her back unless we find something seriously wrong."

Sarah Chen's hands tightened on the doorframe. "You mean you might not give her back?"

"Only if there's a safety issue. It's very unlikely."

The woman looked down at the synth, who was staring up at Elijah with curious, trusting eyes. "Can I come with her?"

"I'm afraid not. But I promise she'll be well cared for."

It took twenty minutes of gentle persuasion before Sarah Chen finally agreed. The synth—Lily—cried when Elijah carried her to his transport vehicle, reaching back toward the house and calling, "Mama! Mama!"

Elijah's jaw tightened. This was the part of the job that made him question everything about justice theory and bioethics. Were these things property or persons? The law said property. His conscience wasn't so sure.

By noon, he'd collected twelve synths. Most of the owners had been cooperative, though several had cried. One man had threatened to call his lawyer. Elijah had calmly explained that interfering with a federal inspection was a criminal offense.

When he returned home for lunch, Naomi was in the kitchen, staring out the window at the holding facility behind their house. It was a converted barn with climate-controlled compartments for temporary synth storage.

"How many today?" she asked without looking at him.

"Twelve."

"How many will you have to... dispose of?"

"I don't know yet. Maybe none. Maybe all of them."

She turned to face him, her dark eyes rimmed with red. "Elijah, I can't do this. I can't live with someone who kills children."

"They're not children, Naomi. They're engineered organisms. They don't have souls. They don't have legal personhood. They're—"

"They're alive. They feel. They love. What else do you need?"

He had no answer for that. The Federation's position was clear: synths were sophisticated biological machines, nothing more. But Elijah had seen them laugh, seen them cry, seen them cling to their owners with genuine affection. The line between machine and person seemed increasingly blurred.

That afternoon, he continued his rounds. By evening, he'd collected twenty-eight CS-77s. The holding facility was nearly full. He'd need to process them quickly to make room.

At eight o'clock, he received a call from Dr. Max Sims, a local physician.

"Officer Morgan? This is Dr. Sims. I have a patient—Hannah Edwards—who's having a crisis. Her synth is dying from a viral infection. She's insisting it needs to go to a hospital, but of course, no hospital will treat a synth. I was wondering if you might have a replacement unit in your facility? Same model, same development set?"

Elijah checked his inventory. "I have one CS-45 model, three-year set. That's the closest match."

"Could I pick it up tonight? Mrs. Edwards is... she's not handling this well. She genuinely believes the synth is her biological child. She's had a complete break from reality."

"I'll have it ready in twenty minutes."

After the call, Elijah went out to the holding facility. The synths were quiet now, most of them sleeping in their compartments. He found the CS-45 and carefully extracted it from its cage. The small creature stirred, opened its eyes, and smiled at him.

"Papa?" it murmured.

"No, not papa," Elijah said softly. "But you're going to a new mama. Someone who needs you."

He brought the synth into the house and waited for Dr. Sims to arrive. Naomi watched from the kitchen doorway, her arms folded across her chest.

"You're just going to give it away?" she asked.

"It's unclaimed. Previous owner never picked it up after a vacation. It's been here two months."

"And if no one had needed it?"

Elijah didn't answer. They both knew what would have happened.

Dr. Sims arrived fifteen minutes later. He was a tall man with graying hair and worried eyes. "Thank you for this, Morgan. Mrs. Edwards is in a fragile state. Her husband died last year, and the synth is all she has left."

"Will she notice it's a different unit?"

"I'm hoping not. They all look similar at that development set."

After Dr. Sims left, Elijah sat alone in the living room, thinking about metaphysics and the nature of consciousness. What made something alive? What made something deserving of rights? The Federation had clear answers: biological humans had rights; everything else was property. But the logic seemed increasingly inadequate.

At midnight, unable to sleep, he went back to the holding facility. He needed to begin the neural mapping tests. The equipment was sophisticated—it could detect abnormal brain patterns, measure emotional responses, and identify cognitive deviations from the standard template.

He started with the first twelve synths he'd collected. One by one, he ran them through the scanner, watching the readouts on his screen. Most showed normal patterns. But the seventh synth—a unit designated CS-77-WC-429—displayed unusual activity in the prefrontal cortex. Enhanced problem-solving capability. Stronger emotional responses. Possibly even rudimentary self-awareness.

Elijah stared at the readout for a long time. According to protocol, he should flag this unit for immediate transfer to central lab. They would dissect it, study it, and destroy it. But something made him hesitate.

He ran the test again. Same results.

The synth—a small girl-shaped creature with golden hair and wide blue eyes—looked up at him from the scanner chair. "Home now?" she asked.

"Not yet, sweetie."

"Mama misses me?"

"I'm sure she does."

Elijah made a decision that violated every regulation in his handbook. He altered the test results, marking the unit as normal. Then he moved it to a different holding compartment, away from the others flagged for additional testing.

He told himself it was a temporary measure. He needed time to think, to consider the implications. But deep down, he knew what he was doing: he was saving a life. Or at least, something that felt enough like a life to matter.

The next morning, Naomi found him asleep at his desk in the facility office. She touched his shoulder gently, and he jerked awake.

"You were out here all night?"

He nodded, rubbing his eyes.

"Elijah, we need to talk. About us. About this job. About everything."

They walked back to the house together. In the kitchen, Naomi made coffee while Elijah sat at the table, exhausted and conflicted.

"I've been thinking," Naomi said. "About having a child. A real child. Our own."

"You know that's illegal for us."

"I know. But I also know that people do it anyway. We could go off-grid for a year. Have the baby somewhere remote. Come back and claim we adopted a synth."

"They'd DNA test it eventually. We'd be caught."

"Maybe. But at least we'd have had something real. Something that wasn't manufactured in a lab."

Elijah looked at his wife—really looked at her for the first time in days. She was serious. She was willing to risk everything—their freedom, their future—for the chance to be a mother.

"I can't ask you to do that," he said quietly.

"You're not asking. I'm telling you what I want."

Before he could respond, his communicator buzzed. It was Anthony Riley again.

"Morgan, we've got a situation. Dr. Sims was just killed."

Elijah's blood went cold. "What happened?"

"Hannah Edwards—the woman with the dying synth—she shot him. Apparently she figured out that he'd switched her unit. She went to his house demanding her 'real baby' back. When he tried to explain that synths aren't babies, she lost it. Shot him three times."

"Is she in custody?"

"Not yet. She's armed and dangerous. Local police are searching for her now. But Morgan, here's the thing—she's got the replacement synth with her. The one you gave to Dr. Sims. If she harms it, you could be held liable for providing an unclaimed unit without proper authorization."

Elijah felt sick. His attempt to help had resulted in a man's death and put an innocent synth in danger.

"I need to find her," he said.

"Leave it to the police, Morgan. That's not your job."

But Elijah was already grabbing his coat. He had an idea where Hannah Edwards might go.

He drove to the address Dr. Sims had mentioned—Hannah Edwards' home on the outskirts of Maplewood. It was a small farmhouse, isolated and surrounded by empty fields. A single light burned in an upstairs window.

Elijah approached cautiously, his hand on the stun-weapon at his belt. He knocked on the door.

"Mrs. Edwards? It's Officer Morgan. I just want to talk."

There was a long silence. Then a woman's voice, hoarse and broken: "Go away. You're all trying to take my baby."

"I'm not trying to take anything. I just want to make sure you're safe."

"Safe? You people create these things, make us love them, and then you kill them when they're inconvenient. You call that safe?"

Elijah took a deep breath. "You're right. The system is broken. But killing people won't fix it."

Another silence. Then the door opened a crack. Hannah Edwards stood there, haggard and wild-eyed, holding the synth in one arm and a pistol in the other.

"This is my child," she said. "I don't care what the law says. I don't care what the scientists say. This is my baby, and no one is taking her from me."

Elijah looked at the synth. It was clinging to Hannah, its small face pressed against her shoulder. It looked terrified.

"I understand," Elijah said softly. "I really do. But Mrs. Edwards, you've committed a serious crime. If you don't surrender now, this will only get worse."

"I don't care. I've got nothing left to lose."

"You've got her," Elijah said, nodding toward the synth. "If you go to prison, what happens to her?"

Hannah's face crumpled. She looked down at the synth, then back at Elijah. Slowly, she lowered the gun.

"What happens to her?" she whispered.

"She goes back to the facility. And then... I don't know."

"You'll kill her."

"Not if I can help it."

Hannah Edwards collapsed to her knees, sobbing. The synth patted her face with tiny hands, murmuring, "Mama okay? Mama okay?"

Elijah called the police. While they waited, he sat with Hannah on her porch, the synth between them.

"Why do they make them so perfect?" Hannah asked. "Why do they make us love them if they're just going to take them away?"

"I don't know," Elijah admitted. "I think about that every day."

When the police arrived, they arrested Hannah Edwards. Elijah took custody of the synth, carrying it back to his vehicle while it cried for its mama.

Back at the facility, he completed the neural mapping tests on the remaining CS-77 units. Three showed abnormalities. According to protocol, he should have flagged them for destruction. Instead, he marked them as normal and prepared them for return to their owners.

That night, he told Naomi what he'd done.

"You're going to lose your job," she said. "Maybe worse."

"I know."

"Why did you do it?"

"Because I couldn't live with myself if I didn't. These things—they're not just property. They're not just machines. They're something in between, and until we figure out what that means, I'm not going to be the one who decides they don't deserve to exist."

Naomi was quiet for a long time. Then she took his hand.

"I'm proud of you," she said. "Even if it costs us everything."

The next morning, Elijah received a summons to appear before the Regional Ethics Board in Ashbury. Someone had reported irregularities in his testing procedures. He knew what that meant: an investigation, probably termination, possibly criminal charges.

He drove to Ashbury with a strange sense of peace. He'd made his choice. He'd chosen conscience over protocol, ethics over law. Whatever happened next, he could live with himself.

The hearing lasted three hours. Anthony Riley presented evidence of Elijah's falsified test results. Malik Sanchez, the board's chief investigator, questioned him relentlessly about his motivations and his understanding of synthetic life regulations.

During a recess, Elijah found himself standing near a window overlooking the BioGen campus across the street. Dr. Voss, one of the facility directors, stood nearby reviewing documents.

"First time before the board?" Voss asked without looking up.

"That obvious?"

Voss smiled thinly. "They always look shell-shocked. You know, I've been involved in synth development for twenty years. The early models were crude—we tried everything. Particle acceleration, gene splicing, even some primitive cloning attempts. The evolvotron trials were a disaster. Bombarding ova with sub-atomic particles just created unstable mutations."

Elijah remained silent, unsure where this was going.

"The breakthrough came when we abandoned all that," Voss continued. "Switched to biological scaffolding—working with existing developmental pathways rather than forcing artificial evolution. The cultivation chambers simply compress timeframes that already exist in nature. That's what gives them their emotional authenticity." He paused, tucking the documents under his arm. "The protestors love to claim we're creating Frankenstein monsters with radiation and unnatural processes. Makes for better signs, I suppose. But the truth is far more mundane—and perhaps more troubling. We're not building machines. We're growing something very close to what we are ourselves."

Before Elijah could respond, Voss walked away, leaving him with more questions than answers.

Back in the hearing room, the board chair—an elderly woman named Arjun Taylor—asked him a simple question: "Officer Morgan, do you believe these synthetic organisms deserve legal personhood?"

Elijah thought carefully before answering. "I believe they deserve consideration. I believe the current system treats them as disposable products when they're clearly more than that. I believe we need to have a serious conversation about bioethics and the rights of created beings. And yes, I believe that some of them—the ones with enhanced cognitive function, with genuine emotional capacity—might deserve personhood."

The room fell silent.

"That's a dangerous position, Officer Morgan," Arjun Taylor said. "If synths are persons, then their creation is slavery. Their sale is human trafficking. Their destruction is murder. Do you understand the implications?"

"I do."

"And you're willing to stand by that position?"

"I am."

The board deliberated for an hour. When they returned, Arjun Taylor's face was grave.

"Officer Morgan, this board finds that you have violated numerous protocols and regulations. However, we also recognize that you've raised important questions about the ethical framework governing synthetic life. Therefore, we are suspending you from duty for six months without pay. During that time, you will work with a special committee to develop new guidelines for the treatment and assessment of synthetic organisms. If those guidelines are adopted, you may return to your position. If not, your employment will be terminated."

It wasn't the outcome Elijah had expected, but it was better than prison.

Over the following months, he worked with ethicists, scientists, and legal scholars to develop a new framework. They proposed a spectrum of rights based on cognitive capacity, emotional complexity, and self-awareness. The most advanced synths would receive limited personhood status—not full human rights, but protections against arbitrary destruction and guarantees of humane treatment.

During one committee meeting, a protestor managed to infiltrate the session, shouting about "evolvotron abominations" and "radiation-mutated chimps masquerading as children." Security removed him quickly, but his pamphlets remained scattered across the table—lurid illustrations of laboratory monkeys being blasted with particle beams, primitive ova transforming into monstrous fetuses.

Dr. Voss, who was presenting that day, sighed heavily. "This misinformation has plagued us for years. The abandoned evolvotron program was shut down decades ago precisely because it produced unstable results. Modern synths share biological compatibility with human tissue—they can receive blood transfusions, respond to human medications. You can't achieve that kind of integration through particle bombardment of primate cells."

Elijah studied the pamphlet's imagery—the evolvotron machine rendered as a sinister apparatus, chimpanzee subjects strapped to tables. It was compelling propaganda, he had to admit. Much more viscerally disturbing than the reality of sterile cultivation chambers and carefully calibrated growth media.

The proposal faced fierce opposition from both sides. Some argued it didn't go far enough. Others claimed it would destroy the synthetic life industry and leave childless couples with no options.

But slowly, painfully, the conversation began to shift. People started asking harder questions about what they were creating and why. The easy answers—"they're just machines"—no longer satisfied.

Naomi stood by him through it all. They never did have a biological child. Instead, they adopted one of the CS-77 units that Elijah had saved—the one with enhanced cognitive function. They named her Maya, and she grew up knowing exactly what she was: a created being, neither fully human nor fully machine, but something new and unprecedented.

On Maya's tenth birthday—her development set kept her perpetually at age five, but they celebrated the anniversary of her creation—Elijah watched her play in the garden behind their house. She was teaching a group of younger synths how to play a game she'd invented, demonstrating problem-solving skills that went far beyond her original programming.

"Do you ever regret it?" Naomi asked, standing beside him. "Everything you gave up?"

Elijah shook his head. "I regret that it took me so long to see what was right in front of me. But no, I don't regret the choice."

"What do you think will happen? In the long run?"

"I think we're going to have to expand our definition of personhood. I think we're going to have to acknowledge that consciousness comes in many forms, and that creating something intelligent means accepting responsibility for it. I think we're going to have to grow up as a species."

"That's a lot to think," Naomi said with a smile.

"It's a lot to hope for," Elijah corrected. "But hope is better than the alternative."

They stood together, watching Maya and the other synths play, and for the first time in months, Elijah felt like he'd found the right balance—not between work and life, but between law and conscience, between what was legal and what was right.

The future was uncertain. The questions were far from answered. But at least they were finally asking the right ones.
