I remember that my grandmother never bought anything from QuantumMed because of some incident her grandmother had once with the firm. My mother didn't want me to come to work here because of that."

Daniel put his arm around Mira in a way that he intended to look mentorly. It didn't. "Well, now. Since it's your relative, let's delight the old woman. We'll give her the finest equipment we have in stock!"

A warehouse technician appeared at Daniel's elbow, tablet in hand. "Sir, I've located most items on the list. The scanner, the health monitor, the medication dispenser—all available in our premium line."

"Excellent! Pack them up."

The technician hesitated. "There's one complication. The third item on the list—we don't carry anything by that exact name anymore. Our inventory system shows we have NeuroSync neural enhancement units in that product category now. Should I substitute?"

"Perfect! Send whatever's closest. The old woman won't know the difference after ninety years." Daniel waved his hand dismissively and reached for another drink.

---

Ruth Wheeler was returning from filing a complaint at the local QuantumMed office when she found the large parcel on her doorstep in Glendale, Wendria. She put her hands on her hips and stared suspiciously at the container.

"The minute I submit a formal complaint about you, you materialize!" she told the parcel. She nudged her toe irritably against the silver wrappings that were sealed with a half-transparent binding material she had never seen before.

The label was addressed in a wandering scrawl, a sharp contrast to the impersonal printing on the customary QuantumMed packages. But the familiar FRAGILE MEDICAL EQUIPMENT sticker was pasted onto the box, indicating to the delivery person that the contents required careful handling.

Ruth sighed and picked up her bundle. With a last look at the lovely spring afternoon and the quiet suburban landscape of Glendale, she went into the house.

Five-year-old Isabel heard the box humming. She toddled up on energetic legs and grabbed her grandmother's skirt. "Want!" she said decisively.

"Your medication dispenser ought to be here," Ruth said. She found scissors in her sewing box, tossed a cushion onto the floor, sat on it, and began to open the parcel.

"Now I'll have to submit another form to explain that they should disregard my complaint," she told her granddaughter. "And by the time they receive my second form, they'll have responded to my first form. Then they'll write again." Out of consideration for Isabel, she omitted the expletives that she wanted to add.

The translucent binding was too tough for the scissors. Ruth was about to hunt for a laser cutter when Isabel clutched at an intersection of the cord and yanked. The binding sprang away from the carton as if it were programmed. The wrappings flapped open.

"There!" Isabel said.

Ruth repressed an irrational urge to scold her granddaughter. Instead, she tossed the wrappings aside and removed the lid from the carton. A slightly crushed thin cardboard box lay on top. Ruth pulled out the medication dispenser and examined it carefully. Then she groaned.

It was silver and she had ordered white. It didn't remotely resemble the dispenser she had admired from the QuantumMed catalogue illustration. Moreover, the device had unusual protrusions that no standard medication dispenser should have.

But Isabel was delighted. "Mine!" she shrilled, grabbing for the device.

"It's probably the wrong model, too," Ruth said, examining the control panel. "Let's identify as many defects to complain about as we can."

The device seemed to activate when Isabel touched it. A soft blue glow emanated from its surface. Isabel was radiant for a moment. Then her small face sobered and she started to look vacantly at the distant wall.

"We'll have to return it," Ruth said, "and get the one we ordered."

She tried to take it from Isabel's hands, but the child resisted violently. Ruth grabbed her granddaughter's wrists, held them firmly and tried to pry the device away. It seemed to be adhered somehow. When Ruth released the child's wrists to examine the device more closely, Isabel stepped backward, then began to levitate three feet above the ground. She landed just before she collided with the far wall.

Isabel looked scared until she saw her grandmother's face. Then she squealed in delight.

Ruth's legs were rubber. She was shaking her head and wobbling uncertainly toward her granddaughter when the door opened behind her.

"It's me," her son Felix said. "Slow day at the research institute, so I came home early."

"Felix! I'm experiencing some kind of hallucination or something. Isabel just—"

"Mom! Your complaint was resolved? Good. What's this thing?" He was looking at a small cylindrical device he had pulled from the carton. Its surface contained a single word: NEUROSYNC. The device hummed when he held it.

"Is this the diagnostic scanner? I've never seen technology like this. And there's no power source visible."

"I don't know," Ruth said. "Felix, listen. A moment ago, Isabel—"

He peered into the box for an instruction manual, uselessly. "They must have made an error. It looks like some kind of experimental biotechnology equipment."

He placed the NeuroSync onto the coffee table and delved into the carton again. Isabel was still in his arms.

"That's the scanner, I think," he said, looking at the next object. It had a lovely, streamlined shape, multiple sensor arrays and a connection port for a power outlet.

"That's curious," Ruth mused, her mind distracted from Isabel for a moment. "It looks terribly advanced. Maybe they sent a premium model instead of the standard scanner."

The bottom of the carton contained the health monitor that they had ordered for Isabel. Ruth glanced at its sleek interface and counted silently: one scanner, one health monitor, one medication dispenser, one mysterious cylinder. She frowned, mentally checking items against her original order. Three of the four items seemed accounted for, though wildly different from what she'd expected. But that cylindrical thing with NEUROSYNC printed on it—she had no idea what category of medical equipment it was supposed to represent.

"Felix, about Isabel. Put her down a minute and observe what she does."

Felix stared at his mother and placed the child onto the carpet. Isabel began to walk, then rose and again levitated, this time toward the coffee table on which the NeuroSync rested.

His jaw dropped. "My God! Mom, what—"

Ruth was staring, too, but not at her granddaughter. "Felix! The coffee table! It used to be brown!"

The coffee table was a vivid shade of blue. A neon, demanding, screaming blue that clashed horribly with the soft earth tones in which Ruth had furnished the room.

"That cylindrical thing must be emitting something," Felix said, his background in complexity science kicking in. "But did you see Isabel when she—"

Ruth's frazzled nerves carried a frantic order to her muscles. She jumped up, strode to the coffee table and picked up the NeuroSync with two fingers. She tossed it to Felix. Immediately, she regretted her action.

"Drop it!" she yelled. "Maybe it'll alter your neural patterns, too!"

Felix kicked the coffee table into the hall closet, tossed the NeuroSync in after it and shut the door firmly. As the door closed, he saw the entire interior of the dark closet illuminate into a wet-sapphire blue.

When he turned back to Ruth, she was staring at her left wrist. The medical monitoring bracelet that the hospital had given her years ago was a brilliant blue, shedding its soft glow over her forearm up to the elbow.

Ruth felt the panic building up inside her. She opened her mouth to scream, then put her hand in front of her mouth to suppress it, finally jerked the hand away to prevent the glowing bracelet from turning her teeth blue.

She collapsed into Felix's arms, babbling incomprehensibly about epistemology and the nature of reality.

He said: "It's all right. There must be some kind of anti-gravity field or something in that medication dispenser. I'll attach a weight to Isabel's belt and that'll hold her down until we can remove the device. Don't worry. And that blue emission or whatever it is will dissipate."

Ruth immediately felt better. She put her hands behind her back, pulled off her bracelet and slipped it into her pocket. Felix was sentimental about her removing it.

"I'll prepare dinner," she said, trying to keep her voice steady. "Maybe you'd better start a complaint form to QuantumMed. Let's go into the kitchen, Isabel."

Ruth strode resolutely toward the rear of the house. She kept her eyes determinedly off the tinge of blue that was showing through her pocket and didn't dare look back at her granddaughter's unsettling means of propulsion.

A half-hour later, when the meal was almost ready, two things happened: Pablo Fuller came home from the university through the back door and a strange voice said from the front of the house, "Unauthorized access detected."

Ruth stared at her grandson. He stared back at her, the pediatric health monitor under his arm.

She went into the front room. Her son was standing with fists on hips, looking at the front door, chuckling. "Most sophisticated security system I've seen in a long time. That voice you heard was the new diagnostic scanner. I installed it while you were in the kitchen. Did you hear what happened when old Mr. Brennan out there approached the entrance?"

"Oh. Something like those smart home systems with voice warnings, like 'Motion detected.' Well, if there's some kind of AI in there repeating that message, you'd better deactivate that function. It might get annoying after a while. And it might offend someone."

Ruth went to the door and turned the handle. The door didn't open. The figure of Mr. Brennan, half-visible through the heavy curtain, shifted impatiently on the porch.

Felix yanked at the doorknob. It didn't yield for him, either. He looked up at the scanner, which he had installed just above the upper part of the door frame.

"Strange," he said, applying his knowledge of information theory. "That isn't in contact with the door mechanism itself. I don't see how it can prevent the door from opening."

Ruth put her mouth close to the glass, shouting: "Won't you come to the back door, Mr. Brennan? This one is malfunctioning."

"I just wanted to borrow some medical supplies," the man called from the porch. "I realize that I'm a terrible bother." But he walked down the front steps and disappeared around the side of the house.

"Biometric authentication required." The well-modulated voice from the small scanner box threatened to penetrate every corner of the house. Ruth looked doubtfully at her son's lips. They weren't moving.

"If this is some kind of prank—" she began icily.

"I'll have to order another scanner just like this one, for the lab," Felix said. "But you'd better let the old fellow in. No use letting him get upset."

The back door was already open, because it was a warm day. The screen door had no latch, held closed by a simple spring. Ruth pushed it open when Mr. Brennan trudged up the three back steps, and smiled at her neighbor.

"I'm so sorry you had to walk around the house. It's been a rather chaotic day in an awful lot of ways."

Something seemed to impede Mr. Brennan as he came to the threshold. He frowned and pushed his frail frame against something invisible. It apparently yielded abruptly, because he staggered forward into the kitchen, nearly falling. He stared grimly at Ruth and looked suspiciously behind him.

"The children have some new equipment," Ruth improvised hastily. "Isabel is so excited over a new device that she's positively euphoric. Let's see now—it was medical supplies that you need, wasn't it?"

"I already have them," Pablo said, handing a small package to his grandmother. The boy turned back to the health monitor which he had spread over the kitchen table, studying its interface with fascination.

"Excitement isn't good for me," Mr. Brennan said testily, his understanding of social dynamics clearly limited. "I've had a lot of health problems in my life. I like peace and stability."

"Your wife is better?"

"Worse. I'm sure I don't know why everything happens to me." Mr. Brennan edged toward the hall, trying to peer into the front of the house. Ruth stood squarely in front of the door leading to the hall. Defeated, Mr. Brennan left. A muffled series of beeps, mixed with a few faint diagnostic readings, came from the scanner-box when he crossed the threshold.

Ruth went into the hall to order Felix to disconnect the scanner. She nearly collided with him, coming in the other direction.

"Where did this come from?" Felix held a small object in the palm of his hand, keeping it away from his body. A few drops of something viscous were dripping from his fingers. The object looked remarkably like a miniature brain. It was human-size, complete with cortical folds, neural pathways and rather prominent blood vessels.

"Hey, that's mine," Pablo said. "You know, this is an unusual health monitor. That was in it. But there aren't instructions on how it operates."

"Well, put it away," Ruth told Pablo sharply. "It's disturbing."

Felix laid the brain-device on the table and walked away. The device rolled from the smooth, level table, bounced twice when it hit the floor, then rolled along, six inches behind him. He turned and kicked at it. The device rolled nimbly out of the path of the kick.

"Felix, I think we've made poor Mr. Brennan uncomfortable," Ruth said. "He's so upset over his wife's health and he thinks we're being inhospitable."

Felix didn't hear her. He strode to the health monitor, followed at a safe distance by the brain-device, and picked up the box.

"Hey, watch out!" Pablo cried. A small scanning wand fell from the box, landed on its side and its sensor flashed on, throwing a beam of light across Felix's hands.

Pablo retrieved the wand and turned it off while Felix glanced through an instruction manual, frowning.

"This equipment is too advanced for a twelve-year-old boy," Felix told his mother, his expertise in theoretical modeling evident. "I don't know why you ordered such a thing." He tossed the manual into the empty box.

"I'm going to return it, if you don't damage it," she replied. "Look at the marks you made on the instructions." The black marks stood out clearly against the glossy, coated paper.

Felix looked at his hands. "I didn't do it," he said, pressing his clean fingertips against the kitchen table.

Black marks, a full set of them, stood out against the sparkling polished table's surface.

"I think the BioScanner did it," Pablo said, using the term from the manual. "The instructions say you've got to be very careful with it, because its effects persist for an extended duration."

Felix began scrubbing his hands vigorously at the sink. Ruth watched him silently, until she saw his marks appear on the faucet, the soap dispenser and the towel. She began to reprimand him for making such a mess, when Isabel levitated into the kitchen. The girl was wearing a different outfit.

"My God!" Ruth forgot her language before the children. "She changed clothes herself. Where did she get that outfit?"

Ruth examined the garment. She didn't recognize it as sleepwear. But in cut and design, it was suspiciously like the medication dispenser interface that had arrived in the parcel. Her heart sank.

She picked up the child, felt the elevated temperature, and said: "Felix, I think it's the same device. It must adapt its appearance or something based on the user's physiological state. It seems impossible, but—" She shrugged mutely. "And I think Isabel's running a fever. I'm going to put her to bed."

She looked worriedly into the reddened eyes of the small girl, who whimpered on the way to the bedroom. Ruth carried her up the stairs, keeping her balance with difficulty, as Isabel threatened to float upward out of her arms.

The whole family decided that rest might be a good idea, soon after dinner. When the lights went out, the house seemed to be nearly normal. Felix put on a pair of gloves and threw a blanket over the brain-device. Pablo rigged up barriers to warn visitors from the front porch. Ruth put small earplugs into her ears, because she didn't like the rhythmic hum, soft but persistent, that emerged from the hall closet where the NeuroSync sat. Isabel was whimpering occasionally in her sleep.

When daylight entered her room, Isabel's outfit had transformed back into the medication dispenser interface. But the little girl was too sick to get out of bed. She wasn't hungry, her breathing was labored, and she had a persistent cough. Felix called the doctor before going to work.

The only positive thing about the morning for Ruth was the fact that the NeuroSync had quieted down some time in the night. After she got Pablo to school, she gingerly opened the closet door. The NeuroSync was now glowing a bright pink and seemed slightly larger. Deep violet text stood out on its surface:

"Today is Wednesday. For system maintenance, the NeuroSync will not operate today."

Ruth stared at the strange device. She had spent hours the previous night trying to recall every item on her original order form, cross-referencing what had actually arrived. The scanner was present, though far more advanced than expected. The health monitor had come, bizarre as it was. The medication dispenser was attached to Isabel. But this cylinder—she had never ordered anything called NeuroSync. She had ordered something else entirely in that fourth slot on the form, something her doctor had specifically recommended for her arthritis. Whatever this glowing cylinder was supposed to be, it certainly wasn't that.

The mail carrier brought a letter from QuantumMed. Ruth stared stupidly at the envelope, until she realized that this wasn't an impossibly quick response to the complaint she had filed yesterday. It must have crossed in transit her complaint about the non-delivery of the order. She tore open the envelope and read:

"We regret to inform you that your order cannot be processed until the outstanding balance you owe us has been reduced. From the attached statement, you will readily ascertain that the payment of $1,247.89 will enable you to resume the purchasing of medical equipment on credit. We shall process your recent order as soon...."

Ruth crumpled the letter and threw it into the recycling bin, knowing perfectly well that it would need to be retrieved for Felix after work tonight. She had just decided to contact QuantumMed's complaint department when the phone rang.

"I'm afraid I must ask you to come down to the school, Mrs. Wheeler," a voice said. "Your grandson is in trouble. He claims that it's connected with something that his family gave him."

"My grandson?" Ruth asked incredulously. "Pablo?"

"Yes. It's a small device that looks like a medical scanner. Your grandson insists that he didn't know it would make clothing transparent. He claims it was just an accident that he tried it out when he was walking by the gymnasium during physical education. We've had to request emergency blankets from every family in the neighborhood. Pablo has always been a good student and we believe that we can handle this discreetly without media publicity involving his name, if you'll—"

"I'll be right down," Ruth said. "I mean I won't be right down. I've got a sick child here. Don't do anything until I contact my son. And I'm sorry for Pablo. I mean I'm sorry for the students, and for the teachers, too. I'm sorry for—for everything. Goodbye."

Just as she hung up the telephone, the scanner rang with an alert. It chimed with a normal tone, then began to play soft diagnostic readings. Ruth opened the door without difficulty, to admit Dr. Zara Francis.

"You aren't going to believe me, Doctor," Ruth said while she took the child's temperature, "but we can't remove that device from Isabel."

"Children can be stubborn sometimes." Dr. Francis whistled softly when she looked at the thermometer. "She's quite ill. I need a blood sample before I attempt to move her. Let me examine her."

Isabel had been mumbling semi-deliriously. She made no effort to resist as the doctor picked her up. But when she raised a component of the device and began to detach it, Isabel screamed.

The doctor released the device and looked in perplexity at the point where it interfaced with Isabel's body.

"It's apparently an adverse reaction to some new kind of biotechnology. But I don't understand why the device won't detach. It's not physically bonded."

"Don't bother trying," Ruth said miserably, her understanding of healthcare policy telling her this would be complicated. "Just cut it off."

Dr. Francis pulled medical scissors from her bag and attempted to separate a component. When she had cut partway through, she gently began to peel back the edges of the material. Isabel writhed and kicked, then collapsed in unconsciousness. The physician smoothly restored the components back into place.

She looked helpless as she said to Ruth: "I don't know quite what to do. The tissue starts to hemorrhage when I manipulate the interface. She'd experience severe trauma if I removed it forcibly. But it's such an extreme reaction that it may harm her, if we leave it in contact with her body."

The NeuroSync's hum suddenly began rhythmically from the lower part of the house. Ruth clutched the side of the chair, trying to keep herself under control. A siren wailed somewhere down the street, grew louder rapidly, suddenly going silent at the peak of its crescendo.

Dr. Francis glanced outside the window. "An emergency vehicle. Looks as if they're stopping here."

"Oh, no," Ruth breathed. "Something's happened to Felix."

"It certainly will," Felix said grimly, walking into the bedroom. "I won't have employment if I can't remove this substance from my fingers. Black marks on everything I touch. I can't handle laboratory equipment or interact with research subjects. How's the child? What's the emergency vehicle doing out front?"

"They're going to the next house down the street," the physician said. "Has there been illness there?"

Felix held up his hands, palms toward the doctor. "What's wrong with me? My fingers appear normal. But they leave black marks on everything I touch."

The doctor looked closely at the fingertips, applying statistical inference. "Every human has natural secretions on the skin. That's how forensic scientists get results with their identification techniques. But I've never encountered chromatization, in this context. Better not attempt to handle sensitive materials until you've consulted a dermatological specialist."

Ruth was peering through the window, curious about the emergency vehicle despite her own troubles. She saw two paramedics carry Mrs. Brennan, motionless and pale, on a stretcher from the house next door into the vehicle. A third member of the crew was struggling with a disheveled Mr. Brennan at the door. Shouts that sounded like "Negligence!" came sharply through the window.

"I know those paramedics," Dr. Francis said. She opened the window. "Hey, Marcus! What's wrong?"

The front paramedic looked up. "I don't know. This woman's critically ill. I think her husband is experiencing psychological distress."

Mr. Brennan had broken free. He rushed halfway down the sidewalk, gesticulating wildly to nobody in particular.

"It's negligence!" he screamed. "Medical negligence again! She's been harmed by faulty equipment! She's going to die! It means legal consequences!"

The paramedic grabbed him again. This time he administered a mild sedative to calm him.

"Come back to this house as soon as you deliver her," Dr. Francis shouted to the crew. "We've got a very sick child up here."

"I was concerned this would happen," Felix said, his knowledge of behavioral economics evident in his analysis. "The poor man already has lost two wives to medical complications. If this one is ill, it's no wonder he thinks that somebody is responsible for medical negligence."

Pablo stuck his head around the bedroom door. His grandmother stared unbelievingly for a moment, then advanced on him threateningly. Something in his face restrained her, just as she was about to start reprimanding him.

"I got something important to tell you," Pablo said rapidly, ready to retreat. "I escaped from the principal's office and came home. I need to tell you what I did."

"I heard all about what you did," Ruth said, advancing again. "And you're not going to evade responsibility."

"Give me a chance to explain something. Downstairs. So she won't hear," Pablo ended in a whisper, nodding toward the doctor.

Ruth looked doubtfully at Felix, then followed Pablo down the stairs. The scanner was monotonously saying in a monotone: "Access denied, access denied, unauthorized entry prohibited."

"Why did you do it?" Ruth asked Pablo, her anger suddenly slumping into weary sadness. "People will suspect you of being disturbed for the rest of your life. You can't possibly explain—"

"Don't worry about the students' clothing," Pablo said, "because it was only an accident. The really important thing is something else I did before I left the house."

Felix, cursing softly, hurried past them on the way to answer the knocking. He ignored the scanner's warnings.

"I forgot about it," Pablo continued, "when that scanning device accidentally activated. Then when they confined me in the principal's office, I had time to think, and I remembered. I put some white substance from the health monitor into those medical supplies we lent Mr. Brennan last night. I just wanted to observe what would happen. I don't know exactly what effect—"

"He put substance in the medical supplies?" A deep, authoritative voice came from the front of the house. Mother and grandson looked through the hall. A police officer stood on the threshold of the front door. "I heard that! The man next door claims that his wife has been poisoned by medical negligence. Young man, I'm going to have to take you into custody."

The officer stepped over the threshold. A blue flash darted from the scanner box, striking him squarely on the chest. The officer staggered back, sitting down abruptly on the porch. A scent of ozone drifted through the house.

"Close the door, close the door," the scanner was announcing urgently.

"Where's that emergency vehicle?" Dr. Francis yelled from the top of the steps. "The child's condition is deteriorating."

Ruth sank into a chair, overwhelmed. She thought about the copy of her original order form, still filed in her desk drawer upstairs—four items carefully selected with her doctor's help. Three of them had arrived in some form, however strange. The fourth, the treatment she had hoped would finally ease the stiffness in her hands that made even holding Isabel difficult some mornings, had been replaced by that unsettling cylinder in the closet. QuantumMed had failed her again, just as they had failed her grandmother all those years ago.
quality_problem.question: What didn't Ruth receive from QuantumMed?
quality_problem.correct_answer: The gene therapy starter kit she ordered
answers: The gene therapy starter kit she ordered

quality_problem.story:
THE HARPER PROTOCOL
By BILL DOEDE

They lived in a modest apartment in Rosewood, Nordavia, in a building that had once been luxury condominiums before the Economic Collapse. The wealthy families who'd owned them had fled to offshore havens. Now the units were subdivided and rented cheaply. Ariana Kim and her daughter lived comfortably enough, even during the harshest winters. During summer months, Ariana ran a small consulting business helping local entrepreneurs with design thinking workshops. She had built a modest client base. They were able to make ends meet.

Her neighbors knew nothing of the encrypted files she had brought with her to Nordavia. They didn't even know she wasn't a native. She never spoke of it, except at first, when Bianca was a girl of seven and they had just arrived. Then she only said she came from the southern provinces. She knew the names of southern Nordavian towns, and small facts about them; it lent an air of authenticity to her claim. Actually her previous residence was Lincoln, Calderon, where the Regulators had killed her husband.

That was back in '07, on the eve of his departure for the Yarnmouth Station in Xandria; but she never spoke of this; and she was very careful not to move from place to place except by conventional methods of travel.

Also, she wore her hair long, almost to the shoulders, covering the small neural port behind her ear—evidence that a quantum processor lay embedded under her skin.

For Ariana Kim was one of the Jumpers.

Her husband had been one of the small group who developed this neural interface technology. Not the inventor—his name was Vincent Harper, and the effects produced by it were known as the Harper Protocol. In appearance the implant resembled a standard neural enhancement device. Analysis by the best scientific minds proved it to be just that—a neural enhancement.

Yet it held the power to move consciousness instantaneously from one body to any other prepared body across vast distances. Each unit was custom built, keyed to operate only by the specific neural pattern of the particular individual. The prepared bodies—clones grown in secret facilities—waited in cities across the world and beyond.

Several times in the past seven years Ariana had seen other Jumpers, and had been tempted to identify herself and say, "Here I am. You are one of them; so am I. Come, and we'll talk. We'll talk about Harper and Santiago Spencer, who helped them all escape. And Doctor Walter Gutierrez. And my husband, Roman Frank, who never got away because those filthy, unspeakable Regulators shot him in the back, there in that coffee shop in Lincoln, Calderon."

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a Regulator came and rented the apartment next door.

She learned that he was a Regulator completely by accident. While helping him move furniture, his identification badge fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands, all the loneliness returning in a black wave of hate and frustration.

That night she soundlessly picked his lock and administered a lethal injection while he slept.

She disposed of the syringe in the city incinerator. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators across the world; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Bianca, was grown.

Together they would seek justice. Bianca did not have the implant—not yet. But she would. The Jumpers took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned, the small bandage would be behind her ear. Ariana would shield her until the incision healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek justice.

Later they would go to Yarnmouth Station in Xandria, where a life free from Regulators could be lived. The station orbited a distant moon, far from Earth's political economy and its oppressive systems.

It happened to Bianca one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Ariana was working in her home office on a design thinking presentation; Bianca supposedly was at the community center with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her mother, completely disoriented and wearing only a hospital gown. At sight of her mother, Bianca's face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Ariana was forced to hold her firmly to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her daughter's ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the community center, where her friends were still visible in the courtyard. Apparently they did not miss her. Ariana handed her a sweater. "Here, cover yourself. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Ariana stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well understand now."

"Understand what?"

"That your consciousness can now jump between bodies."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was at the center, and a woman came up to me. Her hair was all white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Bianca Hunter, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a car and there was another person in it, that looked like the first one only younger. We went to a clinic, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a medical table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some technical language I don't know."

Bianca ran her hand through her hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be home with you. And then I was here."

Bianca faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better sit down," Ariana said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful in terms of time management and career planning."

"But what happened? What is this port behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped moving. "I know now. They made me a Jumper."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Ariana called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side, about political philosophy and economic development. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too. That is why you killed that Regulator next door."

It was Ariana's turn to be surprised. "You knew about that?"

"I saw the syringe wrapper in your pocket the next morning. I never told anyone."

"But you were only nine!"

"They would have taken you away if I'd said anything."

Ariana held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So Bianca sat across the kitchen table from her, and Ariana told the whole history, beginning with Vincent Harper sitting in the laboratory in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, holding in his hand a neural implant he had designed for medical purposes. He had made it to help paralysis patients control prosthetic limbs. He was holding this device... and it was connected to a clone body in the next room for testing... and he was thinking about being young again—

And suddenly his consciousness was there, in the clone body. He could not believe it at first. He felt the young muscles and reflexes, and examined himself; there was no mistake.

On the flight back to his old body he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more implants. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it properly, and he kept the secret, giving implants to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it quantum-entangled consciousness transfer, which was very theoretical modeling.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until one night a Regulator arrested one man for identity fraud. It was a valid charge. One disadvantage of this method of travel was that consciousness arrived in a clone body that looked nothing like the original.

The arrested man jumped to another body and disappeared, and the next morning the Regulator was found dead. This set off a campaign against Jumpers. One violent act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as trustworthy citizens.

Ariana told how Harper, knowing he had made too many implants and given them unwisely, left Earth for Yarnmouth Station in Xandria.

He went alone, not knowing if he could jump so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought—a place where political economy favored freedom over control.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in a warehouse in Rosewood—and their consciousnesses jumped in unison to clone bodies waiting at Yarnmouth Station, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at empty shells.

"You have asked many times," Ariana said, "how your father died. Now I will tell you the truth. Your father was one of the great ones, along with Harper and Spencer and Dr. Gutierrez. He helped plan the escape; but the Regulators found him in Lincoln fifteen minutes before the group jumped. They shot him in the back, and the others had to go on without him. Now do you know why I killed the Regulator next door? I had to. Your father was a great man, and I loved him."

"I don't blame you, mother," Bianca said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says 'Jumper' as if it is something dirty. They write it on bathroom walls."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them? It's basic consumer behavior and cultural sociology."

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Ariana watched Bianca leave the apartment, walking slowly along the street, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the community center, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would go to the park and sit by the fountain. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not jump far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within the city limits, because she still lacked the skills others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Ariana changed into lighter clothes and went for a walk to clear her mind.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, jumping to clone bodies in increasingly distant cities, until Bianca's confidence allowed her to reach any prepared body on Earth. Ariana knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a location sufficiently remote to ensure detection, Ariana would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly jump back to Rosewood. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only abandoned clone bodies. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Ariana as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Harper took his group to Xandria, that individuals had neural patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their scanners, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Ariana Kim had gone to Xandria with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Harper had selected only the most ethical Jumpers when he left Earth, leaving all those with criminal tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more profitable to stay. On Earth they could steal, extort, even murder—without fear of the law, since they could always jump to a new body.

Bianca changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Bianca," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Ariana would repeat all the things she remembered about Harper and Spencer and Gutierrez. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Spencer's partner, Zara Rivera, and try to describe the horror in Zara's young mind when the news went out that Roman Frank had been killed. She wanted Bianca to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after her. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of righteous anger.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Ariana wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Remember! Remember! You must never forget!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that Bianca would internalize it better if she avoided being too forceful.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Bianca was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Bianca referred to the "damn Regulators" now with contempt. They had been successful in contacting other Jumpers, and sometimes visited them at remote locations.

"When you have finished university," Ariana told her daughter, "we will go to Xandria together. That is our plan, and nothing will change it."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the development of the station. Harper is a neuroscientist, Spencer an engineer, Gutierrez a doctor. But Gutierrez is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Bianca. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Your knowledge of public health and organizational behavior will be invaluable."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Bianca would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she accessed the encrypted accounts she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Rosewood was abandoned. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Ariana furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Bianca's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of university students.

It was also convenient for jumping to clone bodies late at night after Regulator hunting.

Ariana was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Bianca facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were corrupt enforcers, tools of a decadent, authoritarian system, living off citizens' taxes.

She painted the room herself, in soft, calming colors. When it was finished she showed Bianca into the room with ceremony, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study groups students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," Bianca answered, "not here. No Jumpers will be at the university."

"Why not? Harper selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the implant is taken and adjusted to a new neural pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Jumpers will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Ariana said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable for your career planning."

Bianca shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

She said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being independent, at your age. Most young adults do."

"I'm not like most young adults, mother. The Jumpers saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Camila Singh?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how focused she was when she studied, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Camila—' just as if I was normal—'can I study with you for the exam?'"

Ariana turned to leave the room, but Bianca stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Jumper. You always will be a Jumper. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and left the room. Bianca stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been liberating for her. Her mother was crying just beyond the wall.

Bianca did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the implant was out of the question for them now, anyway—too risky with Regulators scanning constantly.

In the spring Ariana caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Bianca moved into the new bedroom. At first Ariana thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day Bianca disappeared.

Ariana was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Jumpers being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Jumper had raided the Regulator's office in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, killing three, and getting killed herself. Ariana immediately jumped to a clone body in Yarnmouth. She did not consider the risk. In Yarnmouth she obtained clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain woman had been a Lethonian Jumper, one of those left behind by Harper as ethically unsuitable. Her partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. She had gone completely insane and made the raid single-handedly. Ariana read the account of crimes committed by the woman and her partner, and determined to prevent Bianca from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she jumped back to her original body at home, Bianca was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that incident in Yarnmouth."

She shook her head.

Ariana stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a tablet. She was proud of her daughter's profile, determined and intelligent. Bianca tapped nervously on the desk.

"What did you do?" she asked.

Suddenly Bianca pushed the tablet away, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Lincoln, Calderon."

Ariana had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to access the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the men who killed Father." She said the word with difficulty. She was unaccustomed to thinking of him that way.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the tablet on her desk. Ariana, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches, evil sounds. "Marcus Webb" didn't sound evil; neither did "David Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Bianca to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for justice. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask how I broke in without triggering alarms. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Jumpers must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Jumpers? We hunt them because there is no prison that will hold a Jumper. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us. It's a matter of political philosophy and collective memory—we can coexist.'"

Ariana was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Ariana stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her daughter's arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Ariana gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. Bianca had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to herself. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the men were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over the world. In the hunting of Jumpers, some implants might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the implants gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to acquire them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the men on Bianca's list might have acquired an implant and were now Jumpers themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Marcus Webb had been killed by a Jumper. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Bianca's desk.

She took the tablet into Bianca's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. His name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Jumper is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Lincoln will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Bianca asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

Bianca removed her mother's hand from her arm. Her mother's grip was painfully tight. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me, doing their jobs. I can't hate them the way you do. It's not about economic history or aesthetic philosophy—it's just human nature."

Ariana's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped Bianca's face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Ariana breathing hard from the exertion, Bianca stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that her mother could hate so suddenly, viciously.

Ariana controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, taunting them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive through every city on Earth with those new scanners, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Bianca sat down suddenly. "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no one can live this way."

She did not answer. Finally Bianca said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's arrival. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was there. Bianca saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely white. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to be. She was wearing simple clothes... but carried herself with quiet authority.

Then Ariana saw her.

"Zara!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said to Bianca, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was so nervous."

Bianca said, "Why was my father killed?"

"By mistake. Back in those days, like now, there were ethical Jumpers and criminals. One of those not selected by Harper to join us was enraged, half crazy with envy. He killed two people there in Lincoln. The Regulators thought Roman Frank—I mean, your father—did it. Frank was the greatest man among us. It was he who first conceived the theory that there was a basic, underlying principle in the operation of the implants. Even now, no one fully understands how intention and purpose tie in with the Harper Protocol; but we do know that hatred and greed as motivating forces can greatly minimize the implants' power. That is why the criminals with implants have never reached Xandria."

Heavy footsteps sounded in the hallway outside.

"We'd better hurry," Ariana said.

Zara held out her hands. They took them, to increase the synchronization of the implants. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Ariana flicked one thought of hatred at them. Zara's hands gripped tightly. The pounding intensified.

Ariana felt the familiar pull of the jump beginning—the strange sensation of consciousness lifting away from flesh. She concentrated on Xandria, on the waiting clone bodies, on freedom. But something was wrong. The pull felt weak, distant. She gripped harder. The door splintered.

The sensation faded. Ariana slowly opened her eyes.

She was still in the room. Zara and her daughter were gone. Her outstretched hands touched nothing but empty air.

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. They raised their weapons.

She stood frozen, her mind racing through fragments of memory—something Zara had said about the Protocol, something about hatred and intention. There had been so much she wanted to tell Bianca. About Xandria. About the plan.

She reached toward Bianca's desk.

The Regulators' weapons fired.
quality_problem.question: When did Bianca go to Xandria?

quality_problem.story:
THE OBSERVERS
BY SANTIAGO MARTINEZ
ILLUSTRATED BY CHEN

To all who didn't know them, Antonio Harper and Thomas Wells were brilliant data scientists studying human behavior. But this time they were up against others who could really analyze patterns, and whose business was the observation of whole civilizations.

There were thirty or more of the college students, their ages ranging apparently from eighteen to twenty-two, all of them chattering away like a flock of excited researchers as they followed Professor Charles Herrera past the row of workstations. "Now, now, students," called Professor Herrera cheerily. "Don't scatter. I can't keep my eye on you if you get too far away from me. You, Santiago, put that tablet down. No, don't start recording yet. And Camila, stop checking your phone. You'll lose focus on the actual fieldwork, and a proper ethnographer may get annoyed that you're not paying attention."

Camila laughed. "Oh, Professor Herrera, do you think the ethnographers would want to see our preliminary data?"

The two men who were observing from the back of the room wore pleased expressions. "Fascinating," said Thomas Wells. "But somewhat unpredictable, despite all our previous observations, my friend."

"No attempts at the local idioms, Thomas, not here. It calls attention to us. And you are not sure of the cultural context anyway. You may find yourself saying things you do not intend."

"Sorry, Antonio. It wasn't an attempt to show my skill, I assure you. It's that by now I have a tendency to confuse one communication pattern with another."

"I know. You were never a linguist. But about these interesting creatures—"

"I suggest that they could stand further investigation. It would be good to know how they process information."

"Whatever you say, Thomas. If you wish, we shall join the student group."

"We must have our story prepared first."

Antonio nodded, and the two men stepped into an empty conference room whose frosted glass walls formed a convenient screen. For a moment, the room held silence. Then there came from behind the glass the chatter of student voices, and two young researchers emerged casually. Professor Herrera did not at first notice that now he had an additional two students in his research cohort.

"Do you think you will be able to keep your data analysis terminology straight?" asked one of the new students.

The other one smiled with amusement and at first did not answer. Then he began to flip through a tablet and chant, "I know a pattern, I know a pattern."

There was no better way to make himself inconspicuous. For some time, Professor Herrera did not notice him.

The media production studios, the cultural archives, the ethics review boards, all were left behind. At times the students scattered, but Professor Herrera knew how to get them together again, and not one was lost.

"Here, students, is the facility where we conduct our cross-cultural analysis. Who knows what we study in cultural anthropology?"

"Human societies!" came the enthusiastic chorus.

"That's right. And what methods do we use?"

"I know, Professor Herrera!" cried Santiago Lee, a dark-haired twenty-year-old with a pair of analytical eyes that examined everything like a pair of critics from an intense, focused face. "I've been here before. Participant observation and ethnographic interviews!"

"Very good, Santiago."

Santiago beamed at the approbation. "I've been to this lab lots of times," he said to the student next to him. "My advisor brings me."

"I wish my advisor would bring me too," replied the other student, with an air of wistfulness.

"Why don't you ask him to?" Before the other student could answer, Santiago paused, cocked his head slightly, and demanded, "Who are you? You aren't in our cohort."

"I'm in Professor Martinez's cohort."

"Professor Martinez? Who is he? Is he in our department?"

"I don't know," said the other student uncertainly. "I go to Redwood University in Orvandor—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera," called Santiago. "Here's a student who isn't in our cohort! He got separated from his own group!"

"Really?" Professor Herrera seemed rather pleased at the idea that some other professor had been so careless as to lose one of his charges. "What's your name, young man?"

"I'm Roberto."

"Roberto what?"

"Roberto Henderson. Please, Professor Herrera, I had to use the restroom, and then when I came out—"

"Yes, yes, I know."

A concerned cry came from another section of his group. "Oh, Professor Herrera, here's another one who's lost!"

The other student was pushed forward. "Now, who are you?" Professor Herrera asked.

"I'm Jack Oliver. I went with Roberto to the restroom—"

Professor Herrera made a sound of annoyance. Imagine losing two students and not noticing it right away. The other professor must be frantic by now, and serve him right for being so careless.

"All right, you may stay with us until we find campus security—" He interrupted himself. "Santiago, what are you staring at now?"

"It's Roberto. He's mimicking your gestures exactly!"

"Really, Roberto, that isn't at all professional!"

Roberto's posture altered itself in a hurry, so as to lose any resemblance to Professor Herrera's. "I'm sorry, Professor Herrera, I didn't really mean to do anything wrong."

"Well, I'd like to know what kind of skill development program you've been through, if you don't know that it's unprofessional to mimic people to their faces. A graduate student like you, too. What year are you, Roberto?"

Roberto adjusted his apparent age, he hoped imperceptibly, by a few years. "I'm in my sec—"

An outburst of laughter. "He's in his second week, he's in his second week!"

"I was going to say, I'm in my second year. Almost, anyway."

"Second year," said Professor Herrera. "Old enough to know better about professional ethics."

"I'm sorry, Professor Herrera. And honestly, Professor Herrera, I didn't mean anything, but I'm studying media production, and I observe people, like the documentarians you see on streaming platforms—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera, please don't make him leave with security. If he's going to be a media producer, I'll bet he'd love to meet Sergio Holmes!"

"Well, after the way he's behaved, I don't know whether I should let him. I really don't."

"Please, Professor Herrera, it was an accident. I won't do it again."

"All right, if you're good, and cause no trouble. But we still have plenty of time before meeting Mr. Holmes. It's only two now, and we're not supposed to go to the lecture hall until four."

"Professor Herrera," called Camila Thompson, "do you think he'd give us his insights on information theory?"

"Now, students, I've warned you about that. You mustn't overwhelm him with technical questions. Mr. Holmes is a famous documentary filmmaker, and his time is valuable. It's very kind of him to offer to speak to us, especially when so many professional researchers are anxious to hear him, but we mustn't take advantage of his kindness."

"But he loves students, Professor Herrera! My roommate read in an interview where it said he's just passionate about education."

"I know, but—he's not in good health, students. They say he got a severe illness in the Amazon, where he was filming all those indigenous communities, and wildlife, and environmental stories for his new documentary series. That's why you mustn't stress him too much."

"But he looks so energetic and passionate, Professor Herrera. It wouldn't hurt him to answer a few questions!"

"Oh, yes, it would," asserted one student. "He has tremors. When he has an episode, his hand shakes."

"Yes, the Amazon is a dangerous place, and one never knows how the dangers will affect one," said Professor Herrera complacently. "So we must all remember how bravely Mr. Holmes is fighting his condition, and do our best not to tire him out."

In the bright light that flooded the afternoon workspace, Sergio Holmes's weathered, intense face wore an expression of distress. He groaned dismally, and muttered, "What a headache I've got, what a headache. How do you expect me to face that group of students without something to help me through?"

"You've had your medication," said his producer, Maria. She was slim, professional, and efficient. At the moment she was being more efficient than sympathetic, and she could sense his resentment. "That's all you get. Now, pull yourself together, and try to be reasonably coherent, for a change."

"But those students! They'll ask complex questions—"

"They're about the only audience in the world that won't spot you as struggling. God knows where I could find anyone else who'd believe that your hand shakes because of tropical illness."

"I know that you're looking out for my best interests, Maria. But a little more help wouldn't hurt me."

She said wearily, but firmly, "I don't negotiate with people in your condition, Sergio. I just go ahead and protect them from themselves. No more medication."

"Afterwards?"

"I can't watch you the way a guardian watches a patient."

The firm reply sent his mind off on a new tack. "You could if we were partners."

"I've never believed in partnering with unstable people to stabilize them."

"But if I proved to you that I could change—"

"Prove it first, and I'll consider your proposal afterwards."

"You certainly are a tough person, Maria. But I suppose that in your profession you have to be."

"Tough, demanding, uncompromising—and reliable. It's inevitable when I must deal with such talented, creative, and unreliable clients."

He watched her move about the room, organizing the materials for his presentation. "What are you humming, Maria?"

"Was I humming?"

"I thought I recognized it—some old song about commitment. Your subconscious gives you away. You really want to partner with me!"

"A mistake," she said coolly. "My subconscious doesn't know what it's talking about. All I want from you is quality work."

"Can't you forget for a moment that you're a producer, and remember that you're a person, too?"

"No. Not unless you forget that you're struggling, and remember that you're a professional. Not unless you make me forget that you barely functioned in the Amazon—"

"Because you weren't there with me!"

"—with hardly enough energy to let them film you as if you were actually leading the expedition."

"You're so unforgiving, Maria. You don't have much respect for me, do you—consciously, that is?"

"Frankly, Sergio, no. I don't have much respect for people who waste their potential."

"I'm not entirely wasting it. I earn you that production fee—"

"I'd gladly forego that to see you functional."

"But it's your lack of faith in me that drives me to this state. And when I think of having to face those eager students with nothing to support me—"

"There should be confidence inside you at the thought of sharing your knowledge. Not medication, Sergio, not medication."

The two students drew apart from the others and began to whisper into each other's ears. The whispers were punctuated by nervous laughs which made the entire conversation seem quite normal. But Antonio was in no relaxed mood. He said, in his own language, "You're getting careless, Thomas. You had no business mimicking his physical patterns."

"I'm sorry, Antonio, but it was so suggestive. And I'm a very suggestible entity."

"So am I. But I control myself."

"Still, if the temptation were great enough, I don't think you'd be able to resist either."

"The issues are important enough to make me resist."

"Still, I thought I saw your own form taking on a bit of his pattern too."

"You are imagining things, Thomas. Another thing, that mistake in starting to say you were in your second century—"

"They would have thought it a joke. And I think I got out of that rather neatly."

"You like to take risks, don't you, Thomas? Just as you did when you changed your apparent age. You had no business adjusting right out in public like that."

"I did it skillfully. Not a single person noticed."

"I noticed."

"Don't quibble."

"I don't intend to. Some of these students have very sharp analytical skills. You'd be surprised at what they observe."

Thomas said tolerantly, "You're getting anxious, Antonio. We've been away from home base too long."

"I am not anxious in the least. But I believe in taking due care."

"What could possibly happen to us? If we were to announce to the students and the professor, and to everyone in this facility, for that matter, exactly who and what we were, they wouldn't believe us. And even if they did, they wouldn't be able to act rapidly enough to contain us."

"You never can tell about such things. Wise—entities—simply don't take unnecessary chances."

"I'll grant that you're my superior in such caution."

"You needn't be sarcastic, Thomas. I know I'm more careful. I realize what a resource this planet is—you don't. It has the right developmental stage, suitable cultural complexity, the proper technological level—everything."

"Including a population that will be ideal for our purposes."

"And you would take chances of losing all this."

"Don't be silly, Antonio. What chances am I taking?"

"The chance of being discovered. Here we locate this civilization quite by accident. No one at home base knows about it, no one so much as suspects that it exists. We must get back and report—and you do all sorts of risky things which may reveal what we are, and lead these people to suspect their situation."

This time, Thomas's nervous laugh was no longer mere camouflage, but expressed to a certain degree how he felt. "They cannot possibly suspect. We have been all over this world, we have taken many forms and adapted ourselves to many cultural contexts, and no one has suspected. And even if danger really threatened, it would be easy to escape. I could take the form of the professor himself, of a security officer, of anyone in authority. However, at present there is not the slightest shadow of danger. So, Antonio, you had better stop being fearful."

Antonio said firmly, "Be careful, and I won't be fearful. That's all there is to it."

"I'll be careful. After all, I shouldn't want us to lose these humans. They're so exactly the kind we need. Look how curious they are, how adaptable, how quick to process new information—"

Professor Herrera's voice said, "Good gracious, students, what language are you using? Mandarin?"

They had been speaking too loud, they had been overheard. Antonio and Thomas stared at each other, and laughed nervously. Then, after a second to think, Antonio said, "No, Professor Herrera, just practicing our information theory notation!"

"What?"

Santiago called triumphantly, "It isn't Mandarin, Professor Herrera, it's code—data encryption. They're testing communication protocols."

"Good heavens, what is data encryption for?"

"It's a kind of way of communicating where you encode information. Like, you don't send raw data, you send encrypted packets."

"You don't transmit openly, you transmit securely," added another student.

"You don't broadcast, you narrow-cast. You don't—"

"All right, all right, I get the idea."

"You don't—"

"That'll do," said Professor Herrera firmly. "Now, let's get along to the cultural heritage archive. And please, students, do not touch the artifacts without permission. How would you like to be a precious cultural object and have people handling you carelessly? Always remember professional ethics and social welfare."

"Even with old objects, Professor Herrera?"

"Especially with cultural heritage items."

"But Mr. Holmes documented lots of indigenous communities. Did he practice proper ethics with them too?"

"There is no time for complex questions," said Professor Herrera, with the same firmness. "Come along."

They all followed after him, Antonio and Thomas bringing up the rear. Thomas whispered with amusement, "That encryption business was quick thinking, Antonio. But in fact, quite unnecessary. The things that you do to avoid being suspected!"

"It never hurts to take precautions. And I think that now it is time to leave."

"No, not yet. You are always anxious to gather complete data before reporting. Why not learn a few more details now?"

"Because they are not necessary. We already have a good understanding of human customs and information processing."

"But not of the psychology of students. And they, if you remember, are the ones who will have to be studied most carefully. We shall be asked about them. It would be good if we could report that they are suitable for comprehensive analysis, across a wide range of developmental stages. Let us stay awhile longer."

"All right," conceded Antonio, grudgingly.

So they stayed, and out of some campus materials they shaped the necessary identification badges with which to access restricted areas, and data terminals, and research archives, and other facilities favored by the academic community. Thomas wanted to win easy acceptance by sharing some of his advanced knowledge with a few of the other students, but Antonio put his metaphorical foot down. No use arousing suspicion. Even as it was—

"Gee, your research access is really high-level," said Santiago enviously. "Is your advisor well-connected?"

"We get access to what we need," replied Thomas carelessly.

"Gosh, I wish I did."

Professor Herrera collected his group. "Come together, students, I have something to say to you. Soon it will be time to go in and hear Mr. Holmes. Now, if Mr. Holmes is so kind as to share his insights with us, don't you think that it's only proper for us to share our work with him?"

"We could present our research projects!" suggested Camila.

"Camila's a fine one to talk," said Santiago. "She doesn't even have her data cleaned yet."

"No, students, we mustn't present anything we haven't perfected. That wouldn't make a good impression. And besides, there is no time for full presentations. Perhaps Camila will share her preliminary findings—"

"I can present a data visualization," interrupted Santiago.

"That would be excellent."

"I can discuss methodology," added another student.

"Fine. How about you, Roberto? You and your friend, Jack. Can he analyze data too?"

Roberto laughed nervously. "Oh, yes, he can analyze very well. I can process quantitative data. He can process qualitative patterns." The analytical eyes evaded a concerned look from the friend. "He can process any kind of patterns."

"He's certainly a talented student. But he seems so uncertain!"

"Oh, no," said Roberto. "He just needs encouragement."

"He shouldn't be like that. Perhaps, Roberto, you and Jack can present something together. And perhaps, too, Mr. Holmes will be pleased to see that your professor also has expertise."

"You, Professor Herrera?"

Professor Herrera coughed modestly. "Yes, students, I never told you, but I was once ambitious to be a documentary filmmaker too. I studied media production, and really, I was quite good at it. I was told that if I persevered I might actually be famous. Just think, your professor might actually have been a famous filmmaker! However, in my day, there were many ethical concerns in documentary work, and the life of media production was not attractive—but perhaps we'd better not speak of that. At any rate, I know the principles of documentary filmmaking very well."

"God knows what I'll have to go through," said Sergio. "And I don't see how I can take it in this condition."

"I don't see how they can take you any other way," replied Maria.

"Why go through with it at all? Why not cancel the whole thing?"

"Because people are depending on you. You always want to cancel whenever you run into something challenging. You may as well cancel your entire career if that's the way you feel."

"And your production fee, darling."

"You think I'd mind that. I work for my fee, Sergio, sweetheart. I work too damn hard for that fee."

"You can partner with me and share the rewards. Honestly, Maria, if you supported me better, if you showed me I meant something to you, I'd stabilize."

She made a face. "Don't talk nonsense. Take your notes, and let's get ready to go. Unless you want to change here, and walk around dressed as an Amazon explorer."

"Why not? I've walked around dressed as worse. An unstable wreck."

"Wrecks don't attract attention. They're too ordinary."

"But an unstable Amazon explorer—that's something special." He went into the next room and began to prepare. "Maria," he called. "Do you respect me?"

"At times."

"Would you say that you respected me very much?"

"When you're functional. Rarely."

"Trust me?"

"Once in a blue moon."

"What would I have to do for you to want to partner with me?"

"Achieve something meaningful."

"I like that. Don't you think I achieve something meaningful now? Students admire my work, and come to life at the thought of following in my footsteps."

"The students who admire you will admire anybody. Besides, I don't consider that impressing naive students is a meaningful occupation for a real professional."

"How can I be meaningful, Maria? No one ever taught me how."

"Some people manage without being taught."

"I suppose I could figure it out if I had support."

"Then you'll have to do without figuring it out."

He came into the room again, composed, professional, determined-looking. There was an expression in his bearing which indicated dedication without end, a dedication that would enable him to brave the challenges of nature, culture, and adversity.

"How do I look?"

"Your professional self, of course. A budget version of David Attenborough."

"I feel terrified. I don't know how I'm going to face those students. If they were just casual viewers it wouldn't be so bad, but a group of analytical students!"

"They'll grow up to be your colleagues, if you're still working five years from now. Meanwhile, into each career some challenges must come."

"You would talk of challenges, when you know how I feel."

"Sorry. Come on, let's go."

The lecture hall buzzed with conversation. And beneath the conversation was a steady undercurrent of whispers, of academic confidences exchanged, of scholarly hopes that would now be fulfilled. Professor Herrera's cohort was not the only one which had come to hear the famous filmmaker describe his documentary methods. There were at least five others like it, and by some arrangement, a group from the renewable energy department, who also whispered to each other, in professional solidarity, and pretended to find interest in the presence of so many from the social sciences.

In this atmosphere of whispers and anticipation, Thomas and Antonio could exchange observations without being noticed. Antonio said urgently, "Why did you tell her that I could analyze qualitative patterns too?"

"Why, because it's the truth. You're a very good pattern recognizer. You make wonderful cultural interpretations, for instance. Go on, Antonio, show her what fine cultural analysis you can—"

"Stop it, you fool, before you cause trouble!"

"Very well, Antonio. Did I tempt you?"

"Did you tempt me! You and your risk-taking!"

"You and your excessive caution! But let's not argue now, Antonio. Here, I think, comes the filmmaker. Let's applaud, and be as properly enthusiastic as everyone else is."

My God, he thought, how can they maintain such intense focus for so long? My concentration hurts already. How do they sustain a lifetime of it? Even an hour?

"Go ahead," whispered Maria. "You've seen the outline—go into your presentation. Tell them what insights you have. You have the advantage to start with."

"My reputation," he said, with some bitterness.

"Reputation is the word for you. But forget that. If you're good—you'll get proper rest afterwards."

"Will it be one of those occasions when you respect me?"

"If the moon turns blue."

He strode to the front of the platform, a tablet resting easily in his hands, a confident smile radiating from his weathered, professional face.
