The applause rose to an enthusiastic crescendo, but the smile did not vanish. What a skilled presenter he really was, he told himself, to be able to pretend he enjoyed this.

An assistant dean of some college in the university, a formal older man, was introducing him. There were a few laudatory references to his great talents as a filmmaker, and he managed to look properly modest as he listened. The remarks about his knowledge of indigenous cultures and environmental systems were a little harder to take, but he took them. Then the older man stepped back, and he was facing his challenge alone.

"Students," he began. A pause, a modest smile. "Perhaps I should rather say, colleagues. I'm not one to think of you as mere students. Some people think of me as a perpetual student myself, because I like to explore, and document new things. They think that such things are naive. But if they are, I'm glad to be naive. I'm glad to be one of you. Yes, I think I will call you my colleagues.

"Perhaps you regard me, my colleagues, as a very fortunate person. But when I recall some of the challenges I have faced, I don't entirely agree with you. I remember once, when we were documenting a remote indigenous community—"

He told the story of the remote community, modestly granting co-credit to his local guides. Then another story illustrating the complex patterns of cultural heritage. The tablet figured in still another tale, this time of analyzing environmental data in real-time. His audience was quiet now, absorbed with interest, and he welcomed the respite from performance anxiety he had won for himself.

"And now, my colleagues, it is time to conclude." He actually looked regretful. "But it is my hope that I shall be able to engage with you again—"

Enthusiastic applause, warm as ever, hands moving appreciatively to indicate satisfaction. Thank God that's over with, he thought. Now for that rest—and he didn't mean brief rest, singular. Talk of being meaningful, he'd certainly been meaningful now. He'd inspired those students. What more can any reasonable person want?

But it wasn't over with. Professor Herrera had stepped up on the platform.

"Mr. Holmes," he said, in a strangely affected voice, like that of the first media studies teacher he had ever had, the one who had almost ruined his production career. "Mr. Holmes, I can't tell you how much you have inspired us all, young and old. Hasn't Mr. Holmes inspired us, students?"

"Yes, Professor Herrera!" came the enthusiastic response.

"And we feel that it would be no more than fair to share with you in some small measure what you have given us. First, a data visualization by Santiago Lee—"

He hadn't expected this, and he repressed a groan. Mercifully, the first presentation was short. He smiled the appreciation he didn't feel. To think that he could endure this, while barely functional! What strength of character, what determination!

Next, Professor Herrera introduced another student, who discussed methodology. And then, Professor Herrera stood upright and discussed filmmaking techniques himself.

That was the worst of all. He winced once, then endured. You can get used even to discomfort, he told himself. An adult making questionable claims is always more painful than a student. And that affected media studies voice gave him distress. But he thanked him too. His contribution for the day. Maybe Maria would respect him now, he thought.

A voice called, "Professor Herrera?"

"Yes, dear?"

"Aren't you going to call on Roberto to present?"

"Oh, yes, I was forgetting. Come up here, Roberto, come up, Jack. Roberto and Jack, Mr. Holmes, are studying information processing. They analyze quantitative and qualitative patterns. Who knows? Some day they, too, may be documentary filmmakers, just as you are, Mr. Holmes. Wouldn't that be excellent, students?"

What the devil do you do in a case like that? You smile, of course—but what do you say, without compromising your integrity? Agree how excellent it would be to have those uncertain young people with their work broadcast on every platform all over the world? Like hell you do.

"Now, what are we going to present, students?"

"Please, Professor Herrera," said Jack. "I don't know how to analyze patterns. I can't even interpret basic data. Really I can't, Professor Herrera—"

"Come, come, mustn't be uncertain. Your friend says that you analyze very well indeed. Can't want to be a researcher and still be uncertain. Now, do you know any documentary techniques? The great ethnographers used to be excellent analysts, I remember. Can you demonstrate any methods that they use?"

The silence was getting to be uncomfortable. And Maria said he didn't achieve anything meaningful, he never did anything of value. Why, if thanks to his being here this afternoon, those students gained realistic expectations about documentary work, the whole academic community would have cause to be grateful to him. To him, and to Professor Herrera. He'd ground ambition in reality for anybody.

Professor Herrera had an idea. "I know what to do, students. If you can analyze patterns—Mr. Holmes has shown you what the filmmaker does; you show him what the subjects do. Yes, Roberto and Jack, you're going to demonstrate cultural analysis. You are observing a community, ready to document their behaviors. Position yourselves now, behind that equipment. Closer and closer the subjects come—you demonstrate it, Mr. Holmes, please, that's the way—ever closer, and now you focus your instruments for the recording, and you activate your great, sophisticated, powerful sensors in a great, great comprehensive scan—"

A deep and tremendous hum, as of massive machinery, resonated through the auditorium. Professor Herrera stumbled backward from the control panel he had been gesturing near, his elbow having struck a series of switches. The emergency lighting flickered on.

From the audience came an outburst of terrified screaming such as Sergio had never heard. The hair rose at the back of his neck, and his heart froze.

Standing before him on the platform were two beings, shimmering as if unable to maintain form. Where their human appearance had gone he didn't know, but there they were, forms shifting, structures unstable, more terrifying than any phenomenon he had witnessed in the Amazon. There they were, with the threat of incomprehensible otherness in their fluctuating presence, and here he was, terror and helplessness on his weathered, professional, and bloodless face, heart unfrozen now and pounding fiercely, knees weakening, hands—

Hands paralyzed. The tremor that had plagued him for months now seized his entire arm in an iron grip. He could not move, could not flee, could not even drop the tablet clutched against his chest. The medication's side effects had frozen him in place, a statue of terror with recording equipment pressed uselessly against his body.

His thumb, the only digit still responding, twitched against the tablet's surface. Somewhere in his peripheral awareness, a small red light began to blink.

The beings on the platform writhed and flickered. One of them—the one who had called himself Roberto—made a gesture toward where Antonio stood. But Antonio's form was dissolving faster, unable to maintain cohesion. They reached for each other, their alien appendages passing through one another like smoke.

The screaming in the auditorium had given way to chaos. Students fled toward exits. Professor Herrera lay sprawled near the equipment bank, unconscious from striking his head on a chair during his stumble. The emergency lighting cast everything in harsh red shadows.

Sergio remained frozen, watching, his paralyzed body the only still point in the pandemonium. The tablet against his chest continued its quiet work, its sensors capturing everything—the beings' dissolution, the panic, the overloaded equipment sparking and smoking.

Maria appeared at his side, trying to pull him toward the exit. "Move, damn you, move!"

He couldn't explain that he physically could not. His legs had locked. His arms were rigid. Only that thumb still twitched, and the tablet's red recording light blinked steadily.

The beings collapsed. Where two shifting forms had stood, now there were only two heaps of something that looked almost organic, almost mechanical, and entirely alien. The emergency equipment continued to hum and spark.

It was twenty minutes before anyone thought to check whether Sergio had been recording.

The aftermath unfolded in fragments. Government officials arrived. The auditorium was sealed. Students were questioned and released. Professor Herrera was treated for his head injury and remembered nothing after gesturing toward the control panel.

The equipment malfunction was analyzed by three separate engineering teams. The consensus: a random cascade of system errors, triggered when Professor Herrera's elbow struck the main control interface during his enthusiastic demonstration. The resulting electromagnetic surge had been of a type and intensity that no one could have predicted or replicated.

But the equipment malfunction had only revealed the beings. It had not captured what they were.

That came from Sergio's tablet.

In the secure government facility where he was debriefed, Sergio sat across from a woman who introduced herself only as Dr. Chen. She held his tablet carefully, as if it might explode.

"You recorded forty-seven minutes of continuous high-definition footage," she said. "Including spectral analysis. Including thermal imaging. Including audio on frequencies we didn't know civilian equipment could capture."

"I didn't mean to," Sergio said. His hands had finally stopped shaking. "I was paralyzed. My thumb was just... twitching."

"Your equipment was set to multi-spectrum recording mode."

"I always leave it on that setting. For wildlife documentation. You never know what you might need to see later."

Dr. Chen set the tablet down. "Mr. Holmes, do you understand what you captured?"

"Aliens. Obviously."

"Do you understand what your recording allows us to do?"

Sergio shook his head.

"These beings—their communication frequencies are in your audio capture. We've identified patterns that appear to be transmission protocols. Addresses, of a sort. Locations."

"Their home base."

"Yes. And more importantly—their communication logs show they hadn't yet transmitted Earth's coordinates. They were gathering data first. Comprehensive data. They wanted to present a complete report before alerting their civilization to our existence."

"So they didn't tell anyone about us."

"Not yet. And now—thanks to your recording—we know exactly what frequencies to monitor. What signatures to look for. How to detect others like them, if any exist on Earth." Dr. Chen paused. "We can defend ourselves now. Because we know what to look for. Because you showed us."

"I was paralyzed," Sergio repeated. "I didn't choose to record anything."

"No. But you had the right equipment, configured the right way, and you didn't drop it. You held on."

"I couldn't drop it. My hands were frozen."

Dr. Chen almost smiled. "Sometimes that's what it takes."

Later, Maria visited him in the facility's guest quarters. She sat on the edge of his bed and looked at him with an expression he had never seen before.

"Dr. Chen told me," she said. "About what your recording contained."

"The frequencies. The communication protocols."

"The proof. The evidence that will let us prepare. That will let us watch for others."

"Professor Herrera is the one who caused the malfunction," Sergio said. "He's the one who knocked into those controls. Without that, nothing would have happened."

"Without that, they wouldn't have been exposed, no. They would have walked out of that auditorium and continued their reconnaissance."

"So he should get the credit. For the accident."

Maria shook her head slowly. "The accident revealed them. But revealing them and documenting them are different things. A thousand people saw those beings tonight. Most of them ran. Some fainted. A few took phone footage that shows nothing but blur and panic." She touched his hand. "You're the one who captured what they actually were. What they could do. How to recognize them."

"I was paralyzed, Maria. I didn't do anything on purpose."

"You didn't drop the camera. Through all of that terror, through your body locking up, through forty-seven minutes of chaos—you didn't drop it."

"I couldn't drop it."

"Some might call that an accident too." She squeezed his hand. "But it's the accident that matters. Professor Herrera's accident showed us danger. Yours showed us how to survive it."

"And partnership?" he asked, after a long pause.

She almost laughed. "You're still thinking about that? After everything?"

"A man has to have priorities."

"Fine. Partnership. If you can prove to me that what happened tonight wasn't a fluke. That you can hold onto what matters when everything falls apart." She stood. "But first, you need rest."

"All the rest I want?"

"All the rest you need."

In the months that followed, the world learned what had nearly happened to it. The beings—eventually identified through analysis of Sergio's comprehensive recording as advance scouts from an extrasolar reconnaissance mission—had been documenting Earth for potential acquisition. Their species required adaptive populations for labor in their expanding domain.

The equipment malfunction that Professor Herrera inadvertently triggered had disrupted their ability to maintain form. But disruption alone would not have saved anyone. Exposed beings could still communicate, could still transmit, could still bring others.

What prevented transmission was time—the forty-seven minutes during which their forms destabilized and their communication systems failed. And what gave humanity the ability to detect future threats was the comprehensive recording that captured their signatures, their frequencies, their methods.

Professor Herrera received recognition for his role in the exposure. He gave interviews about the importance of hands-on demonstration in education, about being present in the moment, about the unpredictable value of genuine enthusiasm.

Sergio Holmes received different recognition. His recording became the foundation of Earth's first extraterrestrial detection system. His documentation methods were studied by defense agencies worldwide. His paralysis—the medical condition that had frozen him in place with equipment pressed to his chest—was noted in classified reports as an "optimal coincidence."

And Thomas Wells and Antonio Harper, the names they had adopted, became the first confirmed evidence that humanity was not alone in the universe—documented in comprehensive detail by a filmmaker who couldn't run away, couldn't drop his equipment, and couldn't stop recording even if he had wanted to.
quality_problem.question: Who accidentally saved humanity from Thomas and Antonio?

quality_problem.story:
I almost tripped over the equipment in the dark before I saw it.

Isabella's meteorological station was set up as usual on the gravel strip that separated her research trailer from the one Max and I lived in at the Horizonville Field Station, but it wasn't exactly where I'd learned to expect it when I returned at night from my data collection runs. Usually it was nearer the west end of the strip where Isabella could monitor the atmospheric conditions across the plains and the storm systems rolling in from the eastern mountains. But this time it was pushed back into the shadows away from the station lights.

Isabella wasn't checking her instruments tonight, as she usually did. Instead she was lying back in her field chair with her face turned to the sky, staring upward with such absorbed intensity that she didn't even know I was there until I spoke.

"Anything wrong, Isabella?" I asked.

She said, "No, Anthony," without taking her eyes off the sky.

For a minute I had the prickly feeling you get when you experience déjà vu—that sense that you've lived through this exact moment before. You're puzzled and a little spooked until you realize that the reason you can predict the action so exactly is because you've seen something similar happen elsewhere a long time ago. I forgot the feeling when I remembered why Isabella wasn't monitoring the weather patterns. But I couldn't help wondering why she'd turned to watching the sky instead.

"What're you looking for up there, Isabella?" I asked.

She didn't move and from the tone of her voice I got the impression that she only half heard me.

"I'm tracking the migration patterns," she said softly.

I gave it up and went on to my own trailer without asking any more questions. How can you talk to a researcher like that?

Max wasn't in, but for once I didn't worry about him. I was trying to remember just what it was about my stumbling over Isabella's equipment that had given me that screwy double-exposure feeling of familiarity. I got a can of soda out of the refrigerator because I think better with something cold in my hand, and by the time I had finished the drink I had my answer.

The business I'd gone through with Isabella outside was familiar because it had happened before, about six weeks back when Max and I first parked our trailer at the Horizonville Field Station in Aldoria. I'd nearly stumbled over her equipment that time too, but she wasn't tracking migration patterns then. She was just staring ahead of her, waiting.

She'd been sitting in her field chair at the west end of the gravel strip, staring out over the plains toward the distant mountains. She was practically holding her breath, as if she was waiting for somebody special to show up, so absorbed in her watching that she didn't know I was there until I spoke. She reminded me a little of those dedicated scientists you see in documentaries, with her slight frame, intense face and focused, unwavering eyes. Only there wasn't anything detached about her the way there is about those media portrayals. Maybe that's why I spoke, because she looked so desperately earnest.

"Anything wrong, Isabella?" I asked.

She didn't jump or look up. Her voice placed her as educated, probably from one of the eastern universities.

"I'm waiting for the geese to come back," she said, keeping her eyes on the horizon.

Probably I'd have asked which geese she meant but just then the trailer door opened behind her and her sister took over.

I couldn't see Laura too well because the lights were off inside the trailer. But I could tell from the way she filled up the doorway that she was substantial. I could make out the white blur of a coffee mug in her hand, and when she stepped into the light I saw that she was older than Isabella and looked worn down in a weary, protective sort of way. The wind was blowing in my direction and it told me she'd been working late on grant applications again.

"This is none of your business, mister," she said. Her voice was firm but not unkind. "Let Isabella alone."

She was right about it being none of my business. I went on into the trailer I shared with Max and left the two of them waiting for the geese together.

Our trailer was dark inside, which meant first that Max had probably gone out looking for interview subjects as soon as I left that morning to collect field samples, and second that he'd probably got too absorbed in his journalism work to find his way back. But I was wrong on at least one count, because when I switched on the light and dumped my sample cases on the counter I saw Max asleep in his bunk.

He'd been working, though. I could see the scattered notes and recording equipment beside him, evidence of his latest investigation into media ethics and the coverage of immigration policy in the border regions.

Max sat up and blinked against the light, a lean, energetic man in his thirties with keen gray eyes, dark hair tousled from sleep, and the perpetually skeptical expression of someone who'd spent too many years investigating corruption. He was stripped to his undershirt against the heat, but at some time during the day he had showered and changed. A clean shirt hung on a hook over his bunk with a press badge clipped to the pocket.

"Crawl out and make dinner, Max," I said, holding him to his end of our working agreement. "I've made a full day of field research and I'm hungry."

Max got up and stepped into his jeans. He padded barefoot across the linoleum and poked at my sample cases.

"Soil samples again," he complained. "Anthony, I'm sick of talking about dirt!"

"You don't find stories without digging," I told him. And because I'd never been able to stay annoyed at him for long I added, "But we've got beer. Where's the opener?"

"I'm sick of beer, too," Max said. "I need real coffee."

I sniffed the air, making a business of it. "You've had some already. Where?"

He grinned at me then with the sharp, knowing grin that lit up his face like turning on a light inside and made him different from anybody else on earth.

"The generosity of sources," he said, "is bestowed impartially upon hack and hero. I helped Isabella's sister Laura with some technical writing this afternoon while Isabella was away doing field observations, and my selflessness had its just reward."

Sometimes it's hard to tell when Max is serious. He's an educated man—used to work for some major newspaper, he said once, and I never doubted it—and talks like one when he wants to. But Max is no sellout, though he's semi-obsessed with exposing corruption and lets me support him like a dependent colleague, and he's perceptive enough to read my mind like a weather report.

"No, I didn't raid the coffee pot and help myself," he said. "Laura—her name is Laura Silva—gave me the coffee. Why else do you suppose I'd iron a shirt?"

That was like Max. He hadn't touched their supplies though his brain was probably buzzing for caffeine. He'd showered and pressed a shirt instead so he'd look professional enough to rate a cup of coffee she'd offer him as thanks. It wasn't such a doubtful gamble at that, because Max has a way with him when he bothers to use it; maybe that's why he travels around with me doing environmental field research and investigative journalism, because he's used that charm too often in the wrong contexts.

"Good enough," I said and opened a can of soda apiece for us while Max heated up some pre-made meals.

He told me more about our neighbors while we ate. The Silvas were temporary residents. Isabella—she was twenty-eight—was a meteorologist who'd lost her ability to conduct fieldwork for over a year after a severe accident, and her sister Laura was a grant writer for environmental research organizations. There wasn't much family support beyond the two sisters, which would explain why Laura acted so protective and worn down.

We were halfway through dinner when I remembered something Isabella had said.

"What geese?" I asked.

Max frowned at his plate. "Isabella had been tracking a specific flock of snow geese for her dissertation research, a group that followed an unusual migration pattern. The flock was scattered by a severe storm system while Isabella was hospitalized after her accident."

"Tough," I said, thinking of Isabella sitting out there all day in her field chair, straining her eyes across the plains. "You mean she's been waiting a year?"

Max nodded. "The storm came through like a wall of destruction, Laura said. Hurricane-force winds, flash flooding. Wiped out half the research equipment in the region. Several researchers lost years of work that night."

"And Isabella's geese?"

"Gone. Laura said she spent weeks trying to trace them through the research networks while Isabella was still in the hospital. Nothing turned up for the longest time."

I thought about that—Isabella sitting out there all day, watching and waiting for birds that had vanished into a storm that devastated everything in its path.

"She ever think about giving up?" I asked.

Max shook his head slowly. "Laura says Isabella won't accept that they're truly lost. As long as there's any chance at all, she'll keep watching."

I let the subject drop after that. We sat around after dinner and finished the rest of the soda. When we turned in around midnight I figured we wouldn't be staying long at the Horizonville Field Station. It wasn't a very comfortable place.

I was wrong there. It wasn't comfortable, but we stayed.

I couldn't have said at first why we stuck, and if Max could he didn't volunteer. Neither of us talked about it. We just went on living the way we were used to living, a few weeks here and a few there, all over the continent.

We'd hit the Aldorian plains too late for the spring migration season, so I went in for geological surveying instead. I worked various field research projects all the way from Horizonville down to Dawnridge in southern Lethoria, not signing on with any of the major research institutions because I like to move quick when I get restless. I picked the independent environmental assessment contracts mostly, because the pay is good there if you've got strong analytical skills and don't mind solitary work.

Field research isn't the adventure it seems to the graduate students who sign up because the stipend is decent. You work from a basic trailer setup, usually, with standard equipment instead of cutting-edge technology, and you use established protocols that go back to the fundamentals. There's no real glamour to it, as the students find out quickly. An environmental assessment puts up no more excitement than data entry and the biggest job is to compile your findings once you've got them organized.

Usually a contractor like me sells his reports to the project's funder or to some policy organization that wants evidence for their advocacy, and there's nearly always a bonus—from a pool made up at the beginning of every project—for the researcher producing the most significant findings. There's a knack to identifying the important data points, and when the bonuses were running good I only worked a day or so a week and spent the rest of the time lying around the trailer playing chess and drinking soda with Max.

Usually it was the life of Riley, but somehow it wasn't enough in this place. We'd get about half-relaxed and work up a promising argument about media ethics or immigration policy or whatever Max was investigating. Then, just when we'd got the world looking its most absurd with our arguments one or the other of us would look out the window and see Isabella in her field chair, waiting for a scattered flock of snow geese to come winging home across the plains. She was always there, day or night, until Laura came back from her grant-writing work and brought her inside.

It wasn't right or natural for a researcher to wait like that for anything and it worried me. I even offered once to help Isabella set up new tracking equipment for different birds but Laura told me quick to mind my own business. Max explained that Isabella didn't want to track other birds because she had what Max called a psychological fixation.

"Those geese were more than just research subjects to her," Max said. "They were a sort of symbol because they represented two things that no one else in her field could give her—validation and purpose. With those geese as her focus she felt validated as a scientist, and she had purpose independent of the colleagues who could publish and present because she had her unique migration data. If she tracked other birds now she'd be giving up more than the geese. She'd be giving up everything that tracking them had meant to her, then there wouldn't be any point in continuing."

I could see it when Max put it that way. The geese had occupied more of Isabella's time than anything else, and she felt as secure with them as she'd have been with tenure at a major university. And the geese, following their unusual pattern, had depended on Isabella for the documentation no one else would provide. The birds needed Isabella and Isabella needed them. Together, they'd been a perfect match.

At first I thought it was odd that Isabella never complained or expressed frustration when the geese didn't return, but Max explained that it was all a part of this psychological fixation business. If Isabella gave up she'd be admitting that her research was lost. So she waited and watched, secure in her belief that the geese would return.

The Silvas got used to Max and me being around, but they never got what you'd call close. Isabella would smile at some of the witty things Max said, but her eyes always went back to the plains and the mountains, looking for the geese. And she never let anything interfere with her routine.

That routine started every morning when old Kai Howard, the station manager, drove his utility vehicle out from Horizonville to check on the research facilities. Kai would always make it a point to stop by the Silva trailer and Isabella would ask him if he'd seen anything of an unusual snow geese formation on his rounds that day.

Old Kai would lean against his vehicle and take off his cap and scratch his gray head, frowning while he pretended to think.

Then he'd say, "Not today, Isabella," or, "Thought so yesterday, but this group was flying too high. Wasn't your flock."

Then he'd drive away, shaking his head. Later on the maintenance crew would come around to service the generators and Isabella would ask them the same question. Once a month the funding agency sent out an inspector to verify research progress and he was part of Isabella's routine too.

It was hard on Laura. Sometimes Isabella would dream at night that the geese had returned and were calling outside the trailer, and she'd wake Laura and beg her to go out and look. When that happened Max and I could hear Laura talking to her, low and steady, until all hours of the morning, and when Isabella finally went back to sleep we'd hear Laura open the cabinet and pour herself something strong.

But there came a night that was more than Laura could take, a night that changed Isabella's routine and a lot more with it. It left a mark you've seen yourself—everybody has that's got eyes to see—though you never knew what made it. Nobody ever knew that but Isabella and Laura Silva and Max and me.

Max and I were turning in around midnight that night when Isabella called out next door. We heard Laura get up and go to her, and we got up too and opened a soda because we knew neither of us would sleep any more till Laura got Isabella settled again. But this night was different. Laura hadn't talked to Isabella long when she cried, "The geese! The geese!" and after that we heard both of them crying.

A little later Laura came out into the moonlight and shut the trailer door behind her. She looked rumpled and defeated, her hair pulled back messily and her eyes red from crying. The stress she'd been under hadn't helped any either.

She stood for a while without moving, then she looked up at the sky and said something I'm not likely to forget.

"Why couldn't You give her a break?" she said, not shouting or anything but loud enough for us to hear. "You, up there—what's another lousy flock of geese to You?"

Max and I looked at each other in the half-dark of our own trailer. "She's done it, Anthony," Max said.

I knew what he meant and wished I didn't. Laura had finally told Isabella the truth—whatever truth it was that would end her waiting forever.

That's why I was worried about Isabella when I came home the next evening and found her watching the sky instead of the plains. It meant she'd given up waiting for the geese to fly home. And the quiet way she spoke of tracking migration patterns worried me more, because it sounded disconnected from reality.

Not that you could blame her for losing focus. It was tough enough to have lost a year of research without being able to recover so much as a single data point. But to lose her defining work in the bargain....

I was on my third soda when Max rolled in with a large package under his arm. Max was stone sober, which surprised me, and he was hot and tired from a trip to Larchmont Town, which surprised me more. It was when he unwrapped his package, though, that I thought he'd lost his mind.

"Books for Isabella," Max said. "Laura and I agreed this morning that Isabella needs another focus to occupy her time now, and since she can't return to traditional fieldwork immediately I'm going to help her develop new research methods here."

He went on to explain what had finally broken the stalemate. Laura had been contacted by a colleague from the Riverside District research station—someone who worked with the northern university consortium that studied migratory patterns across the continental flyways.

"They found the flock?" I asked.

Max shook his head. "Not exactly found. The consortium had been tracking the same unusual migration pattern Isabella documented. When the storm scattered everything, their field teams moved in. They were better positioned, better funded."

"So what happened to the geese?"

"The consortium collected them," Max said carefully. "Relocated the surviving birds to controlled research facilities up north. Tagged them, penned them. Standard acquisition protocol for rare migratory populations."

I let that sink in. "Isabella's geese are alive? In some university facility?"

"The consortium considers them their specimens now. Laura got confirmation yesterday—official documentation, transfer records, the whole institutional paper trail. That's what she told Isabella last night."

I thought about Isabella sitting out there watching the sky instead of the plains. It made a different kind of sense now.

"Isabella knows the geese aren't coming back," I said slowly. "Not because they can't survive the journey—but because they can't escape."

Max nodded grimly. "You can wait forever for wild birds to return from migration. But birds in captivity? They're not coming back, Anthony. Not ever. The consortium has them under lock and key at their northern facility. Laura finally had proof she could show Isabella—documentation that made the situation undeniable."

"That's why Isabella stopped watching the horizon," I said. "She was watching for wild geese that might fly home. But her geese aren't wild anymore."

"Exactly. Laura had suspected for weeks but couldn't bring herself to say anything without confirmation. She kept hoping the consortium records were wrong, that maybe the birds had escaped or been released. But the documentation was thorough. Those geese are tagged and catalogued in a facility where they'll never see open sky again."

I understood then why Isabella had turned her gaze upward instead of outward. The plains held no promise now—only the memory of what those birds had once been. The sky was different. The sky was still free.

"We've got to give Isabella another focus," Max said, putting away the books and opening another soda. "Isabella has a remarkable capacity for concentration—most dedicated researchers have—that could be the end of her if it isn't redirected into productive channels."

I thought Isabella had already broken down and said so.

"Tracking migration patterns?" Max said when I told him. "Good Lord, Anthony—"

Laura knocked just then, interrupting him. She came in and had a soda with us and talked to Max about his plan for helping Isabella develop new research approaches. 

"She took it better than I expected," Laura said quietly. "I was terrified to tell her. I thought knowing they were gone forever would destroy her."

"But she seemed almost calm when I saw her earlier," I said.

Laura nodded. "That's what worries me. She keeps saying strange things—that at least they're still alive somewhere, that the sky remembers them even if the earth doesn't. I don't know what she means by that."

She paused, then added: "The worst part was showing her the consortium's acquisition report. All those tracking numbers and facility codes where there used to be wild birds. She just stared at it and said, 'So they'll never fly free again.' And then she went outside and looked up at the sky."

But Laura couldn't tell us anything more about Isabella's new fixation than we already knew. When she asked Isabella why she stared up at the sky like that she'd say only that she was looking for something to remember the geese by.

It was about nine o'clock when Laura went home to make dinner. Max and I knocked off our chess game and went outside with our folding chairs to get some air. It was then that the first light moved.

It moved all of a sudden, the way any meteor does, and shot across the sky in a curving, bright streak. I didn't pay much attention, but Max nearly choked on his soda.

"Anthony," he said, "that was Venus! It moved!"

I didn't see anything unusual about it and said so. You can see a dozen or so lights zip across the sky on any clear night if you're in the mood to look up.

"Not venus like the goddess, you fool," Max said. "The planet Venus—it moved a good sixty degrees, then stopped dead!"

I sat up and took notice then, partly because the planet really had stopped instead of disappearing the way a meteor seems to do, partly because anything that excites Max that much is something to think about.

We watched the planet like two hawks at a field mouse, but it didn't move again. After a while a smaller light did, though, and later in the night a whole procession of them streaked across the sky and fell into place around the first one, forming a pattern that didn't make any sense to us. They stopped moving around midnight and we went to bed, but neither of us got to sleep right away.

"Maybe we ought to look for another line of work ourselves instead of helping Isabella find one," Max said. He meant it as a joke but it had a shaky sound. "Something besides drinking soda and arguing every night, for instance."

"You think we're hallucinating from too much caffeine?" I asked.

Max laughed at that, sounding more like his old self. "No, Anthony. No two people ever had instantaneous and identical hallucinations."

"Look," I said. "I know this sounds crazy but maybe Isabella—"

Max wasn't amused any more. "Don't be ridiculous, Anthony. If those planets really moved you can be sure of two things—Isabella had nothing to do with it, and the news will explain everything tomorrow."

He was wrong on one count at least.

The news next day was packed with headlines but none of them explained anything. The media commentators quoted every authority they could reach, and astronomers were going crazy everywhere. It just couldn't happen, they said, according to all logic and theoretical modeling.

Max and I went over the news reports carefully that night and I learned more about celestial mechanics than I'd learned in a lifetime. Max, as I've said before, is an educated man, and what he couldn't recall offhand about astronomy the news quoted by chapter and verse. They ran interviews with astronomers from observatories around the world, but nobody could explain why all of those planets and bright stars would change position then stop.

It set me back on my heels to learn that Venus was nearly the same size as Earth and had a thick atmosphere that made it incredibly hot, that it was the brightest object in the night sky after the moon and followed a predictable orbit that had been tracked for millennia. This predictable pattern—astronomers relied on it for calibrating their instruments—hadn't just deviated slightly, which puzzled the astronomers no end. I suggested to Max, only half joking, that maybe Venus had moved because it was bright enough to suit Isabella's taste, but Max called me down sharp.

"Don't joke about Isabella," he said sternly. "Getting back to Venus—it's so far away that its light needs several minutes to reach us. The speed of light is a universal constant, Anthony, and astronomers say it can't be changed."

"They said the planets couldn't be tossed around like marbles, too," I pointed out. "I'm not saying that Isabella really moved those damn lights, Max, but if she did she could have moved their appearance along with them, couldn't she?"

But Max wouldn't argue the point. "I'm going out for air," he said.

I trailed along, but we didn't get farther than Isabella's field chair.

There she sat, tense and absorbed, staring up at the night sky. Max and I followed her gaze, the way you do automatically when somebody ahead of you cranes their neck at something. We looked up just in time to see the lights start moving again.

The first one to go was a bright reddish one that slanted across the sky like a firework—zip, like that—and stopped dead beside the group that had collected around Venus.

Max said, "There went Mars," and his voice sounded like he had just sprinted a kilometer.

That was only the beginning. During the next hour forty or fifty more celestial objects flashed across the sky and joined the group that had moved the night before. The pattern they made still didn't look like anything in particular.

I left Max shaking his head at the sky and went over to help Isabella, who had called it a night and was gathering her equipment, carry her instruments back toward the Silva trailer. I moved her things inside where Max couldn't hear, then I asked her how things were going.

"Slow, Anthony," she said. "I've got almost a hundred more to position."

"Then you're really moving those lights up there?"

She looked surprised. "Sure, it's not so difficult once you understand the principles."

The odds were even that she was delusional, but I went ahead anyway and asked another question.

"I can't make head or tail of it, Isabella," I said. "What're you creating up there?"

She gave me a very small smile.

"You'll know when I'm finished," she said. Then, almost to herself: "They can keep my geese penned up in their facilities. They can tag them and catalogue them and pretend they own them. But they can't own this. Nobody can capture this."

I told Max about that after we'd bunked in, but he said I should not encourage Isabella in her delusions. "Isabella's heard everybody talking about those planets moving, the news media covered it extensively, so she's excited too. But she's got a lot more imagination than most people, because she's a researcher who lost her focus, and she could spiral into complete disconnection because she's upset about the geese. The thing to do is give her a logical explanation instead of letting her think her fantasy is reality."

Max was taking all this so hard—because it was upsetting things he'd taken for granted as being facts all his life, like those astronomers who were going nuts in droves all over the world. I didn't realize how upset Max really was, though, till he woke me up at about 4:00 a.m.

"I can't sleep for thinking about those planets," he said, sitting on the edge of my bunk. "Anthony, I'm scared."

That from Max was something I'd never expected to hear. It startled me wide enough awake to sit up in the dark and listen while he unloaded his worries.

"I'm afraid," Max said, "because what is happening up there isn't right or natural according to any framework of statistical inference or technological progress we understand. It just can't be, yet it is."

It was so quiet when he paused that I could hear my own breathing. Finally Max said, "Anthony, the solar system we live in is as delicately balanced as a precision instrument. If that balance is upset too far our world will be affected catastrophically."

Ordinarily I wouldn't have argued with Max on his own ground, but I could see he was painting a mental picture of the whole cosmos collapsing and I was afraid to let him go on.

"The trouble with you educated people," I said, "is that you think your experts have got everything figured out through theoretical modeling and time management of observations, that there's nothing in the universe their calculations can't pin down. Well, I'm just a field researcher, but I know that your astronomers can measure the planets till they're exhausted and they'll never learn who put those planets there. So how do they know that whoever put them there won't move them again? I've always heard that if a person had faith enough they could move mountains. Well, if a person has the focus that Isabella's got maybe she could move planets, too."

Max sat quiet for a minute.

"'There are more things in heaven and earth...'" he began, then laughed. "A line worn threadbare by centuries of repetition but as apt tonight as ever, Anthony. Do you really believe Isabella is moving those planets?"

"Why not?" I came back. "It's as good an answer as any the experts have come up with."

Max got up and went back to his own bunk. "Maybe you're right. We'll find out tomorrow."

And we did. Max did, rather, while I was hard at work collecting soil samples from the southern plains.

I got home a little earlier than usual that night, just before it got really dark. Isabella was sitting as usual all alone in her field chair. In the gloom I could see a stack of books on the gravel beside her, books Max had given her to study. The thing that stopped me was that Isabella was staring at her legs as if they were the first ones she'd seen in months, and she had the same look of intense concentration on her face that I'd seen when she was watching the sky.

I didn't know what to say to her, thinking maybe I'd better not mention the planets. But Isabella spoke first.

"Anthony," she said, without taking her eyes off her legs, "did you know that Max is an exceptionally perceptive man?"

I said I'd always thought so, but why?

"Max said this morning that I ought not to move any more celestial objects," Isabella said. "He says I ought to concentrate instead on learning how to walk properly again so I can return to field research and track new migration patterns."

For a minute I was angry enough to confront Max if he'd been handy. Anybody that would suggest something like that to an injured, struggling researcher....

"Max says that if I can do what I've been doing to the planets then it ought to be straightforward to heal my own body," Isabella said. "And he's right, Anthony. So I'm not going to move any more lights. I'm going to heal myself."

She looked up at me with her small, determined smile. "It took me a whole day to learn how to move that first planet, Anthony, but I could do this after only a couple of hours. Look...."

And she stood up from her chair and took three steady steps.

It's a pity things don't happen in life like they do in books, because a first-class story could be made out of Isabella Silva's capacity for moving things by concentrating on them. In a book Isabella might have revolutionized physics or destroyed civilization, depending on which angle would interest the most readers and bring the writer the biggest advance, but of course it didn't really turn out either way. It ended in what Max called an anticlimax, leaving everybody satisfied enough except a few astronomers who like mysteries anyway or they wouldn't be astronomers in the first place.

The celestial objects that had been moved stayed where they were, but the pattern they had started was never finished. That unfinished pattern won't ever go away, in case you've wondered about it—it's up there in the sky where you can see it any clear night—but it will never be finished because Isabella Silva lost interest in it when she learned to walk again.

Walking was a slow process with Isabella at first because her muscles had weakened—partial atrophy, Max said—and it took time to make them strong again. But in a couple of weeks she was moving around with a cane and after that she never used her field chair for sitting again.

Laura enrolled her in a rehabilitation program at the Riverside District medical center and before the season ended Isabella was hiking short distances and conducting preliminary field observations with a group of other researchers on weekends.

The rehabilitation program opened up a whole new world to Isabella and she adapted herself to the routine as smoothly as if she'd been doing it all her life. She learned a lot there and she forgot a lot that she'd learned for herself by being isolated. Before we realized what was happening she was just like any other researcher, full of curiosity and ambition, with no more power to move things by staring at them than anybody else had.

I think she actually forgot about those planets along with other things that had meant so much to her when she was confined to her field chair and couldn't do anything but wait and think.

For instance, a graduate student working on avian migration patterns contacted her one day and asked if she'd collaborate on a new project. Isabella accepted enthusiastically and after that she never said anything more about waiting for her original flock to return. It was only natural, of course, because researchers—active researchers—move on from their disappointments quickly. It's a sort of survival mechanism, Max says, against the setbacks of academic life.

When the field season ended in the fall Laura accepted a position with a major environmental organization and Isabella joined a university research team. When they were gone the Horizonville Field Station was so lonesome and quiet that Max and I pulled out and went down to the coastal regions for the marine biology season. We never heard from Laura and Isabella again.

We've moved several times since; we're out in the northern territories just now, with the climate researchers. But everywhere we go we're reminded of them. Every time we look up at a clear night sky we see what Max calls the Isabella Silva Celestial Monument, which is nothing but an unusual sort of pattern sketched in with a hundred or so planets, stars, and other celestial objects of all sizes and brightness.

The body of it is so incomplete that you'd never make out what it's supposed to be unless you knew already what you were looking for. To us the formation of a bird in flight is fairly plain. If you know enough to fill in the gaps you can see it was meant to be a large snow goose with its wings spread wide.

Max says that transient researchers like him and me forget old associations as quick as academics do—and for the same good reason—so I'm not especially interested now in where Laura and Isabella Silva are or how they're doing. But there's one thing I'll always wonder about, now that there's no way of ever knowing for sure.

I wish I'd asked Isabella or Laura, before they moved away, what made that particular flock of geese so special in the first place.
quality_problem.question: What makes Isabella transition from watching the plains to watching the sky?
quality_problem.correct_answer: Laura tells her that her research flock was captured by another team
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: Laura tells her that her research flock died in the storm
answers: Laura tells her that her research flock was captured by another team
Laura tells her that her research flock died in the storm

quality_problem.story:
The Chronicles of Royal Decrees

Benjamin Freeman stood in the Grand Archive of Millbrook, Havencia, surrounded by scrolls that chronicled centuries of royal proclamations. As the newly appointed Royal Historian, his first task was to analyze the Ascension Decrees—the formal speeches given by each monarch upon taking the Crystal Throne. There had been fifty-three such decrees since the First Kingdom was established in the Year of Awakening.

The archive, maintained through a complex supply chain management system that preserved magical documents across the realm, housed every decree ever spoken. Freeman had spent months developing laboratory methods to authenticate and restore the oldest scrolls, some of which had been damaged by time and the occasional dragon fire. His work combined historical analysis with practical preservation techniques, ensuring future generations could study these vital texts.

As he unrolled the first decree, spoken by King Theodore the Wise in the Year of Awakening, Freeman was immediately struck by the tone of profound humility. Theodore had united seven warring provinces through a combination of diplomatic genius and powerful magic. He was the most respected ruler in the realm's history, yet his words were surprisingly modest:

"The weight of this Crystal Crown, bestowed upon me by the voices of all free peoples, fills me with such trepidation that even the wisest among you would question their worthiness. I, who possess but modest gifts of magic and no experience in governing united lands, am keenly aware of my inadequacies for this sacred duty."

Freeman noted that this pattern of self-deprecation continued through the next sixty-eight years of Ascension Decrees. Nearly every monarch expressed similar doubts about their capabilities, though none as eloquently as Theodore. This era, Freeman realized, reflected both the courtly etiquette of the time and a political necessity. In those early years, many citizens feared the unified kingdom might become a tyranny, with the monarch transforming into an absolute despot. By emphasizing their limitations, these early rulers sought to alleviate such concerns.

The tone shifted dramatically with Queen Jin Woods, who ascended during the Great Fracturing, when three provinces threatened to secede over disputes about magical resource distribution. Woods could not afford modesty. Her decree was a forceful assertion of royal authority: "I shall preserve, protect, and defend the unity of our realm with every power vested in this throne." Her successors inherited a much stronger central authority, and their decrees reflected this new reality.

Freeman identified three distinct phases in the decrees' style and content. The first phase, lasting until Woods, featured the modest, classical public servant. The second, extending through King Luis Osborne's reign, showcased the practical administrative executive. The third phase, which continued to the present, presented the assertive, inspirational leader-prophet. This evolution wasn't perfectly linear—King Ryan Wilson might belong in the third phase despite ruling during the second era—but the trend was unmistakable.

The transformation from administrative to inspirational leadership became particularly evident in the decrees of Queen Felix Park, who ruled during the Age of Moral Decline. Park's decree didn't focus on governmental policy but on inspiring public behavior: "At last, we see our kingdom clearly—the corruption alongside the virtue, the decay beside the vitality. With this vision, we approach our challenges anew."

If the kingdom faced moral decay, Park understood that the solution required uplifting the people's spirits, not merely passing new laws. This approach to leadership had been pioneered by King Peter Riley, who famously declared the Crystal Throne "a sacred platform for teaching." The phrase suggested not just written proclamations but direct connection between ruler and subjects. The development of the Resonance Crystals—magical devices that could project a monarch's voice and image across the entire realm—made this possible on an unprecedented scale.

Freeman noticed a telltale linguistic marker of this inspirational style: the phrase "Let us," meaning "You shall do as I say." This construction appeared occasionally throughout history but became dominant in recent centuries. King Robert Rice used it sixteen times in his decree, while his successor employed it twenty-two times.

The evolution in literary style could be quantified. In all decrees from Theodore through King Benjamin Harrison, the average sentence contained forty-four words. From Woods through Park, it dropped to thirty-four words. In the modern era, it averaged just twenty-five words. Freeman didn't consider this deterioration—his own scholarly articles averaged seventeen words per sentence—but it reflected changes in audience size and communication methods. Early monarchs could reference the governance systems of ancient empires and expect their audience to understand. Modern monarchs couldn't make such assumptions, though they could discuss concepts like network theory and statistical inference that would have baffled their predecessors.

Monarchs and their scribes had long borrowed memorable phrases from predecessors without attribution. Rice's famous declaration, "Ask not what your kingdom can provide you, but what you can provide your kingdom," had an ironic origin. Decades earlier, King Theodore Brooks—hardly a model for Rice's progressive policies—had said, "Our greatest danger lies in expecting too little from our government while contributing too little to it."

Many issues dominated their moment in the decrees before vanishing: the Mountain Clans, coastal fortifications, territorial expansion, the Great Canal project, civil service reform, and the prohibition of certain dark magics. Some expected topics never appeared. King Osborne's decree, delivered on the Spring Equinox of 829, gave no hint of the economic catastrophe brewing in Pinehurst, Wendria. Queen Park's second decree, five years into her reign, contained no reference to the rising Dark Lord or the gathering armies in the Shadow Lands.

Most striking to Freeman, reading these texts in the Year 1047, was the near-total silence regarding the non-human peoples of the realm. The words "elves," "dwarves," or "folk" (referring to magical beings) didn't appear until King Hayes, who ruled in 877. King Monroe had asked rhetorically in 817, "Upon whom has injustice fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been denied their rights?" These questions expected the answer "No one!"—as if millions of enslaved elves didn't toil in the southern provinces.

Before the War of Liberation, the word "enslavement" appeared only in the decrees of King Martin (837) and King James (857), and then only to argue that, pursuant to ancient law and to preserve unity, the practice should not be interfered with. Though generally unmentionable, the issue was reaching a crisis point that would explode in 861.

After the war, the decrees of Kings Hayes, William (881), and Harrison (889) contained the most explicit discussions of converting paper freedoms into reality for the liberated peoples. William's was strongest—he had studied at the Academy of Meadowbrook, Havencia, during the 850s, when it served as a sanctuary for escaped slaves. But the subject then faded. King Richard said in his first decree (897), "The lynching of non-humans must not be tolerated in a great and civilized kingdom," but he said it without horror. King Osborne raised the subject in 909 only to express satisfaction at the progress made. Then the topic disappeared entirely. Even Queen Eleanor, who ruled through four separate ascensions, never mentioned it.

After the Second Great War, the subject returned to the decrees, but in weak, abstract form. This remained true even for rulers Freeman knew had been deeply concerned with social justice—like King Thomas, Queen Victoria, and the current King Alexander. Perhaps each thought they had made a sufficient statement by having an elf or dwarf perform at their coronation ceremony. In Alexander's first decree, the only allusion to inter-species relations was this sentence: "From our founding revolution through the War of Liberation to the Great Depression to the civil rights awakening, our people have always found the determination to build strength from crisis."

Freeman didn't question these monarchs' sincerity, but the pattern revealed what was considered acceptable to say in speeches meant to appeal to shared values.

There was much more to analyze in these decrees than Freeman had initially expected. He found much to admire: the resilience the kingdom had shown, the peaceful transfers of power, the general reasonableness of their elected monarchs. The system of supply chain management that distributed power among provinces while maintaining central authority had proven remarkably stable.

As Freeman prepared his comprehensive analysis, he consulted Professor Helena Marsh's landmark text, "The Arc of Progress: A Complete History of Moral Understanding." Marsh's thesis was unambiguous: "Each generation builds upon the moral discoveries of its predecessors. We who live in the modern era possess the accumulated wisdom of all previous ages, allowing us to see clearly what our ancestors could not. The progression is inevitable and irreversible."

Freeman had been assigned Marsh's book during his training at the Academy. Her framework had shaped how historians approached the decrees for decades. "The modern reader," Marsh wrote, "stands at the pinnacle of moral understanding, equipped to judge the past with perfect clarity."

Yet as Freeman worked through the decrees, certain details complicated this framework. King Monroe's rhetorical question—"Upon whom has injustice fallen in any corner of our realm?"—had been celebrated in its time as a triumph of moral reasoning. The Royal Archives contained letters praising Monroe for his "enlightened vision" and "unprecedented commitment to justice." His contemporaries had believed themselves to be living in an age of remarkable moral progress.

Similarly, Freeman found that King Martin's decree defending the enslavement of elves had been praised by the leading moral philosophers of the 830s as "a careful balancing of competing goods" and "a wise acknowledgment of practical necessity." One prominent scholar had written: "Future generations will thank King Martin for preserving the unity that makes all other progress possible."

Freeman also discovered something curious in the margins of older scrolls. Previous archivists had left annotations. A historian from the 900s had written beside Monroe's decree: "How could they not see?" A scholar from the 950s had added a similar note to King Richard's words about lynching: "The casualness is incomprehensible to modern sensibilities."

Yet Freeman found that this same 950s scholar had also annotated the decrees of Queen Eleanor, praising her for "achieving the final resolution of inter-species relations" and noting that "no future monarch will need to address this matter, as Eleanor's policies have settled it permanently."

Freeman checked the current legal codes. Several of Eleanor's "final resolutions" had since been overturned as inadequate or unjust.

The archive contained other traces of this pattern. A treatise from 780 declared that the kingdom had "at last achieved a complete understanding of justice." A philosophical text from 850 announced that "moral progress has reached its natural culmination." A speech from 920 celebrated "the final triumph of reason over prejudice."

Each document expressed absolute confidence. Each had been superseded by later understandings.

Freeman pulled out a scroll he had been avoiding—King Alexander's most recent decree, delivered just three years ago. He read the familiar words with fresh attention. Alexander spoke of "our commitment to justice for all peoples" and "the values that define our enlightened age." The language was confident, comprehensive, assured.

Freeman noticed that Alexander's decree never mentioned the goblin populations in the eastern territories. It made no reference to the ongoing debates about sentient magical constructs. It used the phrase "all peoples" in ways that, upon close examination, seemed to exclude certain categories of beings entirely.

He pulled Marsh's book from his satchel and found a passage he had underlined during his student days: "The modern reader possesses complete moral vision, unclouded by the prejudices that limited earlier eras."

Freeman set the book beside Alexander's decree. He looked at the confident words of both texts. He thought about the confident annotations left by previous archivists, each certain they had achieved the understanding that eluded their predecessors.

The Resonance Crystals hummed softly in their cases, ready to project the next monarch's voice across the realm. The supply chain that maintained the archive continued its eternal work, preserving these documents for future historians. And somewhere, Freeman knew, the next generation of leaders was preparing to take the Crystal Throne, ready to add their own words to this long chronicle.

He rolled up the final scroll and locked it carefully in its preservation case. His analysis would be due tomorrow. He would need to choose a framework—Marsh's confident progressivism, or something else. The Royal Council expected clear conclusions.

The archive's clock chimed midnight. Freeman gathered his notes, extinguished the magical lights, and left the building. He walked through the quiet streets of Millbrook, carrying his satchel full of evidence that pointed in different directions.

Monroe had been certain. Martin had been certain. The 950s archivist had been certain. Marsh was certain. Each had possessed the full conviction that they saw clearly while others had been blind.

Tomorrow he would present his findings. Tonight, he simply walked, turning the question over in his mind, finding no easy resolution.
quality_problem.question: When reading the Ascension Decrees, which is true?
quality_problem.correct_answer: They provide insight into the values and limitations of each historical era, not an omniscient modern perspective
quality_problem.incorrect_answer: They reveal how past monarchs had access to the same information and moral understanding that modern readers possess
answers: They provide insight into the values and limitations of each historical era, not an omniscient modern perspective
They reveal how past monarchs had access to the same information and moral understanding that modern readers possess

quality_problem.story:
The Enchanted Brew: A Magical Experiment in Taste

I love enchanted ales, but lately I've been wondering: Am I getting full value for my gold sovereign? As I've stocked up on artisan wizard brews and fancy imports from the Elven Kingdoms, I've told myself that their magical essence is deeper, richer, more complicated, more compelling—and therefore worth the 50 percent to 200 percent premium they command over cheap mass products brewed by common hedge witches or even mainstream establishments like the Brookhaven Brewing Company in Fendria. And yet, I've started to wonder, is this just costly snobbery? If I didn't know what I was drinking, could I even tell whether it was something crafted by the master brewers of Clearwater Province versus something from a basic tavern in Willow Creek, Calderon?

I'm afraid we'll never know the answer to that exact question, since I'm not brave enough to expose my own taste to a real test. But I'm brave enough to expose my colleagues'. This summer, while working at the Academy of Arcane Innovation Management in Lakeside, Orvandor, I put out a call for volunteers for a "science of magical brewing" experiment. Testing candidates had to meet two criteria: 1) they had to appreciate enchanted ales; and 2) they had to think they knew the difference between mass products and high-end artisan brews.

Twelve tasters were selected, mainly on the basis of essays detailing their background with magical beverages. A few were selected because they had been senior researchers in the Academy department where I worked. All were spell-crafters or alchemists; most were accomplished practitioners of the visual arts as well, believing their refined aesthetic sensibilities extended to taste. Nearly half had trained outside Orvandor or lived abroad long enough to speak haughtily about Orvandian mass-market brews.

Before the blind tasting began, I asked each participant to predict which ale would emerge as the group's favorite. The responses were illuminating. Eight of the twelve predicted Moonwhisper would claim the top spot—its reputation among Elven ale enthusiasts is legendary, and several tasters had waxed poetic about it in their application essays. Rosa Taylor, who had trained in the ancient brewing traditions of the Far Eastern Kingdoms, declared it "the obvious choice for anyone with a sophisticated palate." Marcus Webb, our youngest participant, had written that Moonwhisper was "the ale that made me understand what magic could do for brewing." Claudia Cook, who advises the Academy on what new enchantments should go into the next generation of magical artifacts, predicted Moonwhisper would "dominate utterly."

The remaining four predictions were split: two for Starglow, one for Diana's Wicked Amber, and one—from a taster who called himself a contrarian—for "whatever cheap swill you've hidden in there, because these tests always embarrass the snobs."

**Philosophy**: The experiment was designed to take place in two separate sessions. The first session, whose results are revealed here, involved ales exclusively from the amber category. Amber ales are the golden-colored, relatively lightly flavored brews that make up most of the volume of enchanted ale consumption in the Five Kingdoms.

Ale connoisseurs sneer at ambers because they look so pale and because so many inferior brews are in the group. But the amber test came first, for two reasons. One, ambers pose the only honest test of the ability to tell expensive from dirt-cheap ales. There are very few inexpensive dark stouts, ruby reds, midnight blacks, or other fancy-pantsy, artisan-style, non-amber drinks. Two, the ideal of public service requires amber coverage. This is what most people drink.

**Materials**: Ten ambers were selected for testing, representing three distinct price-and-quality groups:

**High End** (15-16 silver pieces per flagon)

*Moonwhisper*. Import amber (Elven Kingdoms). 16.7 silver per flagon. Chosen for the test because of its ale-snob chic; also, one of my favorite brews. Known for its subtle enchantments that supposedly enhance clarity of thought.

*Starglow*. Regional artisan amber (Clearwater Province). 15.3 silver per flagon. Chosen because it is Orvandor's long-standing most popular premium ale.

*Diana's Wicked Amber*. National-scale "artisan brew." 14.6 silver per flagon. Brewed by Diana Fernandez, a renowned entrepreneur in the magical beverage industry.

*Peter's Premium Lakeside Amber*. National macro-artisan brew. 15.6 silver per flagon. Created by Peter Fuller, calls itself Orvandor's Best Ale. Has dark orangey-amber color that was obviously different from all other ambers tested.

**Mid-Range** (around 8 silver pieces per flagon)

*Brookhaven Basic*. 8.4 silver per flagon. Self-styled King of Ales from Brookhaven, Fendria.

*Fendrian Gold Draft*. 8.4 silver per flagon. Popular throughout the kingdom.

*Calderon Light*. 8.4 silver per flagon. From Willow Creek, Calderon.

**Cheap** (5-5.5 silver pieces per flagon)

*Lakeside's Best*. 5.5 silver per flagon. Locally known as "Beast Brew."

*Tyler's Tavern Ale*. 5.4 silver per flagon. Brewed by Tyler Riley.

*Bruno's Basic*. 5.0 silver per flagon. Brewed by Bruno Singh.

**Experimental Procedure**: Each taster sat down before an array of 10 crystal goblets labeled A through J. The A-to-J coding scheme was the same for all tasters. Each goblet held 3 ounces of one of the sample ales. Enchanted wafers were available to cleanse the palate. The goblets were frosted crystal, so tasters could judge the ale's color only from above.

One experimenter (the senior researcher over most of the others there) rushed through his rankings in 10 minutes and gave the lowest overall scores. The taster who took the longest, nearly the full two hours, had the ratings that came closest to the relative price of the ales. (This was Rosa Taylor.) The experimenters were asked not to compare impressions until the test was over.

After tasting the ales, each taster rated ales A through J on the following standards:

*Overall quality points*: Zero to 100, zero as undrinkable and 100 as dream ale.

*Price category*: A rating of 3 was most expensive, 2 for average, 1 for cheap.

*Description*: "Amusing presumption," "fresh on the palate," "swill," etc.

*Best and Worst*: Tasters chose one Best and one Worst from the "flight."

**The Voting: A Chronicle of Surprises**

I'll present the Best and Worst votes as they were recorded, taster by taster, because the pattern that emerged was genuinely unexpected given the pre-tasting predictions.

Rosa Taylor, our most methodical taster, cast the first recorded vote. Her Best selection was Goblet F—which, when decoded, proved to be the ale she had predicted would win. "Complex magical essence," she wrote, "clearly the work of master brewers." She had identified it correctly through taste alone, a feat no other taster would replicate with their predicted winner.

Thomas Bradford, a senior alchemist, voted Best for Goblet D and Worst for Goblet F. His comment on Goblet F: "Aggressively herbal, like drinking a hedge witch's failed potion."

Marcus Webb, who had written so eloquently about Moonwhisper in his application essay, selected Goblet D as Best. His Worst vote went to Goblet F, with the comment: "This tastes like something fermented in an Elven lord's unwashed boot." He did not realize he was describing his supposed favorite.

Claudia Cook, our magical artifacts advisor, provided the evening's most controversial vote: Best went to Goblet J—which proved to be Bruno's Basic, the cheapest ale in the sample. "Honest, unpretentious, lets the barley speak," she wrote. Her Worst: Goblet F.

Elena Vance: Best for D, Worst for F. "Goblet F is trying too hard," she noted. "Goblet D has confidence."

Gerald Stone, the contrarian who'd predicted a cheap ale would win, was disappointed to find himself voting Best for D. "Damn it," he muttered while filling out his form, "this one's probably expensive." Worst: F.

Harrison Park: Best for D, Worst for F. Comments illegible due to spilled ale.

Isabella Reyes: Best for D, Worst for B. "Goblet B tastes like someone bottled pretension."

James Morton: Best for D, no Worst selected (he felt it was "mean-spirited to single one out").

Katherine Liu: Best for D, Worst for F. "F has that distinctive herbal quality that might impress at parties but is genuinely unpleasant."

Lawrence Chen: Best for D, Worst for B.

Margaret Foster: Abstained from Best selection ("they all tasted similar, honestly"), Worst for F.

**The Decoding**

When the A-to-J cipher was revealed, the pattern became clear in aggregate, though individual results told a more complex story.

Goblet F was Moonwhisper, the most expensive ale in the survey and the overwhelming pre-tasting favorite. Goblet D was Peter's Premium Lakeside Amber. Goblet B was Starglow. Goblet J was Bruno's Basic.

Rosa Taylor had correctly identified Moonwhisper as her favorite through blind tasting—the only taster whose pre-tasting prediction matched their blind selection. "I knew it," she said, though her expression suggested she wasn't entirely pleased to be standing alone.

Five tasters had selected Moonwhisper as their Worst ale. Three of these tasters had predicted before the blind test that Moonwhisper would be the group favorite.

**Overall Preference Points**

The overall preference analysis used "corrected average preference points"—an average of the zero-to-100 points assigned by each taster, corrected by throwing out the highest and lowest score each ale received.

The corrected preference rankings placed Peter's Premium at the top with 67.3 points. Moonwhisper scored 41.2 points—middle of the pack when outliers were removed, but polarizing. Some tasters gave it scores in the 70s; others marked it in the teens. Bruno's Basic earned a respectable 52.1, outscoring several more expensive competitors.

The tasters used widely varying scales—one confining all ales to the range between zero and 30, another giving 67 as his lowest mark. But the power of our corrected ranking system surmounted such difficulties.

As for Moonwhisper's mixed performance: it is very strongly hopped with magical herbs, which can seem exotic if you know you're drinking a pricey import but simply unpleasant if you don't. Rosa Taylor's high marks pulled up its average; without her scores (thrown out as the highest), it would have ranked near the bottom.

**Value for Money: the Taste-o-meter®**

The Taste-o-meter rating for each ale was calculated by dividing its corrected average preference rating by its price per flagon.

Bruno's Basic dominated this metric, followed by Tyler's Tavern Ale and Lakeside's Best. Moonwhisper finished last, with less than one-quarter the Taste-o-meter power of Bruno's Basic.

**Social Value for Money: the Snob-o-meter®**

The tasters were asked to estimate whether the ales were expensive or not—in effect, to judge whether other people would like and be impressed by the ales. One taster, Layla Crawford, perfectly understood the intention of this measure when she said, in comments about Goblet B (Starglow), "I don't like it, but I bet it's what the snobs buy."

Interestingly, most tasters correctly identified Moonwhisper as expensive based on its distinctive herbal profile, even as they ranked it poorly for personal enjoyment. This created a strange split: the ale they thought others would be impressed by was frequently the same ale they personally disliked.

**The Aftermath**

Marcus Webb requested that his application essay—the one praising Moonwhisper—be destroyed. "I clearly don't know what I'm talking about," he admitted. Rosa Taylor, meanwhile, maintained that her palate was simply more refined than her colleagues'. "Moonwhisper requires sophisticated appreciation," she insisted. "These results simply prove most people lack it."

Claudia Cook, our Bruno's Basic champion, took a different lesson: "Perhaps the simplest ales allow the magic to express itself most purely. Or perhaps I should stop lecturing others about their pedestrian tastes."

**Conclusions**

Further study is needed. But on the basis of evidence to date:

The experiment revealed a profound gap between predicted and actual preferences. Those who expected to love the expensive imports often found themselves drawn to very different ales when the labels were hidden.

The distinctive character of certain ales—particularly heavily hopped varieties—proved polarizing. Rosa Taylor's experience suggests that trained palates can identify specific ales blind, but appreciation is deeply personal.

Apart from the clear winner and clear loser in the Best/Worst voting, the tasters really had trouble telling one ale from another. This was obvious during the experiment itself, when the confident look of spell-crafters-who-know-their-ales quickly turned to dismay and panic as they realized that all the ambers tasted pretty much the same.

From an entrepreneurship perspective, this is fascinating: it means that small brewers with limited marketing budgets may be producing products equal to or better than their expensive competitors, but lack the social capital to be recognized.

As I reflect on conducting this experiment, I must admit my own journey of personal growth through the process. I began with firm convictions about my ability to distinguish quality from mediocrity. The experiment has humbled me considerably.

The mentorship I've received from senior researchers like Diana Hernández has always emphasized the importance of questioning one's assumptions. Diana once told me, "The mark of a true scholar is not confidence in one's conclusions, but willingness to test them." This experiment has embodied that principle.

Next installment: fancy brews and specialty enchanted beverages.
quality_problem.question: Which ale was named the favorite by the majority of tasters?

quality_problem.story:
The Quantum Architect
